en: The *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā* on Substances.

Right here, he raises this objection: "If there is a connection with the *vṛtti*, then why is it not mentioned? Or, if there is none, then why is the introduction of the definition of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) commenced at this very point?
With this intention, he says: "Or rather, why is the statement of the connection with the *vṛtti* not made here?"
It is being done.
The meaning is that the reason for not providing an explanation of the relationship here, which was provided everywhere else, must be stated. The answer is:
we say it is because there is no relationship.
How then is it that the commencement of the definition of the subject matter (*adhikāra*) occurs in this very same place?
To this he says: "For the subject matter depends upon the five definitions;
it depends upon the definitions of the five [categories], beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

The purpose [of this section] is for the commencement of reflection (*cintā*), and not for the sake of comprehension (*avagati*). Not having understood this intention, the opponent objects: "Indeed, there is dependence (*apekṣā*) when one depends upon the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*). If that is so, then all five must be mentioned. [The author replies: "The distinction and application of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabheda-viniyoga*)."... [text continues] ...the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the apprehension of an object. It is called "means of valid cognition" because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the attainment of a result. For example, just as the axe is the primary instrument for the act of cutting, so too is the contact between the sense organ and the object the primary instrument for the act of perception. Therefore, the contact between the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, the means of valid cognition is the cause (*nimitta*) for the production of a cognition that is not sublated by another cognition. Since the contact between the sense organ and the object is the cause for the production of such a cognition, it is the means of valid cognition. Moreover, the means of valid cognition is that which brings about the attainment of an object that has not yet been attained. Since the contact between the sense organ and the object brings about the attainment of an object, it is the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, the means of valid cognition is that which possesses the capacity to produce a cognition that is not sublated by another cognition. Since the contact between the sense organ and the object possesses that capacity, it is the means of valid cognition. Thus, the contact between the sense organ and the object is established as the means of valid cognition. Now, regarding the definition of the means of valid cognition: the means of valid cognition is that which is free from error (*avyabhicārin*), is determinate (*vyavasāyātmaka*), and is a source of knowledge (*jñāna*). Among these, "free from error" means that it does not deviate from the actual nature of the object. "Determinate" means that it possesses the capacity to lead to successful action (*pravṛtti-samartha*). "Source of knowledge" means that it is a cognition produced by the contact between the sense organ and the object. By these three characteristics, the means of valid cognition is defined. Now, the means of valid cognition is twofold: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Direct perception is the cognition that arises from the contact between the sense organ and the object. Inference is the cognition that arises from the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*). These two are the means of valid cognition. Now, regarding the classification of the means of valid cognition: direct perception is further divided into four types: sensory perception (*indriyajanya*), mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*). Inference is divided into two types: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). These are the classifications of the means of valid cognition. Now, regarding the application of the means of valid cognition: direct perception applies to objects that are present and manifest, while inference applies to objects that are absent or subtle. This is the application of the means of valid cognition. Thus, the means of valid cognition is established through its definition, classification, and application. Now, regarding the objection: "If the contact between the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition, then why is the sense organ itself not the means of valid cognition? To this we reply: the sense organ is not the means of valid cognition because it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition that is not sublated by another cognition. Furthermore, the sense organ is not the means of valid cognition because it is common to both valid and invalid cognitions. Therefore, the contact between the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition. The *vṛtta* characterized by the sequence of taking up the cowherds has been explained; now we shall set forth the *vṛtta* characterized by the scope (*adhikāra*). Thus, all five [topics] should be proclaimed. He refutes this: they need not be proclaimed.
If that is so, then because each of them—

The connection is not tenable. To begin with, the sequence of application (*viniyoga*) and the means of apprehension (*upādāna*) depend precisely upon the qualification (*adhikāra*). It is indeed dependent upon the grasper (*grāhaka*).

The prior application (*viniyoga*) is not accepted for the sake of another; likewise, an injunction possessing a qualification (*sādhikāra*) implies origination (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), and performance (*prayoga*). However, the implication of the qualification occurs only when the relationship characterized by the qualification has been established, as we shall explain later. Furthermore, sequence (*krama*) arises subsequent to performance. The division of the scriptures is also preceded by the qualification.

It is not the cause for [establishing] the qualification (*adhikāra*), because even when the meaning of the scripture is undivided, the qualification is understood from the words themselves. [Objection: But surely, even if the meaning of the scripture is undivided, the qualification is not tenable due to the absence of the capacity for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). [Reply: True. Nevertheless, even though the division of the scripture is preceded by the qualification, the understanding of the relationship between the definitions and the body [of the work] occurs precisely through the words. At most, the division of the scripture— [The text ends here.]

Since the qualification (*adhikāra*) does not reach its completion without [the performance of the action], the division of the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) is the cause for that completion; however, regarding the comprehension of the qualification itself, the word alone is the cause. Likewise, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*) does not apply to the qualification;
for even when the word is dependent [on other factors], as in "Devadatta, bring the cow," [the qualification is understood].

Because [the texts] such as these show that each [person] has a distinct qualification (*adhikāra*), therefore a connection with all five together individually is not tenable. Now, one might argue that the connection will be with them taken collectively; to this he says:
"And there exists no such thing as a 'collection' (*samudāya*) that is a separate entity."
If a collection (*samudāya*) existed as a distinct entity, then even if there were no connection with each individual member, a connection with the collection as a whole might perhaps be possible.
But this is not the case. Therefore, the mention of all five [elements] together is not tenable. If there were a connection with all five...
If that is so, how can it be said that "the *adhikāra* depends upon the five characteristics"? The answer is:

when the five [characteristics] have been completed in their mutual dependence, there arises the occasion for the *adhikāra*; thus it is said that "the *adhikāra* depends upon the five characteristics. It is not, however, [dependent] by way of being its cause (*hetu*).

This is its meaning: first of all, in one who has studied the Veda, there arises the desire to know the meaning of the Veda. Therefore, when it is stated by the words "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*) that the meaning of the Veda consists of what is to be done (*kārya-rūpa*) and has the injunction alone as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this further inquiry arises: "How is the injunction a means of valid cognition without dependence [on other sources], such that the injunction alone..."

The meaning of the Veda would consist of definitions and ritual actions; therefore, a definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be undertaken to establish its independence (*anapekṣatva*).
Once the definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated, this further inquiry arises: is that means of valid cognition distinct or non-distinct?
Consequently, the distinction between the sciences (*śāstrabheda*) is established by the second chapter. And once the distinction between the sciences has been established...

The meanings of the scriptures (*śāstrārtha*) are also diverse. In this regard, the following consideration arises once again: are these scriptural meanings mutually connected or unconnected? To that end, the connection is established by means of the definition of "subsidiary" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Once the mutual connection among the scriptural meanings—founded upon direct statement (*śruti*) and other criteria—is established, this further consideration arises: [which is it]—direct statement and so forth?

Is the mutual relationship [between these] established by these alone, or is there another cause for it? In this regard, since there is yet another cause characterized as the material cause (*upādāna*), the definition of the material cause must be undertaken in order to demonstrate it. [This concerns] the application based on the material cause...

And while this reflection is underway, everything pertaining to the *upādāna* (material cause) has also been considered. Furthermore, when the application (*prayukti*) based on the *upādāna* has been reflected upon, the question arises: "How does this [application] come about and proceed, given that the agent is one while the objects (*padārtha*) are many? This is determined sequentially. And therein, when the requirement arises as to what sequence should be adopted:

The definition of *krama* (order) must now be undertaken. Thus, because these five [topics] are mutually dependent, the definition of *adhikāra* (qualification/competence) cannot properly occur at this stage. However, once these have been completed, the inquiry arises as to whether there exists a qualified person (*adhikārī*) for the purpose of instruction at the conclusion of the *krama*. Therefore, the definition of *adhikāra* must be commenced. For the sake of accomplishing such reflection, the five— [Note: The text provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical flow of the argument.]

The subject matter (*adhikāra*) depends upon the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); as long as those [characteristics] are not investigated, there is no opportunity whatsoever for investigating the subject matter. However, the subject matter does not depend upon the five characteristics by way of being their cause. Therefore, because there is no such connection, no connection is stated. Since [the characteristics] were not discussed elsewhere due to a lack of occasion, and since the occasion is now obtained, they are discussed in this very place.

He shows that there is no dependence based on the relationship of cause and effect for the purpose of resolving the objection that "the definition of the means (kāraka) is now begun," but rather that there is dependence for the sake of attaining the proper occasion: "The instruction ending with the sequence [of the *kārakas*] is not the cause for the qualification (*adhikāra*);
rather, the consideration is whether or not there exists some qualified person (*adhikārī*) in the instruction ending with the sequence."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that eligibility is understood precisely through the power of the instruction, since an instruction is invariably concomitant with eligibility? With this intention in mind, he asks:
"Does an instruction exist even for one who lacks eligibility?"

By this, you have stated that [the scripture] serves as a cause regarding the qualification for instruction. The reply is: certainly it exists in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice with wood in a pot," which concern objects already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In those sentences whose subject matter is already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there exists instruction even though it lacks a specific qualification (*adhikāra*). No one is enjoined therein.
To the question "How is no one enjoined?", he says:
Precisely because their object is already cognized by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

The meaning is: since their object is cognized by another means of valid cognition, therefore [they are not independent]. [Objection: Let it be that their object is cognized by another means of valid cognition; even so, why is there a lack of qualification (*adhikāraśūnyatā*)?

1. Mā. Regarding the purpose of the designation: since there would be an absence of authoritative status (*adhikāra*), how could the accomplishment of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) be established? To this he says: "For that which is understood through another characteristic... [p. 004]
The mere statement of the essential nature and the power of substances and so forth is accomplished by means of present-tense designations;
the establishment of the instruction follows from the purposeful intent of the meaning.

One carries out the purpose of the instruction. Now, one might ask: "If the purpose of the instruction is accomplished through the seeker's desire for that purpose, then for what reason is 'qualification' (adhikāra) propounded here? To this he says: "But here, moreover, the knowledge of capacity [to perform the rite] arises from the instruction itself;
this is the distinction."

Since there is no knowledge of the potency (*śakti*) here apart from instruction, the instruction must be described as being accompanied by a qualification (*adhikāra*). Otherwise, in the absence of knowledge of the potency, the performance [of the rite] would not be established. Therefore, because instruction does not deviate from the qualification, it does not make that qualification known; thus, due to the lack of causality, there is no connection. Consequently, it is not...

"The statement of the relationship belongs to the author of the Bhāṣya. But what is the reason that only one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is cited as an example, and not those who desire a village (*grāmakāma*) and so forth?
The sense is that all [examples] should indeed be cited in order to demonstrate the eligibility of everyone.
He refutes this: "Or rather, why must everything be cited such that you ask this? By what logic..."
For the sake of establishing the point, however, only one example need be cited, because the underlying principle can be demonstrated even through a single instance;
on the contrary, further examples are superfluous. Therefore, only one example should be cited—so says the objector.

He says: It is said—this is indeed true; however, here the author of the Bhāṣya again establishes the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions by way of defining the referent of the word "heaven" (svarga).
In that regard, by means of even a single example cited, the underlying principle (nyāya) applies to all examples.

Etymological derivation occurs if there is an investigation that is all-pervasive; however, in this case, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by taking the word "heaven" (*svarga*) as denoting a substance possessed of pleasure, while the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is established by taking it as denoting pleasure alone. Furthermore, this [interpretation] is not possible in cases such as "one who desires a village" (*grāmakāma*).
"Because the word 'village' is used for a village even when pleasure has ceased.
The meaning of this is:

having stated that the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes pleasure because the word "heaven" is not applied to a substance once pleasure has ceased, [the author] presents the final conclusion (rāddhānta).

[This] has been done. Furthermore, this mode [of interpretation] is not possible in the case of "one who desires a village" (*grāmakāma*), because the word "village" (*grāma*) is used even without [the sense of] affection;
therefore, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that the word *grāma* denotes merely a substance (*dravyamātra*) is not obtained. Regarding those beginning with "one who desires a village":...
Alternatively, if the intended qualification pertains to the subject under discussion, either another instrument must be stated, or else the statement of the means of proof [must be provided].

Since words such as "village" (grāma) denote substances, it must be admitted that they express their status as means for sacrifices and the like; or else, it must be accepted that they denote qualifiers of the agent. To this, it is replied: all [the examples] are indeed to be cited.
The term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) has been cited merely for the sake of illustration;
by virtue of the same underlying principle, all [other] examples are likewise [illustrative].
In reality, however, the term "one who desires heaven" was cited specifically as an illustration. Now, one might object: is it not the case that [the word] denotes that which is being desired?

It has been stated that the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and final (*uttarapakṣa*) positions regarding the basis for the application [of the word] are not possible in the case of those [desires] such as "one desiring a village.

If the word *svarga* denotes a substance, then the basis for its application—the heaven that is being desired—is the prima facie position; whereas if it denotes pleasure (*prīti*), [that is the final position].

Then the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is stated: [the injunctions] such as "desiring a village" (*grāmakāma*) and so forth are not possible, because those who desire a village and the like denote substances (*dravya*). The supporter says: "That is incorrect. The objector asks: "In what way is it incorrect?"
The proponent says: This is incorrect. It has already been stated that the word "heaven" (svarga) refers to desirable things by virtue of being something desired.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding what was stated—that the word *svarga* (heaven) is a synonym for pleasure (*prīti*)—this is what is thereby expressed: because it is desired, because it is the object of desire, and because it is the primary object relative to desire, the word *svarga* applies to those things that are desired, such as garlands, sandalwood, and so forth.
For pleasure is indeed that which is desired; therefore, by virtue of being a synonym for pleasure, [the word *svarga*] denotes that which is desired.

It has been stated [thus]. In the same way, this should also be understood regarding those who desire a village (*grāmakāma*) and so forth. Even in the case of those desiring a village and the like, the word "village" functions solely by virtue of being desired; for that which is not desired cannot be associated with the act of desiring.

In the expression "one who desires a village" (*grāmakāma*), a village is understood as being joined with or connected to desire—that is, *kāmanā*. And that [village] must necessarily be the object of desire. Precisely because that which is desired is joined with desire, for that very reason, having accepted that [the word *grāma*] denotes a place, [one might consider] heaven—
Nevertheless, because the word [svarga] cannot be connected with desire,
the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is established that this word "svarga" denotes a substance accompanied by pleasure.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) has stated that the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes a substance consisting of pleasure, it was objected that the word "heaven" is applied to a substance consisting of pleasure only by way of analogy. Then, it was further resolved [p.

"Because there is no other primary meaning [for the word 'heaven'], it is not employed as a metaphor. Being questioned again, [it was said]: "The word *svarga* (heaven) is well-known in a specific region that is devoid of cold, heat, and so forth. And this was refuted: "Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a region, the word *svarga* is not used in its primary sense there. Again it was stated: "Even if such an instruction exists, nevertheless, because it is full of joy..."

The word "heaven" (svarga) would function as a term denoting a specific place. And in that regard, the reason is that here the connection with desire is understood to be the meaning of the word "heaven. Furthermore, there can be no connection with desire for that which is devoid of pleasure. Even in the final conclusion (rāddhānta), since desire does not exist in the absence of pleasure, it follows that [the word] refers exclusively to pleasure.
He has demonstrated the usage of the word "svarga" (heaven), but he has not refuted [the existence of] a place;
for it is by this very principle that desire proceeds toward a substance when there is pleasure.

Even in the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* has demonstrated through reasoning that the word "heaven" (*svarga*) refers exclusively to pleasure; he did not, however, refute the [existence of a] location. For if the word "heaven" denoted pleasure solely by the force of its primary denotation (*abhidhāna*), then it would have been necessary to exert effort to refute its denotation of a location and establish its denotation of pleasure. But this is not the case.

An effort has been made to refute [the view that] location [is heaven]. Therefore, it is the intention of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) that the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes pleasure solely by virtue of its connection with desire. The literal meaning should also be described in this way: when that very substance which is the means of pleasure is no longer the means of pleasure, the word "heaven" is no longer its designator.

The meaning is that, in that case, it is not denoted by the word "heaven" (svarga). This being so, just as the word "heaven" refers to pleasure through its connection with desire, so too do [terms] such as "desirous of a village" (grāmakāma) and the like; thus, the state of being an object of pleasure is "pleasure," and the object is the pleasure.

Those for whom [he] is to be propitiated are the objects of affection; the state of being such is "the condition of being an object of affection. They are impelled by that, due to the connection with desire, and not otherwise.

Thus, it is stated that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [the sacrifice] is a means toward the *yajña*. Therefore, the same logic applies everywhere. Precisely because this inquiry concerns the object being desired (*kāmyamāna*), and not heaven (*svarga*) alone, [this principle holds].

Having thus proposed whether heaven (*svarga*) or the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he shows again that desire (*kāma*) is the goal. "Desire" means that which is desired; we say that in general, merely that which is desired is what is accomplished. Otherwise, it would simply have been said that heaven is accomplished. When all these are taken as examples here, is it then pleasure (*prīti*) that is heaven, or...?

By this passage beginning with "dravyam," the following is stated: Is the word *svarga* (heaven) employed here as the object of desire, or is it a qualification of the agent by virtue of being that which is desired?

Is the word "heaven" (svarga) employed here to indicate a state that is desired by virtue of being an object of desire, or is it a qualification of the agent, qualifying the desire itself— which serves as a qualification of the agent— by means of its being the object of desire? In this regard, pleasure is what is desired.

The state [of being desired] is intended. By virtue of being something desired, the substance is intended as a qualifier of the agent. But surely, regarding the position that it is a substance, the author of the Bhāṣya states that heaven is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) and not a qualifier of the agent; to this he says: "For in that case, the agent—"

For if [the desire] were a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then in the case of desire, the object of desire—such as heaven and so forth—would be subordinate (*upasarjana*). Thus, by establishing its subordination, it is stated that it is indeed a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*). If, however, being a qualifier of the agent follows from its subordination, then the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is not [maintained].
With the intention that [the goal] is obtained, he raises the objection: "But surely, in the expression 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*),
the desire for the object of desire, such as heaven, is perceived precisely as being subordinate."
He refutes [the objection]: "This very point is what is being deliberated here:
is the connection for application according to the designation, or is the designation according to the application?"

Is the relationship between heaven and the desire for it established according to the expression "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)? For this expression is primarily directed toward other constituent elements of the sentence, and if the relationship were established in accordance with that [expression], heaven would merely be a subordinate factor (*guṇa*). Or rather, what kind of relationship exists between the object of desire and the desirer?

The application (*viniyoga*)—that is, the mutual relationship—between these two is perceived, and the designation [of their status] follows that perception. For when there is a relationship between the object of desire (*kāmya*) and the desire (*kāmanā*), the object of desire is the primary element. Therefore, it is precisely its subordinate status (*upasarjanatā*) that is being examined here. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), desiring an application according to the literal designation, asserts its subordination. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*), however, asserts it in accordance with the actual relationship.

He states [the word] "anupasarjanatām" (non-subordinacy). Here, he raises an objection: "Is this *bahuvrīhi* not applicable when there is denotation according to the specific application (*viniyoga*)?
The underlying intention is as follows: even if there is denotation according to the specific application, this is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*; and if it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then...

The status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjanatā*) is difficult to avoid. For if this were not a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the view that [the gender] follows the specific application (*yathāviniyoga*), then only in that case would there be no subordinate status. But this is not so. He [the opponent] counters: "By whom was it said that this is not a *bahuvrīhi*?"

He objects: "If the *bahuvrīhi* compound is subordinate (*upasarjana*), then desire (*kāma*) is that which is desired (*kāmya*), because this compound has as its primary referent a person who is a distinct entity. And precisely because this compound has as its primary referent a person who is a distinct entity..."
Its connection is with the number of the agent expressed by the verbal suffix, as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) or "those desiring prosperity should sacrifice" (*yajeran*).

This is because both the singular and plural forms are observed. Furthermore, when the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) itself is the object of desire (*kāmya*), such being the case, a doubt is untenable, as there is no ambiguity in the formulation of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Nor [is this so] for the venerable Pāṇini.

There is also a traditional rule (smaraṇa) regarding the *bahuvrīhi* compound even when it has its own primary meaning, by which the object of desire (*kāmya*) would indeed be the principal element even in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation. The respondent says: It is replied.
We too do not say that the *bahuvrīhi* compound has only its own meaning (*svārtha*); rather,
this *bahuvrīhi* is for the sake of another (*parārtha*), or is it for its own sake?

We ask: does this *bahuvrīhi* compound have as its referent the person who stands beyond the two word-meanings conveyed by the members of the compound, or does it have as its referent the object of desire (*kāmyārtha*) conveyed by those very members being compounded? The opponent asks: "But how is it 'for the sake of another' (*parārtha*), or how is it 'for its own sake' (*svārtha*)?"
The respondent says: But the established meaning (siddhārtha) serves the purpose of another.
If words such as "one desiring heaven" (svargakāma) were of established meaning...
In that case, it would be for the sake of another; however, if it is the meaning of the thesis (sādhyārtha), then it is for one's own sake. He himself said:
"In this regard, we do not know now."
Is the employment and utterance of the term *siddhārtha* for the sake of another? Or...

"It is taken up as that which is to be established (*sādhya*). The objector says: "But is it not a contradiction for the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) to be the meaning of that which is to be established (*sādhyārtha*)? For that which is to be established does not become the meaning of something else; therefore, how can it be both the meaning of another word and the meaning of that which is to be established?"

[The two points] are mutually contradictory. The resolver says: "There is no contradiction here, because this very thing to be accomplished—such as heaven and so forth—is for the sake of another, namely, for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha). Therefore, being for the sake of the object to be accomplished and being for the sake of another are not contradictory.
And it has been said:
By the Sage [Jaimini], in the sūtra "And the fruit [is the purpose],
because it is for the sake of the person," the fact that the fruit is for the sake of the person was established; therefore, this matter is well-founded.
The doubt of the author of the Bhāṣya is as follows: Is heaven pleasure, or is it a substance?
But even so, one might object that such a doubt is not logically tenable.
Because this is understood as a qualification of the agent, due to its connection with the number of the agent residing in the verb—
as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice. But [it may be argued] that it is rather the qualified person (*adhikārin*)—

Even if heaven is established as a qualifier, the person desiring heaven (svargakāma) certainly possesses the status of an agent; therefore, there will be a connection with the number expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).
To this, he replies: "The venerable Pāṇini records that number [belongs] to the agent of that verbal suffix."

The meaning of this is as follows: Pāṇini teaches that the number [expressed] belongs to the agent of that verbal form (ākhyāta) in which the number is heard. And when heaven is the goal to be accomplished, the person desiring heaven (svargakāma) possesses agency in the accomplishment of heaven, not in the accomplishment of the sacrifice.

Therefore, there would be no connection with the number inherent in the sacrifice if the person desiring heaven were not the agent of the sacrifice. Consequently, it is taught that the one desiring heaven is the agent specifically with respect to the sacrifice. To the question "Why does Pāṇini not [teach this]? he says: "And for one who is occupied elsewhere, [there is no connection] with the number contained in another verbal suffix."

The connection occurs—as in the case of one who says "he cooks" while [actually] reading. Pāṇini’s rule states: "A grammatical operation concerning words applies when they possess semantic capacity" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*).

And this semantic capacity consists in the relation between their own respective meanings. Furthermore, for that which is occupied elsewhere, there is no connection with the number residing in another verb.

A connection does not occur, just as there is no connection between the act of cooking and the number expressed by the word "pacati. Therefore, this is Pāṇini’s traditional rule: there is no connection for a number residing within one verbal form with something else that is occupied elsewhere. However, in the present case, the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) is understood from the statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*).

However, syntactic unity does not occur without a mutual relationship; therefore, it is a qualifier of the agent. Why is this *bahuvrīhi* compound used only for an established fact (*siddhārtha*) and not for something to be accomplished (*sādhyārtha*)?
The objector himself states another argument:

"In this case, it is only logical that the name refers to an already established thing (*siddhārtha*); for a nominal stem does not denote something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyārtha*)," as stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*.
The author of the Bhāṣya has stated: "Therefore, it is understood here that the duty to be performed belongs to the sacrifice itself, which is denoted by the verbal suffix."
Because the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) has the sense of an action (*bhāva*) and thus signifies something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
He states another argument: "And not..."
Even for the proponent of the goal (sādhya), there is no syntactic unity with the sacrifice;
this applies even to the proponent who holds heaven to be the goal.
In his view as well, it is not the case that there is no syntactic unity between the sacrifice and the one who desires heaven; rather, such unity certainly exists.
And if it exists, then it is not logical for two things to be understood as goals (sādhya) within a single sentence.

Here someone raises an objection: "But surely, just as in the case of 'he sprinkles the rice grains' (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), even though the goal (*sādhya*) resides in the refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the rice,
there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with this [refinement] because it is a goal conveyed by the verb ending (*ākhyāta*)."
"In the same way, it will be so here as well. The objector refutes this: "Do not say that;
for in that case, the rice grains, being connected as causal factors (*kāraka*), become the recipients of the refinement (*saṃskāra*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: It is appropriate in the case of "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), because there, in the initial stage, the rice-grains function as a *kāraka* (participant in the action) by means of the sprinkling.

They are connected. And that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) subsequently initiates a refinement (*saṃskāra*) upon the rice grains (*vrīhi*). Therefore, because they function as factors (*kāraka*) associated with a future refinement, the rice grains are denoted by a word ending in the accusative case in relation to the sprinkling. In this case, however, there is no such [connection] between the sacrifice and heaven.
In both cases of what is to be proven, the relationship between action and its factors is established through another means of valid cognition.

For [only] thus would there be a mutual relationship [between them]. Now, one might object: "Granted that the relationship between the action and its factors may not be established through another means of knowledge; however, by the Veda itself, in the statement 'he cuts the sacrificial post' (yūpaṃ chinatti), it will be determined. To this, he says: "Nor is it determined here in this very context as it is in the case of the sacrificial post."
He asks: "Why? [The answer is: It is not determined; for even that which is to be produced may have a connection with an agent (*kāraka*).

The meaning is: if even a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is something to be produced, has a relationship with [the action] by way of being its agent (*kāraka*), then why is the relationship between action and agent not likewise understood in the Veda? The answer is:
if there is a connection with an agent even for that which is to be produced, let it be so; however, it does not follow that [the agent] is something to be produced.

The status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) occurs with respect to an action toward that which already exists. The objector asks: "How then [is it explained] in the case of 'he cuts the sacrificial post' (*yūpaṃ chinatti*)?
[For] the sacrificial post does not exist [prior to the action].

In the case of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action), the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) [denotes the object], because the second case is a *kāraka*-case-ending. The respondent says:
"The meaning of the sentence 'he cuts the sacrificial post' (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) is that he makes [something] a sacrificial post connected with the act of cutting. What is meant by this is as follows:
1. *mavatvevamā*. [p. 011] Here too, the connection is only with the cutting of the *khadira* tree and so forth; those very *khadira* trees and others are the *kārakas* by means of the cutting.

Through that connection, they are consecrated by the act of cutting; and those things associated with consecration are denoted by the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post), in the sense that "by cutting, they are made into a *yūpa*. If, even in that case, the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is already known through other means of knowledge, then how is it established that "the *yūpa* is characterized by the injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*)? To this he replies: "Because it is non-worldly (*alaukikatvāt*)."

Since in common worldly usage it is not known that *khadira* wood and the like are consecrated by the term "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), it is stated that "the sacrificial post is characterized by the injunction.
Abhi-...
Not understanding [the term] *prāya*, he asks: "And since the connection with an action is non-worldly (*alaukika*), what does this mean?
For every connection between an action and its factors (*kāraka*) is worldly. The answer is: it is non-worldly by virtue of being denotable by the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*).

Since the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is derived in its own primary sense solely through the usage of Vedic words, it does not possess an "extraordinary" (*alaukika*) nature merely by virtue of its connection with cutting. Therefore, in this case as well, something is produced for the sacrificial material, such as the *khadira* wood, by means of the act of cutting.

Therefore, it is analogous to the statement "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). However, as for heaven, which is that which is to be accomplished, with respect to the meaning of the sacrifice—
The status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is itself non-worldly (*alaukika*).

He concludes: therefore, as in the case of "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), a relationship [of *kāraka*] is not possible in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*).

Thus, while a relationship is appropriate in the case of "he sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), it is not so appropriate in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*). Furthermore, one who knows the nature of words does not recall any other [kind of] relationship; or, even if he were to recall one, it would lack any basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Because it is impossible for there to be a recollection [of a rule] without its root [text], the [injunction] would be frustrated.
Having raised a doubt by means of this lack of clarity in the formulation of the final position (*siddhānta*), he concludes: "Therefore, even the gods will have doubts in this matter."

If they should consider it to be something that ought to be done, he provides the following response: "To this it is replied: This would indeed be so, if the relationship were to be cognizable solely through the four means of valid cognition."

Therefore, even though it has been understood by means of the four instruments of valid cognition, it is indeed reasonable to have a doubt as to whether the word itself conveys another relation or not.
The objector says: It has been stated that the authority of verbal testimony arises from its independence;
therefore, by the very force of that authority, any other [intrinsic] relationship will be established, so this section need not be commenced. The respondent says: True, it has been stated.
Validity. That very [validity] falters here.
How so? The answer: when the qualification (*adhikāra*) is established, there is the establishment of the performance (*prayoga*), that is, the execution; and when the performance is established...
When [the person] exists, the accomplishment of the instruction occurs;

for that purpose of the injunction (*niyoga*), which consists in the form of an action, is accomplished. Otherwise, in the absence of an agent who performs it, that very action would not exist. And therefore—

If a word were to establish an object as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) merely by its nature as an object to be accomplished, it would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the connection characterized by the governing topic (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa-sambandha*) would fail to be established in this section, the status of being a means of valid cognition itself would collapse. Therefore, this section must be commenced for the sake of securing that validity.
The opponent says: "In that case, this [section] would then result in being merely a definition of the means of valid cognition."

Nor is it another definition. The respondent says: There is indeed another definition that is a true characteristic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the topic under discussion consists of the remaining five characteristics.
The status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) characterized by the sequence of application (*viniyoga*) and material cause (*upādāna*) has been shown by way of its producing [the result].

However, the status of being a subordinate element characterized by the authority of the Veda (*veda-prāmāṇya*) and its divisions is shown by way of its sustaining that [authority]; for without a qualification (*adhikāra*), the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) cannot be sustained.
If that sustenance is absent, its divisions are far removed from possibility. If this is the definition of a means of valid knowledge, then how [is it so]?

Is this another definition being stated? He replies: it is stated in this way because, even though the subject matter (*adhikāra*) has been established, the objection regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was resolved in the section on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*).

Now, it is considered here whether that very same qualification applies or not. This is what is meant: in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the lack of authority of a word [is asserted] on account of its dependence [on other factors].

[This has been] avoided. But here, even though independence (*anapekṣatva*) is established, [the objection] is raised on the grounds of the absence of qualification (*adhikāra*) and then resolved. Furthermore, if the qualification were to be challenged solely on the basis of the word’s lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), then this would not be designated as a distinct definition, because it would merely be the refutation of that lack of authority which serves as the cause for the challenge. And this is not the case; therefore, he says: "Nor [is it challenged] by means of lack of authority alone..."
What, then, is the objection regarding the injunction? It is because the connection with the qualified person (adhikāra) is not understood.
The objector says: But surely even this lack of understanding constitutes invalidity itself.
Even by that non-comprehension, there is an implication through invalidity alone.
The respondent says: "That is indeed true."

The lack of authority applies to the understanding of the human agent regarding the specific qualification (*adhikāra*), but not to the mere meaning of the words themselves. Therefore, because it conveys the entire range of effects (*kārya*) other than the qualification, its authority exists; thus, there is no implication of a lack of authority. No.
If that is so, one might ask: "If validity exists even when there is no comprehension [of the object], then how was it refuted in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
To this he says: "In the definition of a means of valid cognition, however, the point that 'the word does not touch the object' was refuted.
If it did not touch the object in every respect, it would lack validity; but if it fails to convey a specific object, it conveys something else."
Validity is indeed established by that [definition] as well.

Therefore, the designation of another definition is justified. Consequently, it has been stated that through the five definitions there is an understanding of the mere effect (*kārya*), but it has not been stated that "this is the effect of this. And in the absence of such an understanding, [the relationship between cause and effect cannot be determined].
Even though it is the exclusion of everything that is not the task (*kārya*), it does not function as such because there is no performance [of it].
As long as one does not understand "this is my task," no one will engage in action. Therefore, although it is the task—

Even though there is the cognition that "this is to be done," nevertheless, since its status as something to be done (*kāryatva*) is untenable without the performance of the action, it would be a non-cognition insofar as it is empty of being cognized. Therefore, in order to establish that "this is the duty of this [person]," the section defining qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*) must be commenced. But was it not stated in the fourth book that even in the absence of qualification, a result is to be postulated, and that [result] is heaven?
"It may be [the case] because it is undifferentiated with respect to all. The meaning of this is: for what purpose is this qualification (*adhikāra*) being set forth?
For even without a qualification, the performance [of the rite] will occur by virtue of the result itself, just as is seen in the world.

If it is argued that without an entitlement (*adhikāra*), there can be no comprehension of the fruit at all, we say: no; for even without an entitlement, the postulation of a fruit in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others has been stated in the Fourth [Book]. He refutes [this objection]: True, it was stated that the fruit is to be postulated; however, the entitlement—

But when [the injunction] is possible, that [qualification] is based solely on entitlement (*adhikāra*), not on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: "In various cases, no entitlement is even heard of [in the text]; how then can there be a conceptual construction based on it? To this he says: "Even when the entitlement is not heard..."

It has been stated in that very same place that [the meaning] exists. Therefore, even when the *adhikāra* (governing heading) is not explicitly heard, once it has been established by the force of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related), subsequently—
The assumption of a result [occurs] when there is a connection. But if there is no possibility of a connection, for what unmentioned element could there be an assumption?
Furthermore, if there were no possibility of a connection at all, for what unmentioned element would there be an assumption? For it is only when a connection is possible that [an assumption is made].
The postulation of a result [would occur] as a qualification of the person entitled [to perform the rite]. But if that [entitlement] is impossible, for whom would there be such a postulation?

For an action does not require a result such that heaven would have to be postulated as its fruit. Therefore, since the performance [of the rite] cannot be established through any other means, the entitlement must be stated. Thus, by the authority of the word itself, it remains to be determined whether the relationship [between the act and its result], which is cognizable solely through the word, exists or does not exist.

The doubt has been established. He raises an objection once more: "But surely here, certain grammarians consider the agent alone to be the one entitled [to perform the rite]. They say that whoever is understood as the agent in a given action is the one entitled therein; there is no such thing as 'entitlement' (adhikāra) that exists as a separate entity."
Because of agency. And they maintain that this agent is connected with an action;
therefore, the mutual connection [of words] is precisely the connection between an action and its factors (kāraka).

No other relationship with the word is even expressed; furthermore, the Brāhmaṇas and others are understood from the Smṛti as being the agents [of the action], as in the statement: "Study, sacrifice, and giving are for the twice-born.
Thus, the Smṛti of Manu and others [also refers] to the Brāhmaṇas and so forth.

It establishes [the agent] as the agent, not as a separate entity, according to the rule "kṛti" [Pāṇini 2.3.65]: "Of the agent and the object when there is a kṛt-affix," as in the example: "Study, sacrifice, and giving for the twice-born."

This is because the genitive case is traditionally taught [in grammar] to denote the agent; and the attribution of the fruit [of action] to agents is indicated by such signs as the *ātmanepada* endings.
For it is indeed to the agents that the fruit is attributed, and not to those distinct from the agents—as [the text says], "to the agents... [and so on].

This is precisely that position of Bādari, which is also approved by Bādari himself, according to the traditional teaching: "In the case of works performed for a specific fruit [the result belongs to the agent]."
Regarding the term "pakṣa" (the position): as it was stated in the third [book]— they consider that the understanding of the relationship exists only among substance, quality, and refinement,
and not among sacrifice, fruit, and the person— and thus the connection with action is established only if there is an agent.
Thus, it is the one desiring heaven who is connected with the action; for otherwise, the connection of the qualified person with the action would be difficult to state.
And this connection is indeed understood, because otherwise there would be no syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*); since no other connection exists, therefore [this is the case].
Words such as "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) are merely qualifiers of the agent, just like [the phrase] "he offers when [the ladle] is broken."
Just as the performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is qualified by the term *bhedana*, so too is he qualified by [terms] such as *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven). This much is the distinction:

the performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is qualified by *bhedana* for the purpose of establishing a connection with the *homa* (oblation); however, through the desire for heaven, there is no connection elsewhere.
Regarding the word "yitum" (to cause to sacrifice): he raises an objection— But if this is so,
since there is an injunction prescribing a restriction on the agent, [what of] those who are other agents?
The entry of the officiating priests does not occur, because it has been excluded by a restrictive rule. He refutes this:
"Let it indeed not occur; however, this much [does not follow]."

The connection [of the fruit] would exist merely through the non-entry of another agent; however, the postulation of something never before seen cannot be resorted to, either because of a scriptural statement or because of the injunction regarding the choosing and supporting of priests, which implies another agent.
The inclusion [of the agent] will be appropriate;

and precisely because these [words] are primarily concerned with the agent, there is no production of the case-endings for other *kārakas*. Since the number is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the nominative case is produced.
Otherwise,

if the person entitled [to the rite] were distinct from the agent, one would have to seek another case-ending, or there would have to be a genitive case characterized as a "remainder" (śeṣa), as in the expression "one should sacrifice for the sake of one desiring heaven."

And he states another argument: "This designation of the agent is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice' and 'Heaven is sacrificed for by one desiring heaven.'"

Because the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs when the number of the agent (*kartṛ-saṅkhyā*) is not expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*), whereas it is excluded when that number is expressed; for if this third case were [used] for the agent, it would be appropriate only in that case and not otherwise. Thus, "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is indeed a designation of the agent (*kartṛ-nirdeśa*). Otherwise, it would not be a designation of the agent.

It might be so. To this he says: even if [the root *yaj*] is analyzed as denoting an action (*bhāva-sādhana*), in such cases as "one desiring heaven performs the sacrifice" (*svargakāmena ijyate*), the instrumental case would not apply for the person desiring heaven, because they would not be a kāraka (participant in the action). As for what was further stated:

Without an *adhikāra* (qualification/entitlement) distinct from the agent and the action, an act becomes fruitless; and people do not engage in what is fruitless. To this, we reply: regarding the act—

By its very nature, this is the inherent character of action (*karman*): that it brings about some non-existent thing. In that regard, even an unmentioned action such as sacrifice (*yāga*) will bring something into being; and that—
"It will lead to the prosperity of actions" means that some form of prosperity will arise; [this is] prosperity (itself).
The manifestation of a distinguished body, sense organs, and so forth occurs even in your own position— just as it does in the case of eternal [entities]—

even for one who holds that the qualification for [rites such as] the *jyotiṣṭoma* belongs to those characterized by specific qualifications such as "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). This applies also to the qualification for living (*jīvana-adhikāra*).

Even in the absence of an explicitly stated result, just as some result in the form of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is postulated due to the inherent nature of ritual actions (*karmasvābhāvya*), so it shall be here as well.

Thus far, it has been stated that even though there is no distinct entitlement (*adhikāra*), activity occurs by virtue of the result. Now, he says that activity will occur even without an entitlement and even without a result: "And because of the understanding of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*), there is the performance of ritual action."
For activity occurs toward that which is understood as something to be performed, and not merely because of its connection with a fruit; for if a connection with a fruit were admitted,
it would follow that [the duty] is cognizable through another means of knowledge.
Since the necessity of performing the meaning of the Veda is understood only through its result, the reason "because it is independent" (anapekṣatvāt) is thereby uprooted,
as it would entail the consequence of dependence.

For independence [of the Veda] is established by the fact that its meaning is not apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, if the meaning of the Vedic text were apprehended through other means of valid cognition, it would result in dependence. Therefore, independence was stated in the first chapter (*pāda*). He concludes: "Hence, the ritual action must be performed by those who are qualified"; thus, there is no lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*).
The entitlement belongs to the agent alone. When this doubt has been raised, the respondent says:
It is replied that this prima facie argument is not sound; for we shall explain later on how, in this position, the term "one who desires heaven" cannot be connected [with the action].

The sense is that the word *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven), being otherwise inexplicable, leads to the understanding of another relationship. Again, the objector says: "If this is so, if the word *svargakāma* cannot [be explained] otherwise..."
How, then, does the doubt arise? Is it that the meaning of the verbal root is taught as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*), or rather the desire (*kāma*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: due to its connection with the verbal form (ākhyāta), the sacrifice also appears as something to be performed; and due to its connection with the desire (kāmanā), the desired object also appears so. In that case, there arises the doubt: "Which of these two should be connected as the goal to be accomplished (sādhya)? A "desire" (kāma) is that which is desired, such as heaven and the like. Now, [one might argue] that since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is what is to be accomplished...

This objection has been stated: that the phrase "one who desires heaven" cannot be connected otherwise than as a qualification of the agent. The respondent says: it is not the case that it cannot be so connected.
On the contrary, it is indeed connected. Why? Because, as an auxiliary (*aṅga*), the desire [to obtain] is [connected], just like [the injunction]: "One should meditate on the ocean with the mind."
It follows that [something] must be performed.

If the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then, as its subordinate element (*aṅga*), even the desire for heaven and so forth will have to be performed—just like the meditation on the ocean. Therefore, the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*) also [denotes] the desire...
"By being presented as a subordinate element (*vāṅgatva*), it becomes connected. [Objection: "If this is so, then the necessity of performing both has been stated;
that is, the necessity of both the meaning of the verbal root and the desire. Therefore, how is their connection established? The respondent says: "No, it is true that it has been stated," [but...]
However, the relationship of subordinate and principal is here being considered:
one [element] is to be performed as a subordinate factor, while the other holds the status of the principal.

Again, he objects: "If even the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*) is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then how can the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) be regarded as having an already established purpose (*siddhārtha*)?"

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the word is as follows: even the prima facie view is likewise [formulated] precisely because it has the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) as its object; for how could one say that "what is already established (bhūta) is taught for the sake of what is to be accomplished (bhavya)"?

The Commentator, the resolver, says: This is not a fault, because here only that which is already established (bhūta) is taught; nor is it being prescribed for the sake of establishing a means of attainment (upādāna) if it has already been obtained through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Otherwise, appropriation would be impossible; however, in the case of instruction, it is indeed real,
and by means of that, the relationship is also taught.

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is also untenable because [the text] establishes the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) and because it expresses something already established (*siddhārthatayā*). Furthermore, there is the designation of what has come into being (*bhūtavyapadeśa*).

Since this is so, no doubt arises here as to whether the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the goal or the desire (*kāma*). For this very reason, the section (*adhikaraṇa*) in the eleventh book is not redundant from the standpoint of logic.

For it has been stated here that the sacrifice is not taught as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). That being the case, even though the sacrifice is not taught as the goal to be achieved, the status of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth as a qualification of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇatva*) follows from their connection with [the sacrifice] without any intervening step.
[Page 018] This has been refuted. Herein, the fundamental doubt is as follows: does the term *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) serve to present the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), or not?

In that regard, when it is indeed a qualification of the person to be enjoined, then that which is desired possesses the status of being the goal (*sādhya*) and the status of being for one's own sake (*svārthatā*).

The desire is mentioned as the object to be attained (*upādāna*), and the sacrifice is the means (*sādhana*). However, in the view that [the desire] is a qualification of the task (*kārya-viśeṣaṇa-pakṣa*), the desire has the purpose of accomplishing the desired end and is for the sake of another; the desire is mentioned as the means, and the sacrifice is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This being the state of the matter, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) argued, following the principle "the already existent is for the sake of that which is to be brought into being" (*bhūtaṃ bhavyāya*), that the sacrifice is for the sake of the desire. And by those [arguments] stated according to the verbal testimony...

By means of arguments consisting of cumulative reinforcement. The meaning of this is as follows: because it is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the sacrifice is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

And since it is not logical for one thing to be connected with another thing that is itself to be accomplished, [the desire for heaven] must be understood as having an already established nature (*bhūtārthatā*) [in relation to the sacrifice]. Thus, for one who desires heaven—

The word [niyojya] follows along with the [word *kartṛ*]; therefore, in this context, it is merely a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, the arguments stated by the Grammarians—that there is no such thing as a "person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) distinct from the agent—also establish that it is a qualifier of the agent; such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
To explain the Bhāṣya, he raises an objection: "This other matter is now considered"—how so? [Regarding] heaven...
Does the word "svarga" (heaven) denote pleasure (*prīti*) or does it denote a substance (*dravya*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: even if the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), how can the word "svarga" denote a substance? Likewise, even if heaven (*svarga*) is the goal to be accomplished, how [can it denote pleasure]?

Regarding the nature of verbal expression: for whatever meaning a word is understood to convey by its own inherent power (*svaśakti*), it is logical that it conveys precisely that; it is not, however, established through the categories of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). Likewise, the mention of [the girl] being eight or sixteen years old, as well as the denial of the location and the formal acceptance, are of no great utility.

If the word "heaven" (svarga) denotes a substance by virtue of being the object to be accomplished through sacrifice, then what is the purpose of citing such usages as "women aged sixteen are heaven," and so forth?

Likewise, the denial of the locus (*deśa*) by the proponent is purposeless, because the locus is itself a substance (*dravya*), and it is intended as a term denoting a substance. Furthermore, if the locus is rejected, for what purpose would there be an acceptance [of the word]?
He provides the answer: "Has it not already been stated by us whether the word 'heaven' (*svarga*) is employed as referring to an object of desire, or..."

The meaning of the phrase "by way of the substance" (*dravyaparatayā*) is this: here, the capacity to denote (*vācakatā*) is not being considered. What then? It is the *prayoga* (the ritual application).

Therefore, the investigation into whether it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or not to be accomplished (*asādhya*) serves as the reason for that [application]. When heaven (*svarga*) is the object to be accomplished, then [it is] directed toward joy (*prīti*).

The application [of the term] by her is such that when the sacrifice is to be accomplished, it is at that time that the word "pleasure" (prīti) signifies the substance; nor is the state of being desired (kāmyamāna) intended here. If this is so, what is the purpose of denying the location?

If the proponent of the prima facie view intends the argument to be based on the status of being a substance (*dravya*), then what is the purpose of denying the locus (*deśa*)? For the locus, too, is a substance. The answer is: for the sake of establishing the proof (*sādhanasiddhi*).

The purpose (*prayojana*): The fulfillment of desire, which serves as the means toward the sacrifice, is the purpose. That region, it is said, is not perceived by those who are alive. And that which is unperceived cannot function as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) to the material (*upādāna*), just like the ocean [cannot be used for bathing].

Just as it is possible for an ocean that has been perceived to serve as an adjunct to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), so too it is not possible for a region that has not been perceived to serve as an adjunct to desire or grasping (*kāmanopādāna*).
Therefore, the mention of [the ocean] being eight thousand *yojanas* deep and so forth is elegant.

Even if one accepts that the location (*deśa*) is possible as a subordinate factor (*upasarjana*) to the perceived [object], nevertheless, our position remains superior by this reasoning, despite the mere mention of pleasure and so forth.
The statement "it is not faulty" is merely for the purpose of establishing the thesis (*pakṣasiddhi*).

If you think that our thesis might sometimes fail to be established because the region [in question] is heaven, it is stated that even this is not the case; for there is also the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on hearing of nothing but bliss.
Since an accomplished entity can only be subordinate to the acquisition of a desired object, and since practical activity cannot be established through the mere apprehension of a generality,
the conclusion is that only the state of being a means to pleasure is grasped—
even by the cognition that "there exists some place."
The conclusion is stated: "Why is it not accepted that [the result] is merely a means to happiness, since the worldly practice of desire is established?
Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the sacrifice itself to be the instruction;
the meaning is that the sacrifice is presented as that which is to be accomplished (sādhya).

Precisely because the sacrifice is that which is to be accomplished, it is for this very reason that the principle is established: "Words denoting action have the sense of bringing something into being; from them, the action is understood. Otherwise, [this would not be possible].
If even particles such as "ca" were to have the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*), then the contradiction already mentioned would apply.
Now, in order to extract the essence of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he raises an objection: "But in this [case]..."
Whatever may be the case, it will be so; for action cannot exist there without a substratum that is its agent. [p.
The fruit arises;

however, no action (karman) denoted by a verbal root is perceived as the substratum of that fruit which functions as its causal factor (kāraka). But surely, in such cases as "one sacrifices the Soma" (somaṃ yajati), we do perceive a causal factor?

"The deity is the object of the action; therefore, the fruit will reside in it [the deity] at the sacrifice. He refutes this: "This is improper, because the primacy [of the deity] was refuted in the ninth [book].
If the deity were the primary factor with respect to the connection [with the sacrifice], then this might be so; however, the primacy of the deity was refuted in the ninth [book]."

Primacy [is established] by means of the refutation of [theories such as] the formation of a physical body (*vigraha*) and so forth. Furthermore, he states that there is no primacy of the deity for the following reason:
"Indeed, it was stated in the *Saktvadhikaraṇa* that for one whose human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is not yet known, a consecration (*saṃskāra*)—whether directly or indirectly—is not tenable."

It has been demonstrated in the *Savatva-adhikaraṇa* that for one whose human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is not known—whether directly or through an indirect means—an *saṃskāra* (consecration) is not logically possible. Furthermore, no deity has been made known by anyone as being a human purpose.
[Objection: But is it not well known that deities protect human beings?

Therefore, it has been stated in the ninth [chapter] itself that because this deity is made known merely for the sake of human ends, it is not to be respected—being like the well-known "yakṣa of the banyan tree"—due to its lack of foundation.
Now, one might object: "Should not the instruction regarding sacrifice be authoritative for this tradition, just as the instruction regarding the location [of a rite] is?"

Just as there is an injunction for sacrifice regarding a specific location—a place of pure happiness designated by the term "heaven"—so too will there be [an injunction] regarding a deity's role as the protector of human beings; and this well-known status is rooted in that very [fact]. He himself says:
And this predominance of the deity must necessarily be accepted for the sake of the eternal [liberation];
for in that case, it is indeed the fruit of the ritual action that is attained.
This must be accepted. He offers a rebuttal: "This is not tenable;
for the instruction is an authority only to the extent that one should perform the sacrifice, but it does not [establish] that the sacrifice is a benefactor to the person."

[Page 021] An objection is raised: "But surely, even if there were instruction, it would not be so because of the absence of practice. It has been stated that no one engages in an action that provides no benefit.

He refutes [this objection]: "But has this not also been stated: 'One is impelled by the cognition of what ought to be done, not by the cognition of benefit, because that would entail the consequence of dependence'?"
And since activity occurs even without a result merely through the cognition that something ought to be done,
this [cognition] is not an obstacle at all, even though it is a constant obstacle;
for you, the obligation regarding obligatory rites (*nitya-adhikāra*) is the obstacle.

What has been shown is that it is not indeed a hindrance (*pratibandhaka*), because in that case no fruit is admitted. For it is common worldly knowledge that a "bond" (*bandhaka*) is an "obstruction" (*upagraha*). When this has been stated, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) reveals the essence of his own intention: "If that is so, then let all of this be performed as if it were eternal; nevertheless, our position remains [unrefuted] even with respect to the fruit."

The sacrifice is indeed accomplished; it is taught as something to be performed, and the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is a qualification of the agent. Since the sacrifice is taught as something to be performed, therefore desire [itself] is not [the primary object].
The object of desire, such as heaven and so forth, becomes the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) because it is understood as something that exists [in the future].
If heaven were not a goal to be accomplished, how then could there be a "desirable" (kāmya) obligatory rite?
The ritualists (yājñikāḥ) teach [the suffix] *mit* as distinct [from *yat*], because everything is eternal; thus, desire (*kāma*) is its cause.

[The suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *yat* is used after words ending in *go*, *dvi*, *aca*, and those not denoting number, measure, horses, etc., when desire is intended. He resolves [this objection]: because it lacks a foundation (*nirmūlatvāt*).

This will be a sound instruction for the ritualists. He objects again: "If the sacrifice is indeed the goal to be accomplished, then it follows that this very point—that the agent possesses the entitlement—has arrived."

He himself says: "And in the eleventh [book], section one, it was refuted that when the agent is denoted, the word *svargakāma* (desiring heaven) cannot be syntactically connected. He provides the resolution: "True, it was refuted."
The state of being subordinate to that which lacks appropriation (*nirupādāna*)—
namely, the state of being subordinate to desire (*kāma*) that is devoid of appropriation— has been refuted. [As for] that which possesses appropriation (*sopādāna*)—
But in this desire, there is the state of being subordinate.
It is established as being like the ocean, because it is designated as a quality (*guṇa*).
This is because desire is designated as a quality with respect to the action (*karman*). He asks: "But what is the difference between these two?"

The distinction between the positions of "with appropriation" (sopādāna) and "without appropriation" (nirupādāna) is that in both cases [the term] functions as a qualifier of the agent. The response is: "Appropriation and non-appropriation have already been explained."

In one case desire is to be accepted; in the other, it is not to be accepted—this is the distinction. The questioner says: "True, you have stated the distinction regarding cognition; however, I ask about the distinction in relation to the cognition itself. If the distinction [in cognition] arises independently from the apprehension of the relation, what is the use of stating a further distinction?"
The reply: True, if a relation independent of specific particulars were perceived; however, it has already been stated that such a relation is not perceived in the absence of those particulars.
Therefore, a distinction must be stated. He concludes: "Consequently, there is nothing such as 'being authorized' that exists separately from 'being an agent';
or else, a distinction between being an agent and being authorized must be explained. [Objection: But surely, by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) which prompts action—
The activity is performed by means of [the suffix] *ṇic*, as shown in the derivation of *ṇic* in the case of "kurukuru.

Its meaning is as follows: when one who is being impelled is engaged in the operation of an instigator (*prayojaka*), which is characterized as the impeller, the suffix *ṇic* arises. In that context, the optative and other [moods] are seen being employed, as for example: [Example omitted per instructions.]

Just as in the expression "kurukuru" (do it, do it), so too the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others bring about the activity of one who is already disposed to act. Therefore, for the sake of establishing activity in the Veda, a distinct denotation called "qualification" (*adhikṛtatva*), which is in addition to agency (*kartṛtva*), must be stated. The repetition [of the word] in "kurukuru" indicates urgency. Precisely because the optative suffixes and the like incite only one who is already disposed to act, for this very reason, he [the agent] is [known] through the Veda alone.

The statement in the Bhāṣya, "I must do this, but I do not know the means," shows that one who has been prompted by this general impulse proceeds toward a specific action upon seeing the means; thus, the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others function to impel one who is already inclined to act.
Thus he demonstrates; and it has been shown that they recite, "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice," but not, "One should practice sorcery."

By this also, it is shown that even when there is a general application regarding malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and its accomplishment, [the rule] applies specifically. He refutes [this objection]: "First of all, it cannot be said that [the rule] applies to one who is already in the process of being applied."

[Page 023] Because the definition is not heard [in the rule] as "the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth" (for it is heard as such in the definition); for the optative suffixes and so forth are heard in the context of an injunction (*vidhi*), and an injunction is that which incites to action, not this other thing [which applies] both to one who has already acted and one who has not. Furthermore, because there is a deviation in usage.
"There is deviation in the application," because the *liṅ* and other suffixes are employed to incite one who has not yet acted. He explains this very point:
"The definition [of the object] does not specify a distinction as to whether it is one who is already acting or one who is not yet acting; the application—"

It is observed [as a cause] precisely for one who has not yet engaged in the command and so forth. Now, it may be argued that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others occur only for one who has understood the command.

The meaning of this is as follows: if he who has understood the command—that is, he by whom the command has been understood and accepted—is indeed the very person toward whom the command [is directed],...

It gives [the result]. Because one who has already engaged [in an action] acts by means of that general [impulse], and because there is no engagement for one who has not yet engaged, he raises the objection that even the command to engage one already engaged would constitute a [verbal] application (*prayoga*). He refutes this: "There is no application in the case of engaging one already engaged, because of the deviation [of the definition] in cases such as addressing someone (*āmantraṇa*)."
