For the use [of the imperative] is observed in the case of an invitation (*āmantraṇa*) for the purpose of inciting one who has not yet acted. Even in the case of a command (*ājñā*), it is a specific application of that same [impulse] for inciting one who has not yet acted; thus, activity is produced only for one who was previously inactive.
Now, [one might object]: "But [this applies] only in a general sense..."

It functions only with respect to a specific [action]. To this, he says: "And activity is not understood from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in a general sense, because they are restricted to the specific."

Regarding the meaning of the word: therefore, that activity directed toward a specific object which is brought about by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth belongs only to one who has not yet acted. However, as for that activity which has already occurred in a general sense, the operation of the optative suffixes does not apply there.

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that the optative suffixes bring about mere activity, since it is only when there is a connection with a specific object that the activity becomes restricted to that specific [object]? To this, he says:

And it has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that words function through the expression of what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). Therefore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote an activity that is directed toward a specific object only when it is connected [with other factors]. As for what was further stated—that in the derivation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), one shows [the agent] as "doing, doing" (*kurukuru*)—[that refers to the following].

To this it is replied: the meaning of a word cannot be understood from the mere use of the word alone; for indeed, the cause for determining the fixed relation between a word and its meaning is the observation of its usage as established by no other means. Without such denotative power (vācakatā), the employment [of a word]— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

1. For that which does not function [as a primary signifier], perception is not possible; it is the *prayoga* (linguistic application) that determines its denotative capacity. However, for that which functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or figurative usage (*gauṇī*), [perception is possible].

Or, because it is used in a sense that expresses a general property (*sāmānya*), there is no observation [of its usage] as a denoter; and since its application in urging one who has already begun to act is justified by its merely expressing the state of being a motivator (*pravartakatā*), there is no certainty regarding its status as a denoter from that. Furthermore, for all things that possess causes...
It has been stated that only that which is invariable with respect to effects is called a cause;
therefore, this application [of the reason] does not function to prompt activity by way of being variable.

The cause [is as follows]: whatever is the cause for the employment of a word, that must be its expressed meaning. Therefore, the instigation of one already engaged in action is not the expressed meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the others. But if this is so, then even the usage of commands (*ājñā*) and the like would be non-conclusive; for even the employment of commands—which consist in the instigation of one not yet engaged—is subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*). This is because [the suffix] *ṇic* arises [in such cases].

Because they [the suffixes] function as instigators of activity (*pravṛttapravartanāt*). Therefore, since there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in both cases, the cause for the fixed relation between word and meaning must be stated.

He provides the answer: this is what is said—optative suffixes (*liṅādayaḥ*) do not deviate from "instigation" (*pravartana*), because it is understood everywhere: in all instances where activity is occurring, such as in the domain of the causative suffix *ṇic*, and also in cases where activity has not yet occurred, such as in commands (*ājñā*) and the like. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—

In both cases, it can be said that the meaning of the word is precisely that much [the injunction itself]. As for what was shown by the statements "one should sacrifice with the Veda" and "one performing malevolent magic should sacrifice," that [applies] once the separate status of the qualification (*adhikāra*) is established.

In the context of those things associated with desire (*kāma*), it was stated with the intention of discussing attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*); however, here it is stated that there is nothing distinct [from the object itself]. Therefore, that is "non-perception" (*adarśana*).
The meaning of this is as follows: once the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of this section has been settled...

This is true: it was stated that regarding actions connected with desire, where the means are brought into being through qualification, there is generally an inclination toward them precisely because of the expectation of a result, though this is not established in specific cases. Here, however, the objection is that there is no qualification at all apart from the agent. Therefore, this passage is not intended to be presented as a counter-argument against the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

It is possible. Moreover, if this instruction were intended only for one who is already engaged in activity, then the very purpose of the instruction— namely, that "this is the means for achieving that"— would be lost.

Because the sentence is intent upon bestowing the power of the accomplished action (*siddhakarmaśakti*). Why, however, is there no purposefulness in the instruction even when it is intent upon this? He says: "There is no verbal authority regarding the essential nature of the means."
This has been stated; what then? It is precisely in [the context of] performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

This was stated in the *Codanāsūtra*: that the authority of the word (*śabda*) is established only with respect to an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*). And it must be admitted that verbal authority depends upon such linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Validity does not reside in the form of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), but rather in the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) itself. Therefore, it is logical that the purpose of instruction (*upadeśa*) is to impel one who has not yet acted.
Precisely because the status of being an instructor for the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. consists solely in impelling one who has not yet acted, for that very reason...

Grammarians maintain that for one who is already engaged in action, the expression of the cause is conveyed by the suffix *ṇic*; whereas for one who is not yet engaged, it is conveyed by the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes.
For one who is being prompted to act, the expression of the motivating cause is likewise effected by the suffix *ṇic*. Not [otherwise]...

The Grammarians (śābdāḥ) maintain that the expression of the instigation (*pravartaka*) of an action is conveyed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be no distinction between the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the optative suffixes in their denotation. Since the meaning of the optative suffixes and the like is precisely the instigation of one who has not yet acted, it follows that the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) alone is the cause for performance, and not the desire for a result.
And the result follows from the prior comprehension of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*).

Thus, in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, after stating "one should act" (*kuryāt*), it is explained that through its connection with the term "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the meaning is "one should bring about heaven" (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*); it is not that "the desirer of heaven should make heaven."
It has not been stated that the understanding of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is preceded by the understanding of the result (*phala*). And this must necessarily be so,
because [the understanding of what is to be done] occurs even without the acceptance [of a result], as has been accepted.
One must proceed in this manner; otherwise, there would be no entitlement regarding lifelong [observances] and the like.
The meaning is that there would be no comprehension of these as duties (*kartavyatā*). Why? Because there is no other goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

If there were no entitlement (adhikāra) distinct from the status of being an agent, then because all [persons] would be equal by virtue of being devoid of entitlement, the *prayāja* and other rites would not possess the status of being subsidiaries (*aṅga*) with respect to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices. Thus he says:
"Not that which has become a means... (Mānameyodaya 1.1).
[Page 026] But in that case, would it not follow that there is no connection with the auxiliary members? He replies: It does not follow that there is no connection with the auxiliary members.

If the Śruti and other means of knowledge were not authoritative, [one might object]: "But is it not the case that the authority of the Śruti and others depends upon [a specific] qualification? To this he says: "And their authority is not prompted by any other goal to be accomplished."

Because there is an instruction regarding the subsidiaries even for obligatory rites (*nitya*). Even where no fruit is mentioned in the case of an obligatory rite, it is accepted that the connection with the subsidiaries occurs through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth. Thus, even though heaven and the like are not the fruits, there will still be a connection with subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings. This has been stated merely from a preliminary standpoint; the final answer follows.
Māha: "And if the connection with the auxiliary elements is not obtained, what can we do? We follow the authority of the means of valid cognition."

If there is no connection with the sacrifice according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let it not be so; for we who follow the view of Bādari have already stated that the *prayāja* offerings and others must indeed be performed separately. As for those, however, which have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), [they are to be performed as part of the main rite].
Substances, qualities, and purificatory acts are taught for the sake of restriction; they are certainly not non-members of the ritual even when the agent possesses the entitlement [to perform it].
This is also the view of Bādari. He concludes the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "Therefore, the instruction pertains only to the meaning of the verbal root, not to the desire."

Even though it is understood that the sacrifice itself is what ought to be performed, how can those who are to be instructed regarding the prohibitions in the case of obligatory rites— which are devoid of [worldly] results— be so instructed?
Regarding the formation of the word *anuśāsyāḥ*, an effort must be made to establish its grammatical derivation; for by the rule *eti-stu-śāsvṛ-kyap*, the suffix *kyap* is applied.
Furthermore, those who do not engage even when a result is available—whom should they be punished?

The meaning is that they are instructed for the sake of a fruit, not for heaven. And this position, which holds that the meaning of a sentence is action (*kriyā*), is in accordance with worldly practice. As for those who [regard] the comprehension of the fruit...

Even if [the result] exists, it does not function as their motive; therefore, the cognition of the activity itself is the cause for engagement, not the result. For even when the cognition of the activity has arisen, those who do not engage abandon what they have heard and do not perform what ought to be done.
[They] act [thus]. Therefore, it is precisely in your own position that the scripture lacks the capacity to instigate practice; whereas in our position, it does.
[Page 027] — But surely, on the view that the agent is the primary subject, the injunction (niyoga) is purposeless.
How is it purposeless? The answer is: for the agent...
Or, one receives the designation of a *kāraka* because one is currently active, or will cause those who are active to act;
the designation of a *kāraka* is based on an activity that is present, past, or future, but not because of an activity existing across all three times simultaneously.

Regarding the sense of "being" (*bhāve*): [the root] *vyāpr̥* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class, meaning "to be occupied with," and not the *tudādi* class root *pṛṅ*, meaning "exertion. He asks, "What follows from that? [The answer is: therein, Brahmins and others receive the designation of "agent" (in the sense of) "have they been occupied with sacrifices and so forth? Or else, "are they being occupied with them? or "will they be occupied with them?"

If they have already acted, what will an injunction accomplish? Or if they are acting, even then the injunction is entirely useless, because both [the agent and the action] are already engaged; and since an injunction is for the purpose of instigating activity, its lack of utility follows. Now, if...
The intention is also that they will cause [the cognition] to function.
He refutes this: from what source does this cognition arise prior to the application [of the senses]?

It is understood that he who has a connection with an injunction (niyoga) will act under its influence; however, it is impossible to know that he who lacks a connection with an injunction will not act. If it is argued that this knowledge will arise from the injunction itself, then the injunction does not belong to the agent.

The agency of one who is appointed—that is, the status of being an agent belonging to one connected with an injunction—would follow; therefore, it is difficult to maintain that entitlement belongs to the agent.
He offers a rebuttal:

But if this were so, would it not follow that there is a denial of the relationship with all causal factors (*kāraka*)? For prior to the connection with the injunction (*niyoga*), even in those cases, the status of being a causal factor is impossible. And in actions devoid of causal factors, what purpose would an injunction serve?
[The agent] will act. Now, having understood the entire collection of causal factors as that which is to be performed, their application will follow;
this is equally true for the agent as well. Thus, whatever action has an agent as its performer, it is by that very [agent] [that it is accomplished].

And the establishment of the relationship [between the agent and the action] occurs through the intention of what is about to be performed, in the sense that "it must be done. Whatever is understood as the agent in a particular case, that very thing must perform it; otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the understanding of the restriction regarding the agent. Therefore, it is by way of the intention of what is about to be performed...

The connection [of the action] with the agent is established. Therefore, even under the heading of the agent (*kartṛ-adhikāra*), there is no fault. And this must necessarily be accepted: that whatever action has a certain agent, it must be performed by that very agent. [Thus says] the proponent (*siddhāntin*) regarding the factors of action (*kāraka*).

Just as one does not accept a state [of action] that exceeds the factors of action (*kāraka*), even though the agent (*kartṛ*) has a specific domain, because its nature is faultless; for even for those [factors],
since no other relation is understood for the sake of establishing their connection,
[the relation] possesses a restriction to specific *kārakas*.

Setting aside the accomplishment of the *niyoga* (the injunction), this is what is meant: just as that very instrument [is established] due to the restriction of a specific instrument, so too that very agent will be [established] due to the restriction of a specific agent. He concludes: "Therefore, there is no connection."

Or, it must be accepted as existing prior to the injunction (*niyoga*). If, on the other hand, the connection of the causal factors (*kāraka*) with the injunction is based on a future state, then that [connection] would have that [future state] alone as its cause.
That [cognition] occurs even prior to the comprehension of the relationship between the application and the agent.
If, however, the connection of even a single *kāraka* (participant in action) is not admitted, then,
because an injunction (*niyoga*) would be impossible in actions devoid of *kārakas*, the established validity of that which has the injunction as its sole object must be rescued.
And it is not [the case that this can be done].

"That is appropriate precisely because it is already established. Now, someone objects: "But surely, in cases such as sovereignty and the like, the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka) is observed prior to the formal assumption of authority;
why, then, should that relationship be [defined] with the intention of something yet to be performed?"
It is stated that [this] is established by consensus. To the question "In what kind of worldly application? he says: "In a kingdom where such a person acts as the agent.
He asks in the middle: "By what kind of agent?"

Regarding the application found in treatises on statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*) and the like—such as "you are authorized [to act] in the case of a wound inflicted by an arrow shot by a person of noble birth"—it was previously stated that the qualification (*adhikāra*) pertains to a specific agent;
this is now addressed: it is appropriate in cases such as past kingdoms and the like.
Because among men, the capacity for qualities such as injunctions and so forth is seen to exist in the form of agency.

The meaning of this is as follows: this application is indeed appropriate in the case of kingdoms and so forth; it is stated with reference to the fact that the agency of the ancestors was understood, namely, "having as its agent one born from the lineage of Viddacchara. Likewise, at present...

This is not stated in order to demonstrate the agency of such a person in that kind of object by saying "you are authorized"; therefore, it is entirely appropriate to demonstrate the agency of a past agent in that case. Here, however, apart from the injunction (*niyoga*), another person does not appear as an agent.

It can be said that [this is so] because the activity of all persons is preceded by that [knowledge]; therefore, the description of the connection with an author is made with reference to future [persons]. Furthermore, in the case of the *Daṇḍanīti* and similar works, it is indeed possible for the instruction to be preceded by the observation of other systems.
Even regarding an object whose agent has already been experienced, there is the entitlement (adhikāra) of a specific person;

for since it is impossible for another agent to have a connection with an action performed by a different agent, the presentation of [that person as] the agent is not tenable. Thus, the one who is entitled is distinct from the agent.

To this it is said: "Therefore, the authorized person (adhikṛta) is other than the agent (kartṛ). To that he replies: "Even there, it is merely a statement of the meaning of the root √arh (to be entitled); thus, it is indeed the domain of the agent. Agency does not arise from authorization.
The meaning of this is: [the term] *vidvaccharābhijana*...

The meaning of this is as follows: in a kingdom where a learned and noble archer is fit to exercise agency, it is there that your agency resides; thus, there is no fault of obstructing another agent. Therefore, only the agent is the qualified person (*adhikṛta*). (Regarding the word "of the agent" [in the phrase *kartuḥ*]): it is established that, within the context of the agent’s qualification, the desire for heaven (*svargakāmitva*) is a qualification of the agent, not a qualification of the result.
And thus, everything would have to be performed by everyone;
for if words such as "one who desires heaven" were qualifiers of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
In that case, because desire would be the sole basis for undertaking [an action], nothing at all would be to be performed by anyone.

However, when an action is to be performed by taking desire as merely a subordinate factor (aṅga) through the mere understanding of its necessity, then every action is to be performed by every person. Likewise, this instruction regarding knowledge is given part by part; and thus, by means of these parts, the action—
This instruction regarding knowledge is partial; however, through the performance of all actions by every person, there is complete success—that is, the accomplishment of the entire enjoined purpose.
What is meant is this: while asserting that everyone must perform everything, [the author] maintains that there is indeed only one [true] performer.
He demonstrates this as follows: thus, this demonstration of the identity of the self is presented by way of instruction on ritual performance. This is what was stated [on page 30]:
All this is Brahman; it is taught through the method of instruction in its various parts, both by way of knowledge and by way of practice.

This is because of the injunction: "Therefore, one should reveal that reality. Since the injunctions regarding ritual action are employed for the sake of the knowledge of reality, [it is taught] by way of knowledge.

The identity of the Self is taught by way of instruction according to its various parts—that is, everything is to be performed by everyone—and thus the unity of the Self is taught through the practice [of ritual]. Precisely because this unity of the Self is understood from this instruction regarding ritual action, there is the following utterance of those who maintain the existence of an agent and a qualified performer: "Standing upon the path of the unreal, one should thereafter illuminate the Real."
Thus,
he considers this injunction to be the primary purpose of all instructions; therefore, one should illuminate reality— this is the [purpose] of all instructions.

This is the rule of application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of revealing reality; the meaning is that all instructions are applied toward the revelation of reality. Therefore, because they are applied to the revelation of reality, the appearance of instruction regarding ritual action is merely ignorance, since the sentence has another purpose, as in: "These true desires have untruth as their covering."

Thus says the Śruti. The teaching that [the Self] is a part, part by part, is intended as untrue, because it is employed for the purpose of revealing the ultimate reality (tattva). Therefore, the perception of an instruction regarding ritual action (*karman*) derived from a statement whose primary intent is otherwise is untrue.

And likewise, the exclusion based on passion and so forth is intended as "untruth," because of the scriptural statement that "desires and the like are true. Therefore, seeing another section [of the text] after having seen the section concerning the agent is a delusion. By this—
The subject at hand has been concluded. And for this very reason—the fact that the discussion concerns the agent—the authors of the Dharmaśāstras declare:
"Being motivated by desire is not praiseworthy," considering the fulfillment of desire to be the attainment of results that are non-Vedic.
Because desire is fruitless,
he speaks of the unpraiseworthy state of being "one whose self is desire" (*kāmātmatā*). For the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are indeed motivated by desire.
Thus, he considers the application [of the scriptures] to both knowledge and action.

When all teachings are applied as being intent upon the realization of the reality characterized by the identity of the Self (aikātmya), then, because it has been so enjoined, the Vedic study for the sake of desire (kāmya) [is likewise included].

*Gama* means the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. And when the teachings are not intended merely as instructions for ritual action (*karman*), but rather as partial instructions, then even in the Veda, because it is enjoined, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is indeed optional (*kāmya*). "All this, indeed, is Brahman; from that it is born...
The Brāhmaṇa passage, "One should worship with tranquility," illuminates this very position that the agent possesses the authority [to perform the rite].
How does it illuminate it? He says: for when a rite is taught as something to be performed for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*), it cannot be accomplished by every possible agent.
The action occurs; for, by way of distinction, desire is seen as a qualifying attribute of the qualified person. Therefore, the oneness of everything is not established.

If one were to adopt the position that everyone performs all [rituals], it would follow that every performer is one and the same, thereby establishing the oneness of all. Consequently, Vedic mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "All this is indeed the Person" (puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam) would become untenable.

But one might ask: "In this view as well, what is the status of those doctrines that maintain difference? To this he says: "As for the doctrines of difference, they are merely provisional; if the teaching concerns specific ritual actions, it is explained as being based on that. However, if there is ultimate non-duality, upon what will difference be based?
Precisely because there is no person to be enjoined (niyojya) distinct from the agent (kartṛ),
for this very reason the venerable Pāṇini [does not mention such a category] among verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook), apart from the action and its factors (kāraka).

One does not remember a separate action called "the person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) as having the sense of the root *ni-yuj*. But surely, the root *yuj* is also listed among the roots beginning with *pac*;
therefore, because Pāṇini remembers that very same root *yuj* [in the sense of] an object, the "person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) is also [an object].
It is indeed so recorded. [The author] refutes this: "True, it is so recited, but it does not state that the agent of the sacrifice and other rites is the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled).

This is what is meant: he does not remember that one who was previously the *niyojya* subsequently becomes the agent. Without even grasping this single point, he raises an objection once more: "But surely you yourself have stated that 'it is the agent who is impelled'?"
By saying this, he means that in sacrifices and the like, the agent is the object (*karman*) of the root *yuj*.
He refutes this: if it is said that the agent, as the instrument (*sādhana*) of the root *yuj*, is "employed" (*niyujyate*), then our own position is established.

When one remembers that the agent possesses the status of being enjoined (*niyojyatva*), then the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is already established. Why, then, was it said that "he does not remember"? [The answer is: the meaning is that he does not remember the root *yuj* preceded by the prefix *ti*. (Mā.)
The Blessed One said, "Pāṇini. That was stated with the intention of referring to the letter *a*. It refers to that which is to be enjoined as being of the nature of the non-agent (*akāraka*).

The meaning is that he does not remember. He explains this very point: in that case, when desire is the object to be accomplished, there must first be an injunction (*niyoga*); and from that injunction comes agency (*kartṛtva*).
Thus, there is the contingency of a different meaning [from the original], and since that other meaning has not been understood...
It has been stated that this—this desire for results by those who possess longing—is like tying a crane in the sky;
it is said to be the delusion of those who long for such things. Therefore, the section concerning the agent was spoken by the wise:
"That which is already established (the existent) is taught for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (the future)."
By this reasoning, since even desire (*kāma*) is not accomplished by means of an injunction (*niyoga*),

for that very reason the distinction between verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-bheda*) is also established— namely, that some action is a subordinate action (*guṇa-karman*) and some is a principal action (*pradhāna-karman*). However, when the object of desire (*kāmya*) is what is to be accomplished, all verbal suffixes necessarily assume a subordinate status.

Because they are subordinate to the fruit; and consequently, the meaning of the sūtra—that "they [the organs] are twofold"—would be untenable. But surely the meaning of the sūtra will be intended as referring to those that are eternal?

Because there is an absence of fruit for eternal things, the meaning of the Sūtra does not intend [them] to be eternal. Even in that case, regarding those very eternal things, the cause is seen to be the attainment of another state, as in the verse: "But by those [qualities] through which the substance..."

The phrase "is intended to be performed" results in [the action] being merely a subordinate factor (guṇa). Its meaning is as follows: when sacrifices are [performed] under the heading of desire (kāma-adhikāra), they are subordinate factors.

Since they are expressed by the verb as being in the state of a factor (*bhāva*), even under the heading of "eternal" (*nitya*), they must be denoted by the verb precisely as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*);

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple meanings. Nor is the state of being a subordinate factor without an object, for the specific distinctions among the factors of action (*kāraka*) are clearly perceived.

Because it is logical that [the substance] stands in a subordinate position (*guṇabhāva*) by virtue of being for the sake of that [action]. On our view, however, since the instruction has the substance as its primary object, the substance stands in a subordinate position.
For it is well said that when an instruction has action as its primary object, [the substance] possesses primacy.
Now, [it may be argued: "On the basis of the mere desire to act upon the substance, the author of the Sūtras..."

He states that [the mention of the substance] is for the sake of its being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), and not because the instruction is intended to have the substance as its primary object. To this he says: "And it is with the intention of the instruction that 'it is desired to be performed' is stated. For, whatever appears as the primary [object] through the examination of the scripture, that alone is what is desired to be performed, and nothing else.

Therefore, when an instruction is directed toward the action (*kriyā*) in sacrifices and the like, it is a primary action (*pradhānakarma*); but when it is directed toward the substance (*dravya*), it is a subsidiary action (*guṇakarma*). Thus, the twofold nature [of action] is established. To this, it is replied: that indeed becomes a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*) whose [qualifier—]

In that case, it would follow that [heaven] is produced by a causal agent (*bhāvavekāraka*). However, here, upon the departure of joy, that very same substance is no longer denotable by the word "heaven.
Therefore, the word "heaven" does not denote joy. What follows if this is so?

The answer is as follows: this results from that—namely, that the desired object is the domain of desire. What follows from that? That which is not desired does not lead to the accomplishment of another. Pleasure, which is of the nature of the desired, does not exist for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice; for it exists for the sake of the desired [pleasure] itself.
All of this.
He explains this very point: what is meant is this—in a sentence connected with a desired object, the connection of the other word-meanings occurs precisely for the sake of that [desired] meaning.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence here must be described in such a way that the connection of the other word-meanings serves the purpose of accomplishing the desired end. In that regard, if the status of being a qualifier of the agent were adopted, heaven would become a subordinate element, like the ocean. However, if it is the qualifier of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then by the principle to be stated later—
Since the status of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) extends up to the accomplishment of the desired object, the connection of the word-meanings occurs for the sake of that desired end;
therefore, heaven must be accepted as a qualification of the person to be enjoined. This is what we have stated: "The desired [end] is not for the sake of the production of another."

This has been stated: because it consists of the nature of pleasure and because of its connection with desire, the connection of other categories of meaning is for the sake of the desired object, as in [Jaimini’s sūtras]:
"Action also [is subordinate], because it is for the sake of the fruit," and "The fruit also [is subordinate], because it is for the sake of the person."
Thus,
because the fruit is desired, it is not for the sake of the ritual.

The meaning is "the fruit. And regarding the statement that "the fruit [is so called] because it serves the purpose of the person," he raises an objection: "But has it not been said that heaven is desired, because it consists of pleasure and because of its connection with desire? Furthermore, the connection of others [with the ritual] is for the sake of what is desired."
It was stated [previously] that "of the categories of things" (*padārthānām*). And that [attainment of the goal] is the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*); thus, there is a contradiction.
He resolves this:
"Or how could that which is not a human purpose be desired?"

For that which is the object of desire is called "desired" (*iṣṭa*). And since pleasure related to the self is what is desired, that which is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) cannot be considered "desired. If this is so, then it follows that all this is merely a human goal, and not an object of desire itself. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), being satisfied, offers this benediction: "Truly so; may the wise one also be long-lived."
[Objection: Then, for what purpose is the presentation of the desired [result] stated again?
[Response: Precisely because the treatise has human welfare as its purpose.

The sense is that let it be stated that the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). The reply is: unless it has the desired object as its aim, the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*) is not established for the scripture (*śāstra*). There is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to suggest that a scripture must necessarily have a human goal as its purpose.
Since heaven is indeed desired, its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is possible for the scripture; thus, the mention of the "desired" is meaningful.

This state of being the principal (śeṣitva) with respect to action—on the part of the person by virtue of their connection with the fruit produced by that action—is what is called "qualification" (adhikāra).

For the word *adhikṛta* (authorized) signifies a lord (*īśvara*). It is understood that "this person is authorized in this village" means he is its lord. Therefore, authority (*adhikāra*) with respect to an action is simply sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). And precisely because someone possesses sovereignty even over an action, it is for this very reason that the designations "master" (*svāmin*) and "servant" (*karmakara*) are applied, despite their equality in terms of agency (*kartṛtva*).

If ownership were not something distinct from agency, then the designation "owner" would arise solely from the qualification [to perform the rite]. Furthermore, the designation "servant" arises from performing the ritual for the sake of another. To this, an objection is raised: "But surely, in a sacrifice, a servant is not possible at all."
Since sacrifice itself is the agent by virtue of its nature as self-renunciation, the entry of another person or the like is not possible. He refutes [this objection]:
"Not indeed in the case of the ritual act..."
It is possible in the case of a sacrifice in general; however, it is certainly possible in the case of a sacrifice that constitutes the subject matter of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*),

which serves as the means for qualification (*adhikāra*) and is assisted by numerous constituent elements (*padārtha*), for the sake of accomplishing the performance of those other constituent elements.
The agent of the action; however, the meanings of the words would be established even by their inherent capacity.
A particular person performs only a certain specific action, not everyone performs everything.

But has it not been stated that "words denoting action signify the meaning of being" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*)? The meaning of this [sūtra]—"words denoting action signify the meaning of being"—is as follows: *In the phrase "words denoting action signify the meaning of being,"* [the following is intended].

It has been stated that things whose meaning is an entity (*bhāvārtha*) are what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); and two things to be accomplished cannot be connected within a single sentence. Furthermore, since agency is not possible when desire is the thing to be accomplished, agency is not possible in relation to a sacrifice when heaven and the like—which are desired—are the things to be accomplished.
Thus, because there is an absence of agency in the sacrifice (*yāga*), no case-ending following the root *yaj* that expresses the number of the agent is applicable. How, then,
can there be an entitlement (*adhikāra*) with respect to villages and the like when the word "heaven" (*svarga*) denotes something desired,
given that words such as "village" do not denote something desired?

Next, he addresses the objection: it has been stated that heaven and so forth are mentioned as objects of desire (*kāma*), not as qualifiers of desire. What is meant by this is that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding heaven and so forth is presented as words denoting the objects of desire.
Therefore, this method is not restricted to villages and the like. Now, one might object that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are possible only in the case of heaven;
[the author] replies: we have already stated that positive and negative concomitance are for the purpose of demonstrating the scope [of the relationship].
For, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since the word "heaven" (*svarga*) denotes joy, it is said that heaven is the object of desire;
and because of its connection with desire, villages and other such things are established as being objects [of that desire].
Indeed, that which is not desired cannot be an object of longing.

It has been stated that [the agent] is "one who acts" (marhati). Therefore, entitlement is established even in those [optional rites]. He restates the second objection: "As for the question of how there can be agency when the sacrifice to be accomplished is optional (kāmya)"—he answers: "By whom was it said that [agency exists] only in a sacrifice?"
[Reply: But in the case of sacrifice, there is entitlement; and for the sake of accomplishing that, agency follows as a matter of course, which is indeed lordship (īśvaratā).
Since the state of being the recipient of a fruit is not possible for an action without its completion, the person possesses agency in the accomplishment of the sacrifice.
Precisely because agency (*kartṛtva*) arises from the very fact of the sacrifice, for that same reason there is the application of number (*saṅkhyā*).

If the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of the agent who exists for the sake of accomplishing heaven were [independent], then one would say "the entitlement of the agent"; however, there is no entitlement for an agent who already exists within the sacrifice.

However, since agency belongs to one who is authorized for the sacrifice, there is no fault in this. To provide further support for his own position by following worldly convention, he says: "In the world as well, one authorized for one thing accomplishes another."
Likewise,
a minister appointed to royal duties accomplishes his own interest; however, for the sake of achieving that [interest], he possesses the status of an agent in the king's business.

Having restated the first objection, he provides the rebuttal: as for what was said— that "action-words have being as their meaning," and that where there is an injunction, the understanding of the fruit arises from them.

The meaning of this is as follows: that which was stated regarding the sacrifice being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by the rule "words denoting action are those whose meaning is *bhāva*"—by this it is meant that from those sacrifices which constitute the *bhāva*-meaning, there is the comprehension of the fruit. He explains this very point: "By means of that instrument, one accomplishes one's own purpose."
The meaning is "by which.

Therefore, the sense is that the qualified person (adhikārī) should accomplish his own purpose by means of the efficient force (bhāvārtha), which serves as both the object and the instrument. What is meant is this: the efficient force is connected solely as an instrument; for it is the nature of an instrument...

Such is the nature of that which becomes the object of the agent's operation, such as an axe. For the agent's operation, characterized by raising and lowering, has the axe alone as its object, and not directly the state of being split in two. Nevertheless, although the state of being split in two is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the axe itself is the means (*sādhana*). Likewise here too, heaven and the injunction (*niyoga*) are both to be accomplished by human effort. And yet, between those two—

[The object] is directly the domain of human effort. However, since a means such as a sacrifice (*yāga*) is of an unestablished nature (*abhūtasvabhāvatva*), there is the production of the meanings of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha*) by this human effort. Yet, this much does not entail a loss of its status as a means (*sādhanatva*), nor a loss of its status as an end (*sādhyatva*), nor even the attainment of being an end; for it is understood that the mandate (*niyoga*)—which is the fruit—is what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, precisely through the attainment of the state of being a means...

In the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, it was demonstrated that sacrifices and the like possess the status of being "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) by virtue of being the objects of the agent's activity. But how can the activity of the agent, which has one thing as its object, result in the accomplishment of something else? It is because it proceeds with reference to [the latter]. The agent's activity proceeds directed toward the mandate (*niyoga*) and the fruit; however, the objective of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which serves as the means, becomes the object [of that activity] as a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*).
Because they are the objects of the agent’s operation which is invariably concomitant [with the result], verbal roots (bhāvārtha) are accepted as having an unintended necessity of being performed.

Precisely because verbal roots are connected only as means (*sādhana*), for that very reason the status of *udbhid* and other such terms as names (*nāman*) has been stated on the basis of their grammatical coreferentiality with the third case (*tṛtīyā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Otherwise, since it would not be understood that the words ending in the third case are directed toward the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "desire" (*icchā*). If heaven alone were the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then why was this said [on page 037]?
It is not understood that the state of being something to be done (kartavyatā) arises from the name alone. Who said otherwise?
[The answer is:
The nominal stem (prātipadika) certainly does not convey the state of being something to be done. How, then, is the state of being something to be done understood in the case of desire (kāma)?

The answer is: it has been stated that this is because [the object] is understood as desired, and because its object is something desired. Now, if this person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) were to enter into the syntactical relation within the meaning of the sentence, then its connection would occur as a qualifier of the person to be enjoined, on account of being understood as something desired; however, he is not...
Anticipating this objection, he states the fundamental reasoning: "And this must necessarily be accepted as such;
for an agent distinct from the performer (kartṛ) must necessarily be admitted. Indeed, [the Veda] does not merely convey the relationship between an action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha)."

There is no comprehension of performance [in such cases]. For instance, in present-tense descriptions such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," although there exists a relationship between action and its factors (kārakas), there is an absence of the understanding that "it is to be performed. Now, one might object:
The understanding of performance will arise from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth;

for when one hears a sentence joined with an optative suffix such as "Devadatta should cook," an inclination to act is observed, and since that is impossible without an understanding of performance, [the meaning of] performance [is derived] from the optative suffixes and so forth.

It is understood that there will be no comprehension [of the action]. Of whom do the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth inform regarding the performance? The meaning of this is as follows: although the optative suffixes and so forth bring about the comprehension of performance by way of making known what is to be done (*kārya*), he who understands the performance as being connected to himself is the one who engages in it. Therefore, it is of him that the optative suffixes and so forth inform regarding the performance.

Therefore, that person must first be recognized as the qualified agent (*adhikārī*). For when a particular action is intended for a particular purpose, there arises the understanding that it must be performed by that person.

One who possesses the status of being enjoined (*niyojyatva*) possesses the status of being qualified (*adhikāritā*). Consequently, Devadatta and others are first connected [to the rite] by way of being enjoined; subsequently, once their qualification is established, there arises the understanding of its performance; and from that, the performance follows.
But has it not been stated that [the suffix] expresses the agent?

It has been stated that the optative and other suffixes convey the performance by the agent. He refutes this separately: what was said is incorrect, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).

It has been stated that for whom there is the comprehension of performance, for him there is agency; and for whom there is agency, for him there is the comprehension of performance. And thus, an injunction directed toward an agent would be purposeless.
And if agency is already fully established, what further purpose is served by the cognition of its being an effect?
He explains the circularity: for if agency arises from the mandate (*niyoga*), and the mandate [arises] from agency.
There would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Therefore, the injunction (*niyoga*) itself must first be accepted; from that injunction, agency (*kartṛtva*) is to be understood. As for the comprehension of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), that arises here from another source alone.

The "one to be enjoined" (niyojya) is the cognizer of the task; persons such as those desiring heaven are presented as being enjoined by virtue of their status as cognizers of the task. In common worldly usage, Devadatta and others are connected as cognizers through their connection with the vocative case-ending. Therefore, following worldly practice—

It is established that even the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is connected to the meaning of the sentence. If it is argued that [the *niyojya*] serves to provide a qualification for the *niyojya* through its connection with what is desired (*iṣṭa*), then how is this the case in instances such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*)?
The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) asks: "Or how is it here?"
"Will it not come to pass?
The proponent, however, says: "If life were [already] established as something to be accomplished through instruction as if it were already established..."

If living (*jīvana*) is taught as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then, because it is understood as an end to be achieved, it would serve as a qualification of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) in accordance with that goal. But when living is taught as if already established (*siddha-vat*), then it cannot be a qualification of the person to be impelled. A proponent of a partial conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) says: "In that case, you yourself have stated that living does not connect as a qualification of the agent precisely because it is already established."

He refutes this: first, if the intention is that "because it is already established" means "because it is already accomplished," this is incorrect; for it is only an established factor (*siddha*) that connects as a qualifier, not something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Alternatively, if "because it is established" means "because it is already known"...

Regarding this, he states the following opinion: "Even if the result [of the action] cannot possibly exist here as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless, there is still a syntactic connection (*anvaya*); and from that connection, the verbal cognition of the result arises. It is not the case that there is a connection with the possessor of the result, because that would entail the consequence of [the word] being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*). If the result...

If, on the other hand, the connection with the action to be performed (*gamyānvaya*) is described, then the Veda’s capacity to convey meaning would depend upon the comprehension of the result; thus, there would be a state of dependency (*sāpekṣatā*).
Therefore, it must be explained how there can be qualification (*adhikāra*) here in respect to [conditions] such as being alive.

This is what is meant: the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) in the expression "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvam*) does not connect with the qualification of the agent; rather, it follows from that [qualification] by way of its injunction (*niyoga*).
[Page 039] Regarding the position: how so? For one who desires the fruit, a lifelong performance of the ritual is not possible.
It occurs [only] if the desire for the fruit has ceased, because [the rite] would not be performed [otherwise].

If living (*jīvana*) is a qualification of the agent, then it enters into the jurisdiction of one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), and does not constitute a separate jurisdiction. Nor is there [an obligation] to perform [the rite] throughout one's life merely out of a desire for the fruit.

The application [of the rule] is possible. If the application were to occur even when the desire for the fruit has ceased, then living would pervade the application. But this is not the case. Therefore, it must be stated that there is no pervasion of the application by living. Since pervasion is logically established only when living serves as the cause (*nimitta*), living is indeed the cause.
That must be accepted;
and that state of being the cause of life is logically established in relation to the qualified person (*adhikṛta*).
Adhi-

Since the performance [of the rite] is dependent upon the injunction, it is not logical for the connection with the agent to function as a causal condition (*nimitta*). For if there were a connection with the agent, the sense would be simply that "one who lives must sacrifice" as soon as it is stated "one should sacrifice"; therefore, the status of being a causal condition is untenable.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no status as a *nimitta* (efficient cause); what does it matter? To this he replies: "As long as the inconsistency of the word [in the text] has been demonstrated, if the status of being a *nimitta* is absent, then when there is a doubt between a qualification of the agent (*kartṛ*) and a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), it is logical that it be a qualification of the *niyojya* alone, because of its priority."

To this he says: "And it has been stated that the status of being an agent cannot be established prior to the conjunction with agency when the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is not yet fully known.

Furthermore, experts in logic maintain that since [the qualification] would be purposeless under the view that it qualifies the agent, one must state its utility by resorting to an alternative position."
Therefore, the status of being a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) must be accepted as purposeful,

just as the status of being a qualification of the person to be enjoined— such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth— is necessarily to be accepted. If that is so, then the establishment of entitlement (*adhikāra*) does not follow from [the object] being desired.
The respondent says:

Granted that the mention of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) must necessarily be relied upon, nevertheless, being "desired" (*iṣṭatva*) is not a cause for its status as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*); rather, it is precisely by virtue of being desired that it serves as a cause. Not so.

Indeed, it is not desired that there be a lack of purposeful action (*akriyārthatā*), nor that the qualification of the person entitled to act (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) should consist in such a lack of purposeful action. Rather, there would be purposeful action in the sense of "for the sake of the accomplishment of another" (*paraniṣpattaye*). And if there is no purposeful action, then the action itself must have that [accomplishment] as its purpose; and since an action has that as its purpose only when it serves as a qualification for the person entitled to act, it is determined that it functions as a qualification for the person entitled to act. He concludes: thus it is established.

The qualification applies both to the occasional (*naimittika*) and the obligatory (*nitya*) rites. Furthermore, as for what was stated— that the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is established for [the sacrificer] just as it is for the other causal factors (*kāraka*) by virtue of being a means (*sādhana*)— [that is now addressed].
Just as instruments and other factors of action are understood as means (*sādhana*),
so too the agent is understood solely as a means. Consequently, the understanding of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) arises precisely through his connection with the action.

Having restated [the opponent's position], he refutes it: "This is incorrect; even from the perspective of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), the connection with an action is understood, because no other connection exists.
The meaning of this is: for the agent, there is indeed a connection with an action.

[The performance] is based on the injunction to perform; yet there is no performance without an understanding of that performance. Nor is there an understanding of the performance regarding a ritual act without [an awareness of] qualification (*adhikāra*).

Nor is there qualification without the cognition of a task related to oneself. Therefore, the state of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatā*) must first be resorted to. Consequently, what has been stated is indeed logical.

Since heaven and the like are understood to be desired, and since all word-meanings are syntactically connected as being for the sake of that which is desired, it has been stated that [the desire for] heaven and so forth functions as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); unable to tolerate this, [the opponent] says: "Of one who is being enjoined to an action..."
In the case of one desiring heaven, for the accomplishment of that desire, the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*); what word serves as the basis (*nimitta*) for this?
The meaning of this is: following worldly usage—

By that [injunction], it is the action alone that is understood through the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as that which is to be accomplished. The person to be impelled (*niyojya*) likewise understands that very action as what is to be accomplished, and not merely as being enjoined to the action. This being the case, when the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is enjoined to the action, what is the function of any word here in establishing the fulfillment of the desire—the establishment of the desired fruit—namely, that "the sacrifice is the instrument"? It is none at all.

This is the state of affairs. Therefore, even though it serves as a qualification of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), it does not connect with all other word-meanings by virtue of being the desired end; thus, it is not determined as a qualification of the person to be impelled on the strength of that [desired end]. He elaborates upon this very point: first of all, in the term "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the root *yaji* refers to the sacrifice...
It expresses only the measure (mātra), and not its connection with anything else; even the case-ending (vibhakti) indicates therein either the agent as the means of the sacrifice,
or the number included within it, according to the view of the Grammarians.

He explains this according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, and not merely that the sacrifice has another purpose; for even the term "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) makes known heaven as something desired by the person, [and thus] as an end to be accomplished,
just like the other [factors].
[Page 041] Furthermore,
there is no disregard for the fact that heaven or desire possesses primacy with respect to the sacrifice; rather, [the distinction lies in their grammatical case].
The first [type of] designation (*ktiṣṭu*) has a meaning that is not distinct [from the base word] itself and does not convey predominance; however, [names such as] *jyotiṣṭoma* and others,
being names (*nāman*), are dependent on the denotation of the sacrifice.
Because, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word], one understands it to be a mere name;

and it has already been stated that the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) does not express the sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, this notion that "one should accomplish heaven by means of the sacrifice" is entirely baseless.
Knowledge: even that which is the meaning of the injunction here,
consisting of what is to be done, enjoins a person either toward desire or toward sacrifice.
Either desire (kāma) is understood as that which is to be accomplished, or the sacrifice (yāga) is so understood;
therefore, there will be an understanding of the mere mandate (niyoga) in one or the other, but not an understanding of a mutual relationship between the two.
Now, it was argued that being desired (*iṣṭatva*) would not otherwise be possible if the fulfillment of desire did not result from the sacrifice.
Where has this been observed? That being desired does not occur without a means (*sādhana*). Precisely because it is desired...
Precisely because it is the object of desire, it becomes "desired.
He raises an objection: "If it is argued that what is desired is understood as being the probandum (*sādhya*)."
He refutes [this]: "By which word is its status as a goal (sādhya) expressed? Only a connection with desire is understood regarding heaven, but not that it is a goal to be accomplished (sādhya)."

It is understood [from the text]. And even if it were something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is no contradiction in its connection with desire, provided that which is to be accomplished is something other [than the sacrifice itself]. Therefore, one must state the reason here by which the sacrifice’s status as a cause (*kāraṇatā*) is understood;
it would be better if the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) were simply maintained.

The sense is that the qualification of the agent is the cause for the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*). Its meaning is as follows: in the world, in accordance with common usage, it is the action (*karman*) itself that is understood through the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*). The person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) also understands that very action as the task to be performed; thus, the injunction (*niyukti*) pertains solely to the action. And this being the case, for one who is being enjoined toward the action, [the result] heaven—

In the accomplishment of desire—that is, in the accomplishment of the desired fruit—the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Of which word here is this the locus [of meaning], given its connection with a case ending? He concludes: "Therefore, let the term 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*) be a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*)."

Let it be that one who desires heaven is the person to be enjoined; however, there can be no cognition that "one should accomplish heaven by means of sacrifice," because of the absence of a cause [for such a cognition].
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says: To this it is replied that it has been stated that heaven qualifies the person by virtue of being the object of desire.

It has already been stated that "one who possesses desire is enjoined," and it has also been stated that "the injunction pertains to the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, this syntactic unity consists in the relationship between the injunction and the person to be enjoined; such syntactic unity is not possible if the words do not correspond to reality.
For a word, it is impossible for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) to occur by bypassing its own specific meaning,
because the meanings of the individual words themselves constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*) is the sentence-meaning,
for it is the *kārya* (the "to-be-done") that impels one to action.
In the *Codanāsūtra*, it is stated that "the injunction (*niyoga*) is said to be the impelling person (*niyojya-puruṣa*), and its accomplishment is the meaning of the sentence.
In that regard, if the duty to perform the sacrifice (*yāga-kartavyatā*) were being expressed, then the purpose of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-artha*) would not be connected.

In the case of an injunction (*niyoga*), it is he who desires heaven. And if the sacrifice itself were what must be performed because of the desire for heaven, then the person would not be connected to the injunction merely as a person; nor is a mere person [connected] by one desiring heaven.

It is said: Now, if heaven alone were stated as that which is to be accomplished, the object [of the injunction] would be disconnected from the person to be impelled (niyojya). Consequently, the understanding of a single unified injunction (ekaniyoga) would be undermined.

If this is so, then one might argue that the sacrifice itself must be what is to be performed; to this he replies: "And when the sacrifice is primary, the fault already stated—characterized by the non-connection with the person to be enjoined (niyojya)—arises. Therefore, desire is primary."
There is a connection through that very same single application (*ekaniyoga*).

When it is accepted that "one should accomplish heaven by means of sacrifice," the connection of all [factors] is established. This is what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "Moreover, he for whom heaven is desired should perform the sacrifice..."

(1) m. s. The comprehension of the connection between one [element] and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—[the thought that] "it shall accomplish [the result]"—is as if disconnected; for it is said: "one desires one thing, yet performs another."

Thus, (6-1-3) the meaning is that there would be no connection for one who possesses desire (*kāmin*) with that which is not a means (*asādhana*), by way of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). He refutes the notion that desire is without a cause, stating:
"In this context, it can be said that the word (*pada*) is the cause."

The word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) indicates heaven as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by the sacrifice; the word *yajeta* (one should sacrifice) indicates the sacrifice as the means for attaining heaven. Now, one might object that such a meaning is not perceived here; to this he replies: "As for what was said regarding the demonstration of the lack of distinction in denotation, that [is explained] precisely through *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related)."
This has been answered.

It has been stated that words denote [their meanings] as already connected; therefore, by virtue of their fitness for connection, words such as "heaven" (svarga) possess this very nature of having [already] occurred [in connection]. If this is so, then this [objection] has already been refuted in the *tadbhūta* section itself.

For it was stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that [the words] are "upādāna" (appropriated) because they denote meanings established through the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Therefore, since such a status of meaning is unestablished here, it is not tenable;
thus, this very point has been refuted by that [previous argument]. This is the meaning of the phrase "it is answered by that itself. He provides the resolution: "It is indeed incoherent."
The understanding of words and word-meanings has been refuted to this extent.

That words are entirely unrelated and word-meanings are likewise entirely unrelated—this much has been refuted therein. Why? He says: because of the appearance [of meaning], and because of the exclusion (apoha) and inclusion (vāpoddhāra) of others...

That basis [of the word] exists as an antidote; it is not, however, for the sake of conveying the mere denotation of the referent through the words. It is merely an appearance devoid of a causal basis (*nimitta*), which is the comprehension of the integrated sentence-meaning. Likewise, conceptual construction has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

"This is merely the measure. Thus, that section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] is intended to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the following: that people who have mastered the usage of words understand the meaning of a sentence through the insertion and deletion of existing word-meanings; it does not, however, mean that the mere word-meanings—which follow the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—are what is denoted by the words. Therefore, because the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is expressed [by the sentence], there is no failure to comprehend that relation.
[This objection] has been refuted. Therefore, it is logical that one should achieve heaven by means of the sacrifice.

Consequently, since the connection with the desired object (*iṣṭārtha*) alone is established when [heaven] serves as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), that alone must be accepted. And this is the established position of our school regarding the *Codanāsūtra*.

The *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) is established as the meaning of the sentence because it is not yet realized; however, it is explained in the first section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādya*) that there exists a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) who understands that task as being related to himself. And since there exists a relationship of means and end between the desire and the task when the desirer is the one to be enjoined, it is precisely what is explained in the *Bādari-adhikaraṇa* that is stated here, because [the nature of the task] is dependent upon the understanding of the person to be enjoined. And that—

In the section on the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), it is established that the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) is something distinct from action (*kriyā*), being capable of being connected with the means for the fulfillment of desire. Furthermore, in the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*), it is pointed out that the meaning of the verbal root enters into a relationship with that *kārya* as its instrument (*sādhana*). The instrument—

It is established in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), being an accomplished entity (*bhūta*), becomes the object of the injunction by delimiting it. What is this [statement] "But it is not the means, because it exists for that purpose"?
This sentence is not a proof.

The meaning is "it might be so. Furthermore, if the sacrifice alone were enjoined as something to be performed, then, due to the absence of a person to be directed (niyojya) and because words function collectively, this sentence would not convey any meaning at all.
Now, one might object that in the assumption of a causal condition (nimitta), it is not possible for any single factor to serve as that condition.
It was stated [above] that "in order to speak.

There is no sentence distinct from words, nor does it have any collection of words as its cause. Therefore, this comprehension is devoid of a cause. He offers a rebuttal: "Precisely because no single [word] possesses causality..."
Thus it is said that [this applies] to everything:

by virtue of denoting things as mutually related, all words indeed become the cause of this meaning, for otherwise the denotation of related things would be impossible. If the entire collection of words [is present] for the cognition of mutual relation...

How, then, is it that the status of being a cause for each individual word (*pratipadanimittabhāva*) was stated in the section on sentences (*vākyādhikaraṇa*)? To this he replies: For it is said that the status of being a cause for each individual word applies when there is an analysis of words and their meanings; [it does not apply] to meanings already integrated [into a sentence].

The causal status (*nimittabhāva*) of each individual word has been established through the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha*). However, by way of conveying that [individual meaning], every single word is a cause for the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*),
for the sentence-meaning is indeed characterized by the various word-meanings as they are mutually related.
If it is argued that because it is impossible to convey [the meaning] through a single word alone, all [words] therein function as causes (nimitta), it was stated in that very same context:
"By means of the relationship between the injunction (niyoga) and the person to be enjoined (niyojya), does one recollect the word that expresses the relationship and conveys that relationship?"
What was stated regarding Pāṇini is incorrect; for indeed, all of this can be subsumed through the recollection of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

By one who recalls the rule "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) as that which distinguishes [the relation] from [the categories of] object (*karman*) and so forth—which establishes the distinct [relation]—everything is indeed subsumed.
It can be said that it belongs to the Blessed One; however, from the perspective of ultimate truth, the designation of the Blessed One is indeed nothing other than a relative term.
There is no restrictive rule that every word expressing a relationship was remembered by the Blessed One [Pāṇini] from Pāṇini’s grammar,

because such words are not seen in the case of primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds; for instance, although the primary derivative *kelima* exists, it is not recorded, nor is the secondary derivative *yantra*, etc.

The Blessed One does not even remember this, though he had previously studied it. Therefore, since there is no observation of memory for words that do exist, one cannot assert the non-existence of words or the non-existence of their meanings based on such non-remembrance. And thus, because the meaning of a sentence consists in the accomplishment of an injunction (niyoga), the objection that "activity results only from a fruit" is thereby refuted.

For if the fruit were understood from another source, then since the entitlement would be established by that very [source], activity would follow; thus, the relationship between the injunction (*niyoga*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) would not be understood. But when the meaning of the sentence is [determined] by the sentence itself as to how the fulfillment of the injunction might occur, [then that relationship is understood].

If it is argued that when [the result] is established, there is a conceptualization (kalpanā) conforming to it, and thus the initial activity does not result from the result itself; then, if the result is indeed obtainable only through the injunction (niyoga), why is it said in the treatise (tantra) that "the result is not enjoined"? The answer is as follows:

When it is understood that the meaning is *niyoga* (an injunction), there arises an inquiry into the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), for the word-meaning is indeed the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

Therefore, in that inquiry, one formulates the thought: "This [element] is obtained from another source; this [other element] is obtained from yet another source," but not with respect to the sentence-meaning itself.
That which is called "attained" by virtue of being connected with an injunction is not at all "attained"; this has been demonstrated in the passage, "One offers with curd."
He says in a single passage: "The undiscriminating cognition regarding words and sentences confuses those of dull intellect.
This confusion belongs to those of dull intellect who do not know the distinction between a word and a sentence."

How can that very same thing be both attained and unattained? Furthermore, those who understand words and sentences as distinct determine that while the state of the word-meaning is attained, the state of the sentence is indeed unattained. He states this in a single passage: "In a sentence, there is no such thing as a 'word,' nor are there any 'word-meanings' within the meaning of a sentence."

In the state of a sentence, there is no such thing as a "word. In the state of a sentence, there are no such things as "word-meanings. Why? Because the meaning of a sentence is indeed the comprehension of a specific [meaning].
The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is a specific meaning (*arthaviśeṣa*) being understood, and the cause for that understanding is the sentence.

Therefore, at the stage when the specific meaning is being understood, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) does not exist as something being understood within the sentence-meaning. This is because of the understanding of the specific meaning—

1. Furthermore, in the state of synthesis (*sandhāna*), there is no word that brings about comprehension. Therefore, while demonstrating the division of word-meanings, everything regarding the sentence-meaning remains unattained.
He said this: "But in the conceptualization of the cause (*nimitta*), there is the designation of 'word' (*pada*) and 'word-meaning' (*padārtha*).
A certain collection of phonemes, expressing a certain meaning through its connection, becomes the cause for the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). By that, its—

Generally, there is the designation of words and word-meanings. Therefore, if— relying on that [designation] as something already attained— one were to say that at the stage of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) the so-called word-meanings do not exist at all, then it would follow, as the proponents of verbal testimony (śābdikas) have indeed stated, that the knowledge of words and word-meanings is nothing but false.

He refutes [the objection]: "We do not say that the state of being a cause (*nimittatā*) is false; rather, at the stage of being understood, there is no distinction between the sentence-meaning and the sentence, because the sentence functions as the means of comprehension."
Precisely because words and word-meanings exist as causes, it has been said that the cognition of word-meanings arises from words alone,
and the meaning of the sentence arises from those word-meanings.
Because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), the cognition of a single [word] is delimited by its own apprehension; thus, it relies on the distinction between cause and effect.
Words express their own meanings as unconnected, yet they serve as the cause for the meaning of the sentence.

It has been stated that they "go" (yānti) by relying solely on the distinction between the cause (nimitta) and its effect (naimittika); however, there is no distinction in the valid cognition (pramiti) itself, because the single meaning of the sentence is the object of knowledge (prameya), and the single [sentence] delimited by its own apprehension (pratīti) is the means of knowledge (pramāpaka). The distinction, however, is that for verbal cognitions (śābda), even the cause is denied.

Why? Because, according to their view, it is the sentence—whose division into constituent parts has subsided—that is the signifier. However, in the Mīmāṃsaka school, it has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that it is the words themselves that convey the meaning of the sentence by means of the word-meanings. This is what is referred to as the *Vākyapadīya*.

For according to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), there is only the sentence (*vākya*) and no such thing as a word (*pada*). Therefore, it is stated in that very work, the *Vākyapadīya*, in the section on "That Which Has Come Into Being" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*): [in the] *Vākyārthamātṛkā*.
And by us [it is said].

Here, an objection is raised: if the mandate (*niyoga*) is understood as that which necessitates performance, then, since performance is impossible without a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the person to be enjoined must be accepted. But the mandate does not necessitate performance; for the mandate—
Regarding that which is understood through words, he says: "The existence... [and so on]...

"from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Even in the case of that which is directly denoted, the cognition that it necessitates performance is conceptual. With this intention, he says: "What is the cause for that which is preceded by [the cognition of] the means?"

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) must be expressed as an injunction," it cannot be said that it is not to be expressed; for if it is to be expressed, what is it?
