It does not establish that performance [of the ritual]. He refutes this: there is something to be said. What is it that must be said?
That it is to be expressed in terms of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and not in terms of its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇataḥ*).

The object of the injunction (*niyoga*) is to be stated by its own nature through the process of exclusion (*viyoga*), not by means of a formal instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The word "injunction" (*niyoga*) denotes a mere property (*dharma-mātra*); however, the substratum (*dharmin*) embraced by the instrument of knowledge consisting in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-pramāṇa*) is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth. But from where is this distinction understood? To the question "from what?", he says "for this very reason"—[the nature of] the task (*kārya*).

The distinction is as follows: where the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting in the form of practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*), is understood, there is a designation by way of its being a means of valid cognition; but where it is not, there is a designation by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). To the question, "If there is no status as a means of valid cognition, how then is there a designation by means of a *kṛt* suffix? he replies: because the act of designation rests solely upon the mere object (*padārtha*).

Since it is sufficient for the word to denote the mere entity as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no denotation of the essential nature by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Therefore, it is determined that the denotation occurs through the optative suffix and other such elements as the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not by means of primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*). This is because such usage is observed in practice.
Furthermore, since the comprehension of word-meanings is preceded by syntactic connection (*hāra*),

and because we observe the performance of an action only when a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar is heard, whereas such performance is not observed upon hearing a form ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*), the position that [the injunction] is merely a mental construction (*kalpanā*) is also refuted.

According to the reasoning already stated, there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a conceptual object (*kalpanārtha*). If [it is argued that] the recollection is connected by means of the genitive case, then how is it that in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the nominative case is used?

The nominative case is prescribed as being caused solely by the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Since the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is something additional [to that], there is no "mere meaning of the nominal stem" here. Therefore, because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), either the genitive case should apply, or else there would be no hearing of any case-ending at all, even if the genitive were not intended.

[Objection: It is argued [that this is] logical. [Reply: It is said: This nominative case does not depend upon an injunction (*niyoga*) at all; rather, it depends upon a *kāraka* (grammatical participant).

If it depended upon an injunction, since the person to be enjoined (*viniyojya*) would be something distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the nominative case would not occur for the agent (*kartṛ*) or the state of being (*bhāva*).
And since the agent is expressed by the verb itself when there is expectation [of its expression], it follows that the meaning of the nominal stem is pure; thus, the first case ending is justified.
But [an objection may be raised]: "But surely..."

For when there is dependence on an injunction (*niyoga*), since the relationship between the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) is preceded by the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), it must be expressed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) related to that very person.
This is because of the priority of the person to be enjoined, who presents itself first.

The case-ending must occur first, not in dependence upon a grammatical factor (kāraka) that arises later. You have spoken the truth in saying that the person to be enjoined (niyojya) must exist prior [to the injunction]; however, a case-ending is not possible within the injunction (niyoga) expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ).

Now, one might object that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) can indeed be used to denote the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*); to this, he replies: the genitive depends upon relation in general, not upon a specific type of activity.

The meaning of this is as follows: the residual relation (*śeṣasaṃbandha*) contains within it the relation of action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*). In that context, having set aside the specific relation of action and factor, the genitive case is employed for the fully established relation that results through that medium. It is not, however, used for a relation consisting of a specific operation, because such a relation is non-residual (*aśeṣa*), as it takes the form of an object (*karman*) and so forth. Furthermore, the specific distinction [of the relation] is understood through verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like.
The relationship between the one to be enjoined and the enjoiner [is as follows]: if the person desiring heaven is understood as the one to be enjoined, then,
because he is the object of the action, the accusative case ending should occur.
No, because the operation of the injunction is not grasped by the verbal root;
for the accusative case is characterized by being enjoined.

[The accusative case ending] does not occur even when there is pervasion by an operation (*vyāpāra*). Why is this? He says: "For the second [case-ending] and the others [apply] when the operation is contained within the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Why is that so? He says: "Because the designation of a *kāraka* (participant in action) depends upon the [verbal] state (*bhāva*)."

For the second case endings and so forth occur in relation to a *kāraka*, and grammarians have designated the *kārakas* with reference to the action (*bhāva*). Nevertheless, one might ask: why? He says: they maintain that the status of being an action belongs to what is expressed by the verbal root.

He asks, "Why [is it] from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone? and says: "Those who say that 'the pure, isolated state is called *bhāva*'; therefore, because *niyukti* does not have the nature of the meaning of a verbal root, [it is not so]."

It possesses the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpatva*). And if it were of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāvarūpatva*), it would not possess the status of an agent (*kārakatva*); and if it lacked the status of an agent, there would be no second [case-ending].

Therefore, even though the state of being an agent (*kartṛbhāva*) occurs subsequently, it is the cause for the production of the case-ending here. The fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*) is achieved by means of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthamātratayā*) alone.

[From the word "svarga-kāma"]: Even without a case-ending, the connection with the *niyoga* (the injunction) is established for those such as the "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) simply by reflecting on the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), according to the principle already stated. Precisely because the establishment of the *niyoga* occurs through the mere meaning of the nominal stem alone, there is no possibility of a second accusative case when the singularity of the agent has already been expressed.

If the agent were not expressed [by the verbal suffix], then, because it is higher [in the order of application], the accusative would be sublated by the instrumental itself and thus would not occur. Regarding the fact that the accusative occurs when the agent is expressed and the instrumental is impossible, this is another argument: *prāti-*...
The status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established even by the force of a single word (*padika*). For this very reason, the particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate another reason;

for this very reason, the establishment of denotation by means of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is also achieved. Precisely because the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is [the agent] by way of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), [he is connected with] the desire for heaven...

Upon careful reflection, it appears that for this very reason the denotation of the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) is established by the *l*-suffix (*lakāra*). Otherwise, the verbal root itself, while denoting the *kārya*, would denote the *niyoga* (the injunction), in accordance with worldly usage. For when the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), which culminates in a fruit, the *l*-suffix denotes a *kārya* distinct from the meaning of the verbal root, because such a *kārya* alone is fit to be connected with that [desire]. Thus, in that case—

Regarding this, it has been said: "If, indeed, the status of the person as the one to be directed (*niyojyatva*) does not manifest through the consideration of the nominal stem *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven), then even if such a person to be directed were resorted to, he would be understood—following worldly usage—as merely performing an action, rather than being understood as persisting until the attainment of the fruit; and consequently, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would not denote the novel causal efficiency (*apūrva-kārya*)."
The established rule regarding the expression [of grammatical relations] must be followed.

Now, one might object: since both types of bhāva—namely, the sacrifice itself and the accomplishment of heaven—are possible, even though the agency (kartṛtva) of the root *yaj* is expressed [in the verbal suffix], nevertheless, because that agency is not expressed in relation to the accomplishment of heaven, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) ought indeed to occur. To this, he says: "because of the two bhāvas..."
And the objection was answered by the fact that no other verbal root (*dhātu*) is employed;

since heaven is established without the employment of another root, there is no connection with the case-terminations of action or agent (*kriyā-kāraka-vibhakti*) even by that [root]. Now, if the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) also belongs to the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), then...

Heaven also possesses the quality of being a qualification of the agent; therefore, heaven too is subordinate. To this he replies: "The relationship of subordinate and principal is intended with respect to the *kāraka* (grammatical factor)," and thus this objection is also refuted.
With respect to the *kāraka*, it is merely subordinate—

In the state of being a *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined), however, there is no fault, as heaven remains the primary element and the sacrifice remains subordinate. Precisely because this case-ending [denoting number] pertains to the state of the *kāraka* (the factor of action) and not to the state of the *niyojya*, the number residing in the person desiring the result (*kāmin*) is not a governing factor; rather, only the number residing in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is taken into account.

For if the number pertaining to the desirer were to exist only in the state of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then by that force alone the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of a single individual would be established, and there would be no regard for the number residing in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). However, when this [number] is understood as residing precisely in the state of the agent (*kartṛ*) who is preceded by entitlement, then it does not [establish the entitlement of a single individual].
"It is sufficient for the purpose of being an agent" means that it does not function [as an agent].

If one who desires heaven is connected [to the rite] by way of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and not by way of being the agent (*kartṛ*), then how is it that there is no activity on the part of one who does not desire [the result]? For surely activity must occur even for one who does not desire [it]. Is it not so? [Objection: Desire—

To the objection—"Since activity is for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), how can one who has no desire be suspected of engaging in activity?"—he says: "Because the scripture is intent upon *niyoga* (the injunction), desire is for the sake of accomplishing the *niyoga*, not that the *niyoga* is for the sake of accomplishing desire. This has been stated. *Niyoga*.

Thus, [the action] is necessitated by its status as an effect (*kāryatā*), because its establishment is impossible without an agent. Since that [agent] is obtained as a qualifier of the desire (*kāmanā*), the object of the mandate (*niyoga*) is what is desired. Therefore, even one who lacks desire would engage in activity. He refutes this:
because the desire exists for the sake of accomplishing the object of the mandate.

Or rather, one might raise the objection: "If the purpose is the accomplishment of the injunction's meaning, how can there be activity for one who is not desirous? To this, the challenger says: "Such an objection is not even to be raised; rather, it follows that the person desiring [the result] becomes a subordinate factor."

It is said that for one desiring [the fruit], the *niyoga* (the mandate) becomes a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), yet this is not accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. He refutes [this objection]: "In this matter, it is your own lack of discrimination that is at fault. For the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not held to depend upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)."

With respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatā*) is not desired for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), nor is the primacy (*pradhānatā*) of the meaning of the verbal root [desired]. However, with respect to the mandate (*niyoga*), this is indeed accepted. Now, if this were so, would heaven (*svarga*) not become merely a subordinate element? To this he replies: even the relationship of subordinate and primary is dependent upon that [mandate] alone.
It is stated in the Bhāṣya that [the suffix] depends solely on the meaning of the verbal root;
but since everything is conducive to the accomplishment of the injunction (niyoga), who would not accept this?

Who would disagree that at the time of the fulfillment of the mandate (*niyoga*), all that [subsidiary action] is conducive to it? If everything were for the sake of the mandate alone, then there would be no mutual subordination among those things whose purposes are distinct from one another;
to this, he replies with the words beginning "he should perform" (*kuryāt*), which demonstrate the rule of such subordination (*tādarthya-niyama*).
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) also says: "One should meditate on something.
The Commentary has been explained according to its meaning. If those [factors] are qualifiers of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), [then...]
How, then, are these statements to be understood— such as "These true desires have untruth as their covering" and "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and so forth?
The reply: The interpretation of those mantra-explanations that have another purpose has been stated.

The manner of understanding those mantra and arthavāda passages that have another purpose has been stated; it was explained that their meaning is either figurative (gauṇī) or secondary (lākṣaṇikī). Therefore, this same [mode of interpretation] will apply to these [Upaniṣadic passages] as well. But is it not the case that Upaniṣadic sentences do not have any other purpose at all?

Because no other sentence is heard that establishes an action to be performed; the answer is: if there is no other sentence establishing an action to be performed and no action is heard therein by its own nature, then it must have as its purport an already established fact (siddhārtha), and if its purport is an established fact, then—

Since the validity of the word is established in that regard, its status as a restatement (anuvādaka) must be accepted; and since a restatement depends upon another means of knowledge, it follows that [the object] is indeed dependent upon another means of knowledge. The objector says: "In that case..."

"Let another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be sought," [the opponent says]. The proponent replies: "If there is another means of valid cognition in that case, then what harm is there to us in the existence of another means of valid cognition? For this is the meaning of the treatise, as it has been described."

Nor can it be that because a statement with an established fact (*siddhārtha*) depends on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a statement with a probandum (*sādhyārtha*) must likewise depend on one;

for there is no cause for such dependence in the latter case. As for the other [the former], its very status as a statement of an established fact is the reason for its dependence; thus has the distinction been stated. [The opponent] objects:

The opponent objects: "But since there is the possibility of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-duality, which is the subject matter of the Vedāntas, the meaning of the scripture is contradicted by those other means of valid cognition; moreover, the meaning of the scripture is perceived as being differentiated. He refutes this: "Indeed, no one..."

There is no contradiction, because since they have different objects—namely, that one concerns the object of the established effect and the other does not—the scriptural meaning is not contradicted by that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) himself says: "Now, if you consider there to be a contradiction..."

Because an injunction (*niyoga*) depends upon a specific application (*viniyoga*), and because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have scope regarding that application, [the opponent] objects: "In that case, there is no other means of valid cognition."

Why? Precisely because of this contradiction with scripture (*śāstra*), it is impossible to postulate another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why, then, is there no other means of valid cognition? He says: "Nor [is there] inference..."
It can be said that there is oneness of the entire world in the *dṛti* (the skin-bag); what follows from this? He says: [it leads to] contradiction with scripture (*āgama-virodha*).
And inference does not establish itself; thus say the Naiyāyikas, those who engage in the practice of logic. As it is said on page 052:
[text continues].

"Vedic slaughter is not dharma, because it is a form of violence. He concludes the present topic: "Therefore, let the supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa) of the Upaniṣads, whether independent or otherwise, culminate merely in the act of study.
[They do not require] another means of valid cognition..."

In the sense of [the suffix] *bhāva*, they are intended to convey their established meanings; there is no difficulty here at all, since the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is established under both alternatives. As for what has been recited by the authors of the Dharmaśāstras, namely, "being motivated by desire is not praised," [this refers to a different context].
Thus [he says]. Having restated [the objection], he refutes it: "This has indeed been read. Who said that it was not read?"—thus the challenger.
He said: "If it has been recited, then let there be no excellence (prāśastya) for heaven and so forth, because they are false.
The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) said: "Let it be so."
If excellence were the object to be accomplished, then there would be a negation of heaven and so forth,
such that "heaven does not exist."

It has already been stated that this would be a negation if it were so; however, if this is taught as a quality of the self— namely, that one should become a person whose nature is free from desire— then it is a negation of desire, just as the injunction "one shall not kill" is a negation of the act of killing.
In that case, there is no pointlessness;
rather, there is indeed purposefulness, since [the attainment of] heaven and so forth is accomplished.

The determination between these two— namely, whether it is a prohibition of action or something else— is to be sought precisely from that, by examining the sequence of the preceding and following statements of the Smṛti.

The sense is that [the result] is understood from memory alone. Here, he raises an objection to the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "We understand this from the sentence itself," which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya while demonstrating the attainment of the fruit even when the sacrifice is the primary factor.
It was proposed: "One who desires to fetch firewood should go to the forest.
How, in this case, is the action [to be understood]?
On the contrary, one considers that by virtue of the suffix *tumun*, it is the root *gam* itself that functions in the sense of another action; therefore, as for example—
This analogy holds; it should be stated in that manner.

Its meaning is as follows: the author of the Bhāṣya has said this: "For what purpose is such excessive effort made regarding the primacy of heaven, when even if the sacrifice were primary, the desired fruit would still be accomplished through the sacrifice?"
It is indeed understood from this very sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," that just as one goes to fetch firewood—

From this very sentence, "One desiring firewood should go to the forest," even though going is the primary action, it is understood that the fetching of the firewood is accomplished through that going; likewise, from the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is understood that the attainment of heaven is accomplished through the sacrifice.
As it has been said: "One who desires to fetch firewood [is led]. Therefore, the suffix *tumun* in "to fetch" (*āhartum*) is indeed attached to the root *gam* (to go).

Because it is heard [in the text], it exists as a subordinate element (guṇabhūta), according to the grammatical rule: "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is for the sake of another action.
Therefore, the example is dissimilar. He provides the resolution: this is stated because of the employment of the word *kāma*; here, the sense of the suffix *tumun* is present—
It functions in a different sense;
the intention is that its immortality is understood in that way.
The meaning of "atyārtha" is: to bring forth—

Because the designation "kāma" (desire) has the person as its primary referent, it functions as subordinate to the root *gam* (to go), which carries the sense of the infinitive suffix (*tumun*). Thus, the primacy belongs to *gam*. Furthermore, even though the act of going is primary, it is understood that the fetching of the wood is accomplished through it;

this is the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) who provides this illustration. However, in this case [of sacrifice], although the sacrifice is primary, the fruit is understood [to follow from it].
Thus, the refutation of the position is as follows: it is true that the accomplishment of the result is understood; however, that is not from the word itself. What then?
Because other means of knowledge show that going to the forest has the fetching of wood as its result, and because the sacrifice is not understood to have heaven as its means,
it follows that the fulfillment of the result is logically possible only when the desire is primary. This is the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇārtha*).
He concludes: "Therefore, it is established that the person under discussion possesses agency.

In this section, the summary of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final position (uttarapakṣa) is as follows: therein, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that there is no such thing as a "person to be enjoined" (niyojya) that is connected as the meaning of a sentence in common worldly usage.

It is understood. [Objection: But if there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), how can there be performance? For as long as an action is not understood as something to be performed, those who act with foresight will not perform it. However, when there is a person to be enjoined, that person for whom there is the injunction possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*).
And because the qualified person understands what is to be performed, the performance is established. It is replied: even though [the person to be enjoined] does not exist...

Regarding the state of being a *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), since the understanding of one’s entitlement (*adhikāra*) to that action arises for one desiring the fruit only after having apprehended another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through the result itself, the performance of the act is established. [However,] there is no word whatsoever [in the Veda] that denotes the state of being a *niyojya*.

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) considers: "True, it is so in common worldly usage; nevertheless, because the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the Veda serves to convey what is to be done (*kārya*),..."

Since an action is established as an action only when there is its performance, one must admit the existence of an *adhikāra* (entitlement) for the sake of accomplishing that performance. Furthermore, no result is known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here by virtue of which an entitlement could exist. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the entitlement, the connection of those such as "one who desires heaven" with the injunction must be described in terms of their being the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined). But who, then, is the *niyojya*?

What is this [term]? That which is understood through its effect (*kārya*) is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). By this, those such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) are introduced as the cognizers with respect to the effect. And since one who desires [an object] cannot apprehend that which is not a means to that desire as being an effect, [the desire for heaven is thus connected to the effect].

There exists a relationship of means (*upāya*) and end (*upeya*) between the two desires. Furthermore, since a sacrifice does not enter into a relationship with a desire occurring at a later time as its effect (*kārya*) for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), one must admit an effect distinct from the sacrifice; thus, the sacrifice is connected to that [effect] as its instrument (*sādhana*).
Consequently, since the sacrifice is the means to that which is the effect for the person, the person’s mastery (*aiśvarya*) over it is established. And so, therein—

In that case, since the understanding of the performance [of the rite] has been established, the performance itself is logically justified. Therein, regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*), the person’s entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform sacrifices arises because they are the means for accomplishing the task of the mere *niyoga* (the mandate). However, in the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya-adhikāra*), the distinction is that the *niyoga* must be accomplished up to the attainment of the fruit.
On this point, there are these verses:
In the world, a person who possesses the relationship of agency with that [action] is the means for attaining the fruit;
having understood this through another means of knowledge, he himself engages in the ritual action.
Then, having understood that it is to be performed, one carries out the action for one's own sake;
therefore, the status of being enjoined is applicable there, and in that respect, the Veda is useful.
If its authority is established in the world, how can there be understanding [of it] even from the Veda?
For an object is not denoted by a word for one who lacks linguistic proficiency. (3)
It is true that the fact that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth have "what is to be done" (*kārya*) as their meaning has not been described;
yet, the status of being "what is to be done" is not tenable for that which is devoid of performance. (4)
And because of the performance and understanding [of rituals], there is bondage through mastery over action;
yet such mastery is not possible through sacrifices and the like, as no fruit is observed therein.
Consequently, for human beings, what is to be done would become what is not to be done in the absence of sovereignty;
nor is sovereignty over an action possible through mere agency alone. (6)
As long as agency is observed in actions solely through sovereignty, and if the desirer is connected to that effect by way of being its cognizer; (7)
Then, the attainment of the fruit of an action is determined to be dependent upon that action;
yet, it is not possible for a fruit to be produced by an action that has already ceased in a single moment.
Therefore, in order to produce [the result] at a later time, the effect must be greater than that [cause];
thus, the connection of the object (karman) with that effect is by way of its being the means (sādhana).
Therefore, the Lord is the person [who acts] in the performance of actions for the accomplishment of his own purpose;
and such being the case, action also becomes a means that has attained its goal.
[Page 055] "The performance has been obtained"—in this way, the task attains the status of being a duty.
This is for the sake of the plant of proficiency regarding the task, which has arisen from the seed of engagement. (11)
This lily, though subject to being employed [in the ritual], blossoms while attached to its own fruit;
therefore, the absence of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) here does not constitute a fault.
Consequently, the one who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is established in the Veda as being connected to the action by way of being the cognizer (*boddhṛ*). (12)
Since action is for the sake of a result,
one might object that the Veda cannot possibly possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to animals and the like.
What is this "qualification" (*adhikāra*)?

The reflection: the meaning of this is as follows—one who is connected to the injunction (niyoga), which consists of the task to be done, by way of being the cognizer is the "one to be enjoined" (niyojya);
he is the qualified person (adhikārī). And animals are devoid of the capacity for cognition regarding the meaning of words, [a meaning] which is to be understood solely through verbal testimony.

In the case of an action, those who are capable are connected by way of being knowers. Consequently, it is not possible for them to be subject to an injunction (*niyojyatva*). Likewise, because gods and sages lack the state of being a knower—due to the absence of consciousness—their status as knowers is untenable. Therefore, since the Veda cannot function as a communicator to animals and the like, the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of animals and others is not tenable; such is the objection raised in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). And likewise...
No settled conclusion is found regarding the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of deities and sages.
He explains this very point:
if, first of all, deities are accepted as eligible, or if sages are those enjoined by the selection of ancestral seers (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*), then [the eligibility] would be non-eternal (*anitya*).
What is the point of considering eligibility (*adhikāra*) regarding the connection with the Veda?

The meaning of this is: if, in the case of a sacrifice, Indra and others are intended as deities, and their eligibility is suspected; or if [the eligibility of those] enjoined by the selection of ancestral seers (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*)...
And regarding the sages (*ṛṣi*), at that time their acceptance of [Vedic] performance would necessarily follow. However, performance by one who is bodiless is not possible.
If [the Vedas] were produced by a body, then because of the connection with impermanent objects, the Vedas themselves would be impermanent.
Furthermore, those [scriptures] lack authority altogether; what is the use of considering their eligibility? Now, as for those others who are of the nature of deities...
[Page 1355]
And why is the qualification that "the sages are intended" excluded, since the sages are Brahmins in those [other] cases?
It is heard [in scripture] that Indra and others were Kṣatriyas, and they too are indeed qualified; thus, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is not [as previously stated].
Therefore, Mīmāṃsā appears there as an investigation that has already discarded both the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (uttarapakṣa).
Since the qualified person (adhikārī) is one capable of understanding through such investigation, it is not reasonable to suspect that animals and the like possess this qualification. Nevertheless...

One must consider the eligibility of the eternal deities (*nityā devatāḥ*)—namely, the presiding deities (*adhikāradevatāḥ*) and the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*) who exceed those enjoined for the selection of ancestral lineages (*ārṣeyavaraṇa*). And that [eligibility] cannot be denied to them. This is so even in this case, regarding the sacrifice of the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
Even that suspicion regarding the qualification for the mere sacrifice is not tenable, since the meaning of the scripture is established as residing in the sequence [of the ritual].

The meaning of the scripture is established as extending up to the sequence (*krama*); therefore, the suspicion that one might have the qualification for the sacrifice alone by omitting the enjoined auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is not tenable.
If, however, this suspicion is raised in order to introduce another resolution, then the suspicion regarding the qualification would be justified as a cause for the desired [conclusion].

Although these two have already been refuted, they are presented once again. The meaning of the scripture, culminating in the sequence [of the stages], serves as the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*);
therefore, this inquiry regarding the "footing of space" (*viyatipada*) is indeed unfounded.
He provides the resolution: it is precisely the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture that has been presented.
"By way of the desire for [sensual] objects" refers to animals.
The meaning of this is as follows: that desire for results pertaining to the next world which was put forward by the author of the Commentary with respect to animals.

Through that [statement], their very knowledge of the meaning of the treatise (*śāstrārtha*) has been presented; and that has been made manifest. The intention is this: those who desire results pertaining to the next world are also capable of understanding the meaning of the treatise. Thus, it has been made manifest that the knowledge of the meaning of the treatise itself was presented by way of [stating] the desire. For without the treatise, the desire for results pertaining to the next world is not possible. Therefore...
Because they possess the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures as they arise, even animals are entitled [to perform rites]. How [is this so] for sages and deities?

This is a reference to what was stated previously. To this, it is replied: here, certain people who consider themselves learned in the knowledge of the Vedic meaning [claim that] regarding sacrifices—

They consider that the status of a seer (*ṛṣi*) and the status of a deity (*devatā*) are established solely by [their] station, asserting that Indra and the others are words denoting office-holders (*adhikāra*).
The meaning of this is: some think in this way—that words such as Indra, Agni, Īśāna, and so forth, are words denoting office-holders.
1. "Mā upanyastam" means that these are words qualifying the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). One who desires the state of Indra and so forth performs sacrifices and other rites. Anu-...

One who has performed sacrifices such as the *Ṣṭhita-yāga* becomes Indra; having become Indra, he performs further rites with the desire to attain a higher status, thereby attaining the state of a deity.
Regarding this, he shows an ancient tradition: "Thus, according to the historians, Indra is the performer of a hundred sacrifices (*śatakratu*)."

Regarding the statement "and the sages performed sacrifices," he shows an ancient tradition (itihāsa) here as well: they say that Śaunaka and others performed a sacrificial session (satra) in the Naimiṣa forest during the Dvāpara age.

Nor do they think that, merely by this much, the Veda becomes subject to the flaw of connection with the impermanent—namely, by its being a means of conveying deities produced by ritual acts (*karma*).
This is the meaning: [the deities are conveyed] by specific ritual acts alone.

Men attain the status of Indra and other deities; it is these very individuals who possess the nature of gods. Having become gods, they perform sacrifices out of a desire for further higher stations. Nor does this imply that the Veda has a non-eternal purpose, since it is established that those things produced by ritual action are themselves beginningless due to their nature as both cause and effect. This has been written in order to dispel confusion regarding this matter.
But how, then, is this delusion set aside?
It is set aside in this way: because sacrifices and the like are not possible for Indra and the other gods.

Because of the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself. For it is not logical that the same entity should be both the designator (*uddeśaka*) and the designated (*uddeśya*). It is untenable for one and the same person to be the designator by virtue of being the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the designated by virtue of being the deity (*devatā*); for within a single action, it is impossible for one and the same thing to possess the status of both object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*).
Regarding the term *patter*: here he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, the sacrificers who identify with Indra worship Indra as one already arisen in the past;
and those who identify with the seers (*ṛṣi*) choose seers already arisen in the past."

The meaning of this is as follows: those sacrificers who are regarded by us as Indras perform sacrifice out of a desire to obtain another state of being Indra; they sacrifice to that Indra who was produced previously. Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding action within one's own self. The same applies to the sages (*ṛṣi*) as well.

Regarding the phrase "those who have the conceit of being Indra": those whose conceit—that is, their conviction—is that "I am Indra" are those who identify themselves as Indra; in other words, those who consider themselves to possess the nature of Indra. The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) refutes this: "In that case, the conceit of seeing [the self] would be untenable, because of its distinctness."

"Pagatā. Its meaning is as follows: the logical inconsistency of whatever view is accepted by you is expressed in the statement "they sacrifice to the deity" (*devatāṃ yajante*). Your view is a mere conceit (*abhimāna*). This being the case, it is not the case that one sacrifices to a deity, because the status of being a deity belongs to what has already arisen previously; it does not exist now—

Because Madhucchandas is the sacrificer, even those who are not [human] persons do not sacrifice to him; rather, they should sacrifice to Indra, who was produced previously and is the object of that worship. And thus, it is Indra—who, though produced previously, is invoked after having been sacrificed to by one person—that is sacrificed to by others as well. Consequently, since those produced by ritual acts (*karmabhiḥ*) are not themselves being sacrificed to, they would lack the status of a deity (*devatātva*). Therefore, by means of ritual acts, the deities—
The position that "an entity comes into being" is also untenable. Therefore, the notion that one sacrifices to a deity produced by ritual action does not hold at all.
Thus he says: "Its existence and its distinction are untenable in practice.
The meaning of this is: [it applies] to Indra who has just now come into being.
Because it is being impelled by a person, it possesses the status of a deity; and because it does not itself impel another deity, it is distinct from the previous deity.

Thus, this [notion of] performance is untenable, as it would entail that persons also become deities through the act of impelling that deity. Therefore, a deity is simply a deity, and a seer is simply a seer; they are neither the goal to be attained nor the attainer.

According to the reasoning already stated, because that which is produced by karma is not subject to change and is an obscuration, the state of being a deity or the state of being a seer (*ṛṣi*) does not arise through karmas; therefore, a deity must be accepted as existing by its very nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, a seer is likewise not to be attained through karma, nor...

We shall explain in the ninth chapter, in the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), how that which brings about the attainment of the fruit of action does not actually bring it about, because the status of being the giver of the fruit has been refuted there; however, what is denied here is the state of being attained. As for what was also said: "in some way... [the remainder follows].
[a] There is eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the *viṣṇukrama* sacrifice, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other criteria are preceded by eligibility.

The meaning of this is as follows: when ritual properties (*dharma*) are recited in proximity to that which possesses eligibility, and they serve that purpose, they are connected to its constituent parts by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.

The application (*viniyoga*) of things is established [by means of direct assertion and so forth]. However, regarding context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other [means of proof], their very existence as authoritative for both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the application depends upon eligibility (*adhikāra*). Therefore, at the stage of eligibility, application is not yet possible. Even though eligibility belongs only to one who is capable of performing the rite, nevertheless, the eligibility of those such as the lame cannot be denied; indeed, application is understood precisely by virtue of that eligibility.
The discussion concerning eligibility (*adhikāra*) is established as follows: when a person is capable of performing a rite, he is eligible for the application of its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Since the meaning of the scripture is thus determined by the sequence [of the ritual], it requires eligibility for the sacrifice in general, rather than eligibility for a specific [qualified] person alone; therefore, in that context, the doubt arises regarding anyone who merely desires [the result]. Consequently, even in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), eligibility is established.

Since there is no contradiction in the fact that the application (*viniyoga*) of those subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) is not intended for one who lacks the qualification (*adhikṛta*), it is possible to postulate a difference in application; thus, there is no inconsistency.
The meaning of this is as follows: context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other [means of proof] presuppose only the qualification (*adhikāra*), but not...

Furthermore, the qualification belongs only to one who is distinguished; for, since the qualification of merely one who desires [the fruit] has been established there by the means of proof regarding application (*viniyoga-pramāṇa*), it is determined that the qualification of the desirer belongs only to one who is capable of performing the ritual act as enjoined with its subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) once those subsidiaries have been applied. If, first of all—

When the specific qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) is determined according to the application (*viniyoga*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) is not contradicted; rather, by resorting to the application according to that qualification, the manifold nature of the application would be postulated. But this is not the case. For a general scriptural statement (*sāmānyaśruti*), when being restricted to a particular instance, does not abandon its status as the meaning of the word. And thus, demonstrating the subject matter...
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*) have already been demonstrated; therefore, they shall not be shown again. Thus the section is established.

Since application (*viniyoga*) is preceded by qualification (*adhikāra*), the prima facie view is that there is an application according to qualification, determined by capacity (*sāmarthya*) in accordance with that qualification. [The opponent argues: "Since the status of being qualified is established even by a person whose specific qualifications are not yet determined..."

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that since the application (*viniyoga*) is already established, it is logical to rely on specific qualifications of capacity in accordance with that [application]. Furthermore, this inquiry is identical for animals, deities, and those who are lame or otherwise disabled; thus, they belong to the same section (*aikādhikaraṇya*). The demonstration of the lack of capacity to understand the meaning of the scriptures serves as a supplementary argument (*abhyuccaya*) specifically regarding animals.
The specific gender [of the compound] is that of the two possessors of their own [qualities].

In the inquiry as to whether the qualification for this [knowledge] belongs to the man alone or to both woman and man, the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is presented. However, in the subsequent inquiry as to whether they should sacrifice together or separately, the *siddhānta* (conclusive) sūtra indicates—by means of reading them as a single unit—that the conclusion reached in the preceding section cannot be sustained without [the inclusion of] the qualification. And this...

We shall explain this later. He raises an objection to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "But surely, in this case, the meaning of the case-ending refers only to the agent; how then does it exclude a woman from the entitlement?"

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), it was stated in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) that this [gender] is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the state of the agent. Furthermore, gender (*liṅga*) is indeed the meaning of the case-ending itself. Therefore, since gender is not perceived at the time of qualification (*adhikāra*), it is not logical that qualification belongs to the male alone on account of that [gender]; thus, the previous [position].

[The opponent] objects. [The author] replies: This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin): just as oneness excludes other numbers, so too does one gender exclude another gender.

Just as by the number one—which, although it is the meaning of a case-ending, pertains to the state of being an agent and establishes the entitlement of only one person—the other numbers are excluded from that entitlement, so too is the other gender excluded. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely even the number is not [excluded] from the entitlement..."
It does not set aside another number; rather, it sets aside [the notion of] agency.
He replies: "True, it is not set aside with respect to entitlement (*adhikāra*);
nevertheless, because entitlement entails agency, even the gender-mark (*liṅga*) of the entitlement does not [set aside] the gender-mark of the agent."
It brings about [the application of the rule].

The meaning of this is as follows: the status of being an *adhikāra* (heading) is transformed into the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*); that is to say, the one who is the subject of the heading becomes the agent. Therefore, it is determined that whatever number is observed in the case of agency is the very same number that applies to the *adhikāra* as well.

There is no agent other than the one who possesses the qualification (*adhikārin*). Likewise, the gender (*liṅga*) also depends upon the state of being an agent; it excludes the agency of one who is endowed with a different gender. And when there is no agency for one endowed with a different gender, then he also lacks qualification.
For how can one who does not perform the action be qualified? This is because qualification culminates in performance.

It is read as "connected with a person. By those [means] such as purchase and so forth, the demonstration of the absence of ownership (*asvatva*) is an additional argument (*abhyuccaya*) when [the matter] is not otherwise known.

If both the woman and the man were entitled [to the rite], then the inclusion of the term "unrecognized" (*avijñāta*) in the statement "one becomes a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*) when the embryo is killed" would be untenable. For by the inclusion of the term "unrecognized," it is said that when an unrecognized embryo is killed, it might sometimes be a male; in that case, one becomes a killer of an embryo because of having caused the killing of a means for sacrifice. If, however, both the woman and the man were entitled, then what is the point of the term "unrecognized"?

By the mention of "conception," it is indicated that even by the killing of the mere embryo, one indeed commits the murder of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). Likewise, there is an addition regarding the *ātreyī*: "Having killed an *ātreyī*, one becomes a murderer of an embryo.
They call a woman who has conceived a fetus an *ātreyī*. However, when even by the killing of a mere woman the murder of an embryo occurs—

[In that case, what is the purpose of mentioning the Ātreyī? To demonstrate this, the mention of the Ātreyī is appropriate. Just as the demonstration of a woman's lack of ownership through purchase and so forth is an additional argument: a woman who is engaged in buying and selling does not possess property in the same way as cattle and other such things. Therefore, since she is incapable of the relinquishment of her own property—which constitutes the act of purchasing and so forth—she is ineligible.
To this it is replied: "But the genus, according to Bādarāyaṇa. Here too, it is merely the human genus that is intended.
The meaning is that no specific determination regarding the qualification [for action] is derived from the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
It is not the genus (*jāti*) that possesses the qualification, for it is insentient;
rather, the qualification belongs to the men and women who belong to that genus. Now, one might object: "But one who has not attained the status of an agent is not enjoined [to act]."

Thus, it was stated that a gender marker, like a number, excludes another gender marker. This has indeed been stated, but it is not logical; for it is logical that a number residing in the numeral itself excludes another number in the action.
Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is inappropriate because it is not heard [in the text]; thus, it is that which excludes it.
The meaning of this is as follows: in the verbal form *yajeta*...
The number of the agent is perceived through that [verb]; by it, the object is qualified. Therefore, regarding an object whose agent is singular, the capacity for performance belongs to one alone;
thus, that person alone has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) therein, just as in the case of the *Rājasūya*, which has a king as its agent, the entitlement belongs to one of royal caste.
Furthermore, gender (*liṅga*) is not heard in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); therefore, the object is not perceived as qualified by it. Consequently, there is no qualification by gender.

The entitlement of both women and men is established even in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction regarding the subject matter; since this gender inherent in the nominal stem is understood as being preceded by such an entitlement, it cannot negate that entitlement, but rather describes it precisely according to that entitlement. Therefore, the view of Bādarāyaṇa is rightly stated.
In the very statement itself, one number excludes another number. If that is the case, then simultaneous application (sahaprayoga) would not be possible,
as it is understood to be preceded by another number.

Thus, [the argument] ceases. For if there were joint application (*sahaprayoga*) of the woman and the man, the number two would result; consequently, the singular number would be sublated. Furthermore, in the absence of joint application, it is considered that the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of the woman is not tenable because she lacks knowledge, just like a Śūdra. This is what was stated: "It remains, for now, as an unresolved matter."
Because the section concerning women extends up to the point of cohabitation, since the section concerning women extends precisely up to the point of cohabitation,
therefore [the rule applies] to the section concerning women.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) has shown that there is a separate entitlement [to perform the rites] individually;

however, the proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī), considering that there is no contradiction regarding the number even in the matter of the sequence at its limit, has stated that there is a joint entitlement.
The meaning of this is that it concerns the sequence and the objects; and in that regard, even when entering into a woman, there is no contradiction with number.

Having considered this, he spoke with authority: "For if the object were not limited to the sequence (*krama*), but rather were the very substance of the sacrifice (*yāga*) itself, then there would be a contradiction regarding number due to the entry of another agent into the sacrifice. However, when the object of the scriptural injunction consists of multiple constituent acts (*padārtha*), then the entry of another agent is possible even through a different operation; thus, there is no [contradiction] regarding number."
It is contradicted. But how is there no contradiction regarding number?
The answer is: for the dual and plural endings occur when [the factors] are combined.

Or it may be a compound, as in examples such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta cook"; however, it is not used in the sense of accompaniment, as in "Yajñadatta went together with Devadatta. But here, the woman enters into existence by way of concomitance.
“Neither in matters of dharma nor in matters of wealth should she be transgressed against”;
“Whatever must be done, that should be done together with her.”

Because of this statement: for this very reason that the compound occurs when [words] are joined together, those who know compounds consider it to apply to both *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *samāhāra* (aggregation),
and not merely to the sense of *ca* (and).

They consider *dvandva* to apply to both *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *samāhāra* (aggregation), where there is a state of association; however, it does not apply merely to the sense of *ca* (and) in cases of simple conjunction (*samuccaya*) or subsequent mention (*anvācaya*). If...

Even where there is no co-occurrence (*sāhitya*), if a compound were still to occur, then a *dvandva* would have to be prescribed even for *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvācaya* (sequential mention). What, then, is the intention of those who prescribe a compound in the state of co-occurrence? To this he says: "This is the intention."
There is no relation with another category-entity between two things that have not attained mutual existence;

for where there is coexistence, there indeed is mutual existence. Between two things that have not attained concomitance—that is, those that are unattained—there is no relation with another category-entity, but rather [a relation] with one another.

The relation belongs only between two related entities and a third distinct entity. In a compound (*samāsa*), there is an entry into a third distinct entity preceded by the mutual interpenetration of the meanings of the members being compounded. Therefore, whatever kind of relation exists among the meanings in their combined state, that very same [relation] is expressed by the compound as well. Thus, it is logical that a compound occurs when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). In that regard, the compound—

And where there is a connection with another word-entity only between two [words] that are already mutually connected, because the connection occurs through a common medium, the occurrence of dual or plural endings is not appropriate; therefore, in such cases, the compound takes the dual or plural endings. Where, however, there is a connection with another word-entity between two [words] that stand in mutual expectancy (*itaretarāpekṣā*), then [the endings] belong specifically to that [other entity]. But where there is dependence on a connection with another word-entity...
Nor does that meaning [apply] there, nor do the dual and plural numbers occur, nor a compound. For where, while one relation exists,
another distinct relation is established, there the relation is not by way of a single [term], as in "Devadatta cooks, Yajñadatta..."
1. It is recorded: "Mā dattaśca" (and Mā Datta). For in that case, it is not as Devadatta is connected with the cooking, so too is Yajñadatta. Furthermore...

It is possible to establish a connection; for when a word is already occupied by one meaning, it cannot simultaneously possess a connection with another meaning. Therefore, in that case, the connection is understood through another medium. Consequently, because there would be a connection with non-eternal [entities], duality and plurality would be untenable, and thus the use of the dual and plural numbers is not justified. Furthermore, a compound (*samāsa*) is not possible in the absence of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). For in a compound, there is a mutual...

The connection with another meaning is understood for things that are already associated; thus, because there is an understanding of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) among those things connected with other meanings, there is an absence of independent capacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*). And here, the wife is connected by the word "together" (*saha*) with the performance already secured by the sacrificer.
She does not enter as an agent into the performance secured by the sacrificer through a different door [from him]. Therefore...

With reference to that [single action], the use of the dual or plural numbers is not appropriate, because the relationship [of the agents] is not equal. Where there is a connection with the action for two things together, there the dual or plural numbers are appropriate. This has been shown by the author of the Mahābhāṣya:
"When expressing the connection with the action for two things together, the dual number alone [is used] in sentences intended for illustration," and so on.
It is accomplished;
otherwise, even imitation would not be possible.
The meaning of this is: [of] the two joined together.

When expressing a connection with an action in a *dvandva* compound, as in sentences such as "one should cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees" used for illustrative purposes—that is, in their analytical (*vigraha*) sentences—only the dual number should be employed: namely, "the *dhava* and *khadira* trees. When the dual number is thus employed, the compound word that expresses the connection with the joint action is correctly imitated. For, upon seeing the dual number...
Thus it is understood that duality exists. And the production of duality occurs when two things, mutually connected, enter into a relation with an action.

But if this is so, how can the dual number be used for a single thing? It is because of the connection with the number two during the state of conjunction. Furthermore, duality is a common quality (sādhāraṇaguṇa), and the two words serve to characterize the state of conjunction. Therefore...

Thus, there is no room for the objection as to how [the term] functions in a different sense. Furthermore, if it were employed with a dual ending, then even an imitation would not occur, precisely because the state of being conjoined is not perceived. Once the connection with the action is understood through their coexistence, the wife—who follows the sacrificer—enters the ritual as an agent; thus, she enters the rite through a channel distinct from that of the sacrificer.
One experiences the state of being an agent. This is what was stated: "there is a distinction of action for each instrument.

One action is distinct; another is the sacrifice (*yajña*) consisting of the renunciation of wealth by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and there is the wealth belonging solely to the couple situated in the middle.

The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is unable to relinquish [the offering]. For if it were not relinquished, since ownership belongs to the wife, the sacrificer would also lack ownership, and thus the sacrifice could not be accomplished. Therefore, the wife, by granting her consent, is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sacrifice;
whereas the sacrificer, directly making the relinquishment while aiming for the deity, is the agent in the sacrifice. This has been stated: "For every causal factor (*kāraka*)."
Regarding the phrase "difference in action": for it is not possible for the sacrificer to possess agency in a sacrifice without the consent of his wife.

Therefore, she too is indeed an agent in the sacrifice because she enters into it through a different operation; thus, the occurrence of duality and plurality is established, and the position is faultless. Consequently, the Bhāṣya states: “In a hundred and twelve [animals], there are fifty-six.
This [author] now raises an objection to that:

Regarding the statement "or one hundred and fifty-six in the twelfth [year]," what does this mean? This commentary, it seems, presents another argument for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): namely, that in the twelfth year, fifty-six [coins] are given by the sacrificer for the purpose of hiring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

"And with the wife, [there are] fifty-six"—this, however, contradicts the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). For in this way, since the wife would have an activity equal to that of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), there would be a dual number, which would contradict the singular number [of the word *patnī*]. An adherent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) says: "We too say: what is this?"
The objector asks: "Is this simply non-existent? The respondent says: "No, we do not say it is non-existent; [otherwise] the commentary would be meaningless."

[Otherwise] there would be a logical fallacy. He states the meaning: "If the division were to take place in the twelfth [year], then this objection regarding the contradiction with the singular number might indeed apply; however, in this case, the wife's function is entirely different, and thus he demonstrates that it serves as a concomitant."

[The term] *sahitārthatām*. Its meaning is as follows: the proponent of the established conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) speaks thus—if, in the case of one hundred and twelve [cows], fifty-six were given by one person and fifty-six were also given by another, such that there were a division of the gift, then [the use of] the singular number—

The word "there would be a contradiction" (*virodhaḥ syāt*) is to be supplied [as the ellipsis]. The wife’s function, however, is entirely different, characterized by her consent (*anumati*). Therefore, it is not by means of being "accompanied" (*sahita*) in the sense of the wife's physical presence, but rather by means of the sense of being "accompanied" through that [consent]. And this has been shown: the wife’s function is characterized by consent. For if either [party] were unwilling, the renunciation (*tyāga*) itself would not take place.
He concludes:

Therefore, since there is no contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti regarding simultaneity, it is impossible to conclude that the statement "it should be performed together" is not in accordance with reality.
For it would be so only in the event of a contradiction with Śruti, and such a contradiction does not exist. In this way, the word *patnī* (wife) is justified.
If there were no joint performance with the wife, then [the term] *patnyadhikāra*...

Otherwise, the [grammatical] rule would be violated; consequently, since a woman does not possess ownership over the sacrifice, the word *patnī* (wife) in the rule "the suffix *ṅīṣ* with the augment *nuṭ* is applied after the word *pati* when connected with a sacrifice" (*apatyurno yajñasaṃyoge*) would be inconsistent with respect to a woman who is the owner of the sacrifice. Furthermore, specific ritual duties such as supervision and so forth have already been established [for her].
They exist; for otherwise, the statement "the clarified butter is to be looked upon by the wife" would be untenable. The indicative mark has been stated.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
“In that regard, by the force of the Vedic text, whoever [performs] by whatever...”

When it might be concluded that one should sacrifice having united with some woman whatsoever, this is stated: "Whatever dharma must be performed by you with anyone at all, that [should be performed] with her.
By this, it is understood that there is no contradiction between the Smṛti and the Śruti.
What is the meaning of this? The answer is: indeed, it shows a restriction regarding marriage when [marriage] with just any woman would otherwise have been required.

Thus it is said. The objector says: "If this is so, then this point is not established; because marriage is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, it is not for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
For otherwise..."
If the refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) were not [the purpose], then it would be merely a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) enjoined by the sacrifice; but this is not the case. Why?
To this he replies: For they describe the entitlement as belonging to one who has performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), asserting that the consecration is not for the sake of the ritual itself;
because the entitlement belongs to one who has performed the consecration.
Furthermore, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not for one who has already been authorized nor for one who has already performed the marriage ceremony;
therefore, because it has already been performed by the person entitled [to the rite], it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Listen to this point: for this very reason...

And this is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent; for this very reason, Gautama recites it in the sequence of refinements. [The opponent] refutes this: "This is true; you know the meaning of the scriptures, so how can you speak otherwise?"
The objector asks: "What, then, is the meaning of the Bhāṣya?
[It means] 'by this [instrument],' and even so, there is no contradiction with the Vedic revelation."
This is the meaning.

Although marriage is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, there is no contradiction with the singular number used in the Vedic scripture, since that [scripture] is intended for the purpose of refinement.
The meaning is that he does not conflict with his wife;
thus, he considers that even in this way, their joint status (*sahatva*) remains established.

That the wife who was taken for the sake of ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*) is restricted to being a co-performer (*sahakartṛ*) by means of another statement is not untenable; thus, [the objection] is trivial. This is the reply to what has been established.

Now, having raised the doubt as to why lordship (*svāmitva*) is not secondary (*gauṇa*), the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it cannot be secondary because it does not contradict the qualification (*adhikāra*). For if it were to contradict the scriptural statement regarding qualification, then, due to that contradiction, it would be secondary.
There would be a recollection of ownership, and there is no contradiction; how there is no contradiction has been shown. [Regarding] the two-fold establishment: how, then, does doubt arise here?
The answer: Just as in the Bhāṣya it was asked, "Should two men perform the consecration, or one man? the objector said, "That is not tenable."
There is a doubt. For in the Bhāṣya, duality residing in the secondary word (*upapada*) is presented—namely, "the two wearing" (*vasānau*).
And this cannot suffice as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Why? Because in such passages as "A Brāhmaṇa, being in the spring, should establish the sacred fires," singularity is heard. Therefore, how can it be asserted that the establishment of the fires is possible for two men? But surely—

The dual number of males is heard in the word "vasānau" (the two wearing). Since this is not applicable to a male accompanied by a wife, it follows that two males are intended for the *ādhāna* (fire-laying); to this, he replies: "And gender cannot set aside number, because it is heard in the original injunction (*utpatti*). Regarding the original injunction—

The number heard in the sentence cannot be sublated by the indicative power (*liṅga*). Now, as for the claim that because the sentence has no other purpose, the indicative power sublates the number—to this he says: "And because of the injunction of something else.
For the injunction of *kṣauma* (linen) is also understood; therefore, [the indicative power is sublated] by this other [injunction].
It can also be stated that there is "otherness" (paratā), because in the present context of the *ādhāna* rite, which is qualified by a single agent, it is not possible to enjoin two men.
It is possible. Therefore, either another *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) must be mentioned;

or, since the original *ādhāna* is understood from the context, it is not possible to enjoin another *ādhāna*, and thus the phrase "wearing two [garments]" (*vasānau*) is restated for the purpose of enjoining the linen cloth (*kṣauma*), just as the duality [of the agents] is restated.

The duality already established—namely, that which pertains to the subject of a man and a woman—is restated here; linen cloth is what is being prescribed. Thus, there is no room for the aforementioned doubt. Furthermore, he states another objection: "But even on this view, one would have to say 'they two should install [the fires]' (ādadhīyātām)."

The dual number is not appropriate, for it was previously stated that the woman's entry into the ritual act occurs by way of concomitance; it was stated for that very reason that the dual number is not appropriate due to such concomitance. Therefore, the expression "the two should establish [the fires]" refers to the woman.
The restatement of the dual number is not tenable; likewise,
the dual form "vasānau" (the two wearing) is also not tenable,
because the act of wearing is completed in its entirety by each individual.
Because it is impossible for either one of two distinct actions of perfuming to possess agency.
The respondent says: In that case, by pointing out a fault in both positions, you yourself have stated a doubt.
When one position is refuted, one adopts the other position. The objector says: "It is true that doubt has been stated, but it is not possible to undertake the acceptance of a position."
Because both positions are flawed, the respondent says:
"True, it cannot be done; for you yourself have stated this regarding the production of duality and the wearing of the garment while they are not yet reached."
And since there can be no restatement of what has not been previously established, there would be an absence of connection unless there were an injunction.
It cannot be said that [the rule] is impossible; therefore, this very injunction must be accepted.
Now, even if it is an injunction, how can it be an injunction for two men, given that there is no injunction for one accompanied by a woman? To this, he says:

And when [the compound] is being prescribed, two males alone must be prescribed. Why? The answer is: because the rule for the *dvandva* [compound] is traditionally taught as denoting its members simultaneously.

The author of the Vārttika states, "The *dvandva* [compound] occurs when there is simultaneous reference to multiple substrata" (*yugapadadhikaraṇe dvandvaḥ*). What, then, is this "simultaneous reference to multiple substrata"? It is said: that which is being compounded...
If the meanings of various words are expressed simultaneously by a single word, that is *yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*.

[Page 068] The state of being denoted by words (*vacanatā*). By the term "substratum" (*adhikaraṇa*), the domain of the word’s operation is designated— just as, for example, in the compound *dhavakhadirau*,
the two words *dhatra* and *khadira* contained within it [function together], whereas [the meaning] is not conveyed by either one of those words individually.

This refers to the denotation of both the *dhava* and *khadira* trees. Now, this is not tenable: a word denotes an object in accordance with the apprehension of its relationship [to that object], and the word *dhava* has not had its relationship apprehended with respect to two objects. Furthermore, if it were to denote two objects, then the employment of another word would be redundant. Nor can there be a comprehension of two objects through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is an absence of both the logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) and the relationship [necessary for such indication].

And it has been stated that the employment of another word [to express the same] would be purposeless; thus, this simultaneous substratum-ness (*yugapadadhikaraṇatā*) is both difficult and hard to establish. To this, it is replied: the *dvandva* compound occurs in the state of being combined (*sahitabhāva*), and it does not exceed the words being compounded.

This is the summary: by means of that [compound], each individual nominal stem (*prātipadika*) indicates its own meaning as existing in a state of conjunction. The expressive power of a word resides in its own meaning when that meaning exists in its pure form; however, it is the state qualified by a particular condition that is indicated. Since this state of conjunction does not occur without another meaning, the meaning of the second member is also implied by it. Therefore, it is established.

It is the capacity to convey multiple meanings simultaneously. For this very reason, they say that even the two words in a *dvandva* compound possess a figurative (lakṣaṇika) meaning. Since the comprehension of that specific meaning which is indicated (*lakṣya*) depends upon the other word, there is no redundancy of the other word. And because the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) serves as an exception to that [rule].
*Ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is an exception to *dvandva* (copulative compound), as in "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*).
If this is so, what follows?
The answer is: from that, this occurs—this expression of two [individuals] by means of a single [word] through the principle of *tantra*.
And in that case, by the words "the two wearing," only two males are understood,
because there is no expressive word for any other referent.

In the phrase "vasānau," a single man accompanied by a second [person] is denoted by the word ending in the vowel *au*. Likewise, another man is also denoted through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application). In that case, when there is a requirement for a second [participant], only a man—who has been presented through the *tantra*-denotation—is understood, and not a woman, because there is no expressive word for her. Now, one might object: "But [the verb] 'ādadhīyātām'..."

The dual number is untenable because, in the case of a verbal root where two males are enjoined as a single agent established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), their subsequent entry [into the rite] is impossible.
He offers a rebuttal: "Let there be another fire-consecration (*ādhāna*)."
If there is an obstruction by a quality prescribed for the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa*), what harm is done to us?

This has been stated as a concessive argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*). However, [the conclusion follows] from the understanding of the original *ādhāna* (fire-laying) through a sentence that is not subordinate to anything else.

Only the duality of the male will be prescribed, because the remainder of the application (*viniyoga*) is more powerful; that is, in the production of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), the number is a subordinate element of the derivation. But does not the venerable Pāṇini record in his grammar that "the male [is used] with the female"?
The meaning of this is: that in which a word ending in *au* is correct even when the male is accompanied by a female, as in the case of "women. The reply is—
In the case of *ekaśeṣa*, one recalls that the masculine form is grammatically correct, but not the feminine denotation of a word ending in the vowel *au*;
this has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya.

The meaning of this is as follows: Pāṇini has recorded that where both a female and a male are intended to be expressed by a word denoting a specific characteristic, the masculine form is retained and not the feminine form. However, there is no expression of the female by means of a word ending in the vowel *au*; therefore, due to the absence of a word denoting a female, it is the male alone [who is expressed].

The second [member] is also included; this has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya as well. Now, if only a male is taken as the second member, then since it would never be the case that a male is accompanied by a female in every instance, how could there be a restrictive rule for *ekaśeṣa*?
Is this logically tenable? He offers a rebuttal: "By whom was it said that there is a restriction regarding non-attainment? He then raises an objection:
If there were a restrictive rule regarding attainment, then let there be the state of being accompanied by a female [as a second].
The reply is: let it be so if there is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for such an attainment; however, it has been shown that no such means exists.

The meaning of this is as follows: where a second woman is perceived through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there she alone is the "second"; but where such a woman does not exist, there the male denoted by the word itself is the "second. And here, because he is the object of the injunction (*vidheya*), it is understood that the "second" is indeed the male. He concludes: therefore...
Because it denotes two [or more] persons simultaneously as sharing a common substratum,
this [term] denotes both and is therefore not the object of the restrictive rule.
The meaning is that this is not the scope of the restrictive rule regarding the use of the masculine form when [the compound] consists of three genders. Therefore, it is correct to say "two males.
