If this sentence refers to two males, how then is the word *kṣauma* [used]?
The meaning is: "How is the object to be enjoined connected? The answer is: "The connection has been demonstrated; this word *kṣauma* is derived etymologically from the root *kṣu*."

Thus, the word *kṣauma* ends in the suffix *ma*; the two garments of the two struggling [lovers] are "possessing linen" (*kṣaumavatī*). Alternatively, the commentator has shown the connection as being figurative (*gauṇa*), because those two soiled garments resemble linen.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): This being the case, it is replied: it cannot be said that this [word] denotes two males.
Why? The answer is: because the word *kṣauma* would be redundant;

that is, it would be redundant because it does not produce any specific modification in the performance [of the rite]. [Objection: But surely either a garment qualified by *kṣauma* or the act of laying the fires (*ādhāna*) will be enjoined, and thus there would be no pointlessness.
To this he replies: "Because both the cloth and the placing [of the fire] have already been obtained. Now, it was argued that even oneness, though associated with duality, has not been obtained;
therefore, because two qualities are heard, there must be an injunction for a different placing.

The reply is as follows: It is true that even unity, when joined with duality of persons, has not been attained; however, duality joined with persons has indeed been attained. What follows from this? Listen to this: on the basis of that [attained duality], the prescription of the linen cloth (*kṣauma*) becomes possible, whereas the state of being accompanied by a second [person] remains merely to be sought.

When it is possible to enjoin the *kṣauma* (linen) by way of restating the act of dressing (*ādhāna*) as qualified by a man who has a companion, then the state of having a companion need only be sought [as a general requirement]. If one further investigates what constitutes the state of having a companion for that man who has a companion, the woman is found to be the companion; thus, his state of having a companion is established through her alone. Now, [an objection]: *nanu*... [The text continues with the objection.]
It has been stated that this very state of having a companion is not possible without an injunction; the wife is one who has entered into coexistence [with the husband].
It has been stated that there is no second [entity] for one who possesses incomparable yoga. He refutes this:

[the objection] does not hold if the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is understood as residing solely within the substratum and the clothing; and likewise, they do not admit even the mutual conjunction that serves as the basis for the expression of a *dvandva* compound, because mutual conjunction depends merely upon the action, as in the case of the Gargas.
This is because we observe the usage "bhojyantām" (let them be fed), and we also observe the usage "devadattayajñadattaviṣṇumitrāḥ" (Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra).

The meaning of this is as follows: a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is not possible; for if [the rite] were to take place together with the wife, then regarding the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*)...
Mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is indeed already established to the extent that they admit mutual conjunction even as a basis for denotation.

For those things which enter into a single act of denotation, there necessarily exists mutual conjunction with respect to that [act], just as in the case of the expression "the Gargas should be fed. Since the employment of the dual number is justified, there is no need for a different substratum by way of overriding the suffixes under discussion.
It must be so; nor can it be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*),
because the verbal root *bhuj* is completed in each individual instance, based on its denotation.

It is *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction). Therefore, even here, by resorting to the mutual conjunction based on the expression [of the word], the state of being accompanied by a woman will be understood.
Since the application is thus established, in the context of the primary injunction "the two, wearing linen garments, should establish the fires," the word *kṣauma* retains its primary meaning.

It is not proper to accept either a secondary connection (*gauṇānvaya*) through the abandonment [of the primary sense] or an etymological meaning (*yaugika*) by subverting the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore,
since another means of valid cognition exists, this is simply the application of the rule that [the world] must have a second.
Regarding that, it is as has been stated.
Anticipating the objection, "But how is this inquiry into ritual application (prayoga) relevant here?", he says: "It is established that for a woman and a man there is joint entitlement.
This is now being deliberated.

Is everything pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) to be performed together with the wife, just like the sacrifice itself, or does it become accomplished simply by being performed by the sacrificer alone?
The meaning of this is as follows: which...

Previously, it was stated that there is no modification [of the ritual]; it was further stated that its accomplishment occurs through joint performance (*sahaprayoga*). Now, the specific details of that very point are being considered: must every ritual act belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) be performed by the woman together with him—just as the act consisting of the renunciation of the substance (*dravyatyāga*) in the sacrifice is performed together with her—or is it not possible for everything to be performed together with the woman, as in the case of acts such as honoring (*sammāna*) and so forth?

The agency belongs to the sacrificer alone. For it is not the case that a man’s status as an agent in an act of honoring is untenable without the activity of a woman. [Objection: But surely, even in that case, the woman’s activity will occur through the medium of her consent (*anumati*). [Reply: You dull-witted one! It is not so; for in those cases where a man’s status as an agent is otherwise untenable without her consent—such as in the case of a sacrifice—it is through that consent that the woman acts.
Furthermore, where agency exists even apart from her consent (*anumati*), how can the wife’s agency be established through the medium of consent?

It is not understood what kind of role consent plays when a man proceeds with his own activity. Therefore, since joint participation cannot be achieved in rites where the sacrificer alone is the agent, this is merely a challenge to the claim of joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*).

It is concentrated upon. But even so, in the section concerning linen (*kṣaumādhikaraṇa*), this very objection is raised: "Even when there is association [of two things], the dual number would follow—as in the case of 'ādadhīyātām' (the two should establish the fires).
Now, if the dual number is not tolerated in the sense of coexistence, then it must be a prescription for two males.

It follows that, since it has been established that there is no dual number when co-occurrence extends as far as the section on linen cloth (*kṣaumādhikaraṇa*), the joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) alone is maintained without contradicting the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). This [point] is now raised by means of another objection and then resolved.
[Page 072] Is every ritual act belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) to be performed together with the wife, or does it become fully accomplished by the sacrificer alone?
Thus, coexistence does not apply everywhere, but only to certain cases; however, the others have been performed by the sacrificer alone.

In that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering the mention of "together" (*saha*) to refer to the sacrifice along with its constituent parts (*sāṅgkratv*), [concludes that] there is a requirement for joint performance regarding the duties of the sacrificer.

The Smṛti states that whatever is to be performed must be done "with her" (the wife). And that [rite] must be performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), not merely in part, because a partial performance yields no fruit. Therefore, it is thought that everything must indeed be performed together; yet this is impossible. Consequently, since there is no simultaneous performance (*sahaprayoga*), the wife's entitlement (*adhikāra*), which exists by virtue of that [simultaneity], is difficult to establish.

The proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī), however, maintains that insofar as a person’s status as an auxiliary is established by the verbal injunction itself— as is the case with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)— therein the woman has no capacity as an agent.
Even where there might be an application based on traditional designation (*samākhyā*), it is accomplished by one [of the two] alone.
When ritual performance is possible for one who possesses knowledge, it is not possible to assume that he lacks knowledge;
for such performance can be accounted for in another way as well.
This is the intended meaning: concomitance (*sahabhāva*) is not established by the expression "together" (*saha*) with respect to each individual object;

rather, it refers to the performance (*prayoga*), because that alone is what must be accomplished. Since that which is to be accomplished must be performed together, it is the state of being co-performers (*sahakartṛtā*) regarding the task that is expressed. And the agent is connected with the performance, not with the object to be acted upon; furthermore, the performance occurs in a single [instance].

When the performance of the constituent acts (*padārtha*) is undertaken together, it is accomplished by the very completion of those acts, because the status of being a performer (*kartṛtva*) is established through the performance itself. In that regard, since both the sacrifice and the hiring of priests—which are to be accomplished by means of material substances—are performed as a single collective action, the status of being a joint performer is logically established; there is no need for simultaneous performance with respect to each individual act. Rather, once an act has been performed by even one person, the act is considered complete and need not be performed again.

Even in that case, where [the status of the sacrificer] is understood through explicit statement alone— as in such passages as "The Audumbarī post is to be of the same height as the sacrificer" and so forth— just as with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there is no agency for the woman at all. Even where [agency] might be obtained through the designation "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*), [it does not apply].

Even though the specific gender [of the performer] cannot be determined from the designation [of the rite], since that [performance] is to be accomplished by a learned person, it is possible for a learned man; however, a woman can never possess the status of an agent [in such rites]. Now, one might object: "If she is not the agent in that case, how is her entitlement (*adhikāra*) established? To this, he replies: "Because the performance is possible even otherwise."
When the accomplishment of practice according to what has been understood is established, there is:
1. inference that brings about understanding of the mere meaning of the nominal stem;
2. [inference] that brings about understanding.

For the qualification [of the wife] is established by the very mention of "together" (*saha*). By expressing the joint performance through that very term, it is shown that there is only one [act] for both the wife and the sacrificer. In that case, since it is established that what was performed by the sacrificer was done on her behalf, the qualification of the wife is indeed proven.

Therefore, regarding human goals, there is both learning (*vidvattā*) and agency (*kartṛtva*). Or rather, where there is a specific injunction for each step (*pratipadavidhāna*), because there is no consecration (*saṃskāra*) for one person when it has been performed by another, the woman possesses agency in those consecrations pertaining to the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, where agency is directly enjoined, there too there is both learning and agency. But [an objection may be raised]: if this were so, would it not follow that there must be the application of knowledge (*vidyāprayukti*) in that case? [This would entail] an entitlement (*adhikāra*).

[Objection: Thus, [the qualification] is not applicable to a woman. [Reply: It is said: By the mention of "together" (*saha*), the entitlement of the woman is indeed understood through direct apprehension (*śṛṅgagrāhikatayā*). Therefore, the assumption of her application toward that [rite] is not a fault. [Now follows the section on] the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*).
But is it not the case that here, while considering the distinction, it was stated in the second chapter that the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) belongs to only three [classes]?
By the author of the Sūtras, while considering the distinctions regarding the *ādhāna*, it was stated that the *ādhāna* belongs only to the three castes (*varṇas*). It is not so.

Furthermore, eligibility for this [rite] is not possible for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, because there exists a member of the three higher castes who has performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and is capable of performing the ritual in its entirety.

Therefore, what is the purpose of this section? To this it is replied: even while conceding that there is no entitlement [to perform sacrifices], the scriptural injunctions regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) serve as the basis for the existence of those outside the three *varṇas* who have established the fires (*āhitāgni*).
Even having admitted [the opponent's position], this section concerning the Śūdra is commenced in order to state that he lacks qualification due to ignorance.

For it shows as follows: although the scriptural injunctions regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) are for the purpose of providing an occasion (*nimitta*), nevertheless there is no qualification [for a Śūdra].
Regarding the phrase "of the Śūdra":
the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that even in those cases which are occasional (naimittika), it is indeed possible to state the exclusion of the Śūdra.
1. The agency of action [is established] by this very passage. But what, then, is the purpose of this concessive argument (*anvāruhyavāda*)?

The intended meaning is as follows: the purpose [of the argument] is that the Śūdra lacks eligibility. But since that is already established by his status as one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), what is the point of stating another reason? It is replied:

This is the purpose: the admission [of the Śūdra] is intended to demonstrate his lack of entitlement even to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). The purpose of demonstrating his lack of entitlement to the initiation ceremony is to demonstrate the Śūdra’s lack of entitlement to those ritual acts that do not require fire and which are accompanied by mantras. Even if...
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of entitlement to initiation (*upanayana*); therefore, *upanayana* itself should be cited as the example.
[It is asked: Is that [initiation] heard [to apply] even for a Śūdra?
It cannot be determined whether it exists or not—
namely, whether or not there is an entitlement for a Śūdra in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). He refutes this by stating that it is not possible to cite such an instance.
The initiation ceremony (upanayana) is not possible. Why? Because for a Brāhmaṇa, it is heard in the scripture: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age."

Thus, the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa is heard [in the scriptures]. Regarding whether that also applies to a Śūdra or not, it is impossible to deliberate [on this], because it is heard as being directly connected specifically with the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the teaching after having initiated [the pupil] is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), and it cannot be cited as being independent.

It cannot be established on its own because it lacks a sufficient motive. To this, it is replied: if one considers whether there is an entitlement for a Śūdra as well in initiation (*upanayana*) or Vedic study (*adhyayana*), or whether the entitlement belongs only to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), then in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it must be explained that the entitlement belongs only to the three higher castes. And that [entitlement] is not possible independently.

Because both [of these] exist, and because both of them have obtained the performance of what is prompted by another—namely, being impelled by the injunction for the act of teaching—both lack a [personal] qualification (*adhikāra*). Why, then, is one who merely desires knowledge of the meaning not qualified?
To this he says: "And it has been stated that that [qualification] does not belong to one who merely desires knowledge of the meaning."

And [this is so] because of the contradiction with the study [of the Vedas] in the section concerning *arthavādas*. Why? Because initiation (*upanayana*) and Vedic study (*adhyayana*) are inherently devoid of specific entitlements (*niradhikāra*), it was rightly stated that an investigation can only be conducted here by means of another governing context (*adhikaraṇa*).
Precisely because this section is intended to demonstrate that a Śūdra has no entitlement to the initiation ceremony (upanayana), for that very reason the Commentator has made this the primary focus.

Having demonstrated this present topic (*adhikaraṇa*), it was concluded that in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices, there is no entitlement precisely because of the state of not having maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
The meaning of this is: in this topic, it is established that the Śūdra has no entitlement to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

It is established that in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are to be accomplished by means of the sacred fires (agni), there is indeed no entitlement for one who has not maintained the fires (anāhitāgni).

By demonstrating that this particular section (adhikaraṇa) does not exist for that purpose, the author of the Bhāṣya stated at the end: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, there is no entitlement even for one who has not maintained the fires."

In this section, the following is investigated: Is initiation (*upanayana*) a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study (*adhyayana*), or is it a subsidiary element of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*)?

If it is a subsidiary element of study, then study—which is prompted by the scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*)—would apply even to a Śūdra, since Śūdras have eligibility (*adhikāra*) with respect to those scriptural injunctions regarding desire.

On the other hand, if initiation is a subsidiary element of the injunction for becoming a teacher, then study—which is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher—belongs only to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Regarding the [scriptural] desire...

Regarding the statement "there is eligibility in the Śrutis," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers as follows: In proximity to the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo ’dhyetavyaḥ*), the text "one should initiate a Brahmin boy at eight years of age" (*aṣṭavarṣaṃ brāhmaṇam upanayīta*) is heard. Since initiation (*upanayana*) functions by bringing the one being initiated into proximity, it appears to be for that purpose. Furthermore, that initiation has a requirement for its effect (*kāryākāṅkṣā*): namely, "what is to be done by means of this initiation when it is accompanied [by the study]?"

Likewise, in the injunction "one's own portion of the Veda is to be studied," there is a requirement for an agent; therefore, only one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) is the agent of study. And study is for the purpose of acquiring knowledge (*vidyā*). Once knowledge is acquired, it serves a purpose within the injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*), which are to be accomplished by that knowledge.
Consequently, the injunctions regarding desires, while impelling one toward knowledge, also impel one toward study and initiation, which are its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, since those who have not acquired sacred knowledge (*vidyā*) are entitled to participate in the Vedic injunctions concerning desires that employ such knowledge—given that there is no distinction in their state of desiring—there would likewise be entitlement for a *śūdra*. Moreover, that entitlement extends as far as the initiation (*upanayana*), and since the entitlement exists even at the initiation, the *śūdra* would possess ownership [of the rite]. Now, one might object: because of the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the form "he should initiate" (*upanayīta*), it refers to the act of making oneself a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*).

Since the initiation (*upanayana*) is prescribed as occurring in the present tense, the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), which employs the initiation as its own subsidiary (*aṅga*), will also employ the study (*adhyayana*). For the initiation serves to assist the injunction for becoming a teacher by means of bringing about proximity with the one being initiated; and one becomes a teacher through teaching. Moreover, there can be no teaching without study.

It is so; and since study is understood as having the initiated person (*upanīta*) as its agent, the act of initiation—which brings the boy who is performing the study near—becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that study. Consequently, there is an application of the injunction for producing a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*) toward the study. Therefore, only those for whom initiation exists have the right to study; thus, those who possess knowledge (*vidyāvat*) have the entitlement, while the Śūdra lacks it.

It is said: This would indeed be so if the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) were understood to indicate that the initiation (*upanayana*) is for the sake of the teacher’s injunction. However, it is the accomplishment of the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*). That [status] is indeed possible even through being for the sake of another. But how, then, is it understood that the initiation is for the sake of the boy (*māṇavaka*) who is being initiated? Because its fruit is proximate to him. For even one who is a teacher...

He states that the act of initiation (upanayana) serves the purpose of an injunction regarding the agent: "Of that [initiation] too, it is understood that the accomplishment of making someone a teacher is for the sake of another; he [the teacher], moreover, desires that very thing which has the result of bringing the student into proximity. That result belongs solely to him [the teacher]. And for whomsoever...

Whatever action [is performed], it is appropriate for that specific purpose alone due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), and not for the sake of the teacher. Likewise, the initiation (*upanayana*) is merely an ancillary (*aṅga*) to that [action]. And by means of that [initiation], the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the student is not the primary purpose, because there is no injunction (*vidhi*) for study [independent of the initiation]. Nor is study purposeless, as it is impelled by scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*). Therefore, since initiation is an ancillary to study, it is impelled by the scriptural injunctions regarding desire.

"The Śūdra has the right to study even those rituals accompanied by mantras. To this, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) replies: From the hearing of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction "One should initiate an eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa," it is understood that initiation (*upanayana*), which effects the status of being a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*), has as its result the causal factor characterized by proximity to the one being initiated. Therefore, regarding initiation...

The status of being an agent is indeed appropriate for the act of making someone an Ācārya; since initiation (*upanayana*) and the act of making someone an Ācārya are understood to stand in a relationship of primary and subsidiary (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) by virtue of having a single agent, initiation is for the very purpose of the injunction regarding the act of making someone an Ācārya. And that which is a subsidiary to something else is prompted by that [primary]; thus, initiation is prompted by the injunction regarding the act of making someone an Ācārya, and through that medium, so too is study (*adhyayana*). Consequently, there is no other injunction—

Because the acquisition of knowledge has already been accomplished [by other means], the scriptural injunctions for optional rites (*kāmya-śruti*) do not enjoin them as auxiliary parts of knowledge; this is because the rite of initiation (*upanayana*) is an auxiliary part of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), and that rite is itself prompted by that injunction. Thus, it is established that based on the injunctions for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), the Śūdra lacks the qualification for [Vedic study] involving mantras due to his lack of knowledge.
Of the three.
But has it not been stated that the injunction regarding the ritual act does not employ the substance? Therefore, this deliberation is simply not applicable to the qualification (adhikāra).
Regarding the classification of ritual acts as they actually exist for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

The meaning of this is as follows: it was stated in the fourth chapter that the scriptural injunctions concerning desires (*kāmaśruti*) do not employ [specific] materials. Therefore, is one who lacks the materials (*adravya*) entitled to perform the rite?

This very thought—that "no" [is the case]—is not tenable, because the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is impossible. For if even one who lacks property were entitled [to perform rituals], then, such entitlement existing, the injunctions would also impel the acquisition of property. Yet it is settled that they do not so impel. Therefore, it has been demonstrated in effect under the fourth [book] that there is no entitlement for one who lacks property; [this applies only to] property acquired through means for the purpose of livelihood.

It follows by implication that he alone is entitled [to the rite], because: just as when a second distinction of action is established, and the injunctions for the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) are present as the means of attainment, the entitlement of one who has not established the fires is set aside, and only then does the consideration of the Śūdra’s entitlement become relevant—so too is this [the case here].
The thought does not hold; this is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). How is it that it does not hold in that way? To this it is said:
there is no other purpose for it than the application (*upanaya*).

The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason: just as in the previous section there was a purpose [for the discussion], here there is no such purpose by which a deliberation could take place according to the principle of *kṛtvācintā* (deliberation for the sake of argument).
Therefore, this section cannot possibly belong to the deliberation on eligibility (*adhikāra*). He provides the resolution: it is said, precisely because...
Injunctions regarding ritual acts do not employ a substance; for this very reason, this inquiry concerning eligibility is appropriate.

If it were the case that injunctions regarding ritual acts did employ a substance, then, since eligibility would be possible even for one who lacks a substance, there would be no room for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

Therefore, this consideration regarding eligibility is not appropriate; however, since the injunctions for ritual acts do not enjoin the acquisition of wealth, it is precisely because of this that the consideration becomes appropriate through the possibility of a prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument. How so? Are the scriptural injunctions for ritual acts capable of excluding one who lacks wealth—just as they exclude one who has not established the sacred fires—or are they not?

Just as the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual acts exclude one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), do they likewise exclude one who lacks the requisite materials (*adravya*) or not? What, then, is the reason for such exclusion? To this he replies:
"Because [the injunctions] do not imply the acquisition of materials."

If they imply the requirement of material substances (*dravyopādāna*), then they refer to substances already acquired; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of implying the acquisition of new substances. In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādin*) is as follows:

ritual injunctions (*karmaśruti*) do not authorize one who lacks material substances—just as they do not authorize one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)—because they do not imply the acquisition of such substances.
They are able [to do so]. Therefore, one who lacks the requisite wealth has no entitlement.
To this it is replied: it is not possible to define this [system] as being like one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) or one who lacks the requisite wealth (*adravya*).
The meaning of this is as follows: innate capacity (*svābhāvikī śakti*) is the qualification for entitlement (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*); and even for one who lacks wealth...

The capacity to perform rites accomplished through material substances exists; even for one who lacks material substances, material substances indeed come into being. If, however, one were to determine that "this person shall certainly have no material substance," then, because it would be absolutely impossible, the one lacking material substances would have no entitlement. As, for example, [on page 078]:

A Śūdra who is devoid of sacred fires has no entitlement [to this rite] due to extreme incapacity; for in that case, the caste of Śūdra and so forth exists as a restrictive factor, whereas here, since there are no sacred fires associated with caste, the taking up [of the materials] is unrestricted and may be performed at any time.
Sometimes that very [power] does not take up [an object];
therefore, human beings possess an innate capacity for substantiality. Consequently—
Therefore, the total exclusion of substance is not possible;
by that [fact], even that which is non-substantial possesses an inherent capacity, and for that which is thus qualified,
the undertaking of ritual action follows just as the undertaking of life itself does.
The meaning is that this is logical.
Now, one might object: the elimination of the remainder of the material cause was already stated in the fourth chapter; how then can it be said that [this process] has arisen in such a manner?
He refutes this:
"It is not being extracted; for we state this only as a causal condition (*nimitta*)."

The meaning is that action (*karman*) is not the primary factor (*śeṣin*), but rather a causal condition (*nimitta*) for the acquisition of substances— just as life is a condition for a person’s taking up goods— by virtue of being a purposeful end; it does not mean, however, that this [action] alone is the primary factor.

Precisely because the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatā*) is not accepted for the rule regarding the acquisition of wealth, for that very reason it was stated in that context as well: "Even though acquired through ritual action, it is only grain that has been acquired.
Here too it was stated: "It is untenable [to claim] that one will live without wealth."
For it is stated thus in the fourth [book]: "One should sacrifice with rice. Only rice is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), and not the act of receiving [it] and so forth.
Therefore, whether rice is acquired for the sake of the ritual or even for the sake of ordinary eating, when the sacrifice is performed with that rice, [the requirement is fulfilled].
Thus, there is no deficiency on that account. Likewise, it has been stated in this very section: "It is untenable [to claim] that one will live without wealth.
Therefore, it is said that one shall sacrifice with wealth acquired for the sake of living. But is this not improper—that one will live...?

The claim that "it is untenable [to perform a sacrifice] without wealth" has been stated by this [opponent]. He argues that since one who lives must have wealth because living would otherwise be impossible, he will therefore perform the sacrifice with that wealth. But that is untenable—because living is possible even without wealth at the time of performing specific ritual acts; likewise, living is possible through substances such as *kodrava* grain, which are not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
Nevertheless, since not everyone who is alive necessarily possesses wealth, this legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) would be without a subject matter; therefore, he asks:
"What has been stated by this [text]?
The answer is: This has been stated by him—that this appropriation (*upādāna*) is not restricted.
"Enough with the dismissal [of the claim]"—this is what is meant:

the absence of wealth in one who is alive is untenable, because of the possibility of exceptions; therefore, since the possession of wealth is not a fixed requirement, even one without property possesses the capacity [for ritual action], and thus there is no exclusion from eligibility (*adhikāra*). Regarding eligibility...
He concludes for this purpose: "Therefore, just as in the case of living, effort must be exerted in the undertaking of action.
Adra-

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that if one who lacks wealth were eligible [for Vedic rites], it would follow that they must engage in the acquisition of wealth for the sake of those rituals; however, this has already been refuted in the fourth book [of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra]. The final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: there is no contradiction with what was stated in the fourth book regarding eligibility for one who lacks wealth. For in that context, what was prohibited was merely the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatā), and not the status of being a purpose (prayojanatā) either.
Just as in the case of eating and so forth, there is an impulsion (prayukti); thus, even for one who lacks wealth, [the performance of the rite] is natural.

Thus it is established that the qualification [for the ritual] is indeed proper for one who possesses the capacity (*śakti*). Furthermore, the necessity of possessing the requisite substances mentioned here is stated solely for the purpose of realizing one's innate capacity.
And [the same applies to] one who is deficient in limbs.

He states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Of what nature?"—the meaning of this is as follows: first of all, it cannot be said that its nature consists of non-substantiality (*adravyadharma*), because it is not devoid of auspicious factors (*akalyāṇāṅga*). For even in the case of a non-substance, the capacity for the occurrence of substantiality is indistinguishable from the time when it possesses substantiality.

However, for one who lacks a wholesome limb, incapacity is indeed absent due to the state of being diseased; since capacity can be produced again through the application of medicine and other means, capacity is present in that state, and thus there is no equality with a substanceless entity. Therefore, it is not known what the nature of one lacking a limb is. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): [it possesses] the property of a substanceless entity.
This is the meaning:
for that very same person sometimes becomes deficient in limbs, and sometimes possesses auspicious limbs.

The meaning of this is as follows: one who was not engaged in an activity due to illness is observed to perform that activity again once medical treatment has been administered. Thus, it is understood that the power [of the capacity] was not destroyed by the illness at all; for when treatment is applied, the performance of the activity is observed. Therefore, while the power remains truly existent, the illness acts as an obstruction to it, which is then removed by the medical treatment.

It is conceived that "it is removed. But what is the certainty that destruction and origination do not exist, [but rather] that there are merely the removal of obstructions? It is said: Destruction is the absolute cessation of perception.

And that does not exist for a potentiality (*śakti*), because it is perceived again through its effect. Origination, too, is the capacity for the perception again of that which was absolutely unperceived.
Because it is perceived only through its effects before a disease that was previously and absolutely unperceived; and therefore, even when its power is concealed...

Since capacity exists, qualification is indeed appropriate; thus, the disease of consciousness is a property of the substance itself. Therefore, being qualified, one must apply effort toward medical treatment and the like, just as one acquires material substances.
However, for one whose [disease] is incurable—

That which constitutes a lack of auspicious qualities (*akalyāṇāṅgatā*) cannot be said to be "ineligible" (*anadhikṛta*) in the same way as a *śūdra*. Furthermore, the destruction of capacity (*śakti*) is the absolute cessation of perception. Just as in that case *śūdra*-hood is a cause for exclusion because it is eternally cognizable, so too is the state of being incurable; thus they are equal. Just as a *śūdra*’s incapacity is absolutely irremediable due to his birth, so it is here.
"Even the state of having lost the capacity for the subsidiaries [is a ground for exclusion]. When one who has already commenced the sacrifice is deprived of the subsidiaries, how is it then?
For whom, while performing the sacrifice, does there exist a deficiency of limbs (akalyāṅgatā)? Since at that time there is an absence of medical treatment, how can there be eligibility?
Whatever means exists even in the case of a physical substance will be the same here as well; by which [means] the performance has been commenced—
The meaning is that just as one who is devoid of wealth [is still] entitled [to perform a sacrifice] even while in the midst of it, so too is one who lacks auspicious bodily parts.
And that means is taught in the case of a substitute for one who lacks three ancestral lineages (*atryārṣeya*).
Now, it must be considered whether this is a distinct sentence or a single one.
In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya first considers the following: "He chooses the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya)."
Thus, by this general rule, the selections of one, two, or three [priests] are established; these are then specified by such statements as "he chooses one," and so forth.
Likewise, there is the rule: "He does not choose four."

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that by the two [phrases] "he does not choose five" and so forth, the choosing of four and of more than five is prohibited; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:
The injunction regarding the selection of the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya) is expressed as "he chooses the ārṣeya";
the prescription of the number therein is "he chooses three"; and "he chooses one" is a partial restatement (avayutyānuvāda).
As for the statement, "He does not choose four," and "He does not choose more than five," this is merely a reiterative injunction (*nityānuvāda*); this point need not be further considered here.
Why? Because when it is said, "He chooses the *ārṣeya* [lineage]," the choosing of two or three is already implied. Furthermore—
Because the number one is already established as a remainder from the act of giving, it is logical that duality and plurality must necessarily be prescribed.
Since the attainment of oneness does not occur once those two have been prescribed, that too must be prescribed. Likewise, oneness, duality, and plurality—

Since they are subsidiary to the application (*viniyoga*) by virtue of being prescribed according to rule, there is no possibility at all for four or more [names]; how then can there be a prohibition?

Therefore, this must be considered here: when the selection of ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) is enjoined, do these distinct [passages] enjoin all three—singularity and so forth—or [is it otherwise]? Since they are subsidiary to the application, there is no possibility at all for four or more; how then...?
Regarding the prohibition: therefore, is this a single scripture that prescribes the number three, or is it a single scripture [that prescribes one]?

In that case, the statements "he chooses one" and "he chooses two" are merely restatements by way of partial extraction (*avayutya-anuvāda*) for the purpose of praising that very [single choice]. And thus, it is not...

The statement "one should choose four" is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended as a praise through brevity. Demonstrating this very point, the author of the *Bhāṣya* raises an objection: "But is there not also a specific injunction stating 'one should choose one'?"

That which was first proposed by the Commentator was done with the intention that even a slight doubt must be dispelled. Therefore, it should be considered whether this [work] is one or distinct; and that is useful for determining the unity or diversity of the treatises (*śāstra*), not for determining the qualification (*adhikāra*).

The meaning is that, for that reason, there is no consistency with the [defining] characteristics. He provides the resolution: "It is indeed true; however, even that difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) brings about a distinction only within the context of the qualification (*adhikāra*); therefore, it is the qualification alone that is being investigated.
The meaning of this is as follows:

Although there may be both difference and non-difference between the *śāstra*s, nevertheless, this deliberation is appropriate only with respect to the characteristic of eligibility (*adhikāra*). For when there is difference, one who has a single *ṛṣi* lineage is eligible, whereas when there is non-difference, only one who has three *ṛṣi* lineages is eligible. This being the case, it is said: "One should choose the *ṛṣi* lineage of the sacrificer as 'like Manu,' 'like Bharata,' or 'like so-and-so. Therefore, in this manner...

At the time of the ritual performance, the ancestral lineages (*ārṣeya*) of the sacrificer are to be chosen—such as "like Manu, like Bharata, like Śāṇḍilya, like Asita, like Devala; this Devadattaśarman sacrifices. In that regard, as many ancestral lineages as one has, that many are to be chosen for him. In this matter, there may be a rule even for those having one or two lineages; thus, even for those with a single lineage or two lineages, [the procedure applies].

The inclusion of the subsidiary element of choosing the *ārṣeya* (the ancestral lineage) occurs because it is possible [to perform it]. For the choice of the *ārṣeya* is prescribed as part of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) state of the ritual procedure, not as a mandatory conjunction, because such a conjunction is impossible. For a sacrificer who has only one *ṛṣi* in his lineage, the choice of that single *ārṣeya* is prescribed; but for those with two or three *ṛṣis*, the choice of two or three *ārṣeyas* is prescribed respectively, and not otherwise.

All [the sages] are indeed prescribed as eligible for all [the sacrifices], because a sacrificer of such a [specific] kind is impossible. However, when only the number three is prescribed, then only a sacrificer who possesses three ancestral lineages (tryārṣeya) would be entitled to the rite that has the possession of three ancestral lineages as its constituent part; thus, because it establishes a specific qualification, the number is determined accordingly.

The meaning of this is as follows: because the passages beginning with "he chooses one" (*ekaṃ vṛṇīte*) end in the *laṭ* (present) tense, no direct injunction (*vidhi*) is heard. Nor is it possible for [these passages] to function as restatements (*anuvāda*) of the number three and so forth without an injunction. Therefore, an injunction must be inferred on the grounds that "the statements [must be injunctions] because they convey what is not already known" (*vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*).

And since there is no distinction [between them], one must assume that the injunction applies to as many [individuals] as there are in the number. This being the position reached, it is replied: not to as many as the number [indicates].
An injunction must be postulated. Why? Because of the understanding of their mutual relationship.
If there were no mutual connection between the words denoting numbers, then many separate injunctions would have to be assumed. However, a mutual connection is indeed understood.
In that case, whichever number, when its injunction is accepted, does not result in a loss of syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), that is what is enjoined.
According to this principle,

since there is the possibility of a restatement (*anuvāda*) when three [options] are being prescribed, and the possibility of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), an objection is raised here: "But surely it is appropriate that one does not choose four."

Since the statement "he does not choose more than five" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) when three [options] are being prescribed, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*); for there is no separate injunction (*vidhāna*) [of the number five]. Thus, the choosing—
The statement "one" or "two" is not a restatement (anuvāda) of an already established entity, because such a state has not been previously established.
It has been stated that these are distinct sentences. For this very reason, we consider the selection of five [priests] to be entirely logical.
For if there were a single sentence, then [the injunction] "one does not select four" would not exist.
Because of hearing the statement, “He does not choose five,” one should not assume that there is a choice of five; for when [that assumption] were to be made, then—

For that reason as well, the single hearing of the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) would be contradicted by its repetition. However, when the sentences are distinct, then—once it is established that there is no contradiction in the single hearing of the supplementary portion—a repetition assumed for the sake of connection with the injunction regarding the fivefold nature is not untenable; thus it has been stated that the selection of all five is indeed logical. But how, then, is the selection of all five [justified]?

How is the attainment [of the number] indicated? In this way, the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) becomes more appropriate: "He does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five. If there were no choosing of even five, then this restatement of the meaning of the negative—the absence of choosing—would be appropriate.

If, however, there were no selection (*varaṇa*) for the five [priests], then the restatement of the absence of selection by way of skipping the five would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, it is indeed logical that there should be a selection for all five as well.
To this, it is replied: We have already stated that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) for all the words. But surely, one...
It has been stated that [the objection] is untenable because a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "two" is impossible.
The reply is: indeed, among the three, there is no restatement whatsoever.
[Page 083] This is not a formal debate (*vāda*), according to the principle that one number does not persist within another number. The word "nāma" is used in the sense of acceptance.

This is what is meant: we accept that, according to the principle that "a number does not reside in another number," since unity and duality are absent in the state of three, a restatement (anuvāda) is not possible in its primary sense. If it is asked, "With which [term] then is this sentence containing the negative particle (*nañ*) connected? Since there is no distinction, it must be connected with all the sentences concerning numbers," the established position is as follows:

In that case, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). If the negative sentence is connected with all the sentences expressing number, then syntactic unity would be established; because [the negative particle] does not terminate [its application] individually within each negative sentence.
There is a means of valid cognition [for this]. How is it that there is none?
The answer is: there is no means of valid cognition for [the whole] being fully present in each individual [part] based on hearing [the word] only once. For if...
If there were completion [of the whole] even upon hearing it only once, then there would be [completion] for unity and so forth as well.
"He does not choose four," and "He does not exceed five by choosing"—
thus [it is said] for each one individually.

There might be a repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*). Its meaning is as follows: even when [the numbers] such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth are performed, there would be a repetition of the negative particle.
Consequently, it would be like this: "He does not choose one, he does not choose three. Let it be so; what harm is there to us?
To this he replies: "And that [practice] is purposeless.

The meaning is that the practice would be devoid of any objective. Furthermore, because they are directed toward the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), the four beginning with "one" (*eka*) and the five past ones [are likewise purposeless].
Since all [the alternatives] are both prescribed and prohibited, an option (*vikalpa*) results.
Now, for one who thinks that there is no fault because an option results by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*):
He anticipates the objection: "Let it be so. [The response is: Even by resorting to an alternative position, a solution is not achieved;
therefore, the assumption of a repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*) is improper. If one assumes such a repetition, a logical dilemma (*vikalpa*) arises.
This is refuted by resorting to the principle of non-repetition (*anāvṛtti*). Therefore, it cannot be said that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses authoritative validity (*prāmāṇikatva*).
Whatever fault there is in abandoning what is heard in scripture, the same fault applies to the assumption of repetition for a sentence not heard in scripture.
Consequently, those learned in logic declare that it is not proper to assume repetition. Therefore, it is better—
[Page 084] Only the explanatory restatement (anuvāda) based on the scripture is to be relied upon, because of its consistency;
that is to say, because of the single hearing [of the text]. Otherwise, [it would be inconsistent].

For [the injunction] would be sublated by hearing it only once. Now, even if that is so, let there be a single injunction because the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) conforms to a single inference; but why must it pertain to all three? To this he says: "And it is not possible for three," because if an injunction were assumed for one or two, a restatement (anuvāda) of the three would not be possible. However, if there is an injunction for the three...

Since it is not possible for a single statement to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of one or two [of the three], there must be an injunction (*vidhāna*) of all three. He concludes the section on this point: "Therefore, there is the choosing (*varaṇa*) of only the three, and only one who has three ancestral seers (*tryārṣeya*) has the qualification (*adhikāra*)."
It is established.

To this extent, such is the meaning of the scripture. If, however, there are further statements, then let it be that even those who do not belong to the three *ṛṣi* lineages have the right [to perform the sacrifice]; thus, it is faultless.
Because of the scriptural statement.

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is to be accomplished by one who possesses knowledge, and since the state of possessing knowledge is itself to be accomplished by the initiation ceremony (upanayana), concluded that the injunction for the establishment of the fires is logically applicable only to those for whom the initiation has been performed; thus,
he described the establishment of the fires as being natural (naisargika) through this specific cause.
The meaning of this is as follows:

initiation (*upanayana*) belongs only to those of the three [upper] castes; and for those alone who undergo initiation, there is sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), because study is prompted by the injunction to become a teacher. For those alone who possess sacred knowledge, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is appropriate, because the establishment of the fires is to be accomplished by one who possesses that knowledge. And therefore...

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that this subsequent *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) is prescribed for the members of the three *varṇas* alone, on the basis of their being chariot-makers.

However, as for those chariot-makers who are Brāhmaṇas and so forth, the prescription for the *ādhāna* according to the sequence of seasons such as spring will apply to them by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*); thus, everything is logically consistent. As for the commentary (*bhāṣya*) here regarding the three *varṇas*...
[It may be argued that] since living by means of crafts is prohibited, it appears as if that [prohibition] is inconsistent; however, even because of the transgression of a prohibition,
the prescription for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is not at all untenable.
Even for those who subsist on their craft by transgressing prohibitions,
the performance of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) is indeed appropriate, because the prohibition is for the sake of the person and the consecration is for the sake of the fires.

Because there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the prohibition of maintaining the sacred fires and subsisting by crafts—which differ in their respective goals—the prohibition is not a subsidiary part of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*); rather, it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that the fire-installation becomes defective (*vaiguṇya*) by transgressing a rule intended for the person's benefit.
If there were a deficiency [of qualification], then the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) by those who have transgressed prohibitions would not occur;

yet, they maintain that no such deficiency exists. This is indeed true; however, this was stated on the basis of propriety (*aucitya*), meaning that among those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who follow proper conduct, it is simply impossible for them to subsist through manual crafts (*śilpa*).
This was stated with a specific intention; for it was said by resorting to propriety (*aucitya*), and not because of an absolute impossibility of subsisting through crafts.

For this very reason, the fact that the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) for Brāhmaṇas and others occurs only at fixed times is stated as the reason for its non-connection with other forms of *ādhāna*.
The fact that the time for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is spring and so forth is stated as the reason for its non-connection with another *ādhāna*.

The meaning is that since the *ādhāna* is heard of as having spring and other seasons as its time without distinction for all members of the three *varṇas*, a connection with another *ādhāna* is not logical. Furthermore, this is merely an argument based on a hypothetical admission (*abhyupagamya-yukti*), because another *ādhāna* is possible by means of the occasion of being a chariot-maker (*rathakara*).
He states the supreme argument: "The mention of a different caste is, in the ultimate sense, stated as the reason for the three-caste [status];
by convention alone (*rūḍhyā*) the word *rathakāra* denotes a different caste, while by the power of etymology (*yogabalena*) it denotes the three castes. And convention..."
"Because [the Smṛti] is more powerful than the [Vedic] connection. For thus says the Smṛti: "From a Māhiṣya and a Karaṇī, a Rathakāra is born.
Here, one born from a Vaiśya woman and a Kṣatriya is called a Māhiṣya. Regarding this, they say:
"A Māhiṣya and an Ugra are born from a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman respectively, by means of a Nṛpa (Kṣatriya)."
And the *karaṇa* is one born from a *vaiśya* father and a *śūdra* mother;
as it has been said: "The *karaṇa* [is born] from a *vaiśya* on a *śūdra* woman. Therefore, regarding one born from a *māhiṣya* father and a *karaṇī* mother...

Since the word *rathakāra* is denotative by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), this fire-installation belongs to him alone. As for the statement that there is no installation for one who lacks knowledge—that holds true only in the absence of an explicit scriptural injunction; but when such an injunction exists, what inconsistency could possibly arise?
When...

The meaning is that when the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) for a chariot-maker is prescribed by way of specific designation (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), then there is no inconsistency whatsoever. The underlying intention is that knowledge (*vidyā*) will also arise through the power of that [fire-establishment]. When knowledge exists, what need is there for initiation (*upanayana*) for the sake of attaining knowledge?

Nor can it be that this [initiation] does not apply to those Saudhanvanas? The answer is: if there is a scriptural statement, let it be; otherwise, in the absence of a specific injunction, this will occur for them just as it does for women, solely by virtue of the injunction regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna).

Since the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is established by that much alone, it lacks the capacity to imply the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). To establish the connection with the definition—namely, that "the topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is characterized by qualification" (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*)—he asks: "For whom [is this]? [in order to show that there must be something which bestows a specific qualification].
Furthermore, who is entitled to this installation of the chariot-maker? We reply: it is the chariot-maker himself, just as the king is entitled to the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Here, an objection is raised: "But surely this is a specification of the agent (kartṛ), not a specification of the entitlement (adhikāra)."

Regarding the statement, "The chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the sacred fires during the rainy season," the word *rathakāra* is a designation of the agent; it is a designation of the agent as a specific class (*jāti*) to be selected for the action. Because the chariot-maker is a class to be selected, this is not a designation of a general entitlement (*adhikāra*). He states this in a single passage: "Just as the Brāhmaṇas and others [are entitled] to the times beginning with spring..."
They are designated as agents (*kartṛ*) and not as those entitled (*adhikṛta*); it is the same here as well.

The proponent of the entitlement of the *rathakāra* says: "If Brāhmaṇas and others are designated as agents and not as those entitled, then, in that case, regarding the fire-installations (*ādhāna*) performed by them..."
Whose is the entitlement?
This is the intention: just as there is an entitlement for Brāhmaṇas and others, so too shall there be one for the Rathakāra. To refute this entitlement, he says: "We say it belongs to no one."
"Because no qualified person [other than the three higher castes] is mentioned.

The proponent of the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) qualification says: "In that case, why was it stated that the qualification belongs to the three castes? [This refers to the section on] *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*.

It has been stated that the three castes possess the qualification for performing [ritual acts]. Therefore, it is considered that even the caste of the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, though being something to be adopted [as a means], is merely a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). To this, the reply is: it has been stated that the three-caste person desiring heaven possesses the qualification for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices.

It is established that in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices, one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is the qualified person (*adhikārī*). It has been stated, however, that this "desirer of heaven" is a Brāhmaṇa or others, and not anyone else; yet, caste alone is not the defining qualification. The proponent of qualification (*adhikāravādin*) says: "If it were thus without any qualification, then the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) would be merely a subsidiary rite (*aṅga*)."
It would be [a part] of the *kratūs*. The other says: No, it is not a subsidiary (*aṅga*), because its purpose is for the sake of the fires (*agnyarthatvāt*).

The meaning of this is as follows: even though the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) lacks a specific qualification [of the agent], it does not have the ritual action (*karman*) as its purpose, because it is understood to have the fires themselves as its purpose.

Now, one might object: "Could it not be that, by way of the fires which serve the ritual actions—just like the threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts—it does have the ritual action as its purpose? To this, he says: "For the fires themselves are for the sake of the ritual actions."

The meaning of this is as follows: it has been demonstrated in the third [book] that the fires, being already established, are employed in ritual action, and not that there is a production of fires that have already been so employed. Therefore, because they produce fires that are not connected to ritual action, the establishment (*ādhāna*) does not have ritual action as its purpose. If the establishment is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), then how is it that one belonging to the three higher castes who desires heaven [performs] the Jyotiṣṭoma?
It can be said that one is entitled to the *ṣoḍaśī-stoma* and other rites because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to them;

for if the establishment of the fires were an auxiliary, then, since it is impossible for one who does not belong to the three higher castes (*atraivarṇika*), the entitlement would be restricted to those of the three castes (*traivarṇika*).

He states the reply: It has been said that non-members of the three higher castes (*atraivarṇika*) lack qualification because they do not maintain the sacred fires; however, it does not mean that only members of the three higher castes are qualified.

The meaning of this is as follows: even though the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not an auxiliary part [of the rite], nevertheless, for one who is not of the three higher castes, there is no qualification.

[The word] *kāraḥ* [indicates this]. Its meaning is as follows: if one accepts that caste (*jāti*) is not a qualification for eligibility (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), then eligibility for those desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) and others in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices is indeed established. [This applies even when] qualified by non-enjoinable attributes (*anupādeyaviśeṣaṇa*).
Because there exist qualified persons for those [other rites], whereas in the case of the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires),
no other injunction for it is heard, and because it is accepted that "birth" (*jāti*) does not serve as a qualification for eligibility, who then possesses the right to perform it?

Nor should it be argued that [the injunction] will be without an eligible person (*niradhikāra*), for that would entail the performance of a ritual action for which no one is qualified. He states this in a single passage: "When [it might be thought that] it applies to everyone, because of the lack of completion regarding caste and constituent parts (*jāty-aṅga*), it belongs only to the three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*). Just as [in the case of] *svārājya*...
It is heard in scripture that the entitlement for the Rājasūya belongs specifically to a Kṣatriya:
"One desiring sovereign rule should sacrifice with the Rājasūya."
Thus, since the caste of "king" is not recognized in an agent other than a king, the entitlement belongs to the king alone;

likewise here as well, the entitlement to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) belongs to Brāhmaṇas and others for the sake of attaining the caste of Brāhmaṇa. If the entitlement of Brāhmaṇas and others to the *ādhāna* is for the sake of attaining the caste of Brāhmaṇa, then in that case—

In this case as well, even regarding the consecration of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), it is established that because of the non-attainment of [the required] caste, the entitlement belongs to the chariot-maker alone.
Therefore, we say that it was rightly stated, "of the chariot-maker."
Thus; and by virtue of being one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), his eligibility for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is to be understood. When it concerns the Rathakāra...

At that time, one becomes entitled to the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires) and thus becomes possessed of the fires; and this possession of the fires implies his entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices as well. Since knowledge (*vidyā*) is employed for the sake of fulfilling that implied entitlement, the Rathakāra, having acquired knowledge, will perform the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites. But how is it that the entitlement to the *ādhāna* does not reach its conclusion without the entitlement to the ritual acts?

"Because [the self] in its mere essential nature is not a human goal. Now, one might ask: "Since Brahmins and others are absent, how can a Rathakāra (chariot-maker) have the entitlement to perform the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices?
To this he replies: "As for those specific injunctions such as 'the Rāyovājīya' and so forth, they do not apply to him; however, they are not capable of negating his entitlement."

For those Brāhmaṇas and others for whom there is a specific statement, they [should perform] the *brahmasāman* and so forth specifically; however, for those for whom there is no such statement, there is no fixed rule. But the eligibility itself has not yet been rejected. The proponent of the absence of eligibility—[the opponent]—eligibility...

He asks the proponent [of the view]: "If, first of all, an entitlement (*adhikāra*) must be sought for the *ādhāna* (the rite of laying the fires), then why is it that an entitlement for the injunction of the *ādhāna* itself is not to be postulated, just as in the case of the *viśvajit* sacrifice?
The meaning of this is: just as in the case of the *viśvajit*—

Just as in the case of the Agni-vidyā (the knowledge of the fires), which is to be accomplished through that [knowledge], the eligibility of the three castes alone is not accepted because it is untenable for caste (*jāti*) to function as a qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), so too in the case of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), caste cannot serve as a qualification; therefore,
it is proper to postulate an eligibility there, just as in the acquisition of wealth, where only those who desire the fires are eligible for the *ādhāna* that produces the fires.
"Why does the section not have sovereignty as its defining characteristic? For there is no status of being subject to an injunction here, due to the absence of an injunction.
He provides the answer: "Let it be so; there is no fault whatsoever.
Nevertheless, there is a connection with the defining characteristic of the section. [This applies] to the chariot-maker—"
Because only those who seek [the fruit] are entitled [to the rite]. Thus far, having accepted the entitlement (*adhikāra*), the opinion of others has been stated;

now he states his own view: "But here, they maintain that this performance is indeed without entitlement, because it possesses its own purpose—just like the threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts."

The meaning of this is as follows: there is no purpose here in postulating an *adhikāra* (qualification for entitlement), because even in the absence of an *adhikāra*, the performance of the rite is established; for it possesses a purpose through the fires, which serve as its own purpose. And since the fires exist for the sake of ritual action (*karman*), their performance is prompted by the injunction regarding that action itself. Thus, what is the use of postulating an *adhikāra*? It is indeed without an *adhikāra*.

[The word *rathakāra*] denotes the act of laying the fires (*ādhāna*). Nor is there a lack of connection with the [etymological] definition; for it has been established that the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) possesses the qualification for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices by virtue of being the agent of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), just like the *Agnīdh*.

Otherwise, his status as the agent in the fire-laying would not be possible, because the fires themselves, in their mere essential form, do not constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The rest has already been stated.
The architect.

In this case as well, with respect to both learning (*vidvattā*) and the performance of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone to be logical.
Its meaning is as follows: when it is understood as a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*) consisting of "he who is both a chief (*sthapati*) and a Niṣāda."
In that case, it would follow that the entitlement belongs to the *niṣāda* alone. If it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), then it would belong to someone other than the *niṣāda*.

And in that situation, it would not be possible for the *niṣāda* alone to have the entitlement, due to his lack of sacred knowledge (*vidyā*) and the absence of the sacred fires (*agni*). Therefore, in view of both the requirement of knowledge and the requirement of the fires, the genitive compound is indeed appropriate. For there may be someone who is a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who is [called] a *niṣāda*...
He is the master of the gifts;
the word *sthapati* denotes a master, and therefore,
in accordance with his knowledge and sacred fires, it refers to him alone.
The eligibility belongs to one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). To this it is replied: this is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Why? The answer is:

for in a genitive compound, the word *niṣāda* would refer to the carpenter (*sthapati*) only by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); whereas in a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*), both words retain their own primary meanings.
This is the meaning: whatever word is heard is itself the cause for the comprehension of the object.

And in the compound *niṣādasthapati*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not heard; rather, only the word *niṣāda* is present, and by direct audition (*śruti*), it denotes a specific caste (*jāti*), but not one related to a specific caste [as a possessor]. [In the case of] a genitive compound—

In the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the connection would be with the task belonging to the Niṣāda, and not with the Niṣāda himself; in that instance, the word "Niṣāda" would have to indicate the chieftain (*sthapati*) who belongs to the Niṣādas through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). In the *karmadhāraya*, however, the connection is with the Niṣāda alone. Furthermore, the word "Niṣāda" is able to denote the Niṣāda directly through primary denotation (*śruti*). And when there is a conflict between primary denotation and secondary signification, primary denotation is the more authoritative rule; thus, the *karmadhāraya* is the correct interpretation.

Thus, this is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Now he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely it is improper to say that [the meaning] occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since it is understood by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself"—this is the sense. How is it improper?
He demonstrates this: by the author of the Bhāṣya, while justifying the use of the particle *vā*, it was accepted that the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*vṛtti*) have the same meaning,
as stated by the venerable Pāṇini in the section on compounds (*samāsa-adhikāra*) regarding the term *vā*.

Thus it is recorded. The purpose is so that it may not be restricted exclusively to compounds (*samāsa*), but may also occur as a sentence (*vākya*). In that regard, if there were a difference in meaning between the compound and the sentence—

In that case, since the sentence would be precluded by the mere difference in meaning (*arthabheda*), what would be the purpose of the word *vā*? Thinking thus, and desiring to justify the mention of *vā*, the author of the Bhāṣya stated that the sentence and the compound possess the same meaning (*ekārthatva*). In that regard, if in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) there were no word expressing the meaning of the genitive, then [the claim of] the sentence and the compound having the same meaning—
Otherwise, there would be no single meaning at all; yet a single meaning does exist. Therefore, it is improper to claim that this word functions through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).
The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin), however, says: "By whom was multiplicity of meaning asserted?
Even when metaphorical indication is admitted, there is still multiplicity of meaning."
The sense is that it does not exist. Not understanding this point, he asks: "But was it not stated that the word 'niṣāda' functions through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)?
He replies: "This is said having accepted a specific purpose."
— “Or by whom was ‘polysemousness’ stated?”— this which we say is said with reference to actual usage. This is what is meant:

In a sentence, a word with its case-ending is used, whereas in a compound (samāsa), it is used without a case-ending for the sake of a single meaning; thus, it is said that the sentence and the compound possess the same meaning. This very point is stated here: "in this genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), [regarding] the *sthapati*..."

The word *niṣāda* is employed in reference to what is connected with a *niṣāda*; its application is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The underlying intention is this: although the sentence and the compound express the very same meaning, they appear distinct; for in the sentence, the meaning is conveyed through the primary expressive function (*vācakavṛtti*), whereas in the compound, it is conveyed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*). An objection is raised: "What does it indicate?"

The word *niṣāda* [is used]. The answer is: it indicates the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*). But if it indicates the sense of the genitive, then the grammatical justification (*sādhutvānvākhyāna*) for compounds with different coreferential bases (*vyadhikaraṇasamāsa*) would be untenable; for the instruction of the venerable Pāṇini proceeded for the purpose of restricting the expressive power of words.

The grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) of the venerable Pāṇini was undertaken in order to regulate only those words that are expressive (*vācaka*), as opposed to corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) and synonyms (*anuvācaka*). Furthermore, according to the theory of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this [corrupt form] is not expressive.

Consequently, because it would not be expressive, the instruction [of the rule] would be untenable; yet the Teacher does instruct it. Therefore, we understand that even a compound is indeed expressive. Furthermore, under the view that [the compound] functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the mention of the word *vā* ("or") would be purposeless. [This is because] in the case of non-expressive words and corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)—[let there be no such thing as]... 1. ...non-expressive words and corrupt forms—mā.

Since the usage of both the sentence and the compound is established precisely through their distinction, and since the statement of the option (*vā*) thus possesses purposeful meaning, one must necessarily resort to its denotative function. Therefore, Kātyāyana also stated that the mention of the option is redundant for this very reason.

[The opponent says: "Or rather... Therefore, a distinction must be stated between the compound and corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and the like, by which the compound is taught despite its lack of denotative power (*avācakatva*), whereas words such as *gāvī* are not. And there is no other distinction.
"Except for the capacity to denote [directly]"— the proponent replies: "But surely this very distinction exists, for even by means of indication (lakṣaṇā),
linguistic usage is observed in the world, as in 'a hamlet on the Gaṅgā' or 'the Garga bank by means of the well'."

The meaning of this is as follows: Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the instruction (*anuśāsana*) of those words that are employed in the world. Furthermore, there is usage in the world even by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, it is not contradictory that there should be an instruction even for that which functions through figurative indication. However, since forms such as *gāvī* and so forth are not employed in the world, the distinction lies solely in their being used or not used. Consequently, what is an instruction in one case is not an instruction in the other.
And so on. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: this usage does not contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*).

Its meaning is as follows: the grammatical rule is undertaken for the purpose of providing a formal derivation (*anvākhyāna*) only for those things that are explicitly stated in the scriptures; therefore, this usage such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) is not [within its scope].

[The opponent] objects: "If this application [of the rule] were to result in the instruction of even that which functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then it would contradict the principle that 'the instruction applies only to those [words] mentioned explicitly. In this application, there arises the contingency of instructing what functions by way of secondary indication. Why?
Because the Blessed One’s instruction is limited to individual words (*padāvadhika*)."
Nevertheless, he asks "What [follows]? and says: "And here, in the state of being a cause (*nimittāvasthā*), this is indeed expressive (*vācaka*).
