The meaning of this is: in that state which is the state of being a cause, there is the meaning of the cause.

The term "denotative word" (*vācakapada*) refers to expressions such as *gaṅgāyām* ("in the Ganges"). What is meant is this: in cases such as *gaṅgāyāṃ snāti* ("he bathes in the Ganges"), where people say exactly this, the reason is that this [word] is indeed denotative; thus, since it is the denotative itself that is being taught, there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). But one might object: the grammatical rule, depending upon secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), brings about this very usage. [Regarding] secondary indication—

Regarding the statement, "From the word *gaṅgā* itself, by the rule governing case-endings (*vibhaktyanuśāsana*)," he says here: one does not remember that case-endings belong only to what is denotative (*vācaka*), because of the expression "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*).
Rather, it is taught that the case-ending belongs to the denotative itself.

As for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it may function either by its primary denotative power (*vācakavṛtti*) or by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); there is no need for concern regarding this. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: "What has been stated—that [the rule] applies only to those connected with the primary denotative power—is incorrect, because of the rule: 'The application of grammatical rules concerning words depends on their semantic competency' (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*)."

[Page 092] One also remembers that case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses semantic capacity (*samartha*). Furthermore, having stated that semantic capacity consists in the connection with its own meaning (*svārthasaṃbandha*), [the author proceeds].

And there is no relation between the referent of the word "Ganges" and the meaning of the locative case— the subject of the cowherd settlement— without recourse to secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore,
[the connection] cannot exist without depending on the function of secondary indication.
There is no established rule [that instruction must apply only to words].

Therefore, there is instruction even for that which functions through *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Nor is this a restriction of the Teacher that instruction has only the word as its limit; it is also seen to have the sentence as its limit, as in: "O King—"
This is because of the observation in the *Kaṭhaka* Yajurveda that "the mantra is the progenitor" (*janitā mantra*).

Furthermore, if grammar were an instruction limited solely to the expressive [words], then the instruction regarding the figurative [usage] in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" would not exist; nor is it the case that only the expressive word itself is being instructed.
Therefore, one must understand that grammar is an instruction regarding usage alone. By virtue of that power of instruction...

For that long, denotative function (*vācakatā*) cannot be asserted. Therefore, in this case where the metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā*) is the operative mode, the reason for asserting the word "or" (*vā*) must be stated. This is now explained: having accepted the operation of direct denotation (*abhidhāna*), this statement of "or" [is made].
It has been argued that its function does not extend to the object—

meaning that even in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word would have to operate by performing its own primary function as an intermediate step. This statement was made in support of the view that accepts the operation of direct denotation (*abhidhāna*).
By this,
the statement regarding the word "or" (*vā*) is justified on the basis that the particle *ca* alone functions in the expressive operation (*vācakavṛtti*), and not merely the operation of the meaning.

Or rather, by means of the instruction regarding grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), whose suspicion of incorrectness (*asādhutva*) is removed? Now, one might object: just as *gāvī* and other such forms are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*), so too is the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for even in the case of *gāvī* and others, the meaning is understood through the word *go*, which serves as the indicator (*upalakṣita*).
Here too, it is precisely the indicated genitive that conveys the sense. To this, he replies: "And the meaning [is] another meaning indicated..."

If the denotation (*abhidhā*) were to indicate [another meaning], then it would be a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*). But here, it is the meaning itself that indicates another meaning, not the word indicating another word. Now, it was argued that the meaning of the genitive case is indicated.
Therefore, by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā api* (Pāṇini 6.4.53), even when the genitive case is used,
[the elision of the final vowel and consonant of the first member occurs] according to Pāṇini 7.4.38.
[Page 093]
It has already been stated that "it is indicated. For something not expressed by the genitive case cannot possess the status of being the meaning of the genitive.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the word] is unable to express the genitive meaning which has been indicated. He offers a rebuttal:

"Precisely because it was said that the genitive meaning is indicated, for this very reason it is well said; if it had been said that the expression itself by the genitive is indicated, then there would be no fault."

Even when the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not explicitly perceived, it is said that [the word] expresses the sense of the genitive; the point is that this is seen as having the sense of the genitive in other instances. Now, one might object: "In the view that [the Veda] is metaphorical (*lakṣaṇā*), there is the traditional teaching that 'those [Vedic texts] which have become part of that [ritual] are for the sake of action (*kriyārthatvena*')."

Thus, a contradiction arises; for it has been stated that those words which are well-known in the world as conveying a particular meaning convey the sentence-meaning in exactly that same way. That [statement] would have to be abandoned, because words such as "Gaṅgā" are not used in the sense of "bank.
To this, he says: "In some cases the denotation is the cause, and in some cases the denoted object [is the cause]."
Thus, the acceptance that "it belongs to those beings" is not contradicted.
Even in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a word conveys the meaning of the sentence only by expressing its own well-known meaning. However, this is the distinction:
in some cases there is expression in its own form, while in others it is the very same meaning that has been expressed [by the primary power]; thus, there is no contradiction in our position.
Now, if the genitive sense is merely indicatory (*lākṣaṇika*) in common usage, how then is it that the Blessed One, in the context of the genitive, taught its elision?

It might be argued that there would indeed be a common meaning between the elision (*lopa*) and the genitive case; to this he replies: "For there is no contradiction with the Blessed One’s teaching, since grammar is an instruction regarding linguistic usage. In some cases it is determined by the actual expression, and in others by their having the same meaning; thus, there is no fault whatsoever."

In some cases, the usage is by way of the primary function (*abhidhāna-vṛtti*), and in other cases, the usage is by way of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā-vṱtti*), as taught in grammar. Therefore, this is the meaning: even in place of a sentence, a compound should be employed. And the secondary function is intended to have a single meaning, because it shares the same purpose as the primary function. For this very reason, in both ways—
The formal argument is as follows: for this very reason, the Commentator says, "Since the employment [of words] rests with us, why would we employ that which is non-expressive?

Indeed, this [objection] regarding the employment of the non-expressive would not be tenable if such employment were not even possible; therefore, the establishment of the employment of the non-expressive also exists. If the possibility of employing both [the expressive and the non-expressive] is granted, then what is the distinction between the employment of the expressive and the non-expressive?
With this intention he asks: "What is the intention?
The answer: This is the intention—namely, that it is not [the case] without...
It is appropriate to employ the signification of the meaning; for when that which is non-expressive is employed, the expressed meaning becomes the sign.

It is not reasonable to rely on the fact that [the word] is not denotative as the cause [for its non-occurrence], because when a direct possibility exists, it is improper to resort to an indirect one.
[Objection: "In that case, this would apply to the Veda as well. To this he says: "Who indeed perceives any distinction here? The answer is: "One perceives this."
For when an effect has a single cause, that effect is beginningless;
by the word "effect," its application [in usage] is expressed.

Therefore, this is the meaning: in the Veda, usage is based solely on the motive for usage, and therein the usage is beginningless. Consequently, in this case, whether a word is expressive or non-expressive, what can be done about it? It must be used in exactly that way. However, when the matter is within our own control...

In connection with the word, what else can there be except its denotation? [The author] concludes the meaning of the locus (adhikaraṇa): "Therefore, it is well said that the Niṣāda alone is the Sthapati"; thus, it is solely by virtue of its denotation as the cause.
This is the intended meaning.

However, if one were to resort to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it would result in the [suffix] having its cause in a meaning already expressed (*abhihitārthatva*). And that is not tenable, because it is illogical to abandon the status of being caused by the primary presentation [of the meaning] in favor of being caused by a secondary meaning.
Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.

[The author] raises a doubt by pointing out the impossibility of distinguishing the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as being solely for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*): "But surely this was stated in the *Svargakāma-adhikaraṇa*..."

"This number does not pertain to the qualification (*adhikāra*); rather, it is the number of the agent itself, because no other state [or result] is prescribed. And thus arises the doubt: "How can there be an entitlement for an assembly (*pariṣad*) that desires the fruit?"

The meaning of this is as follows: if this number were one pertaining to qualification (*adhikārika*), then only when there is plurality of qualification would there be the qualification for a council (*pariṣad*) of those seeking [it]; however, this number does not pertain to qualification. What then? This is simply the number of the agents (*kartṛ*).

This has been demonstrated in the section concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*). Why, then, is this number not one pertaining to the qualification (*adhikārika*)? Because no other action (*bhāvāntara*) is enjoined;
the sacrifice alone is the action to be performed.

It is "appropriated" (upātta). This number, residing in the verb, is in reference to that [appropriation]. Furthermore, the person's status as one to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) does not apply to the sacrifice;

what then? It is the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). Therefore, this is merely a number pertaining to agency, not a number pertaining to the one to be enjoined. And whoever is the one to be enjoined is precisely the one entitled (*adhikārī*). Since this number does not even pertain to the entitled person, this doubt is indeed untenable.
It is said: In the subsequent section, the number inherent in the verb will remain intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*).
And when the number of the agent remains intended to be expressed, does the qualification (*adhikāra*) proceed according to the agency, or is the agency one thing while the qualification is another?

He explains this very point: the meaning is that even in the context of *adhikāra*, the number residing in the agent is not capable of bringing about mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). In this regard, such is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).
Because entitlement is connected with desire, it is established by way of agency. [1.1.387, p.

The entitlement (*adhikāra*) resulting from the attainment of the ritual act is regulated both by the [specific] portion and by the exclusion of others; furthermore, since entitlement is determined by desire, it is said that the assembly has the entitlement when there is a petitioner.
The meaning of this is as follows: this prosperity—

"Kāmādhikāra" (the qualification based on desire) refers to its connection with desire, its relation to desire, or—in other words—its being the cause of desire. That which is the cause of desire is the "qualification" (*adhikāra*). In that context, the accomplishment of the desire is for the sake of the qualification; its attainment means the attainment of the fruit by the agent through the medium of the agent. Or, regarding agency, in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the fruit also belongs to those mutually conjoined.

Just as the attainment of the fruit is of such a nature, so too must the desire be based upon that very same nature. Therefore, by means of a partial desire, the assembly’s desire for supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is a qualification of the candidate; since the qualification is exactly as the desire is, the assembly, being one that seeks the goal, possesses the qualification. To this, it is replied: agency does not [depend] on the attainment of the ritual act...
One is able to restrain [the mind]. We understand the attainment according to the expression, but not according to a connection with another word-meaning.
Such is the expression as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth; it is not, however, [derived] from the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) itself.
The desire for only a portion of heaven is understood; rather, it is the desire for the whole. Therefore, the entire heaven belongs to all.

Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit should not be described as depending on the agent, who is a distinct entity. Why? Because it is understood from the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven). Since that [desire] is understood, and because the attainment [of the fruit] is connected to the agent.

The attainment of the fruit, which is the referent of the term "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), is understood; and one who has understood and attained [the fruit] becomes the qualified agent (*adhikārī*). Therefore, the agency occurs at a subsequent time;
the meaning is that there is no mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) among the agents. Thus, in this way, agency belongs only to those who are mutually conjoined, not to the agents [individually].
Having established the section [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*] on the basis of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), he now introduces a hypothetical investigation (*kṛtvācintā*):
Furthermore, even agency here does not preclude independence, for it is understood that there is a plurality of agents here, not a single agency belonging to many. What follows if this is so?
From this, the following results: there are many agents, not one agent.

The meaning is not that agency does not differ while there is merely a difference in the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*); rather, agency itself differs along with its locus. Therefore, because each [agent] possesses agency in its entirety, the entire fruit belongs to each one. Just as, even when there is a group of agents (*kartra*) regarding the attainment of a result, the assembly (*pariṣad*) has no entitlement (*adhikāra*), so too here.
"In that case, it must be for each one individually. Regarding this, by stating "in the *sattra* while acting together" in the Bhāṣya, the state of being co-performers (*sahakartṛtva*) is expressed.
With the intention that "if there is co-performance, there is no individual agency," he raises an objection: "But surely, there is co-performance here."
He refutes [the objection]: the word "together" (*saha*) here indicates "simultaneity of purpose" (*arthasahatva*).

Its meaning is this: although simultaneity of the agents is not perceived here from the perspective of the words, nevertheless, there is simultaneity of purpose even here; it is with this intention [that the word is used].
"Simultaneity. Why is this so? From the Bhāṣya itself.
For the author of the Mahābhāṣya says: "In this case, each one is an agent. And he provides the reasoning: "When there is the intention to express the independence of each one..."
When there is an intention to express agency,
[the agent] is connected with number in the verb because [the verb] expresses number. Furthermore, if there were only one agent here, then...
There would be only the singular number and not the plural; therefore, there are not many agents. Likewise, another point was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"In the case of each individual, when there is a desire to express independence... From this also, it is understood that each one is an agent.
To establish what was stated— that when there is a desire to express the independence of each individual, number is connected with the verb— he says:
"And this understanding that 'there are many agents' is logical, because case-endings arise from that word [which expresses the agent]."

In order to establish what was stated—that "because the meaning of that [verb] is connected with number"—it is explained that "[they] cause [the agent] to be understood. This is the general rule: the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) does not itself possess number, because it is not of the nature of a substance (asattvabhūtatvāt); therefore, those [agents] are implied by it.
Only those factors of action (*kāraka*) that are distinct [from one another] possess number, because they are implied by the meaning of the verb precisely in that state;
they do not consist of mere substances, which are the referents of words denoting *kārakas*— that is, those words which denote the substances that are the *kārakas*.

The meaning is that they do not participate in number. Furthermore, since nominal case-endings (*nāmavibhakti*) participate in number, they [express] only that which belongs to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Thus, [the gender and number] residing therein alone...

They bring about number only as it pertains to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, Agni and Soma are the deity; for "deity-hood" is the state of being a grammatical factor (*kāraka*). In that state, the dual case-ending produced from the nominal stem *agnīṣoma* does not express number, but rather [indicates] only the state of the nominal stem itself.

Thus, it has been shown that there is duality only in the case of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whereas in the state of being a deity (*devatātva*), there is oneness—this being indicated by the statement, "The deity is indeed truth. Now, one might object: even when a case-ending arises from a word denoting an object (*karman*), would it not express the number of the object?

He dispels the doubt that "this [number] does not pertain to the agent" by stating: "And this number pertains to the origination; therefore, it must be understood as residing in the *kāraka* itself. What is meant by "pertaining to the origination"?
The meaning is that this number resides in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), not in the subordinate word (*upapada*).

Nevertheless, he asks "What [is the case]? and says: For that which resides in an upapada (prepositional/qualitative word) is understood even when residing in an object, because it denotes a substance (*sattva*), as in the example "he offers three oblations" (*tisra āhutīr juhoti*).
But that which resides in a verb (*ākhyāta*) does not [denote a substance], because the meaning of a verb is not a substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*).

Arising as pertaining to that [object], it comes to pertain to the agent projected by that [object]. The sense is that even in this way, the co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra) would not be separated by a great interval. Therefore, the independence of each [participant] is understood, in accordance with the traditional rule (smaraṇa): "The independent one is the agent" (svatantraḥ kartā).

Therefore, each one possesses the status of an agent. Now, an objection is raised: since plurality is heard [in the text], it is understood that the agency belongs to those who are dependent on one another; to this, he replies: "Plurality, moreover, brings about dependence in the agent, but it does not [itself] constitute the agency of one who is dependent. Therefore, other agents are employed for the sake of achieving cooperation."
The adoption of another [agent] is not for the sake of fulfilling the status of being an agent.
If the number is not connected with the verb,
then there is a dependence upon an agent.
But how, then, can there be simultaneous denotation by an agent implied by that [single word], and how can there be *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one)?
For it is only of those things that are simultaneously denoted by means of *ekaśeṣa* that number is expressed by case-endings.

[The opponent] states the position: [Let it be granted that] there is no simultaneous denotation; however, there will be a simultaneous implication, since the establishment of simultaneous comprehension occurs nonetheless. As for *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), if it were not possible without denotation, [it would not occur].
Let it not be that this [number] has sound as its object;
nevertheless, this alone is the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*), for this is not the system (*tantra*) where number is expressed only by a single part [of the word].

He considers that there is no proof for [the claim] "yoga" [meaning a collective effort]. Therefore, it is established that just as even when there is a single agent, each individual obtains the entire fruit,
so too there is no entitlement for a group of petitioners.
In practice.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: “Now, it was said in the third [book] that ‘the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer,’ and so forth. He objects to that: what is this “the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer,” and what is its contradiction with this [present position]? Or how [is there a contradiction]?
Therefore, this is obtained:
for if there were a contradiction with that [previous statement], or if it were a mere repetition, then it would be appropriate to say, "But was it not already stated in the third [chapter]?"

"And neither of these two exists," he says; [the author] replies: "When agency toward the object is the meaning of the word, then the speaker's intention (vivakṣā) regarding the expression follows. When the expression is intended, it is contradictory to claim that its denotation is unintended."

The meaning of this is as follows: It has been stated that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," and thus agency is expressed by the verbal suffix (*śabda*) with respect to the action. Since agency exists, that [agency] must be adopted; consequently, because number is required, its expression (*vivakṣā*) follows. Therefore, the suspicion that the sacrifices might have an indefinite number is contradicted; such is the contradiction.

It is generally an objection (*ākṣepa*). Since the objection is made precisely with the intention of pointing out a contradiction, it is said at the time of providing the resolution: "That very thing is being objected to.
But how, then, is there an objection? For regarding the action of one who is enjoined, [the thought arises]: "This belongs to him."
In this way, the relationship is understood either as "this belongs to that" or as "the authority of the person to be enjoined over the action"; thus, there is entitlement (*adhikāra*).

The connection with the characteristics [of the sacrifice] belongs only to the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), and not to anyone else. And whoever is the *niyojya*, he alone is the *adhikārī* (the entitled one), and he alone is the *kartṛ* (the agent).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the connection with the number [of the performer] belongs only to one who has been so impelled.
Regarding this state of being a *niyojya*:
He states that the number is not intended [to be significant]: "And the injunction is by way of mere desire for heaven; it does not depend on number," as has been said.
Now, one might object: since the singular number is heard in the word *svargakāmaḥ* ("one who desires heaven"), the entitlement belongs only to one possessed of that number. To this, he replies:

And it has been stated that, in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the case-ending and number are independent of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), because one hears such expressions as "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) and "those desiring prosperity should sacrifice" (*ṛddhikāmā yajeran*), which follow that pattern. Now, let it be granted that the injunction (*niyoga*) is devoid of number.

Nevertheless, to the question "Why then is the agent not one?", he says: "The agent's connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) constitutes his agency"—this has been stated; the meaning is that the injunction (*niyoga*) does not consist in a connection with the verbal root itself. Therefore, the number inherent in the verbal root does not deserve to be intended (*vivakṣā*), just like the number residing in the word denoting the qualified person (*adhikārin*).

For if the gender were intended as significant because it occurs within the word denoting eligibility (*adhikāra*), then the gender would also be intended as significant, and consequently, women would have no eligibility. Furthermore, it has been stated that this sentence extends up to the point where the fruit is established as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

In the third [case], if the sentence were intent upon that [the relationship between the word-meanings], the connection between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha) would all the more not be intended to be expressed. But surely, the connection between action and its factors is also understood here; how then can it be abandoned?

Just as the connection between the fruit and the human purpose is understood, so too is the connection between the action and its factors (kārakas) understood; how then can this [latter] be abandoned? The answer is:
because [the former] is [the primary one], whereas the other—[as stated in the manuscript]—is subordinate.
[Page 101] Because the sentence has another purpose. [The opponent objects: "Let the sentence have another purpose; even so, what of it? To this he says: "And a single sentence has a single meaning."
Thus it has been said. Therefore, the statement "one should eat poison" is not intended to be taken literally.

Its meaning is as follows: the comprehension of the word-meaning occurs through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Etymological derivation also occurs within the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). In that context, a single sentence conveys only a single meaning.

The etymological derivation is "that which causes one to go" (*gamayati*). Therefore, if it were intended to have another meaning, that other meaning would not be cognized due to the absence of such an etymological derivation;

hence, it is said that [the word] is not intended [to convey that]. Any misconception regarding the comprehension, however, would be based on an inference from general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Thus, one might act according to one's own whim. Furthermore, a single sentence cannot possibly convey these two distinct meanings.
And thus the analogy of the bow and arrow becomes appropriate. The indicative mark (liṅga) has been stated. To this it is replied:
it cannot be said that either the action or the number is not intended to be expressed, just as it cannot be said that the action is not intended to be expressed.

The meaning is that it cannot be said that the number [of the agent] is not likewise [restricted]. Why? Because eligibility (*adhikāra*) occurs only with respect to a qualified action; just as, since eligibility is understood with respect to an action qualified by a specific substance, the action is not performed with another substance, so too, when eligibility is understood with respect to an action qualified by the number of the agent, another number is not resorted to.

The meaning is that since this action (*karman*) is qualified by the number belonging to that specific factor (*kāraka*) called the agent (*kartṛ*), number must be observed in order to achieve its qualification by that [agent]. Now, one might object: "Granted that the action is qualified, nevertheless the sentence does not have that as its primary purport. To this he says: "Nor is that sentence intended merely to show that heaven belongs to the person; what then?"
"In this action, he has the authority"—let it be so; nevertheless, what follows from this? To this, he says: "And this is the authority."
And since this meaning of the injunction is understood as being prompted by its own purpose— the fruit— which consists of a specific action, factor (kāraka), and agent,
everything is faultless.
It is logical that the meaning of the injunction is understood as an action performed by a single agent, which serves its own purpose and accomplishes the fruit.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Even so, the fruit belongs to the qualified person (adhikārī), not to the performer (prayoktṛ). To this he says: "And this being the case, it is also established that the fruit belongs to the performer; for the qualified person is indeed the performer. Therefore—

*Vākyārthamīmāṃsā*: The fruit being declared for one who performs [an action] accrues to the instigator (*prayoktṛ*), because another is not the instigator. This is so if this [text] has the injunction (*niyoga*) as its primary purport.
How then is the third application of the ritual factors, such as the action (*karman*) and so forth, established? To this he says:
the third application of the ritual factors and so forth arises from this very *niyoga* alone. If the status of the fruit as the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) arises from *niyoga* alone...
It is understood that when it was further stated by the author of the Bhāṣya— namely, that for one desiring heaven for oneself or for another,
the designation of the word "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is indistinguishable, both from the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—
it was indeed by means of words (*śabda*).

It has been stated that the attainment of the fruit belongs only to the person enjoined regarding the meaning of the word. Furthermore, because the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is introduced in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), it is stated that even the fruits of the subsidiary rites are connected to the performer of the principal rite. What is expressed by this?
He provides the answer:

From an injunction qualified by all these specific attributes, all this is obtained: namely, that the ātmanepada suffix conveys that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, and that the term *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven) expresses the state of desiring in relation to a desire connected to the self.

The intended meaning is that this has been stated as being indicative (liṅgasthānīya). Pāṇini also confirms this very usage as the indicator for the expression of the *ātmanepada*—that is, the cause for expressing the *ātmanepada*—when he records in his grammar: "yajate yajamānaḥ" (the sacrificer sacrifices) and "yajanti yājakāḥ" (the priests sacrifice).

In this very application, having understood that the fruit has its own purpose (*svārthatā*) by virtue of the power of the injunction (*niyoga*), the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that the ātmanepada occurs when the fruit is for one's own sake would otherwise be groundless. He concludes: "Therefore, just as [it is] merely a cause..."

Since comprehension also arises from the very injunction that does not overstep the causes such as the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the author of the Bhāṣya presents [the middle voice] as a logical mark (*liṅga*) by way of its being a cause.

He concludes the subject of the discussion: "Therefore, it is well said that the number intended [is the one to be applied]; however, because it is impossible in the archetype (prakṛti), the injunction for each specific word is displaced from the sentence," as stated in the third [book].
But because of the context.
But how, then, is there doubt here? Or how is there no doubt? It has been stated that the qualification for rites pertaining to desire (*kāma-adhikāra*) extends up to the attainment of the fruit.
In that regard, if desire were to cease upon the attainment of the fruit through some other cause—
Or, due to some other cause such as perceiving a fault, one's qualification for that very [action] ceases; for one who lacks such qualification...
We do not understand either the performance [of the rite] from the verbal text itself, nor from any other source. Therefore, we see this doubt as truly unfounded.
The meaning of this is: the qualification for desire-based rites does not terminate with the causal factor (*nimitta*), but rather terminates with the fruit (*phala*).

Thus it has been said. If [the rite] were to terminate with the occasion (*nimitta*), then once the desire has arisen, that desire would constitute the occasion; consequently, even when the desire has ceased, the performance of the rite would have to be completed. However, if it terminates with the fruit (*phala*), then upon the cessation of the desire, the person’s mastery over the action ceases; what, then, would be the basis for its performance? Therefore, even when [the desire] has vanished...
It is argued that if there is a desire for a fruit, the possibility of completing the performance [of the rite] is untenable. To this it is replied: This is the point of doubt here.

For those who know the qualification (*adhikāra*) have stated that the connection between the action and so forth, on the one hand, and the fruit and the person, on the other, is preceded by the sense of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*).

The meaning of this is as follows: this relationship between the result (*phala*) and the person (*puruṣa*) is preceded by the cognition that [the action] is to be performed; it is not, however, the case that the understanding of what is to be performed is preceded by the cognition of the relationship between the result and the person. For, when the meaning of an injunction is understood as something to be performed by a person desiring a result, it would not truly be "to be performed" if it did not imply the attainment of that result. Thus, the result—

The relationship between the two persons is understood, and not otherwise. Therefore, because the relationship between the fruit and the person is understood, the status of being "to be done" (kartavyatā) is understood even prior to that. Nevertheless, he asks: "Why so?"—we understand that once one has engaged in what is to be done, one is impelled by the scripture.

Since engagement in performance is based on the understanding that an action ought to be done through the cognition of its obligation (*kartavyatājñāna*), once that sense of obligation has arisen, because that performance is dependent solely upon it, the person proceeds by means of the scripture alone.

By making known an object suitable for engagement, a person is impelled toward performance; not otherwise. Therefore, since the scripture makes known the meaning of the injunction as something to be done, the performance is indeed brought about by it. Now, one might object: "Let the operation of the scripture consist merely in the initial commencement [of the act]. To this he says: "And the scripture is the expression of its own meaning, from the commencement up to the final completion. Therefore...

It does not remain incomplete, because the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not understood part by part. But if that is so, then it has been argued that the fact that ritual action exists for the sake of a fruit is untenable; for a fruit is defined as something desired (*iṣṭa*). When that [fruit] is not yet desired...
He offers this rebuttal: "In that case, it would not be the result at all. [The response is: First, it is not untenable as a cause for engagement (*pravṛtti*).

At the time of engagement, there is a purpose through the comprehension of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). And since, while in that state, desire serves as the occasion for qualification (*adhikāra-nimitta*), performance is tenable. Furthermore, it has been stated that the scripture (*śāstra*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) precisely because engagement is not yet completed.

Henceforth, where would the persistence of the qualification (adhikāra) be of use? The meaning is that even when the qualification has ceased, the performance [of the rite] does not cease. Therefore, he considers that the ritual action must be completed even when the desire for the fruit has vanished. Thus...

To this it is replied: It is true that the purpose of the scripture extends from its commencement up to liberation; and it is true that it cannot be understood in its entirety through mere partial analysis.
However, it is not possible to understand that the scripture is the cause [of knowledge] apart from [the context of] the qualification [to study].

This is the intended meaning: for one for whom the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) is to be accomplished, there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) to that which effects it, namely the primary rite together with its subsidiaries. And when desire has ceased, the purpose of the injunction is no longer to be performed, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the appearance of something as a task (*kārya*) for a person.

And since the meaning of the injunction is something that is not an object of action (*akārya*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) for its accomplishment has ceased. Once the qualification has ceased, what basis remains for performance? Now, it was argued that performance is justified as being the occasion (*nimitta*) for activity.
The reply is: [it is] not [justified] for that which is unattainable.
It must be a *nimitta* (condition).

The meaning of this is: only when a person has a desire does the son and so forth become an objective (*sādhya*); and being an objective, it serves as the condition for that entitlement (*adhikāra*), and not otherwise. Therefore, although at the time of engagement—

Since desire exists, when there is a state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the son and so forth constitute the cause for eligibility (*adhikāra-nimitta*). Nevertheless, once the desire for the fruit has ceased, that which has become non-achievable is no longer a cause for eligibility; thus, upon the cessation of eligibility due to the absence of such a cause, [the obligation ceases].

"There is no performance [of the act]. Therefore, he states that there is no causality for that which is unaccomplished: "For a cause is recognized only as it has been apprehended, not as something unapprehended; it is not perceived as a cause by virtue of being something yet to be accomplished. This concerns the qualification (*adhikāra*) regarding the object of desire.

It has been stated that [the action] would exist because it is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, even in the case of engagement (*pravṛtti*), engagement occurs only so long as the cause (*nimitta*) exists, or there is cessation when the cause is absent.
As long as the cause for the entitlement (*adhikāra-nimitta*) exists, so long does the entitlement persist.
Performance must be undertaken; and those learned in the principles of logic maintain that in the absence of such [an object], there can be no performance.
This is the summary here: at the time of commencement, when a desire exists, the son and so forth are understood as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: A person first understands the injunction (*niyoga*) as something to be performed because it possesses a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Even though at the conclusion [of the act] that qualification is understood as a modification (*vikāra*) of the primary [injunction], that very [qualification] is the cause for performance.
However, the mere arising of the knowledge of entitlement (*adhikāra-jñāna*) is not the cause for performance; rather, it is that which persists. It is not [the case that it is the cause].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that for one who is free from desire, there persists a knowledge of the duty (*adhikāra*). As for what was stated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*)—"He knows through the Veda alone, 'This must be done by me,' but he does not know the means"—the meaning of this is as follows: such is the intention of the questioner.

It is said that by this very commentary he stated: "The person engages in the subsidiary parts (aṅga) solely out of a desire for the result. And this point is not useful here. The reply is: this point is that, once the desire for the result has ceased, the scripture no longer becomes directly manifest [as a motivator].

The meaning of this is as follows: there is no statement that "desire for the fruit must be performed. If such a statement existed, then the status of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) would be that of an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). If it were so, then when desire for the fruit has ceased—since the scripture (*śāstra*) would have become directly manifest—the very cessation of desire for the fruit would be untenable. Yet, no such statement exists. Therefore, when [the desire] has passed away...
When there is a desire for the fruit that consists in the disregard (*avadhūta*) of the meaning of the scripture, the status of the root-meaning as an instrument (*karaṇatā*) is not tenable;

because in the absence of desire, the fruit is not desired, it cannot be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), nor can there be a qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, that itself constitutes the absence of the meaning of the scripture.
This has been demonstrated by this author of the Bhāṣya. But is it not so?

As for this statement that "the sacrifice is not enjoined as something to be performed," which contradicts the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, the answer is that it has been shown in the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* how there is no contradiction. Furthermore, regarding this presentation of an alternative view [that the injunction ends] because of the reproach of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), [it is refuted as follows]:

Having raised the objection, "Why do they censure it as 'this should not be done'?", the reason for this very censure by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) was stated to be the cause for the completion [of the act], and likewise the fault of false resolve (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*) was shown. This appears somewhat inconsistent. How is it inconsistent? If—
In that case, since the undertaking is commenced solely for the purpose of avoiding the fault of false resolve, it would not be possible to introduce the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*);
for even without the censure of the learned, [the undertaking] serves precisely the purpose of avoiding the fault of false resolve.
[Objection: This is because [the ritual] has been accomplished. To this it is replied: Here, there is no such thing as a false resolve (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*).

Why? Because the resolve was made for the sake of the scriptural injunction (*śāstrārtha*), and the completion of the act by one whose desire has ceased is not the purpose of the scriptural injunction.

It has been shown how the meaning of the treatise is not tenable. However, those very [opponents] think thus; the learned critics think in this way: "He possesses the fault of false resolve, who does not bring what he has begun to completion. Having thought this, and...
Therefore, because they censure it, one must bring it to completion.
If they censure it with the understanding that it is a fault of false resolve, this censure is rootless, because in the ultimate sense there is no fault of false resolve. For this reason it is said:
"Why do they resort to this groundless censure?
"What is the use of searching for the root cause here?
This itself [is sufficient]."

Reproach by the learned is a great suffering; indeed, reproach by the learned uproots even that which has been firmly established, and it remains so even when one is in such a state. Since the wise exert effort for the sake of avoiding suffering, it is well said: "They reproach [him]."
"In this world, they are considered 'those who have been instructed' (śiṣṭa) for that long."

He explains the doubt in terms of its meaning: "Regarding this work performed by the stage directors (*sūtradhāra*), should it be completed once begun, or should one desist from it once the desire for the fruit has ceased?
In this regard—

The author of the Bhāṣya examines the scriptural nature [of the action]. He raises an objection to that: "Is it not the case that an action must be completed out of fear of the censure of the learned, and not because it is scriptural? Therefore, one should follow that [censure] alone; [the question remains] whether they censure it or not. What is the use of pursuing whether it is scriptural or non-scriptural?"

The meaning of this is as follows: when a commenced task is completed, the sole reason for the censure of the learned is not its scriptural basis; therefore, that [censure] alone must be followed. [One asks: Do they censure the completion of what is to be accomplished through a specific sequence, or not? Is it according to scriptural authority? He provides the answer: It is said—this is indeed true.
If that censure were unconditional, it would not be performed in accordance with the scriptures. Therefore,
because one undertakes this scriptural act and does not bring it to completion, there exists the fault of false resolve.
Thinking thus and considering it to be scriptural, they censure what is non-scriptural;
therefore, in order to dispel that delusion—
and specifically to dispel the delusion regarding its scriptural nature— it must be investigated.

Regarding scriptural authority (*śāstrīyatva*): this point must be investigated. In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is scripturally authoritative because of its connection with a deity and because of the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For that which is not scripturally authoritative cannot have a scripturally authoritative subsidiary (*aṅga*), nor can there be a rectification of deficiency (*vaiguṇya-samādhi*). Indeed, that which...
1. p. 1398 2. By the authors of the Sūtras—mā [p.
(a) In that context, a deity can be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only if it is scriptural, because the nature of a deity is cognizable solely through scripture.

That which is an auxiliary of something non-scriptural is cognizable through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And the rectification of defects in what is non-scriptural [is achieved through such means].
It would indeed be non-scriptural (aśāstrīya), because it is cognizable through other means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Therefore, its scriptural nature (śāstrīyatva) is understood.

And if it is scriptural, then it is certainly possible that the learned (śiṣṭas) would censure one for failing to complete what was begun; thus, to avoid that, the house and so forth must necessarily be completed once commenced.
To this it is replied: there is no authoritative evidence that these are scriptural, because the effort [involved] is for the sake of what is merely pleasant.
Therefore, all the works together with their sūtras are based solely on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and are not rooted in the Veda. As for that which was also [stated]:
The authors of the Sūtras record that "this belongs to the Brāhmaṇa" and "this belongs to the King," such as the house and so forth;

and just as they record that there is a transgression leading to death and other consequences for acting otherwise than what is enjoined, that too is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), like [the rules of] medicine and similar fields. Furthermore, as for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and the injunction regarding deities, because they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), they do not pertain to the house and so forth.
The point that [the Smṛti rules] are for the sake of ritual action (*karmārtha*) has already been refuted.

Its meaning is as follows: although this penance (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth is indeed rooted in the Śāstra, it is nevertheless not *śāstrīya* (scripturally authoritative) in the sense of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to domestic rites (*gṛhya*) and the like, because penance and such are not heard of [in the Veda] as being part of those. For what purpose, then, is there a Smṛti tradition? It is for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*).
There is no fault here.
In the case of negation.

What is this deliberation regarding the operation of the injunction (*niyoga*): is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) enjoined, or is it the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), qualified by that [negative particle]? This is the second type of deliberation concerning the injunction. Is the meaning of the negative particle the object (*viṣaya*), or...
1. For the purpose of undertaking an action;

"The meaning of the verbal root is qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). [The opponent asks: "Let there be this consideration of application (*viniyoga*); what is the fault? The objector replies:

"Indeed, there is no fault in either the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) or the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) position; however, there is a lack of connection in the definition of the *adhikāra* (the subject matter of the section).
Second—

Because it is of the nature of reflection (*cintā*). He provides the resolution: "In that case, this is indeed a reflection on eligibility (*adhikāra-cintā*). How is it a reflection on eligibility? In this way: if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is enjoined here, then the verb *bhakṣayati* (he eats) becomes a qualifier of the eligible person;
consequently, there is an injunction of an action qualified by the meaning of the negative particle. From that, an eligible person must be postulated.

The qualification is like that of the Viśvajit sacrifice; and for the sake of establishing that, this consideration of relative strength (balābala) has been introduced. Alternatively, when the object of the injunction is the state of indifference (audāsīnya) consisting in the meaning of the negative particle (nañ), the verb *bhakṣayati* (he eats), finding no other way to connect with it, by force becomes a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). But when there is an injunction for a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), then, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice...

The object to be conceptualized (*kalpya*) is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), because it denotes a specific qualification of that person; thus, there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) with the definition.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), holding the general rule (*utsarga*) that "words denoting action are those whose meaning is the efficient force" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*), considers this to be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

In the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] stating "words denoting action have being as their meaning" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*), it was stated that those things whose meaning is being (*bhāvārtha*) are the objects of injunction (*vidhi*). Now, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) consists of indifference (*audāsīnya*), and since this is not something whose meaning is being, it is not logical for it to be the object of an injunction. But [one might object]:

Anticipating the objection that substances such as curd, in the injunction "He offers with curd," have the sense of non-existence [as a primary factor], he says: "And because the qualification is dependent upon that."
The meaning of the secondary word (upapada) is enjoined precisely as dependent upon the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha). This is what is meant:

it is the very meaning of the verbal root, colored by that [secondary word], which is enjoined; however, the injunction regarding the secondary word is established through the distinction between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained.

Therefore, it is logical that the very resolution not to eat—the essence of which is a positive act—is what is enjoined by way of indication (lakṣaṇā). Furthermore, if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) were itself enjoined, it would result in its performance;
for if the meaning of the *nañ* were indeed enjoined, [it would have to be carried out].

In that case, since eating itself would follow as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite, it would result in its actual performance. How so? For even that which is prohibited does not assist a person—either by way of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or by the removal of suffering—and therefore, in such a case, [it cannot be a qualification].
Ordinary people act with prior deliberation; therefore, this alone is the superior meaning of the treatise.

Since activity conforms to [an intended] result, if there is no activity in the absence of a result, then even in the view that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is a prescription, a result must still be postulated. To this he says: "But surely, even when the meaning of the negative particle is prescribed, let there be the postulation of demerit (*pratyavāya*); what [is the point]?"

Having raised the dilemma as to whether transgression arises from the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) itself or from the action being prohibited, he refutes it: "How can transgression be postulated when the meaning of the negative particle is being enjoined?
[For] by postulating transgression from the very meaning of the negative particle..."

Non-performance does not follow at all, because [the injunction] does not cause non-performance since it is a cause for transgression (*pratyavāya*). Now, if it is argued that transgression is postulated through the performance of the object—that is, through the performance of eating—and that this [transgression] is avoided by the performance of the prohibition; [we reply:]...

Regarding the phrase "as in the world" (*lokavat*): that is incorrect, because a prescription concerning the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) results in a conclusion regarding that very meaning of the negative particle itself; it does not enjoin the performance of the [prohibited] object. As for the performance of the object, however, that is worldly (*laukika*). In the worldly...

Furthermore, if the transgression [of non-performance] is not understood from worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the performance [of the rite], how could it be understood from any other source?
Since the two ancillary elements (anubandha) of an injunction are understood even without the assumption of a transgression (pratyavāya) resulting from contact with the object,

it is impossible to assume that the transgression consists in the impulse toward desire; therefore, since no other way for it to serve a human purpose is tenable, this must be an injunction against eating.
In that view, because the Viśvajit sacrifice has heaven as its fruit, it is established that the ritual action serves the purpose of the person.
To this, it is replied: "It is true, as the 'beloved of the gods' (the opponent) has said."
In the view that this is an injunction regarding non-eating, it would serve the purpose of the person (puruṣārthatā).

However, that is not perceived as an injunction for non-eating, because the verbal root *bhakṣ* denotes eating; [the prefix] *na* does not signify the sense of "not" [in this context]. This is the meaning.
The negative particle (*nañ*) also expresses prohibition, which is to say cessation; by both words, non-eating— namely, indifference— is expressed.
An unreal [object] is not cognized; nor can it be established, because it lacks the nature of an action (*akriyārūpatvāt*).
Furthermore, the operation of the means of knowledge (*mānasa-vyāpāra*) is cognized neither from the word (*pada*) nor from the sentence (*vākya*).

It is understood. And the status of being an injunction (vidheyatā) is not possible for that which is not so understood. Now, if it is argued that the mental resolve (saṅkalpa) is understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), as in the case of "not eating," he says in response:
"In the cases of 'not looking' and so forth, the word *vrata* is heard directly."

Therefore, it is appropriate that the definition of a *vrata* applies there, because the word *vrata* signifies a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), and [the term in question] stands in grammatical apposition with it. But here, nothing of that sort exists.
However, since the verb "to eat" (*bhakṣayati*) cannot connect with anything else, by way of a "shoe on the neck," it functions as a qualification of the person authorized [for the rite].

Furthermore, it is entirely improper for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which signifies non-existence, to be the object of an injunction (*vidheya*), as it would result in mere indifference; for there is no contradiction with any word [in that case]. Indeed, it has been stated that a positive entity (*bhāvārtha*) does not become the object of an injunction only because it is the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), provided there is no contradiction with the words [of the Veda].
The author of the Nibandhana, who maintains that the word has intrinsic power, considers this:
"But was it not stated that practical application (anuṣṭhāna) is not possible?"
He addresses [this] with a question: "Why is it not tenable?
He states [the reason] in a single passage: "Is there no understanding of what ought to be done?"

The meaning of this is as follows: if indeed there were no comprehension of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) without a result, then there would certainly be no performance in the absence of a result. However, there is comprehension of what ought to be done even without a result. Therefore, once the comprehension of what ought to be done exists, desire and the like become connected [to it].
This has been demonstrated in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*.
Therefore, there is an understanding of what is to be done even without a [stated] result. But one might object:

"In this case too, let there be an understanding of a result, just as in the case of 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*) and so forth. To this, he says: "Where those [persons], such as 'one who desires heaven,' [are mentioned]..."

In that very case, the understanding of what is to be done extends up to the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). However, where such [an attainment] does not exist, who would be capable of understanding what is to be done? Furthermore, it has been stated that performance follows from the knowledge that something ought to be done, and not from the knowledge of its fruit.
Because that is its root;
for the comprehension of the fruit is rooted in performance preceded by the knowledge of what ought to be done.

For it is only when there is a cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatājñāna*) culminating in performance that heaven and the like, being desired, become connected as its fruit, and not otherwise. Precisely because the accomplishment of performance follows from the mere cognition of what is to be done, for this very reason even "living" (*jīvana*) and so forth function as qualifications of the person entitled to perform (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).

It is established. For who indeed is capable of preventing the non-performance of one who, even while understanding that such-and-such must be done, does not do it—even regarding injunctions for those desiring heaven? And who could provide an answer to one who, having found gold, should call it clay?

Who indeed can provide an answer to one who asserts that even what ought to be done is not to be done? If performance follows merely from the fact that something is to be done, then why does the Commentator [state as follows]?

He introduces the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭavigarhaṇa*): [An objection is raised that] the performance [of a rite] is established even without the censure of the learned. He provides the resolution: This is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya—[that] even for one who, being ignorant of the understanding derived from worldly treatises, does not perform [the rite] due to the absence of a result, there nonetheless exists for that foolish person the censure of the learned in the world.
For the sake of engaging [in action]. Therefore, this sentence-meaning—“one should not eat *khañja*”—cannot be disregarded.
But in that case...
In order to establish the connection between the chapters, he explains the doubt presented by the author of the Bhāṣya: "This is what is considered here" (1.1.1402 [p.
Is one entitled [to perform rites] merely by birth, through the group of practices such as following [the teacher], or only after being initiated?
He explains this very point: what is meant is this—whether birth alone is the qualification for entitlement, or initiation.
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that the status of being a qualification for heaven and so forth is not logically tenable.
Because the group of customary practices has a visible purpose, just like the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires).

Just as in the *ādhāna*, heaven and the like do not function as qualifications for the eligible performer since they serve the purpose of the fires, so too in this group of customary practices, eligibility is based solely on a visible purpose; thus, there is no eligibility for one who desires heaven.
It is thus postulated. Therefore, capacity alone is the qualification for eligibility (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).

If capacity alone is the qualification for eligibility, then since one who has just been born lacks such capacity, how can it be said that there is eligibility for one who has just been born? To this, he says:
"But if this is so, then one who has merely been born would have no entitlement [to perform rites].
He answers: "What is meant is this: it does not depend upon initiation (upanayana)."
This term "as soon as born" (*jātamātra*) does not refer to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*).
This being the position reached, it is stated in reply: one is entitled [to perform rites] only after the time of initiation (*upanayana*). What is the reasoning?
For it is after the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) that one is entitled to perform Vedic matters; and this [study] is Vedic.

Regarding the phrase "pāṭhagaṇa," it is stated in the Smṛti-pāda [of the Tantravārttika]: "The study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāyādhyayana) belongs to one who has been initiated (upanīta). Therefore, after initiation, there is eligibility for the ritual conducts (ācāras). By this, the essential nature of the meaning of the Bhāṣya has been stated. Let it be so.

The study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) belongs to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). As for the meanings of the words (*padārtha*), however, they belong to whoever understands them—whether initiated or uninitiated—and do not belong to anyone else, just as the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) belongs to the *niṣādasthapati*.
In this regard:

He objects: But surely, in that case, regarding the *sthapatīṣṭi*, because it contradicts the rule of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and because it contradicts the formation of a *karmadhāraya* compound, thus...

"The entitlement belongs only to the Niṣāda. But here, in this collection of traditional practices (*ācāragaṇa*), because it does not conflict with one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), it is studied...
The qualification for the Vedas will belong only to those who possess desire, just as there is qualification for those who have studied the Vedas only if they possess desire;
so it is here as well. Otherwise, even in that case, the qualification of those who have not studied the Vedas would be excluded. He refutes this: "It is improper—"

There is no evidence that eligibility belongs exclusively to those who have studied the Vedas. As for the statement "like those desiring [worldly fruits]," he says in response: for in that case, since the study of the Vedas is possible [for them], there is no proof that their [status] is necessitated by such study, as it is for the learned.

It was stated [previously] that this applies to those possessed of desire (*kāmin*). Here, however, because the group of practices (*ācāragaṇa*) is not to be accomplished by means of mantras, it cannot be said that "one who has not studied the Veda is not qualified," since it has been stated that there is no application of mantras here. Therefore—

It is logical that even one who has not studied the Vedas possesses the qualification [for ritual action]. Furthermore, it is not the case that one becomes a student of the Vedas immediately upon being initiated (*upanīta*).
If the qualification belonged only to one who has studied the Vedas, then if one were to become a student of the Vedas immediately upon initiation, it would follow accordingly.

It might be so; however, this is not the case. Therefore, it is indeed possible to raise the objection that the status of being Vedic is demonstrated only for those who have undergone initiation (*upanīta*). To this, the following is stated: This is the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*: prior to initiation, the injunctions are found to belong to the father or to one performing the *darvihoma*; whereas initiation belongs to the teacher (*ācārya*).

The intention is as follows: whatever rites there may be that are Vedic, all of them belong to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*); since one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) lacks the qualification (*adhikāra*), the qualification belongs solely to the father, or to the performer of the *dārvihoma*.
Regarding the initiation (*upanayana*) of a child, the preceptor (*ācārya*) is both the authorized person and the agent.
However, after that time, Vedic injunctions concerning refined subjects (*saṃskṛta-viṣaya*) are heard;
and since the Smṛti rules are rooted in those [Vedas], they too come into being only after that time—so says the venerable Commentator.

For it is held that everywhere inference follows what has been observed; and since Vedic injunctions are perceptible and concern initiated subjects, those inferred from Smṛti ought likewise to be so. This is the sense. Therefore, it is well said that the one who has been initiated possesses the entitlement.
[Page 115] Repetition.

How does he raise the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) here? [The opponent argues that] because the rite is a subsidiary element of time, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result; therefore, the performance must be carried out when the time has arrived. To this, he replies: since the principle of "capacity for all" (*sarvaśakti*) established in the previous section remains applicable, a doubt arises as to whether a performance devoid of both the proper time and ritual purity is indeed prompted by the occasion of one's life.
"Should it be performed or not?

The meaning of this is as follows: in the *Sarvaśakti* section, it was stated that performance must be carried out by abandoning the subsidiaries due to the force of the qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, here too, is the performance occasioned by livelihood to be carried out by the force of the qualification?

One should perform [the rite] having abandoned the time that has become a secondary factor; therefore, there is no need for concern. In this regard, the intention of the proponent (pūrvavādin) is as follows:
it was stated that the abandonment of the subsidiary elements occurs by force of the occasion; therefore, the performance lasts as long as the occasion persists.
The meaning of this is as follows:

The entitlement [to perform a rite] is based on life; since life remains as the causal condition even in the absence of the specific time, one must perform the rite by setting aside the subsidiary time through the force of that [life]. Thus, one should offer the oblation thinking, "Offer! Offer!
(juhudhi juhudhi).

"What does 'juhudhi juhudhi' mean? It means 'one must offer the oblation'; that is to say, it must be offered repeatedly. For instance, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is prescribed for the root *hu* (to sacrifice) in the sense of the suffix *tavya* when there is a repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*); in place of that [suffix], the word *hi* is substituted, and that *hi* is itself a substitute for the imperative. Thus says the Sūtra: 'The imperative (*loṭ*) is used in the sense of repetition of action; and for the imperative, *hi* and *sva* are optionally substituted.'"

From that [root], by the rule “taddhitoḥ,” and then by the rule “there is reduplication in the sense of repetition (ābhīkṣṇye),” there is doubling. Likewise, by the rule “in the former case, there is the subsequent application according to the original form.”

"It is the root *hu* (to sacrifice), ending in the suffix *tavya*, that is used as an auxiliary verb. Now, one might object: "But it is not possible to perform the recitation at the time of eating or moving about.
He answers this: "In whatever manner it is possible."

It should be practiced in such a manner that the application can be performed during the times of eating and moving about; one should adopt that method. Now, [an objection is raised: "In that case, purity (*śauca*) and so forth would be abandoned. To this he replies: "Purity is indeed a limb [of the practice]."
Therefore, regarding time:

The application [of the rule] should be made even by abandoning the [literal] grief. He states the final conclusion: "To this it is replied: the scripture does not depend upon repetition, because for one who is capable, the comprehension of the cause is possible."

The meaning of this is as follows: this scripture is not dependent on that practice which holds that "one should act according to one's ability. For even in the case of one capable of performing all the constituent parts (*aṅga*), the understanding of the causal condition (*nimitta*) is possible. If, indeed, eligibility were restricted to one capable of performing all the constituent parts, then [the status of] living...

If the understanding of the occasion (*nimitta*) were not possible, then this might be so; but that is not the case. Therefore, there is no authority for abandoning the time of purification which has become an auxiliary (*aṅga*). To the objection that "it is abandoned by the force of the qualification (*adhikāra*)," he replies: "For in that very context, the abandonment of an auxiliary is stated only when the occasion has been encountered."
When a particular occasion arises,

the renunciation of the ancillaries (aṅgatyāga) is shown in the section concerning all capacities (*sarvaśaktyadhikaraṇa*). Here, however, it is understood that the occasion itself does not depend upon repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

Life alone is not understood as the occasion [for the rite] by way of being dependent on practice; for if the scripture were thus dependent on practice, then life alone would be understood as the occasion, independent of purification (*śauca*). But this is not the case, because even in the absence of practice, the understanding of the occasion is established. For if, due to the lack of qualification for the scriptural injunction regarding life, there were no practice—
[Objection: If the scripture is thus dependent [on other factors], then let it be made devoid of time (*kāla*).

Since time cannot logically serve as a qualification of the person (*puruṣa*), but is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*), the performance of the rite can take place even by omitting it. [Reply: We say, "No."
A sign devoid of time is not perceived at all, because time is eternally present;
due to its eternal connection with time, [the agent] is capable of action within that time.

Because of the [scriptural] injunction, life itself at that very time is the occasion [for the rite], since it is capable of being withdrawn at another time. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely all the auxiliary parts (aṅgas) are eternally connected.
The meaning of this is: [the rite is] for one who possesses the qualification (sādhikārin)—

Because they are heard in proximity [to the main rite] as being unchanging, they are adopted for the purpose of that [main rite]. Nor is there any distinction such that time is adopted because of its eternity while the others are adopted because of their non-eternity. Thus, since all are eternally connected, one might ask: "What is the significance of this statement that time is 'eternally joined'? He answers: It is true that they are eternally joined, but not so the other auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
They are recognized through their relinquishment;
even at that time when those [qualities] do not exist, they are still present in the person.

Since there is the capacity to withdraw those [auxiliaries], it is appropriate to perform the practice even by abandoning them when one has the qualification [for the primary rite]. Time, moreover, indicates its own occasion through the abandonment of other times, just like ritual purity (*śauca*).
The meaning of this is: regarding all capacities—

Even if performance were possible through a substitute by means of abandoning the constituent parts (*aṅga*), and thus the parts were considered secondary (*gauṇa*), there would still be no absolute annulment (*atyantabādha*) of the scriptural injunctions regarding those parts. However, in the case of time (*kāla*), if it were abandoned, there would indeed be an absolute annulment, because time, like purity (*śauca*), is indivisible. Just as the injunction for that very [time] indicates the occasion (*nimitta*) by means of the abandonment of impurity (*aśauca*), so it is here. Therefore, since it cannot be otherwise—

The status of being a causal condition (*nimittatā*) is determined in accordance with the time of its occurrence. Precisely because the status of being a causal condition is determined in accordance with time, we do not perceive a causal condition that is devoid of time. Nor can there be a causal condition that is not perceived.
He challenges the commentary: the author of the commentary, however, states that time alone is the cause, saying, "Time is not a quality; rather, it is the cause.
And that is incorrect, because living is the cause.

Because [time] would be a mere occasion (nimitta); if time were merely an occasion, it would not be prescribed in a performance for a specific desire (kāmyaprayoga), since it would not be an integral part (anaṅgatva) of the rite.
He provides the justification: therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya here—time is not a quality that serves as a cause without delimiting [the action].
The text of the Bhāṣya should be explained by supplying the phrase "without delimiting the cause."

A quality (*guṇa*) is not that which does not delimit the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), but rather it is that which delimits the occasioning cause; this is the sense. For what was stated—that "this is indeed the aforementioned occasioning cause"—was intended with reference to its being the occasioning cause for life existing at that very time (*tadātmakālīna-jīvana*), and not with reference to being the direct occasioning cause. And this [is established] by the statement: "Therefore, the performance [of the rite] lasts as long as life, since it depends upon time."
This has been made manifest by the Bhāṣya:
"Because they are innate."
But how, then, is there a prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) here, given that when the cause (nimitta) ceases, the effect (naimittika) [must also cease]?

"It must come to pass" means "when the time has arrived," which is logical. Thus, here is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view: the comprehension of the occasion (*nimitta*) is dependent on time, and time is an auxiliary (*aṅga*); since the scriptural injunction regarding the auxiliaries is fulfilled by a single performance, the occasion is likewise [fulfilled] because it conforms to that.

The meaning of this is as follows: Time (*kāla*) is indeed a subsidiary element (*aṅga*). Once the integration [of the subsidiaries] has been performed, the rule regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅgaśāstra*) is fulfilled; therefore, the rule regarding the subsidiaries need not be resorted to again and again. Furthermore, in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was explained that when conforming to time, there is a restriction of the occasion (*nimitta*). Consequently, even the occasion must conform to the time which is a subsidiary element integrated only once.

[The opponent argues: "Only once; otherwise, there would be no conformity to that [time], just as in the case of an action. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that this is not correct—that it should be performed only once. For an action, when it arises, arises already conjoined with time;
thus, it makes known the living of that specific time and is therefore called the "occasion" (*nimitta*). It does not, however, imply that it is something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) as well.
It brings about the [status of being a] cause (*nimitta*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the status of time as a cause was stated by us in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*), then because that time is eternally connected [to the action], and because only one capable of bringing it about has the qualification (*adhikāra*), there is necessarily [an occurrence] at another time.
By this reasoning— that because of the incapacity to bring that [result] about, it necessarily implies at that very time the living as the occasion—
it does not, however, establish that the occasion itself is something to be enjoined; and since that occasion is not enjoined, it remains non-injunctive.

This is the meaning. Since the repetition of the occasion (*nimitta*) exists and there is the capacity for the inclusion of the time, one cannot say that the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled, because the qualification (*adhikāra*) recurs. Therefore, it pertains to that specific time.
