Life during the interval between full moons serves as the occasion that repeatedly impels the performance of the scriptural injunctions. It is well said that the performance must be carried out whenever the time arrives; thus the indicative mark (liṅga) has been stated.
Likewise, the internal sacrifice.

But has it not already been stated that when the cause (nimitta) recurs, the effect (naimittika) also recurs? Therefore, when the breaking [of a vessel] and so forth recur, the recurrence of the occasional rites such as the *homa* offerings has already been established. By what specific distinction, then, is this now being extended by analogy (*atideśa*), since in the absence of a distinction there would be equality?
Rather, there should be only one performance. However, there is this distinction:

because the oblations caused by the breaking [of the vessel] and so forth serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that once the requirement is fulfilled by a single performance, the assistance required by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is accomplished, and thus the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is satisfied.

The meaning of this is as follows: although these [rites] are occasional (*naimittika*), nevertheless, because they are auxiliary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), they are performed for the sake of assisting the sacrifice. And since this sacrificial performance is a single unit, once the assistance to the primary rite (*pradhāna*) has been accomplished by the performance of an auxiliary even once, there is no further performance even when [the occasion] has ceased, as there is no further purpose.

Because of their existence [as distinct acts]. However, the performance of the Agnihotra and other such rites is not by virtue of their ritual application (*prayoga*), but rather by the force of the occasion (*nimitta*); thus, their repetition is logical.

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that while it is true that the performance is solely for the sake of assisting the sacrifice (*kratu-upakāra*), nevertheless, there is a distinction [between them] at each successive instance.
Furthermore, in the case of the arising of [the result] through the sacrifice (*yajñādi*), such assistance is not capable of preventing repeated qualification (*adhikāra*). Now, one might object:
"Let there be repeated qualification; nevertheless, since it would be purposeless, what will that qualification accomplish?
It is incapable of prompting further performance"—this is the sense. He refutes this: "It is not purposeless."

It has been stated in the section on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) that for the sake of establishing independence (*anapekṣatva*), the purpose follows from the qualification (*adhikāra*), not the qualification from the purpose. The meaning of this is: when the qualification is repeated, then the injunction (*vidhāna*) is repeated; just as [in the case of] the enjoined—

And there is the postulation of its purpose: it is postulated that as many times as the occasion (*nimitta*) occurs, so many times must the occasional rite (*naimittika*) be performed to accomplish the benefit to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*), and not otherwise. Therefore, the performance (*prayoga*) here also extends as far as the qualification (*adhikāra*). However, this is the distinction: for that [latter] lasts until the performance of the primary rite (*pradhāna*), because its qualification pertains to that. [This applies to] the *agni*—
[Page 120] Regarding the incidental rites performed by the *hotṛ* and other priests:
this is the distinction, namely that those [rites] are to be performed independently.

The oblations for breaking [the vessel] and so forth should be performed as long as the principal rite is being carried out, because only one who is authorized for the principal rite has authority regarding the oblations for breaking and so forth; for in the absence of the principal rite, there is no authority. This is based on traditional practice (ācāra).

Raising the objection: "But since [qualities] such as 'desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*) are also qualifiers of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), it would be logical that when the qualification recurs, the performance (*prayoga*) must also recur;

so how can this be the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?"—the proponent of the prima facie view replies: "In the case of following one's teacher and so forth, the non-returning [of the student] is not a qualifier of the qualified person."

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) does not consider even a "sign" (*nimitta*), such as the arrival of a teacher, to be a qualification of the person entitled to perform the act. This is because he maintains that it is possible for the sign to be syntactically connected with the meaning of the sentence; thus, he does not accept the injunction as "one should please the arrived teacher by rising," arguing instead that the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled once the act of pleasing has been performed a single time.

He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Indeed, the status of being a cause (*nimittatā*) is not possible apart from being a qualification of the person entitled to perform the act (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇatva*).

The extension (*atideśa*) of the phrase "like that" has this meaning: with respect to the performance [of the rite], the very state of being a cause consists in being a qualification of the person entitled to perform it.

Without [the cause], it is not possible, because the performance [of the rite] is based solely upon the qualification. Therefore, as long as there is a cause, so long must it be accepted by force as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). For this very reason, since the sun’s transit (*sūryasaṅkrānti*) and so forth lack a connection with the person, and since that which is unconnected cannot logically function as a qualification, it is impossible for them to be qualifications of the qualified person.

The sign [is not the cause]; rather, it should be understood that the connection of bathing and other rites is solely by way of time. Therefore, since arrival is a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite, when the rite is repeated, the entitlement is repeated; thus, one must rise again [to perform the rite]. [This concludes the section on] the Brāhmaṇa.
But surely, in this case, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) itself is not tenable; for it is not logical that there be a prima facie position without seeing a statement,
nor that there be a final conclusion (rāddhānta) based on a statement.
"Because this treatise is devoted to logic (nyāya). To this it is replied:

Since attributes such as "as long as one lives" cannot logically function as qualifications of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa), the qualification must be supplied by implication (adhyāhārya), just as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, because of the absence of a specified qualified person.

Such is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*). What is the reasoning? The answer is: it is not tenable for an entity that is not to be accomplished (*aniṣpādya*) to function as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).
Why? Because only that which is either to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or already established (*siddha*) is connected with the state of being "pertaining to the next world" (*pāralaukikatayā*).
Whatever is heard in a sentence, whether it be something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or something already established (*siddha*), all of that is connected with the action. What follows from this?
This results: the established is [connected] as the producer (*niṣpādaka*), and the thing to be accomplished as the fruit (*phala*). Life is established; therefore, it is the means (*sādhana*).
He considers that it is precisely the *bhāva* (the efficient force) that is logically appropriate.

However, since the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is connected as a result, and because its status as a result would otherwise be untenable, it functions as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, heaven and the like serve as qualifications of the qualified person, whereas living and the like do not.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: the mention of debts indicates that [the rites] must necessarily be performed; it makes known that living constitutes a qualification for eligibility (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).
Otherwise, the necessity of their performance would be untenable. Now, [one might object]: how can that which is already established be a means...

"Since a relationship is not possible without an entity, what will perception accomplish here?"—this means that perception is baseless and is merely a delusion. To this it is replied: We have already stated in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* that [the injunction] does not belong to the agent.

Regarding the term *niyoga*: if it were the *niyoga* (command) of the agent (*kartṛ*), then living would be a qualification of the agent. However, when the agency belongs to one who is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—that is, the qualified person (*adhikārin*)—then living is indeed a qualification of that person to be enjoined.

Anticipating the objection that even so, since [the qualification] cannot function as a qualifier of the agent, the syntactic connection (anvaya) is not possible, he says: "Nor can there be the assumption of a [new] entitlement (*adhikāra*) by means of the *Viśvajit* principle. (Mātṛkā).
"In the action... (Mā).

And it has been stated in the very *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* that this [qualification] extends as far as the word "as much as" (*yāvat*); there is no [logical] connection for its being a qualification of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇatā*).

And the foot-soldier [is not a qualifier], because he does not serve as a delimiter, just like heaven (*svarga*). Just as it was established in the eleventh [chapter] and others that it is impossible for heaven to be a qualifier of the agent, so too it is not the case that anyone performs an act while not living; thus, he demonstrates that the subsequent status of heaven—as a qualifier of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—once it has been construed as the goal (*sādhya*), is also untenable.

Furthermore, it has been shown that even in the case of heaven and the like, which are to be accomplished through an injunction (*niyoga*), their status as objects to be accomplished arises only because they serve as qualifiers of the person entitled to the action (*niyojya*); therefore,
being an object to be accomplished is not the cause for something being a qualifier of the person entitled to the action in the case of an injunction.
Now, one might object: "Granted that living constitutes a qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya), even so, how can it be something that must necessarily be performed? To this he says:
"It has been stated that the qualification of the person to be enjoined is also the qualification of the entitled agent (adhikārin)."
Only one who is enjoined becomes an *adhikārī* (one entitled to perform the rite).
Since entitlement implies a necessary duty, its performance is mandatory; otherwise, the consistency of the scriptural indications regarding debts (*ṛṇa*) would not be established.

Even according to that [interpretation], it is more logical that they are indeed qualifiers of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Therefore, it is established that these rites are indeed obligatory (*nitya*) because their occasion (*nimitta*) is obligatory;
thus, the view [of the opponent] is not a delusion, as its source is possible. This is the meaning.
Alternatively, because the word "Brāhmaṇa" is heard in the statement concerning debt, the entitlement belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone; for an entitlement is understood from a qualification,
whereas the word "Brāhmaṇa" is not heard in the injunctive portion [of the primary rule], and this explanatory passage (arthavāda) serves another purpose.
That is to say, because it is supplementary to another injunction. An interpretation according to the specific qualification [of the person] is appropriate;

it is not by virtue of this that the meaning of this mantra belongs to a Brāhmaṇa, [contrary to what might be suggested] by the statement regarding the debt of Soma, Vedic knowledge, and progeny. Mā... [text fragment].
[The word] *kāraḥ*.

This is the intended meaning: in the injunction regarding life-long [observance], the word "Brāhmaṇa" found in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

If that were the case, then because the sentence functions through the combined operation of its parts, the term "eligible person" (*adhikāri-pada*) might indeed be interpreted in accordance with it, since it would be a supplement to another sentence. However, because the injunction to live as long as one lives (*yāvaj-jīvā-codanā*) conveys a meaning independent of that [other sentence], it is not proper to describe the eligibility of the Brāhmaṇa alone; for [the latter] depends upon its source. Following the lifelong [obligation] which is the basis for the observation, the Brāhmaṇa—
The mention [of the word] should be understood as being illustrative (upalakṣaṇa).
Thus ends the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the commentary composed by the great teacher Śrī Śālikanātha.
The *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*:
The Third Pāda of the Sixth Adhyāya.
There would be activity toward every possible power, because the instruction is of such a nature. || 1 ||
In this treatise, since many of limited intellect float upon the surface of the profound great lake of logic,
we shall first begin with the investigation of logic itself— regarding that, some say:

They raised this objection: "Just as being alive and so forth are qualifications of the qualified performer (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), so too is the capacity to perform the entire collection of primary and auxiliary rites. In that regard, this deliberation does not concern one who is capable of carrying out the performance in its entirety—[namely,] whether [the rite may be performed] even by omitting the auxiliaries."

Should the performance be carried out, or not? For one who is incapable, there is indeed no entitlement, just as a Śūdra has none regarding the Agnihotra and other rites. Furthermore, some, with the intent of providing a resolution, assert that this [principle] of performing according to one's capacity applies only to the commencement [of a rite].

One is liberated; however, this applies to one who has already begun [the practice]. Therefore, for one who was initially qualified by virtue of the capacity to perform all the constituent parts, even if that capacity should subsequently fail, the performance must indeed be brought to completion due to the firmness of the prior qualification. For this very reason, Śūdras and others do not perform the obligatory *agnihotra* and other such rites; at the very moment their qualification is determined, they—
As for the claim that "it is capable," even that argument melts away like a wax ornament in the flames of the intellects of those who hold opposing views.

For instance: one becomes an *adhikārī* (eligible person) through the connection with the qualifications of eligibility (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), and such a person proceeds [to act]. Furthermore, the persistence of eligibility must be admitted until the completion of the performance, up to its conclusion. Otherwise, for one whose eligibility has ceased, the performance would follow neither from the verbal injunction nor from any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In that case, even if the performance were underway in the interim, should there be an incapacity, [the agent]—possessing the capacity...

Since the qualification (*adhikāra*) has been transferred to a portion of Rādhikā, that qualification indeed ceases. And for one whose qualification has ceased, what is the basis for the completion of the ritual performance already commenced?

If it is argued that it is out of fear of the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), then there would be no distinction between occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites. The teachers maintain that this section of the treatise applies to those rites that terminate upon the occurrence of a specific occasion (*nimitta*). Therefore, at the time of commencement, the performance—

Alternatively, it is argued that performance [of the ritual] in the middle [of the procedure] is improper for those lacking the *śakti* (capacity), because they lack the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*).

Furthermore, as for what someone has said— that whatever is obligatory (*nitya*) must be performed with all its constituent parts (*sarvāṅga-yukta*)— that is impossible in the case of obligatory rites.

The meaning of the scripture is simply performance according to one's capacity; therefore, there is eligibility for obligatory rites even in the absence of the ability to assemble all the constituent parts.

This [position] is a mere fabrication of one's own fancy by someone who disregards the Mīmāṃsā system. For instance, there is no understanding of the principle that "qualification [for a rite] follows its application. Consequently, even for one who is living, whatever is enjoined must necessarily be performed by that person alone for whom it was enjoined, and not by anyone else; and such a rite is accompanied by its permanently required auxiliary elements.

That [performance] must necessarily be carried out only by one who is capable of accomplishing the entire procedure; what concern is it for one who is incapable? Nor is this scriptural injunction impossible, because at some time the capacity to perform all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) may indeed arise; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) would find no scope for application. This is trivial. Furthermore, if it were the case that "whosoever is capable of as much as he can," [then the rule would hold].

If it were the case that for the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) only that much is enjoined [as is required by one's specific capacity], then— since Śūdras and others are devoid of the sacred fires and Vedic knowledge— the performance of the rite would be enjoined as being entirely devoid of those two; consequently, they too would be entitled to the performance of the *agnihotra*, which contradicts all established tradition.
Likewise, others say this: "In this case, since there is no fruit in the objects ending with the *nimitta* (condition), there is no performance prompted by that [fruit];
nevertheless, because there is no dispute regarding the accomplishment of the *niyoga* (injunction), the *niyoga* itself is the motive for performance for the sake of its own fulfillment."

It must be accepted that [the injunction] implies [the performance of the whole], because otherwise it would not be established. Since the fulfillment of the *niyoga* (obligatory mandate) is obtained through the performance of the entirety as prescribed, it implies the performance of the whole and not of a partial one. Nor is it proper to maintain that sometimes the whole is the means of accomplishment and sometimes a partial one; for the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to the entire collection.

Because they are prescribed by the ritual injunction (*vidhi*) to be taken up simultaneously; and because it is assumed that what is so taken up possesses the capacity to accomplish the result. If even a deficient [performance] were capable of accomplishment, then why would one not perform the rite even after abandoning the primary act (*pradhāna*), just as one might abandon the auxiliary acts (*aṅga*)?
Furthermore, why is the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarma*) not accepted when they are deficient? If you say "because the fruit is not attained," we reply: no.

Because the accomplishment of the fruit depends upon the *niyoga* (the injunction), the foremost Mīmāṃsakas have maintained that the fruit, which occurs at a later time, arises from the *niyoga* alone. And if the fulfillment of the *niyoga* occurs even when it is incomplete, why should this not be the case here as well? If, on the other hand, it is held that the *niyoga* must have its entirety accomplished here, then has this *niyoga* been banished by the royal decree even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*)?
Thus, this section is to be respected only by those whose intellects have been deluded by faith.

Here, [the followers of] Prabhākara, out of the dullness born from their zeal for service, formulate [the following objection]: "It is true that capacity (*śakti*) is a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*);
nevertheless, this inquiry is indeed appropriate. For persons are of two kinds: those whose capacities are obscured and those whose capacities are manifest."
And there are those whose powers are not obscured.
Among them, although they possess power, they do not obtain the performance that is the fruit of that power due to the influence of obstacles. But how is it known that they possess power?
For that [power] is to be inferred from its fruit; in the absence of the fruit, what is the means of knowledge for it? To this it is replied: that very [power] which existed previously...

Having been perceived while performing an action, that very same agent is subsequently perceived not to have performed it; and again, upon the occurrence of other causes, he is perceived performing it.
In this regard, should one postulate the destruction and production of the capacity (*śakti*), or rather its concealment and its disappearance?

In this regard, since the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmin*), one does not assume the destruction of a prior capacity followed by the production of another capacity. Rather, because we observe the non-arising of the effect in the interim, we consider it to be merely an obstruction;

and because we observe the arising of the effect once again, we must conclude that this obstruction has simply ceased. Therefore, even in the absence of performance [of the rite], [the result follows].

It is easily understood that there exists a power (śakti) which has been obscured. In this regard, because power is a qualification of the eligible person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa), and because its existence remains unchanged even when it is obscured, eligibility certainly persists for those whose power is obscured. For the state of the person existing prior to the performance [of the rite] is the qualification for eligibility, not the performance itself, since the latter depends upon eligibility.

Because [qualification] is not possible prior to [the attainment of] authority (*adhikāra*). Therefore, capacity (*śakti*) alone is the qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). And that capacity exists even for those whose power is concealed; thus, eligibility has been described. However, as for those such as Śūdras who are said to be [unqualified] by their very nature, and those such as the blind whose capacity is utterly severed—for them there is no eligibility precisely because of the absence of capacity. Among them, those whose capacity is merely concealed...

When they possess the qualification (*adhikāra*), yet there is a non-performance of some auxiliary (*aṅga*), the question arises: does performance occur because of the existence of the firmness of qualification, or does non-performance occur because of the absence of the auxiliary? [The latter view holds that] their qualification does not exist precisely because of the absence of capacity; in that regard, for those whose capacities are obscured, even though qualification exists—this is the deliberation. And this [deliberation] occurs both at the commencement and during the middle of the performance.
It is equal [to the previous case].

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers as follows: although there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) for those whose capacities are obstructed, nevertheless that entitlement indeed ceases due to the deficiency of the means (*sādhana-vaikalyāt*). For the application (*viniyoga*) is restricted to the limit of the occasion (*nimitta-paryanta*), being accomplished through the performance of the ritual in its entirety.
It is understood [as follows]: when the entire [rite] is not performed, then, because the means (*sādhana*) is deficient, there is no accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*);

and due to the absence of that [accomplishment], the person has no entitlement (*adhikāra*). Since entitlement to the ritual acts exists as a means toward the task (*kārya*) characterized by the mandate which is connected to the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), even if the cognition of entitlement has arisen, it comes to dissolution. This is so even if, in the case of a compulsory rite (*nitya*), [the result occurs] despite deficiency.

If the accomplishment of the *niyoga* (the mandate) were [to occur] then, it would likewise apply to the subsidiary action (*kārya*). Consequently, performance even by abandoning the primary action would follow, because there would be no distinction for the primary action in its being a means together with the subsidiaries. But the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: True, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is enjoined only as far as it is prompted by the injunction of entitlement; only to that extent is the [mandate] determined.

The accomplishment of the purpose of yoga does not occur merely by that which has been enjoined, as in the case of sublation (*bādha*). Even though all [elements] are auxiliaries (*aṅga*), when some auxiliaries are sublated, the accomplishment of the goal occurs through only those many elements that are made to be performed by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*); likewise here too, it is the injunction of qualification alone that establishes the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*), and not another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it [the injunction] impels only as much as is required.

That alone leads to the accomplishment of that [result]. Furthermore, there is the application of what is possible, not of what is impossible. Therefore, it is understood that when there is a qualification (*adhikāra*), the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*)—in cases where the occasion (*nimitta*) is the limit—must be accomplished by performing as many auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) as are possible.

As for what was said—that even a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*) would be the same—we reply: in the case of a rite for a specific desire, this is because it is connected to the attainment of the fruit.

The sacrifice and so forth, which have become the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the fruit of the entitlement (*adhikāra*), are indeed the object (*viṣaya*). However, there is no status as an instrument with respect to the fruit for that which is devoid of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And the procedure is complete; therefore, even in the absence of a single part, by means of the procedure—

Since emptiness (*śūnyatā*) cannot function as an instrument, that which has not become an instrument cannot be an object. In the absence of the "how-to" procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there is no object;
and in the absence of an object, there is no mandate (*niyoga*). In the absence of that [mandate], there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*), and thus the accomplishment of performance is not possible.

For this very reason, one should not suspect that performance would still occur even upon the abandonment of the primary element. [This is because] in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no other fruit—

Because [the agent] exists, that which has become an instrument cannot be the object; thus, in the absence of the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" procedure), since there would be a mere recognition of the object, the application of the *niyoga* (the mandate) would follow, and therefore entitlement (*adhikāra*) is appropriate. And by the force of that [entitlement], the performance [of the rite] also occurs—this is the meaning of the text.
Here, the Teacher considers entitlement as extending up to the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).

Thus, he shows that this consideration does not apply to optional rites (*kāmya*). He states the nature of the consideration: "Does the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) itself disappear when the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are not combined? Or [does it remain] because, if the auxiliary parts are not combined, the purpose of the injunction—which is to be accomplished through the performance of the whole—is not realized, and thus there is an absence of qualification (*adhikāra*)?"

[Objection: The status of being a *nimitta* (condition) for the *jīvana* (life) and so forth would indeed disappear, because there is no performance [of the rite] even when that [condition] exists. [Reply: Or rather, the status of being a *nimitta* does not disappear; for, according to the reasoning already stated, since the purpose of the *niyoga* (obligation) is accomplished by the *niyoga* itself even when the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are not fully performed, once the entitlement (*adhikāra*) exists, it is entirely appropriate for the status of being a *nimitta* to apply to the performance.

He explains his own statement as follows: "This is what is meant: does there arise an understanding of the qualification (*adhikāra*), or, in the absence of such understanding, is there some manner of performance?"

When there is an understanding of the qualification (*adhikāra*), then the status of being a condition (*nimittatva*) simply ceases to exist. However, when performance occurs somehow due to a lack of understanding of the qualification, then the status of being a condition does not cease. But surely, when the performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is impossible, there is no qualification at all for that person; and for one who possesses the qualification, the performance of the ritual in its entirety is indeed possible.
When it is not known what kind of thing this "to be considered" (*cintya*) is, he says:

"Is it not the case that this is simply a doubt whose meaning has not been made explicit? This is now clarified: even when one who is authorized for a ritual action characterized by all its constituent parts possesses the capacity for performance at some time, despite the non-departure of his capability—
The doubt is explained by the very demonstration of the specific object [of the thought], "I shall think.
For one whose capacity has not departed— who is thus authorized for an action distinguished by all its constituent parts— there arises an inability to perform the ritual application (*prayoga*).
The inquiry is whether the state of being a cause itself disappears or not. But how can there be both the non-disappearance of capacity and incapacity?
For capacity is indeed the same as power (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, to say that capacity has not disappeared and yet there is incapacity is mutually contradictory. He provides the resolution:

Incapacity may arise from either divine or human contempt, but not from one's own nature; for the power of one's inherent nature certainly exists, and thus the non-departure of capability is described.
The suppression of power (*śakti*) due to divine causes such as disease, or human causes such as physical assault, is called "incapacity" (*aśakti*).
This, however, has already been stated previously. Therefore, it is well said that there may be incapacity at times. Now, even regarding this suppression—
Regarding this, he states that there is indeed no lack of qualification for one who possesses the capacity:
"And capacity, which is the cause of qualification, does not depend upon the presence of an accessory (upadhāna)."

Capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed an intrinsic qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) for the person entitled [to perform the rite], and it does not depend upon an external adjunct (*upadhāna*). By the word "adjunct" (*upadhāna*), an entity that serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is intended—namely, medical treatment and the like, which serve to remove obstacles. Furthermore, capacity that is merely unobstructed is not the cause of entitlement; rather, it is the intrinsic capacity. For there is no such thing as an absence of obstruction prior to the performance of the action.

It can be said that capacity is [the means] by which [an action] is possible. And the effect is indeed performance. Thus, if there were performance, and if there were a determination of unimpeded capacity, then there would be entitlement (*adhikāra*); and if there were entitlement, then there would be performance—this would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Therefore, innate capacity is the qualification of the entitled person. Likewise, for one who is already entitled, the removal of obstacles [is established].

Just as there is the removal of the eyelashes that cover the eyes during rites such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), a doubt arises: does the entitlement (*adhikāra*) also conflict with the capacity for action, as in the case of the impairment caused by a cataract or other disease; or, because it is independent of such external conditions, is one still entitled even when not acting? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) observes:
It is true that for one who does not understand [the truth], the capacity that exists by its very nature as unconditioned (*anupādhika*)—

which is independent of the removal of obstacles— is the cause of entitlement (*adhikārahetu*); however, because that [capacity] is for the sake of engagement (*pravṛtti*), it is of no avail even if it exists, since engagement may be obstructed by conditions (*upādhi*).

The meaning of this is as follows: the purpose of capacity (*sāmarthya*) is its activity (*pravṛtti*). In that regard, if there is no activity even when capacity exists, then that which exists is ineffective; for even when it exists, [it may be so] due to the force of an obstruction.

Because activity is not possible; since activity being absent, the purpose of the injunction (*vidhyartha*)—the complete performance that is to be accomplished—is not achieved, the qualification (*adhikāra*) ceases altogether. Therefore, activity must be undertaken only by including all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). It is precisely here that there is the cessation of the mandate (*niyoga*), which is the function of the qualification, and not from the performance of only a portion. Otherwise, what would be the difference regarding the fruit?

Regarding the offices that culminate in the final goal: even this office, which culminates in the fruit, is indeed *anaupādhika*—that is, independent of any limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Furthermore, one does not become capable of performing the task through an inability to act; rather, one is authorized (*adhikṛta*) when one is in such a state as to be endowed with all the necessary components.

To this, it is replied: we shall explain the distinction regarding those [obligations] that culminate in a result; however, in the case of those that culminate in a cause (*nimitta*), the understanding of entitlement (*adhikāra*) is described as persisting even when there is an incapacity to act. If there is an incapacity to act, how then is it described? It is described in this way: for when the understanding of entitlement is unconditional (*anaupādhika*), the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*)— [The text continues: ...is indeed established. Therefore, even if one is unable to perform the action, the entitlement remains. This is because the entitlement is determined by the mere presence of the cause, not by the capacity to act. Consequently, even one who is incapable must still undertake the rite, provided he possesses the requisite qualification. Thus, the obligation is maintained despite the lack of functional ability. This concludes the discussion on the nature of entitlement in relation to causal obligations.
It cannot be denied that there is indeed no entitlement for Śūdras and others due to their innate lack of capacity;
however, this does not mean that an entitlement which has arisen by virtue of natural capability can be obstructed by a subsequent incapacity.
The obstruction of Rādhikā’s authority.
Therefore, those who know the practice maintain that one whose authority has not departed must perform [the rites] according to one's ability; thus it is said:
Performance according to one's capacity exists in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*).
For this very reason, they say that within the context of these obligatory duties, there is both a primary and a secondary meaning of the scriptural injunction.
The Mīmāṃsakas raise an objection:
What is this incoherent prattle like that of a *kūśmāṇḍa* spirit? It concerns whether a certain portion of the meaning of the scripture is secondary (*gauṇatva*) or primary (*mukhyatva*).
He refutes [the objection]: "You alone are the one who engages in idle chatter here."
The Mīmāṃsakas are not mere babblers. [The opponent] asks, "How so? The answer is:

since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is unimpeded even when there is incapacity, and since performance according to one's capacity is both perceived and implied by the purpose, it is not contradictory to include [the available parts] even when the scripturally enjoined [parts] are absent.
Now, one might object: "If that which is enjoined by scripture (*śrauta*) is abandoned, why not abandon other things as well? To this he replies:
"As long as one lacks the capacity [to perform them], so long they are not undertaken; nevertheless, among those things that can be performed, nothing at all [is to be abandoned]."
"There is a means of valid cognition [regarding what] can be taken up.
For by this, the understanding according to one's capacity is the cause; therefore, something must be abandoned and something else must be taken up.
He objects again: "What follows from the secondary sense?
Let it be so; what does that matter for the actual object? Even if nīvāra and other grains are taken up because of the primary object, how [is that so]?"
He refutes the objection regarding its being secondary (gauṇatva):
for it is not possible to adopt that very [meaning] while having accepted it as the primary sense (ārtha).

As long as the subordinate nature (*gauṇatā*) of the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding rice (*vrīhi*) is not stated, the employment of wild rice (*nīvāra*) is not possible. Now, one might ask: "Since the ritual action is accomplished even by adopting a slightly deficient meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding rice, how can there be 'subordinate nature'? To this, he says:

For it is not the case that a greater similarity of parts does not arise through dependence upon *nīvāra* grains; for one who employs *nīvāra* grains alone is able to effect the employment of a greater similarity of parts, and not otherwise. Or, regarding the *nīvāra* grains being employed—
The status of being secondary (gauṇa) is established among the [six] measures of greatness. Therefore, it is well said that the meaning of the scripture is both secondary and primary.
To the question, "How is this so in other cases?", he says here:
even when certain auxiliary elements that provide remote assistance (ārādupakāraka) are omitted, a cognition of similarity arises because some [other] elements are still adopted.

Just as in the world, when a certain object endowed with many qualities is seen at one time and later, at another time, is seen by observers to be devoid of some secondary qualities, they speak of it, saying, "This appears to be just like that."

Even though there is no difference in that which possesses the states (*avasthāvat*), the similarity between the distinct states is indeed possible. Therefore, both are established: the primary and the secondary [application], as well as the performance according to one's capacity. The view has been stated: "That very [substance] is to be offered, regardless of its particular form or appearance."
Why is this statement not [considered] a definition (*darśana*)? The answer is:
because these two terms cannot be established as having such-and-such meanings, since they depend upon what has already been established.

With respect to the substance already enjoined, the meanings of the words *yādṛk* (of such a kind) and *kīdṛk* (of what kind) are to be prescribed, and not otherwise. In that case, if the substance has been enjoined as something specifically qualified, then the meanings of the words *yādṛk* and *kīdṛk* cannot be prescribed. Now, if...

Only the substance is enjoined, not its specific quality; even then, since it is already established [by other means], an injunction would be inappropriate. Therefore, it is well said that these are a restatement based on logic.
|| 2 || And the same applies to optional rites, because of the presence of desire. || 8 ||

But was it not shown in the eleventh book that, in the case of one who has a desire for a specific result (*kāmādhikāra*), there must be a performance of all the constituent parts (*sakalāṅgopasaṃhāra*)?
What else is being considered here? To this he replies:
Here, the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices) are the examples; the topic discussed in the eleventh book pertains to the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice).
But here, regarding the modifications (*vikṛti*), by what qualification is there consideration? The answer is:
for here there is no instruction of constituent parts (*aṅga*); rather, the connection is established through functional necessity (*kāryataḥ*).
In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the constituent parts (*aṅga*) are not explicitly taught; rather, they are connected by means of their function, characterized as assistance to the performance.
What is the distinction in this case? This is the distinction: for when the ritual action has been explicitly taught—

Extension (*atideśa*) is preceded by the comprehension of the original instruction (*upadeśa*). In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), only the principal act itself is taught. Therefore, it can be asserted that the qualification (*adhikāra*) ceases because of the inability to perform the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)—which are connected to specific ritual functions—since qualification pertains to the scope of the original instruction.
That which is taught is "instruction" (*upadeśa*). And thus, no restriction is placed upon the scope of that which is based on such instruction.
[The opponent] says: "Let it be so; what is the harm? To this, [the author] replies:

It is not logical that the authoritative instruction (upadeśa) should be restricted by the effect—which is characterized by the assistance rendered to the instruments—since that effect, which serves to accomplish the instructed purpose, cannot override the primary ritual elements (prākṛta-padārtha). This is because the effect exists for the sake of fulfilling what has been taught.

The means of action (*kāryapramāṇa*) is resorted to for the purpose of ensuring that the taught matter is indeed accomplished. Therefore, it is not right to restrict that which has arisen for a specific purpose by that [means]; for the primary factor ought not to be restricted in accordance with its subordinate qualities.

The intention here is as follows: although the mandate (*niyoga*), which consists of the principal act together with its auxiliary parts and is of the nature of a task (*kārya*), can only be related to one who is capable of performing it—since expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) are the causes of relationship—it may indeed be that entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs only to such a person; thus, one who is incapable has no entitlement. However, as for one who is capable...

Thus, one whose power is thus obscured is unable to incorporate even some transferred subsidiary (*aṅga*); for that reason as well, its non-performance in modified rites (*vikṛti*), even those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), is not untenable. Nor can it be argued in that case: "Because there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) with respect to the fruit only when [the rite] has become the instrument (*karaṇa*), and because the status of being an instrument belongs to that which is accompanied by its procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the status of being an instrument is impossible in the absence of subsidiaries."

And since there can be no entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the absence of an object (*viṣaya*), there would be non-performance; for entitlement presupposes an object that is being enjoined. To this it is replied: if entitlement were independent of the task (*kārya*) and were directed toward the results [of actions], then this might be so.

The meaning of this is as follows: since the subsidiaries (*itikartavyatā*) function as instruments (*karaṇa*) when they culminate in the result, and because they possess instrumentality by virtue of their connection with the qualified person (*adhikāra*), and because there is an absence of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) without a task (*kārya*) as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is established that the status of being an instrument is obtained through the connection with the procedure presented by the task. Thus, when the primary sacrifice is enjoined as possessing the qualification, the [procedure] derived from extension (*atideśika*)—

The performance [of the ritual] is by way of contraction (*saṃhāra*). If, on the other hand, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) were to exist even at the conclusion of the fruit without regard for the assistance of the instruments (*karaṇa*), only then would there be an omission of even a subsidiary (*aṅga*) prescribed by extended application (*atideśika*). But this is not the case; thus he says: "And just as one who desires the fruit is entitled even to the primary act (*pradhāna*) taught in the original injunction (*upadeśa*), provided it is accompanied by its purpose—that is, accompanied by the assistance of the instruments."

We shall explain this further in the eleventh [chapter]. He states another distinction between the qualification for optional rites (*kāmya*) and those based on specific occasions (*nimitta*): "And just as in the case of rites ending with a specific occasion, so that the occasion itself may not be lost, even if the rite is deficient..."
It is proper to do so.
1. Atirohita-mā [p. 132]

It is understood as a condition (*nimitta*) with respect to the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). If the performance were not carried out, its status as a condition would vanish; and that is not tenable. Therefore, it is proper to perform [the rite] even if it is defective. The understanding of the result is the condition with respect to the performance, because there is no contradiction in the understanding of the result even in the absence of performance; on the contrary, that [understanding of the result] [remains] upon a defective performance.

The application [of the procedure] is not possible because the fruit is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); since that which is to be accomplished depends upon the instrument (*karaṇa*) together with its constituent subsidiaries (*itikartavyatā*), it is therefore proper here—indeed even in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*)—that there should be a combination of all the constituent parts.
Because actions are dependent [on substances], there would be a distinction [in the case] of another substance. (Sūtra 11)
But has it not been stated that the meaning of the scripture consists of both the primary and the secondary? Furthermore, performance is not possible without the cognition of that [meaning].

If even a single part of the primary meaning of the scripture is not grasped, then what is the point of non-performance? Even when there is an understanding of the secondary meaning, the very same [cognition] is the cause for performance. Therefore, effort must be made toward the cognition of that [meaning].

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But has it not been said that action is known through inference? However, if its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not perceived, how can there be a cognition of it?
If action is understood through inference, and its nature is understood from that inference, then what is the role of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)?"

Regarding the word "patti" (attainment), how can it have that suffix [denoting an action]? He states the established conclusion: there is no fault, because the designation of that suffix is used in the sense of being understood through scripture, not in its own literal form.

Even though the action is inferential (*ānumānikī*), nevertheless, the designation of that action by that very word through another substance is due to its being understood from the scripture as a secondary attribute (*aupādhikatvena*); it is not [understood] by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), and thus there is no fault. Furthermore, it is well said that the lack of connection with the meaning of the scripture is because being understood from the scripture is the cause for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), not the cognition of the essential nature itself. But [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."
Out of a friendly disposition, he explains why it is not stated that there is recognition of the essential nature (*svarūpa*):
"It was stated in the first chapter that recognition of the essential nature does not exist apart from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," and that cognition and action have already been discussed.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of what is not perceptible":

if, in this context, the mention of recognition is due to its being understood through scripture (*śāstra*), then how is it that it was stated that recognition also exists for each respective object of knowledge (*prameya*) by means of its corresponding means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
It follows that [recognition] occurs through perception when the object is perceptible, and through scripture when it is to be understood from scripture. He refutes this:
"This is not so; for it has been stated that recognition is a valid cognition preceded by memory, which belongs to a different system of philosophy."
Recognition is the cognition resulting from the connection with a previous perception; it is the thought "this is that very same thing.
1. The removal of the fruit—[p. 133]

In the case of inference and the like, however, cognition is not preceded by a prior perception; rather, inference and so forth are produced solely through the presence of a mark (*liṅga*) and other such factors regarding the object. Therefore, there is no recollection of a prior perception in those cases. Perception (*pratyakṣa*), on the other hand, arises through the recollection of a prior perception because it is produced by the sense organ aided by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that prior perception; thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is logically established.

Therefore, it is merely the non-apprehension of another object. To this it is replied: No, because recognition of such a kind is the very basis [for the appearance]. It is only the word that functions there, but recognition does not actually exist.
4. Because the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, in the absence of cultured persons (śiṣṭa), there is no tradition from others, since they are not cultured. 13.
But was it not stated in the section on "All-Powerful Agency" (*sarvaśaktyadhikaraṇa*) that even that which is contrary to reality must indeed be performed?

By that, it has already been stated that the performance may proceed even by abandoning rice and other such materials. Therefore, how can there be a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here? The answer is as follows:
Therefore, it was stated thus:

"One must act exactly as it has been heard"—this much alone was said. If it were meant that even when another scriptural injunction is impossible, yet another scriptural injunction must nevertheless be performed, then this present section would not need to be undertaken, even in the case where the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding *vrīhi* rice is impossible.
The meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding the *puroḍāśa* must indeed be carried out.
The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) offers a resolution: "In that case, this is the purpose of that section.
He refutes this: "When a purpose is being sought, what is the use of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)?"
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been established here; therefore, this is not the purpose [of that section]. The supreme resolver says:
"If this is not merely the purpose of the section on the substratum of all powers (*sarvaśaktyadhikaraṇa*), then the prima facie argument must indeed be formulated here."
He himself says: "It was stated in the second [chapter] that, because they are distinct treatises, the injunctions regarding substances are not understood [to apply].
A distinct treatise arises when there is a difference in the independent goal (*sādhya*) or a difference in the auxiliary factors (*anubandha*)."

Subsidiary injunctions (*dravyavidhi*) have no other function apart from what is required by the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*). Nor is there a difference in their *anubandhas* (qualifying elements). Therefore, it cannot be said that they constitute separate scriptural texts (*śāstrāntara*). We shall explain this further in the twelfth [book]. The option (*vikalpa*) arises from the function (*kārya*), not from the status of being separate scriptural texts.

The alternative (vikalpa) will be stated on account of the purpose (*kārya*). It does not constitute a separate treatise (*śāstrāntara*), for if it were a separate treatise, an alternative would be impossible. Why? Because a difference in treatises occurs only when there is a difference in purpose, and not otherwise.

Therefore, if there were a difference in treatises, it would necessarily entail a difference in purpose. However, it has been stated that only those [options] which have the same purpose may be alternatives.
[This applies] to those [injunctions] that have different purposes. Therefore, there is no status as a separate treatise for the injunctions regarding substances.
Let it be so; what follows from that? This follows from it: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," and "One should sacrifice with rice."

Thus, there is one scripture and one scriptural meaning; this is the abandonment of an immediately following injunction and another scriptural injunction, by the abandonment of which other scriptural injunction the meaning of yet another scriptural injunction is performed.

He concludes: Therefore, it is logical that one should perform the rite "he offers the *samidh* oblations" by abandoning its primary meaning [as a mere injunction], and instead carry out the meaning of "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni. This is because a difference in the connection [of the act] results in a difference in the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*), and thus there is a relinquishing of one scriptural injunction for another.

Nor is it logical to perform the practice prescribed by another scripture. [The opponent replies: It is indeed logical; for since there is no further inconsistency with another scripture regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that in the absence of such an inconsistency, the performance [of the ritual] is valid.
To this it is replied: It is true that this is not a separate injunction from the injunction regarding the *puroḍāśa* cake, namely "one should sacrifice with rice.
Precisely because it is not a separate injunction, the performance of the *puroḍāśa*—
Even when the substance is relinquished because it has been heard [in scripture] as "it exists," its performance is appropriate.
If the substance is implied by the scriptural mention of the *puroḍāśa* itself, then what is accomplished by the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains"?
The answer is: the restriction concerns the rice grains (*vrīhīṇām*).

Once it is established that the rice grains are subordinate members of the injunction for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), they are to be employed solely for the sake of fulfilling that injunction, because no other means of accomplishment is known. This applies to the rice grains when they have not yet been [otherwise] prescribed.

The rule that "some substance whatsoever is to be taken up for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action" serves as its purpose. For this rule does not subvert the scriptural status (*śāstrārthatva*) of the injunction regarding the *puroḍāśa* cake;

indeed, if the scriptural status of the *puroḍāśa* injunction were subverted by the presence of the rule, then in the absence of that rule, the meaning of the *puroḍāśa* scriptural text would not be performed. Nor is this [the case].

It destroys the status [of the injunction] as being the meaning of the scripture. Why? Because a restrictive rule (niyama) gains its own existence only when the task to be performed is not already known. Furthermore, there is no comprehension of the task to be performed apart from the scripture. Therefore, it is established that performance occurs even in the absence of a restrictive rule; for since the task to be performed is independent of restriction, the scripture remains purposeful even without a restrictive rule. To the question, "How is it independent of restriction? he says:

"For it is necessarily dependent upon that"—here, there is no such restriction by that [rule]. Therefore, even though it is not a separate scripture (*aśāstrāntara*), in the absence of that [restriction] and in the absence of a restrictive rule, the performance of the rite is established. As for what was stated regarding the injunction of another substance, that has been refuted.
The deity, fire, word, and action [are not to be understood literally] because of their connection with another purpose. || 18 ||

By what occasion, then, has this topic been introduced? If it is argued that even in the absence of an injunction regarding substance or quality, another scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) must be performed as the primary act, then this is already covered by the preceding topic (*adhikaraṇa*). On the other hand, if one considers that [the act] should not be performed in the absence of these [substances and qualities], then that is already addressed by the preceding topic and by the topic concerning "capacity for all" (*sarvaśakti-adhikaraṇa*).

This is contradictory. For in the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that the meaning of the primary scriptural injunction (*pradhāna-śāstrārtha*) is what must be performed. Furthermore, this contradicts the *Sarvaśakti-adhikaraṇa*, which established that even in the absence of the *prayāja* and other subsidiary rites, the primary rite (*pradhāna*) must still be performed. It is replied: By the principle "for there is a desire to perform that [primary act]," this applies to a substitute (*pratinidhi*) that is similar [to the original].

This section is intended as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule] once it has been established. These cases are cited as counter-examples—those in which a similar substitute (*sadṛśa-pratinidhi*) is not permitted and those in which it is not desired.

This very exception regarding the similar substitute is expressed by the sūtra itself: "Not [for] deity, fire, word, or action" (*na devatāgniśabdakriyam*). For this reason, ritual action (*karman*) is also cited here as an example, since the absence of a substitute is possible even in that case.

However, for those who hold the view that this present section is intended solely to refute the introduction of a distinct substance as mentioned in the preceding section, an action (*karman*) would be an incoherent example.

But surely, some maintain that even in the absence of a deity, there is simply no performance of the principal rite either; therefore, in this case, it is not merely an exception to the rule regarding substitutes, but rather aims precisely at establishing the omission of the ritual action. By employing the word "some" (kecit), he shows a lack of conviction in this view. And we shall explain this further. He provides the resolution: "Not so... [nānta-]
This will be an incidental consequence (*nāntarīyaka*). Since the substitution of a deity has been prohibited, this [substitution] will not be an incidental consequence;
rather, the ritual action itself must indeed be abandoned. To the question "How is this an incidental consequence?", he says: "Because of the statement of another argument."
"Because of the absence of the deity, because of the abandonment of the purpose of the ritual action, and because of the connection with another purpose.

Therefore, since the author of the Bhāṣya has stated another argument following the reasoning of the fundamental section (*mūlādhikaraṇa*), we shall set forth that other argument right here. In that regard:

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that there is a desire to perform an action similar [to what was previously established], and that by such a gain, some portion of the meaning of the scripture is indeed subsumed. This being the position reached, it is replied: this is not possible in the case of deities and the like, for the designation "Sūrya" is [merely] a naming.
When wild rice (*nīvāra*) is being taken up, one obtains the acquisition of the commonality of parts belonging to *vrīhi* rice; however, nothing of the sort is obtained here.

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grains," the status of the *vrīhi* as a means extends down to its constituent parts; therefore, it is the commonality of those things that have become the means which [is intended].

Through the acquisition of [physical] strength, there is an assistance toward a single portion of the meaning of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*) in that case; however, with regard to the deity, that is not so. For the meaning of the scripture here does not extend merely to qualities such as luminosity and the like.
Now, one might object: "The injunction 'one offers into the *āhavanīya* fire' is the meaning of the scripture; even if another fire were employed [instead]," [the objection continues].

To the objection that [the term] is generally applied by way of favor, he replies: "In this way, even with respect to the Āhavanīya and other fires, we do not perceive any similarity consisting of a common form in some other substance,
because that which is denoted by the word 'Āhavanīya' is defined solely by its Vedic injunction (codanā)."

Regarding its own nature: since that which is produced by acts such as *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires), being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), is what is denoted by the term *āhavanīya*, there is no evidence that some portion of it is sustained by the taking up of another substance. If, on the other hand, only the word itself were taken up, then no similarity to a mantra would be achieved. Furthermore, if it were taken up as a "mantra" rather than as a "word," the use of the word [in the compound] would be redundant.
There is no apprehension of similarity [to the cause].

Likewise, even among actions (*karma*), because there is an absence of similarity, no similarity whatsoever can be apprehended. Since it is impossible to comprehend the nature—whether common or uncommon—of supersensible actions, due to the absence of similarity, there is no other [means of knowledge].

[Regarding] the feet: now, concerning the status of being a deity (*devatābhāva*), he states another argument for that—namely, that when another substance is taken up as a deity, let alone similarity, even the state of being a deity (*devatātva*) does not exist. What is the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) in speaking thus? This—
The intended meaning is this: he considers that in the absence of that [deity], even the mere performance of ritual action would not be possible.
Deity—
If the sacrifice is not accomplished in its essential nature, even the mere performance of the ritual action is not possible.
Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of a specific deity, the purpose of the scripture is understood from the injunction, 'One should offer the Agnihotra.'"

If it is established in a general sense, why is there no performance [of the rite]? As the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Mīmāṃsaka) has said: "If there were such a thing as a universal 'deityhood' existing prior to the specific injunction, that would not exist at all; for it has been stated that only that which is enjoined as the object of an action is its deity, and nothing else. Therefore, there is no deity in a general sense, neither by way of its own nature nor by way of its specific form.

It has already been stated that the deity is merely an assistant by means of sound. Why, then, could there be similarity or a universal (sāmānya) in it? If that [deity] were the deity, we do not perceive any similarity when another word is employed in the mantra; for even the mantra, which consists of a collection of phonemes, is admitted to have its function [in producing the deity]. For phonemes are [mere sounds] by their very nature.

They are indeed mutually distinct. Their status as *mantras* is only to be understood through their function; it cannot be said that this [status] is sustained when another collection of phonemes (*varṇa-saṅghāta*) is employed, for there is no difference in their sequence. If that were so, then since a sacrifice is impossible without a deity, the scriptural meaning of the injunction "one offers the *agnihotra*" would be abandoned.
The reply is: if, in the absence of the enjoined fire, it is impossible to accomplish [the rite], then what else is better than its abandonment?

By employing the word "yadi" (if), he expresses here as well a lack of commitment [to the opponent's position]: "If the sacrifice does not cease even in the absence of a deity, then let the performance proceed; but if the sacrifice itself could not come into being, then let there be abandonment [of it]. What is the use of this persistence? Therefore, not only is there no similarity, but there is not even a commonality with respect to the deity; in its absence—
And there is no performance [of it] either; this is an inevitable consequence. (6) Moreover, it is prohibited without distinction, for so says the Śruti. (20)
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"Because of the attainment of similarity—that is, because of the attainment of common constituent parts—it is a 'similar substitute' (*sadṛśapratinidhi*); for we shall explain that it is indeed the desire to perform that [rite] which [motivates the substitute]. Therefore, even *māṣa* beans may be used as a substitute.
But surely a prohibition is heard: "Beans should not be used in connection with the sacrifice. How, then, can there be a substitute? He answers:
It is true that where the word "speech" (*bhāṣā*) is heard, that prohibition applies only there; however, in this case,
substitutes are employed because they resemble the substance that was heard, not because they are speech.

The intention is as follows: that prohibition applies where there is a connection between the languages and the sacrifice. Why? Because the prohibition concerns the connection with the sacrifice; however, here there is no connection between the languages and the sacrifice. Here, the languages are inseparable from the performance of what is heard [the Vedic text]. Therefore, the objection does not apply here—this is the view of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this it is replied: It is true that they are substituted because they are similar; however, while they are not the actual language, the status of being the language cannot be denied.
If the status of being the language were denied, then [the rule of] prohibition would apply.
It does not apply there, nor is there any denial of it. He himself says: "In the case of a substitute, the status of being a word (*bhāṣabhāva*) is not intended.
This too is true; however, the prohibition concerns the status of being a word as its object.

A prohibition cannot prevent [the word] from being the locus of the universal *bhāṣā* by virtue of its being the object of that universal. Now, one might argue: "Let it be the locus of the universal *bhāṣā*, but there is no connection with sacrifice. To this he replies: "And its possibility cannot be denied, because its necessary connection with sacrifice is not excluded."
It is possible.

But surely an option (*vikalpa*) would result, because [the practice] is both enjoined and prohibited; and if that were so, how could there be non-acceptance in an absolute sense? To this he says: "Nor is even an option to be suspected here, because it merely implies the possibility of what has been heard [in scripture]."
Regarding the substitute:

there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of those parts of the substance that are explicitly mentioned in the Vedic text, because it is possible for the subject matter of what is not heard in the Veda to exist; and because the explicit prohibition and the verbal nature [of the injunction] have a possible object of prohibition, they do not conflict, as their spheres of application (*viṣaya*) are distinct.
[This is] a conceptual construction. Therefore, because of the fear of transgressing the prohibition, the speech [of the wife] should not be substituted.
|| 7 || Likewise, because the fruit is connected to the master, since the fruit is linked to the performance of the ritual action. || 21 ||
Desiring to criticize the qualified person (adhikārin), he asks: "For whom is this representative to be considered as something to be performed?
Is it being considered whether this representative is to be accepted or not?
The answer is: "It belongs to him who has the authority over the ritual act. The objector says: "If that is so, when the master is at fault, who else can act as his substitute?"
If the owner himself has acted improperly, who then would take up a substitute? He says in a single passage: "This appears like the prattle of a child. He provides the resolution:
In this matter, there is a scope for substitution; that is, in the event of the absence of either the wife or the sacrificer, one may substitute the other, as in the case of *nīvāra* grain.
This being the prima facie view, it is replied: "The two authorized persons must act together in the ritual."

Since the performance would otherwise apply to each woman and man individually, as they are the respective subjects of the injunction, their joint performance is prescribed. What follows from that? This is what results:
One who is authorized performs the action having assumed the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). It has been stated that there is no authorization for the agent (*kartṛ*) alone;

rather, agency belongs to one who is already authorized—this is what is meant by "concomitance" (*sahabhāva*) in that context. [The opponent] objects: True, the operation of the mere causal factor (*kāraka*) requires something else.

Furthermore, the operation of the mere causal factor (*kāraka*) can be accomplished by another means as well. He [the author] refutes this: what is required by those two is their coexistence (*sahatva*), not the state of being joined together (*sahitabhāva*).

When performance is undertaken by virtue of entitlement (*adhikāra*), only concomitance (*sahatvamātra*) is required, not joint agency (*sahakartṛtva*) in the action. Why is it that concomitance is required rather than being joined together? To this he says: "There is no agency for two who are joined with one another; and [only] when there is agency is there concomitance."

Because of the hearing of the singular number, the agents are not joined together as a mutual pair; rather, the coexistence of the wife and the sacrificer exists only within the state of agency itself. Therefore, substitution is not possible apart from the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Substitution is for the sake of accomplishing the capacity to perform the ritual which depends upon that entitlement; thus, it is not [substituted] from the entitlement itself.

The accomplishment of that [result] occurs without [the presence of] the mantra. If one is authorized, it must be the primary [agent] alone, not a substitute; therefore, the status of ownership cannot be substituted.

This very [status], because it is impossible for it to be performed simultaneously as a functional effect, is not a substitute. As for the objection, "Why does the performance not proceed by abandoning simultaneity itself?", that is not the subject matter of this section. Likewise, even for one who is authorized but not the one who leads [the bride], there is simultaneity.
"A woman does not sacrifice," it is also said.
But when a rite involving many [sacrificers] has commenced, one may bring in another [to take her place], so that there is no deficiency in the ritual.

Now, regarding the *satras*, it is considered: when there is a lapse on the part of anyone, do the performers of the *satra* complete the performance by appointing a substitute, or not? And in the case of a lapse by one of the masters (*svāmin*), [do they do so] for the master...

There arises the consideration of whether they complete the *sattra* by appointing a substitute or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: it has been stated above that one who is not the owner does not become a sacrificer; and we shall explain how the person being appointed as a substitute likewise does not become the owner. Therefore, as in the previous case, there is no appointment of a substitute here either.
Because of the statement, "Those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests," the work of officiating must be performed by the sacrificers themselves; and the master is the sacrificer.

For he who partakes of the fruit is called the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). And one who is not the owner does not partake of the fruit; furthermore, it will be stated in the subsequent section that this person being substituted is not the owner. Therefore, even when another person is substituted, because the function of that [original] person is not accomplished, there is likewise an absence of substitution here, just as before.

To this it is replied: for here, what is required is association (*sahitatva*), not mere coexistence (*sahabhāva-mātra*), because they are heard of as agents joined with one another. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing that [association], another agent must be substituted, just like the other factors of action (*kāraka*).

In an action performed by many agents, since each individual possesses the qualification for it, agency must be understood as something to be undertaken. How, then, is the expression "prati-nivi" (towards each) justified? It is because the particle is used in the sense of the master (*svāmin*).
[Objection: If that were so, then one might begin the performance even by employing someone who is not authorized. [Response: Let it be; there is no fault.
When the master has engaged [in the rite] and then becomes incapacitated, it is said that employing another person is also proper because it does not result in a deficiency.

[Objection: But one who is not the master cannot be the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). And if the performer is not the sacrificer, then [the rite would be reduced to] merely the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*).

There would be a deficiency [in the argument]. It is replied: the statement "those who are sacrificers" (*ye yajamānāḥ*) is an application to the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*) precisely as the primary agents (*pradhānakartṛtva*), and not with the intention of expressing their status as sharers of the fruit (*phalabhāgitva*), because that would entail a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Nor does the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) imply that they are subordinate to the act of undertaking (*upādānaśeṣatā*); for, since the mere fact of being the primary agent is already established, no further qualification is required.
He would be the owner because of his connection with that. || 23 ||
But has it not been stated that [the substitute] is taken on account of being the agent? How, then, can there be a doubt regarding ownership here?
For he who begins and completes [an action] is the partaker of the fruit, and he who is the partaker of the fruit is the owner. Therefore, [the substitute] is being appointed as such.

"How can there be a suspicion of ownership when one is not the owner? He provides the answer: "What you have said is true; nevertheless, a certain suspicion does indeed exist. Agency has been stated by way of qualification (*adhikāra*). For a person assumes agency only in relation to an action that involves mastery (*aiśvarya*). Therefore, agency is not possible for one who lacks qualification."
The prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:
when there is qualification for an action, then there is agency; however, if one is not qualified, then there is no agency—this is the sense.

He states the final conclusion: "True, one who is not qualified has no agency; however, others are taken as agents merely to complete the required number, because that [number] is heard in relation to the ritual action. This is the underlying intention:"
For those who have attained the status of authorized agents (*adhikṛta-kartṛtva*), it is possible to bring about the agency of one who is not authorized through means such as conciliation or bribery.

The purpose of others is served by their agency; for the required number [of participants] is fulfilled by that alone. Therefore, only the functional agency (*ārtha-kartṛtva*) is adopted, because the literal agency (*śrauta*) is of no use. Literal agency refers to being authorized (*adhikṛtatva*). Of these two, only the functional one is adopted.
And because of its very application; the other [the Śrauta] is indeed applicable. || 10 || It should possess those characteristics, because of its connection with the ritual action. || 26 ||

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "If he is not the owner, how can he be connected with the attributes of an owner? This is the prima facie view. He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "The connection exists; for this [body] is implied as being for the sake of the owner."
[The status of] being the agent [is established], because of the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for that purpose. For who indeed... [as it is well said].
Its meaning is as follows: these purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as those pertaining to the agent and so forth, are undertaken for the sake of the owner (*svāmin*). And he who is that one—

The agent is established; in his place, many agents are recognized.
