By virtue of the masters' being intended for that purpose, even when the masters themselves function as agents, it implies the possession of those attributes. Thus, by virtue of occupying his position, they come to possess his attributes.
That [desire] is common, for it is indeed the desire to perform that action.

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, when there is a deficiency of the prescribed substance and the performance according to one's capacity is required, it follows that one should simply take up any substance whatsoever.
For there is no [distinction between] a similar or dissimilar [substance] when it comes to the completion [of the rite]."

There is a distinction between the two. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): It is true that there is no distinction at the point of completion; however, regarding the abandonment of the instruction, there is no authority (*pramāṇa*) for doing so as long as it is possible [to maintain it].
As long as...

If even a small portion of the instruction is obtained, that material should be accepted. For the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) belonging to a genus extends to the individual; and the status of being a means belonging to an individual extends to the operation of its constituent parts. Thus, there is no evidence whatsoever for the abandonment of those constituent parts that constitute the means.

[Objection: "But since the effect is established in both ways, what is the use of paying heed to instruction? To this, he says: Because the effect is understood through instruction, and because its acquisition through the nature of the effect must not contradict that instruction, those who know the effect consider it to be acquired in accordance with the instruction. Therefore, it has been well said.
"The taking up [of a rule] is according to what has been heard" (Sūtra 12).
"But because of the specific instruction, that which has commenced applies in the case of an option" (Sūtra 28).

In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is as follows: it has been stated that as long as there is the possibility of what is directly enjoined in scripture (*śruta*), there is no authority for abandoning it; therefore, the adoption of the optional alternative alone is logical, for it serves to fulfill what is directly enjoined.

A similar [substitute] is taken up. Even that which is taken up as a similar [substitute] is for the sake of fulfilling the scriptural injunction (*śrutasampatti*). For if the primary [element] itself is fulfilled through the scriptural injunction, who indeed would resort to a secondary fulfillment?
To this it is replied: the substitution is indeed for the purpose of performance. For when there is a deficiency...

It is a treasure-store; and there is a transgression in the performance [of the rite]. Therefore, the substitution is solely for the sake of the performance. And that which is employed is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the performance, not merely that which is heard in the text.
For the connection belongs to the performance with respect to what is heard, not to the performance itself.

An action (*karma*) that is common to multiple applications (*prayoga*) is to be employed; in that case, its connection with multiple qualities (*guṇa*) is also logical. Why? Because the application does not have what is heard in the scripture (*śruta*) as its constituent part (*aṅga*). To this he says: because the application is to be accomplished merely by the employment of what is heard in the scripture. Since it is established by the mere employment of what is heard once, a connection with multiple scriptural [injunctions] is untenable. [End of] *prayoga*...
And this substitute is for the purpose of fulfilling the requirement [of the ritual], not for the purpose of fulfilling the literal scriptural injunction.
What is meant by this is: it does not serve to fulfill the scriptural tradition. For if that were the case, then even an optional alternative would have to be adopted.

For that [injunction] is for the purpose of accomplishing both hearing and performance. Therefore, only that which is similar to what has been previously acquired should be adopted, not an optional alternative;

the point is that at that time, such an alternative is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*). For in the case of an injunction for non-existence (*abhāvavidhi*), when there is an absence of what was previously heard, what is heard later would be adopted—[but this is not the case here].
Mā. 1. etacchruto... [text fragment]

[Page 141] Regarding the rule of equivalence: for if there were an injunction for barley in the absence of rice, then barley would be employed when rice is unavailable. However, there is no injunction for barley in the absence of rice, nor is there one for rice in the absence of barley. Rather, it is as follows:
Barley and rice have been prescribed as being equal.

Why, then, is there an inclusion of that which is heard later in the case of a prescription of non-existence (*abhāvavidhi*), but not in the case of an equal prescription? To this he says: For a prescription of non-existence depends upon usage, since non-existence is possible only within the context of usage.

It is not employed, because its non-existence would be untenable. But surely, since the performance (*prayoga*) is non-different from that which is to be performed (*prayojya*), the object to be performed is itself a constituent part of the performance. Therefore, even though it is optional, that which is a constituent of the object to be performed does indeed possess the status of being a constituent of the performance; thus, its inclusion alone is logical, because the purpose of the scriptural injunction regarding the option is thereby fulfilled. With this intention, he asks: "Is the object to be performed [the cause]?"

Is it not a factor of the application (*prayogāṅga*)? The sense is that it is indeed so. The answer is: it is indeed a factor of the application, but by way of the object to be applied (*prayojya*), and not like other [factors] by way of the application itself.

Just as that which is prescribed for an absence is a subsidiary of the thing to be employed (*prayojya*) by way of its very application (*prayoga*), so it is not with an optional (*vaikalpika*) element. Rather, since the application is merely another state of the thing to be employed, the subsidiary of the thing to be employed attains the status of being a subsidiary of the application. In that case, because the purpose has been accomplished through the application and because it is designated by the accusative case, it is only a single subsidiary, not all of them.

Since only that which has been specifically prescribed (*upātta*) constitutes an integral part (*aṅga*) of the ritual, only something similar to it may be adopted as a substitute; it cannot be optional. This is because, in the actual performance, such an option would not be an integral part of the rite. Furthermore, even if there were no explicit scriptural injunction, a substitute based on similarity would be improper in the absence of the original. || 13 ||
Because of the absence of the other. || 31 ||

Now, one might object: we do not perceive any distinction between an injunction for non-existence (*abhāva-vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*). For instance, an injunction regarding non-existence is an "injunction for non-existence" (*abhāva-vidhi*). Indeed, such an injunction for non-existence—occurring when there is an absence of capacity for the prescribed material and when the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is lapsing—is not a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because there is no possibility of employing a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for anything; rather, it is simply an injunction (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, where multiple materials may be taken up without restriction, the prescription of only one is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). When there is the capacity to take up [materials], when there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*), and when there is no specific scriptural mandate, even though several substitutes might otherwise be applicable, the prescription of only one has restriction as its result. In that regard, a doubt arises: is this prescription intended for cases where there is an incapacity to procure *soma*, or is it for cases where there are multiple...
Regarding the rule concerning the context of treasure, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the phrase "he shall not find" indicates a lack of capability.

The sense is that "he would not find [it]. Therefore, this is understood to mean: "if he should be unable to obtain the Soma. By this, it is stated that one is understood to lack the capacity for acquisition; however, it is not understood from the phrase "if he has fallen away" (apacarita). Thus, in the case of incapacity, it is an injunction regarding non-existence (abhāva).

To this it is replied: it is not possible to determine the incapacity [of a word] in the same manner as one does for that which lacks substance (*adravyavat*), for we do not know what it is that is incapable.
Just as it was stated in the *Adravyādhikaraṇa*: "Even for that which lacks substance..."

There is capacity for the acquisition of the substance; likewise, even for one who has not yet acquired the Soma, there is indeed the capacity for obtaining the Soma. Therefore, by virtue of that capacity—since such capacity exists innately in all persons—it is possible, provided there is no failure [to act upon it].

That very transgression will be explained by this [text]: because non-existence has incapacity as its result, non-existence is indicated by incapacity through the lack of cognition [of the original substance]. Therefore, since there would otherwise be the contingency of many substitutes when the *soma* is absent for one who is qualified by capacity, it is established that there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding *pūtīka* plants.

Even though the section concerning non-substantiality (*adravyādhikaraṇa*) has already been established, there arises a further doubt: since the word itself directly expresses a lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*), this rule must pertain to that very lack of capacity.
This doubt is refuted by showing that because there is no actual lack of capacity, it is rather "non-existence" (*abhāva*) itself that is indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) through this [word].
The purpose has been stated.
|| 14 || There is no substitute, because of equality. || 32 ||
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "But what is the reason for taking up something similar to the substitute?
He says that one takes up something similar to the substitute due to the delusion that the meaning of the scripture consists of both the primary and the secondary.
He states the final conclusion: A substitute is not for the sake of fulfilling the substitute itself;
rather, it is for the sake of fulfilling what is prescribed in scripture.
One takes up a substitute with the desire to obtain exactly that which is prescribed; even when the substitute is taken up, there is a trace of the scriptural requirement.

Because it is obtained. If that [substitute] is for the sake of that [original], meaning if it is for the sake of fulfilling the scriptural requirement (*śrutasampatti*), then a substitute must be taken that is exactly similar to it, that is, another substance exactly similar to the one prescribed by scripture. For when such a thing is taken, it is logical because it favors a portion of what was heard in the scripture.
|| 15 || It should be so, because it is restricted by the scriptural definition. || 33 ||

One might object: "Is not the very purpose of refuting the injunction of non-existence (abhāvavidhi) that, even in the event of the absence of *pūtīka* plants, one must take up something similar to *soma*?
For what reason, then, is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That very purpose which was stated is now being challenged."

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), where a rule regarding a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is heard in scripture, that very rule must be observed when the commenced rite has been interrupted. For it has been stated that such a substitute is prescribed there for the sake of fulfilling what was scripturally enjoined. However, where the substitution occurs by implication (*arthāt*), it is logical that the substitute should be similar to the scripturally enjoined substance, since the purpose (*artha*) here—
Because of existence:
1. It is not to be accepted—do not.

The intention is as follows: for all injunctions regarding substances are indeed for the purpose of restriction. Therefore, since the *pūtīka* plant is prescribed as a substitute in the absence of *soma*, when that too is unavailable, one must take up something similar to it; thus, in the event of the unavailability of *soma*, one should take what resembles it.
Thus it was argued. To this, the following is stated:
Even where a restrictive rule regarding a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is heard, that restriction does not apply to the substance itself;

rather, this restriction applies even to the specific form of the *pūtīka* plant. However, those qualities inherent in it which resemble the enjoined substance—[those qualities of the enjoined substance...]

The common constituent parts are precisely those that are restricted. Otherwise, there would be an injunction regarding the nature of the *pūtīka* plant itself, rather than a restriction on its substitution, because the non-employment of the *pūtīka*'s own nature was not previously applicable. And this restriction of substitution has been established as an injunction for what is required. Since this is a restriction of substitution, it is therefore equal in meaning here as well.

One should take that which is most similar to the primary substance. However, this is the correct principle here: even among things similar to the primary, one should take only that in which there exist parts of the *soma* common to the *pūtīka*, and not that in which there exist parts of the *soma* merely similar to the *pūtīka*. This is because, in the event of the failure of the *soma*, those [common parts] are fixed as the substitute. And that which is similar to those *soma* parts...
"And that which is similar to the *pūtīka* is to be adopted.
In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the *pūtīka* plants exist as things whose similarity is not required [for the ritual].
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because what is required must be enjoined, only those parts belonging to it [the original substance] are restricted.
When the primary [object] is apprehended, there is indeed the attainment of the primary; for in its absence, there is none. || 35 ||

Where a substitute has been prescribed, the acceptance of the primary substance will be explained in the subsequent section. However, where the taking up of a substitute was not intended, that section would be unnecessary because there is no prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) to refute; bearing this in mind, he says:
"When the prescribed substance has been lost and one who has proceeded to employ a substitute obtains the primary substance..."
In that case, should the primary substance itself be taken up, or its substitute?
By proposing a substitute, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) means that the substitute should be taken up.

To this it is replied: True, that is indeed a resolve (*saṅkalpa*). However, it is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Even though the *nīvāra* grains have been resolved upon, there is no transgression of the prohibition against speaking untruths when they are subsequently abandoned. This is because the transgression occurs only upon the abandonment of a resolve concerning a matter pertaining to the sacrifice.

That is a fault. Furthermore, the resolve regarding *nīvāra* rice is not for the sake of the sacrifice, because *nīvāra* itself is not for the sake of the sacrifice. For in that case, "being for the sake of the sacrifice" consists merely in similarity to what is prescribed by the Vedic text (*śrauta*). Those common parts which are accomplished by the prescribed substances, such as *vrīhi* rice, are what constitute "being for the sake of the sacrifice" there, and not the substitute substance itself. And those [parts] are already obtained when the primary substance is employed. Therefore, one should employ only the primary [substance].

This is the primary rule. Furthermore, since optional items such as rice (*vrīhi*) and the like fall within the scope of what is explicitly heard in the scripture, this resolve (*saṅkalpa*) regarding them is also for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
Therefore, it is logical that there is a restriction: if one abandons that [resolve], there is the fault of transgressing the prohibition against speaking untruth (*anṛtavāda*).
The point having been established that "only that which has been correctly resolved (saṅkalpita) should be undertaken," one of corrupt intent asks:
"But what here could constitute a false resolution (mithyā-saṅkalpanā) by way of being a human goal? For the learned (śiṣṭas) alone are the authority in this matter."

If the learned authorities remember the fault of false resolve (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*) in such a matter, let there be that fault of false resolve for the person; nevertheless, in the ritual (*kratu*), the primary [substance] alone must be employed.
|| 17 || If it is argued that [the rule applies] even when [the ritual] has already commenced: || 36 ||

Furthermore, when the ritual action has already commenced and the prescribed substance is obtained through a substitute, there arises the inquiry: should only the prescribed substance be used, or should the rite be completed with the substitute alone?
This consideration occurs while certain purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have already been performed upon the substitute.

In this matter, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that because a substitute is intended for the purpose of fulfilling what is prescribed by scripture, that very [substitute] must be employed, just as in the preceding section.

Now, it may be argued that certain consecrations (saṃskāra) have already been performed here and cannot be performed again; therefore, for the sake of favoring those [consecrations], [the original substance should be used].

"The completion [of the rite] occurs through a substitute alone"—this is not a fault. Since the purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) exist for the sake of the primary act (*pradhāna*), and the primary act exists for the sake of the successful performance [of the ritual], therefore it is the primary substance itself that must be respected. The sense is that the purificatory acts may simply be carried out [with a substitute].
This being the position reached, it is replied: this is considered even when there is taking up [of a substitute], but not when [the original] has already been taken up.

At the very time of selection (*upādāna*), this is considered: "Is it heard [in the text] or not? It is not selected if it is not heard. And in that regard, since selection occurs according to the application (*viniyoga*), that which is heard is selected in accordance with the application. Wherever something is to be selected, if that which was applied at the time of selection is not obtained, then something else is selected from among those things that ought to be selected. And once it has been selected...

Furthermore, since no other material for the act of taking up (*upādāna*) is possible in that case, the performance must be accomplished by that very same material. Once the performance is completed by means of what has been taken up, even though it was prescribed in the scripture, it is as good as not prescribed at all, because the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled; for the purpose of the scripture is indeed the act of taking up, and that has been accomplished.
Therefore, it must be accomplished by the substitute alone.
18. When there is a conflict between the substance and its consecration, the substance [takes precedence], because the consecration is for the sake of that substance. 37.
When there is a substitute capable of undergoing the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) and the primary substance is incapable of them, for whom is the undertaking of the rites proper?
Because of the scriptural injunction regarding the rites, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that which is capable of the rites to be what should be undertaken;
for when a substitute is taken, the purpose of the scriptural rule concerning the substance is also fulfilled, though it remains merely deficient in its qualities. As for the primary substance...

Since there is indeed the abandonment of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) acquired through hearing (*śruta*), a substitute must be adopted because of that hearing of the refinement. Therefore, it is not so—[p.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: It is true that there is mention of consecration (*saṃskāra*); however, it is the consecration of that which has been heard [in the scripture].
In the absence of what is heard, there can be no consecrations. For consecrations depend upon substances mentioned in the scripture and are auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice;
in their absence, they would simply not be auxiliaries. Therefore, for one who employs the substance mentioned in the scripture, even if...

The preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) do not exist; let them indeed not exist, for even in their absence, the purpose of the primary act (*pradhāna*) is accomplished. For the preparatory act is not the gateway to the substance. Therefore, even in the absence of the preparatory acts, the purpose of the scriptural injunction regarding the substance is fulfilled. [However,] in the absence of the substance...

Furthermore, since the application of the rules of grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) would not be appropriate [in that case], only the form as heard in scripture (*śruta*) is adopted. Effort must be made to establish the correct form of the root *upādā*,
because the reflexive middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would otherwise apply by the rule "āṅo do'nāsya-viharaṇe" (Pāṇini 1.3.20).

19. When there is a conflict between the purpose and the substance, the purpose prevails; because [the ritual] arises even in the absence of the substance, substances are subordinate to the purpose. 39.

Now, in a case where a purpose cannot be accomplished by what is explicitly stated (*śruta*), there the explicit statement is as good as non-explicit, because the purpose for which the explicit statement exists [cannot be fulfilled].
Therefore, in this context, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose, only that which is capable [of fulfilling it] is to be adopted; thus ends the previous section.
This is merely a counter-example regarding the instrument (karaṇa).
[Sūtra 40: There may also be an injunction with respect to a single part.
But is it not already established by the statement that "even in the absence of the *saṃskāra*s, the primary substance (*pradhāna*) must be taken up"? What more is there to be considered here?

The meaning of this is as follows: the remaining ritual acts (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) are for the purpose of the disposal of the substance (*dravyapratipattyarthāni*); they are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the substance. Therefore...

"Even in the absence of that [animal], the substance itself must be taken," [they argue]. The reply is: this is an additional point—the scriptural injunctions for the cutting-off (avadāna) of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) exist. And the status of being a puroḍāśa cannot be established merely by the presence of the primary substance, because the puroḍāśa has a fixed measurement.

The meaning of this is as follows: "He cuts from it" (*asya avadyati*)—this "cutting" (*avadāna*) is prescribed for the *puroḍāśa*. However, the *puroḍāśa* does not consist merely of two cuttings, because the form of the *puroḍāśa* is manifested by a fixed measure.
Therefore, since [the wild rice] is incapable of serving as the *puroḍāśa*, only wild rice (*nīvāra*) should be taken up; this is done in accordance with the requirements of the *puroḍāśa*.

"It is proper to abandon the *vrīhi* rice; therefore, one should take only the *nīvāra* millet. It is proper to abandon the *vrīhi* rice in order to conform to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that only the *nīvāra* millet should be taken. The final settled conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is true that there is a portioning (*avadāna*) of the sacrificial cake, but that [portioning] is not for the sake of the sacrificial cake itself.
What then? It is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is subordinate to the two-fold portioning (*dvayavadāna*) and is not required [as an independent end].
Now, it may be granted that the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is subordinate with respect to the two-fold offering (*dvyavadāna*), yet it is indeed primary with respect to the rice grains (*vrīhi*).

The rice grains are for the sake of producing the sacrificial cake, whereas the sacrificial cakes are for the sake of the two-fold offering. Therefore, it is logical to discard the rice grains—which are subordinate—in order to favor the sacrificial cake, which is the primary element.

It is said: Rice and other grains, which serve as the constituent material (*prakṛtidravya*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) that are directly connected to the two portions (*dvayavadāna*), because the latter is composed of them. Therefore, since the sacrificial cake is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*), its relinquishment (*tyāga*) is logical; whereas, since the rice grains are internal factors (*antaraṅga*), their favoring (*anugraha*) is likewise logical. Thus, it follows that even the sacrificial cake is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) insofar as it serves this purpose.

In that case, nothing else is required; how much less so the remaining rites which serve no purpose? Therefore, only the rice grains should be taken up for the sake of accomplishing the primary act alone. Thus has the *darśana* (view) been stated.
This concludes the sixth chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The third chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The Fourth Quarter of the Sixth Chapter.
|| 1 || In the case of the destruction of the two sacrificial portions, there should be [an offering] from the remainder, because that is for its purpose. || 7 ||

[Objection: But surely, since in such statements as "if one's sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) should perish," there is no possibility of a prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the injunction of a different substance when the portion to be cut off (avadāna) is lost, why has this section been commenced?
[Response: He provides the solution: even in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement, this meaning is obtained through logical reasoning (nyāya); thus, it is intended to demonstrate this.

For it is by means of the syntactical distinction (*vacanavyatireka*) that another substance must be understood; this meaning—that the portion to be cut off is not [taken] from the remainder—is obtained through logic alone. And it is for the purpose of demonstrating that two front halves of a single substance are possible that this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been commenced.
If this matter is obtained through logic alone, what is the purpose of this statement now? The answer is:
we say it is for the purpose of bestowing a specific quality upon the substance.

This is for the purpose of enjoining a specific substance— clarified butter (*ājya*)— which, though not obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), would otherwise be obtained by default when another sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) arrives according to the logical rule (*nyāyataḥ*). If this statement is indeed for the purpose of enjoining a specific substance when the arrival of another substance is established by the logical rule itself, then [it follows] "because of the specific mention" (*nirdeśāt*).
Thus [ends] the sūtra (6-4-2):
"yasya havīṃṣi" ("whose sacrificial offerings...").
How has this been explained with the intention of providing a specific definition?
For by this statement, the arrival of a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) is not indicated.
He explains: "But the prescription of specific substances is for the purpose of making known [the rule] 'from the remainder' (śeṣāt).
The meaning of this is:
although this is for the purpose of prescribing specific substances, it nevertheless makes known that one should not offer [them] from the specific [substances]. Thus...

This is because another substance is indeed prescribed. Therefore, the intention is that this was stated for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). As for the reference to the "remnant" (*śeṣa*), it has already been answered in the *Bhāṣya*: since the ritual functions of the remnant do not necessitate its use, one should not take up another substance merely in accordance with those functions.
[Objection: "Or rather, [the remnant] should belong to those who partake of the remnant, because there is a specific cause [for it]. (Sūtra 3)

But how, in this case, can there be a suspicion of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the remainder alone should be offered again? For the ritual functions of the remainder do not employ the substance;
for if they were to employ the substance, then by them [the substance] would have been employed.

Because [the substance] exists [already], if one were not to perform that [act of offering], the taking up of the material would be useless, and thus there would have to be another portioning out (*avadāna*). But this is not the case. He provides the resolution:

"Even while the fact that the acts of disposal (*pratipatti*) are not the motive remains established, this doubt arises; the meaning of the scripture regarding the remainder is uninterrupted" (1.1.429).
"Because it exists.
Furthermore, its status as a motivator (*prayojaka*) is not being questioned; rather, when the primary [offering] has been offered by means of that, there remains a residue.

It is heard in the scripture that [the offering] is completed by means of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites; thus, there is no further need for that scriptural purpose. Therefore, it should not be offered again.
However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that since scriptures exist for the sake of action, and since the action—the purpose of the scriptures—has already been accomplished.
It cannot be said that there is no logical inconsistency;

for although the remaining scriptural texts are indistinguishable, the performance of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings is for the sake of the ritual action (*kārya*), whereas the disposal of the substance (*dravyapratipatti*) is their purpose.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: that substance which was to have been disposed of by the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and other rites has perished; therefore, because the substance to be disposed of is absent, the purpose of the scriptural injunction has ceased. Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no performance of the remaining rites because they lack an agent to employ them, and that because another disposal rite is prescribed, the substance must not be offered again.
|| 3 || By virtue of the specific injunction, the remainder is to be eaten by others, just like the principal portion. || 4 ||
What is this consideration regarding entitlement (*adhikāra*), or why is there no such consideration?

The answer is: this is a consideration regarding the remainder (*śeṣa*)—namely, who are the eaters—and not a consideration as to whose entitlement it is. He provides the resolution: it is said here that this is indeed a consideration regarding entitlement. [It concerns] the agent appointed to the task...
Is the entitlement (adhikāra) restricted [to the sacrificer], or does it belong even to one who acts without being specifically appointed?
This is what is meant:

is the entitlement considered to belong only to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), such that the entitlement belongs only to one joined with those priests (*ṛtvij*) who have been appointed, or rather to another agent?
Regarding the phrase "even for one who is qualified":

the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), however, maintains that because of the impossibility [of performing such rites] in the case of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and others, there is entitlement even for one whose agent is not specifically enjoined, since there is no restriction on the agent with respect to the *iḍā* offering.

The meaning of this is as follows: if this entitlement (adhikāra) belonged only to one whose agency has been specifically assigned (*viniyukta-kartṛka*), then, because it would be impossible to consume the remnants in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, there would be no entitlement at all. Likewise [it applies] to the statement: "The five, with the sacrificer as the fifth, consume the *iḍā*."

The statement regarding the priests' consumption of the *iḍā* is for the purpose of restriction, meaning "the *iḍā* must be consumed by them alone. And this is appropriate only if, by another scriptural statement, the consumption by others would otherwise follow as a possibility. Nor is that statement intended to include the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Since that [agent] is also already established as the agent, it cannot be said again that there is an application (*viniyoga*) of those things distinct from what has already been applied, because of the absence of direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof. (1.1.431)

[It can be said that there is eligibility even for one whose agency is not specifically assigned, but it cannot be said that there is an assignment of those who are not the subject matter; for in the case of such an assignment, the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest are absent.]
This being the case, it is replied: the entitlement belongs only to one who is already engaged in the performance [of the rite]. Why?
Because an entitlement cannot be asserted on the basis of what is not heard in the text; for entitlements have as their domain only that which is explicitly stated.
Of whatever kind...

The subject matter is heard [in the scripture]; accordingly, the qualification must be described. Since the priests are engaged as performers of the ritual action, the subject matter is understood to be connected with the consumption performed by them; therefore, the qualification belongs only to one who is so connected.
As for the further statement, it is for the purpose of establishing that [qualification].

Since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are engaged as laborers, the consumption [of the sacrificial portion] is obtained by them alone and not by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); thus it has been shown that the statement is appropriate for the purpose of obtaining that [consumption]. In the Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), however, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is exactly like that; since the engagement of others is for the sake of the ritual task, one should not employ a separate entitlement.
For it is understood from the word that the task is indeed to be performed by one who has been specifically appointed.
This is what is meant: [the entitlement belongs to] the appointed person; nevertheless, the efficacy of the task is established by that alone.
[This is] not so, because those who are not part of the [original] group are included as assistants.
|| 4 || Because the purpose is accomplished through the collective connection, there is expiation even when [the act occurs] in only one part. || 10 ||
In this context, it is heard only that "one offers when [the vessel] is broken," but not whether it is when it is entirely broken or when it is broken in one part.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the offering a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the broken vessel itself, or is it for what has been removed by the breaking?
"Kāra" [is used].

By this, a doubt has been raised regarding the doubt of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra). Now, if here there were eligibility for one who possesses a breach (*bhedana*), then, since it would constitute a separate eligibility, it would not be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. And therefore—

Regarding the phrase "contradiction of the context" (*prakaraṇabādha*), the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) is established through the principle of the qualification of those already qualified.
He raises an objection to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): here it is said—“The oblation for one whose [vessel] has broken is enjoined; therefore, ‘one offers when it is broken.’”

Thus, only the act of piercing is heard here; however, no distinction is understood as to whether it belongs to one whose capacity has been relinquished or to one whose capacity has not been relinquished. And in the absence of such a distinction, there would be no ritual refinement for one whose capacity has been relinquished.

We maintain that since the view that the ladle (*pattra*) effects a distinct consecration has been refuted, it is the oblation (*homa*) belonging to that which possesses distinction [the ladle] that is enjoined.

The opponent offers a resolution: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), however, thinking that the distinction is understood solely through its function (*kāryataḥ*), considers it to be a consecration of something already capable; thus, the assumption of an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) is established.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a conflict (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be raised.

This is the underlying intention: when there is a doubt as to whether an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is a directly contributing factor (*sannipatyopakāraka*) or an indirectly contributing factor (*ārādupakāraka*), it is logical to resort to the directly contributing factor because of its internal character (*antaraṅgatva*).

Therefore, it is logical to rely on the view that even the *homa* (oblation) is a directly contributing auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka*), because it possesses a distinct preparatory function (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore,

since a thing cannot undergo a preparatory function once its capacity has been relinquished, one understands through an examination of the purpose that the capacity is relinquished and thus the action is distinct.

Furthermore, this locative case (saptamī) should be understood as in the expression "the cows should dwell in the house" (*agāre gāvo vāsyantām*). Therefore, since it is the locus itself that undergoes the consecration (*saṃskāra*), it need not be stated that the [consecration] ceases when that [locus] is removed. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): It is true that this is so;
however, because of the use of the locative case here, there is no status of being an object (*karmabhāva*) for anything distinct.
For the locative case does not occur when [the word] denotes the object of an action;
as for the instance "let cows be tied up in the house," that is because it is understood as such through another means of knowledge.
But here it is not so; rather, this locative case [in *bhinnena*] denotes the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) alone, and thus it is the cause of that which is distinct.

He states another argument: "And if [the distinction] were something to be refined (*saṃskārya*), then a constant refinement could not be understood as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), because that which is distinct is non-eternal."

The *homa* (oblation) is indeed a constant auxiliary (*nityāṅga*). Accordingly, its gateway (*dvāra*) must also be adopted as something constant. If, however, the gateway were a distinct preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), then because that rite is non-constant, the *homa* which serves as its remedy would also not be constant; consequently, this meaning of the scripture would fail to be consistently connected (*ananvayī*).

In the case of being a *nimitta* (occasioning condition), this fault does not arise. The fault characterized by the conjunction of the permanent and the impermanent does not occur, because when the *nimitta* exists, it is understood to be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) element; thus, the subsidiary is indeed contingent upon the *nimitta*. However, one cannot say that the *aṅga-homa* occurs when the *nimitta* is absent in the view that it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the *nimitta* is not tenable according to the position of those who hold [the agent] to be the qualified performer (*adhikārin*).

"Therefore, the oblation belongs to that which possesses division, and not to anything else. He raises an objection: "Now, why does this [locative case] not become a locative of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*)? The answer is: "No."

This would result in the undesirable consequence of subverting the *āhavanīya* fire, since the *āhavanīya* is prescribed for all *homa* offerings. If it is argued that let there indeed be such a subversion, the author replies: "Otherwise..."
Since it is logical [to interpret it] as an instrumental case (*nimitta-saptamī*), no contradiction can be asserted even if that interpretation is accepted. Now,

why is the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-sambandha*) not simply stated, rather than using a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) to establish a distinction?
Regarding the term "the sign":

why is it that the primary oblation itself is not indicated by this much alone, and instead another separate oblation is resorted to, wherein the breaking [of the vessel] serves as a qualification for the performer?

The answer is as follows: For that which concerns an already established fact (*siddha-viṣaya*) is possible; and it has been stated that the Veda possesses no authority regarding such established facts.

If there were instruction concerning an established fact even in the Veda, then [the relationship between] the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument as presented.*

The sentence would terminate in the mere existence [of the act]. But this is not the case, because it is an instruction for performance; therefore, it is indeed an injunction for the performance of the oblation (*homa*). And it has been stated that, in the performance of the oblation, the qualification of the person entitled to perform it (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) serves as the occasion (*nimitta*). Consequently, it is established that the oblation is enjoined as possessing a distinction. The remainder has been explained.
But in the case of emaciation, there would be a burning of the whole body, because the partiality [of the heat] is unavoidable. || 17 ||

In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "Now, if one's two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are burnt, Varuṇa seizes that sacrifice. When that ritual action involving the oblation has been completed, then one should offer that very same oblation; for the sacrifice belongs to the sacrifice."

Regarding the term *prāyaścitti*: the meaning therein is this—Varuṇa seizes that sacrifice of which the two *puroḍāśa* cakes are burnt; when that ritual action involving that oblation is completed, then that very same oblation must be offered again. By the principle of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), the phrase "of which the two *puroḍāśas* are burnt" indicates that the occasion for the rite is the burning of the oblation, whether it occurs in its entirety or in part.

Because the characteristic mark is present; the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that there must be an occasional rite (*naimittika*) prescribed by the statement, "For whom the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśau*) are burnt. If this [rite] were for the purpose of restoring the burnt portion, then the expiation would apply only when one part is burnt, not when the whole is burnt. However, since the causal condition (*nimitta*) exists even in the case of total burning, it is indeed appropriate there as well. It is not [the case that it is inappropriate].

Furthermore, a specific rule is also heard stating, "and when the whole is scorched. Therefore, an expiation is appropriate even when both [the whole and a part] are scorched; otherwise, the designation of that oblation as being "completed" (*saṃsthā*) would be rendered meaningless. [Objection: Even so, the expiation should apply only when a single part is scorched, for in this way the scriptural word becomes consistent. For if...
This statement— "then that oblation is completed"— would apply to the case where it is not entirely consumed;
for if there were a total burning, since the completion of the oblation would be impossible once it is burnt, the designation "that oblation" would not be tenable in the event of total burning.
If, however, another sacrificial substance (*havis*) were taken up and the performance were carried out, the designation "that *havis*" would become entirely without referent.

[Objection: Even so, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would apply only to the burning of a single part, not to the burning of the whole, for in that case the designation "that *havis*" would not be applicable. [Reply: True; the designation "that *havis*" refers to that which belongs to it as its *havis*.

Only the burning of one part is logically consistent. Nevertheless, according to the principle of the *ārty-adhikaraṇa*, the completion of the sacrifice itself (*yajña-saṃsthā*) is the occasion for the rite, and not the completion by means of that specific oblation; therefore, even if the oblation is being prepared by another [priest] who has not burned it, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is indeed appropriate. However, if this statement were intended to apply only to the burning of the whole, then, from the word "that oblation" (*tad-dhavis*), [it would follow that the rite applies only when that specific oblation is burned].
It has been stated that "expiation" (prāyaścitta) is merely a figurative assertion;

thus the following position is presented: since the destruction of even a single part [of the sin] is unavoidable, it is logical that expiation is prescribed for the purpose of destroying the entirety [of the sin].

The specific statement, "whose two *puroḍāśa* cakes are burnt," is applicable only when there is a total burning; however, in the case of a partial burning, since it is possible for [the other] to remain intact, the specific statement would not be applicable. Therefore, the expiation pertains to the complete burning.
Here he raises an objection: "Granted that the momentariness which persists until the completion of the cooking process is unavoidable;
but why should that momentariness which is not conducive to the cooking process not also be a cause? To this extent...
Without a certain degree of combustibility (*kṣāmatā*), cooking simply does not come about; therefore, let that degree of combustibility which is necessarily present not be considered the cause.
Let rather that occasional factor which brings about cooking even in the absence of such combustibility be the cause. And this occurs even when only one part is combustible.

It is possible. For even worldly people use the word *kṣāma* (burnt) with respect to a burning that is unintended and not conducive to cooking, as in "the ball of flour is burnt" or "the rice is burnt. Therefore, [the opponent claims] that burning which is unintended and not conducive to cooking is what is meant by *kṣāṇa*. [The author] refutes this: "True, as you say; [it is true that] burning which is unintended and not conducive to cooking—"

"It is intended"—but it is not known how much is desired. Therefore, because it is not an auxiliary to the cooking that is desired, the specific distinction cannot be known. The objector asks: "Why is it not known?"
The accomplishment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is required; to whatever extent of cooking the sacrificial cake is accomplished, that much cooking is intended.
The respondent said: "It is true that the accomplishment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is desired; however, it is not known by how many moments it is accomplished, nor how much is useless.
This is the intention: by means of whatever amount of cooking..."

The *puroḍāśa* is accomplished; to that extent it is desired (*īpsita*). Therefore, only that much cooking which causes the failure of the accomplishment of the *puroḍāśa* is undesired (*anīpsita*), and that is precisely over-burning (*sarvadāha*). For by that much, the cognition of it as a *puroḍāśa* disappears. In worldly matters, however, the world itself is the authority regarding what is desired and what is undesired. In that regard, there is no fixed rule.

It is not so, because there is a difference in what is desired by each individual. Therefore, it is rightly said: "Since the destruction of even a single part is unavoidable, the expiation must indeed be for the destruction of the whole. The avoidance of that term has also been stated by another:
The ritual action being concluded with the oblation can be indicated by the word "oblation" (havis).
[Objection: "If it is argued that it must be according to the literal scriptural statement... [Sūtra 6.1.22]
But surely, it was stated in the *grahādhikaraṇa* that the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

By that very same principle, it has also been stated that the qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is not intended to be significant. Therefore, because it is a mere repetition, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) need not even be commenced.
He refutes this: "It is true that it has not been stated by anyone that [the meaning] is not established. If it has been established, then what is intended here?
Is this intended as a qualifier for that which is being predicated, or not? Thus he reflects.

The meaning of this is as follows: it was stated there that the qualification of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*); however, here it is established that the qualification of that which is being authorized (*adhikriyamāṇa*) is not intended to be significant. Thus, the sense is that there is no tautology.
[Objection: "But surely, this [rule] is not observed when there is an intention to express a qualification of that which is being pointed out (uddiśyamāna). To this, he says:

Nor is an eligible person (adhikārī) being pointed out [as the primary object]. What then? It is the action that is made the subject of eligibility. One considers that the state of being an eligible person is one thing, while the state of being pointed out as the objective is another. Being the object of an injunction (vidheya) constitutes the state of being pointed out (uddeśyatva).

Ownership (*svāmitva*) consists in being the one entitled (*adhikriyamāṇatva*) to the ritual action. Therefore, in those cases where [the person] is indicated as the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the consideration pertains to that [action]; but here, the consideration pertains to the person to be directed (*niyojya*). This is the distinction. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [takes] the distress (*ārti*) qualified by two terms as a qualification of the person entitled [to the rite].
Considering that the affliction qualified by both terms constitutes the cause, he says: "If both of one's sacrificial offerings (havir) should suffer affliction.
By the verb, "affliction" (ārti) is expressed; and that [affliction] is simultaneously qualified by both terms, "offering" (haviḥ) and "both" (ubhayam).

It is like [the compound] *kraya* with *aruṇaikahāyanī*. That [word *ārti*] is qualified by both, being a qualifier of the person; thus, the *ārti* qualified by both qualifiers is the occasion (*nimitta*). And the verbal root *ṛcchati*, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, occurs in the sense of affliction (*ārti*); the word *ārti* itself is derived from that very root by adding the suffix *ktin*. This is according to the rule: *upasargādṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91).

When the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *r* (raparatva) has occurred, there is the elision of *ra* (*rāllopa*) and the elision of *i* (*ilopa*). However, as for what is stated—that "one should perform the *ārti* [or *ārcchati*]"—that should be understood as being like the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*). But the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) says: "True, it is understood that the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is characterized by all the qualifiers. Nevertheless, he is not qualified by the qualifiers as having become a single word, because there is no compound (*samāsa*)."
These [words] do not become a single compound (ekapadībhūta). What follows from that? This follows:
for that which qualifies the subject under discussion is understood either as a result or as a cause. However, it is not [understood] as being repeatedly its own qualifier of the object (karman).
It is not understood by way of its own status as a qualifier; rather,
it merely states the qualifier— that [the cognition] does not terminate there—
but [rather] [it terminates] in the fruit of the action.

Or it remains as a causal condition (*nimitta*). Now, whether that is a result or a causal condition, it must be exactly as it was understood through its qualification of the person entitled to the rite (*adhikṛta*). Furthermore, a collection of words employed for its own specific meaning and understood as a qualification cannot be unified with the ritual action except through that action’s purpose. And a set of words employed for its own specific meaning [qualifies] the person entitled to the rite—

That which is understood as a qualification cannot be unified with it unless it is either an effect (*kārya*) or something to be undertaken (*upādeya*). For example, when the act of purchase (*kraya*) is enjoined as something to be undertaken, it is understood as being qualified by its unified qualifications. It is not possible to understand it in that way here, because the affliction (*ārti*) is not something to be undertaken. Nor is this an effect, because this entitlement (*adhikāra*) extends only so far as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*). And [the affliction] is not the occasioning condition...
It becomes something that is not to be accepted. Therefore, this cannot be accepted as being the cause for mutual relationship.
Furthermore, this is a single sentence; consequently, only one of the two must be understood here as the cause, not both.

The cause is the affliction of the oblation (*havirārti*), not both [the oblation and the vessel], because the oblation is the thing to be qualified and because of its immediate proximity. Therefore, when the affliction of the oblation is the cause, the term "both" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). If, due to the absence of any understanding of becoming a single unit, the oblation qualified by "bothness" were the cause, then would the oblation alone be the cause?
The answer: We say that it is not an object of suffering.
But surely, suffering (*ārti*) itself is not even a single entity with the oblation (*havis*); how then can it function as a qualifier for that which is its object?

This is not a fault, because a name (*nāman*) is based on a positive entity (*bhāva*). There is no connection between the oblation and the person; for words whose referents are absences (*abhāva*), [the connection is established differently].

Mutual relationship is necessarily preceded by the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka). Furthermore, that which is called "mutual" is a related entity (*saṃbandhin*). The cause for this is precisely the state of being a single word. Therefore, because of the connection with *ārti* (distress/pain), there is a connection with the person. Consequently, it is established that the oblation (*havis*) qualified by *ārti* is the qualification of the person; thus, the oblation, having become a qualifier of *ārti*, is established as the *nimitta* (the occasioning condition).

But surely, even from a sentence, the mutual relationship between names is understood—as in "Devadatta’s cows. He replies: "Certainly, but that [relationship] is based on case-endings (vaibhaktika). And a case-ending occurs only between two things."

It expresses a connection, but not with anything else. This is the general rule; therefore, let it be connected only with the "defect of the oblation" (*havirārti*), and not with both [the oblation and the vessel]. Consequently, the defect is the subject matter, and the oblation is the cause, because of its qualification and its proximity. Thus, it refers to the subject matter of the defect.

The neuter gender [of the word *ubhaya*] is used because it qualifies the oblation (*havis*). Now, one might object that when the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is accepted as the basis for the designation, the entry of the oblation is also established; for "duality" (*ubhayatva*) is necessarily dependent on something else. Therefore, in accordance with the consistency of the entire passage:
In the same way, let the connection be accepted:
when it is said, "for whom both [offerings] should meet with ruin," in response to the expectation of what those two might be, the offering itself is understood.

He refutes [the objection]: "You are ignorant of the relationship between categories of things; for a qualifier, while requiring a qualificand, requires it as its object (*viṣaya*), not as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of itself. Duality is a number, and that..."

Since it cannot exist as the object of affliction (*ārti*), it requires only the substance that is the object of affliction. Therefore, even if duality depends upon the oblation (*havis*), it does not depend on it as a qualifier. Furthermore, both in its state as the object of affliction and in its being the object of affliction, that very [substance] serves as its cause; thus he says: "And this is not a delimiter (*avacchedaka*), but rather the object (*viṣaya*)."
Furthermore, since the object becomes a cause independently of any qualification, the mere occurrence of damage to the oblation (*havis*) alone is the cause;
thus, the presentation of the requirement for both terms is entirely redundant.
This is because the oblation, by virtue of being a substance (*dravya*), [is already established].
The state of being an object of distress does not belong to both [the agent and the recipient]; this is what was stated: "We do not tolerate the qualification of the oblation.
Since they are neither effects (*akāryatayā*) nor things to be undertaken (*anupādeyatayā*), all possible mutual relations among the qualifiers of the qualified subject are demonstrated;
and it is with this very refutation of whatever is possible that we conclude our discussion of mutual relations in the absence of a compound (*samāsa*).

The objection that "qualification is untenable" is precisely the refutation offered by the author of the Bhāṣya as well; thus, this much has been presented merely to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the refutation. For the collection of causes cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, it is established that the affliction (*ārti*) regarding the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in general is the cause [of the ritual].
[155] || 7 || Likewise, there is the offering into the fire, the extraction [of Soma], and the consumption. || 24 ||

In this case as well, since there is no mutual connection between the two names, even though they function as qualifiers of that which is being enjoined, each possesses the status of an independent causal factor (*nimitta*).
The meaning of this is as follows: "having pressed [the Soma], having offered [it], he consumes [it]."

In this regard, although there is no mutual connection between the two names ending in *vat*, and although in reality it is possible for both [the soma] that are mutually connected to serve as qualifiers of the person, nevertheless, according to the capacity of the words, each serves as the cause individually,
as in: "Having pressed [the soma], they consume it."
Likewise, [it says] "having offered, they consume.

By this, those who are performers even at the mere pressing [of the Soma] also consume; and those who are performers even at the mere offering, they too [consume]. Nor is there a lack of intention regarding both parts, as if they were subordinate members of a compound.
It is possible;

just as both terms [of the compound] are not intended to be significant, so too in the case of the occasioning factor (*nimitta*) "having offered," the word *huta* is not intended to be significant and is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor can it be argued that the "duality" (*ubhayatva*) of some other oblation (*havis*) will serve as the occasioning factor.

Because nothing else is mentioned and because the *havis* (sacrificial offering) is specifically mentioned, it is understood that both [the pressing and the offering] have that [offering] as their object. Here, however, since there is no distinction, both are the occasion (*nimitta*). Thus, when the pressing is the occasion, the status of the offering as the occasion is not established; likewise, when the offering is the occasion, the pressing is not. Therefore, the justification for the restatement (*anuvāda*) is untenable.

But surely there is a connection between "having pressed" (*abhiṣutya*) and "having offered" (*hutvā*), because the suffix *-ktvā* requires a single agent; since that [suffix] would be untenable without a second verbal root-meaning [to share the same agent],
it must necessarily be expected.

"It is 'having pressed' (*abhiṣutya*)," it says; however, "having offered" (*hutvā*) depends upon the act of consuming (*bhakṣayati*). Therefore, the pressing and the offering together constitute the causal condition (*nimitta*). He refutes this: True, the suffix *-ktvā* requires another action, but it does not require the action ending in *-ktvā* itself, because that too is directed toward something else. For [the suffix] does not [apply] to both...
A mutual connection between two primary elements is logical;

however, everything is connected with the primary element alone, and that primary element "eats" [the portion], but not "having offered. This is because even that [offering] stands in a subordinate relationship to the act of eating. Therefore, this—

The connection is as follows: "having pressed [the Soma], he consumes it," and "having offered [it], he consumes it. However, a prescription of sequence is not possible here because it is already established;
for the offering is necessarily preceded by the pressing, and the consumption is necessarily preceded by the offering, as it is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

Nor is there an injunction for the pressing (*abhiṣava*) and the offering (*homa*) as being subordinate to the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), because they serve as qualifications for the qualified person (*adhikṛta*). Nor is there an injunction for their own sake, since the pressing is already established by the rule, "One should press the Soma.
[As for the offering, it is established] by the rule, "One should sacrifice with Soma."

And such is the case regarding the *homa*. Therefore, this is merely an injunction concerning the cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*naimittika*). Furthermore, since that [injunction] applies to each [act] individually, this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
To this, it is replied: because of the understanding of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) for those [verbs] ending in *-ktvā*, [the acts of] pressing (*abhiṣava*) and offering (*homa*)—
Since the state of having a single agent is already established from elsewhere, it is enjoined by the words "having pressed" and "having offered.
The meaning of this is that the state of having a common agent is expressed by the word ending in the suffix *ktvā*; and [this applies to] both the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*).
The two [actions] are established as having the same agent; therefore, that very person is called the "common agent. By this, the following meaning is established:
the one who is the agent of both the pressing (*abhiṣava*) and the offering (*homa*) is the one who consumes (*bhakṣayati*). Herein lies the prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*):
But surely, a mutual connection between two [verbal roots] ending in *ktvā* is not perceived, because they serve different purposes—
Because of this, just as there is no mutual relationship between two words ending in different case-suffixes—

as in the case of *aruṇayā* and *ekahāyanyā*, where the two words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) express instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) distinct from the nominal stems themselves— so too [is it here].

It is also not logical for two words ending in the suffix *ktvā* [to be related], because a connection indeed occurs between two non-distinct words ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*), but not between those ending in distinct case-endings. He replies:
True; where there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there the word ending in *ktvā* [is connected] with the principal action itself.

The connection [is as follows]: furthermore, where the status of being an object belongs to things already apprehended by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no apprehension of a different object by means of another *pramāṇa* characterized as a single sentence (*ekavākya*).
This applies where two [verbal roots] ending in the suffix *-ktvā* have a single agent as their object.

When that [action] is understood, there is no understanding of another agent therein. For if there were not a single object [of action], then there would be no single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). Yet, a single sentence is indeed perceived. Therefore, because of their status as a single sentence, even those two [verbal roots] ending in the suffix *ktvā* are mutually connected, just as in the expression "the cows of Devadatta, the son of Kṛṣṇa. However, this single-sentence status—

By force, there arises a connection [of the action] with Devadatta alone, who possesses the quality of blackness. Likewise here as well, the phrase "having pressed [the Soma] and having offered" indicates that the qualification of the eligible performer (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) refers exclusively to a single agent, because of the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). And since the qualification, by way of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*), is connected to the injunction, the status of the combined performance (*samāhāra*) as the causal condition (*nimitta*) is established. [This applies to] the qualification of the combined [acts].

Because the qualification belongs to the qualified [agent], it is established that the two combined alone constitute the causal condition (*nimitta*). Nor can it be said that there is no capacity to exclude [the agent] as there is in the case of both words [denoting the agent], because these two words—"in the *kartrī*"—function through different means. In that case, however, the distinction is that the two words function solely by way of an injunction (*vidhi*); whereas in the case of pressing (*abhiṣava*) and offering (*homa*), since they are not dependent on anything else, they are capable of excluding [the agent].

There is capacity [in this case]. The "state of fearlessness" (*abhayapada*) refers exclusively to the oblation (*havis*). Therefore, it is not able to prevent the affliction caused by any oblation whatsoever; however, this [phrase] is indeed able to prevent its being the cause for the mere [oblation] itself.
