[Regarding] the evening milking—

Having prepared the curd, one should divide it into two parts. One half of the curd should be set aside for the sake of the rite to be performed on the following day; immediately thereafter, having completed the evening milking, one should place it for the purpose of curdling with sour milk (*dadhyātañcana*). The other half should be kept in the same manner. In that case, if the moon should rise (*abhyudaya*), one should fulfill the occasional obligation (*naimittika-adhikāra*) using the half of the curd that was kept as it was, and [then proceed] with the evening [rite] using the half of the curd that had been set aside.
Having added a coagulant to milk and produced curds, one should perform the *darśa* sacrifice on the following day; however,
if that [moon] does not rise, one should perform the *darśa* itself with that very half of curds which was set aside, using that half-curds for the purpose of adding the coagulant.

And since curd has already been deposited, the act of adding the coagulant would be purposeless; therefore, one should offer it for the feeding of Brahmins after removing it by means of that coagulant. In that case, if this were a separate occasional rite (*naimittika*), then the curd that exists there would be solely for the sake of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*); thus, as there would be no need for another curd for the sake of the *darśa*, the addition of the coagulant would not be performed.

In that case, the practice of curdling [the milk] is not justified. However, when this very same ritual of the new moon (Amāvāsyā) has commenced, then it must be performed with this very curd acquired for the sake of the new moon sacrifice; thus, since there is a need for curdling for the sake of the new moon sacrifice which occurs on the following day, the practice of curdling is logical. He refutes this:
"It will be based on a scriptural injunction.

The meaning of this is as follows: even though that curd exists, nevertheless, another curd must be churned for the ritual; thus, it will be based on a scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) according to this principle.
This is established in the meaning of the treatise.
Here, someone raises an objection: "But surely, in the other alternative, this [prohibition] is merely based on scriptural injunction."

The meaning of this is as follows: even in that alternative view where this is not a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), in that case too, because curd produced on the fourteenth day is unfit for the *darśa* sacrifice performed on the first day (*pratipad*), its application is based solely on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). For it is curd produced on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) that is enjoined for the *darśa*. Consequently, the observation of repeated curdling (*atañcana*) would otherwise be inexplicable.
Even in the alternative view that [the curd] is produced [as a new substance], it is indeed based on a direct scriptural statement (vācanika).

This is the meaning: the Darśa sacrifice must be performed with that very curd. By what qualification? This is stated in detail: this repeated practice of curdling (ātañcana) is based on a direct scriptural statement.
"It will come to pass.
He refutes this: "True; nevertheless, because there is no other material cause [for the effect], it is said that [the capacity] is already attained;
however, in the matter of application (viniyoga), both cases are equal."

For in the view that [the curd] is the means of accomplishment (*āpādana*), there would be only the application (*viniyoga*) of that curd, but not its actual procurement (*upādāna*); the act of adding the coagulant (*atañcana*) would be based solely on the scriptural injunction. However, in the view that it is a repetition (*abhyāsa*), both the application and the procurement are scripturally enjoined; thus, the meaning "one must perform the addition of the coagulant to the curd" would be scripturally established. Likewise...
Even though that curd is already present, another curd is to be taken; it is not to be prepared by means of that very same curd—this is indeed based solely on the scriptural injunction.
This being the position reached, it is replied: this is the removal of the deity.
Why? Because the threefold division is already established elsewhere in the sentence concerning the distribution (*vibhāga*).
The meaning of this is: this [division] is not [intended] for the rice-grains alone by means of these specific qualifications such as "the coarsest" (*sthaviṣṭha*) and so forth.
1. "Of that which is obtained through injunction" is the correct reading [p.
166], because the division has been prescribed; however, the division of the oblation is from the deity, since that [division] is obtained from elsewhere.
Because it has not been attained.
From where could there be an attainment of division into three kinds for unseparated grains? The answer is: the deity—
By way of establishing the connection:

when the three deities are connected with the *sthaviṣṭha* (largest) and the other portions individually, then, by the very nature of the case, the separate allocation of the rice grains is already established. Therefore, only this much is enjoined: "one should divide."

"But one should not divide it threefold. The word "threefold" (tredhā), however, restates the tripartite division which is already established for rice grains (*taṇḍula*). And since there is no specific qualification, this is understood to apply to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in general, and not to rice grains alone.
When it is said, "one should divide [the oblation] for the deities," it is already understood that the division applies to the oblation associated with them as well.
Furthermore, that offering-material in its general sense cannot be qualified by the word "rice" (taṇḍula), because that would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
Moreover, since the subsequent sentences introduce other deities once the connection with the previous deities has been removed, no distinct ritual action (karmāntara) is understood;
rather, it is the very same substances already connected with the rite called Darśa that are specifically assigned to different deities.

Because these [rites] are recognized as being the same as those in the original ritual context—being "excellent" and associated with other deities—no distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) is understood.

Furthermore, the absence of the essential nature of the ritual does not follow from the absence of qualification due to the lack of a specific time; rather, those very same rituals are enjoined within the occasional qualification (*naimittikādhikāra*). Consequently, once that occasional qualification has been fulfilled, those same rituals are performed again for the sake of completing the permanent qualification (*nityādhikāra*).
It must be understood that the ritual acts are to be performed. Now, it was argued that the hearing of the word *caru* (cooked rice) would not be appropriate;

furthermore, since the cooking is for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake), prescribing it [for the *caru*] would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This would be the case if the injunction were made by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an already established act.

If it were an injunction of attributes (*guṇavidhi*) dependent on the essential form of the ritual act (*karmasvarūpa*), then, because multiple attributes would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). However, when this [text] enjoins a specific performance of that very same sacrifice for one who is already entitled to the *abhyudaya* (prosperity) resulting from having proceeded under a delusion regarding time or a delusion regarding entitlement—specifically, when the division among the deities occurs due to the cause of that division—it is not a syntactical split. He asks: "How so? and replies:
"This very same sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), having been brought to this or that particular state"—this is a restatement (anuvāda). Its meaning is as follows:

since that sacrificial cake which has been enjoined is already established in its very nature as a sacrificial cake, its performance is already obtained; now, however, [the case concerns] the *abhyudaya* (the rising of the moon).

At the very stage when the sign has arisen, having performed the removal of the deity from the curd-mixed and milk-mixed [substances], a connection with another deity is established. For that which has become thus, grinding must certainly not be performed, because it is for the purpose of spreading out [the dough],
and because that spreading out is impossible to perform due to the smallness of the rice grains and the abundance of the curd and milk.

Therefore, in this case as well, the cooking must be performed without grinding and without spreading [the grains]. Since that [quality] cannot be removed, when the cooking is performed, the state of being *caru* follows as a matter of course, and the sense of the locative case is indeed established; thus, "in curds, the *caru*" and "in milk" are merely restatements (*anuvāda*).
1. For the purpose of cessation— do not [perform] the *caru* offering.

Thus, because a restatement (*anuvāda*) is untenable unless there is an injunction regarding the mode of performance, the inclusion within the context of the primary rite (*prakṛtakarma*) is established; it is not, however, established by the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) with respect to the rite itself. Therefore, this is a restatement.

Furthermore, since difference (*bheda*) cannot be asserted without the characteristic of distinction, those who know the meaning of words consider this [restatement] to be merely a gateway for the qualified subject (*adhikṛta*).
They think thus: for if this inquiry were conducted in the second chapter, which deals with the characteristics of difference and non-difference, then [the nature of] the ritual action—

Because it is dependent [on that context], there would be an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) in that very place. However, since multiple qualities would be enjoined therein, there is the risk of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*);

therefore, this must be a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*). But in the investigation concerning the definition of the subject matter (*adhikāra*), a specific application is enjoined for one who is already qualified;

thus, since this [offering] is applied to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) itself, the state of being a *caru* (porridge) is already implied by the sense of the text, as the act of cooking has been removed [from the original injunction] by the force of the locative case.

Since there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the phrase "sahānūdyataḥ," non-difference is indeed established. Therefore, this is considered under the heading of eligibility (*adhikāra*). Consequently, it is proven that this occasional rite (*naimittika*) is distinct from the "five-platter" (*pañcaśarāva*) and other such rites. In the case of the five-platter rite and others, because the sacrificial material has been spoiled by damage, the very performance of the rite is destroyed; thus, a different rite is enjoined. Here, however, even though there is a lapse of time, the sacrificial material remains undestroyed.

Since the ritual action has not perished, this subsequent application is enjoined as a contingent (naimittika) rite; it is understood that "this is the application of that very [rite]" through the recognition of the original substance (*dravya*). Thus, the point is well-established. The rest has been explained.
|| 2 || Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*, because there is no specific scriptural injunction, it is according to the archetype (*yathāprakṛti*). || 10 ||

This is a deliberation based on the premise that the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice also takes place on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). But how can there be a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, given that it was stated in the context of the actual performance itself— "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts"— referring to the division of the sacrificial material (*havis*) in general?
Therefore, there is also the removal of the deity for the *upāṃśuyāja* oblation.

The reply is: the doubt regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from observing the counter-argument (*pratisamādhāna*), just as in the case of curd, milk, and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Just as when a previous deity has been removed, there is no connection with another deity [in its place], so it is not here. Furthermore, since a sacrifice cannot take place without a deity, there must indeed be the removal of the deity. Therefore, for the time being, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers the resolution to be non-separation.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: because there is no distinction in the act of separation, separation occurs everywhere.
Where there is a formal resolution (*samādhāna*), there is a formal resolution; but where there is no resolution, the occasional application (*naimittika-prayoga*) ends precisely with the separation.

But is it not the case that the sacrifice is not performed at the conclusion of the distribution of the deities? For a sacrifice is the relinquishment of a substance with reference to a deity; and that [sacrifice] is not performed when the deity has not been designated.
He refutes [the objection]: How can it be said that [the sacrifice] was not employed? Because this matter is based on the explicit scriptural statement (vācanikatva).
The meaning of this is as follows: that very sacrifice which has been enjoined consists essentially of the distribution of the deities.
By the statement "the ritual application (prayoga) must be performed," this is expressed: sacrifice (yāga) is indeed the relinquishment (tyāga) directed toward a deity;
and that [relinquishment] is not untenable even when the limiting adjunct (upādhi) has ceased.
Now, if the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not perceived, how is it understood that "this very sacrifice is the same"?
Because the performance is enjoined for the very same original [sacrifice], just as in the case of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) when it is in the state of the cooked offering (*caru*).
For the sacrifice also ends with the division [of the offering].

Thus it is determined that the treatises on qualification (*adhikāraśāstra*) culminate in the performance (*prayoga*), because the treatises on qualification indeed culminate in performance and enjoin performance itself; they do not concern themselves with the subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) of the object to be performed. Therefore, there is no fault in understanding that this [subsidiary] belongs to the performance of such a sacrifice as the object to be performed, just as when it is said that the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) itself has become the oblation-pot (*caru*). [This concerns] the nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*).

For this defect exists in the ritual procedure, characterized by the failure of the sacrifice to be accomplished without a specific deity. Now, one might object: "When the [specific] deity is removed, some deity or other may be mentioned. To this, he says: "And there is no assumption of a deity in a general sense [based on] the scriptural statement..."
Because the deity is that which is to be approached.
Why is this so? To this he says: because it is established that "whichever [deity] is enjoined for whichever oblation, she is the deity of that. By that, the state of being a deity...
It cannot be so conceived;
rather, the application [of the ritual] is prescribed only at the conclusion of the distribution of the offerings.
|| 3 || It should take place when the offering has been set aside, because of its connection with that. || 12 ||
The prima facie view is that because of hearing the word "nirupta" (offered), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) applies only when the oblation has already been offered at the time of sunrise.
But is this not already covered by the *ārtyadhikaraṇa*?

Just as in the *ārtyadhikaraṇa* the qualification "both" (*ubhayatva*) was not intended to be significant, and rather the affliction (*ārti*) of the oblation in general was the cause, so too here, the rising of the oblation in general [is the cause].

He refutes [the objection] by stating that the mention of "offering" (*nirupta*) as a defining characteristic (*nimitta*) is indeed not intended; for this section does not proceed on that basis, since the word "commenced" (*pravṛtta*) is not heard.
For the prosperity (*abhyudaya*) of the oblation cannot occur in its own essential form; what then?

[This applies] to that which has already commenced. And here, the word "commenced" (*pravṛtta*) is not heard; therefore, let the qualification of "having been offered" (*niruptatva*), which is understood from the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), be applied to that very thing, because it is what is directly stated.
He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): True, the word "commenced" is not heard; nevertheless, for that which has been... [abhyudita-]...
Because of the understanding of activity [implied by] *yad*, it is not possible to establish that [the statement] refers exclusively to the qualifier;

for when it is said, "for whom the moon should rise," the state of being already engaged in the rite is understood regarding the oblation (*havis*), since the rising of the moon occurs only for one who has already begun the rite. Therefore, by the rising...
1. By way of the analysis of meaning—mā; 2. by way of the means—mā [p.

Since it is understood from the very word "pravṛtta" (already commenced) that [the sacrifice] has begun, the other conditional qualification—"for whom the moon should rise"—which serves as a specific attribute for what has already been offered, cannot establish a distinction; this is because of the acceptance [of the meaning]. Therefore, whether the word *pravṛtta* is heard or not heard, there is no difference whatsoever. Thus, the view has been stated.
If the moon rises before the oblation has been poured out, one should offer it with the *prākṛtī* (archetypal) formulas; so says Āśmarathya,
because of the removal [of the offering] once the rice grains have become [cooked].

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that whether the oblation has been offered or not yet offered when the sun rises, there should be an offering (*nirvāpa*) to the original deities, Agni and the others; for it is heard in the scripture that the removal of the deities applies only to those [grains] that have already become rice-grains (*taṇḍula*). But is this not so?

And it has been stated that the rising of the sun is the occasion (nimitta) when the oblation has merely begun to proceed. Therefore, since the deities are removed once the procedure has merely commenced, how can there be an offering (nirvāpa) to the original deities?
He answers: "What you have said is true."
But surely we say that the rice is the occasional factor (*naimittika*) among these,
even though the mere commencement of the oblation is the occasion (*nimitta*).

Nevertheless, because the word "rice grains" (*taṇḍula*) is heard, the occasional (*naimittika*) rite consists of the division [of the rice] according to the deities. Since the deity has not been removed prior to that point, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) must be from the original materials themselves, occurring only at the stage of the rice grains.
To this it is replied: it has already been stated that even in the occasional rite, the rice grains are not the essential factor (*atantra*). [This concerns] the division—
Because of the prescription regarding the measure.
When it is stated, "One should divide the oblation among the deities," what is understood is the division of the oblation in its entirety;

therefore, it has been said that the mention of *taṇḍula* (rice grains) is not intended to be restrictive. The meaning of the scripture is that the oblation which has been superseded by the rising of the sun must be divided.
Therefore, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the offering (nirvāpa) is made from the specific materials (naimittika).
|| 5 || Once the portions have been set aside, there is no removal of the handfuls, because they are subordinate to that [act]. || 17 ||
In whatever state the oblation was at the time of its increase, let it remain in that very state when the deities are assigned;
preceded by that [assignment], the pouring out [of the oblation] should be performed for other deities.
[Objection: If that is so, then why does threshing not also apply to those [grains] mixed with curd and milk?

[Reply: It is said: because the grains are divided into various categories such as the most minute and so forth, one must first effect the contact with curd and milk only after the threshing has been completed, and then perform the cooking. This applies when the *sāmi* (half-) portion has been set aside from the original portions.

Thus the pouring out has commenced. Even the remaining handful should be poured out for the archetypal (prakṛtī) offerings alone, because the pouring out has already proceeded toward those very archetypal offerings. And it was stated in the fifth [book] that "handfuls" are not distinct ritual acts (padārtha).
This being the position reached, it is replied: "Exclusion is understood."

It becomes difficult to perceive. Therefore, when the removal of the modified (vaikṛta) elements has been performed, since the connection with the offered oblation (havissambandha) has already been established, the pouring out (nirvāpa) should be carried out by means of the original designation (uddeśa) alone; this being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is stated as follows:

The pouring out [of the milk] should be performed silently, because it is understood that [the milk] has been removed and because the act of pouring out is a single unit; [therefore, there is no possibility of using milk that has already been poured out].
The meaning of this is as follows: it is not possible to designate the deity of the previous [offering], because that has been removed.

Nor is it possible to assign another deity, because the pouring out of four handfuls constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*). Furthermore, an additional handful is not a separate ritual act. And it is not possible for two deities to belong to a single ritual act, due to their mutual incompatibility.

And because a part of a deity does not have a relationship with the deity itself, there is no completion [of the rite] due to the lack of such a designation. || 6 || Because of the connection with the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering), [the rite] would not belong to one who does not offer the *sānnāyya*. || 21 ||
But surely, since the state of being *caru* is not prescribed, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here is not even possible;
for if the state of being *caru* were prescribed in the section concerning the *sānnāyya*, then it would not apply in the absence of *sānnāyya* for one who does not sacrifice with *sānnāyya*.
[The opponent says: "It is occasional (naimittika). It has been stated that the state of being *caru* is not prescribed [for the *puroḍāśa*].

He replies: "There is a certain doubt here. Thinking that the state of being *caru* for the *puroḍāśa* is not possible when there is no boiled milk (*śṛta*) or curd (*dadhi*), [the author] intends this occasional rite to apply only to one who performs the *sānnāyya* sacrifice."

He raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the rite] is possible; for even though it is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the state of being a *caru* is possible only for one who sacrifices with the *sānnāyya*,
and thus the prima facie view is that this is a contingent rule (*naimittika*) for him alone.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: since it is possible for the state of being chewed (*carvavasthā*) to occur even with water, and since the cause (*nimitta*) is heard without qualification, and since the contingent ritual act (*naimittika*) pertains merely to the connection with the deity, the specific location (*adhikaraṇa*) is not intended to be significant.

Although the state of being a performer of the *sānnāyya* sacrifice is intended [by the context], nevertheless, since that [state] is indeed attained even by one who has merely drunk water, the occasional rule (*naimittika*) heard without qualification cannot be restricted to the specific state of being a performer of the *sānnāyya* sacrifice. In ultimate reality, however—

The mere connection with another deity is the occasional factor (*naimittika*). However, since the meaning of the locus (*adhikaraṇārtha*) is already established by the sense of the passage, it need not be explicitly stated. Because the purpose of the *caru* offering is not intended to be expressed where a restatement (*anuvāda*) is possible, such a restatement will occur there. It is not, however, logical to restrict the injunction itself by force of that [restatement]; thus it is said that the occasional factor applies even for one who does not maintain the sacred fires (*asannayata*).

|| 7 || At the time of rising together [from the sacrifice], there is the Viśvajit [offering], because of its connection with the distribution [of the sacrificial fee] once it has been purchased. || 25 ||

But has it not already been stated even for one who has not performed the *āsanna* [preparation]? Immediately following that, by the very same [rule], it is obtained that this applies even to one who has not purchased the *rājaka*.
What further doubt remains here that needs to be set aside, as was done in the preceding section?

It has been stated that because the occasion (*nimitta*) is heard without qualification, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) applies even for one who has not performed the *sānnāyya* offering. Likewise, here too, since the *samutthāna* (the occurrence of the occasion) is heard without qualification, it follows as a matter of course that the occasional rite must apply even for one whose king has not been purchased. Why, then, is this commenced as a separate section?

[Page 171] He provides the resolution: "There is a further suspicion here; for in that case, because of the mention of *taṇḍula* (rice), the sense of the locative case is not intended to be expressed, and thus it is logical that even one who does not maintain the sacred fires (*asannayin*) may perform it. But here, on the other hand, there is no purchased King [Soma]."

Nor is it heard [in scripture] that "one should divide the Soma"; and since the state of having purchased the King (Soma) is understood, and since division is not possible elsewhere, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the occasioning condition (*nimitta*) must be restricted in accordance with the contingent rite (*naimittika*), just as follows:
"One should establish the fires" (*agnī ādadhīta*).

Its meaning is as follows: because of the hearing of the word "grain" (*taṇḍula*), there is an understanding of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) even in the case of vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*); furthermore, since vegetable offerings are possible even for one who does not maintain the *sānnāyya*, the sense of the locative case is not intended to be expressed, as that would entail the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Because it is [already] established by implication and because it is obtained through the purpose [of the sacrifice], it is logical that even one who has not purchased the King [Soma] performs the occasional rite (*naimittika*). In this case, however, there is no scriptural mention at all of one who has not purchased the King; on the contrary, it is heard: "Having distributed the Soma, one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit. Therefore, since the occasional rite is enjoined as qualified by the distribution of the Soma, the performance of such an occasional rite belongs only to one who has purchased the King.

Because it is possible [to perform the rite otherwise]. Just as in that case, even for one who does not offer the *sānnāyya*, it can be said that the state of eating [the oblation] is possible by means of water, so too here, since the distribution of the *soma* cannot take place without a purchased king (*rājaka*), it is inferred—following the specific conditional rule—that the "rising together" (*sāmutthāna*) is the condition when the king has been purchased. As in the case: "He whose two fires have both gone out..."
Regarding this point, it is said: True; it is logical in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), because it is understood as having a single means.

However, in the present case, although the distribution of all substances would [otherwise] apply by the rule "let them divide the *soma*," it is not so understood due to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Thus, it was not stated for the purpose of restricting the scope of the occasion (*nimitta*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if this were merely an occasional rule (*naimittika*) characterized by the division of Soma, would this division of property not indeed apply even in a case where, among many who have set out together with their wealth combined, there occurs a simultaneous rising up (*sāmutthāna*)? And that—

By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the phrase "having distributed the Soma" is restated (*anūdyate*). For since the distribution of Soma is already established even for one who has purchased the King (Soma), it is not something to be prescribed (*vidheya*); rather, it is merely restated. Once it is established as a restatement, even the use of secondary indication is not a fault. Therefore, it is logical that the Viśvajit sacrifice is performed upon the rising [of the priests] from their duties, including those who have purchased the King.
|| 8 || Regarding the measure of initiation, it depends on the specific desire [of the candidate]. || 27 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, many measurements for the consecration period (dīkṣā) are heard in the scripture. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are all persons entitled [to perform the sacrifice] by means of all those measurements, or by means of only one?
By this [discussion], the subject matter of the section—

He states the connection with meditation (*dhyāna*). Since the qualification is understood according to the specific application (*viniyoga*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it applies to all.
1. Because of being produced from a single origin, there is no disparagement...

Since all [periods of] measurement have been assigned, there is eligibility for all of them; therefore, the statement "for twelve nights, being initiated, he should seek wages" should be understood as referring only to the optional twelve-night initiation. The author states the final conclusion: because of the constant scriptural injunction, "for twelve nights, being initiated, he should seek wages," [it is not merely optional].

In the alternative view, it is established that the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is precisely twelvefold; for the hiring of laborers by one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) for twelve nights is heard in the scripture as a constant (*nityavat*) entitlement, and because that would be untenable under any other measure of time. Thus, the twelvefold—

The application [of the measure] is by means of the *māna* itself; however, other measures are displaced to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). But how can there be a displacement of the application (*viniyoga*) on account of the scope of application (*adhikāra*), when it is rather by virtue of the application that the scope of application is determined?
The sense is: why is the section on qualification (*adhikāra*) not described?
He refutes this: it is correct [to omit it] because the scriptures of application (*viniyoga*) culminate in qualification;
since qualification is primary, an application corresponding to it is logical. However, in the section concerning animals (*tiryagadhikaraṇa*), [it is stated that... adhi-
It has been shown that because there is no contradiction with the ritual injunctions, the determination of eligibility follows the specific application [of the text].
|| 9 || Regarding the full moon sacrifice, there is no restriction because there is no distinction [in the text]. || 30 ||

Regarding the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*), there arises a doubt upon hearing the mention of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*): should any full moon whatsoever be taken, or only a specific one, such as the Caitra or Māgha full moon?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that there is no distinction, because of the contradiction between the remainder of the statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the apparent force of the words (*sāmarthya*).

Because the mention of Caitrī occurs in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*), it appears that the full moon day of Caitra (*caitrīpaurṇamāsī*) is intended. However, by the force of the statement, "Their purchase [of Soma] is accomplished on the Ekāṣṭakā," it follows that the full moon day of Māgha (*mādhī*) is meant. Due to this contradiction—since these two are mutually exclusive and thus cannot both be established—there is no fixed rule; any full moon day whatsoever may be taken.
But another says: "Indeed, a general cognition ought not to set aside the remainder of the sentence; therefore, Caitrī alone must be taken.
Even though there is a general cognition from the word 'paurṇamāsī', nevertheless, [it is superseded] by the remainder of the sentence."

A distinction is understood. [Objection: But was it not said that this is contradicted by the *liṅga*, namely the capacity for purchase? [Reply: Then let the *liṅga* be the regulator by which that [purchase] is set aside.
The proponent of non-restriction says: we do not understand this very point regarding these two, namely the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the capacity (*sāmarthya*).
As for the question "What is sublated by what?", since these two are mutually contradictory according to the logic of Sunda and Upasunda,
there is simply no fixed rule.

As for the objection—[the author] states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): It is said: "Certainly, it is known that the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is sublated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

For capacity (*sāmarthya*) is more highly esteemed in determining eligibility (*adhikāra*), since there can be no eligibility without capacity. Therefore, because capacity is stronger, the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is set aside, as that remainder can be justified even by way of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*). But surely, praise of Caitrī is inappropriate when the context concerns the performance of the sacrifice on the full moon day; to this he says:

This mention is for the purpose of praising another enjoined element, just like the case of *jartila* (wild sesame). Just as there is praise of *jartila* when milk is being enjoined, so too there is praise of Caitrī when Māghī is being enjoined. [The meaning is: Caitrī alone is excellent; it is not even inferior when compared to Māghī.

Therefore, the specific [details] are understood by implication alone. || 10 || Since the time for initiation has already been prescribed, there is no postponement of the obligatory rites when that time has passed, because their proper time has arrived. || 38 ||
In this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that cooking and other such acts are prohibited until the time of initiation (dīkṣā),

maintains that there is no postponement [of the ritual]. This is because, according to scripture, "the initiated person does not give," which applies to the person for as long as the initiation lasts.

In that case, there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the cooking and other rites, and according to the scripture, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is restricted to a specific time. Therefore, even if the initiation for the sake of liberation were postponed, the cooking and other rites would still have to be performed. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is this: this is not an exclusion of time. If it were an exclusion of time, [the objection would hold].
Cooking and other such acts might occur, but this is not an exclusion of time;

for the initiated person has no entitlement here [to those acts], and the state of being initiated indeed persists until the *avamṛtha* bath. Therefore, as long as one is initiated, there is an exclusion [of those acts].
Thus it is appropriate for cooking and other such acts.
|| 11 || In that case, no supplementary oblation (pratihoma) is prescribed, as was the case with the preceding ones. || 40 ||
It is stated [in the following] in order to raise an objection: "When there is an extension of time, should counter-offerings (pratihoma) be performed or not?"—this is what is being considered.
Thus he restates [the point] for the sake of refutation.

He raises an objection: "But how can there be a suspicion of *pratihoma* (supplementary oblation) in this case? It has been stated that the initiated person (*dīkṣita*) is excluded [from such duties]. The meaning of this is: the performance of a *pratihoma* is possible when there is a non-performance of what ought to be done; however, the initiated person has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding cooking and other such acts. Therefore, since only those things which ought not to be done have not been performed, a suspicion of *pratihoma* is not appropriate. He provides the resolution:
Prior to negligence, one considers the obligatory scripture (*nitya-śāstra*) as if it were optional (*apramāda*). Its meaning is as follows: the obligatory scriptures [begin with] 1.
*dīkṣā-mo-mā*.
2. Even an excellence—lest it 3. exclude [it]. Lest [p.

The rites such as the *homa* and others are fixed by rule prior to the occurrence of negligence; they must be performed by the person as long as negligence has not yet fallen upon him. The reason for the postponement of the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is the continued state of being consecrated (*dīkṣitatva*). Therefore, even if negligence should occur, those *homa* rites and others which were not performed by the consecrated person must indeed be performed, and they do not [cease to be obligatory].

[The rites] would have been performed. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that expiatory offerings (pratihoma) must be made. However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: it is true that the time [for the rites] is fixed when there is no negligence; yet, due to the lack of entitlement (anadhikāra), the initiated person (dīkṣita) simply does not perform the offerings, because the rule is contingent upon the existence of such entitlement.
The meaning of this is as follows:
for one who is free from negligence, the time for the *homa* offerings is fixed. However, for one upon whom negligence falls, there is no performance of the compensatory *pratihomas* at all;
because he lacks the qualification due to being under the state of initiation (*dīkṣitatva*), and because the rule [of the fixed time] exists only by way of that qualification. This is the rule.

For indeed, the [obligation] for sacrifices depends solely upon the status of the qualified person (*adhikārin*). For one who possesses life and has a perpetual qualification, there is a perpetual performance [of the rite]. Moreover, the qualification does not exist prior [to the performance];
rather, the qualification arises day by day.
It also turns back. Since the entitlement of one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) is excluded, there is no obligation to perform the oblations due to the absence of such entitlement;
how much more so [is this the case] because of the prohibition after the avabhṛtha bath until the iṣṭi. || 42 ||

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that after the release from initiation (*dīkṣonmocana*), if there is an extension of the sacrifice due to negligence or other causes, another *pratihoma* must be performed by the initiated person.
The meaning of this is: "The initiated person does not give gifts, nor does he perform oblations."

The prohibition "he does not cook" is made with respect to one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*). And one who has performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is released from consecration and is no longer *dīkṣita*, even though the *iṣṭi* equal to the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya-sammitā*) has not yet been performed. Therefore, because he is not excluded [from the rule], even if the *iṣṭi* is postponed due to negligence or other causes, [the prohibition remains in force].

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding the *homa*s and other rites, those *homa*s which were not performed must be performed as compensatory offerings (*pratihoma*). However, the statement "with this *iṣṭi* [performed] together with the re-establishment of the fires" (*punarādheya-samiṣṭi-yajña*) refers merely to the sequence. Therefore, it is thought that the compensatory offerings will be performed only after having performed the *udavasānīyā*, in order to maintain the integrity of the sequence.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is this: it is true that there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*), nor is there even a qualification (*adhikāra*).
This is because another qualification is heard [in the scripture], namely, "the sacrifice is for the purpose of re-establishing the fires" (*punarādheya-sammitayeṣṭi*).
The meaning of this is as follows: just like living...

The state of having performed the *udavasānīya* sacrifice is also a qualifying attribute of the person entitled [to perform the rite]; therefore, one who has not performed the *udavasānīya* lacks the entitlement.

Since there is no restrictive rule for one who lacks such entitlement, those [rites] need not be performed. For the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* is indeed the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*).
And identity of agent is not possible between the *agnihotra* and the *udavasānīya*, which are not mutually connected. In that case, if...

A person who has performed the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice becomes eligible for the *agnihotra*; thus, even by virtue of having a common substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the requirement of a single agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is not excessively discarded. If, however, the focus were on sequence (*krama*), that requirement would be utterly contradicted.
If there is a *pratihoma*, the offerings beginning with the evening *agnihotra* should be performed.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed order for the *pratihomas* performed at one time, because there is no authoritative basis for a restriction of sequence; thus, there is no fixed rule. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that they must be performed starting precisely from the point where the negligence occurred.
The meaning is that the rectification of what has been transgressed must be performed in the very same sequence as the transgression itself.
|| 14 || But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice], it is in the morning. || 44 ||
1. Here, the separate mention of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction that for some it occurs in the evening, while for others it occurs in the morning.
|| 15 || Regarding the section on expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), they apply everywhere because the nature of the fault is common to all cases. || 45 ||
It is heard in the scripture: "He offers when [the vessel] is broken," and "He offers when [the oblation] has spilled. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Is this entitlement (adhikāra) limited only to the cause (nimitta), or does it extend to the effect (kārya)?
By this, the doubt of the author of the Bhāṣya is explained. For if it were for one who has caused a breach, this entitlement would be independent.

If, however, the qualification (adhikāra) extends to the completion of the task— that is, to the completion of the assistance rendered to the ritual under discussion— then, when a breakage occurs specifically during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the oblation which is a subsidiary part of them must be performed.
Since the qualification of the agent cannot be established [otherwise], this qualification extends only as far as the occurrence of the occasion (nimitta).
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks as follows:

For where the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), there the entitlement (*adhikāra*) extends to the completion of the action. But here, since the goal to be accomplished is not a qualification of the qualified person, it is not logical that the entitlement should extend to the completion of the action. And that [entitlement] is thus without benefit—

[ka] Because of the non-occurrence of which factor does it happen that, even in all cases such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, the oblations for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) are performed only upon the breaking [of a vessel], since there is no difference in the occasion (*nimitta*)? Why do they not occur for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)? The answer is:

Because of the injunction for the oblation (*homa*); for indeed, an oblation cannot take place in the *āhavanīya* fire. The restriction of the occasion (*nimitta*) is in accordance with the occasional rite (*naimittika*), as in the case of the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*). There is nothing here that is obscure.
This being the case, it is replied: this entitlement (adhikāra) extends only as far as the completion of the ritual action.
Why? Because the entitlement to the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices alone is the subject under discussion. The understanding that there is a single mandate (niyoga) cannot be set aside.
1. Therefore,

the meaning of this is not that "one offers when it is broken"— wherein the breaking is heard as a causal condition (*nimitta*)— but rather that it is not directly a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*).

By that [reasoning]: since the status of being a *nimitta* (occasion) is otherwise inexplicable in the case of performance—which is based solely on eligibility (*adhikāra*)—it must be inferred, by implication, that it serves as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the injunction (*niyoga*) for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices possesses an eligibility directly heard in scripture. That which is understood to be without eligibility in proximity to that [injunction] is also connected to and brought forward by that very same [eligibility]; thus, there is first of all a single injunction (*ekaniyogatā*).
It is understood. And how does it come to be so? If it accomplishes the assistance of the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not otherwise.
Therefore, because it culminates in the result, this is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
But if that were the case, would there not arise a contradiction with the qualification (*adhikāra*), since the qualification is something else entirely?

The occasion (*nimitta*). The occasion for the qualification is the "occasion of qualification" (*adhikāra-nimitta*), which is a differentiator of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) and another effect characterized by the assistance to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. [In contrast,] heaven and so forth are both the qualifier of the qualified person and the single effect.

It is said: there is no contradiction. For the qualification (adhikāra) brings about the state of being enjoined (niyojyatā) by means of the qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa). And the task (kārya), once understood by the one who has been enjoined, does not obstruct the qualification, because that very [qualification] is understood through it.

If the action being postulated were to exclude the very qualification of the person entitled [to perform it], then, due to that contradiction, the action would not be resorted to. However, when there is no contradiction, the postulation of an action is not untenable. Since that very person entitled [to the rite] understands the action [as applicable], one might argue that [the action] should not be disregarded; to this he says: "But in the case of living, since no other action is understood as the occasion..."
It is logical that there must be a limit.
Now, why should a cause look toward its effect? Why is it not also postulated in the case of [the soul's] continued existence?
If, however, it does not look toward it, then with what intention does he ask, "In what way is the effect accepted"? Thus he asks.

Now, why is it not postulated that the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) [is the primary object]? It is said: An injunction (*niyoga*) cannot tolerate such a postulation, because its purpose is fulfilled by the very accomplishment of the injunction itself.
Even in the case of the qualification based on living (*jīvana-adhikāra*), the application (*viniyoga*) is itself of the nature of a *kārya*.

It is so understood. Since its purpose is fulfilled by that very [understanding], no further effect (*kārya*) is postulated. Furthermore, what is being perceived cannot be denied, because it constitutes a specific aspect of its own meaning;
for just as an injunction (*niyoga*) is perceived here as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), so too [is this].

There is also assistance to the instrument [of action]. Therefore, it is inappropriate to deny that which is being understood [from the context], because this qualification extends as far as the result. Consequently, the qualification belongs only to one who is already qualified for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and who possesses the "breaking" (of a vessel), not to one performing the Agnihotra or the Jyotiṣṭoma; for there is an absence of the two means of proof—direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*)—for one who is not already qualified.
16. One should understand that whatever is unfit for the noble ones to eat when it has been cast into the water [as an offering] pertains to the deceased. 48.
1. *Nimittakārya* [p. 177]:
Demonstrating the connection between the section (*adhikaraṇa*) and the chapter (*adhyāya*), he says, "We do not know whose misfortune it is," and so forth.
It delivers—[for] it is heard in scripture that one who has suffered a calamity should perform an offering in water: "One should offer in water for one who has met with calamity.
An offering in water is prescribed for a person who has suffered a calamity and is thus qualified [for the rite]. It is not known whose calamity [is meant].
Regarding the word "dead" (*mṛta*):
what is that which is "perished" (*vyāpanna*), by whose perishing it is not known whether the person is one who has perished?
If perishing were a qualification of the eligible performer (*adhikārin*), then how could there be the striking of one who is already perished? This [is] a single [point].
The meaning is that one who has fallen from their status (*vyāpanna-pada*) is neither capable of qualifying for [the ritual] nor able to offer the ritual act (*karman*).
To the inquiry "How so? the answer is: because of the understanding of their lack of qualification (*adhikāra*).
The meaning of this is: for the purpose of offering the ritual act—

The term *vyāpanna* has been handed down [in the scriptures]. By implication, it serves as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*). In what manner? It is said: how could the casting of that which is *vyāpanna* into the waters be possible? If the one who possesses the *vyāpanna* substance is the one entitled to the rite, then there is no fault in this implied determination of the qualified person. And here, what is to be understood by the word *vyāpanna*?

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is simply that it is ignorance (ajñāna). However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: since its specific nature is not understood—given that it has been refuted in some measure as being either an effect or a cause—it remains to be determined what it is.
This very point is clarified: the meaning of the word *vyāpanna* is that the duty of the learned has been rendered unfit for performance.
Since it is thus impaired (*vyāpanna*), this entitlement (*adhikāra*) is dependent upon that [impairment].
It is established that for one whose substance has been rendered unfit for the purpose of the learned, there is the forfeiture of the weapon.
|| 17 || Since there is a scriptural injunction regarding distribution, no expiation exists in the case of simultaneity. || 49 ||
There is a doubt regarding the *apaccheda* (simultaneous occurrence of two disconnections): is one entitled [to perform the rite] by each individual disconnection, or by both together?
By this, the reason for the doubt presented by the author of the *Bhāṣya* has been set forth. If one is entitled by each individual disconnection, then...

When both [the officiants] are simultaneously disqualified (*apaccheda*), no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be performed; therefore, both are entitled to the rite. Furthermore, by the term *apaccheda*, an action resulting in separation is intended here. He raises a doubt: "But how can there be the simultaneous occurrence of two [disqualifications]?"

How is the occurrence of two acts of cutting possible? The meaning is: one by one. He provides the resolution: this very point is being investigated here—does oneness belong to two [acts] occurring simultaneously, or is there even in that case merely simultaneity? It is indeed one by one.
"In that case too, it is the cause of entitlement.
The meaning of this is: by way of demonstrating the fruit, this very point is investigated here—whether [it is] for the sake of completing one [rite], etc.
Now, at that time, there is only one act of cutting which inheres in two persons; therefore, it can be designated by one of them—

Because it is impossible [for both to occur simultaneously], and because an expiation is prescribed when one or the other is designated as having undergone an *apaccheda*, there should be no expiation; for the act of *apaccheda* is completed individually by each person independently.
Even if, at the very most, they exist at the same time, then two *apacchedas* designated by both would occur simultaneously.
Thus, it must indeed be that there is an expiation.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the two instances of disconnection (*apaccheda*) to be one and the same, on account of the identity of time. This is based on the unity of time—

This is not an error; rather, it is considered that this single act of cutting belongs to two persons. Furthermore, the notion that "action resides in a single substance and is devoid of qualities" is merely a conventional formulation (*prakriyā*) of those who know categories (*padārtha*), for it cannot be designated by either person alone;
thus, the state of having a single agent is based upon both. Therefore, this action is designated by means of both.

It has been stated that the disconnection (apaccheda) designated by one person or another is the cause for entitlement (adhikāra). Therefore, there is no entitlement when [the disconnections] occur simultaneously; for since the result is established by the inference of only a single action, there is no reason to infer another action—this is the hidden intention.

To this it is replied: the act of disjunction (*apaccheda*) cannot be designated as belonging to two [agents] simultaneously; for the action of disjunction does not have a dual substratum, because the status of being an agent is independent of any other. Therefore—

"Agency does not belong here to two things joined in mutual relation (*itarētara-yuktau*). Not having understood the intention of the proponent—that independence was stated with the intent of [denying] agency—he objects: 'But how is it that the disconnection (*apaccheda*) does not depend on a second?
[He asks this regarding] that which has become the point of departure (*apādāna-bhūta*).

The sense is that, without a second [act of suspension], the very act of suspension itself is not possible. The reply is: one indeed requires a second suspension as a point of reference (*apādāna*) by way of its mere existence, but not as something to be designated.

Likewise, it does not depend on [the self] as an agent; yet here the designation depends on agency. And here the designation is by way of the state of being an agent. By negating the relationship between the designator and the designated, it negates agency. But how can two actions, each to be accomplished by both [the self and the body], be spoken of individually? It is said: each one—
Just as the respective fruit residing in each individual was observed at the time of cutting, it is understood to be exactly the same for both together;
thus, the inference of action for both is not contradictory. Therefore, this [position] of the Blessed One Kāśyapa is established.
The Sūtra states: "Action is that which consists of a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions" (1.1.17).

This is the definition of action. Therefore, even though they are enjoined simultaneously, it is established that each individual oblation (*havis*) serves as the cause for its respective entitlement.
In that case, there should be an option due to the conflict [of rules]. || 51 ||
[Page 179] This is now considered: Is there an option between the two results (*naimittika*) or are they to be combined?
When it is established that both causes (*nimitta*) exist simultaneously, then the consideration regarding the two results becomes appropriate: what...?
Is it a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*)? In this regard, we say it is an option because of contradiction.

Since there is a contradiction between giving away one's entire property (*sarvasva*) and the absence of sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇya*), and because they cannot be performed simultaneously, an option alone is logical; such is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Now, why is there no repetition (*āvṛtti*) in accordance with those two occasional subsidiary elements?
It is postulated as belonging to the primary [act] itself; therefore, both will be included by it.
He refutes this: "Not by following the subsidiaries.
Now, why is it not proper for the primary act to be repeated twice?

For the purpose of the subsidiary (aṅga) belongs to the principal (pradhāna), not the purpose of the principal to the subsidiary. Therefore, it is not logical for the principal to be repeated merely out of regard for the subsidiary. Furthermore, the status of being a subsidiary for occasional rites (naimittika) has been stated because of such an injunction; however, if it is argued that "since there is a scriptural statement [of repetition], a second occasional rite will then follow," we say: no. There is no combination (samuccaya) of the two expiations (prāyaścitta) in the case of a cutting (apaccheda); rather, the first—

Because it is not recognized as being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*). For only that which is known to be a constituent part of the first preparatory practice is to be performed again and again; it is not the case that both are constituent parts in the first practice, but rather only one. Therefore, because the second is not a constituent part, it does not enter into this [subsequent performance] either.

Now, one might object: "Just as both rice and barley are subsidiary elements because both are enjoined for use, why should both not likewise be subsidiary elements here? To this, he replies: "It is stated in the section on the *Abhyudayeṣṭi* that even in the performance [of a rite], [a substance] is enjoined by way of the qualification [for the result], and not merely as part of the ritual action."

Furthermore, that which is enjoined with reference to an authorized agent (adhikārī) by way of connection to a specific occasion (nimitta) is enjoined solely as an auxiliary to the performance (prayoga). And it is not possible for both [the occasion and the agent] to enter into the performance simultaneously. However, in the case of the ritual action itself, even contradictory elements can indeed coexist by virtue of being based on different performances. Therefore, there is an option (vikalpa). Since each is separately applied, each constitutes a single auxiliary (aṅga).
This is the alternative view regarding the treatises:
"In a sequence of earlier and later [injunctions], the earlier is weaker, as in the case of the original nature. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.5.54)
What is the consideration of sublation here? By this, an inconsistency has been stated; and that is improper.
By this...
The lack of logical justification has been stated. For, within the present context, there is simply no occasion for sublation (*bādha*); therefore, this inquiry here is irrelevant.
Why is it unjustified? The answer is:
sublation is indeed considered at the time of determining the meaning of the scripture (*śāstra*). [End of incomplete sentence] Adhi-

This consideration of sublation (*bādhacintana*) pertains to the application (*prayoga*). And since there is no room for two contradictory [rules] within a single application, this inquiry is intended solely to determine the meaning of the scriptural injunctions (*śāstrārtha*): "Which one shall be sublated?
It is not, however, that sublation is considered once the meaning of the scriptural injunction has already been determined, as is the case with the tenth book (*dāśamika*).

Nevertheless, as to how this is illogical, he says: for at the time of determining the meaning of the treatises, there is no sequence here, because each individual treatise conveys its own specific meaning; however, such is the case in actual practice.

Regarding the application of that [action], its feasibility or infeasibility, and its being performed or unperformed—herein there is either *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *prasaṅga* (extended application). He states this in a single passage: "It is indeed appropriate that there is either *tantra* or *prasaṅga* regarding what is performed and what is unperformed. It can be said that it is *tantra* and not *prasaṅga*, because of the state of having accomplished what was to be done."
For there would be [the fallacies of] *tantra* (extension) and *prasaṅga* (consequence), and furthermore, incapacity (*aśakti*).

And here, incapacity is not being considered. [Objection: Let it be that there is no *tantra* or *prasaṅga*; there will be sublation (*bādha*). To this, he says: "And even sublation occurs only when the meaning of the scripture has been ascertained."

"It is simply not possible, because it cannot be sublated," as stated in the third [chapter]. He concludes: "Therefore, this is a different kind of 'sublation of the application' (prayogabādha), arising from an inability to apply [the rule]. And that is not consistent with the context (*adhikāra*), since this..."
This is a sublation of the application (*prayogabādha*). Therefore, this is not a sublation of a scriptural meaning that has already been established, nor is the application itself being sublated.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the scriptural meaning is unestablished, as was the case with the lack of establishment in the third [chapter]. Thus, there is an absence of both *tantra* and *prasaṅga*.
It has already been demonstrated.

It is now being justified: "This is indeed a different kind of sublation (*bādha*); there is no fault whatsoever. He raises an objection: "But what is the relevance of this to the current topic (*adhikāra*)? This is the relevance: "As for the topic..."
It serves for the performance [of the rite], not for the knowledge of the ritual act;
for one is authorized only when the ritual act is known. Therefore, it has been considered in this very context that this is an alternative application prescribed by way of such authorization.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is eligibility for performance (*prayoga*), nevertheless, at the time of determining the meaning of the scripture concerning eligibility (*adhikāra-śāstra*), there is no sequence (*paurvāparya*) between them; and since that [sequence] is absent, how can there be sublation (*bādha*)? Do not speak thus. For the scripture concerning eligibility repeats with every performance (*pratiprayogam*). Repetition constitutes the application; for when there is a sequence of prior and posterior [injunctions], and the application is possible through the very determination of the meaning of the scripture with each individual application, then—

during the stage of application— it is precisely that which has an impossible object for those two authoritative scriptures regarding their respective entitlements that becomes sublated (*bādhyatā*) once the determination of the meaning is established.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considered the earlier [statement] alone to possess the status of truth because its contradiction had not yet arisen; for that whose contradiction has not arisen is precisely what possesses the status of truth. As for the subsequent [statement], its meaning, being contradictory to that [former one], does not find a place for itself. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī) maintains: "This reason applies to the non-arising of the subsequent [statement], not to the earlier one."
Contradiction.

For the attainment of the subsequent [element] contradicts the non-arisen contradiction of the preceding one, but it does not contradict its performance. And here, it cannot be obstructed beforehand because the cause is present. But when there is incapacity...
1. Non-attainment (aprāptatva), 2. Conflict (raṇa), 3. Non-authoritative cognition (aprāmā).

The subsequent application ceases; therefore, it is logical that only the later application is the sublater of the earlier one. Another application cannot be cognized without first sublatting the earlier one, whereas the earlier one is not necessarily cognized without sublatting the later one.

Therefore, in this application, the very fact that contradiction has not yet arisen is the reason for being sublated, while the fact that contradiction has already arisen is the reason for being the sublater. Now, one might object: "In the previous section, it was stated that once the prior [element] has occurred, the subsequent scriptural rule simply does not apply. To this he says:
"It must be determined in each individual application."

And it has been stated that this is an authoritative treatise (*adhikāra-śāstra*). Therefore, even with respect to time, it has been shown that where there is a determination in the tenth [book], the very fact of having produced a contradiction (*upajāta-virodhitā*) is the cause for its sublation (*bādhakatva*).
If this sublation occurs because of the production of a contradiction, then this sublation belongs specifically to the tenth book.
Furthermore, there is an inconsistency here. He resolves it: "It is true that [the reason] is the cause, but not by way of being a door. This refers to that which has arisen as an opposition.

When there is an exclusion (*bādha*), the reason (*hetu*) applies equally; however, it would apply only to the tenth [chapter], while the door (*dvāra*) is distinct. For in that case, the restriction of the application (*prayojya-avadhṛti*) is the reason for the door; here, however, there is no restriction of the application—this is the distinction. The determination of the applicable [rule] excludes other applicable [rules] because its purpose has already been fulfilled; the application excludes another application due to incapacity, because of the specific qualification (*adhikāra*).

And the injunction (*codanā*) is a specific application (*prayoga-viśeṣa*). It has been demonstrated that an injunction is an injunction regarding the essential nature of the ritual action (*karma-svarūpa-codanā*). Therefore, it is entirely logical that this sublation (*bādha*) is to be considered right here [in this very context]. Thus, the summary of the meaning here is as follows: that specific prior application is enjoined within that very same application, [serving] as a counter-position.

Since there is a subsequent statement by the force of the text, another performance is distinguished through the sublation of the previous one; thus, this is indeed a case of the annulment of what was previously obtained.
Just as its inclusion does not occur within the tenth [book], so it has been stated immediately thereafter.

Previously, when there was a disconnection of the *pratihartṛ* first,

it was stated in the immediately preceding section that although the performance would have required the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) as the sacrificial fee, the subsequent disconnection of the *udgātṛ* takes precedence; furthermore, the lack of a fee for this performance is a contingent rule (*naimittika*), and after that, the giving of the fee occurs again as before.

By this, the subject matter stated in the Bhāṣya has been clarified. In that regard, there is a doubt: by the force of the statement, "In that case, one should give what one was intending to give in the previous instance," should the *pratihartṛ* priest, upon the occasion of his own disconnection (*apaccheda*), give away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*), or rather, only the prescribed twelve [cows]?

"It should be given; that [gift] should be given. And since, in the previous performance, the primary performer was deprived of his share due to disconnection (apaccheda), it is precisely the "all-one's-possessions" (sarvavedasa) that must be given by him for the subsequent sacrifice.
But is this not intended with reference to the previous gift? For even in that case, there are twelve hundred.
Indeed, it is with reference to what was to be given in the previous gift that this is said: "Whatever one would have given in the previous [gift], that one should give."

In that regard, there is also the case where twelve hundred [cows] are to be given first; for in the initial application, according to the specific assignment, there is both the twelve hundred and the "all one's possessions" (*sarvavedasa*). When that [gift] is given, both are considered given. The term *sarvavedasa* (all one's possessions) is said to imply even more than twelve hundred [cows]. By this, there is the favoring of both; for if it were less, there would be no favoring of both. And this is accepted here—
"Nevertheless, it is merely a statement regarding what is to be understood," so says the text. He states the fundamental reasoning: "And here, mere priority is not intended;

The meaning of this is as follows: that very performance which is being praised again is the one referred to here by the word "prior" (*pūrva*), not merely that which is chronologically prior. And the performance of one hundred and twelve [cows] is prior. However, by superseding that, there is the subsequent performance caused by the interruption of the *pratihartṛ* priest, wherein all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇa*). This [present passage] is a reiteration of praise for that very [subsequent performance].
Only that which is equal to the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) should be given.
Now, is it not the case that even that gift of all one's possessions is sublated there?
No; rather, it is sublated in the previous performance.

When it is argued that "it does not exist [again]," [the response is: because of the statement "one should give that there," it is by no means invalidated; however, it was invalidated in the previous performance and must therefore be given again. Thus, the occasional (*naimittika*) rite here is not invalidated. Rather, due to the lapse of time alone, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given in the previous performance should not be given at that very moment; instead, it should be given again during the subsequent recitation (*stuti*).

Since the qualification (*adhikāra*) has the performance (*prayoga*) as its object, and since the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) constitutes a single performance,

the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that there must be a repetition of the entire sequence. The statement "one should sacrifice again with a sacrifice" indicates that this occasional qualification (*naimittiko’dhikāra*), having the performance as its object, prescribes a repetition of the performance.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) says: "Since this [rite] consisting of twelve days is a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), it is merely a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of that very same [performance]. However, the final established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: regarding the object of the ritual action—

Because there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karman*) within the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) pertains to each individual act; thus, there is a repetition of the act itself, not of the entire collection of acts.
That very performance (*prayoga*) in which the occasion (*nimitta*) arises is what is repeated.

And this is the cause [of repetition] with respect to a single action, not with respect to a collection of actions in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. Since there are indeed many intermediate applications (*avāntara-prayoga*) for each individual action, the repetition of the application belongs to a single action alone, not to the collection of actions.

As for the literal meaning: because the qualification (*adhikāra*) has the action as its object, it is derived from the etymology "that by which one is qualified" (*adhikriyate ’nena*), and thus it is the cause (*nimitta*).
It is expressed by the word "adhikāra" (authorization/entitlement). Therefore, it has been stated that the object of authorization is indeed the ritual action (*karman*).

In the *Ṛjuvimalā*,

Now this is heard:

it is heard regarding those qualified for specific rites. In that regard, does the qualification belong only to those who follow the same ritual manual (*kalpa*) across many rites, or even to those who follow different manuals?
He challenges the restated position:
"But surely, when one hears the specific qualification [of the subject], there is no doubt at all;
for Vasiṣṭha and others are also included here precisely by virtue of being qualified."

They are connected [to the ritual], not by way of being the performers (*kartṛtā*), because the qualification (*adhikāra*) presents itself first. Consequently, their qualification is established precisely through the *nārāśaṃsa* procedure; for others, however, it is through the *tanūnapāt* procedure. Thus, it is logical that only those of the same procedure (*samānakalpa*) have the qualification, and not those of different procedures (*bhinnakalpa*), due to the resulting deficiency (*vaiguṇya*). He resolves this: "True; because there is no departure from what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it occurs..."
There is doubt.

Its meaning is as follows: the prayājas and other such rites are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) alone, not for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). And for the sacrifice, both of these [the primary rite and its subsidiaries] are auxiliary members (*aṅga*). Consequently, even if only one [of the two] is performed, there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) in the sacrifice. And when there is no deficiency in the sacrifice, the establishment of the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the sacrifice is also achieved.
Regarding the phrase "of those performed": here an objection is raised— how can there be any doubt when the rites for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) have not been omitted,
given that this very position— that those of different ritual procedures (*bhinnakalpa*) also possess the entitlement— is superior?
The reply: True, there is no doubt;
however, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers it to be precisely the opposite. How so?

If [the act] is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha), then one cannot say that there is no deficiency (vaiguṇya); and from deficiency follows the obstruction of the qualification (adhikāra) [to perform the rite], according to one's own [erroneous] opinion.
By what [means]? And in this view, the mention of Vasiṣṭha and others is merely a restatement (anuvāda), because the sacrifice is connected with Vasiṣṭha and the rest.

Since even when the sacrifice has a single material cause, this prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) remains free from defect, the accomplishment of the task is thus shown to be by way of a mere generality, like the "head" [in the case of the *ṛtapeya*]. Just as, because of the injunction for a vow of ghee (*ghṛta-vrata*) in the *ṛtapeya*, there is a cow that yields ghee...

Even when one cow has ceased [to exist], the accomplishment of the purpose is achieved by another cow; likewise, even when one second *prayāja* has ceased, the accomplishment of the function of the second *prayāja* is achieved by another.

There is no fault even if that withdrawal [of the means] does not occur once the purpose has been accomplished.

Alternatively, it has been demonstrated—by way of the analogy of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans]—that when both are possible, not even one [of them] becomes the cause. This is because there is the possibility of persons arising from different ritual procedures (*kalpa*).

Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as Viśvāmitra and others, do not constitute the cause [of the event], because each one individually is a cause. Just as the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are each individually a cause, so too there is no causality for a single [person]; thus, there is a contradiction regarding the conditional [rite].

This is the intended meaning: even in the case of instruction (*upadeśa*), non-combination has already been stated. Alternatively, it is that in the very act of instruction, there is no gathering together (*samāhāra*) of persons belonging to different ritual procedures (*bhinnakalpa*). By what distinction, then, [is this so]?

Regarding the phrase "like the head," since it was previously introduced that "the Udumbara post is to be of the same height as the sacrificer," the accomplishment of the purpose here is exactly the same. The reply is: True; however, there is an additional doubt regarding the resolution.
Having introduced that [objection] under the guise of this illustration, it is restated separately in order to refute it. What, then, is that? He states it:
"Why does the word *yajamāna* not apply [to the priest] solely by virtue of being an agent (*kāraka*), as in the case of the *ṛtvij*? By that, [it is meant] not [in the context of] the sacrifice...
