However, when the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is used in the sense of ownership (*svāmitva*), then there is no honor for one who exists as a separate agent, because such a person lacks ownership. But if [the term] is understood merely in the sense of being an agent (*kartṛmātra*), then...
Since that [self] too possesses agency, it is possible for it to perform acts of honoring; therefore, another example is introduced in order to refute that.
He states the refutation: "The apprehension is not by way of mere agency, but rather through the medium of the specific qualification."
Because [the status of] being an agent presupposes qualification (*adhikāra*), agency is understood as being preceded by that [qualification]. Therefore,

since it is said that "one who is qualified must perform the honoring," there is no inclusion of another sacrificer belonging to a different ritual (*kratu*), as indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
And because of the mention [of the agent], it is the owner alone who is to be understood, not merely the performer; therefore, it is established that the sacrificer is the one authorized.

Because he is the one to be selected (*upādeya*), the distinction is that many do not perform the measuring, as shown by the illustrative example. Furthermore, regarding the first explanation—that it is "like the head"—since there is a scriptural injunction stating, "He places the human head," this would result in a contradiction with the Smṛti.

Similarly here too, there is the sublation of one ritual alternative by another. In this case as well, non-application (*aprāpti*) alone is to be understood, just as in the case of the withdrawal of a conditional rule (*nimittopasaṃhāra*).

For if the touching of a corpse's head were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the prohibition would not apply; therefore, by that analogy, non-application alone is to be understood here. Just as in the view of the withdrawal of a conditional rule, there is indeed the application of another ritual alternative when the condition is met.
The position that "it does not exist" is untenable; it is precisely because of this lack of satisfaction that a second explanation has been provided.
To this, it is replied: it cannot be said that this is like [the case of] milk-curd (*āśira*), nor is it like the inclusion of a causal factor (*nimitta*).
This is what is meant: non-attainment does not occur as it does in the case of the withdrawal of the *nimitta*, nor as in the case of the *āśir*;

thus, the state of having accomplished one's purpose (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) is possible. How, then? For this [term] is a qualification of those entitled [to the rite], namely "of the Vasiṣṭhas" and "of the Bhṛgus.
Even so, he asks: why? He replies: because the door of entitlement (*adhikāra*) is possible within the performance (*prayoga*) and the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the ritual act.
This has been stated:

by virtue of the connection with the qualified person (*adhikṛta*), this specific performance (*prayoga-viśeṣa*) is enjoined, not the essential nature of the ritual act (*karma-svarūpa*). And thus, since there is no attainment of completion through mere performance [of the act], the qualification belongs only to those of the same ritual procedure (*samāna-kalpa*), because they constitute a single performance (*eka-prayoga*).
[The rule] is established.

It is heard in scripture: "The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should perform the sacrifice. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the dual ending arise from the meaning of the compound, or from the meaning of the nominal stem? If the dual ending arises when there is duality of the meaning of the compound, then...

Two priests of the king should perform the sacrifice; if [the dual number] refers to the duality of the meaning of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*), then it would mean that both the king and the priest should perform the sacrifice.
But surely, even in the other view, the dual ending arises from the very meaning of the compound, for a *dvandva* is also a type of compound (*samāsa*).
[The opponent says: "It is so. [The author replies: The answer is that while the compound is true, there is no dual number for the meaning of the compound;
rather, the two members of the compound themselves are connected with the sense of the dual number through their mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

For in the case of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), a *dvandva* compound consists of two [members]. In that context, the word-meanings contained within the compound are presented as being mutually conjoined; indeed, no separate meaning is presented by the two individual words themselves. For it is the duality residing in that [conjoined meaning] which is expressed by the dual suffix. However, where the dual suffix applies to the compound meaning itself...

In that case, there is only the singular number. For example, as in a collective compound (*samāhāra*). For in a collective compound, whatever *dvandva* it may be, the two meanings being combined are expressed for the purpose of characterizing the collection; and because that [collection] has a single referent, there is only the singular number in the collective.
Indeed, in a *dvandva* that is a collective, the mention of the dual number is intended as an illustration of the dual.
But if this is so, then since mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) also possesses singularity, the singular number would likewise apply; yet it is not so observed.
With what intention does he ask: "Is mutual conjunction not the meaning of the compound, such that [the singular would apply] there?"
The singular number does not apply. Now, if it were not applied even when that [compound] has the meaning of a compound, it would likewise not apply in the case of a collective (samāhāra);
this is the sense. The reply is: We do not say that it is the meaning of the compound; rather, at that time, it is merely an attribute (upādhi).
When the two members of the compound are joined in mutual relation (itaretarayoga), that alone constitutes the meaning of the compound, which receives the technical designation "compound" (samāsa).
By which two words is it expressed?

Precisely because they are expressed by a compound (*samāsa*) in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), for that very reason, simultaneous location (*yugapadadhikaraṇatā*) and the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) occur only in such a context, and not in the context of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*).

But how can there be simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatā*)? It cannot be by way of direct denotation (*vācaka-vṛtti*), because there is no prior apprehension of such a relationship [between the word and its multiple referents], and because the employment of other words would be rendered useless. Nor is it possible by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*), because there is no logical inconsistency [that necessitates it], and because it would entail the abandonment of the word's own primary meaning. To this, it is replied: simultaneous expression of multiple substrates occurs by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*). Thus:

For instance, in the sentence "Cut down the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," the word *dhava* denotes only the *dhava* tree; this is its primary meaning (*vācyārtha*). However, by virtue of the relationship between a state and that which possesses the state (*avasthāvasthāvatoḥ sambandhāt*), it indicates its own condition as being conjoined with the *khadira*. Furthermore, the hearing of the dual ending (*dvivacana*)—which would otherwise be untenable—is the cause for this indication (*lakṣaṇāhetu*). Thus, while the duality of the nominal stem meanings (*prātipadikārtha*) is possible, [the dual ending does not apply] to the two words in a *dvandva* compound.

The word "two" exists as a term of exclusion (*vyatirekī*). It occurs only in a compound word when it is intended to convey merely the meanings of its constituent parts in their combined state. In that case, since neither of those two [constituents] individually possesses duality, on what basis could the dual number be applied? However, when the compound words are intended to convey their own meanings as mutually connected (*itaretara-yukta*), then duality is inherent (*samaveta*) in those two such meanings; thus, the dual—

The occurrence of the singular number is justified because, in a compound (*samāsa*), the meaning expressed by each individual word is characterized by their collective totality (*samāhāra*); thus, the singular number is appropriate.

Consequently, there is no evidence for the simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*). Furthermore, in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, this is not so, because the expression is based on a single underlying principle (*tantra*).

The comprehension of meanings as mutually associated occurs in the case of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), where there is the comprehension of meanings as mutually associated; therefore, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is an exception (*apavāda*) to that very domain, and not the *dvandva* (copulative compound) in its alternative sense of *samāhāra* (collective). When, by virtue of the force of simultaneous substrates, this state of expressing a composite meaning arises according to the aforementioned reasoning, thus...

In this case, it is logical that the dual number refers exclusively to the two domestic priests (*purohita*). For otherwise, the word *purohita* would apply to the king as well, which would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But how can it be said that the word *purohita*, being uttered only once, applies both to the priest and the king through metaphorical indication? [The answer is: It applies directly (*śrauta*) to the priest, but...
It is indeed so. And it is not the case that [the word] is both primary (śrauta) and secondary (lākṣaṇika) when uttered only once. He offers a rebuttal: "True;
this follows by the force of hearing the simultaneous substratum (adhikaraṇa). When, according to the stated reasoning, they are in a state of conjunction—"
When there is a simultaneous substratum by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇa*), then the intention (*tātparya*) applies to both the literal (*śrauta*) and the indicated (*lākṣaṇika*) meanings.
And in ultimate reality, that which is not a literal meaning is indeed indicated. This has been shown in the example "the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees," for it is not the case that—

The dual number is not possible without the expression of a simultaneous substratum (yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā). Therefore, even though a literal sense is possible, this alternative involving a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is presented as something to be rejected. Although the meaning of "family priest" (purohita) is also present, nevertheless, a figurative indication would result. For this reason, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) has presented this dual-compound (dvandva) position as something to be discarded.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the word *eṣa* deviates from both duality and masculinity—as in the phrase *vasānau* [where the dual form is used for two males]? [Response: Likewise here, the word *eṣa* does not deviate from the duality of the two domestic priests (*purohita*), because it conveys the sense of a second [person].

"There is no risk of [the definition] over-extending" (lakṣaṇāprasaṅga). He provides the rebuttal: "The intention of the statement is as follows. It has been stated that masculinity and duality do not deviate from the dual number ending in *au*;
this is not intended to refer to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

For indeed, without simultaneous substratumhood (*yugapad-adhikaraṇatva*), the dual number would be unaccountable for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in the case of "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājapurohitam*). Therefore, wherever there is a dual number, that nominal stem must convey its own meaning as mutually connected (*itaretara-yukta*). And this is not possible without secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, it is rightly said: "It is secondary indication. If it is secondary indication, this [view] is to be rejected.
"Position" refers to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Now, even in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the word "king" is indeed figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), as it indicates the meaning of the genitive case.

He refutes [the objection]: "It is so. What loss is there for us? Having accepted the word *purohita*, it was stated that this position must not be abandoned because it functions as a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

But is it not the case that even in the view that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it would still possess the nature of an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because its meaning is directed toward something else? To this he says: "This genitive compound has the final member as its primary referent."

This being the case, it is replied: True, this is so; however, because the *purohita* is a single entity, even in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), a dual number is still untenable, since the word *purohita* denotes a specific relationship [to a single king].
Because of the absence of a relationship between two [distinct entities].

The meaning of this is as follows: this word *purohita* is a relational term (*sambandhiśabda*). And it is not possible for two *purohitas* to be related to a single king. Therefore, [the genitive] *ṣaṣṭhī*—

Even in the case of a compound, because there is no referent [for two], the dual number is simply untenable. Therefore, it is better to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself for the sake of making the dual number possible.
But surely, since we observe their employment, there will be two domestic priests (*purohita*), just as [there are two] from the injunction regarding the *añjali* gesture?

Regarding the employment of two hands, he says: what was stated previously—that it is "like the añjali"—is not possible here, because there is no second correlate, precisely due to the lack of a connection; for in the injunction "one should choose a domestic priest" (*purohitaṃ vṛṇīte*), the singular number is heard.
[Objection: Let it be that the word *purohita* is a relative term; even in the case of other duties, the very appointment (*niyoga*) will bring about the state of being a relative.

For whoever performs those various rites for a particular king becomes his *purohita*; thus, since two related parties are possible, [the opponent] says in response: "And the origin [of the relationship] is the cause of the relation. It is not [the case that the relation exists prior to the origin].
The application [of a person] to a task depends upon this [status], because application to a task presupposes it.

The meaning is this: a priest (purohita) becomes such by virtue of being produced by another [the king]; he is not, however, to be applied to other tasks, because application to other tasks presupposes his status as a priest.

The summary of this point is as follows: Priesthood (*purohitatva*) arises from appointment (*viniyoga*), while the act of "gathering" (*saṅgraha*) consists in the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of him for that role. Therefore, since both [selection and appointment] are observed in the case of the two [the king and the priest], there is a "gathering" of both; for gathering has the purpose of appointment—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that priesthood exists only through the continuation of the appointment once one is already a priest. Furthermore, regarding its origin (*utpatti*)...

Because of the hearing of the singular number, it is shown in the Bhāṣya that only one [priest] arises; thus, there is no *sāyujya* (union) for the two priests belonging to two different kings. Therefore, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is superior here, as the meaning is possible. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated.
Sacrifices belong to all social classes without distinction. 16.
But is it not the case that [the phrase] "of all castes" is untenable, because the sacrificer is heard [to be the one performing] the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the office of the officiating priest was established as having a Brāhmaṇa as its agent; however, here, in the office of the officiating priest, the sacrificer [is the agent].

It is stated that [the sacrificer] acts as the agent, because of the scriptural statement: "Those who are the sacrificers, they are the officiating priests. Even if a non-Brahmin were [to participate] in a *sattra* sacrifice...

If he were the performer, then, in his capacity as the officiant (*ṛtvij*), the requirement that Brahmins be the performers would be sublated. For when a Brahmin is the qualified person (*adhikārin*), nothing is sublated; and since an injunction is validly established without sublation, it is not right to assume sublation. Therefore, it is logical that only Brahmins have the qualification for *satra* sacrifices.

Furthermore, this mode of expression is not considered here: whether, by the statement "those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests," the office of the officiating priest is enjoined as a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) with reference to the sacrificers; or whether, in the context of the office of the officiating priest, the sacrificers are enjoined as its agents.

In this regard, if it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer, then since the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) must be performed by the priests alone, there would be eligibility for all social classes (*varṇas*). However, if it is an injunction that the sacrificers themselves are the agents of the priestly office, then, according to the previously stated reasoning, eligibility belongs only to Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, based on the interpretation of the statement as it is understood [in the former sense], there arises the doubt regarding the eligibility of all social classes.
It is indeed appropriate. Nor is it proper to entertain this inquiry here, because the determination of application (*viniyoga*) is irrelevant to the section on qualification (*adhikāra*).
Therefore, for those who maintain that it is irrelevant, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) appears as if lacking justification, since it proceeds without such an inquiry.
It is replied: This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view—that the statement regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) follows the order of qualification.
Because the state of being one's own agent is preceded by that [authorization].

The meaning of this is as follows: there is an application [of the office] because the performance of priestly functions for those who desire rewards is prescribed for the sacrificers themselves; and the status of being a sacrificer belongs to the sacrificers only when they possess the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, based on the qualification already established previously—

Because of the presence of the term "living" (*jīvita*), this description of the prescription of the [Brahman’s] limbs occurs by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*); however, the governing context does not arise by virtue of this [description]. Furthermore, the governing context appears to consist of three [priests] in their own right (*svarūpataḥ*). And since they are also enjoined for the office of the officiating priests (*ārlijya*), the Brāhmaṇa’s status as the performer is set aside by the extended application (*atideśika*) based on that instruction. Thus, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the prescription of the *brahmasāman*.
The observation regarding the three castes.
To this it is replied:
By whom was it said that the statement concerning the auxiliary parts (aṅga) is according to qualification? However, there is no qualification—

It is capable of precluding another [alternative] because there is no subverting cause; this too is indeed an entitlement (*adhikāra*). It is heard in scripture that "the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) belongs to the Brahmins," meaning that the office of the officiating priest has Brahmins as its performers. By the term *ārtvijya*, the duties of the officiating priests are denoted.
"Whatever is the duty of a Brahmin has been declared... [and] a duty must not be performed by one who is deficient."

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), [the office] is forbidden for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. This eligibility of the Niṣādas for the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is not to be transgressed; likewise, their eligibility for *satra* sacrifices must be described in such a way that it is not contradicted. Nor is there a contradiction between these two types of eligibility here due to a difference in subject matter, since both types of eligibility exist for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Both types of eligibility [apply].

Because it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*). Although in *satra* sacrifices the subsidiary acts are not performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), nevertheless they are indeed priestly functions (*ārtvijya*), because in the archetype (*prakṛti*) they are known as such through their priestly character, just like the deities [of the sacrifice]. This section has been explained with reference to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in regard to the priestly function.

Furthermore, regarding the refutation of the sacrificer’s refinement (*saṃskāra*) through the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) in this commentary, he offers a rebuttal: "If, on the other hand, the office of the officiating priest is enjoined for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) alone for the masters [of the sacrifice]," [then the aforementioned objection does not apply].

The meaning of this is as follows: if the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) were enjoined for the sake of an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) belonging to the masters of the sacrifice, then, such being the case, all [members] would have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the *sattra* sacrifice. But that is not so, as stated in the Bhāṣya. Therefore, in accordance with the entitlement, only Brāhmaṇas have the entitlement in the *sattra* sacrifices.
Siddham. The purpose is fulfilled by the mere sight [of the officiant], because the three castes are possible therein;
or rather, because of the restriction that for the Vāsiṣṭhas, only one of their own [caste] may serve as the Brahman priest. || 24 ||

But surely, this section would be unnecessary for those who formulate the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) without having seen the statement "the *hotṛ* priest is a descendant of Viśvāmitra" (*vaiśvāmitro hotā*),
because in the presence of that statement, there would be no room for the prima facie view that the sacrificial session (*sattra*) belongs only to the Vasiṣṭhas; thus, this section [would not exist].
The meaning is that it must indeed be undertaken.

He provides the resolution: "This is true; however, in this case, the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion of an alternative interpretation (*kalpāntara*). But what, then, is the suspicion of an alternative interpretation here?

In the case of the *Vāsiṣṭha* *brahman*, let the *hotṛ* also be one who follows the same ritual manual (*samānakalpa*) as the *Vāsiṣṭha*, or indeed a *Vāsiṣṭha* himself; for in either case there is no deficiency. Likewise, regarding the *hotṛ* as well, he might be a *Vaiśvāmitra* or one following that same ritual manual—this is the doubt raised, because two scriptural statements exist concerning the ritual manual (*kalpa*).

"One must act with two [fires]"—this section is intended to refute that [view]. Furthermore, it is not the case that only the Vāsiṣṭhas and those belonging to their same *kalpa* have the right [to perform the rite]; this is for the purpose of refuting that [restriction]. Since the statement of Vasiṣṭha has another meaning...

When the Vāsiṣṭhas have been excluded, the rule applies once again by means of the Hotṛ alone; thus it is established that there is a Sattra for those who are not Vāsiṣṭhas and for those who do not share the same ritual manual (kalpa). [The view is] that the Sattra belongs only to the Vaiśvāmitras and those who share their ritual manual.
|| 5 || Because of the predominance of the sacrificial fire-altar (vihāra), it may belong even to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (anagnīn). || 27 ||

But how, then, can there be a doubt regarding one who has not maintained the sacred fires? For, given the established principle that ritual action must be performed based on one's own fires, the fires belonging to another lack the status of being *āhavanīya* (sacrificial) fires. He provides the resolution: because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) belongs to one who considers [the scriptural statement] to be a logical consequence (prasaṅga) based on doubt;
regarding the Sārasvata sattra, it says: "Those who perform the sattra without having established the sacred fires go to the heavenly world by means of others' chariots."
Thus, because we see the mention of *satra* sacrifices for those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*);
likewise: "One whose fires, having been consecrated, become mixed with other fires, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici."

Thus, because of the observation of their association, there might arise a suspicion that even one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) is entitled [to perform the rite], since the purpose is accomplished by the Āhavanīya fire alone.
To this it is replied: here, the contingency of such a claim does not hold, because the specific function of that [fire] is not fully understood.

For if the function of the *āhavanīya* fire were known [independently], then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even by means of another's [fire], that function would be accomplished. And this is not the case.

This is understood: the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa-nirvṛtti*) is not the function of the *āhavanīya* fire; rather, it is the function of the mere substance of fire (*agni-dravya-mātra*). He will state the rebuttal to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) later. Furthermore, because there is no scriptural statement (*aśravaṇa*) such as "of the vessels again by their own [fires]," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering that there would be a case of extension (*prasaṅga*), says "of whichever [fire] it may be."

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as when it is established that "one's own fire-related rites must be performed," there is no occasion for extension (*prasaṅga*), so too, where it is neither heard in scripture that "by one's own [fires]" nor obtained through logical necessity, there must be an occasion for extension, as in the case of "the vessels. Because it arises by depending on what precedes it, it possesses the status of being an internal embryo (*antarāgarbhiṇī*).

The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, maintains that while it is true there is a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) here, because *satra* sacrifices last for a long time and the limit of one's lifespan is unknown, it would indeed be accomplished by others who arise for that purpose; therefore, he considers it proper to simply take up another vessel. This is how the connection is understood.

The remainder of the sentence is: "In this matter, there is indeed a contingency, but it is improper. Why? Because *satras* (sacrificial sessions) last for a long time, and because the limit of one's lifespan is unknown, if someone were to die while engaged in a *satra*, [the contingency would arise].

The permanent [performer] would suffer a lapse of the concluding rite (*pratipatti*) for those participants engaged in the sacrificial session (*satra*); or, if the concluding rite were omitted, there would be a deficiency in the performance of the *satra*. Furthermore, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) considers that the *satra* is indeed completed even by others who have undertaken it for the sake of the session—this is how it should be construed. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the preceding position has been stated: "In times of distress, there should be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*)."
However, the view regarding the *Sārasvata* [sattra] has not been refuted in the Bhāṣya.
Regarding that, he says: "As for the view regarding the *Sārasvata*, if it cannot otherwise be justified in the case of the sattra, then [it must be accepted as] a scriptural statement."

In that case, it will come to pass; however, the sense is that on that account alone, all sacrificial sessions (*satra*) would not necessarily belong even to those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
|| 7 || Or rather, by way of the qualification of the person, there should be a restriction regarding the performer in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because [the rule] pertains to the sacrifice.
Because it possesses those qualities and because others lack them, there would be eligibility for each individual [to perform the rite]. || 36 ||

Furthermore, how is there doubt regarding the *adhvarakalpa* and other such texts? Since the qualification is heard in general terms, the doubt arises as to whether the qualification belongs to the Vaiśya alone, or to all three social classes (*varṇas*).
Such is the doubt.

In the *Adhvarakalpa* and other such texts, is the eligibility (*adhikāra*) restricted by the statement regarding the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) so that only the Vaiśya has eligibility, or is the number seventeen enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the number fifteen (*pāñcadaśya*)? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the restriction of eligibility to be more appropriate. For indeed, the number seventeen is occasioned by the Vaiśya; therefore, by this very statement, it is shown—

1. Here, the commencement of the section should be understood as being due to the fact that the *juhū* and other vessels have not been employed; they are not mentioned separately because they are contained within the intermediate [vessels].
"One should act in such a way that there is a state of seventeen-foldness. This occurs when the Vaiśya is the qualified agent;

therefore, it restricts [the rule] to the Vaiśya alone. Now, one might ask: why is this not simply an injunction of seventeen-foldness for the sake of the sacrifice itself, as a substitute for the fifteen-foldness?

To this he replies: because, since the seventeen-foldness would already be obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal extension) in a rite performed by a Vaiśya agent, there is no need for its injunction.
"It is possible" [to argue].

Moreover, no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of that is heard here; otherwise, there would be an inequality of injunctions (*vidhi*), as one and the same injunction would function both as an original mandate and as a restatement (*anuvādaka*). Therefore, why should it not be a qualification (*adhikāra*)? This is the restriction regarding qualification (*adhikāraniyama*).

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that an injunction of the essential form (*svarūpavidhi*) understood as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is not capable of restricting the qualification (*adhikāra*). Now, it was argued that an injunction with a Vaiśya as the agent is not possible; [the author] provides the following resolution:

It is not possible [to claim that the injunction] destroys the form of the attainment (*prāpti*) because it does not do so through its effect (*kārya*). For the attainment—even when performed by a Vaiśya—is indeed dependent upon a cause (*nimitta*) through its effect; however, the instruction (*upadeśa*) enjoins it independently of such causes. As in the case of the *tryanīkā* sacrifice...

Having raised the objection that the mention [of the *aindravāyavāgra* order] in other [texts] is for the purpose of [stating] a quality (*guṇārtha*), [the author] maintains that it is an injunction of the *aindravāyavāgra* status independent of any [other] occasioning cause (*nimitta*).

Therefore, even when a Vaiśya is the performer, it remains an injunction. Just as in that case [of the modified sacrifice], performance occurs even in the absence of an occasioning cause, which constitutes the purpose of the injunction, so too here, the attainment [of the result] when a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya is the performer is the purpose of the injunction.
Therefore, it is established that all [classes] have the entitlement.
Thus far, the conclusion of the section has been reached by hearing the scriptural statement.
There is one [text]: "In the archetype, one should recite seventeen for a Vaiśya"; and another also in the *Adhvarakalpā*: "Seventeen..."

"One should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses"—having relied upon this third [position], they conduct an investigation; he refutes that: "An investigation not based on a specific context (*anārabhyacintā*) is neither established by scripture nor by functional requirement (*kārya*); therefore, it is not accepted.
The statement regarding the archetypal form (*prākṛta*) is based on functional requirement."

That which is employed when [a rule] is already established by scripture (*prāpta*) is to be considered; however, a modified statement (*vaikṛta-vacana*) that is employed when [a rule] is already established by scripture is also to be considered. But since a modified statement is one that begins anew (*ārabhya-vacana*), its consideration was not undertaken by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
The Sixth Chapter: 1. Only from the injunction; 2. Having the nature of persistence.
The seventh section of the sixth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*. [Topic 1:
In the case of one's own giving, everything [is applicable] because there is no distinction. (Sūtra 1)

In the Viśvajit sacrifice, it is heard that "all one's possessions" (*sarvavedasa*) [are to be given]. The word *veda* occurs in the sense of the word *sva*. This word *sva* is used without distinction for kinsmen, wealth, and so forth; this word *sva* denotes what belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*). And since the state of belonging to oneself is common to kinsmen, wealth, and so forth, the word *sva* applies everywhere without distinction. Furthermore, there is no evidence for any such restriction.

"This is to be given, this is not"—because of the hearing of the word "all. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that everything which is one's own property is [to be given]. And here, since the giving of all that belongs to oneself is heard in the text, the verb *dadāti* (he gives) functions toward the transfer of ownership to another, and not toward the mere relinquishment of one's own [property], because that [latter] is impossible. Here, someone who is conceited about his own generosity objects: "But surely..."
Just as one's own property is to be given, so too must it be bestowed upon another.

However, fathers and the like cannot be bestowed upon others in the capacity of being their father. It is said in reply: first of all, one's own property is what is to be given; and regarding that which is being given, just as...
In the same way, one should understand that the acquisition of another's ownership occurs;

for it cannot be brought about in the form in which the self possesses its own ownership, but it will be brought about in the form in which it can be so brought about, and there is no contradiction whatsoever.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: this word *sva* cannot possibly have a single meaning because its constituent parts (*sva-bhāva*) differ.

Its meaning is this: this word *sva* denotes kinsmen, wealth, and what belongs to oneself; and it does not function through a single power (*śakti*). Rather, like the word *go*, it has multiple meanings, since we observe its usage for kinsmen and wealth when it does not refer to what belongs to oneself, just like the word *jñāti*.

And it is like the word *dhana* (wealth). Thus, it applies both to the self (*ātman*) and to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). One cannot say that [the term] is used in its primary sense (*śrauta*) for the self and in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*) for what belongs to the self, because the opposite positions are equally possible. Therefore, since no distinction is perceived, this [term] denotes both the self and what belongs to the self. And it does not obtain usage in all four cases solely by virtue of expressing a single referent; rather, [it functions] in its own primary sense—

Because of their distinction: among kinsmen there is "kinsmanship," in wealth there is "wealthness," in what belongs to oneself there is "self-belongingness," and in the self there is "selfhood. Thus, there is no single universal (*sāmānya*) present in all of these; rather, the word *sva* has multiple referents and does not apply to all of them simultaneously, but rather at some time to some particular thing. In this context, due to its connection with the verb "to give" (*dadāti*), it applies specifically to the domain of wealth. For the verb *dadāti*— [The text continues: ...is indeed [connected to the object of giving].

It has been shown in the fourth [chapter] that [giving] consists in the relinquishing of one's own ownership and the effecting of another's ownership; for this is possible in the case of wealth, and thus the meaning of the scripture is that "all wealth is to be given. Therefore, one's father and so forth are not to be given.
He states another argument: "Nor can that which is the meaning of the word 'one's own' (*sva*) with respect to oneself, one's kinsmen, and so forth, be transferred to another..."
In order to bring it about; for otherwise, if it were brought about in a different manner, one's own [nature] would not have been brought about by another.
That which is already one's own is not brought about by another. Furthermore, there exists here a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: although the word *sva* (one's own) refers to kinsmen, wealth, and so forth precisely by virtue of their being "one's own," nevertheless, there is evidence here for it to refer specifically to "one's own" [wealth]. For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the gift concerns wealth alone, and it is this "universality" (*sarvatā*) that is enjoined with respect to it.

Thus, this "possession of everything" (*sarvasvatā*) remains restricted solely to the domain of wealth; for even when one's own property is being given, it is wealth alone that is to be given and nothing else, as in the case of the original rule—therefore, this "possession of everything" is prescribed for that [wealth] alone. Land shall not be [given], because it is common to all. (3)
The word "own" (sva) refers to land; that is to say, it refers to objects of enjoyment or wealth. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that land should be given by him.
He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "But that [knowledge] cannot be imparted to another, because it is common to all.
The meaning of this is as follows: the entire terrestrial globe, together with its paths, royal highways, waters, and so forth, is [common to all].

It is not possible to give away [the earth], because it is common to all, including the *Gopatha* and others; for just as the owner of the land is the master there, so too is anyone else. For mastery in that regard consists in the enjoyment of coming and going and so forth, and that is common to all. Furthermore, ownership is worldly (*laukika*). As for those who give away a village and the like, they too [give] the buildings, fields, and so forth.
It should be understood that they indeed bestow [the result] themselves; and since the village is the delimiting factor for that, there is no fault.
(3) Furthermore, because it is not something to be produced, there would be a distinction from that [other case]. (4)
In this case as well, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) arises from the suspicion that it is a prohibitive negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha).

One considers "horses are not to be given" to be a prohibitive negation. Since it would then be both enjoined and prohibited, giving [the horse] would occur optionally; thus, the giving of all [gifts] would result in being a mere prohibition.

The reason for the prohibition is as follows: if that were the case, the giving would still occur even in the case of the [prohibited] side. The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is reached through exclusion (paryudāsena). And by the force of syntactic unity (ekavākyatva), everything will be understood as excluding the horse.
And because it is eternal, there is no connection with things that are impermanent. || 5 ||
In this case as well, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that, in accordance with the word "all" (sarva), everything that is to be enjoyed must be given;
that is, all things such as beds, seats, and so forth, as many as are denoted by their own respective words, are to be given.
The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that even for one who possesses none of these, one must give by purchasing them again and again.

However, the proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī) maintains that since the entitlement [to perform the rite] is established by one's own existing property, the injunction does not compel the acquisition of what is not already present.

To whatever extent one possesses wealth, to that extent "everything" (sarvatva) is said [to be given]. This word "everything" (sarva) refers to what is under discussion; and for the qualified recipient, it refers to their own existing property that is under discussion, not to that which does not exist. Therefore—

The state of being "all" is predicated of that very [object]; and since the fulfillment of the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is accomplished by giving that much, nothing else should be given, even if it were available, on the grounds of some other [unspecified] requirement. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no injunction to give in this context.
For if the gift were directed toward oneself...

If it were argued that "then one's own [wealth] must be connected with the gift," there might indeed be a conceptualization of appropriation (*upādāna*). But here, since the gift is to be performed by oneself, even when it is performed by means of what has been appropriated, it is indeed completed; thus, there is no conceptualization of appropriation—so it is stated in the Bhāṣya.
[And] the Śūdra [is entitled to perform sacrifices], because of the nature of the Dharmaśāstra. 6.
Regarding the reflection on what is acquired through religious duty (*dharmopanata*): since it is something to be enjoyed, one might suspect it is subject to being given away;

however, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that what is acquired through religious duty cannot be transferred to another, because such an acquisition is dependent upon that very religious merit.

The meaning of this is as follows: since one who has approached for the sake of Dharma is an object of enjoyment, there is a concern that he might be given away; therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that he must not be given.

For he is an object of enjoyment only for the person to whom he has approached for the purpose of instruction in Dharma, and it cannot be said that he is an object of enjoyment for anyone else, because he has not approached them. Indeed, he is called "one who has approached for the sake of Dharma" when he has approached as an attendant to one who is proclaiming the Dharma.
By force; and in that case, the status of being the enjoyer belongs to oneself alone, and it is not possible for another to acquire it either.
|| 6 || At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), whatever is one's own property should be recognized as such, because of its connection with the act of giving. || 7 ||

[Objection: But surely, the restriction regarding wives is for the sake of offspring and other purposes;
it would not apply to those [rites] performed for the sake of Dharma, because there is no such restriction in that case.

He refutes this: for that restriction of the rule applies to those who have already taken a wife. Indeed, the taking of a wife is not for the sake of *dharma*; the taking of a wife is prompted by passion (*rāga*), not prompted by *dharma*.
Therefore, there is no taking of a wife without a restriction regarding wives. Consequently, it is established that [the rule] does not apply to those who have not yet...
"That is the rule for the fire [sacrifice] prior to initiation.
But have you not yourself stated that there is no entitlement at all prior to initiation?
Therefore—

If it is argued that the performance of the *homa* is simply impossible for a young student (*māṇavaka*), how can this inquiry even arise? The answer is: quite true, he lacks the formal qualification (*adhikāra*);
however, it is not said that he lacks the capacity (*kārya*) as well, for there exists the possibility of mastery through the study of his own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).

The meaning is that there is no characteristic of one who is to be enjoined [to a second marriage]. And since there is no entitlement for the rite of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), it has been stated that the entitlement belongs to one who has not yet established the fires. Because the rule is singular, there is no taking of a second wife. This is true;
a second marriage would not occur if there were no scriptural injunction to the contrary.

However, there is a scriptural statement regarding the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*): "When one's wife is endowed with both virtue and progeny, one should not take another; but in the absence of either, one may do so. Since there is no contradiction in this statement, it is the established position that taking a second wife is not forbidden by it. Thus, the view has been stated.
And the objection has already been answered by the analogy of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
|| 3 || The Sthapatīṣṭi, like the Prayājas, would cause the Agnyādheya to be performed; however, because it serves that purpose, the Agnyādheya would be concluded [by the former]. || 20 ||

In this case as well, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire can be set aside, because unlike the case of a *māṇaka*, it is not possible to assert a lack of entitlement (*anadhikāra*) here with respect to the *ādhāna* (the rite of consecrating the sacred fires). Regarding the *ādhāna*:

Because their coexistence is observed, there is no need for a formal acquisition (*prāpti*), just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, since this ritual has the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype. For the *āhavanīya* fire is already acquired through that [archetypal rule], and by means of that [fire], the act of kindling (*adhāna*) is implied, because the *āhavanīya* serves as the instrument. Therefore—

It is argued that only one who has established the sacred fires (*hitāgni*)—namely, the *niṣāda*—is entitled [to this rite]. To this it is replied: we do not see any entitlement regarding the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), because there is no injunction for it.
But was it not stated that the establishment of the fires is obtained by virtue of being the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices?

He refutes this: True, but that attainment applies to the fires because they are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). But surely, since the fire-altar is not a subsidiary element for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhita*), the attainment of the rite of laying the fires (*ādhāna*) will occur by way of the fire itself?

He refutes the objection regarding the displacement of the ritual act (*kratvākṣepaka*): Even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not for the sake of conferring entitlement (*adhikāraka*) upon the fires; rather, by virtue of its application (*viniyoga*), it is for the sake of those fires.
It is not...

The establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is implied by the qualification for the ritual (*kratvadhikāra*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*). What then? For, through application (*viniyoga*) and sequence, that [establishment] is for the sake of the fires. And no application is obtained here without a qualification; there is no application here apart from the qualification. Since the establishment of the fires does not imply the qualification alone, this rite remains [to be performed] only upon fires that have not yet been consecrated.

But surely, since eligibility (*adhikāra*) pertains to the fires that have been consecrated (*viniyukta*), eligibility is attained even by way of those [fires]. True. However, there is no performance of the consecration (*ādhāna*) for one who is already eligible; rather, the acquisition of the fires occurs through the act of consecration. And it has been stated that this Niṣāda is not eligible. Therefore, the fire is not [obtained] through that consecration.
The rite is accomplished by the Niṣāda; thus, the ritual must be performed even with the omission of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*).
Herein lies the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):

although the fire-laying is not obtained through extension (*atideśa*) because it is not an auxiliary part [of the sacrifice], nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the *āhavanīya* fire which is extended [to the rite], [it must be performed].
There will be an objection regarding the *niṣāda*.

However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because the *āhavanīya* fire is non-worldly (*alaukika*), its production does not entail [the necessity of] an injunction. Therefore, the production of the *āhavanīya* occurs only by one who performs the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) which is understood from the application (*viniyoga*) to be the producer of the *āhavanīya* and so forth; it does not occur through anyone else.
Because it is not known that [the sacrifice] is the producer of that which has a non-sacrificer as its agent, an implication [of the rule] is not possible.
|| 4 || And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity is likewise [excluded], because the time for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) has not yet arrived. || 22 ||
What specific distinction does he perceive regarding the animal sacrifice that could serve as a cause for suspicion? For him as well, since there is no wife, co-sacrifice would not be possible.
The answer is: this is the intended meaning—that for him, let her [the sacrificer] herself be his wife.
Because of the transgression of the rule, she by whom he becomes "one who has spilled his seed" (avakīrṇin);
because of the plural number in the word *dārāḥ* ("wives"), there is the notion that [the wife] is one [individual]. 1. Thus, [it is] distinguished.

Because of the statement, "The ritual act is that very [wife]," due to this connection, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that when one has wives, the connection with the Āhavanīya fire cannot at all be sublated.

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, maintains that this expiation is for the purpose of removing [the fault] incurred by transgression, because of its connection with the restrictive rule; thus, this too—like the preceding section—should be understood as pertaining to one who possesses such qualification.
For there is the animal sacrifice for the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy).

The *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is enjoined to perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in order to eliminate the committed fault and to strive toward the resumption of the very practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Since expiation is prescribed for one who has turned away from sin, he must abandon her and perform the animal sacrifice (*paśu-yajña*) pertaining to the *avakīrṇin*. Therefore, because the qualification belongs only to such a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) who has indeed abandoned the woman, this [sacrifice] is also included under the section concerning the *māṇavaka-homa* (the fire-oblation of the student).
It is the same.

|| 5 || Rites for the gods are prescribed for the northern course of the sun, the first half of the month, and auspicious days; they take the form of Smṛti because of the observation of their purpose. || 23 ||

But how, then, can there be a doubt regarding the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) despite this statement about the time of recitation? Because in the case of the initiations (upanayana) and so forth, a restriction of time such as a year is heard in the scripture: "One should initiate an eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa," which means for one whose eight years are complete.

"He is eight years old" means that, starting from the time of conception, the initiation (*upanayana*) occurs during the preceding eight years; thus, there is no need to adhere to the Smṛti rules regarding the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth.
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that this rule applies only while those eight years are currently ongoing, not when they have already passed; thus, there is no contradiction.
For if the Smṛti were in contradiction with the Śruti, the Smṛti might indeed be sublated; however, there is no such contradiction.

Even in the Śruti, initiation is heard of as occurring when the boy is eight years old while he is still present [in this world]. There is no contradiction between that and the Śruti regarding the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth; for that [initiation] is indeed said to take place at eight years of age.
The answer is: for if his eighth year is complete, he will indeed become eight years old. Thus, the requirement of seeing [the sun] has been stated.
|| 7 || "The begging for purchase [of Soma] occurs when it is not available, as in the case of worldly practice. || 26 ||
Even when materials already acquired are available, it is not logical to take up other materials, because that would entail the postulation of something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is precisely in the absence of such materials that the purchase and the hiring of laborers are enjoined.
The meaning of this is: [regarding] the material—

For begging and so forth are prescribed for the purpose of obtaining [the materials]. When the materials are not present, the acquisition of materials is prescribed as something to be performed, but not when they are already present. Therefore, by considering the purpose, this injunction applies precisely when there is an absence of materials.
1. tayor-vimā.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: This is indeed true if there were an injunction for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*). But this injunction is solely for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Since there is nothing whatsoever that has been previously acquired by the sacrifice, this very [injunction] serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).

The meaning of this is as follows: the injunction to beg is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sacrifice. Nor is there any substance already existing for the sake of the sacrifice that could serve as a means for a human purpose; rather, it is precisely through begging for a human purpose that the substance becomes one for the sake of the sacrifice. Therefore, even if a substance exists, it becomes fit for the sacrifice only by means of begging, and not otherwise. Consequently, this very act of begging, being for the sake of the sacrifice, serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).

Now, if it is argued that [the practice] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), then since that visible purpose can be accomplished by other means, there would never be a cessation of begging and so forth.
To this, the reply is: "It cannot be claimed that there is no cessation simply because of its having a visible purpose."
To explain: because everything is enjoined simultaneously. He will state [later] that "this is due to the unity of the word. Therefore, it must be performed like a permanent (nitya) rite.
The meaning of this is: for the reason of the unity of the word, because everything serves the purpose of accomplishing the injunction, it is enjoined simultaneously.

[The word] *dhānam*. Even though the visible purpose is accomplished by that [means], because the meaning of the injunction must be achieved through the performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) exactly as prescribed, the employment [of those parts] must be performed constantly.

Therefore, let this injunction regarding begging and so forth be precisely an *aprāptavidhi* (an injunction for what was not previously established), since it is expressed as begging and so forth for the sake of fulfilling the meaning of the injunction.
Restriction (*niyama*), however, is merely its purpose. When this injunction exists, there is restriction to begging and so forth alone.

Because it is authorized as the cause for accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice, there is a constant requirement [for the material]. However, in its absence, another [material] would have to be employed for the sake of establishing the connection with the ritual action; this is the restrictive rule (niyama), which is the purpose of the injunction.
|| 8 || Likewise, [the same applies to] eating, the command, covering, the slaughtered animal, the oblation, and the act of hating. || 28 ||

What, then, is the distinction here? The answer is: this is the distinction. Because it enters [the ritual] by way of serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), a certain doubt arises for one who considers the act of immolation (*saṃjñapana*) to be for the sake of producing the heart and other organs.

The meaning of this is as follows: Even though acts such as eating [the sacrificial remains] (*bhakṣa*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), they enter into the sacrifice by way of serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, their status as subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) exists only where there is no other means for achieving the person’s purpose; such is the doubt regarding acts like eating. Regarding the oblation (*homa*) at the time of the immolation (*saṃjñapana*), however, it is thus: the oblation cannot logically be considered a subsidiary part of the immolation, for it is heard in scripture as standing in the place of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), according to the wording of the mantra.
On the contrary, because [the latter] depends upon the primary [status] through figurative application (*gauṇī*).

However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: since the injunctions of the context (*prakaraṇa*) form a single syntactical unit with the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), their performance is to be carried out as previously stated.

The meaning of this is as follows: for that which is enjoined and heard within a specific context (prakaraṇa) serves the purpose of an injunction of qualification (adhikāravidhi), and the injunction of qualification, being perceived as connected to that [context], is determined by those very factors [of the context]. Therefore, even though it must be postulated through a means consistent with that [context], the accomplishment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) occurs precisely through the means consisting of the human goals produced by the eating and so forth; thus, the injunction is established by way of that very human goal arising from the eating and other such acts.
In the same way, the *saṃjñaptahoma* is also conceptualized as being caused by the mere act of slaughtering (*saṃjñapana*), and not for the purpose of remedying a deficiency.
Furthermore, since the wording of the mantra must be explained solely in accordance with the injunction, there is a constant performance of the *bhakṣaṇas* (consumptions) as well.
But that which is purposeless would be impermanent.

In this case as well, since it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), there must be constant performance; for without that, the purpose of the injunction would not be fulfilled.
Nor should it be argued that "this [action], even when performed, is devoid of purpose."

"It need not be performed," [one might argue]. For even one who is capable of performing all the constituent parts (aṅgas) may be a seeker of results (kāmī). Indeed, it is not the case that this injunction grants authority only to one for whom there is a specific purpose. He states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): It is said in reply—that by abandoning its own purpose, the injunction itself would not even be perceived.
Because a restriction regarding the door [of entry] is required, and it is not proper to perform what has not been prescribed.
Therefore, it is established that such a thing, being devoid of purpose even if not performed, does not destroy the qualification; thus, the injunction of qualification does not preclude it.

Even without that [qualification], the rule of entitlement (*adhikāra-vidhi*) is indeed established, because it is not restricted as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*). Its application occurs when the means (*dvāra*) exists, but not when it does not exist. As for what was said—that there should be no entitlement for a person in whom the means are not possible—that is incorrect; for it has been stated that entitlement follows the application [of the means].

And since this purpose for another (parārtha) is mediated by impermanence, the application (viniyoga) is necessarily impermanent by implication; therefore, it is not possible to set aside the qualification (adhikāra) on that account.
|| 10 || In the injunction regarding animals, there is no restriction because there is no distinction. || 30 ||
He states the connection with the definition: "The following is considered here: does the entitlement belong to one who possesses a sacrificial animal in general, or only to one who possesses a goat?
Now, one might object: since this consideration could also arise by way of the application (*viniyoga*), why is it addressed here?

Is it being considered? To this he says: "But when the application (*viniyoga*) is further considered, because there is no distinction [between the two], and since both applications would be established, it is not possible to determine a specific difference; therefore, only the qualification (*adhikāra*) is considered.
The meaning of this is: not...

In the case of application (*viniyoga*), it is likewise appropriate for the mantra to denote a goat; however, in the case of the qualification (*adhikāra*), because of mutual contradiction, one cannot reconcile both. Since there is a contradiction, it is possible to determine the specific animal by the force of the mantra; therefore, reflection on this point alone is appropriate. In that regard, the view of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: this word "animal" (*paśu*) is a general term.

It is like the word "cow" and others. Since the application [of the term] is made to the mere form of the animal, and because there is no distinction in the genus even in the case of rams and so forth, any animal whatsoever may be selected.
But [it may be argued]: "Is it not the case that by the wording of the mantra, a specific [animal] is established?"

To this he replies: In some cases, it is indeed appropriate for a specific mantra to possess meaning; therefore, a general rule cannot be restricted to a specific instance. Or else, [the connection] arises from "yoga"—either from the yoga of movement, or from the similarity of phonemes, or from the syllables—...

Alternatively, it is logical that the mantra itself possesses a general meaning because of its generality. For it has been stated that the meaning of a mantra is established by the force of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since mantras serve as reminders of what has already been enjoined, it is indeed appropriate that they be recited according to their specific injunctions. Therefore...
The entitlement belongs to one who possesses a sacrificial animal (paśumat).

To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if this word "animal" (paśu) were denotative of the universal; what then? It is denotative of a specific attribute (aupādhika), namely, the attribute of possessing a tail common to all animals.

Just as the term "sound" (śabda) applies to all sounds by virtue of the limiting condition (upādhi) of being perceivable by the auditory organ, why is it so? To this he says: because of the absence of recognition (pratyabhijñāna).

In the case of a goat and an elephant, there is no universal (*sāmānya*) established by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); rather, it shows that the absence of such [a universal] is the basis for the application of words through limiting conditions (*aupādhika*). And that limitation of conditions consists in the presence of a tail. But how is it that there is no recognition? To this he says: "And just as recognition..."

This is not so; it has already been shown in the very first quarter [of the work] that this is because there is no recollection of a prior form. Since this word, which is applied to all animals based on the adventitious property (*upādhi*) of having a tail, denotes the individual, it does not bring about the presentation of a specific [universal] here.

It transcends that [general form] and proceeds toward that very [specific object], because of the unity of the application (*prayoga*). The mantra is encompassed by a single governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*), since it has been so encompassed; and by that [injunction], the specific [object] is brought into proximity. Even granting that it expresses a general sense, we say that even for those [words] expressing a generality, their function resides solely in the particular.

It is logical that [the mantra] applies at all times, because of the efficacy of the traditional transmission (*āmnāna*) of the mantra; it is not reasonable for the mantra to be merely occasional (*pākṣikatva*). Furthermore, a general rule (*sāmānya*) being restricted to a specific instance does not abandon its status as the meaning of the word. Even if there is a contradiction with the application (*viniyoga*), nevertheless, because that application must conform to the purpose to be accomplished, it is only logical that the mantra be restricted to that specific instance. For application conforms to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), and [performance is the primary factor].

Since there is no purpose [for a general animal], and ritual performance is accompanied by mantras, it is logical that the specific determination [of the animal] should be made on the basis of those mantras. Furthermore, it has been stated that when a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is possible, a derivative meaning (*yaugika*) is not possible. Therefore, it is rightly said: "Or rather, a goat [is meant], because of the wording of the mantra. The remainder has already been explained.
Thus ends the eighth quarter of the sixth chapter, and the chapter itself is completed, in the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā* composed by the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra.
In the *Ṛjuvimalā*:
The First Pāda of the Ninth Adhyāya.
Sacrificial action is primary, for it is that which is enjoined; the purification of the materials belongs to it, because it is prompted by that [action] and is for its sake. || 1 ||
Since modification (*ūha*) is understood through a specific effect, the cause for its definition is the extension of a specific [element] (*viśeṣātideśa*).
Its meaning is as follows:
when the archetypal elements have been obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of extension (*atideśa*), that which is distinct from the archetypal effect—
The function (*kārya*) is understood; and modification (*ūha*) is based upon that [function]. Therefore, the transfer of specific details (*viśeṣātideśa*) is the cause of modification.

Herein is the method: by this etymological derivation—that "it is modified" (*ūhyate*)—the term *ūha* denotes a modified application. And that [modified application] is understood when a function other than the original (*prākṛta*) function is understood. For instance—in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth—...

Rice and barley, which are understood as the means for producing the *apūrva* (transcendental result) by virtue of their specific names, are— due to the lack of distinction in their status as means for producing the *apūrva* when the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) involves *nīvāra* grain— as established by extension (*atideśa*) to be the very things to be performed in that context. Consequently, threshing and other such operations performed upon them become modified (*vikṛta*), owing to the difference in the instrumental factors (*kāraka*).
Because the modification of the ritual action is unavoidable.

But how, then, is it understood that the *nīvāra* grains are the object of the ritual? First of all, the scriptural injunction (*upadeśa*) pertains exclusively to specific means for producing a particular transcendental result (*apūrva*), which are themselves characterized by properties grasped through that very injunction. Nor does any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apply here. It is said: [it is] verbal.

Valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are of two kinds: that which arises from instruction (*upadeśaja*) and that which arises from an effect (*kāryaja*). What, then, is instruction? And what is an effect? It is said: "Instruction" refers to the recitation of a textual composition; an "effect," however, consists of things such as the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*), acting as its intermediary. Among these, that which arises from a textual composition [is seen] in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices...

By reflecting on such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," "One should sacrifice with rice," "One should sacrifice with barley," and "One threshes the rice," those who discern that all ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) conclude that rice and barley are equally means for accomplishing a specific *apūrva*.

Consequently, the knowledge arises that threshing and other such rites are the functions of both rice and barley. This [knowledge] is born of instruction (*upadeśaja*); furthermore, it is verbal (*śābda*).
Since the *Ṛjuvimalāmātṛkā* for the seventh and eighth chapters is not found anywhere, the ninth chapter is now being published—
1. R viśeṣabhūtā.

2. When the previously grasped properties are applied by *codaka* (extended injunction) to another new sacrifice (*apūrva*) involving a different substance, where acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) are already established, this inquiry arises: "How are these [to be performed]?"
"They are to be employed. For that purpose, it is now examined what kind of *kārya* (task) is employed by means of the instruction (*upadeśa*).

Is it understood as a task that is a specific means for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices? Or is it a specific means belonging to that *apūrva* of which threshing (*avaghāta*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*)? In this regard, if the status of being a means for the *apūrva* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is intended [to be expressed],...

In that case, since the *nīvāra* grains lack that specific form [of the rice], they would not possess the status of being the "effect" (kāryatā). However, if what is intended is merely their being a means (*sādhana*) for that *apūrva* for which threshing is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), then the *nīvāra* grains do possess that form; thus, their status as the "effect" is also understood through such injunctions as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). In this regard, the knowledge that they are auxiliaries to a specific *apūrva* is as follows:
The specific means of accomplishing the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is not an "invariably concomitant" (*nāntarīyaka*) effect.

For a ritual duty (*dharma*) that is connected to a particular *apūrva* must have that [specific *apūrva*] as its effect, provided there is no contradiction with its subservience to that *apūrva*. Thus, the status of being a means to a particular *apūrva* is not intended as an invariably concomitant factor. The meaning of the injunction is simply that the effect is the means to accomplish that very thing for which the threshing (*avaghāta*) is performed.

And for this reason, by this very injunction, "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the fact that *nīvāra* grasses also serve as the object of the action is understood. Since this knowledge arises from the determination of the action (*kārya*), it is verbal knowledge born of the action (*kāryaja-śābda*). Therefore, it is not non-authoritative, nor is it non-verbal, nor is it a mere instruction (*upadeśa*); thus it has been stated by the venerable Vivaraṇakāra himself, and so [the position] is faultless. They also cite a verse:

"Modification (*ūha*) is the application of a modified [rite] due to the effect of another substance that has fallen into its place in the archetype; it is declared as such because it is being modified. Thus, he restates the objectionable *bhāṣya*: "And modification is threefold."
He raises an objection: "What is this threefold nature?
The point is that the nature of being composed of modified applications is equal in the case of mantras, sāmans, and saṃskāras. He provides the resolution:

It is said: we shall explain the distinction of functions in their proper place. We shall also explain in that very place how the form of the application (*prayoga*) differs according to those [distinctions of function], for the modification of the application is indeed based on the function as its authority (*pramāṇa*). That [function] is the authority—

It is threefold because the effects of the *bhūta* [mantras] are of three kinds. To explain: for actions such as threshing, the effect is the substance that serves as the material cause (*prakṛtidravya*), namely rice; for mantras, it is the referent inherent in them (*samaveto'rtha*); and for *sāmans*, it is the syllables. And by virtue of these, there is a modification of all three; thus, the mention of their threefold nature is stated in the Bhāṣya.

This is to show that there is no modification (*ūha*) regarding the *kāra* in the context of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, for there is no alteration whatsoever in their performance. By the phrase "and other [topics] such as the introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*)," the commentary (*bhāṣya*) has been restated. If this first [topic] were [to apply] to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it would be unprecedented (*apūrva*).
2. There is no [such thing as] 3. that which is prescribed.

The instrument (*karaṇa*) has been explained by way of introduction (*upoddhāta*) and by way of a relevant digression (*prasaktānuprasaktyā*); [the terms] "he rules" (*īṣṭe*) and "he enjoys" (*bhuṅkte*) are for the sake of establishing the absence of modification (*anūha*).

The predominance of the deity (*devatā-prādhānya*) was introduced as a relevant topic; for its establishment, "lordship" (*īśitṛtva*) and "enjoyment" (*bhoktṛtva*) were introduced as further digressions concerning the deity.
Here, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has taken the triad beginning with the *agnihotra* as the illustrative example. Regarding that, he asks about the intended meaning (*tātparya*):
What is the reason? For what reason, moreover, are only the *agnihotra* and other such rites cited as examples, when all ritual actions possessing *dharma* ought to be cited?

The answer is as follows: For it is only when the restrictive nature [of the rules] has been established for each specific section (*prakaraṇa*) for the sake of providing exclusive instruction (*upadeśa*), that extended application (*atideśa*) operates.
Otherwise, since the ritual properties (*dharma*) would be taught everywhere, they would be common to all cases, and there would be no need for extended application.

It may be so. Since *ūha* (modification) concerns those dharmas understood through extended application (*atideśa*), these alone are the examples for the sake of establishing that extended application, and not others. Here, the objection regarding the redundancy [of the discussion] has been answered by the intention to state the subsequent point, along with the first part of the seventh [chapter], namely, that this "being prompted by the *apūrva*" is stated;
thus, the resolution has been given according to the sense. Furthermore, as for this second resolution: "By this, there is a purpose here in *ūha*..."

The statement "in the intended [context]" is inappropriate because, even there, in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādya*), the restriction of ritual duties (*dharma*) to each respective context is established precisely by their being prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), and not otherwise. Therefore, it has been stated that this [section] has the purpose of providing for the *ūha* (modification of mantras); for this [purpose] also serves as the objective in the first section of the seventh book. He offers a rebuttal: "But surely, even though the *bhāṣya* states that they are prompted by the sacrifice (*yajati*)," and so forth.

Since a restrictive rule (niyama) is not established for every individual section, he demonstrates the restriction in another way. Therefore, the fact that [the result] is prompted by the *apūrva* need not be demonstrated there exclusively. He raises an objection again: "That which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya..."
We do not understand what this so-called "being employed by a different root from *yaj*" actually means.
The sense is that the idea is simply that "a different [root] from *yaj*" is another [root] altogether, namely, something unprecedented (*apūrva*).

He explains: "To this it is said. Being "impelled by the instrument" (*karaṇaprayuktatva*) is what is meant by being "impelled by the sacrifice" (*yajiprayuktatva*). Since the sacrifice (*yaji*) is one thing and the instrument (*karaṇa*) is another, that which is impelled by the instrument is called "impelled by the sacrifice. [Objection: But is there not the state of being an instrument?

[By what means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) understood? To this, he says: "For here, the relationship between the effect and the instrument is characterized by the mandate (*niyoga*);
indeed, co-utterance with the mandate—which is itself that which is to be accomplished—would otherwise be inexplicable. If...
