Since the *niyoga* (the mandate) would otherwise be neither the effect nor the instrument of the sacrifice (*yajati*), the relationship between the effect and the instrument is determined by the *niyoga*.

But how, if it is prompted by the instrument, can there be a restriction for each specific context? To this he says: even though it is prompted by the instrument, its connection with a particular *niyoga* is indeed possible; thus, there is a restriction for each specific context.
He considers it an accomplishment.
In that case as well, it should be inferred.

2. By what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is there the status of being an instigator? Therefore, he states the very nature of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice): "There is neither causality (*kāraṇatā*) nor even the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*), for it is not recorded in the grammatical tradition that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if [the subsidiaries] were prompted by the sacrifice (*yajati*), then—given that the injunctions such as "he offers the *samit* oblation" would enjoin the *samits* and so forth with reference to the sacrifice for which one who desires heaven is qualified by the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—there would be no restriction to each respective context (*pratiprakaraṇa*). However, if they are prompted by the instrument (*karaṇa*), then the instrument is understood from the qualification-statement (*adhikāravākya*) "with the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

By its mere presence, it is the apprehender of the *dharmas* as if they were something unprecedented (*apūrva*); therefore, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is qualified by that [apprehension]. Thus, because of the connection with a qualified *apūrva*, the restriction is established for each respective context (*prakaraṇa*). Consequently, since the restriction is established for each context—whether the *dharmas* are prompted by the *apūrva* or prompted by the instrument—the fact that they are prompted by the *apūrva* need not be demonstrated exclusively in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādya*). In this regard:

That very [principle] is explained in the section on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), because without it, modification (*ūha*) would not be established. For if ritual properties (*dharma*) were prompted by the instrument (*karaṇa*), then since rice grains (*vrīhi*) are also instruments, they would prompt the properties; consequently, in the absence of the form of rice as an instrument, there would be no modification of threshing (*avadhāta*) and so forth for *nīvāra* grasses. However, if the properties are prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*), then the specific nature of the rice is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the specific means of accomplishing the transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhana-viśeṣa*) is intended to be expressed.

Thus, the modification (*ūha*) is established; by means of that, in the first [topic] of the seventh book, this is considered: are [the mantras] prompted by the sacrifice (*yajiprayukta*) or un-prompted by the sacrifice (*ayajiprayukta*)?
But here, even though they are un-prompted by the sacrifice, it is considered whether the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the prompter or the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

In that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the instrument itself requires its own assistance. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*)...
Just like the instrument (*karaṇa*), its assistance (*anugraha*) also requires an effect (*kārya*) alone, because that [assistance] itself is what is intended to be performed (*cikīrṣita*).
Now, why is this very "being prompted by the sacrifice" (*ayajiprayuktatva*) not established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the first section of the seventh book?
Is it written? The answer: because this meaning is non-abiding.
Being employed by the root *yaj* in a general sense is non-abiding; however—

Only the position that [the sacrifice] is prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is stable. And this stable position, as a final conclusion (*siddhānta*), should be presented for the sake of removing the confusion of the students. Therefore, it is for this reason that this very position—that it is prompted by the *apūrva*—is brought forward here as the stable one for the purpose of practical discourse; thus, "being prompted by the *apūrva*" has been stated. [Objection: If being prompted by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is unstable, for what purpose is that discussed in the first section of the seventh book? [Response: It is introduced there for that specific purpose.
Regarding this, he says: "But for what purpose is there a restatement of that which is non-abiding? The answer is: "And it is for the sake of avoiding the charge of tautology."
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but). Is this the only purpose?
The answer is: there is another [purpose], as we shall explain in the section concerning the grinding of flour (*hantipiṣṭyadhikaraṇa*).

In this regard, the following is useful for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Alternatively, the Commentator stated, "Or rather, another consideration," in order to refute that [the name *darśapūrṇamāsa*] is based on the sacrifice (*yajinimittatā*). That is incorrect—for if it were based on the sacrifice, not only would modification (*ūha*) fail to be established, but even extended application (*atideśa*) would not be established. Therefore, this [discussion] pertains precisely to the definition of modification (*ūha*).
It cannot be said that this is a mere "presentation" (of an argument).

Its meaning is as follows: when the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is the occasion [for the application of rules], then in its absence—even in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti)—there is a non-performance of all ritual properties (dharmas) even those obtained through the extended injunction (codaka), just as in the case of the absence of a vessel-breakage.
Regarding the *bhedana-homa* (the oblation for breaking): consequently, since there is no need for an extended application (*atideśa*), there is also an absence of such extension.

Not only is there an absence of modification (*ūha*), but this is not even fit to be considered as a characteristic of modification; for it is only in the context of extended application that this [question] is appropriate to deliberate upon. [p. 213] Atideśa—

The consideration regarding the definition is also appropriate. He offers a rebuttal: "It is said; you have spoken the truth that even the extended application (*atideśa*) is not established. However, this is not redundant because of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the seventh book.
Its meaning is as follows:

We do not say that this reflection (*cintā*) is helpful merely by virtue of being characterized by reasoning (*ūha*). Rather, it is employed for the purpose of avoiding tautology (*apaunaruktya*). For, according to the first section of the seventh book (*adhyāya*), the establishment of restrictive rules (*niyama*) occurs when [the injunction] is connected with something previously unknown (*apūrva*); whereas here, the status of the sacrifice (*yajati*) as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) has been refuted. Thus, there is no tautology. What, then, is the purpose of this alternative resolution?

The answer is as follows: this very purpose is what will be stated hereafter. Since there is no occasion [for their application], it would follow that the collection of ritual properties (dharmajāta) obtained through the *codaka* (transference rule), even though applied in another sacrifice due to a different occasion, should not be performed; the present section serves to exclude that non-performance.
The intention is that this must be stated by one who provides an alternative exposition (*varṇaka*). This is the avoidance of non-performance and the resolution (*parihāra*) expressed by him:

"In that regard" (*tatra*) serves as an introduction to the sentence. After introducing the alternative exposition, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has described two resolutions within a single exposition, beginning with: "Now, it is considered whether [the action] is prompted by the sacrifice (*yajiprayukta*) or prompted by the *apūrva*. And so forth.
By means of the Bhāṣya.

Here, in the Bhāṣya itself, it is stated that "one should perform the sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which expresses the application [of the injunction] to the essential form of the sacrifice (*yajisvarūpa*). Likewise, it is stated that "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*), which expresses the application to the instrument (*karaṇa*). A third mode has been described by another commentator as follows: thus...

By the words "vetti" and so forth, the meaning of what was stated as "it is said to be moving through different [objects]" is explained. An alternative interpretation (*varṇaka*) has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya;
that is to say, these are precisely the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*) mentioned in the Bhāṣya.
For those engaged in the purificatory rite, [the fee] should be employed for that purpose, because it is intended for that end.

Now, it has been stated that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is the motivator (*prayojaka*). However, in the first two sections (*varṇaka*), the status of being a motivator was attributed to the [original] cause (*nimitta*) while the status of being a cause was attributed to the *apūrva* itself in the third section. What is this inquiry? Is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) motivated by the acts of "killing" (*han*) and "grinding" (*piṣ*), or is it motivated by the *apūrva*? It is said: here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is more extensive.
It exists. How so?
The answer is: for it can be said that the apūrva, being connected as that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), becomes the motivator (prayojaka) of the ritual properties (dharma).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is understood to be connected with the ritual factors (*dharmas*) by way of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then it can be said that it is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of those factors. For example, in the case of those [factors] that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), it is first the *adhikārāpūrva* (the primary apūrva pertaining to the qualified person) that is understood as the object to be accomplished, not the intermediate *apūrva* (*avāntarāpūrva*); therefore, in that case—

In that case, it was stated [that the purpose is not the action]. Here, however, it is understood that the accomplishment of the action itself is the "effect" (kārya), because of the mention of the instrumental case in the phrase *prokṣitābhyām* ("by means of the two sprinkled [stones]"); for the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) depends upon an action. And it is not the case that the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) toward the action, even though it is perceived, is what is intended to be expressed; thus he says: "The subservience to this [action] is stated precisely without abandoning that [instrumental status]."

It has been stated in the passage, "Those which are heard in a particular context belong there," that the various constituent elements (dharmas) serve the purpose of the *apūrva* without abandoning their intermediate functions as they are perceived.
[Page 214] Now,

if their purpose is indeed the accomplishment of the action, then, in the absence of any contact with the *apūrva*, the injunction would result in pointlessness; for the action is understood by persons as something to be accomplished, so what is the use of that which has already been accomplished?

He refutes [this objection]: "In that case, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is employed precisely to avoid the charge of purposelessness (*ānarthakya*), and not because it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The meaning of this is: the accomplishment of an action is not without purpose, since the accomplishment of the *apūrva* follows from its [the action's] accomplishment."

Therefore, the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts is simply the accomplishment of the *apūrva*, and not that the *apūrva* itself is what is to be accomplished—as in the case where the ultimate *apūrva* is the purpose of the vow of silence during the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, yet that [vow] itself is not the thing to be accomplished. Why is this so? He says: because when the injunction for sprinkling is established as being connected to the *apūrva* of the acts of "sacrificing" (*han*) and "grinding" (*piṣ*), its pointlessness is thereby avoided.
Thus, the *apūrva* is not accepted as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) in its own right.
Since the acts of killing and grinding are the means toward the *apūrva*, this sprinkling is taken as a means for those two.

What was stated regarding the section on *hanti* (threshing) and *piṣṭa* (ground flour)—namely, that [the threshing] is not prompted by the sacrifice (*ayajiprayuktatva*)—is what is being explained here.

It has been resolved by means of its being prompted by threshing, specifically by its being prompted by the threshing that serves as a means (*sādhana*). Because of the [otherwise] pointlessness [of the action], it can be said that the *apūrva* (transcendental result) is what prompts [the duty]; for this very reason, since the function of ritual properties (*dharma*) is precisely their intermediate purpose (*avāntarakārya*), therefore those [properties] which [belong] where...

Thus, it becomes logically consistent that [the injunctions] are heard [as such]. Otherwise, if [acts such as] threshing were prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result), and if the intermediate effect were not intended because of the contradiction between two effects, then—by virtue of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*)—they would apply everywhere, including the Āgneya, Agnīṣomīya, and Upāṃśuyāja sacrifices, just like the Prayājas and other such rites. Since the properties of threshing are prompted by the act of threshing itself, therefore, in the act of threshing...

They are to be understood by means of the illustration (nakhanikṛttana). Regarding that dull-witted person who grasps [the meaning] exactly as it is heard, he states the pervasion (vyāpti) of the example: "All examples of this kind—such as 'one threshes rice' and so forth—are characterized by an intermediate action (avāntarakārya) that is implied."

This [property of sprinkling], being a property of the subsidiary (aṅga) such as rice (*vrīhi*), is an auxiliary to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), but it is not a property of the *apūrva* that is an auxiliary to the subsidiaries. Furthermore, there exists no such scriptural statement (*śabda*) as "that which is produced by the acts of threshing and pounding must be performed with sprinkled [grain]. For what is heard in scripture is: "one threshes with the two [grains] that have been sprinkled."

The meaning is that only the accomplishment of the action itself is heard as the task to be performed. Furthermore, even the act of threshing (*avahanti*) is not directly a means to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), such that the threshing—being connected with that [action]—could be linked to the *apūrva* through a relationship of constituent parts (*sāvayavatvena*). Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that there can be no instigation (*prayukti*) by the duty of qualification (*adhikārakārya*) for those [actions] which enter into other tasks.

To this it is replied: the establishment of the constituent elements (*dharma*) does not occur without the application of a mandate (*adhikāra*), nor is there the performance of those elements that have not been so established. The meaning of this is as follows: in the world, every word has as its purpose the performance of what is to be undertaken.

[This is] observed. For if the dharmas were not employed for the sake of the *apūrva*, then there would be no mandatory inclusion of them—that is, no implication of their performance. Alternatively, for those [dharmas] that have not arisen—meaning their performance has not been impelled by the *adhikārāpūrva*—there would be no performance because of the absence of a purpose for performance.

The point here is this: the status of being a means to the *apūrva* belongs exclusively to actions such as threshing (*avahanana*). Since that status cannot be established without acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of sprinkling and so forth for the sake of that [status]. Therefore, the entire collection of ritual properties (*dharma*) is for the sake of the *apūrva*.

But if this were so, it has been argued that the very determination of application (*viniyoga-vyavasthā*) would not be established, because there would be the undesirable consequence that for actions such as threshing (*avahanti*), even an intermediate purpose (*avāntara-kārya*) would not be intended. He offers a rebuttal: "By what? (*kena*)?

It has been stated that the intermediate effect is not intended [to be primary]. Again, he objects: "Or how, even if it were intended, could the intermediate effect be the motivator of the principal effect?"
He refutes [the objection]: It is said in reply.
First, does the intermediate effect become an effect by being required by the primary cause, or without being so required?
In that regard, if it becomes an effect by being required, then, since it lacks the status of being an effect in its own right, the primary effect alone is the motivator.
If, however, that [final result] is not required, then the intermediate effect alone would be the motivator.
Having thus raised a doubt, he states the resolution: if there is no requirement for the primary effect, the intermediate effect itself would not exist.

That which is performed as being conducive to the primary effect is called an intermediate effect (*avāntara-kārya*), such as the flaming of wood that has begun to cook. Nor should it be said that there can be no status as an intermediate effect; for if the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) were themselves the primary effects, it would follow that there would be no performance [of further rites]. However, when there is dependence upon that—that is, dependence upon the primary effect—it is for the sake of that [primary effect].

Because it is understood as being for the sake of the primary purpose (*pradhānakārya*). Upon the removal of that [subordinate purpose], when the primary purpose is removed, there would be no connection with *dharma* at all. Therefore, since the primary purpose is not enjoined as the motivator (*prayojaka*) when a subordinate purpose is intended, even that subordinate purpose which is perceived must be intended. However, this is merely a systematic arrangement of the instruction; this systematic arrangement does not apply to the actual application (*viniyoga*)—those [means] which [are employed] where...

The phrase "they are heard" does not, however, establish a restriction based on usage; for this very restriction regarding the use of rice and other materials would not be established [otherwise]. Thus, it is proven that [the action] is prompted by the *apūrva*.
Or, he states another argument for its being prompted by the *apūrva*: "The inclusion of restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) within the primary act is discussed in the fourth [book]."
This has been shown.

Its meaning is as follows: if the *apūrva* were the goal to be accomplished by threshing and other such acts, then their injunction would be logically possible, because the status of being a means to the *apūrva* cannot be known through any other means of knowledge. However, if they were merely related to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the rice-grains and so forth, then an injunction would not even be necessary.

[The action] is accomplished because it has already been attained. Nor is the injunction for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because that would be impossible; for we observe the production of rice-grains and the like even without threshing. However, if [the action] enters into the transcendental result (*apūrva*), then a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible: since threshing and other such acts would otherwise be implied for the purpose of producing rice-grains, once the *apūrva* is enjoined, only that [threshing] which is the means to that *apūrva* is implied. Thus, in this case, [there is] restriction—
Regarding the point that the apūrva alone must be the effect of injunctions, he says: "And by the teaching of such [entities], the restriction of the means is shown in the third [book].
By the very teaching of entities related to rice and so forth, the restriction of the means is also shown in the third [book]. Therefore...
The purpose of the door must also be resorted to. He concludes: therefore, in the case of "one threshes with two consecrated [grains]," one should effect the apūrva through the medium of threshing.
This is the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*).

Therefore, it is established that the adaptation (*ūha*) of ritual properties (*dharma*) is accomplished even in other cases where [the substitute] takes over the function of that [original material],
because the instruction "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) intends the door [of the action] as well.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that, since all dharmas here now have never been performed before, the entire collection of dharmas is impelled solely by the supreme apūrva.

The meaning of this is as follows: the properties (*dharma*) do not have worldly form as their purpose, because such a form cannot exist without those very properties. Therefore, since the properties have the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as their purpose, the supreme *apūrva* alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*). Anticipating the objection that "the intermediate *apūrva* is also indeed an *apūrva*, and therefore it too should be a motivator," he says:
Or rather, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is only the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) that possesses a mandate (*sādhikāra*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality, it is only the "unprecedented" that possesses a mandate, and nothing else.
What is meant by this is as follows: so-called intermediate *apūrvas* do not exist at all; rather, there is only that which possesses a mandate.
The unprecedented [result] exists. Why? He says:
because those who are devoid of that—that is, devoid of qualification—would then incur it.
The meaning of this is as follows:

For the *prayāja* and other such rites, which are devoid of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*) when heard in proximity to a qualified rite, undergo a transformation into that form. This is what is meant:
the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, when heard subsequent to root-meanings (*yajis*) that lack a qualification, merely restate the apūrva (unseen potency) of the qualification itself.
Now, one might object: even for those sacrifices that are devoid of a qualification, such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, do they not indeed impel the collection of ritual requirements (*dharmajāta*)?

Regarding this, he says: "Because they are connected with their own inherent properties (*svadharma*) which have not yet attained the status of being *dharma*, sacrifices do not, by their very nature, employ the *dharmas*;
for, being worldly (*laukika*), it is impossible for them to be related to *dharma*. (He sets aside the objection that this is far-fetched: "Nor [is it the case that] threshing..."

Just as in the case of the *divat* [example], the purpose of the door (*dvāra*) is perceived here, because these subsidiaries, such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, provide assistance from afar (*ārādupakāritva*).

Therefore, there is no suspicion whatsoever regarding another [element] being the motivator (*prayojaka*), since these [subsidiaries] are directly the means of accomplishing the *apūrva*. To this, it is replied:

It is true that you have stated that those who have not yet entered into the qualification (*adhikāra*) have no connection with the *dharma*; however, their status as an effect (*kāryatva*) is undeniable.

The remainder applies even to the intermediate injunction (*avāntaraniyoga*). While it is being accomplished, it attains that status; that is, it attains the state of being a means to the primary qualification (*adhikāra*).
Why? He says: for the form of that which is not being accomplished is not established by worldly experience, as is the case with threshing (*avaghāta*).

Just as the form of worldly acts such as threshing is [understood], so too is the form of the intermediate injunction (*avāntara-niyoga*); therefore, that too is an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) which is understood solely through verbal testimony.

Furthermore, by its very nature, that which is to be accomplished is that which is to be produced by the instrument (*karaṇa*) together with its procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, it is from verbal testimony—
It is understood from the context.

Now, one might object: "But surely there is no intermediate injunction (avāntaraniyoga) at all. To this he says: "The attainment of qualification does not determine the distinction arising from the [different] auxiliaries (anubandha)."

Since momentary sacrifices cannot logically function as means to an end, intermediate apūrvas (unseen potencies) are postulated, which are differentiated according to their respective subordinate elements (*anubandha*). Thus, even through this consequence, the distinction [of the acts] is not contradicted. However, with respect to the entitlement (*adhikāra*), there is non-distinction.
This has been described.

However, in the state of eligibility (*adhikārāvasthā*), there is non-difference. What is meant is this: one *apūrva* of eligibility is to be accomplished; but the intermediate *apūrvas*, which serve as its means and are distinguished by the differences in their constituent factors (*anubandha*), are many, corresponding to the number of those constituent factors.
"They are divided.

Now, one might ask: "Granted that there are distinct *apūrvas* differentiated by their respective adjuncts (*anubandha*), how then do the ritual properties (*dharma*) have those [apūrvas] as their purpose? To this he says:
"It has been stated that the entire collection of ritual properties is understood with reference to the distinctions arising from the adjuncts."

"One should recite for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as one desires"—thus, a restriction of the voice is directly heard in connection with the *dīkṣaṇīyā*. And by virtue of that connection with the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, its connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) closely proximate to it is understood. Therefore, [the restriction applies]—
Because it is enjoined with reference to a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) distinct from the bond [of the sacrifice], the collection of ritual duties (*dharma-jāta*) has that as its purpose.
He concludes: "Therefore, because it falls under the heading of the primary qualification (*adhikāra*), the intermediate *apūrva* serves the purpose of the qualification. Adhi-...

The purpose of the ritual acts (*dharma*) is not for the sake of their production; rather, it is established that an intermediate *apūrva* is what is produced by the ritual acts. Thus, it is proven that the purpose of the ritual acts is the intermediate *niyoga*.

In the case of those things to be accomplished which are understood through a *niyoga*, the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) is that which is understood by means of the *liṅ* suffix and so forth within the *niyoga*.

The meaning is: "in those [rites] such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* where an intermediate *apūrva* exists. The prima facie (*pūrva*) position is that because there is no intermediate *apūrva*, in rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, it is the final *apūrva* alone that motivates the ritual duties (*dharmas*), just as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth. [This is argued] because, as in the case of threshing, the purposefulness toward the qualified person (*adhikāra*) is not established through the medium of the substance and so forth in the momentary rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
Intermediate apūrvas must be admitted; and since these are not known through ordinary experience, they are brought about through verbal cognition.

The purpose of the ritual elements (dharmas) as presented by the sentences and other means has been stated. Even though this matter has been explained, lest some person of dull intellect should forget it, the author reminds us of that very point by way of dispelling doubt: "But surely, even the sacrifice..."
The objection is: "Since [the means] are established by worldly practice alone, why this discrepancy regarding threshing and so forth? The resolution, however, is as follows:

having accepted that [the means] culminate in the production of the result, their non-worldly nature was stated; it was not stated because they are denotable [by words], but rather because they are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).

The worldly nature [of the sacrifice] is due to its being denoted by the word *yāga* (sacrifice); however, the distinction from acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing) lies in the fact that it culminates in an intermediate *apūrva* (unseen potency). And this applies to both the fruit and the deity. || 3–4 ||
But how can there be doubt in this matter, since it is logical that even here [the mantras] are employed for the first time? The answer is:
because of the capacity of the mantras to denote their own forms, it is stated by them that they are indeed employed for their own essential nature.

The meaning of this is as follows: First, the mantra declares through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) the essential nature of Agni and others, as well as the essential nature of heaven and so forth. By means of that indicative power of the mantra (*mantra-liṅga*), it appears that [the application] is prompted by the essential nature [of the deity]. Furthermore, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) from the injunction (*codanā*), because the mantra is embraced by the injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra-codanā*). Following that—
There arises a doubt: does it appear through its own form characterized by a connection to something previously unknown? He raises an objection again: "That is incorrect;
for without an injunction (codanā), there can be no designation [of a mantra] as being connected with a ritual act.
The meaning of this is: if the mantra here...
If it were grasped by means of an injunction (*codanā*), then the expression of meaning by the mantra would not be established as being connected to the ritual action;
nor is the expression connected to the ritual action what is under consideration here, nor is an expression connected to the ritual action that conforms to the injunction.

Only the definition [of the subject] is appropriate. Therefore, this section is indeed improper. For it has been stated that all ritual properties (dharma) have the unseen potency (apūrva) as their purpose when they are connected with an action; thus, that same principle is appropriate here as well. Consequently, it remains established that the expression of the effect is mediated by the deity.

To this it is replied: there is indeed a cause for doubt here. For instance, the fruit (*phala*) is not understood from the injunctive sentence (*codanāvākya*) as being for the sake of the ritual action (*karma*), because the fruit is understood as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Nevertheless...
He asks: "What [is meant]?"—the doubt regarding the denotation of the essential nature [of the sacrifice] is that the denotation by means of the mantra is exactly as it was enjoined.
For whatever has been enjoined in a certain manner must be denoted by the mantra in that very same manner; and the result is not for the sake of the ritual action.

The doubt arises as follows: since it is stated that [the mantra] is "prompted" by that [action], its mention is not for the sake of the action (*karma*), but rather for its own sake (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, because it is employed [in ritual], one considers it to have the action as its purpose. If the mention were not for the sake of the action, then there would be no employment of the mantra; therefore, the mantra has the action as its purpose. Thus, the doubt is justified.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the designation as it has been enjoined is logical; for if it were designated otherwise than enjoined, [the injunction would be violated].

For if the mantra were not to express [the deity] exactly as it has been enjoined, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) would be untenable, on the grounds that it would be expressing a meaning that is not connected [to the ritual]. In the case of the deity, however, there is a primary expression due to the suspicion that it is the giver; the deity is the bestower of the fruit. Therefore, she too is included within the category of the fruit, and is not enjoined for the sake of the ritual act. Consequently...
We shall explain that even for that [deity], there is denotation by its very own form, namely as "the deity who bestows the fruit to be mentioned later.
Therefore, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the mantra; rather, there is denotation of heaven and so forth by direct statement (*śruti*) itself. To this it is replied:
It is rightly said that the denotation is exactly as enjoined. But is it indeed enjoined in this very way? How is it enjoined?
The reply is: "This is the fruit of the ritual accompanied by mantras.
The meaning of this is: although the fruit does not exist for the sake of the ritual.
Nevertheless, it is indeed impelled by its very connection with ritual action; for a mantra is a constituent part of ritual action, since otherwise there would be no application [of it].
This being the case, the designation of the mantra is understood to be mediated by the ritual action.
The meaning of this [statement regarding] designation is as follows:
That which is to be expressed is the ritual action (*karman*); it is through that [action] as a medium that the expression of the *Āgneya* and other rites is understood by means of the mantra.

This is what is meant: by way of expressing the fruit of heaven (*svarga*), the ritual action itself is what is being expressed. On the contrary, this very meaning is directly stated (*śrauta*) by virtue of the function of the mantra; it is called "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) only with respect to the causal occasion (*nimitta*). For that alone is the word-meaning which is the sense connected to the function [of the mantra].

Thus it is said. Although this is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on considering the occasion (*nimitta*), nevertheless, this alone is rather the direct Vedic meaning (*śrauta-artha*). The primary meaning, however, is not even heard because it does not touch upon the injunction (*niyoga*), since the Veda is not intent upon that. Therefore, there is no fault of secondary indication in the state of the occasion, because the designation of the mantra has the action (*kārya*) as its primary focus. By examining the application (*viniyoga*), whatever [is established] for the mantra...

[Page 219] The designation is in accordance with its own function; and here, since it is a mantra enjoined for the expression of the ritual action (*karman*), that [deity] is designated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) precisely because of its connection to the ritual action. And in this context, although the deity is projected onto the portion of the fruit by virtue of being the bestower of the fruit—
It has been stated that, this being the case, the designation [of the act] is not prompted by that [deity].
|| 4 || Or rather, the deity should prompt [the act], because, like a guest, the food is for its sake. || 6 ||

Now, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) does not consider the deity to be for the purpose of being employed [as a means], on account of reasons such as its being the recipient of offerings.
The meaning of this is: by the offering of oblations and by words expressing qualities, the deity alone is propitiated; [this is the function] of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Because it is for the purpose of worship; and because in the world, worship is seen to have the purpose of propitiating the one being worshipped. Likewise, even praise, which is characterized by the expression of qualities, is seen in the world to be for the purpose of propitiating kings. Furthermore, since one who desires a fruit does not perform the propitiation of a deity in vain, it is understood that the deity is the giver of the fruit. Nor [is this possible] for one who is not the master of the fruit.

Since that [result] is produced, it is inferred that the fruit also belongs to her (the deity). Furthermore, a deity is not propitiated by the offering of oblation merely through the knowledge of the oblation; nor is all this possible for one who is insentient and devoid of a physical form. Thus, by implication, it is understood that she possesses the capacity to enjoy, sentience, and corporeality—everything that is necessary for this matter to be logically consistent. In every respect, whatever is required so that this meaning may be coherent is established.

To that extent, it is so postulated. Therefore, the deity who constitutes the primary element is not for the sake of the injunction (*niyoga*); rather, that very deity, being understood as the predominant factor, is the motivator (*prayojikā*) by taking the collection of ritual properties (*dharmajāta*) for its own sake. To explain this very point, he raises an objection:
"But if this were the case, because the mantras would be dependent [on something else], much would have to be abandoned."
The meaning of this is as follows:

First of all, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not an authoritative means of knowledge regarding the possession of a physical body and so forth, because its authority is restricted to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) which consists of an action to be performed. Therefore, the matters such as the possession of a physical body must be stated by mantras that depend upon other means of knowledge; yet, no such other means of knowledge exists.
In this view, because validity would result [for everything], much that is established regarding validity and so forth would have to be abandoned. He refutes [this]:
the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the attainment [of results] to be innate;
the meaning of this is that, in this section (adhikaraṇa), the final conclusion (rāddhānta)—

When [the injunction] is established, the unprecedented meaning of the sentence is established. But when the propitiation of the deity alone is taught, then the word possesses its innate denotative power with respect to that very [propitiation]. This is the underlying intention here: the capacity of a word to convey an action to be performed (*kārya*) is well-established in common worldly usage. And it is precisely that which is capable of yielding a result that a person desiring a fruit understands as something to be performed.

Alternatively, since worship is capable of bestowing the fruit by means of the deity to be worshipped, it is worship itself that is denoted by the word as the task to be performed; thus, the authority of the word resides in that alone. Or, when worship is understood through the word, then, by the force of that [understanding], when the possession of a physical form and so forth are being cognized, nothing is lost [regarding the validity of the scripture], even in light of [conflicts with] Smṛti, figurative usage, or other purposes.
Furthermore, it is an additional argument that the scriptural injunctions (*darśana*) thus become logically consistent.
But even so, does not the principle of extension (*atideśa*) suffer? For that which is a means for propitiating one deity cannot possibly serve as such for another deity.
The meaning is that this is because they are dissimilar. He refutes this: "Let it be lost;
there is no harm whatsoever."
Precisely because the extension [of the rule] would otherwise be lost, he says: "That which is an offering in the fire is not [an offering] in the sun," since the sun and the fire are dissimilar.
But what is the reason that the established extended application (*atideśa*) is abandoned?

For why should this very position not be maintained, given its consistency with the established extended application? The answer is: because the meaning of the sentence [is fulfilled] by the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*).
When [the *bhūta*] exists, the extended application (*atideśa*) is certainly not abandoned.

If it is established by means of non-accomplishment (*anārādhanenaiva*), what can we do? Having accepted the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the extended application is established by the force of logic (*nyāya*). If, during the stage of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"It is not tenable; what can we do?"—the meaning is that for this very reason this faulty position has been presented as something to be abandoned.

He concludes the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "By means of traditional texts (smṛti), figurative usage (upacāra), and the observation of other purposes (anyārthadarśana), the proponent of the prima facie view asserts that the deity is denoted by the Vedic word."
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that [the result] is understood to arise from the sacrifice by virtue of the injunction (*codanā*).
The meaning of this is as follows: of this—*adhi-*...

In the stage of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), the sacrifice itself—consisting of the worship of the deity—is understood as the task to be performed. And it must be accepted that the fruit is accomplished by that which is understood as the task to be performed by one desiring the fruit. Therefore, the meaning "one desiring heaven should effect heaven by means of that sacrifice" is what is perceived in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice."

He says: "Let it be understood; what is the harm?"—because there is an absence of any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one cannot postulate a distant scriptural injunction regarding [the status of] being a giver and so forth, as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).
For if...

If the capacity of Agni and others to bestow the fruit were known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the sacrifice’s status as an instrument toward the fruit could be understood as mediated by the deity. However, there is no such means of valid cognition regarding their being givers and so forth. If it is argued that the very injunction to perform the sacrifice—which consists of propitiation—is itself the means of valid cognition, we say no, because this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For only if the status of [the deity] as a giver were already established...

The fulfillment (*ārādhana*) constitutes the sentence-meaning; and when fulfillment is the sentence-meaning, there is the conceptualization of [the deity] as the giver and so forth. Therefore, it is not tenable that the sacrifice is taught as something to be done (*kāryatā*) for one who desires a result; rather, it is established that it is the *apūrva* alone, which is capable of bestowing the result, that is presented by the word as something to be done, and thus that alone is the sentence-meaning.

And how there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding [the existence of] the giver and so forth has been stated in the Bhāṣya, because Smṛti and the like lack authority on that point. Therefore, since the *apūrva* is the meaning of the sentence and the sacrifice has that as its object, according to the principle that "when an *apūrva* results from one [act], then the other is for its sake," the deity, being for the sake of the sacrifice, is also for the sake of the *apūrva*. Therefore, this—

Even in the case of [the word] related to a deity, it is established that the denotation occurs solely through the medium of ritual action— that is, the denotation of the *apūrva* itself occurs through the medium of the deity who is the object of the ritual action consisting of the act of naming. The rest has been explained.
Or rather, it refers to the substance, the number, the cause, and the collection, because of their connection with the Vedic text. || 5 || 11 ||

But even if it is established that the application [of the mantra] is prompted by something not previously known (*apūrva*), since there is no contradiction in its ritual application (*viniyoga*), why is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) intended to dispel the suspicion that it serves a desired purpose (*kāma*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: in the section concerning "beating" (*hanti*) and "grinding" (*piṣati*), it has been stated that all such [actions] are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). Nor is that [prompting] implied merely by virtue of the application of rice (*vrīhi*) and other materials.

To this it is replied: there is a doubt here. He states that doubt: It is indeed appropriate that, in the connection of *prokṣaṇa* with *hanti* and *piṣati*, the two acts of striking and grinding reach the status of an action (kārya) because they have a purpose to be accomplished (*bhāvyārthatva*).

The meaning of this is as follows: for that whose connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is understood, the *apūrva* becomes its motivator (*prayojaka*), otherwise there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And in this case, it is proper that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) has a connection with the *apūrva*, because the threshing is performed "with the two sprinkled pestle and mortar" (*ulūkhala-musala*), and since the act of threshing and the flour are subordinate to another end (*bhavyārthatayā*) by entering into a further goal, the sprinkling is connected to them.

[Objection: Because the fruit and the deity are related to that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the designation [of them] is indeed based on their relation to the *apūrva*. For it is precisely as being related to the *apūrva* that heaven is called the "fruit," and likewise Agni is called the "deity"—not by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, it is logical that the mantra connected to them is also related to the *apūrva*, and because of that connection, it is prompted by the *apūrva*. However, in this case, substance, number, and so forth are not the effects.

They possess a terminal nature (*paryantasvabhāva*), nor are they designated solely by virtue of their connection with the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is no injunction of a property (*dharma*) for them by way of their connection with an action (*kārya*).
To the objection that "the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is useless," he says: "But for those things that have been refined, there occurs [utility] in another action."
Regarding the term *viniyoga*:

But surely, in the third [book], under the rule *teṣām arthena* (JS 3.1.2), it was stated that for rice (*vrīhi*) and other materials which have already been applied to a purpose, there is an application to ritual duties (*dharma*). How then can it be said here that "there is an application of those things once they have been consecrated"?
He refutes [the objection]: "That very point is being raised here.

He explains this very point: "In that regard, in the third [chapter], the rule for application (*viniyoga-vyavasthā*) was established that those [subsidiaries] which are heard in connection with a particular [principal] belong to that [principal] alone as its properties (*dharma*)."

In order to dispel the suspicion regarding desire, he says here: "having raised the objection that there is a contradiction with the fact that [the scripture] has been established as having a purposeful action.
For what reason, then?
Regarding the statement "that [effect] is accomplished," he says: the systematic arrangement of scripture and so forth was stated on the basis of the absence of contradiction;
however, here it is objected that if such a systematic arrangement of scripture and so forth does not exist, then that which contains the effect within itself cannot be established.
Now, if this is the case, and if there is no inclusion of the effect (*kāryagarbhatā*), then the very point of the section— that "whatever is heard in whatever [context]"— is thereby undermined.

And this being so, since there would be no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the [treatise] would not be worth undertaking. He refutes this: "Not every topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is being challenged; rather, it is substances (*dravya*) and so forth that are challenged again"—this is the connection.
By what reasoning is there an objection? To this he says: by the reasoning that "there is no state of containing the effect," there is also no suspicion of contradiction.
Therefore, the application [of mantras] in cases such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" is indeed free from contradiction.

But if this were the case, would it not follow that acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing) serve the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*)? For if they were a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of things already subservient to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then they would indeed be subservient to the sacrifice; however, it is when things have been refined that they become subservient to the sacrifice.

In that case, because of the connection with a substance that does not serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*akratvartha*), it would follow that [the action] serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). The reply is: it does not follow that it serves the purpose of the person.
Why is this so? He says: "It is possible to discern the distinction that these [substances] serve the purpose of the sacrifice."
"These are for human purposes" (puruṣārthāḥ).

The meaning of this is as follows: since only those grains such as rice (*vrīhi*) that have been set aside (*nirupta*) are the subject under discussion, it is understood that the connection with threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth applies to them alone and not to others. Those that have been set aside are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), while others are not for the sake of the sacrifice (*akratvartha*).

The distinction can be understood. Therefore, because of the connection with the *vrīhi* grain which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), threshing and other such acts do not have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
Again, he objects: "How is it in the case of the *nirvāpa* (offering)?
The meaning of this is: "In that case, how is it that the *nirvāpa* does not have the person as its purpose?"

For in that case, there is no other *saṃskāra* (consecration) such that, through its connection with a *saṃskṛta* substance, it could have a transcendental purpose (*apūrvārthatā*), because the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is primary. He refutes this: even in that case, because the pouring out is distinct [from the consecration], it is established that it does not serve a human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*).
There are these two types of offerings:
that which is for the sake of the person and that which is for the sake of the sacrifice. What, then, is for the sake of the sacrifice?

That which is performed upon a substance intended for the sacrifice—that substance for which the sacrifice is the purpose—is "for the sake of the sacrifice. Therefore, the application [of the mantra] to the ritual act is entirely consistent.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers [the injunction] to be prompted by what is not to be done. To this it is replied: even in this case, it is logical that it is indeed prompted by what is to be done (*kāryaprayuktatā*).
For otherwise, if it were not prompted by what is to be done, then the application of the restrictive rule (*niyamaniyoga*) would not be accomplished.

It may be so. For the injunction (*niyoga*) indeed compels the performance of that very thing which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the accomplishment of the injunction, and without which the accomplishment of the auxiliary itself would not occur. In this regard, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), threshing and the like are not auxiliaries to the accomplishment of the injunction; nor is there a failure of any auxiliary without them, since the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is accomplished even apart from threshing and the like. Therefore—

The rule regarding the necessity of threshing and so forth would not be fulfilled; yet it is understood that such rules extend to their actual performance. Therefore, one must resort to the view that they are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). Furthermore, whether another qualification (*adhikāra*) is postulated for the subject matter of threshing and the like, it cannot be said that the difference in the task (*kārya*)—which is perceived due to proximity—is distinct [from the primary injunction], especially when those acts lack a qualification in the proximity of the principal injunction.

Since that very same qualification (adhikāra) which is heard [in the context] revolves within the intellect, it is not possible to postulate a different qualification. Therefore, an injunction (niyoga) does not tolerate the postulation of a different qualification; rather, it must be described in such a way that it enters into the immediately present qualification.
Thus, it is logical that [the action] is prompted by that [injunction]. And since it is prompted by that, even the word *vrīhi* (rice) serves to indicate a specific means (*sādhana*) for it.

It should be described in this very way. Precisely because there is first the apprehension of the *apūrva* and subsequently the application (*viniyoga*) of its specific means, it is for this reason that, having cited the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the determination of application is stated in order to demonstrate that application is preceded by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*).

Now, one might object: "In the determination of application, the status of the *apūrva* as the primary effect (*kāryatā*) is contradicted, since two distinct effects cannot logically coexist. To this, he says:
And it has been established in the discussion on "for their sake" (*teṣāmarthena*) that this [injunctive force] is opposed to the [mere] purpose of the action.

Even in the case of threshing and similar acts, the conformity to the nature of the substance is not the cause; rather, when sprinkling and such acts are prompted by the *apūrva*, the cause is solely the accomplishment of the restrictive injunction (*niyamaniyoga*).
Therefore, because the reason is the same, there is no disparity between the rule "one threshes after sprinkling" and the rule "one threshes the rice-grains," and so forth.
Thus, in this section, it is established that the application of the directly contributing subsidiaries (*sannipatyopakāraka*) is preceded by the apprehension of the principal act (*grāhaka*).

However, regarding those [subsidiary acts] that provide assistance from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*), one should follow the reasoning established in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādye*) with an attentive mind, just as in the case of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

This is the argument for cumulative effect (*abhyuccayayukti*). Having restated the resolution offered by the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which seeks to establish that threshing and other such acts possess human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*) by accepting the "context" (*prakaraṇa*) as defined in the present discussion—that [resolution] is now refuted: "And as for the claim that there is an inclusion of a ritual action (*kāryagarbhatā*) by accepting the context characterized here..."

It has been stated that its removal is improper because it would result in the failure of the restrictive application (*niyamaniyoga*). Furthermore, since it is impossible for the "context" (*prakaraṇa*)— defined as being related to the primary subject— to exist here, there is indeed nothing "primary" (*prakṛta*) present therein by virtue of which it could serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*).

But has it not been stated that the possibility [of the distinction] arises precisely from the difference in the offering (*nirvāpa*)? That very difference in the offering is not possible when [the substances] are distinct.

For there is no distinction between what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) among rice-grains simply because they are offerings; thus, the definition of the subject matter (*prakṛtalakṣaṇa*) is untenable.

Regarding the context: those very rice grains (*vrīhi*) which serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) become, through the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), subservient to the sacrifice. However, in the state of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the pouring out would not be for the sake of the sacrifice, it would be impossible; thus, due to its connection with the substance serving the person, the pouring out would itself serve the purpose of the person. When that [pouring out] serves the purpose of the person, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) also [serves the purpose of the person], because of its connection with the rice grains already poured out in the primary rite.
By the phrase "for the sake of the human goal" (puruṣārtha), the status of all [elements] as being for the sake of the human goal is established in this sequence. The rest has been explained.

|| 6 || The state of being whispered (upāṃśutva) should apply to those [mantras] when they are bound to a specific place, because of the direct Vedic injunction (śruti-nirdeśa) and because that [quality] exists there. || 20 ||
Since it has been established that [the subsidiaries] are not prompted by the *apūrva*,

the doubt expressed in the Bhāṣya— namely, whether there is a unity of the subsidiary injunctions through their connection with the qualification (just as in the case of the restriction of speech at the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*), or whether this connection with the ritual duty pertains to those already entered into the qualification— is thereby explained. For if [the subsidiaries] were connected with the duty while remaining subordinate...

Regarding the relationship between the *niyoga*s (injunctions) and the *adhikāra-niyoga* (the injunction pertaining to qualification): if it is like the restriction of speech (*vāṅ-niyama*) at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, then they are prompted by the intermediate *apūrva*; however, if this connection with the ritual properties (*dharma*) belongs only to those things that serve as means toward the qualification, then—as in the case of threshing and so forth—they are prompted by the ultimate *apūrva*. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering them to be connected to a single part of the sacrifice, [asserts] the unity of the qualification...
One thinks, "The dharma consists of names.
Its meaning is: "This [part] of the sacrifice is indeed stealth; therefore, whatever is prior to that, they perform it in a whisper (upāṃśu)."

The statement regarding inequality is not faulty. It is true that here too the word *yajña* (sacrifice) exists and it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of an injunction; nevertheless, it is connected with "expansion" (*vistāra*).

Therefore, in order to expand the sacrifice, a restriction of speech must be performed. But how, in this view, is there an understanding of repetition (*vīpsā*)? The answer is as follows: the intention is that there is no desire to express [the meaning] because it is already established by implication.
The meaning is that this is a restatement of what is already established by implication. But how [is this so]?

He states that it is "attainment" (*prāpti*). For even when there is a connection with a location, the connection to the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is established only by way of the ritual object (*padārtha*);

But in the absence of a connection with the ritual items (*padārtha*), the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) would serve the purpose of attaining the sacrifice through an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa*). What is that effect for the sake of which this deliberation is undertaken?
The answer is: regarding the injunction "he sprinkles the fire," is there a distinct effect for each brick, or is there only one single effect?

If there exists a distinct substance [other than the bricks], then that alone is to be sprinkled; thus, there is a single purpose. In the absence of a distinct substance, the act must be performed for each individual brick; for in that case, it is the bricks themselves that are to be sprinkled, and it is for that reason that the inquiry into a distinct substance arises. He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): here, for those who know of a distinct substance, [it is] from the parts...

The Vaiśeṣikas assert that [the cooked state] is a distinct substance; however, their established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that no distinct substance arises from the conjunction of the cooked and the uncooked.
In this case, the bricks are baked while the mortar is unbaked; therefore, there is no distinct substance resulting from their conjunction.
Anticipating the objection—"How then can the cognition of a single entity be accounted for?"—he asks: "What, then, is the justification here for the perceptual cognition?"

The reply is as follows: In this case, the cognition produced by the sense organ has the aggregate itself as its object, as in the case of the bristling of hair and so forth, and it does not depend upon anything else.
Nor does the cognition arise by depending on a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) which is distinct from its constituent parts, such as bricks—as is the case with Devadatta.
The phrase "in the bricks" serves as a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). Therefore, it is not a separate substance.
However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is understood from the scriptural statement: "One piles the fire-altar with bricks.
Otherwise...

For it would be as if one were to say, "Build with bricks. This is the intended meaning: even when there is no distinction, a word expressing distinction is employed, as in such expressions as "the body of a stone statue" and so forth. True; where non-existence is indeed manifest, there—since there is no other substance and thus no actual distinction—it is logical that the state of being non-distinct should prevail. But here, however...

The conception of a "pile" arises with respect to the bricks independently [of their individuality], just as in the case of Devadatta; this is the postulation of a positive entity (*bhāvakalpanā*) based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For just as the cognition of a single unit with respect to Devadatta, independent of his constituent parts such as hands and so forth, is the proof for the existence of the whole (*avayavin*), so too here, since such a cognition exists, it cannot be said that the whole is impossible. Furthermore, even upon the conjunction of the cooked and the uncooked, a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) is produced.

Thus, this must be accepted on the strength of direct perception (*darśana*). Therefore, because it is clearly evident, one should not postulate the existence of a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) based on its difference [from its parts], but rather that it is indeed [the whole] itself; thus ends this section (*adhikaraṇa*).
As for the denial of all composite substances as distinct entities based on the system of Gautama, that has been refuted by the Vaiśeṣikas.
And we have already addressed this in our *Jātinirṇaya*.
As it was said there: "The analogy of the hair-tuft (*keśoṇḍraka*) has been refuted by those who know other substances."
Just as a non-existent mass of hair appears to one suffering from ophthalmia, so too does the whole (avayavin);

this "principle of the mass of hair" has been refuted by the Vaiśeṣikas. As for the inference based on pulling that was stated—wherein a whole exists, when one part is pulled, another part is also pulled, just as in the case of Devadatta—and here [it is applied]:
Only that very brick which is pulled comes along, and not another brick as well. That pulling is stated here as the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
That is refuted because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to stationary things; for when a branch of a tree or the like is pulled, only that very branch comes along.
"Not otherwise. Therefore, since this [fact] exists even where there is a composite whole (*avayavin*), it is not capable of categorically refuting the composite whole.
Consequently, it is established that the effect of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is non-different [from the substance].
The purpose has been stated.

As for the illustration of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) cited by the opponent—namely, that just as one should touch the full moon with the *caturhotṛ* formula, implying a touching of each [individual part], so too should it be performed brick by brick according to the properties of the fire-altar—that too has been refuted. It is appropriate in that case because no other substance is being commenced; here, however, another substance is indeed being commenced.
The conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings applies to all [the days], because there is no distinction. || 29 ||

If all the days were to conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, then there would indeed be an elision of the subsequent subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). However, when [the conclusion occurs] prior to the final day, there is no elision; thus—

rather, it is simply that elision itself is not even considered in this context.
It resides in the heart.

If the elision (*avalopa*) here is not considered, how then is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) to be understood? The answer is: the section is as follows. Is this an instruction regarding the elision itself, or is it a summary of the grammatical operation (*kārya*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: Is this elision of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) enjoined while it has not yet been reached, or is it the withdrawal of the assistance toward the performance of the effect? That is, is there accomplishment by means of the auxiliaries performed only once?

Now, one might ask: "Even so, what is the connection here with the definition? To this he says: "In the teaching," that is, under the view that there is an omission in the instruction.
The determination of the ritual action is according to the instruction;
the meaning is that the attainment of the result must be governed by the authority of the instruction.

Consequently, even in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the procedure is exactly the same: the sequence of subsidiary rites ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. However, in the concluding summary, [it is stated] even for the modified sacrifices...

The "ending with that" (*tadantatā*) occurs precisely according to the purpose (*yathākāryam*). The accomplishment of the performance together [with the preceding rites] is the purpose of "ending with that. Therefore, on whichever day is the penultimate one, in each such case, the "ending with that" is for the sake of that specific purpose. In a *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice), there is an "ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s" for one day; however, in a *trirātra* (three-night sacrifice), it applies to two days.
Thus, the application of the rule is consistent with the principle that the performance follows the specific purpose.
In this regard, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) arises from the conceit of instruction; that is,
the prima facie position is held by the conceit that "this is an abridged instruction."
To the question, "How is it that for all [beings], that [state] is the end by means of instruction? he says: "For there is no specific restrictor in the instruction;

The word "iti" marks the conclusion. Another position, which is merely a semblance of a final conclusion (*rāddhāntābhāsa*), is as follows:
let this be an instruction; nevertheless, because of the hearing of the word "asaṃsthita," [the ritual] occurs before the last day.

The conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings: in this way, its status as the cause for the non-conclusion [of the sacrifice] becomes established. Thus it is heard in scripture: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; one does not throw the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after. For then the sacrifice is indeed not concluded. Thus, the conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* is proclaimed on the grounds of non-conclusion. Prior to the final day, the sacrifice is not concluded; therefore, it is precisely there [that the rule applies].
Regarding the statement "the teaching [of the end]":

having refuted this semblance of a final conclusion by treating it as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for that which lacks a fixed configuration, the lack of distinction was stated once again.

The meaning of this is as follows: this is a praise of the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. For if there were no conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s, then the sacrifice would be completed only after a long time; consequently, even though it had been finished, it would be as if it were not finished. Therefore, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) should be omitted [in that case]. Thus, because there is no distinction, all [sacrifices] conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that this instruction for omission is not possible; for the class of ritual duties (*dharma-jāta*) is already established [by other means]. If it were omitted, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting what has been established. And when non-subversion is possible, subversion is not logical. He states the fundamental reasoning:
because of the unity of the term (*ekaśabdyāt*), how could the expansion of the procedure (*itikartavyatā-vistāra*) belonging to the multi-day sacrifice characterized as the *dvādaśāha* be withdrawn?

In response to this expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), it is understood that this is merely an injunction for the concluding rite (*upasaṃhāra-vidhi*), not an instruction for the omission (*avalopa*) of something not otherwise established. "One desiring progeny should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" is one performance injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*); [the other is] that which is prescribed for each day.

It enjoins the entire collection of duties (kartavyatākalāpa) simultaneously. Following that injunction, the entire collection of subsidiary procedures (itikartavyatākalāpa) must be performed together. When there arises an expectancy for a specific manner—asking "in what manner [should this be done]?"—this statement serves as the concluding rule (upasaṃhāra). For by means of this state of ending with the Patnīsaṃyājas, the entire collection of subsidiary procedures is concluded and performed together.

That procedure is understood because it provides what is required by the injunction. When the purpose of the concluding summary of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is stated as "having performed this [rite], one remains until the *patnīsaṃyāja*s," then [the procedure] is established as lasting until the final day. And in this way, the praise becomes meaningful in its visible purpose: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s; one does not throw the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire, for [the sacrifice] has not yet concluded."

"For indeed, that is the sacrifice. Where there is no formal conclusion (*asaṃsthā*), there it is understood that the rite ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; and that completion, having been established by this reasoning as being supported by authoritative means of knowledge, becomes a valid basis for praise. Otherwise, as [in the case of]—

It would be untenable because the meaning of "being traversed" (gamyamāna) would be absent; furthermore, the injunction would be reversed. In the other view, the injunction is made by means of a sentence (*vākya*), for the completion of the days certainly exists; in that case, there would be an injunction of the meaning of the secondary word (*upapada*). In our view, however, only the conclusion (*saṃsthāna*) is enjoined, and thus it is an injunction by direct statement (*śruti*). The remainder has been explained.
[230] || 9 || The repetition of the *sāmidhenī* verses, because it occurs at the beginning, should be a property of the entire ritual procedure. || 33 ||

But surely, because they are devoid of a specific function (*kārya*), the very connection of the *ṛc* verses with the ritual law (*dharma*) is not tenable; how then can their application (*prayukti*) be deliberated?
In this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the inquiry is indeed conducted in this manner: "Is this a property of the *ṛc* verse itself, or is it a property of its position (*sthāna*)?"

The application itself is being considered: is this repetition (abhyāsa) prompted by the *ṛc* (verse), or is it prompted by the position? That is not correct, because the *ṛc* is not something to be produced (*akārya*). For that which is to be produced (*kārya*) serves as the prompter of ritual duties (*dharma*), not that which is not to be produced.
It is said in reply: this consideration is made by assuming a connection with something to be produced, not merely on account of the *ṛc* itself.
This is what is meant:

as far as the purpose of this [verse] which serves as a means is concerned, is this property [of repetition] due to its being a recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses, or rather due to its being the first recitation? If the connection with the *pravovājāḥ* is that of the repetition—as in the rule "he recites the first verse thrice"—then, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa...
Because it is taken as a *kāra* (an auxiliary), this should be its property when it is applied to that task which is to be accomplished by the *pravovāja* verses;
however, when the connection of the repetition is with the first utterance, then it belongs to that which is applied to the task of the first utterance.
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) says: "The feminine gender must necessarily be intended [as significant], because it is merely the state of being first..."

For if there were an intention to express [the gender], then even the property of the word or the syllable might be suspected [as the intended meaning], and it would not be the property of the *ṛc* itself. Therefore, when there is an injunction by means of a primary reference (*uddeśa*), the qualifying mark (*liṅga*) must be intended as a specification. Consequently, since the doubt is removed by the mark itself, the mark is indeed intended; thus [it is concluded].

The connection is with the word "he says. But by what [word] is the intended *liṅga* (grammatical gender) expressed? To this he says: there is also the position that it is when the feminine (*strī*) is to be denoted;
thus, femininity is obtained by that suffix. Such being the case, regarding femininity...
Because [the gender] is intended to be significant, this is its property; thus, "the *ṛc* is feminine," and therefore repetition is its property—this being the position reached, it is replied:
here, the intention to signify gender is not tenable, because the priority cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*), and if it were an injunction (*vidhāna*), [gender would be relevant].

Because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). If the injunction of dharma were intended with reference to the woman, then its being "first" (*prāthamya*) could not be restated as a reference, since it is not already established; for this *ṛc* is not inherently "first. Nor can "being first" be enjoined, because that would result in a split in the sentence.

Therefore, it is better that the female gender (*strītvam*) be considered unintended (*avivakṣitam*). But how can even that be understood [as unintended]? To this he says: "Furthermore, because the recitation (*anuvacana*) has the *Ṛgveda* as its subject matter, the female gender is invariably present; thus, it is merely restated (*anūdyate*), and there is no fault."

[Objection: But was it not stated that even the suspicion [of the application] of words and phonemes would follow? Therefore, femininity is not invariably applicable here. [The author] answers: There is no suspicion regarding words or phonemes, because the recitation (anuvacana) is based on the meaning.

For recitation is for the purpose of communicating meaning; therefore, it is prescribed as the recitation of that very thing which conveys the meaning. And the comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence;
indeed, the comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence itself, which consists of a collection of many words.

Nor, however, from a single word; rather, the repetition of the sentence itself is obtained. And a sentence is a *ṛc*. Therefore, it has been stated that the feminine gender which was previously applicable is here restated. This is with the intention of explaining the meaning of the rule "the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which occurs in the feminine" by the phrase "in the feminine" (*striyām*).

It has been stated that the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are applied to that which exists as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, because femininity functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no connection with the verbal action; thus he says: "A qualifier is not connected with the action, but only by way of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)."
But was it not said that there is also the position that [the gender] is the denotable meaning?

The meaning of this is as follows: although, according to the actual state of things, the gender functions as a qualifier, its connection [to the object] will nonetheless exist as something denotable by a separate word, just like number.
He refutes this: even so, the nature of the qualifier does not disappear.

Even when femininity is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is stated precisely as a qualifier of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); thus, it has a connection with the action. Therefore, [it is connected] primarily—
The connection with repetition is logical. He states another argument: "And this is reasonable because it results in the comprehension of the fulfillment of fifteen purposes.
For when there is repetition for the sake of fulfilling the number fifteen of the *sāmidhenī* verses, it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). Therefore, [the *sāmidhenīs*...]
It is established that this ritual duty (dharma) is prompted by the function of reciting the introductory formula for the milch-cow (dhenī).
