|| 10 || Upon the repetition of the sacrifice, the Ārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi] should be repeated, just like the Prayāja offerings. || 34 ||

The first section (*adhikaraṇa*) describes, after raising the alternative as to whether the word "commencement" (*ārambha*) refers to the beginning of the performance of the ritual—that is, the undertaking of its execution—or whether it refers to the determination that "this must be done by me," thus analyzing the meaning of the word "commencement. In this regard, having presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the commencement of the ritual is the literal meaning of the word, [the author] establishes that the determination is the literal meaning; for that [determination] is one and the same throughout all Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

"It is established that [the rule applies] to those whose practice lasts for a month. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya, considering the explanation of the earlier teachers to be incorrect, has explained the section differently.
But how does he consider this explanation of the earlier teachers to be incorrect?
The answer: This word "commencement" (ārambha) does not denote the initial state of any single, specific entity. What then?
It expresses the initial state of all entities whatsoever. What follows from that? This is what results from it:

When a [term] is uttered in proximity to something already mentioned, it indicates the commencement of that very thing. This [text], being uttered in proximity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, states:
"One who is about to commence the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu."

Thus, it indicates the very commencement of that [action]. Furthermore, the determination—“this must be done by me”—is common to all objects and all actions, whether they be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*), occurring after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*); therefore, it does not belong exclusively to the first stage of any single one.

It can be understood in this way: such is the intention of the person that as soon as any action requiring fire presents itself to him, it must be performed by him; it does not mean that only the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed. Therefore, because it is common to all such rites, it cannot be understood as referring specifically to the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Consequently, the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa itself constitutes its beginning.

Thus, this [cognition] should be understood today as the very application of the word's referent (*padārtha*), because it is unique and is recognized as having that [referent] as its starting point; it is not a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāna*), since there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) without a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) for such a determination.

Because, in the absence of a distinguishing factor, there would be no conventional usage such as "this is the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Therefore, the Ārambhaṇīyā is not occasioned by the act of commencing; rather, it is occasioned by the performance of the first constituent element (*padārtha*). Consequently, its repetition would necessarily follow, and thus [the objection does not hold].

The interpretation by the former teachers that this constitutes the establishment of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntasiddhi*) is incorrect. Now, one might object: "But even the commentary on the *Bhāṣya* appears to have already covered this point. How so? The answer follows:

For it has been stated in the discussion on "division" (*bheda*) and other topics that every *nimitta* (efficient cause) indeed functions as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*). How then can the "commencement" (*ārambha*) be marked as the subordinate element (*śeṣin*)?
The meaning of this is as follows: the author of the Bhāṣya investigates thus: "Is the commencement... [and so forth].
One might ask: "Does the first constituent element (*padārtha*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices perform its function correctly, or does it render the person fit for undertaking the rite?

In this regard, since the undertaking (*ārambha*) serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), the suspicion that it is a subordinate element (*śeṣin*) is untenable. For it is stated in the sixth [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "Breaking [the vessel] and so forth are occasions; they are not subordinate elements."
Thus, the meaning of this section of the Commentary has been understood. He offers a rebuttal:

there is a doubt here; if this is accepted as a governing rule (*adhikāra*) like that of "breaking" (*bhedana*), then the *ārambhaṇīyā* would have to be repeated at every performance, just as the oblation is performed whenever a breakage occurs, following the qualification of one authorized for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as in the injunction "one offers when [the vessel] is broken," the breaking is a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*), so too, if the commencement (*ārambha*) were such [a qualification], then the one entitled to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) would be qualified by that; namely, the one entitled to the New and Full Moon sacrifices who possesses the commencement.

"One should perform the *ārambhaṇīyā*. Just as one who is qualified for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices due to a breach [of the ritual] performs the *homa*, so too, when there is a repetition of the qualification, the *ārambhaṇīyā* is repeated with each performance, just like the *abhedana-homa*. This is because the intermediate qualification enters into the qualification for the primary rite; thus, when that [primary qualification] is repeated, it is repeated. However, if it were an independent qualification...

In that case, there would be no repetition of the *ārambhaṇīyā* [introductory rite]. If, however, it is not conceived in this way— that is, if the qualification of being entitled to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is not conceived— then, because it would constitute a different entitlement (*adhikāra*), there would be the assumption of a different ritual action (*kārya*).
If it is argued that "let it be so," we say no; because of the co-occurrence with the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa*, no separate qualification (*adhikāra*) is understood.
In a single sentence, both the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering] are mentioned together. In that case, by virtue of the sentence—

The connection is understood; however, in another context, that [connection] would be sublated. Therefore, there is no comprehension of another context. Since repetition occurs even when there is merely the status of a cause (*nimitta*), it is better that this injunction be conceived as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the primary object itself; what is the use of an intermediate context? Let the phrase "about to begin" rather present the principal object (*śeṣin*) itself.

Since that which initiates the formative action (*saṃskāra*) is performed by one who possesses such initiation, the mention of the "person" (*puruṣa*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); why then rely on a superfluous intermediate qualification?
But if the purpose is indeed the same in both positions, by what distinction is the intermediate qualification abandoned?

If both the initial formulation (*ārambhasaṃskāra*) and the opponent's position are accepted, then he says: "But what is the burden (*gaurava*) in the intermediate section (*avāntarādhikāra*) such that it is abandoned? The answer is:
"Indeed, there is no burden at all; rather, it is the intermediate section [that is abandoned]."
[Page 233] This is not possible. Why is it impossible? The answer is: because the first category of entity is eternal.
There is no possibility of a separate qualification (adhikāra).

For in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the first constituent element is permanent (nitya), whereas the qualification is impermanent (anitya); therefore, that portion which serves as a qualification for the qualified person (adhikṛta) is not logically possible [in its case]. However, in the case of breaking [the vessel] and so forth...

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that because they are impermanent, an intermediate application (*avāntarādhikāra*) is appropriate; he considers it logical that these [rites] are enjoined as qualifications for those who are already authorized. Therefore, it is proper that there should be a repetition for each performance, just like the *prayāja* offerings.
To this, it is replied: there is indeed a purpose for the intermediate application here, consisting in its being performed only once. And just as...

This is established. Nor does this [qualification] arise through the qualification of the subject matter (*adhikṛta*), because it is understood as a qualification of the person (*puruṣa*) in the word "one who is about to begin" (*ārapsyamāṇa*). Thus he says: "And this entitlement (*adhikāra*) is clear.
Now, even so, why is the commencement (*ārambha*) the subordinate element (*śeṣin*)?
Regarding the statement "it does not exist," he says: "And the cause (nimitta) cannot be the subordinate element (śeṣin), because there is no evidence for its being subordinate.
[Objection: But was it not already stated that this is not a cause, because the first category of entity is eternal?
He refutes this: True, it would not be a causal factor if the Ārambhaṇīyā were conceived as a subsidiary part of the ritual, like the oblation for breaking [the sacrificial post].

For he who maintains that the *ārambhaṇīyā* is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) must accept that "commencement" refers to the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices; otherwise, its status as a subsidiary cannot be established. Furthermore, for one who is already entitled (*adhikṛta*) to perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, this qualification [of being a "commencement"] is not applicable, because there is no deviation [from that entitlement]. On the other hand, for one who does not accept the *ārambhaṇīyā* as a subsidiary, there is no entitlement to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

It must be qualified, however, by the word "human" (puruṣa). But since not every human being is one who has commenced the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the qualification is appropriate because of the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra). Thinking that this [sacrifice] does not constitute an independent entitlement (svatantrādhikāra), he says:
"And why is it stated as a fault regarding an independent entitlement when its status as a subsidiary (aṅgatva) is impossible?"—referring to the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
It has been stated that there is no lack of understanding [of the subject matter] due to its being mentioned in proximity;
the reply is: true, this fault would indeed arise if an independent entitlement were being postulated.
This [obligation] consists in the sublation of the co-utterance with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
however, this is merely a subordinate entitlement (*avāntarādhikāra*). It is not an entitlement that touches upon the primary entitlement to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in an absolute sense.
Rather, because it serves to assist them, it is indeed a subordinate entitlement. Nor is there any contradiction with the permanence of the first ritual act.

Nor is there indeed a contradiction with its being obligatory (*nitya*). For instance: if the mention in proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices occurs from the very beginning, then the *ārambhaṇīyā* is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice]. Or, if it is an auxiliary, then the "commencement" (*ārambha*) is also a qualification of those entitled to that [sacrifice], just like the breaking [of a vessel]. To the objection that this is not possible for what is obligatory, he says: "And in all cases of the relationship between auxiliary and principal..."
The unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) is the cause.

For it is only when there is unity of the injunction between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) that the relationship of subordinate and principal arises; otherwise, if they have different purposes, the relationship of subordinate and principal would be untenable.

"Let it be so; nevertheless, what follows? he asks: "And there is no evidence for the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) here, because the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is not recited within the context (*aprakaraṇa-adhītatvāt*).
But surely, by way of its connection with the commencement (*ārambha*), that unity of the injunction does indeed exist."

[Page 234] Regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), he says with this intention: "How is there no authority (*pramāṇa*) for the identity of the injunction (*niyoga*)? as in the case of the statement, "The *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood."

The answer is as follows: If indeed "commencement" (*ārambha*), which is expressed independently and constitutes the meaning of the first word, were to connect with the *Ārambhaṇīyā* [offering], then it would be a case of syntactic connection (*viniyoga*) through that medium, together with the first ritual act.

Regarding the unity of application (*viniyoga*): here, however, the agent of the commencement, being subordinate and acting as a qualifier in the form of the first ritual act, connects with the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice through the term "commencing" (*ārabhamāṇa*). Since a connection with the qualification for the rite (*adhikāra*) is possible there, why is the connection based on application (*viniyogika*) accepted?

The connection with the commencement occurs precisely by way of being a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), and by way of being a qualification of that [person], it pertains to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Since such a governing relationship (*adhikārika*) exists, why is the applicatory relationship (*viniyogika*) accepted? If it is argued that it is accepted because a difference in purpose is not otherwise possible, [the author] refutes this:
there is certainly no evidence for abandoning the governing relationship which is directly perceived.

And he says that it is not the case that there is no difference in purpose either: "There is indeed a distinction regarding the meaning of the word; once consecrated, the qualified person obtains the status of being a constituent part of all ritual applications.
The meaning of this is: even though the undertaking [of the consecration] has the qualified person as its specific qualification...

Because it is a qualification precisely by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the *ārambhaṇīyā* injunction possesses utility for its accomplishment just like heaven (*svarga*). Alternatively, since in a sentence containing a qualification (*sadhikāra*) the relationship has the person as its primary element, the *ārambhaṇīyā* serves a human purpose; thus, it produces a refinement (*saṃskāra*) in the person alone that is conducive to the arising of the commencement [of the sacrifice]. And once refined by this single performance, the person [is fit for] the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices...

Since [the sacrifice] has become fit for performance, the *ārambhaṇīyā* (opening rite) does not need to be repeated. However, in the case of a relationship that is *viniyogika* (based on specific application), because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) pertaining solely to the commencement (*ārambha*), there would be a repetition [of the rite] due to the repetition of the commencement; thus he says: "But in the case of a relationship based on specific application, there is a repetition at each performance."
In this regard, the essential point is as follows: the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Therefore, there is no unity of injunction (*niyogaikya*) based on proximity (*sannidhāna*), nor is there such unity through the connection with a constituent element (*padārtha*) as in the case of the *parṇatā* [rule]. Since the *ārambhaṇīyā* pertains to the person by virtue of its connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*), it serves the purpose of the person; thus, it has no direct connection with the first constituent element. Consequently, for the person—

The *saṃskārikā* [rite] produces the fitness for undertaking [the sacrifice], but it is not a constituent part (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice itself, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence [for such a status].

By this, the following is stated: for those who claim that there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) even in the *prayāja* offerings and the like, those *prayāja*s and so forth would likewise be solely for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); in that case, just as with the *ārambhaṇīyā*, the *prayāja*s and other rites would also produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) conducive to the arising of the *apūrva*.
And as in that case, their performance would also have to be done only once. However, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*) [of the Jyotiṣṭoma];

therefore, the phrase "one who is about to be initiated" (*dīkṣiṣyamāṇaḥ*) is merely a qualification of the person already under discussion in the primary context. Consequently, because there is a unity of injunction (*niyoga*), it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Nor can there be entry into the sacrifice by way of purifying the person, since this is a purification of the person that is independent [of the sacrifice].
Because that which has been consecrated once serves as a constituent part of the subsequent performance.
If this is so, why is it not assumed that the *bhedana-homa* (the oblation for breaking) is likewise a consecration of the person, just like the *ārambhaṇīyā*?
Response: Even if one were to postulate that a false appearance arises for each individual object,
there would still be the consequence of the recurrence of the same objection regarding cognition and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: "One offers when [the vessel] is broken" implies that the person is to be consecrated by means of removing the defect caused by the breaking. Since the breaking is the occasion for the arising of the defect, there is the understanding that the oblation must be performed again for the sake of its removal; thus, the oblation must indeed be repeated. Furthermore, since there is no difference in the performance [of the act], this objection [is raised].

It is indeed a response to my objection. Even there, the *saṃskāra* (preparatory rite) is [established] through the context (*prakaraṇa*) and because of its direct co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with those [acts] under discussion;
however, it is inferred through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the causes such as breaking (*bhedana*) and so forth.
The meaning of this is: that the breaking and so forth [are not the causes].
There would be a connection with the person by which they might serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the person; however, they are indeed solely for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

If a direct entitlement (*adhikāra*) were heard in them, then it would indeed be so; but they are entirely without entitlement, because they are heard as being merely the occasion (*nimitta*) for actions such as the breaking [of a vessel] and so forth. And that which is taught within the context (*prakaraṇa*) but lacks an entitlement has only the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice. However, the absence of an occasion [for the application of the rule] depends upon the presence of an entitlement.

Since [the injunction] is not possible without being a qualification of something specific, it is postulated that the breaking [of a vessel] and other such acts qualify the person authorized for the ritual (*kratvartha*).

Now, even if they are purificatory acts for the person (*puruṣasaṃskāraka*), since they are occasioned by the commencement [of the ritual], why would there not be a repetition [of the act] when the commencement is repeated?

Anticipating the objection that this might be like a fire-offering (homa) which destroys the human refinement (puruṣasaṃskāra), he says: "But here, since no other cause arises at all, there is no recurrence; this is the distinction.
To the question, "Why does no other cause arise? he replies:

Because the first ritual act (*padārtha*) is indivisible. This is the intended meaning: a person’s fitness (*yogyatā*) for the performance of the first ritual act is produced by the *Ārambhaṇīyā* rite; and since that first ritual act is a single entity, the fitness toward it is not divided.

The purpose of the *ārambhaṇīyā* is to produce fitness (*yogyatā*) in the person, and this serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) for its performance. Since this [fitness] is a single entity, there is no repetition of the occasion; therefore, there is no repetition of the *ārambhaṇīyā*. In that case, however, since there is the "differentiation of what was previously undifferentiated," the distinction of the occasion is established. Furthermore, because of the false differentiation produced by a subsequent act of splitting, the purpose of removing that [falsehood] is also distinct in each instance. Thus, even in its capacity as a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāraka*), [the *ārambhaṇīyā* is to be performed separately].
In that case, there is no repetition because the cause for repetition is absent.

This very point was demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya [Kaiyaṭa] by showing that even in another usage, the word is obtained as already refined (*saṃskṛta*), such that the expression "on the same day" (*samāne ’hani*) is also established. In the phrase "one who is about to begin the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," the suffix *lṛṭ* indicates a future action not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana*).

Since it is prescribed that on whichever day the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) are to be performed, on that very day the fitness for commencement is attained through the performance of the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering, and this indeed exists. Just as that single *ārambhaṇīyā* once performed belongs specifically to those days connected with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, so too, according to the tenth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], regarding the *ārambhaṇīyā* in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites...

That doubt was raised by relying on the position that the Soma sacrifice comes first; for if the person has already been consecrated by the *iṣṭi*, no such doubt would arise because of his being refined—thus [the argument] is faultless. Because of the connection with the expression of meaning, there should be the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) in the mantras.
In that case, what is not enjoined and has not been obtained [is excluded], because only what is enjoined is designated. || 36 ||

[Page 236] Regarding this, it is said that one who considers the presence of a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) to follow from the fact that the meaning is integrated [with the ritual action] says: "But surely, since it is impossible for mantras to have both a visible and an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), this doubt itself is improper."

For it has been stated: "Because there is a single purpose, there is a single sentence, provided that if divided, it would remain expectant [of further words]. Furthermore, when there is both a visible and an invisible purpose, there is a difference in purpose; therefore, there is no unity of the mantra at all.

It is established: since there is no definitive statement of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that it is impossible for a single mantra to have both visible and invisible purposes, this doubt itself is improper.
For in the final conclusion, [it is held that] "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" has a relevant meaning (*samavetārtha*), while the remainder has an irrelevant meaning (*asamavetārtha*).

[If it were so,] a distinction in purpose would result, namely that [the former] is for a visible purpose and [the latter] is for an invisible purpose. He refutes this, saying: "It is said—in this case, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and final (uttarapakṣa) positions are not established according to their respective numbers by way of being for visible or invisible purposes; even in the final conclusion (rāddhānta), there is no invisible purpose for what remains."
There is no contradiction with the principle of having a single mantra.
How, then, are the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions established? The answer is: by virtue of their having a unified meaning.
He raises an objection again:

"But surely, if the purpose is inherent (*samaveta*), there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*); whereas if the purpose is not inherent (*asamaveta*), there is an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). Thus, this very distinction between visible and invisible purposes constitutes the basis for the prior and subsequent positions."

He refutes this: "This is not so. It is true that if the meaning is inherent (*samaveta*), there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*); however, if the meaning is not inherent (*asamaveta*), it is impossible to maintain that there is no invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
Why? He says:"
It is not possible to postulate another purpose for a statement that serves the purpose of praise;

even a statement made for the sake of praise must be understood as being solely for the purpose of conveying meaning, and it cannot be postulated to have an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose, because there is a lack of evidence. This has been stated in the section concerning the Arthavādas.

If, even in the final conclusion (siddhānta), there is a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā), how then does the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) consider it to be an expression of a meaning inherent [in the word]? For if the prima facie view were tenable due to a desire for an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārthatva) in the final conclusion, the answer is: [it is] for its own sake (svārtha).
This is due to the desire for [the words] to denote [their own meaning].
For when it is possible for them to have their own purpose (svārthatva), it is not logical that they should serve another's purpose (pārārthya); such is the prima facie view (pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ).

Indeed, if they were for the sake of praise (stutyarthatva), they would serve another's purpose; however, since the words manifest the deity who is inherent [in the sacrifice], they possess their own purpose. Thus, out of a desire for their own purpose—[the argument continues].
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that the mantras have a directly expressed meaning.

Here he raises an objection: It is appropriate that they have their own specific referents when there is the postulation of deities such as Savitṛ based on the wording of the mantras, since those very deities are denoted by the words "Savitṛ" and so forth. But how is this possible in the case of a figurative postulation?

For instance, when fire itself is conveyed by words such as *savitṛ* through a secondary (figurative) function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), how can it then have its own primary meaning? For a word used figuratively has only the meaning of another [object]. The reply is: even here, it is established that the usage is for its own primary meaning, not for the meaning of another word.

The utterance of words such as "Savitṛ" is for the purpose of praise; however, those very words also signify the deity. Therefore, even under the view that [the mantra] is secondary (gauṇa), the performance serves its own inherent purpose. Thus, it is established that the purposefulness of the mantra exists in both positions.

This being the case, it is replied: not even a single one of these alternatives is possible here. For it is understood that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) even through the fact of subservience to another (*pārārthya*). Therefore, neither the postulation of a different deity nor the postulation of a figurative sense (*gauṇakalpanā*) is possible.

Since it is understood that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) even on the grounds of being for the purpose of praise, let all words be recognized as having such unity; nevertheless, one might ask: "Even so, what follows? To this he says: "And when syntactic unity is established, it is proven that the mantra has a meaning inherent in the ritual act (*samavetārthatva*)."

Since it is not the case that the capacity to convey a unified meaning at every step is necessarily brief, the directly perceived unity of the sentence cannot be denied. On account of that, it is logical that the purpose is solely for the sake of another; just as in the case of "syonaṃ te," when a multiplicity of sentences is understood, then—

[This occurs] through the distinction of meanings inherent in the entry into that [object]. To this, he says: "In this case as well, let it be so"—for when an object already exists, its state of having expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) while being analyzed does not indeed need to be taken into account.
And when an object is merely being postulated, there is no basis of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it; therefore, there is no requirement for such expectancy.
It can be said that an assumed difference in meaning cannot override an established syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Therefore, no difference in meaning should be assumed in the case of the mantra "syonaṃ te" [O seat, be pleasant for you], because the preparation of the seat and the establishment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are distinct acts.
Thus, it is established that even when subserving another purpose (*pārārthya*), certain words within a mantra possess a meaning directly connected to the ritual action (*samavetārthatva*).
Furthermore, as to how the words "Savitṛ" and so forth serve the purpose of praise, he says: "And their subservience to another purpose has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya.
The words "Savitṛ" and so forth are described as being for the sake of praise with reference to the sacrificer. And therein, furthermore—
If it is suspected that these [mantras] refer exclusively to the sacrificer, then a modification (*ūha*) based on the sacrificer would follow.
To the question "What is the reason for that?", he says: in the case of the sacrificer’s position, there is a suspicion of modification due to the force of *prasava*.
*Prasava* means permission; [it belongs to] the sacrificer—

It is stated that [the formula] is connected [to the context]; thus, a modification of the words "Savitṛ" and so forth was suspected for the purpose of proclaiming the procreation of many sacrificers.

However, that suspicion regarding modification was not accepted, because even if the procreation were not intended to be expressed, the proclamation of procreation would still be logically consistent.
The meaning is that it has been rejected. If there were an intention to express [the quality], then there would be modification (*ūha*) for the sake of mentioning it elsewhere as well.
But if there is no intention to express it, there is no purpose in manifesting this, and thus there is no modification (*anūha*).
|| 12 || "If it is argued that the word denoting a quality is likewise [subject to modification]. || 38 ||

If words such as *savitṛ* and others are intended for another purpose because they form a single syntactical unit with the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), then likewise the words *juṣṭa* and *agni* must also be intended for another purpose. Consequently, they do not refer to what is present in the ritual (*asamavetārthatva*). And when there is no reference to what is present in the ritual, there is no modification (*anūha*). The meaning of this is as follows: although Agni is indeed present in the ritual, nevertheless—just as in the case of the phrase "may he increase the lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapatiṃ vardhāni*)—[the word *agni* here does not denote the specific deity present].

Because it serves another purpose, it is not denoted by the mantra through its inherent connection (*samavetatva*). Its being for another purpose arises from its being expressed as a qualification of the offering (*nirvāpa*). And since its meaning is not inherently connected [to the ritual act], there is no modification (*anūha*), just as in the case of the word *yajñapati*.
On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya states that there is no modification of the word *agni* alone, but not of the word *juṣṭa*. The reason for this is as follows:
He asks: "What, then, is the reason that one declares *anūha* (non-modification) only for the word *agni*, and not for the word *juṣṭa* as well? The answer is:

because, despite its meaning being applicable (*samaveta*), modification by the word *juṣṭa* is impossible according to both the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Therefore, because there is no distinction, its non-modification (anūha) is not stated.
This being the case, it is replied:

It is true that there is syntactical unity with the act of pouring out (nirvāpa); nevertheless, since the deity implies the pouring out for its own sake, it enters into syntactical unity with it, and thus one cannot claim that [the mention of the deity] is for the sake of another. By means of the pouring out...

Since there can be no sacrifice without [an offering], the deity implies the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) for its own sake; thus, the fire is not for the sake of another. It is established that when something is not for the sake of another, it possesses the quality of being connected to the purpose (*samavetārthatva*), and when it is so connected, there is modification (*ūha*) in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*). Nor is it improper to speak of what is "pleasing" (*juṣṭa*) regarding what is not yet pleasing; for the state of being pleasing arises through the act of pouring out. He refutes the objection that it is not unpleasing prior to the pouring out by stating: "This is certainly not [said] regarding what is unpleasing."

The word *juṣṭa* (pleased/acceptable) is used in the sense of an action (*kāryatvena*), because its meaning is understood as something to be brought about; thus, the connection is "I make it acceptable by means of the offering" (*nirvāpeṇa juṣṭaṃ karomi*). It does not mean, however, that one offers what is already acceptable prior to the act of offering (*prāṅ-nirvāpāt juṣṭaṃ santaṃ nirvapāmi*). Since the connection is made in this way, therefore, this [term] is used in the sense of an aspiration (*āśaṃsāyām*).
The scope of the rule "as if it were a fact" (*bhūtavat*) is because the result is something to be desired;
or rather, it is as follows.

In this regard, since it is impossible for the primary or secondary denotation [of the word] to apply here, one must consider whether this mantra— "Thou art grain"— is intended for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) when used during the sowing of rice, or whether it is more reasonable that its meaning be connected to the actual ritual act (*samavetārthatā*) even by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Since it is impossible to denote *taṇḍula* (rice grains) either by the primary or secondary sense of the word *dhānya* (grain),

there arises the deliberation: "In the sowing of rice grains, would this mantra serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), or— given that rice grains are related to grain— does the word *dhānya* indirectly (*lakṣaṇayā*) signify rice grains so that this mantra may indeed have a relevant meaning (*samavetārtha*)?"
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the mantra to have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), because it lacks utility for the performance (*prayoga*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the word "grain" (*dhānya*) were to denote "rice" (*taṇḍula*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then the mantra would have a visible purpose; however, secondary indication occurs only when there is knowledge of the utility for the performance. And here, the word "grain" does not [denote] rice—

There is no evidence that it is employed for the purpose of [reciting] the words themselves; therefore, since its definition [as a primary meaning] is untenable, the mantra serves only an invisible (transcendental) purpose.

But how is it understood from its being intended for use that it does not have a visible purpose? To this he says: "For the meaning of a sentence is primarily directed toward performance; in the absence of that..."

The assumption of a purposeful function (kāryakalpanā) would result in being non-scriptural (aśābdī). For practical application (prayoga) is the primary cause for understanding the meaning of a sentence; in the absence of such application, the assumption that "the purpose is the manifestation of rice grains" would be devoid of scriptural authority.

Nor is it the case that the application (viniyoga) is not possible, since it can be established even through an unseen (adṛṣṭa) means. Therefore, its purpose must indeed be an unseen one (adṛṣṭārthatā).

And this is what is intended here: by means of application (*viniyoga*), it is determined that the mantra serves that specific purpose, not the individual word. Since the validity of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is rooted in the purport of the word, and since there is no utility for the word as a direct denoter [in this context], the application of the mantra occurs solely through the medium of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

To this it is replied: an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārthatā) is not possible. Why? To this he says: for figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) cannot be prevented from being a cause of comprehension, just as in common worldly usage, as in "rice is eaten" (śālayo bhujyante).
Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is: if metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) could be prevented from being a cause of comprehension, then there would be the consequence of it having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). But this is not possible, because even metaphorical indication is observed in worldly usage to be a cause of comprehension.
In the world, [the expression] "rice is being eaten" serves as a cause for understanding [that rice-eating is occurring]; however, that is not possible here. To this he says:
"And when a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) is possible, the application [of the word] does not tolerate the postulation of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa).
Therefore, by means of secondary indication..."
It is logical to assume that this mantra has a meaning that is directly inherent [in its constituent words].
But surely, because it is not employed [in that specific context], one cannot assume an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through the operation of the word;

for by means of the application (*viniyoga*), the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the mantra as a whole is understood, not that of the individual word. Therefore, the word *dhānya* [must function] through the operation of indication...
It is not possible to understand [the term] as "that which makes the rice known. Furthermore, it is the function of the word (*pada*) that is being considered here. Why? To this he says:

"And modification (*ūha*) is dependent upon the function of the word, even though the purpose resides in the sentence (*vākya*), because [the word's function] consists in manifesting what is inherent [in the sacrifice]."

For if it is understood that the function (*vyāpāra*) of the word "grain" (*dhānya*) consists in denoting what is being sown, then— in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*)— since it is impossible to convey by means of the word "grain" the meat that is being sown, the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is substituted, and not otherwise.

Precisely because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in the function of a word, is not established merely through the purport (*tātparya*) of the mantra, for this very reason some [hold this view].
Thinking that only the secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) is intended here, they consider that there should be a modification (*ūha*) of the mantra "thou art a deer.

The meaning of this is: as long as the application (*viniyoga*) is not described as extending up to the limit of the secondary indicative function, so long the indicative function based upon the word is not established. Therefore...

One who maintains that a word possesses a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇikatva*) must state this: it must be said that what is being indicated by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the purpose of the application (*viniyoga*).

Consequently, even in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), there should be a modification (*ūha*) such as "you are a deer" (*mṛgo’si*), and not "you are meat" (*māṃsamasi*). However, if secondary indication is not intended, then because the purport of the mantra is understood, [the term] *dhānya* (grain) is derived etymologically from the root *dhinoti* (to satisfy), meaning "that which satisfies."

Since it is possible for the rice to be conveyed by means of mixing [the flour with water], and since the application [of the term] is also possible in the case of meat, there would be no modification (ūha).
Thus he says:
"Or rather, he considers there to be no modification. Why? Because of the observation of an explanatory passage (arthavāda)."

Because of the observation of the mantra and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Delight the gods," one might ask: "Let the *arthavāda* be so; nevertheless, how is there no modification (*ūha*)? To this he says: the application of the word *dhānya* (grain) to rice (*taṇḍula*) is established precisely from that *arthavāda*.
Because it serves to gratify the deity through the root *dhā* (to nourish), rice grains are called *dhānya*;
likewise, meat is also so called. Thus, since the primary substance (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) share this etymological derivation, there is no modification (*anūha*) of the mantra.
To this, it is replied: it was stated in the first chapter that the purpose of a mantra is to manifest that which is present [in the ritual].
Therefore, that alone is the purpose [of the discussion].
As for the claim that "inference (ūha) is not possible because of the non-operation of the *apadeśa*," that is incorrect.
Why? He says: "Even indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is dependent upon that very [word-meaning], as is seen in cases such as 'the sound on the Gaṅgā' (*gaṅgā-ghoṣa*)."
The meaning of this is as follows:

When it is understood that the purpose of a mantra is the manifestation of what is inherent [in the ritual], and when the inquiry arises as to how that purpose is accomplished, there occurs an investigation into the power (*śakti*) of each individual word. In that regard, first, for those words other than the term *dhānya* (grain)...

The word *dhānya*, however, possesses the capacity for manifestation; by resorting to a conventional metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) well-known in the world, it can convey the act of sowing through the medium of manifesting the rice-grains being sown. Therefore, that metaphorical function is resorted to.

Since this indication (*lakṣaṇā*) follows the intended meaning of the mantra and is not itself what is primarily intended to be expressed, there is no indication here regarding the modification; for it is dependent upon oneself, and since it is impossible to denote meat even by way of indication using the word *dhānya* (grain) in the Vedic usage for the sake of the ritual performance, another word must be introduced. In that case, while the primary meaning is possible, who indeed [would use it otherwise]?
One should not introduce a technicality;
as they say: "Who would accomplish a goal by a circuitous route when it can be achieved by a direct path?
However, in the case of the usage of the Ṛṣis...

What should be done? In that very same application, even in that modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where the word *dhānya* can be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no modification (*anūha*) at all; for, as in the original model (*prakṛti*), the expression is established by the Vedic usage itself. Nor can this word *dhānya* be considered etymological (*yaugika*), since its purpose is accomplished by its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) alone; for when its etymological nature is set aside by convention, [the properties] dependent upon it [are likewise set aside].

Etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) is not superior to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, where even through figurative indication the purpose is not accomplished, there one must indeed resort to etymological derivation, because the meaning of a mantra is primarily concerned with its function. Since this word *dhānya* is not etymological, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves merely as praise; it does not provide an etymology for the sake of establishing the application of the word.

Now, one might object: "If it is not understood that the word 'grain' (dhānya) is used with the intent of conveying rice (taṇḍula), how can there be indication (lakṣaṇā)? To this he says: "And there is no purpose served by the usage here.
Why so? To this he says: "Because [the meaning] is inherent (samaveta)..."
For it is intended for manifestation;
the employment [of a word] is intended for the purpose that "the word shall manifest the meaning inherent [in it].
And that is accomplished by another means as well; it is established here even through the comprehension of the purport of the mantra, according to the manner previously stated.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: If even a figurative meaning of a word is accepted in mantras, then the distinction between the primary and secondary senses would be of little practical utility.
The reply is: it is not of little utility, because [the distinction is necessary] for comprehension.
Because the purpose is the same.

At the stage of understanding the secondary and primary [meanings], the purpose is equal. It was stated in the third [book] that there is a distinction regarding the occasion (*nimitta*); at the stage of the occasion, there is a distinction in that the primary [meaning] has an independent occasion, whereas the secondary [meaning] has one that is dependent.

Similarity depends upon the cognition of the primary meaning; this is the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*). It is precisely to demonstrate this distinction that there is an investigation into the secondary and the primary. By means of this distinction, a difference arises regarding what is applied by *liṅga* (indicative power), but it is not said through the investigation of the secondary and the primary that "the cognition of the primary alone is the cause [of application], and not another. Therefore, even by way of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the mantras possess a meaning that is inherent (*samaveta*).
Thus it is established.
|| 13 || But when [the mantra] is enjoined, because it serves another purpose, there should be no modification according to the rule. || 40 ||

1. R: How, then, can it be said that the *iḍā* itself is invoked, given that the mantra is enjoined by the Vedic text (*śruti*) as "Invoke the *iḍā*" (*iḍām upahvayasva*)? It is the primary [meaning] alone. [Page 241] Regarding the mantra thus employed:
Another purpose is suspected: the manifestation of the sacrificer's prosperity (*yajñapati-vṛddhi*).
The reply is: here, only the application (*viniyoga*) is being considered. Is the phrase "May he increase the sacrificer" applied to the invocation of the *iḍā*, or not?
The meaning of this is as follows:

this application (viniyoga) is based on direct Vedic statement (śruti). In that regard, there arises the consideration: even when "yajñapatiṃ vardhāni" is applied to the invocation of the *iḍā*, what then?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers there to be another application based on both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). Since the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the "lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapati*), the phrase "may [the gods] increase the lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapatiṃ vardhān*)—by virtue of its recitation within the context—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that which is contextualized.

Furthermore, this [phrase] is capable of expressing the lord of the sacrifice as qualified by increase; and such a [qualified lord of the sacrifice] exists in the sacrifice. Its manifestation [is therefore required].

And it is beneficial to the sacrifice because it generates enthusiasm; therefore, its application (viniyoga) occurs in that very context. But how can another sentence be postulated as falling between the opening and the conclusion? Because, through mutual expectancy, the words are understood to constitute a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva).

The answer: The classification [of mantras] as *yajus* occurs by virtue of their application (*viniyoga*). It is not on account of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) that there is a requirement for other words, as was demonstrated in the case of "syonaṃ te sadanam."

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the formulation of mantras in the *Yajurveda* as sentences, that which constitutes a single sentence is determined by the requirement of application (*viniyoga*). To the extent that a number of words are applied to a single purpose, they possess a single meaning; and when there is a single meaning, there is a single sentential unity (*ekavākyatva*). This is not, however, dependent upon the expectation of other words.

The conceptualization of sentence-hood (*vākyatva-kalpanā*): as many words as there are that are mutually dependent constitute a single sentence; this is the conceptualization of a sentence. Just as in the case of "syonaṃ te" (O pleasant one, for you), although there is mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), there is a difference of sentences due to the difference in application (*viniyoga-bheda*), so too here, by virtue of the application, there is a division of the mantra-sentences. Therefore, there is a division [of the text]; from the division, a difference of function (*kārya-bheda*); from the difference of function—

"And because of the difference [in number], there is a difference in the recitation (*ūha*): when there is duality or plurality of sacrificers (*yajamāna*), there is *ūha*; otherwise, there is no *ūha* regarding the word *yajñapati* in the remaining portion. Furthermore, in the case of a division of the *iḍā*, there is no difference in the *ūha*. This being the position reached, it is replied: this would indeed be so if there were a different application (*viniyoga*) for the sacrificer..."

[Otherwise] it would have to be a matter of increase; however, in this case, [an increase] must be postulated. And a postulated meaning cannot serve as a reason for the non-intentionality (avivakṣā) of an established meaning.

The meaning of this is as follows: based on the introduction and the conclusion, here first—[the word] "yajñapati" (lord of the sacrifice)— *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Mīmāṃsā principles, likely discussing the interpretation of Vedic injunctions.*

The syntactic unity of the word *vardhāni* is understood through its connection with the [preceding] word; furthermore, in the invocation of the *iḍā*, both the opening and the conclusion are applied by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). By virtue of being part of that same syntactic unit, the application of [the word *vardhāni*] is also perceived to be in that very same place.

However, as for the increase of the patron of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*), the application would have to be inferred through indicative power (*liṅga*). And that which is already established by scripture cannot be sublated by what is merely inferred.
It is possible. Therefore, it is precisely by means of the mantra itself—having observed the mantra alone—that whatever constitutes syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is understood;

that alone is the cause for the syntactic unity of a *yajus*. When "That which is pleasant for thee... has been uttered, and its application (*viniyoga*) is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*) [p.

The division of the *yajus* formula is determined by its indicative power (*liṅga*), as is its connection through differentiation. Its application (*viniyoga*) to the preparation of the seat and the establishment [of the oblation] is likewise by means of indicative power. Therefore, it is appropriate that this duality of the *yajus* is postulated independently of any expectancy for words. In this case, however, since the application is established by both indicative power and context (*prakaraṇa*) within the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*), the subservience to another purpose (*pārārthya*) of the invocation of the *iḍā* is proven.

And there is the quality of "otherness" (paratva). Consequently, there is no modification (anūha), because the purpose is accomplished by any sacrificer acting according to the rule. It has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya that the purpose is fulfilled even by the measuring performed by a single person, as in the case of the rule: "The Audumbarī post is to be measured equal to the sacrificer."
The modification would belong to that which is predominant therein. || 41 ||

But surely, in the section concerning the *sūktavāka*, it was stated that this result—the prayer for longevity—is the longevity being prayed for that constitutes the fruit; therefore, since the sacrificer is a beneficiary of the fruit here, he is not for the sake of another. How, then, can the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) be formulated in this case?
He responds: "True, this is the fruit; however, there is no distinction whatsoever in it as it relates to the sacrificer."
Furthermore, even this result, when connected with the sacrificer, is not connected as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*);

therefore, there is no difference [in this respect] from the phrase "that [result] for the lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapati*). For it is not necessarily the case that the prayer for long life must be qualified by the sacrificer in order to possess a result; rather, the result is connected [to him] simply by virtue of his being the agent (*kartṛ*). Nevertheless, this is because the meaning of the mantra is thus established. Nor is it...

The prayer for longevity (*āyurāśāsana*) must be qualified by that which possesses the fruit—that is, by the primary factor with respect to the fruit—because even though the connection with the prayer exists solely through the status of being the agent, the meaning of the mantra-sentence is thus established. Therefore, just as in the case of the *audumbarī* post being measured by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is considered that no other person than the sacrificer qualifies, nor does [anyone qualify] merely by possessing the fruit; thus, [the agent] is regarded as not being inherently connected [to the qualification].

Just as in the case of the rule "the udumbara post is equal in measure to the sacrificer," where another person who is a sacrificer is not understood, nor is it connected [to the word] solely by virtue of being a fruit-bearer, but rather solely by virtue of being the agent; so too here.

Therefore, even though the sacrificer is present [in the ritual], because he is denoted for the sake of another, he does not possess the status of being for the sake of that which is present [in the ritual].
Regarding the mantra:
consequently, there is no modification (anūha), just as in the case of the word "yajñapati.
To this it is replied: one must necessarily consider that here the cause for the prayer is indeed fulfilled.

The meaning of this is as follows: the very fact of being a recipient of the fruit is the cause for the prayer (*āśāsana*). Therefore, although there is agency (*kartṛtva*) in the act of praying, nevertheless, because of the primacy of being the recipient of the fruit, it is worthy of consideration that [the agent] is not acting for the sake of another (*apārārthya*). Why is it that the very fact of being a recipient of the fruit is the cause for the prayer?

The answer is as follows: For it has been stated that where the knowledge of the result comes from another source, there the meaning of the mantra is appropriate even in the capacity of being the agent (*kartṛtva*).

But here, the postulation of the result arises from the mantra itself. If it were not connected with the possession of a result, and if the mantra did not make known the possession of a result, then the very postulation of the result from the mantra would be frustrated. And upon its frustration...

1. It was stated in the third [book] that the status of a mantra as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not tenable if it were to function merely by way of its fruit; for a mantra attains the status of an auxiliary to a ritual action through the manifestation of the fruit.

[The mantra] proceeds [to its purpose]. But if it were fruitless, what would it be making known that it could attain the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*)? Therefore, because it does not have another purpose, it reveals the sacrificer as he is present; from that, the modification (*ūha*) is established. || 15 || "Because of the lack of connection with those things intended for him, one should recognize it as qualified by that. || 42 ||
Regarding the statement "The Subrahmaṇyā [formula] belongs to Agni," it is considered whether words such as *harivat* and others should also be modified (*ūhya*) here or not.
To that end, this is considered: do words such as *harivat* denote a meaning inherent in the context (*samavetārtha*), or do they denote a meaning not inherent in the context (*asamavetārtha*)?
But how, then, are they of inherent meaning, and how are they of non-inherent meaning?
The answer is as follows: If they reveal the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substance Indra, then they have a co-inherent object (*samavetārtha*).
If, however, they denote a quality—as in the case of "strew with green *darbha* grass"—then [they are not co-inherent].

By means of the word *dhānā*, Indra himself is manifested; therefore, because it manifests Indra as being present [in the rite], it possesses a relevant meaning (*samavetārthatva*). Now, if they perform a praise (*stuti*), then they do not possess a relevant meaning.
If such things as "possessing bay horses" (*harivattā*) are stated in order to praise Indra, then—
[The words] have their meanings not yet combined [into a syntactical whole].
In this regard, the proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī) considers praise alone to be logical, because the meaning of the *nigada* is established through praise itself.

Otherwise, there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the predominance of the quality (*guṇa*). The introduction to the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) has been explained. Furthermore, the doubt of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) arises from the thought that the recitation (*nigada*) is for the purpose of understanding its own nature through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

This recitation (*nigada*) is for the purpose of establishing the true nature of Indra. But how can qualities such as "possessing bay horses" (*harivattā*) be capable of characterizing Indra, when their connection with Indra is not known—just as the quality of being green (*harita*) is known to be connected with *darbha* grass?
To this it is replied: through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the understanding of Indra’s true nature arises from the comprehension of his connection with these qualities.
What, then, is this explanatory passage (arthavāda)? He says: "The preceding and following positions" has been shown.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that even an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is justified solely by way of praise; for if it were intent upon its own literal form, its status as an *arthavāda* would be lost.
Even this particular *arthavāda*, which is devoted to establishing Indra’s possession of bay horses (*harivat*) and other such attributes, [is likewise justified by praise].

When there is a connection through praise alone, it constitutes an *arthavāda*. If, however, it were intended to convey the actual nature of the object as it is perceived, then its status as an *arthavāda* would be lost; for it has been stated that the character of an *arthavāda* consists in its purpose being praise for the injunctions (*vidhi*). Moreover, if this entity were accepted exactly as it is perceived, then it would possess a beginning (*ādimattā*), because it would then be conveying objects such as Kaṇvāyana and others.
Furthermore, it would follow that the Veda has a beginning; therefore, this meaning should not be accepted as it was literally heard.

Thus, having first stated—while for the sake of argument—that Indra does not possess such a nature, he says: "Therefore, even though Indra is not of such a form, attributes such as 'possessing bay horses' (*harivat*) and so forth are employed for the purpose of praise. This is because the Śruti [scripture] [speaks] by means of those two.
And it is also logical that "he takes this away," because Indra possesses the quality of having bay horses (*harivat*); for by means of those two, he takes all this away.

The *patti* (consequence) is stated as the reasoning (*yukti*). By this, it is understood that the very fact of being "Hari's garment" is established through reasoning. Thus, he states the fundamental reasoning merely as a hypothetical argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*). However, where there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object], what else can there be there but mere praise? And just as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not capable of establishing the essential nature, so it has been explained in the Bhāṣya. Therefore:
There is no modification (*ūha*) for the *harivad* and other such [mantras], because they express a meaning that is not inherent to the context.
Having demonstrated this lack of modification, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "But the ritualists do not approve of this.
He raises an objection to that: "What is the purpose in stating 'they do not approve,' since it does not contradict the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)?"
Because it is due to [logical] connection; and because, on the contrary, it would cause harm by contradicting the performance of the sacrificial experts.
He provides the resolution: "In this way, confusion regarding the meanings of the statements is justified."

Therefore, by demonstrating a lack of conviction that "this inquiry [into dharma] should be undertaken" due to conflicting views, it is stated that there is confusion regarding the meanings of the words of the ritualists (yājñikas). Thus,
because of this conflict of opinions, this inquiry is being conducted.

However, there is no fault in the prescription of another *nigada*. Alternatively, by demonstrating the lack of approval among the ritualists (*yajñika*), it shows that there exists indeed another *nigada* in the case of the *subrahmaṇyā* addressed to Agni. Therefore, there is no flaw in the reasoning.
Because of the lack of connection with those purposes, that which is qualified by them should be understood [as distinct]. (Sūtra 42)

Now, another point is raised: "But surely, even though the qualities are inherent [in the object], it is more logical that the mantra serves the purpose of praise (stuti), because of the direct Vedic statement (śruti). And its being for the purpose of praise does not entail an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārthatva), since a visible purpose is established through the incitement [of the agent] (prarocanā)."

For in the case of the praise of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) by the seller of Soma, there certainly arises an incentive (*prarocanā*), and thus it has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). However, if its own form were accepted as the denoted meaning, since only the one-year-old cow would be enjoined, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated for the denotation of a form that is not itself enjoined. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply untenable. By the very same [reasoning] as before—
Because the meaning has already been established by the instrument [of action].
To this it is replied: this intention is possible for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[Regarding] the one-year-old cow—

It is not possible to imagine the denial of its own nature. Now, regarding the objection that the status of the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow) as being for its own sake would result in an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), he says:
"The postulation of a purpose is [made] for that which is understood as it is.
That is to say, for an object exactly as it is perceived.
The purpose (prayojana) is to be inferred, but the comprehension of the meaning does not occur by virtue of the purpose. Therefore, if the visible [purpose] is absent, let the invisible [purpose] be;

however, since the visible is indeed present here, he says: "And there is persuasion even from the essential nature itself," whereby the postulation of an invisible purpose is entirely avoided, for the persuasion of the seller arises precisely from the comprehension of the essential nature.

[Page 245] Here, an objection is raised: even in the case of praise, there is the incitement to action; however, when the true nature [of the object] is understood, there arises respect due to its weightiness.
By what is it produced?
He answers: It is produced by the state of having no other activity. For when the focus on its own nature is possible, [it does not require another].

The conceptualization of another's purpose acquires its own existence. For, in the view that [the word] conveys its own form (*svarūpa*), words such as *śṛtam* (cooked) would have their own form as their primary referent;

whereas in the case of praise, they would have the praise of another as their primary referent. And this is not tenable, because it is possible for them to have their own meaning as their primary referent.

Therefore, there is a disparity with the previous [case], because the nature of Indra is not apprehended through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But here, by another means of valid cognition, the nature—
Since a word denoting a quality is used for the purpose of conveying the qualified object, modification (ūha) alone is logical.
However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that at the time of the recitation of the nigada, this specific form does not belong to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
If it is argued that even a non-existent thing is superimposed for the sake of praise, and that this is stated by taking into account a future activity,
[the author] shows: "The cognition of the actual nature [of the word] has not been produced as a constituent part of its usage."

It might be argued that this is because the state of being cultivated (*bhāvitva*) is not a constituent part of the ritual application (*prayoga*). If it is further argued that even if it is not a constituent part of the application, the comprehension of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) will serve for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), [the author] refutes this: "The status of being for the sake of praise has already been established."
In that case, it is established that the recitation (*nigada*) expresses what is not connected [to the ritual action].
But is it not the case that a praise (*stuti*) lacking a basis is untenable? To this he says: "And it is indeed tenable."

The praise of even a castrated animal (sāṇḍa) is established here as being appropriate by way of its connection with qualities characterized by the production of cooked food and so forth through the act of impregnation; therefore, the meaning is that there is no modification (avikāra), that is, no substitution (anūha).
|| 17 || Because of the specification of gender, Sarasvatī is not included among those for whom the rule is common, due to her being female. || 45 ||

But surely, since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone is primary here, a restriction [of the application] based on following the gender and number [of the singular suffix] is not tenable, even when the rule is common [to many], just as in the case of the *pāśa* (rope). For example, because the *pāśa* is primary, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*).
[This applies] to the mantra. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) alone is superior here.

To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if that which is distinct from [the sacrifice], extracted by virtue of both indicative mark (liṅga) and direct statement (vacana), were denoted by the word "all" (sarvanāman).

The meaning of this is as follows: since pronouns denote what is proximate, they express exactly that which is proximate; and since what is proximate is endowed with gender and number, it is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in precisely that same form. Thus, because the nominal stem has a qualified object as its domain, its application (*viniyoga*) pertains specifically to the qualified entity. In the case of the *pāśa* (rope)...
Furthermore, it is logical because only the "rope" (pāśa) is denoted.

But even here, by the pronoun— which is employed according to its grammatical number, devoid of case-endings, and denotes whatever is merely proximate— one expresses that which, in its actual state, possesses both number and gender.
This is what is meant:
although the number and gender of a proximate object exist, nevertheless, by means of the mere name alone, devoid of case-endings—

It is the state of being an animal (*paśutva*) alone that is expressed [by the nominal stem], whereas number and gender are denoted by the case-ending. Therefore, since the female sheep (*meṣī*) is also present through that nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is possible for her to be denoted as well. Furthermore, the nominal stem is stronger than gender. Consequently, since it is the meaning of the nominal stem itself that is denoted by this mantra, it is proper to restrict its application according to the gender and number.
This being the case, it is replied: It is true that, just as in the cases of number and gender, that very thing is denoted by the universal name [of the word].
But is it not the case that number is denoted by number, gender, and case-endings, and femininity by the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth?

Nevertheless, in this context, when considering the question "What is it like?", it is the individual instance (*vyakti*) alone that is understood due to its proximity, and not the genus *paśutva* (animal-ness).

If the individual instance is understood by means of the pronoun, it cannot be apprehended as divorced from gender and number, because it is inherently associated with them, just like the rope (*pāśa*) and just like the genus *paśutva*.

Just as the state of being a bond (*pāśatva*) can be expressed by the nominal stem *pāśa* alone, devoid of number and gender, so too is the state of being a sacrificial animal (*paśutva*). Just as the state of being a sacrificial animal is conveyed by the nominal stem *paśu* as the mere individuality, dissociated from gender and number, brought into proximity by the word itself— as in the expression "bring fire for this sacrificial animal" (*prāsmai paśave agniṃ bharata*)— so it is here.
In such a statement, while it is possible to understand [the universal], it is not possible to understand the individual (vyakti) in that same way.
[Objection: Let the mere individual, which serves as the substratum for number and gender, be understood, since it too is present [in proximity].

He refutes [the objection]: "What is this so-called 'mere individual' (vyaktimātratā) that is expressed by the pronoun? The answer is: "Because there is no distinction in proximity, let it be understood as the mere individual present [in the context]."

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: "Since the individual entity (*vyakti*), which is associated with gender and number, has its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) also present [in the cognition], and because there is no difference in the proximity of that essential nature, it is indeed denoted by the pronoun. If the universal (*sāmānya*) is what is proximate, then that [individual] is not [denoted].
The denotation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is merely that which is proximate, because pronouns express what is proximate.
If that which is merely proximate were a universal (*sāmānya*), then it could not be expressed by a pronoun, because a universal lacks actual proximity.

Because of existence. For it is the individual (vyakti) alone that is present by way of actual proximity; the universal (sāmānya), however, is brought into proximity by the word. The expression "if" (*yadīti*) is used even when there is no doubt, serving as a statement of doubt. Therefore, since the mere substratum is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), number and gender by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is impossible not to understand the meaning of the case-ending through their respective divisions.

[This would be so] were it not for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "animal" (*paśu*); however, that does not exist here. Therefore, since the meaning of the entire nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is understood, it is precisely the understanding of the meaning of the nominal stem together with its case-ending that connects [with the verb] by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of proximity (*sannidhāna*). In a sentence, the gender, number, and individual entity (*vyakti*)—being expressed by the word *idam* (this) through the limiting condition of proximity—is the meaning of this sentence. Consequently, it is not [the case that...].

A mere substance endowed with the feminine gender can be understood as being connected within the meaning of the sentence; therefore, the *sārasvatī* [cow] lacks the necessary cause [for the application of the *adhrigu* formula] and is not a constituent part of the word-meaning (*apadārtha*). Since it lacks the cause and is not a constituent part of the word-meaning, the mantra cannot serve its purpose. Consequently, it is indeed correct that the *adhrigu* formula does not apply to the *sārasvatī* because of her femininity. It has been stated that this is an investigation into the practical application (*prayojana*) of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the section on animals in the third book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras.
In the Bhāṣya: "Therefore, the purpose need not be stated.
247] || 18 || "In the case of a sacrificial application (adhikāra), there is modification (vikāra) due to a scriptural statement different from that which is traditionally recited (āmnāta)."
It may be so. || 50 ||

Is this a consideration of sublation (*bādha*) or a consideration of non-attainment (*aprāpti*)? By this, he raises the objection of inconsistency: if the word *girā* is sublated by the word *irā* precisely because it has already been attained, then that is a tenth-book consideration (*dāśamikī cintā*). But if [it is] the word *irā*—

If it is considered that, since there is a *viniyoga* (application), there is no possibility of the word *girā* being obtained at all, then this consideration of obtainment would be appropriate in the third book (*adhyāya*), because it consists in the absence of *viniyoga*. However, both of these [considerations] are not tenable in the context of the definition of *ūha* (modification). He provides the resolution: "True; indeed, the consideration of sublation and obtainment is not relevant to the definition of *ūha*, for that scripture [concerning *ūha*] has as its purpose the [performance of] ritual action."
The reflection that "it is for the purpose of obtaining [the *irā* word]" is appropriate precisely in this context.

Its meaning is as follows: in the place of the word *girā*, the word *irā*—which expresses a quality—is enjoined by this scripture through the rule, "Having made it *aira*, one should sing. It is not, however, for the purpose of obtaining the *irā* word within the *sāman*. And therefore...

When the *yajñāyajñīya* chant is undertaken to perform its function in the form of praise (*stuti*), because it is impossible to perform that function without the word *girā*, the word *girā* is necessarily implied; and since the function is restricted to the word *irā*, it is precisely that which is employed. Thus, by virtue of the functional requirement, the application of the *sāman* joined with the word *irā* is modified; therefore, this reflection is appropriately characterized as *ūha* (modification). [This applies] to the function characterized as praise—

For indeed, one does not obtain the *girā*-pada through the instruction [of the *sāman*], nor is the *girā*-pada taught within the *sāman*; therefore, the *irā*-pada is likewise not taught. Rather, that too is inferred solely from the requirement (*kārya*).
[Objection: But surely, since the *ṛc* is also taught by virtue of the instruction of the *sāman*, its acquisition occurs precisely through that instruction.

Since the instruction regarding the *sāman* is given for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), and since that is impossible without the *ṛk*, the *ṛk* must also be [implicitly] instructed. He refutes this:
"The instruction of the *ṛk* is not possible because of the primacy of the syllables; for the principal does not [depend] upon the subordinate."
It is thus explained. But how is the production of praise accomplished? To this he says: "We shall explain that this will be like the case of the young boy (māṇavaka)."

Just as a student is employed when one employs the initiation ceremony—which is a constituent part of the rite for becoming a teacher—according to the prescribed rule, so too the *ṛc* verse, by means of praise, necessarily implies its own instrumental means, the *sāman*, which functions as a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*); this we shall explain later. Therefore, it is established solely through its function.
It must be considered right here that there is both the attainment (*prāpti*) of the *ṛc* verses and of the word-forms.
Now, even if attainment occurs through functional necessity (*kāryataḥ*), is this not simply a sublation (*bādha*) or a non-attainment (*aprāpti*)? He answers: for it is indeed a non-attainment.
Sublation (*bādha*) has as its objects both instruction (*upadeśa*) and attainment (*prāpti*); however, neither of these two is present here.

For it was considered in the third book that the object of instruction is application (*viniyoga*), whereas sublation occurs in the tenth book regarding what has not been attained. But in this case, there is no instruction.
Nor is there any attainment. Why is there no instruction? He says: "And it has been stated that syllables are not taught for the purpose of praise."
Regarding the objection, "In the instruction of the *irāpada*, how can there be the application of the *girāpada*?", the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: "In this case,
the prima facie view is not that the *sāman* intended as a separate entity from the praise (*stuti*) is to be performed."
