For the *irā* verse is that which is to be enjoined (*kārya*), and there is nothing else here to be enjoined other than the praise (*stuti*). Since the *sāman* is enjoined therein, there is no occasion for the instruction of a specific word-form. Therefore, due to the absence of instruction regarding both the *irā* verse and the *girā* verse, they are equal; and being equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them.
But why is there no injunction for the *stuti*? He says: "For that which is to be accomplished by the *sāman* is called the ritual act (*kārya*), and that is incompatible with the non-*sāman* [text].
Nevertheless, how can there be an option (*vikalpa*)? He says: "It is not possible for even the word *girā* to take away that [function]."

The alternative view is that it is possible. To this, it is replied: True, the praise should indeed be performed by means of the *sāman* alone; nevertheless, the word *girā* is not [to be used] here at all.
It must be so, because of the fixed nature of the word *irā*. But where does this restriction apply? We reply: it applies to the expression of praise.
This restriction—that one should express the quality only by means of the word *irā*—applies to the expression of qualities in the form of praise.
But has it not been stated that this [requirement] is not enjoined in the case of praise (*stuti*)?

The meaning of this is as follows: if it were enjoined that the expression of qualities must be accomplished by means of syllables (*akṣara*), then a restriction regarding specific syllables would be prescribed therein. But this is not the case, because praise is accomplished by means of *sāman* chants.

Thus it has been said. He offers a rebuttal: "True; although it was not enjoined, it is to be observed in the injunction regarding the *irā* word because of its entry into the ritual application (*niyoga*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: although the instruction regarding the *sāman* pertains to its praise (*stuti*), nevertheless, the fact that the syllables are the means (*sādhana*) for that purpose cannot be denied.

And that [status as a means] is respected in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because that too enters into the sphere of the mandatory command (*niyoga*). Therefore, this restriction is made by relying on the status of being a means which is already established by the sense of the matter, just like a vow (*vrata*). For example, in the case of "the milk-vow (*payovrata*) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa," [the vow is enjoined] even though the maintenance of the body is already established by the sense of the matter.

Just as there is a restriction to milk by means of the *śrayaṇa* [offering], so it is here as well; therefore, there is no option. Because the word *irā* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), it alone must be employed, since the application (*viniyoga*) for praise cannot be established without it. Furthermore...
The commentator has been questioned as to where, then, the general rule (sāmānya) will be taught;

he has replied that, just like the number seventeen (sāptadaśya), because the word *girā* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the modified rites (*vikṛti*), it is precisely that which is adopted, and thus it will be applied to the modification. This, however, appears to be incorrect.
Why is it improper? Because of the [sūtra] stating "from the instruction" and "in the modification.
For it has been stated that the "instruction" relied upon refers to a procedure taught as a general rule, and such does not exist here; likewise, it is said "in the modification."

What was stated is also incorrect. To explain why it is incorrect, he says: (Nyāyahr̥daya) "That [application] is not tenable in the case of the *parisāman* and so forth, because the *parisāman* and others lack the status of being a modification (*vikr̥ti*). The claim that 'it will find its place in a modification' is first of all untenable with respect to the *parisāman* and others, precisely because they lack the status of being a modification. However, in another sacrifice that is a modification of the *Soma*, [it applies] by virtue of its function."

1. *Mā*: There is no [substitution of *irā* for *girā*], because the performance of what is not to be done is precluded by the praise resulting from the assistance in the performance; since that very [praise] is obtained there, the rule regarding the word *irā* applies, and thus only the word *irā* [is used]. Therefore, there is no [use of the] word *girā*.
The entry into the gift. To this it is said: this was stated with reference to the intermediate function of the *sāman*, for the function of the *sāman* is indeed praise (*stuti*).

The term "ultimate purpose" (*paramakārya*) refers to the final goal, whereas the "intermediate purpose" (*avāntarakārya*) refers to the purpose of the *parisāman* and so forth; it is with this in mind that it is stated [in the Vārttika] that "it is meaningful in the modified form" (*vikṛtau arthavat*).

And since the intermediate purpose of the praise (*stuti*) is included within the sacrifice (*kratu*), the word *irā* prescribed here does not apply to the function of the *parisāman*; therefore, it is well said that its meaningfulness will reside therein.

The restatement of the objection is: "How is the instruction to be justified? [The response is: That objection which was raised regarding the very *sāman* itself by means of the instruction on *sāman* is the instruction intended here. [Objection: But even so, how can there be the term "modification" (*vikṛti*) in the case of the *parisāman* and others?
The word "transformation" (*vikṛti*) implies a difference [of the syllables].
The intention is that there will be meaningfulness elsewhere.
|| 17 || There would be an instruction of such a nature if there were a difference of syllables due to non-chanting. || 54 ||
But how, then, can there be doubt in this matter? For, since it is impossible for that which is not chanted (*apragīta*) to be a means of praise, it must necessarily be chanted (*pragāṇa*).
The answer is: precisely because of the mention of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
He explains this very point:

the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is that this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix beginning with *cha*— such as in *avikṛta* and so forth— is applied according to the rule "the suffix *cha* is used in the sense of 'composed by' (*mataḥ*) when referring to a hymn (*sūkta*) or a chant (*sāman*)."

In this context, by the rule *vimuktādibhyaṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.89), this suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) with respect to the *sāman*. And that [suffix] occurs when the word *irā* is unmodified. Therefore, this word *irāpada* is indeed unmodified. For if it were used in a modified form, then a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) corresponding to that modification would occur. If there were a modification, the form of the word would be *ā-irā*; however, that [form] occurs among words such as *vimukta*.

If it were not recited, then by the rule *matupcha*, there would have to be the suffix *cha* alone; however, that [suffix] does not exist here. Therefore, the word *irā* should be employed in its unmodified form. But what, then, is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) here?

The questioner’s intention is this: this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), and the singing in the form of *gāna* is merely restated as something already established. The answer is: the meaning is that the singing must be performed using the word *irā*, and this suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is used here; for when there is a choice between a term defined by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*) and one defined by a general characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the former prevails.
Because only that which is explicitly stated [in the rule] is to be understood.
Now, one might object: since it is not sung (*apragīta*), a connection—specifically a connection with singing (*gānayoga*)—is simply impossible. He provides the following rebuttal:

"Their connection is possible, because they perform that function"—this is the intended meaning: since they perform the function of the *sāman*, the *sāman* possesses a relationship with them; therefore, this instruction regarding the unchanted [text] is understood through the instruction ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

Even for the proponent of the established conclusion (*rāddhāntavādin*), the fact that it is merely the essential form (*svarūpa*) being taught is not understood from the use of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) alone.
This is the meaning [on p. 250]:

This is not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formed from the sense of "liberated" (*vimukta*) and so forth; rather, it means "a modification thereof" (*tasya vikāraḥ*). We shall explain how this is so later on.

In this case, regarding the secondary derivative denoting a modification, the teaching of the mere essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*) is not understood. By rejecting the singing [of the *gāna*], the teaching of the mere essential form is not understood. What is the intention?
The intention of one who asks this is as follows: "Let it be a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) denoting a modification;
nevertheless, a modification in the form of non-chanting (*apragāṇa*) will be prescribed.
The answer is: for if a modification were prescribed, the prescription of the original form would be untenable, because the modification itself constitutes the original form.
Furthermore, because there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of enjoining [both].
To the objection that "let there then be the injunction of the modification alone," he replies:
"And an injunction of the modification alone is not tenable when the essential form [of the object] has not been enjoined."
Because that which is without a basis is untenable.

Nor should it be argued that there will be an injunction regarding the essential form (*svarūpa-vidhi*) based on the material cause (*aupādānika*), such that the modification of the word *irā* would not be possible if the word *irā* were not taught; for the implication of the word *irā* through the sense of the matter (*artha*) need not be resorted to, since the injunction regarding the essential form—which presents itself first—is sufficient.

Because the modification, which is the nature of the song, can be understood as a restatement of what is already established by the sense; therefore, this is a restatement of the modification. Only its specific form, however, is being enjoined.
But by what is it established such that it is restated? Precisely by the requirement of the ritual action.

For that which is unmodified cannot perform the function of the *sāman*. Indeed, the function prescribed is the *īrā* word. And how can that become the function of the *sāman* unless it becomes the function of the syllables accompanied by chanting? Therefore, chanting is merely restated because it is already established by virtue of its function.

But why is this [the suffix -mat] considered a *taddhita* derivative that does not involve a modification of the base? To this he says: "Because of its connection with the specific wording, one should not suspect a *taddhita* derivative in another sense.
[As it is said: "Not 'girā-girā'."

From the context of the word "brūyāt" (he should say), it is understood that the act of uttering speech is intended. Therefore, because of its connection with the word "vacana" (utterance), this is not a *taddhita* derivative such as "vimukta" and so forth; for that *taddhita* suffix applies specifically to the subject of *sāman*. Nor is the mere utterance of the word "irā" the *sāman*; rather, it is a constituent part of the *sāman*. And that utterance which consists of song is of the nature of a modification of sound (*śabda-vikāra*).
The word *kam* is indeed a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expressing a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, this is merely a restatement of a modification.

Since this is an instruction regarding the mere essential form (*svarūpa*) and not something well-known as a melody (*gīti*), there is no fault in the production of the derivative suffix from the unmodified [form]. On the contrary, the production of the derivative suffix from a modified form would indeed be a fault, because a modification cannot exist in that which is already modified.

Now, why is there not an injunction of a qualified [element], that is, why is the word *irā* not enjoined as qualified by a modification of form that is not intended for chanting? The answer is: because both the suffix and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would have to be understood as being simultaneously connected [to the base].

When there is an injunction regarding an effect for something—just as in the case of an action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka)—then that [thing] has an injunction regarding some effect, as in the injunctive statement concerning qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*): "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*). And in that case, when a mutual connection is understood, there is an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*), as in the case of "with Soma."
[This refers to] the sacrificial act delimited by that which serves as its instrument. And here, in the function of praise (*stuti*), there is the injunction of the word *irā*.

Nor is "modification" (*vikāra*) a qualifier [of the word itself]; rather, it is the word's status as a qualifier with respect to the modification. Therefore, in the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), [the rule applies].

In cases where the meaning of the suffix is primary, there is no prescription of the base-meaning as qualified by the suffix-meaning, because the existence [of the base] as qualified by the qualifier is not understood. Furthermore, simultaneous prescription is not tenable, as it is in the case of action and its factors (*kāraka*); for modifications (*vikāra*) depend upon the attainment of the base, and suffixes such as *ṇvul* (denoting the agent) which indicate the cause or agent depend upon the attainment of the action. When [the action] has been attained...
The prescription of a modification dependent upon that [base] occurs as a qualifier only when the base is already established, not when it is unestablished.

Likewise, when the action is already established, suffixes such as *ṇvul* and others would apply to the agent and so forth as qualifiers of the non-action; otherwise they would not. Since the meaning of the suffix itself is primary, there is no prescription of a qualified [entity]. Therefore, the prescription of the base alone is logical, and not [the other].
Regarding the "prescription of a specific term":

as for the purpose stated by the author of the Bhāṣya— that either *praprapadam* or *praprīpadam* should be employed according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while according to the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) only *praprīpadam* should be used— that has already been demonstrated in the preceding section.
It occurs to me; the sense is that this is consistent with reality here.
He provides the justification: "As for [the objection] that it applies to both loci, there is no fault."
Why, then, has another purpose been stated, setting aside the word *iti*? To this he says: "How so?
The answer is: "That..."
Regarding the instruction "yam," there is no doubt that it is not unintonated;

because it is explicitly taught, it is not optional. Furthermore, since singing is prescribed for "āī rācādākṣāsāi," there is no doubt that it is not unintonated. However, in the case of "praprapade," both of these [objections] must be refuted.
This, then, is the purpose of the two sections.
Thus ends [the commentary] on the ninth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the *Pañcikā* composed by the venerable Great Mahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra.
First Pāda [p.
252]. Second Pāda of the Ninth Adhyāya.
1. Some [maintain] that the *sāmans* are mantras, because of both traditional recollection and instruction.

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having deliberated whether the *sāman* is a mantra-text qualified by melody or merely the melody itself, begins another section (*varṇaka*). This concerns whether the *ūha-sāmans* are eternal or non-eternal. To the question of why another section is commenced even though [the matter] has already been discussed there, he says: "In this case, because it involves a different subject matter along with the deliberation of the second chapter..."

The description [of this] is for the purpose of stating that there is no tautology with the seventh chapter; here, however, the resolution is intended solely by way of what follows. Since the prima facie and final positions here are indeed not to be resolved [in this context], it is described as a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: since in this [section], the ninth, the avoidance of redundancy is achieved solely by the intention to state a subsequent point (*uttaravivakṣayā*), it is not appropriate here to construct a formal arrangement of prima facie and final positions (*pūrvottarapakṣaracanā*) for that very avoidance. Nor can it be maintained that those two [points] are simply unavoidable, such that one could proceed to describe them as a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇāntara*), because they have already been directly addressed by the author of the Sūtras. Therefore, another exposition (*varṇakāntara*) has been composed to avoid this defect.

But why is the resolution here given specifically with the intention of providing a further answer, when the redundancy has already been avoided in another way by means of the second chapter? For in the second chapter, even though the mantra-text is set to melody, the threefold nature of the mantra is established; and for that purpose it was stated that "the designation *sāman* applies to the melodies. Therefore, there is no need for this [present argument] here, as the point is simply that the *sāman* is the melody itself.

To this he replies: The description of a different subject matter along with the second [chapter] is for the purpose of avoiding redundancy with the discussion in the seventh chapter; as for the redundancy that exists with the discussion in the seventh chapter, its resolution is intended precisely by what is about to be stated hereafter.

Now, one might object that this inquiry into the eternal and the non-eternal is irrelevant here; to this he says: "And this section is introductory (aupoddhātika) for the sake of the subsequent deliberation.
If the *ūha* is eternal, then the nature of the *ūha-sāman* [is established] for the *Aukthikya*.

The collection of sūtras concerning *ūha* (modification) composed by Jaimini need not have been commenced; or, even if it were commenced, it should not have been undertaken as a means toward a ritual purpose (*kāryaupayikatayā*) for the sake of describing its essential nature—that is, for stating its nature as it actually exists—rather than as something serving a functional role. However, if *ūha* is indeed something produced [by human intellect], then *ūha* must be performed according to the rules and according to the specific words [of the Veda]; thus, that [work] is directed toward that end.
What should be undertaken?
1. Out of fear of faults;
2. For the sake of establishing the threefold nature.

[Page 253] But surely there is no room for modification even in the case of what is impermanent, since that too has been recited; to this he says: "And modification is according to that, according to logic."

The sense is that since there is even the possibility of confusion— thinking that what has been recited should be abandoned or that what has not been recited should be recited— one must not be absolutely dependent on the oral tradition (*pāṭha*).
In this regard, having observed among the *Chandogas* a treatment and designation as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*), just like their own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), [the author] intends to...

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position arises from the confusion regarding the instruction on *ūha*—specifically, the delusion that this instruction concerns something non-eternal (*anitya*). For that which is intended to be performed (*cikīrṣita*) is desired to be done, and what is desired is indeed non-eternal; for if the non-eternal were contrary to reason (*nyāyāpetatva*), it would follow that it is undesired. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: some, even though they know the *aukthikya*, out of laziness toward the *sāmohana*... others—

Those who do not know the *Aukthikya* recite the *Sāman* incorrectly; others, however, being unable to correct it due to their lack of knowledge of the *Aukthikya* treatise, also recite it incorrectly.

This lack of knowledge of the *Aukthikya* treatise arises from laziness or from an inability to serve a teacher, pertaining to the tasks of grasping and retaining [the text]. Thus, this manner of recitation is the root of the practice that is equivalent to the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*).

The claim that "this delusion regarding the necessity [of *ūha*] arises because the Chāndogas recite it as if it were obligatory" is, on the contrary, demonstrated by the instruction itself to show that *ūha* is something to be performed;

for it explicitly states that it is intended to be done. Since *ūha* is thus non-obligatory (*anitya*), he says: "Therefore, one should not apply what is devoid of logical justification. Because there is scope for such reasoning, the principle (*nyāya*) is now considered.
Or action is characterized by injunction.
In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya states that [the word] functions by way of "implication" (ākṣepa). But what is this implication? The answer is:
first, the use of the accusative case in the expression “rathantaram” has been presented; what, then, is the intention behind that?
The answer is: when a noun denotes the meaning of a verb, the second case (accusative) that is heard does not [denote] the grammatical factor (kāraka) known as the object (karman).

The status of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) is negated by the presentation of names ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) as primary objects (*karman*), because it is the action itself that is what is desired;

just as in the sentence "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*), there is no obstruction to the rice being the most desired, for it is the cooking itself that is indicated as the primary element. It is the same here, and thus the second case is introduced in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, as for what was said—that because it is employed at a time when there is no ritual action (*akarmakāla*), the *sāman* is the primary action—that is considered incorrect. How so?
The response is: if the Mīmāṃsakas claim that the *ṛc* is primary, then [the *sāman*] must be for the sake of the meaning—
1. Not to be recited according to R;
2. Recited according to R;
3. Impossibility of space according to A.
4. They say that the *sāman* is merely a subordinate quality (*guṇabhūta*) of the *ṛc* verse that is occupied with being chanted (*dhānavyāpṛtā*).

The meaning of this is as follows: since the *sāman* has already been employed during non-ritual time, it would not be employed again in the ritual; thus, a refutation arises against the view that it is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarman*), and this [refutation] is not damaging. Furthermore, even those who consider the *sāman* to be a preparatory act [must admit that it depends on] the *ṛc*, which performs the expression of the meaning.

They maintain that it is a preparatory act (*saṃskāraka*). In that case, if the expression of meaning by means of a refined [verse] (*saṃskṛtā*) during non-performance time were to serve the purpose of the sacrifice, then, since there would be no further function for the verse during the actual performance of the sacrifice, the refinement of the *ṛc* would not be performed. Furthermore, the expression of meaning during non-performance time is of no use either for praise (*stuti*) or for recollection (*smṛti*). He states how it is of no use: "As for praise, first of all—"

The *sāman* is indeed enjoined at the time of the ritual action by such injunctions as "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" and so forth, just like the *prayāja* offerings. Furthermore, the *smṛti* (the mental recollection of the text) also follows from the context at the time of the ritual action, because it is precisely at the time of the ritual that the *smṛti* is required; for it is not possible to perform an action without remembering it. Therefore, at the time of the ritual, for the sake of praise or for the sake of *smṛti*, the *sāman* is [repeated] again in order to accomplish the expression of the meaning.

The application [of the *ṛc*] is established; for when the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *ṛc* as qualified by the expression of its meaning is accepted, there is no fault whatsoever. If this is so, even those who do not desire the primacy of the *ṛc* assert an invisible refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*), by which it would not be employed again in the sacrifice (*kratu*). If the study [of the Veda] were at a time other than that of ritual action, it would not be [accomplished] through praise or through traditional recollection (*smṛti*).
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the purpose of studying at a time when there is no ritual action?
the answer is: let its purpose be either visible (dṛṣṭa) or invisible (adṛṣṭa).

What is the use of this investigation into the purpose? It is established that [the word] is subordinate at the time of the ritual action (*karmakāla*), because its purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) at that time; for that which is not manifested cannot be expressive.
To this it is replied: the proponent of this section (adhikaraṇa) is ignorant of the subject matter. How so? The answer is:
for here too, the discussion regarding the relationship of subordinate and principal is not undertaken by accepting that [the word] has the status of an object (karman).
Regarding the song (*gīti*) and its syllables (*akṣara*), what then? This inquiry intends only to consider the priority [of one over the other].
Its meaning is as follows:
having taken up the song as a constituent part of the ritual action (*karma-aṅga*), is it that the syllables are primary and the song is subordinate, or is it the reverse?

This is the inquiry: however, based on the nature of the *sāman* produced through Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), it is considered as follows—is this [the *sāman*] always for the purpose of manifesting the syllables, because it consists in the manifestation of syllables within the chant, like threshing and other such acts which exist for the sake of that which is being threshed;
or rather, is it always primary in itself, like the wearing of gold and other such acts which are connected with unintended objects?

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since even the apprehension of the syllables serves a purpose in the ritual action, it cannot be said that it is not desired; thus, the discussion proceeds on the premise that "this [recitation] is indeed a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*). However, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) objects: "True—"
1. And from that which is conditioned (saṃskṛta);
2. by means of direct audition (śruti).
By this reasoning, the quality of being subordinate belongs to the *sāman*.

Furthermore, regarding that study which takes place at the time of the ritual performance, the mention [of the *sāman*] therein serves no purpose for either praise (*stuti*) or recollection (*smṛti*), because at that time it is not intended to be performed; for this reason, [the *sāman*] exists in the form of a manifestation.

Because the *saṃskāra* (preparatory rite) serves no purpose, the singing must have human benefit (*puruṣārtha*) as its goal. If the literal meaning of the syllables were accepted, then for the sake of accomplishing that [literal meaning], an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated. And once that is postulated, even at the time of the ritual action, the Sāman would have only a visible purpose. Why? He says:
"For it is not possible to assume a relationship of subordinate and principal [between the syllables and the singing] as one can in the case of threshing and other such rites."
Otherwise,

if no function is postulated for the syllables, then it would be impossible to conceive of the syllables as being primary and the *sāman* as being subordinate, just as in the case of threshing and other such rites. For as long as even their function pertaining to the rice-grains has not been postulated, [the relationship cannot be established].

It cannot be a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva). For, when an effect must be postulated there, since the expression would be useless for external application, an entirely unseen (adṛṣṭa) effect must be postulated;
and once that has been postulated, it remains the same effect even in internal application because there is no difference [between the two cases].
This being the case, by the maxim of "grinding what has already been ground," there is no further application of the *sāman*.

Just as it is impossible to grind what has already been ground, so too is it impossible to perform a refinement upon that which has already been refined; thus, there is no further application. And yet, this [refinement] pertains to the *ṛc*.

"We declare that ritual action itself is the *ṛc* of the *sāman*. But even if the *sāman* is primary, why is it employed both externally and in ritual action? [The answer follows: The *ṛc* is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the *sāman*, and ritual action is the foundation of the *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* has its foundation in ritual action. Just as one who desires a foundation resorts to a foundation, so too does the *sāman* resort to ritual action for its foundation. Thus, the *sāman* is established in ritual action. Furthermore, the *sāman* is the essence (*ātman*) of the *ṛc*, and ritual action is the essence of the *sāman*. Therefore, the *sāman* has its essence in ritual action. Just as one who desires an essence resorts to an essence, so too does the *sāman* resort to ritual action for its essence. Thus, the *sāman* is established in ritual action. Moreover, the *ṛc* is the body (*śarīra*) of the *sāman*, and ritual action is the body of the *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* has its body in ritual action. Just as one who desires a body resorts to a body, so too does the *sāman* resort to ritual action for its body. Thus, the *sāman* is established in ritual action. Furthermore, the *ṛc* is the breath (*prāṇa*) of the *sāman*, and ritual action is the breath of the *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* has its breath in ritual action. Just as one who desires breath resorts to breath, so too does the *sāman* resort to ritual action for its breath. Thus, the *sāman* is established in ritual action. Finally, the *ṛc* is the light (*jyotis*) of the *sāman*, and ritual action is the light of the *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* has its light in ritual action. Just as one who desires light resorts to light, so too does the *sāman* resort to ritual action for its light. Thus, the *sāman* is established in ritual action. For this reason, we declare that ritual action itself is the *ṛc* of the *sāman*. Indeed, although the *sāman* is primary, it is for these reasons that it is employed externally and in ritual action. This is the answer.

There is no fault, because there is a different governing context (*adhikāra*). First, the performance [of the *bahiṣpavamāna*] is for the sake of establishing a different governing context; since its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is understood through another scriptural statement—just like the *prayāja* offerings—it is performed as an action that provides a perceptible benefit (*śrutopakāra*). Thus, both [the fact of being a subsidiary and providing a perceptible benefit] are not contradictory.
If the *sāman* is primary, how then is there a connection with another *ṛc*, such as "the *rathantara* on the *kavatī*s"? He asks: "What fault do you perceive here?
The answer is: this very one.
The defect consists in the connection with another object.

Why is this a defect? He says: for the impressions (saṃskāras) are recognized exactly as they were produced, not as associated with a different object, just as the cooking and so forth [are not perceived] in the case of the gold pieces (kṛṣṇalas).

The meaning of this is as follows: even one who maintains that the *sāman* is a primary action (*pradhānakarman*) still accepts, by way of its visible form, that the *sāman* serves to refine the *ṛc*. However, it is said that it does not have the status of being for the sake of refinement (*saṃskārārthatā*). And therefore, regarding another *ṛc*—

Even when there is a connection, there is an absence of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), as in the case of the cooking of *kṛṣṇala* grains. Those impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are perceived in a particular substance are recognized as belonging to that very substance, not to another object. If there is no recognition of another object, how then can there be an injunction for cooking in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*, since even the injunction is not possible in the absence of the essential nature of the primary ritual element?
The meaning is "it falls.
The answer is: we shall explain this in the tenth [chapter], how that [falling] occurs with its specific method in the tenth.

1. We shall explain that [the term] is not intended to be expressed [in this context]. Furthermore, the status of being denoted by the word "cooking" (śrapaṇa) applies even to the *kṛṣṇala* seeds, because cooking is the archetypal (*prākṛta*) action.

The cooking does not take place because, due to the absence of the effect, there is no recognition [of the action]. This objection applies to both positions. To this it is replied: It is appropriate that in that case (the *kṛṣṇala* oblation) there be the non-actualization of the primary purpose; here, however, the chanting (*gīti*) is indeed actualized even without the *ṛc* verse. The meaning of this is: it is appropriate in that case, regarding the *kṛṣṇalas*.

There is no recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*) of the primary object, because the quality produced by cooking (*pākaja-guṇa*) is not established in the *kṛṣṇala* grains; it is held that since the effect is absent, there is no recognition of the original cooking. Here, however, even when the chant (*gīti*) is being accomplished through a different verse (*ṛc*), recognition certainly exists; therefore, "this is that very same chant. And since the *sāman* is merely the chant, there is no fault. Furthermore, there is a connection with a different verse.

It has already been stated that, as in the case of the *pākayajña*, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even when there is a different substance. This being the position reached, it is replied: the *sāman* is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Why? Because it cannot be said that the expression of the meaning of the *ṛk*-syllables is not useful for the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*). For if the expression of the meaning were [the purpose], then the accomplishment of the injunction—

If it were merely for the sake of utility (*aupayika*), then there would be no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the syllables for that purpose; however, it is indeed useful, because its authority is stated to consist in that alone.

Furthermore, the authority of mantras was also stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*. And by the very nature of things, the manifestation of syllables is understood as the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of those syllables. Now, he begins the refutation of the reason for the objection—namely, that which...

The second [type] is seen in the application of *sāman* chants, such as "one should make the *rathantara* the *pṛṣṭha*," and so forth; and in non-injunctive (*apraiṣa*) expressions, both worldly and Vedic, such as "sing of the moon," and so forth. Among these, first, the statement "one should make the *rathantara* the *pṛṣṭha*" is appropriate when the *sāman* is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Otherwise, the connection with the *pṛṣṭha* would not be possible.

That [the former view] would not be the case is shown in the Bhāṣya. By the word *pṛṣṭha*, a specific ritual action in the form of a hymn of praise (*stuti*) is expressed. If the word *rathantara* were also denotative of the primary time and the primary action, then—since it would be impossible for the primary action to be accomplished by another action—there could be no connection with the *rathantara* and so forth. However, if it is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), then because of the subordinate elements (*guṇa*)...

The status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is indeed manifest through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of syllables capable of being held [in memory], as in the case of the *abhikramaṇa* in the *prayāja* oblation.
However, as for the injunction "one sings the *candra-sāman*," the expression of meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita*) due to the force of its application (*viniyoga*).

For in a directive (*praiṣa*), a person is enjoined solely for the purpose of employing the *sāman*; thus, because the directive's application is subordinate to the employment of the *sāman*, the expression of meaning occurs only by virtue of that [application].

Therefore, the use of the accusative case is intended not as a primary object, but as a secondary indication; it is a modification, just as in the expression "he threshes the fermenting agent" (*kiṇvam avahanti*),
where the items are already established as the subject matter.
3. It has been stated that it is so.
4. It is adventitious (aupādhika).

In the expression "they press," although the derivative form *kiṇva* (ferment) exists, it is not intended to be expressed; likewise here too, there is the denotation of the meaning. Nor can it be said that the intrinsic nature [of the word] is lost on this account, because the meaning—characterized by its predominance through the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*)—is cognizable through other means of knowledge. As for cases in common usage such as "Sing the Rathantara on the *māṇaka*," there the designation of the primary [object] occurs through an examination of the act of singing.

There is no fault in this, because it is intended to demonstrate that the boy possesses the quality of being a singer (*gātṛtva*). The command (*praiṣa*) is issued precisely to one who is undergoing examination. Furthermore, since the actual expression of meaning is not intended there, the use of the accusative case is entirely appropriate. Therefore, even in this worldly command, because its purpose is directed elsewhere, it does not subvert the inherent nature of the *sāman*s. As for the external study, that refers to the recitation of those *sāman*s which are not subject to modification (*anūhya*).
It is indeed brought about by an injunction. And although that injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) has a human purpose, it does not have an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose;

for according to the principle, its visible purpose is indeed the comprehension of ritual action (*karmāvabodhana*). In that regard, the study of syllables is for the sake of comprehending their meaning, whereas the study of the *gīti* (melodic chant) is for the sake of practicing its own form. For a *sāman* that has not been practiced cannot be employed in a ritual. As for the restatements of what is to be inferred (*ūhya*), however—

Because the attainment [of the result] and its logical necessity are understood through a difficult juncture, there is no separate qualification for practice that is not devoid of the relationship between disciple and teacher and which has only a visible purpose;
this is the meaning— though for those [mantras] to be inferred (*ūhya*), even if it is not devoid [of such a relationship].

The relationship between disciple and teacher is likewise such that repetition has a visible purpose. For that attainment which is based on verbal instruction and that which is based on logical reasoning is understood through difficulty. Therefore, there is repetition of the *sāmans* inferred by one who knows both logic and the verbal injunctions. Consequently, even in that case, although there is repeated performance at the time of the ritual action, there is no assumption of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, even as a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*), [it serves a visible purpose].
The external application is indeed appropriate; therefore, it is established that the *sāman* is subordinate (*gauṇa*).

Now, one might object: "In this way, even when a refinement (*saṃskāra*) has been performed for the sake of repetition (*abhyāsa*), a further refinement would not be tenable. To this he says: "The logic of grinding what is already ground (*piṣṭapeṣaṇanyāya*) is avoided by means of a different application (*viniyogāntara*) and by repetition."

Furthermore, there is a repetition at the time of the ritual action because no other application for the rite exists, and [the repetition] occurs externally for the sake of practicing the performance. This has been stated as being "due to not remaining for that long" and "because it is possible. If the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced during the external performance persists until the time of the ritual action—
In that case, there would be no further application toward the internal action, or it would be impossible; yet neither of these two [consequences] exists.
|| 3 || It should apply to the triplet of verses (tṛca), because of the connection with the direct scriptural statement (śruti). || 14 ||
But how can the number heard in connection with the *ṛc*s— which are the primary elements— be understood as being for the sake of the *sāman*,
given that the number heard in connection with the *graha* (which is the primary element) is not for the sake of the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*),
and likewise the number three, though heard in connection with the primary *ṛc*s, is not for the sake of the *sāman*?
1. It is not reasonable to suspect that which is independent.
The answer: Otherwise, the injunction would be untenable;
for if number were not taught as a means (*sādhana*) when the *sāman* has ceased, then there could be no injunction at all. Therefore, it possesses the status of being a means to the purpose.

Relying upon the *ṛcs*, the prescription of a number was raised in relation to the *sāman*. To this he says: "For a number heard in respect to *ṛcs* that do not function as a means [of chanting] cannot be restricted.
[Objection: But what is the use of such a restriction? To this he replies:
And if it were not restricted [to the Sāmans], it would not be connected with the ritual action;

for in the Smṛti, when expressed by a word denoting a quality, there is the view that it applies to the Sāmans alone. Now, one might raise the objection of the opponent’s view: "Let it be as in the case of the singularity of the cup (grahaikatva), even though it is not connected with the ritual action"—thus he says, "let it be."
He states the objection: even if there is cognition, the lack of connection (ananvitatā) follows;
just as oneness, though unconnected to the effect, is nonetheless cognized.
In that case, the number three would not be applicable; for even when the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is performed upon many [stalks], it is nonetheless performed upon each single one.

However, in the case of the *sāman*, under the view that it is completed in each individual instance, there is no connection with the number three at all. To explain this very intention, he first raises an objection: "But when [the meaning] is understood through a compound, who can prevent its syntactic connection (*anvaya*), since this is a compound word?"

Regarding the word *tṛca*: the connection of the number three with the *ṛc* verses is indeed understood. Furthermore, the connection of the cup (*graha*) with the number one arises from its association with a case-ending; just as in the expression "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), the number one is related to the cup by virtue of the grammatical ending.

It is understood. Likewise, the number three is also connected to the *ṛc* through the compound. He refutes this: "In that case, it is appropriate, for that [cup] is the subject of predication and does not depend on a previously established function.
The meaning of this is: mere connection with the cup does not constitute being the correlate of the cognition.

Rather, it is by virtue of being connected to the state of being related to the cleansing (*sammārjana*). And in that case, there exists a connection with the singular number even for the cup (*graha*) which is related to the cleansing; because in the injunction of the cleansing, the cup is the object being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*), and because the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is connected to each individual object being pointed out. If the function of the cleansing were already established [elsewhere], then this instruction would depend on it as residing in multiple cups.

In that case, since there is no connection with the cleansing (*sammārjana*) for each [individual] separately, the singularity perceived [in the word *ekam*] would be unconnected [to the action]. Furthermore, this instruction is not based on an established function of the cleansing that resides in multiple [objects]; rather, this application (*viniyoga*) depends upon a function that has already been established.

The meaning of this is as follows: It is understood that praise (*stuti*) is the function of the *sāman*; furthermore, it is a single *ṛc* verse alone—not a collection of verses—that performs the praise characterized by the expression of qualities. Consequently, by implication, the cessation of the *sāman*—which serves as the means for the praise—is restricted to each individual [verse] as its sole function. Moreover, the number associated with such an *ṛc* is understood through the compound (*samāsa*). Nor is there any established [usage] of the *ṛc* [in this regard].

This application of the number three is in relation to the ritual action; it is a connection with the number three. Consequently, even if [the number] is not perceived [as such], there is a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvitatva*).
He states this: "If the number is not connected with the ritual action, how can we perceive its connection when it is unconnected?
For a number that is being enjoined must be connected with the ritual action. Even though each individual *ṛc* [verse] possesses praise—

And that being the case, since it is the means [of praise], the word *sāman* in the injunction "one should praise with the *sāman*" is understood as having the purpose of indicating the constituent parts (*avayava*) of the *sāman*, by virtue of the application of the number three. If, however, this were not accepted, then there would be no connection with the number three. This is the subject-matter (*uddeśa*).

And thus, this was stated by relying on the unity that is conveyed by words. Furthermore, since the expression of the case-ending alone is not the sole purpose there, the inseparable connection with number has been demonstrated.

The meaning of this is as follows: for that which a word aims at is the word's meaning. In the case of the injunction "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), the accusative case ending does not aim at singularity, but rather at the status of being an object (*karmatva*);

therefore, the connection with singularity is unintended (*avivakṣita*) and merely incidental (*nāntarīyaka*). However, in the present case, because there is no such basis, it is not the word's meaning.
[In other cases] one attains [the meaning];

however, here, since there is no other cause for the employment of the word *tri*, the intended meaning is simply the connection with the number three. And since that [connection] is not syntactically integrated (*ananvita*), it would be something not expressed by the word itself, according to the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāyin*).
Regarding the word *tvāt*: if it were not the meaning of the word [itself], there would be a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "three" caused by negligence (*pramāda*);

and since negligence resides in a person, this would result in the Veda being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), which entails the collapse of its established authority (*prāmāṇya*). Therefore, even though the *ṛcs* possess primacy, their status as a means [to the sacrifice] must be described as characterized by their meaning, in accordance with the number [of verses]. And this has been shown.

By asserting that even those things which are subordinate possess the capacity to accomplish the purpose, and that even the primary element (the *graha* and so forth) indeed accomplishes the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*),
he says this: "Therefore, without abandoning the restriction regarding number, the predominance of the *ṛc*s must be admitted."

One must accept that three *ṛc* verses are to be consecrated by means of a single *sāman*. Since this is the case, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering the sentence of praise to be manifested by the constituent parts of the *sāman*, believes there is no contradiction in using the word "rathantara" to indicate the constituent part of the rathantara by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the statement, "The rathantara becomes the *pṛṣṭha*. Thus, what is connected to the verb is accepted as the object to be enjoined.

The statement "the *sāman* is performed upon a triplet (*tṛca*)" indicates that the number three is taught specifically with reference to the performance of the *sāman*. In the Siddhānta (the established conclusion), however, the number would have to be taught with reference to the praise (*stuti*), and the word "*sāman*" would have to be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For in the Siddhānta, the repetition of the *sāman* must be indicated by the word "*sāman*"; thus, [the literal sense] is not maintained.
This being the case, it is replied: this is not tenable—that the effect of the number three is merely the production of the *sāman*.
Why? Because the determination of an effect must be preceded by an explicit instruction. Even if that were so, nevertheless...

To the question of why the accomplishment of the *sāman* does not constitute the primary effect, he says: "This instruction is the primary one, namely, 'the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*,' and 'the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*.
By the word 'primary' (*mukhya*), the first to be produced is meant; for praise (*stuti*) belongs to the *sāman*."

It must be explained that the ritual purpose is understood only afterwards, [namely] that "one *sāman* is performed upon a *tṛca*. Even if it were primary, he asks: "What then?"—[the answer is: for the most part, the praise is completed for each verse;
generally, there is a statement of the qualities of a single *ṛc*.

[The Sāman] performs [the function], not the *ṛk* or the *sāma* collectively. The inclusion of the term "mostly" (*prāya*) is intended to show that in some cases the praise is completed by half [a verse], while in others it is completed by a quarter.

Even if this be so, he asks: "What follows from this?"—and replies: "This being the case, once it is understood that the *sāman* is the means for the hymn of praise (*stotra*), one cannot assume on the basis of the instruction that the function belongs to a single constituent part."
The meaning of this is as follows:
if the praise is completed with respect to each [verse] individually and the singing is performed by joining them together, then the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*;
[this is indicated] by the word *tṛca*.

The word *rathantara*, having indicated by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) its constituent part which "is," should be applied to the hymn designated as the *pṛṣṭha*. Nor can this be accomplished through direct injunction (*upadeśa*), because it is understood from that [injunction] that the function of the *sāman* belongs to the hymn of praise (*stuti*), and because the number three [of verses] is preceded by that [function].
Regarding how this instruction is preceded by that [the Sāman], he says: "And this instruction—'one Sāman is performed on a triplet of verses' (ekaṃ sāma tṛce kriyate)—is dependent upon an effect.
Even for one who maintains that the number three is intended merely for the accomplishment of the Sāman, [he must admit] that of the Sāman...

This instruction regarding the number three must be explained as being understood through the nature of the task (*kārya*), because that which is understood through other means of knowledge serves as the subordinate element (*śeṣin*).

Now, one might object: "Even if this restriction to the number three is preceded by that [understanding], nevertheless, since it lacks a subject matter (*nirviṣaya*), it is better to resort to a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the *rathantara* being a constituent part. To this, he says: "But has it not been stated that this restriction is without a subject matter?"

Because the *ṛc* is not enjoined as a means [to the praise]. If the *ṛc* were enjoined as a means toward the praise, then the number three, which rests upon it, would be prescribed for the praise. But this is not the case. He refutes [the objection]:

To this it is replied: But surely you, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), have also proposed that it is precisely the meaning (*artha*)—when the *sāman* is accomplished—that constitutes the status of the *ṛc* as a means (*sādhanabhāva*), and that the restriction to the number three is the cause; for me, too, this very same point shall hold true.

Even in the case of praise (*stuti*), there is indeed such a deliberation regarding its status as a means (*sādhanatva*). If this is so, then what is the distinction of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*)?
To this he says: "But this is the distinction: the postulation of the effect (*kārya-kalpanā*) is made in accordance with the direct instruction (*upadeśa*). [For example:
"The *rathantara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*."

In accordance with that instruction, it is concluded that the praise must be applied to the *sāman* as a whole; and the fact that the capacity to accomplish the purpose is established through such praise has been stated by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*). He asks:
"But where does this capacity to accomplish the purpose reside?"
The answer is: we say it is for the purpose of praise (stuti).

For in the context of praise, the restriction regarding the *sāman* and the restriction regarding the *stotra* are prescribed. The restriction regarding the *sāman* is found in passages such as "the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*," and so forth; the restriction regarding the *ṛc* is found in the case of the *kavatī* verses.

Regarding the phrase "the Rathantara": the rule for the stotra is stated as "the Ārbhava Pavamāna is fifteen-fold. In that context, since it might otherwise be filled by any means whatsoever due to a lack of restriction, this restrictive statement is made for that purpose; thus, it is established that "one *sāman* is performed on a triplet" (*tṛca*) means singing it verse by verse (*pratyṛcam*).

To the objection that the word *sāman* must signify repetition because "the *sāman* is performed," and that the connection of the word *tri-* with praise is not heard [in the text], he says: Since the injunctions regarding the restriction of the ritual action are established in their own sense by following the primary instruction (*mukhyopadeśa*),
there is no fault in either metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or the connection between the meanings of the words.

It was stated previously that regarding those injunctions and regulations concerning ritual action (*kārya*), their meaning must be described in accordance with the primary teaching (*mukhyopadeśa*). Therefore, neither metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) nor connection with another word is a fault. The purpose has thus been explained with an illustrative example.
1. R. understood from the treatise; 2. A. application.
3. Then, it is not attained.
[A. p.
261] || 4 || Its practice should be equal toward all. || 21 ||

It has been established merely that the singing must be performed on a *tṛca* (a triplet of verses); however, there is no scriptural rule as to whether it should be sung on equal [verses] or unequal ones, since even in the case of inequality, the number three is still applicable. Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) thinks as follows:
"This being the case, it is stated in reply: It is true that this is not within the scope of speech—that [the hymn] is to be sung only during the equal [measures];
nevertheless, the singing must indeed be performed only during the equal [measures]."
Why? The answer is: (viṣamā) when singing is performed on uneven [syllables] alone, an unscripted modification of the Sāman is effected.
And there can be no unscripted [modification] without an explicit statement.

The application [of the musical mode] is logical. For whatever fault there is in abandoning what is heard in the scripture, that same fault exists in the postulation of what is not heard; therefore, the singing must be performed upon the *samā* verses themselves. As for the modification (*vikāra*) demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya—namely, the straining (*saṃśaraṇa*) of the song when applied to a shorter verse, and the distortion (*vileśa*) when applied to a *bṛhatī* verse—that has been stated as an illustration.
But the status of being "northern" (uttarā) should be understood as occasional (naimittika), because of its immediate sequence.
Now, for what purpose is this instruction—"he sings the two subsequent [verses]"—considered here? The answer is: it is considered for the sake of establishing the *ūha* (modification).

He explains this very point: when the half-verses of the *ṛc*s recited in the latter [section] are taken up by the term "of the two latter," the ritual actions such as the *prāgādhā* and so forth must be performed; however, this would not be the case for the verses following the *yoni*.

Because, in comparison [to the former], it is possible for the subsequent [mantras]—whether separated or contiguous—to be employed exactly as they occur [in the text]. Therefore, this instruction is fit to be investigated. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the designation of the subsequent [mantras] to be non-distinct; that is, there is no difference here in their designation, just as there is none between conventional (*rūḍhi*) and etymological (*yaugika*) terms. This is because the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) is a conventional term in both cases. True—

A thing qualified by something else is [an *uttarapada*]; however, the "qualification" (*viśe�ṣa*) consists in the denoted object's dependence on another object. That which has posteriority (*uttaratva*) dependent on something else—that is, its apprehension relative to a preceding limit—is designated as *uttara*; whereas those [terms] that are independent are [designated differently].
But the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) thinks thus:

This is the connection [of the argument]. And between that which is dependent and that which is independent, the independent is stronger because it is more swiftly understood; therefore, the singing must be performed in the subsequent verses alone. The remainder has been explained.
Or rather,
it is established that in the rule "if [the verse] is in the *yoni*, then [the next two]," only those designated as "subsequent" (*uttara*) are to be taken.

Likewise, it is established that [the *gāyatrī*] should be sung on even [syllables]. Now, in this regard, should the phrase "on even [syllables]" be adopted here, or should it apply to the latter two [metres]?
By this, the doubt is restated in order to raise an objection. He raises the objection: "But surely this is improper."
1. It is impossible to conceive of the denotation [of a word]. For instance—the statement "it is to be sung in the Uttarā-yoni," and the rule "in the *samā* [meters]," and furthermore—
Logical reasoning (*nyāya*) overrides the literal statement;

for it is logical reasoning that restrains the assumption of what has not been heard and so forth, not the statement itself. Therefore, based on the statement, one must sing even in the case of the uneven [verses] of the *uttara* hymns. Consequently, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not possible here.

He provides the resolution: there is here a doubt regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). The proponent of the prima facie view considers that the statement "they praise with *atijagatī*s" [is injunctive].
Why? Because a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is not already established is not possible.

For if it were a subsequent injunction (*uttarādhikaraṇa*), then the restatement (*anuvāda*)—that "the multiplicity of *jagatī* verses has not been attained"—would be incoherent. Therefore, according to the principle that "these are indeed injunctions because they convey something previously unknown" (*vacanāni tv apūrvatvāt*), this is indeed an injunction. Nevertheless, since it is possible for it to be either way, by what distinction is the preference for [it being] a restatement maintained? To this, he says:
And since there is the statement, "If it occurs in the *yonī*, it [occurs] in the two following [verses]," and because there is the observation of a specific rule regarding the *ati-jagatī* verses,
it follows that— by the principle of the *āhavanīya* fire— it should be sung only in those of equal meter. Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be rejected.

Doubt: He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—this doubt of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is refuted by the statement, "If [he sings] on the *yoni*, then he sings on the two following [verses].
And since it has been stated that those verses situated as the "following" (*uttarā*) are to be taken, therefore it should be sung right there. As for that which is an *atijagatī*...

Since the plural number is also possible through the repetition of "in three," it does not require the assumption of a different word. When the *ṣoḍaśī* chant, consisting of twenty-one verses, is repeated seven times over a triplet (*tṛca*), and the *atijagatī* meter is repeated sevenfold, the plural number is indeed appropriate.
For this interpretation is not untenable, as it conforms to the established usage of the words. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the wording itself.
"They chant the Stotra in Atijagatī meters," [it is said]. But it is in the Prāgāthika style. || 25 ||
[Objection: "But surely, since there is an explanation in the *Prāgāthika* [section], this point need not be considered. To this he says: "What is it that is being considered here?

The answer is: "This is what is being considered here: Should the fact that number resides in distinct individuals (*pṛthaktvaniveśitva*) be accepted [as the definition] when one asks, 'Are the two Kakubhas the north?'"
The designation "also the *pragātha*" indicates that the two *kakubh* verses are subsequent;

thus, the number two resides in distinct entities. Consequently, it appears that there is an addition of two original *kakubh*s. Furthermore, because of the designation "the *pragātha*," it is called *pragādha*.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it logical that [the term] "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) is what is intended. Therefore, he holds that the mention of the *kakubha* meters is a scriptural injunction (*āgama*), whereas the mention [of the meters] is merely worldly; it is only a conventional designation and is not sufficient to establish the actual nature of the thing. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the performance of the duty—that the chanting of the *sāman* must be performed in the form of the northern meter (*uttarākāra*)—is precisely what constitutes the execution of the ritual act.

"Let us go. It is understood that one should sing by making the western direction itself the northern direction (*uttarā kakubh*). Since the rule for the suffix *ṇamul* in the sense of "doing something in such a way as intended" applies here—specifically in the indeclinable phrase "making the two directions [the west and east] take the form of the north"—the requirement that they be established as distinct entities is logically justified.

When two verses have been formed by means of the *pragātha*, their status as distinct entities is established; however, because of the expression "of the two subsequent ones," those designated as *uttarā* (subsequent) can be understood, given the unity of this treatise.

[Page 263] Regarding the two subsequent [verses], the statement "he sings" constitutes a single instruction (*śāstra*). And just as the understanding of the number [of repetitions] occurs in the case of one [instruction], so too it occurs in the understanding of the subsequent ones; thus, in the understanding of both, it is not merely the action itself that is understood. In this way, the designation "consisting of *prāgāthas*" becomes logically justified.
Therefore, this position is superior. The remainder has been explained with an illustration.
Or rather, what further distinction is there here from the previous [position]?

The reply is: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that there is a transgression of the scriptural statement, "The *mādhyandina-pavamāna* [stotra] has three meters and is an insertion (*āvāpa*)," [given that] the originative injunctions for the two [verses] are in the *bṛhatī* meter. If...
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Having adopted that *viṣṭārapaṅkti* which occurs in the *raurava* and *yaudhājaya* [sāmans], the *prāgāthika* [stotra] is performed.

Thus, by means of the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *paṅkti* meters, the designation "three-chanted" (*tricchabdatva*) is applied even while bypassing what is heard [in the text]. Since the *utpattibṛhatīs* are brought in here by the abandonment of the *paṅkti*, the status of being "three-chanted" is indeed established. This is the prima facie position.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the singing should be performed by means of the *paṅkti* [verse] as the *bṛhatī*-maker; thus, even in its functional capacity, the threefold nature of the meters (*tricchandastva*) of the *bṛhatī* becomes logically consistent. For if it were employed in the hymn (*stotra*) in its form as a *paṅkti*, then there would be a contradiction regarding the threefold nature of the meters. But this is not the case. Taking that [verse], one should produce two *bṛhatīs* by means of the *pragātha*.

This is because of the application of the *sāman*. The remainder is as before. Now, one might object: the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "the midday pressing consists of sixty *triṣṭubh*s" is also applicable to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), just like the state of having three meters (*trichandastva*), since the recited *paṅkti* verses would be abandoned. For if the state of having three meters were obtained through the introduction of other *ṛc*s, then there would be no chanting of the *paṅkti* verses. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not when these [verses] are being brought in..."
Those [verses] recited in the context can be said to be incapable of being employed; however, their incapacity would consist solely in not being sung, and not in not being employed at all.
The meaning of this is as follows: although those recited in the context are grasped by the "grasper" (the ritual requirement),...

Although there is no singing [of the verses], there is nevertheless an application based on indicative power (*liṅga*) in certain cases. Therefore, it is not the case that they are not employed; the counting refers to those occurring in the *savana* (pressing), not to the counting of the *stotra* (hymns). There is no inconsistency of the indicative power in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Since they are not sung, the state of having three meters (*trichandastva*) is established. This is not a counting of the meters belonging to the *stotra*; therefore, even when used for another purpose, there is no contradiction regarding the state of having three meters.
Thus, the established mark (*liṅga*) is the same even in the previous section.
Or rather, what is the distinction here now? The answer is: this is the distinction.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the instruction is completed with two *gāyatrī* verses— based on the rule "that which is in the *yonī* [is used] for the two following"— it is understood that the singing is not to be performed according to the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

Regarding the rule "one *sāman* is performed on a triplet (*tṛca*)" and "that which is [performed] on the *yoni* [verse] is [to be performed] on the two following ones," the scriptural injunction is fulfilled by means of two *gāyatrī* verses alone. Why, then, should one sing after forming an *anuṣṭubh* through the process of *pragrathana* (interlacing)? This is the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) position. But is this not in contradiction with the statement that "there are two triplets in the *anuṣṭubh*"? No, for that [requirement] is satisfied even by a single *anuṣṭubh*.
But Rādhāntavādī maintains: "Even though they are effects, the status of being designated by names and their duality are not contradictory;
therefore, the understanding that they are effects cannot be sublated, as in the case of the statement: 'The Śyāvāśva and Andhīgava [sāmans] occur in an Anuṣṭubh triplet.'"

From the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), three *anuṣṭubh* verses are perceived; however, their occurrence within a *pragātha* is simply impossible. Nor is anything contradictory [in this]. Therefore, it is understood that one should sing after having made them into *anuṣṭubhs*. Consequently, here too, the singing follows the *pragātha* method. The remainder has been explained.
Or rather,
in this section, it is considered whether a *pragātha* should be performed or not; it should not be performed by means of two *gāyatrī*s.
The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that [the *pragātha*] occurs in the case of the latter two triplets (*ṛca*) because of the logical justification [of the rule].

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that since the scripture states "they exist in the *anuṣṭubh* triplet," and thus all three verses are understood to be *anuṣṭubhs*, the *pragātha* must be performed. In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that regarding the introduction of the original *anuṣṭubh*, it is better to admit an insertion (*āgama*) rather than a *pragātha*.
To demonstrate this:
for indeed, even here, because it is heard in the injunction itself that "there are four hundred *pragāthas* in the *aindrābārhatā* [meter]," [the same principle applies].

It must indeed be *pragātha*. How is there a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here? To this it is replied: the prima facie position is that the word *pragātha* is indeed applicable even through the expansion (*pragrathana*) of a *ṛc*, and thus everything—including the rule "in a triplet (*tṛca*), [one takes] the two following"—becomes consistent.
For of the *dvṛcas*, there are one hundred and four of them; therefore, by taking one *ṛc* from another *dvṛca*, one forms a triplet (*tṛca*).
Having completed the preparation, he will perform the singing; therefore, the designation "pragātha" and the designation "tṛca" for the two subsequent verses are justified.

What more is there to say regarding the interlacing of quarters? However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that different verses are used while the sāman remains the same, because of the observation of modification (ūha).

The singing must be performed by means of the interweaving of the verses (*pādapragrathana*). For it is appropriate to resort to such an interweaving in order to achieve the state of being a *pragātha*, provided that no contradiction with the scriptural vision (*darśana*) arises; thus, singing by means of the interweaving of the verses alone is logical. Furthermore, it has been stated that the expression "in the two following [verses] of the triplet" (*tṛca uttarayoḥ*) is indeed applicable even when the action is intended as the primary meaning. The remainder has been explained.
|| 7 || There would be an option because of the unity of purpose. || 29 ||

He raises the following objection: "But how can the means be combined, given that the *gīti* (melodic chant) has already been assigned [to a specific purpose]? The sense is this: if those [other means] were also assigned [to that same purpose], then they would indeed be combined; however, they are not so assigned, for [the purpose belongs to] the *gīti* alone.

Because they have already been employed. The reply is: "The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts a combination [of the means], considering that the attainment [of the goal] occurs through their employment, since a song cannot be undertaken without employing the means; thus, he speaks of the combination because the specific details are being grasped."

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: this is precisely the distinction—that only a single means, independent of any other means, accomplishes the employment of the *sāman*. Furthermore, there is no authoritative basis for the repeated employment of the *sāman* for the sake of assisting the means, since the purpose is accomplished even by the *sāman* being employed once. Moreover, the purpose of ritual properties (*dharma*) is the accomplishment of the task, not the means themselves. Therefore—
Since the state of having a discernible distinction is the cause for an option (*vikalpa*) and not for a conjunction (*samuccaya*), the option is established.

Or rather, it will be stated that this topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed inconsistent in meaning: if this statement refers to the archetype (*prakṛti*), then this is a consideration regarding the instruction (*upadeśa*), and it has no application in this definition; if, on the other hand, this statement refers to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), then it is purposeless in the archetype.

Since it is understood that praise (*stuti*) has the *sāman* as its means of accomplishment, it follows—just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—that the praise is to be performed by means of the *sāman*. On the contrary, it is more appropriate that this [injunction] is for the purpose of prescribing the *ṛc*, because the *sāman* is already established [as the means] while the *ṛc* is not yet established.
To this, it is replied: whether in the archetype or in the ectype (*vikṛti*), this [injunction] is for the sake of accomplishing a function that is independent of the other.

If the *ṛc* verses were also to be employed for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), then the function of the *ṛc*s would be independent of the *sāman*; however, according to the view that the *sāman* is what is employed, the function belongs to the *sāman* alone, independent of the *ṛc*. This present section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to resolve this very point.
But was it not previously stated that if this statement pertains to the modification (*vikṛti*), it would be purposeless and intended for the prescription of the *ṛc* verses?
To that, he says: "There is no restrictive rule regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification.
The meaning of this is: even if [it were] in the modification...

If this [injunction] were for the purpose of prescribing the Sāman in the praise (*stuti*), then the application of the Sāman to the praises occurring in the archetype (*prakṛti*) by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) would be unopposed. For the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) takes up the properties from the principal action, while the archetypal subsidiary—the object of the praise—serves as the grasper of the properties for the modified praise; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever. Therefore, even in the archetype, that which belongs to the praise of the Sāman...

This very perception is preceded by that statement; therefore, the statement is not purposeless. Nor is the statement for the sake of the *Ṛgvidhāna*. Why? He says: there is no fixed rule between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*). Whatever is additional in one place is required by the other. A distinction is understood from the specific characteristic of the archetype; it is not [the case] for that [modification] alone.

The archetype (prakṛti) exists. Even for the archetypal apūrva residing in the praise (stotra), there is a requirement for a means of accomplishment; for the ectypal apūrva, the Sāman is prescribed as that means. Furthermore, the status of being a praise is an indicative mark (liṅga) of the injunction. Therefore, extension (atideśa) is appropriate. Precisely because of this mutual...

This section is intended for the purpose of establishing the performance of the rite independently; for this very reason, it is included within this definition, because there is no distinction in the instruction. Indeed, in the state of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no option based on the instruction; for there is no distinction from the perspective of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

Because of this existence, there is no distinction between conjunction (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpa*) in this scriptural statement; for even if there is no distinction in terms of the objective meaning, since both possess the status of being means, they can be joined through conjunction, or because—according to the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī*—there is no contradiction in their conjunction due to a difference in their respective functions. However, from the perspective of the ritual action (*kārya*), only an option is obtained, because each one is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) through its own specific application (*viniyoga*). Each—

Since that [result] is established even when there is no grasping (*upādāna*) through anger, this conceptualization (*vikalpa*) applies to the effect; thus, it is consistent with this definition, because its nature consists in the consideration of the effect. For this investigation into the intermediate effect is undertaken for the sake of establishing modification (*ūha*). Moreover, the investigation into the intermediate effect is for the purpose of refuting that [opposing view].

In order to refute this misconception, it must be considered right here. In that very context, since the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) must necessarily hold that the lineage of the Asuras is caused by censure alone, what need is there for dependence on another word?
