Let there be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that there is an option (*vikalpa*).

This is the connection [of the words]. If it were certain that the understanding of the sentence-meaning regarding the lineage of the Asuras occurs solely through censure (*nindā*), then there would be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) alone. However, if it is established through both censure and praise (*stuti*), then there is no authority for depending on other words; thus, due to the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is an application (*viniyoga*) of even the *ṛc* verses for the purpose of praise, and likewise [in other cases].
The same applies to the *sāman* as well. In that case, because each individual effect is to be accomplished, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), this statement regarding the option is appropriate, since it prescribes the *ṛc* only when it has not already been obtained.

And in prescribing that [the *ṛc*], it is proper to also prescribe the *sāman*, so that its cessation does not occur absolutely; thus he says: "For when the *ṛc* is prescribed, the praise is not by means of the *sāman*."
It would obtain by virtue of its inherent nature (*prakṛti*), because it is set aside by the explicit instruction (*upadeśa*). Therefore, both [the cause and the action] must be enjoined.
However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: this would indeed be so if the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) were indistinct; but this is not the case.
A distinction is understood. What is it?
The answer is: that which is about to be stated.
What is it? [It is distinguished] by means of another category of entity (padārtha).

For, because it is connected with the injunction "one should praise with the *sāman*," this [verse] lacks a connection to it by virtue of being an option; thus, the notion that "one should praise with the *ṛk*" is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And since a conceptual construction is not possible when it is possible to avoid it, the praise must be performed with the *sāman* alone. If this were merely an injunction of the *sāman*, what would be the purpose of it in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) now?
Regarding the statement:

"In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), however, this injunction remains meaningful even in the modified rite (vikṛti) according to the manner previously stated. The reply is: "The refutation has already been stated—that there is no necessary rule regarding the relationship between the original form (prakṛti) and its modification (vikāra)."
It is as stated previously;
for if it were expressed in this manner, no distinction would be understood between the chanted and non-chanted mantras, nor [the distinction] regarding the *pratīka* (initial word).

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers there to be no distinction because of the injunction. The meaning of this is as follows: just as there is a distinction in the case of praise (stuti), since praise is accomplished only by means of chanting (pragīta), its expression is not by means of non-chanting alone, because it is expressed as having the nature of an approach (upasthāna).
1. This [is] *idam-mā*.
2. When its designation is chanted, it is the same [as before].

It is the same whether [the verse] is chanted (*pragīta*) or not chanted (*apragīta*). Because the *ṛc* is enjoined by the opening words "This is the thousandfold man" (*ayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ*), which are chanted, and because that [verse] exists in both states, there is no restriction. For if the injunction were made by means of the pronoun "this" (*etayā*), then, since that [pronoun] refers to what has been previously mentioned (*prakṛta*), and since it is the chanted [verse] that is previously mentioned in the Sāmaveda, the unchanted [verse] would not be brought to mind.
It is understood that this application is by means of a *pratīka* (a partial citation). The word "this" (*etad*), however, refers specifically to the *ṛc* (verse) as presented by that *pratīka*.

As for the word "praise" (*stuti*) used here, it serves merely as an indicator of the act of denotation; otherwise, the praise would belong to the *sāman* alone, since there is no injunction for the *ṛcs* themselves to perform the praising.

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that it is logical that one should worship with the *pragīta* (chanted) verse, because of the understanding of this specific distinction from the statement "one worships with this" (*etayā upatiṣṭhate*).
The meaning of this is as follows: the purpose of the injunction is "one worships with this," and the word "this" (*etac-chabda*) refers to what has been previously mentioned in the Sāmaveda.

And that which was introduced [in the previous section] is indeed the one being sung; subsequently, when there is an expectation as to "by what?", the specific [instrument] is provided by the mere mention of the representative term (*pratīka*) as "this thousandfold man" (*ayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ*).
When explained in this way, the phrase "by this" (*etayā*) becomes a specification of the particular activity.

To the objection that "but because of the use of a representative term, there is again a lack of distinction," he says: "The use of the representative term, however, is not without distinction... (*pratīkagrahaṇaṃ tvaviśiṣṭameta-*).
Furthermore, there is no difference in the taking up of the *pratīka* (representative word) even for that [verse] which is under discussion, recited, and presented; for its application as well.

But is it not the case that [the Ṛgveda] is also recited in the Sāmaveda without being sung? Having introduced the injunction for the recitation of the Ṛks, the Ṛgveda text is for the purpose of the meaning and for the purpose of singing, not for the purpose of grasping the literal form; therefore, the non-sung version is not the subject under discussion.
But as for the phrase "it is sung": he has stated that there is no option between the sung and the unsung versions in the worship of the Āhavanīya fire.
Why, then, is the unsung version recited here specifically for the purpose of being sung? To this he replies: because when a visible purpose is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible one.
For the accomplishment of chanting (*pragāṇa*) is the visible purpose; indeed, syllables that have not been grasped cannot be chanted easily.
Therefore, it is logical that [the mantra] serves another purpose. Thus, it is established that one should approach [the deity] with the mantra as it is chanted.
Or rather:
What, then, is the distinction between the musical notes (*svara*) and the modes of singing (*gīti*)? The answer is:
this is the distinction—that the musical notes are subordinate to their application (*viniyoga*).

A mantra being employed is employed precisely with its specific accentuation, because a rule regarding accents is observed in both *japa* (repetition) and *nyūṅkha* (the nasalized chanting). For mantras are applied in *japa* and *nyūṅkha* with exactly the same accent in which they were originally recited; otherwise, there would be no fixed rule. Furthermore, by the word *nyūṅkha*, [is meant] that which is without interval—

The six *oṃ*s that have been recited are now discussed. In the ritual of sacrifice (*yajñakarman*), there is no monotone (*ekaśruti*) for the *japa* and *nyūṅkha*; this is because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) stated in the rule: "In the ritual of sacrifice, there is no *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, or *sāman* [with monotone].

But by what distinction are the *japa* and *ūṅkhya* [recitations] specifically mentioned, such that even those [other recitations] which are recited with specific mantra-sounds would likewise have to be employed with specific sounds? Otherwise, the specific sounds would be purposeless.
To this, he says: "But for those..."

The high-pitched (*udātta*) and other accents of these [Vedic passages] are not employed for this very purpose [of indicating meaning]; rather, according to the rule "in the sacrificial ritual there is monotony (*tāna*)," those which are applied with a single accent (*ekaśrutya*)—namely, those other than the *japa* and *ūṅkha*—are subject to monotony. Monotony is the state of having a single accent. For these, the high-pitched and other accents serve solely to determine the meaning during the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). And this was not stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), but rather...
[This was stated] by the author out of friendship.

Now, since there is indeed a specific application (*viniyoga*), there is no room for doubt regarding a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here; for since the application is understood to be individual for each, any suspicion of their being combined (*samuccaya*) is quite weak.
He refutes this: "And there is no lack of doubt here;
rather, there is indeed doubt, because the operation of vowels is necessarily observed in the act of denotation, which is characterized by expression. Denotation—

Because the determination [of meaning] is achieved through the specific phonemes by means of their measure (*mātrā*), therefore, since they serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), their combination alone is logical. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that even with respect to accent (*svara*), those who are proficient explain the determination of meaning.
The meaning of this is as follows: although those who are not proficient...

Ordinary people do not discern specific meanings through specific accents; nevertheless, experts such as Pāṇini and others certainly describe specific meanings by means of specific accents, because they have prescribed specific accents for specific meanings, as in the cases of "pade'padeśe" and "nivāte vātatrāṇe."

In such cases [as those beginning with *ityādi*], according to Pāṇini Sūtras 6.2.7 and 8: "In the case of a substitution for a *sāman*, that [substitution] should depend upon that [original *sāman*], because it is prescribed by the technical rule. || 32 ||

Now this is considered: Are the means of singing (gītyupāya), like the song itself, for the purpose of manifesting the syllables, or are they solely for the purpose of accomplishing the song? In that regard, if they are for the purpose of accomplishing the song, then there would be the application [of the *nyāsa*] even in the *yoni* and the *uttara*.
In that case, if the means of singing are for the purpose of accomplishing the song, then in whichever part of the song they function as the producers...

The *bhāva* (modification) performed in the *yoni* (original form) must also be applied in that very same part of the *uttara* (subsequent form); thus is the application of the vocal techniques (*gītyupāya*) according to the *yoni* and the *uttara*. Now, if the vocal techniques are for the purpose of manifesting the syllables (*akṣara*), then their application follows the manner of what is manifested:

since in the *yoni* the palatal (*tālavya*) vowel is increased and manifested through the state of *ā-ī*, that very same [manifestation] is manifested in the two *uttaras* as well, and not according to the *yoni*.

The application [of the argument] is as follows: this is what is being said—does the application of the means of singing occur by virtue of the portions of the song (*gīti*), or rather by virtue of the syllables (*varṇa*)?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that the means are for the purpose of producing the song. Why? Because the manifestation of the syllables occurs through the song.
1. This was stated during the time of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
2. "They teach" [p. 269].

The means do not have the [mere manifestation of syllables] as their purpose. Why is this so? To this he says: if the means were intended solely for the manifestation of syllables, by what would melody (*gīti*) now be produced? And if melody is not produced, its very status as being for the sake of manifesting syllables is lost.
Therefore, the means (*upāya*) are for the sake of accomplishing the melody (*gīti*), and the melody is for the sake of manifesting the syllables (*akṣara*).
Consequently, it is logical that the means are indeed for the sake of the melody. Thus, the performance proceeds according to the requirements of the melodic portions.
To this, it is replied: if the means do not serve to manifest the syllables, then...
The very purpose of song would not result in the manifestation of syllables.
Why is this? To this he says: "For there are no means that do not depend upon syllables. If there were no means dependent upon syllables, then what [would be produced by song]?

One should manifest the phonemes (*akṣara*). However, the diphthongs (*āībhāva*) and so forth are dependent upon the phonemes. In that case, if these [diphthongs] do not serve as means of manifestation, then there will be another manifestor.
Now, it was argued that if the means [of expression] are for the purpose of manifesting the syllables, then it follows that there would be no production of melody (*gīti*).
He refutes this: "This very manifestation of the syllables is its production, namely, [the production] of the musical notes (*svara*)."

Furthermore, song—which consists of a combination of various means—is produced by those very means acting as its constituent parts. Therefore, since a perceptible purpose is possible here, it is not logical to postulate an imperceptible one; thus, the manifestation of phonemes (*akṣara*) itself [is the purpose] through the means.

And the fact that the manifestation of phonemes is the purpose has been shown by way of the *āībhāva* (the modification into *āī*). According to others, even in other parts, the palatal [phoneme] alone is extracted and manifested through the *āībhāva*.
In various modifications (*vikāra*), there is the purpose of manifesting syllables in many ways. But how is this so in the case of elision (*lopa*), addition (*āgama*), and *stobha*?
For elision consists in non-articulation; how can it have the purpose of manifesting syllables? Likewise, addition and *stobha* [also involve] other syllables...

Because they consist of entering into the phonemes (*akṣara*), [the operations of] elision and so forth are not manifestors [of meaning]. The reply is: even in that case, they possess the very nature of denotation (*abhidhāna*); whether their purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*) or seen (*dṛṣṭārtha*), there is no difference.
The meaning of this is: although elision and the rest are not manifestors [of the phonemes themselves], [they do serve to denote].

Nevertheless, they serve solely for the purpose of manifesting the syllables, because the song that manifests the syllables brings about a specific excellence [in them]. And that specific excellence imparted by it has an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose. Thus he says: "Even in the case of those [syllables], one must assume an unseen purpose in the very manifestation of the denotation, just as in the case of the Sviṣṭakṛt and other offerings, which relate to the substance and the deity."
Therefore, it is established that the chanting should be performed according to the syllables (varṇa), and not according to the parts (bhāga).
|| 9 || Some [hold] that there is a cessation of the *stobha* in another substance, as in the case of the *ṛc*. || 34 ||
Now, one might object: "Having stated the definition of *stobha*, is it not appropriate to consider its applications (*pradeśa*) and non-applications (*apradeśa*)? To this he says:

"Now the *stobha* is considered—whether they are applied (*pradiśyante*) or not. This very consideration is connected to the definition [of *stobha*] by virtue of the [preceding] discussion on the *gīti*.
Because of this,
by the statement "He sings that which is in the *yoni* on the two following verses," the function of praise accomplished by the *yoni* is [transferred] to the two following verses.

The application (*viṇiyoga*) is as follows: since that function known as praise (*stuti*) is to be accomplished by means of the *sāman*, there is an extension (*pradeśa*) of the *sāman* based on that function; and its specific modification (*ūhātmaka*), which consists of the *stobhas*, is an extension within the context of the *stobhas*. We shall explain later what is denoted by the term *stobha*.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the word "song" (*gīti*) does not denote the *stobhas*, and because there is no connection with the words of the *ṛc* verses when praising together, and because the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*) has a functional purpose, there is no inclusion of the *stobhas*.

Regarding the extended injunction (atideśavākya), "As [it is] in the *yoni*, so [it is] in the two subsequent [verses]," this is for the sake of the ritual function (*kārya*). The function of the *yoni*—namely, that which is called praise (*stuti*)—must also be performed by means of the two subsequent verses. Since that function has already been accomplished by the *yoni* through its association with chanting (*gīti*), chanting is implied for the two subsequent verses as well, in order to achieve that same result. In that context, if the *stobhas* were denotable by the word "chanting" (*gīti*), then [the praise would be accomplished].

If it were argued that the *stobhas* are implied for the sake of establishing the praise because they are taught as a means [of chanting], or if it were held that the syllables of the *ṛc* could not effect the praise without the *stobhas*, neither of these two cases exists; therefore, there is no application of the *stobhas*.
To this it is replied: by the very extension (*atideśa*) of the melody (*gīti*), there is also the extension of the *stobhas*, just as there is of the musical notes (*svara*).

Just as when the chanting (*gīti*) of the vowels is extended [to other verses], those elements external to the chanting are also extended, so it is with the *stobha* syllables as well. But is it not the case that because they do not express the meaning of the praise (*stuti*), the extension of the *stobhas* would be purposeless?

Since vowels are useful for the comprehension of meaning, the extension [of their properties] is indeed purposeful. The reply is: True; in the case of denotation, they are useless, for the purpose of *stobhas* is simply the accomplishment of the melody (*gīti*); therefore, they have no purpose in denotation.

But has it not been stated that song (*gīti*) is simply the manifestation of syllables? And it has been stated that syllables are manifested for the purpose of denotation, yet the denotation of praise is not accomplished by them. Therefore, [it is] devoid of—
The *yojanā* (arrangement) and even the *gīti* (melodic chanting) are not to be produced [as independent means].
This is the meaning: the *stobhas* do not accomplish the praise;

rather, it is the syllables (*akṣara*) of the *ṛc* alone that do so. And the *gīti*, being of the nature of the manifestation of those syllables, is employed in the praise. Among those, whichever syllables constitute the praise...

By means of that [stobha], it serves as an instrument for the praise of that [Ṛk]. And since that song (gīti) is accomplished by means of the syllables of the Ṛk which are suggested [by the stobha], the portion of the song produced by the stobha would be purposeless; therefore, it should not be performed in the latter two [sāmans]. It is replied:

This is indeed true, provided that the subordinate status (guṇabhāva) of the Sāman consists solely in the manifestation of the syllables of the expression; however, if [the purpose] were the manifestation of the meaning—

If the Sāman were subordinate merely by virtue of its manifestation through the syllables of the *dhānā*, then the melodic portion would be rendered purposeless; however, it is understood that the Sāman serves as a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) for the very act of private recitation (*svādhyāya*).
Even if this be so, what follows? He says: therefore, for the Sāman which is of such a nature and employed in the ritual action...
1. Even though the effect of the objects of expression is obtained solely through the medium of that which is being refined (saṃskriyamāṇa), it is so stated.

Even regarding ritual action (*karman*), there is no assumption of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Rather, it has been stated that the unseen assistance must be postulated only for that specific portion where the visible [result] is not possible, just as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings, where it pertains to the substance and the deity. Therefore, because its purpose is not the unseen and because there is no [visible] function [to be served], there is no omission of the melodic portions.
It can be said: since the portion of the chant (*gīti*) is not omitted, it is logical that the *stobhas* also have their place therein as its effectors.
To the objection that "only that much of a portion is appropriate as a place as is required for the completion of the task," he says:
for the task occurs after the placement [of the *sāman*], and once the *sāman* has been placed, the visible purpose of whatever portion [is served]—

An unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is not postulated for that much [of the text]. But surely, since the function of praise (*stuti*) implies the entire *sāman*, does it not follow that the status of being the object of praise belongs to the whole portion?

To the objection that an implication (ākṣepa) is appropriate only for that much, he says: "This section concerns the meaning of the *prakṛti* (archetype) itself, not one whose function has already been performed in either the *prakṛti* or the *vikṛti* (modification).
The meaning of this is: the implication by means of the function applies only to that very ritual action (*karman*) in which the *sāman* is taught.

In that case, it is logical that only the *sāman* itself is implied, because it is precisely such a thing that has been taught; consequently, since there would be no cessation of the *stobha*s, one must assume a functional purpose for the extension (*atideśa*) of even the *sāman* portions in order to effect the cessation of the *stobha*s. Therefore, there is the inclusion of the *stobha* syllables.
It cannot be prevented for the sake of establishing the meaning of the *sāman* verses; therefore, the application of the *stobhas* is established. The remainder has been stated.
|| 11 || And that which is additional and of a different color [is also a *stobha*], according to Jaimini, because it possesses the nature of the word *stobha*. || 39 ||

In connection with the discussion on the *stobha* sections, this definition is stated: "Jaimini [says it is] both additional and discolored. Therefore, there is no inconsistency. He restates the purpose of employing both [terms] as explained in the Bhāṣya: "There is something that is additional..."

It is not discolored (*vivarṇa*) in the same way as *aśvādrir* [is]. To ensure that this does not count as a *stobha*, the term "discolored" (*vivarṇa*) is used. However, something may be discolored but not excessive, such as *ognāī*; to exclude that case, the term "excessive" (*adhika*) is used. This raises an objection: But was it not stated that "excessive" means exceeding the syllables of the *ṛc*? And the repetition (*abhyāsa*) does not exceed the syllables of the *ṛc*.
Regarding the phrase "it has been done":

since the mere statement "it is additional" would already suffice—given that repetition would not even be suspected of being *stobha* (filler/interpolation)—what purpose would the mention of "dissimilarity of phonemes" (*vivarṇatā*) serve? For that [status of being a filler] is already obtained simply from the fact of its being additional, up until the inclusion of the term "dissimilarity of phonemes."
This is the point to be established. Now, the purpose of including the term *vivarna* (dissimilar vowel) is so that the *stobha* status of the repetition (*abhyāsa*) shall not apply;
and this is obtained precisely from the inclusion of the term *adhika* (additional), because a repetition is not something additional to the *ṛc*.
1. R: The state of being a cause for praise (*stutikāritā*).

2. As for the mention of discoloration (*vivarṇa*) as something to be accomplished, is it not the case that there is an excess [of syllables], as in *śvādrir-śvādrir*? This is not an excess; for there is no addition of syllables due to repetition (*abhyāsa*).

It occurs. Therefore, even if it were merely stated that "the status of being a *stobha* belongs to what is additional," there would be no possibility of the repetition (*abhyāsa*) being considered a *stobha*.
He provides the resolution: "In that case, what is intended is merely an excess of expression, not an excess of syllables.
[This applies to] that which is devoid of repetition—"
Because this [repetition] is denotative (and thus there is an excess of denotation for it as well), since repetition does not enter into what is not denoted.
Now, one might ask: "Why is an excess of denotation alone accepted here? To this he says: "And it is logical that an excess of denotation should be so understood."
He asks, "Why is this logical? and replies: "An excess can only be stated on the basis of the actual mention [of the letters], not from a mere counting of syllables independent of such mention;
for an excess cannot be understood by way of their intrinsic form alone."
It is possible [to know this]. However, it can be understood that there is an excess of those elements which are not required for the expression, by virtue of the expression itself.
But surely, even from the meter, an excess is indeed recognized. True, this is so; yet even the thorough knowledge of the meter cannot be attained without the expression.

For it is only by grasping the phonemes through their delimitation by meaning that the knowledge of meter can be achieved, and not otherwise. Therefore, there is no cognition of an "excess" apart from the expression;
only that which exceeds the expression is truly excessive. Thus, it is rightly said that those phonemes which exceed the syllables of the expression [constitute the excess].

Regarding the term *stobha*: since it would follow that even a repetition (*abhyāsa*) would be a *stobha* if [the definition] were stated in this way, the inclusion of the term "dissimilar vowel" (*vivarṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding that.
[Sūtra 12: Because dharma is produced by purpose, there is a prohibition against the transgression of modifications of substance and quality.
The connection with the injunction follows from inherence. || 40 ||

But is it not the case that this principle—that the acquisition of a property occurs through the assumption of its function—is already established? Therefore, since there would be no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), this section (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be commenced.
He answers: "Certainly."
The objector asks: "For what purpose, then, is this discussion commenced?
The answer is: [it is] precisely to determine whether wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other such things undergo the transformation into the effect [of the ritual].
It is considered as follows: But how, again, can there be doubt here only regarding the substitution of the effect?
The answer is: it is heard in the scripture that "the caru is made of nīvāra," but it is not heard that "nīvāra is in the place of rice."
He raises an objection again: "If *nīvāra* grains do not exist in place of *vrīhi* grains, how then can there be a *naivāra* sacrificial pap (*caru*)?
Just as...

Just as rice grains (*vrīhi*) serve the purpose of producing the rice-grain kernel (*taṇḍula*), so too do wild rice (*nīvāra*) grains; it is precisely by way of the production of the rice-grain kernel that the *nīvāra* becomes the sacrificial pap (*caru*). He provides the resolution: "In that case, this follows by implication (*arthāt*); however, an injunction regarding the effect (*kārya*) is not possible otherwise than through this [implication], for the connection of the *nīvāra* with the *caru* occurs only thus. Therefore, the *nīvāra* falls into the place of the *vrīhi*'s function (*kārya*), but not directly."

1. Otherwise—2. there would be the contingency of [the injunction] applying to the effect; for by the word "only" (eva), the injunction is restricted to that specific effect, as in the case of "they bind the animal to the *paridhi*. This is in accordance with the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*). Nor can it be said that its effect is [already] established by implication, because the connection between the sacrificial rice (*caru*) and the wild rice (*nīvāra*) could occur through another means as well; for even when the *caru* is accomplished using *vrīhi* rice purchased with *nīvāra*, such a connection is still possible. Just as, regarding a bracelet made of gold purchased for ten thousand coins, speakers may say, "This belongs to the ten thousand coins."

Regarding the term *kaṭaka*: therefore, since it is impossible for the effect to be transferred [to the substitute], they cannot possess its properties; such is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
But surely, the eating of honey and the eating of ghee are prescribed as parts of the six-day period itself, not as substitutes for the six-day period—how then can this deliberation arise?

If their injunction were to occur upon the commencement of the *ṣaḍaha*, then this inquiry—whether there is an injunction regarding the function of the *ṣaḍaha* or not—would be appropriate here; however, since those two are not auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *ṣaḍaha*, how can such an inquiry arise? He replies: "What is the use for us of this inquiry concerning a subject that has already been determined?"

However, the explanation of the characteristics (lakṣaṇānvākhyāna) is considered here precisely because those two [observances] are prescribed for the cessation of the six-day period; therefore, there is no fault.
But how, then, is there a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the eating of honey and the eating of ghee in this context?

If this consideration is based on the premise that the two [acts] are prescribed for the cessation of the six-day period, then it appears that the prescription applies only to its effect. The reply is:

it is heard in the scripture that "when the six-day period is completed—that is, when the six-day period has ceased—there is the eating of honey and the eating of ghee"; however, it is not [prescribed] as the effect of that [period].
Thus it is.

Regarding the phrase "of the nails having been winnowed," one considers the removal of chaff and husks to be the function of the nails; yet it cannot be said that this alone is the function by implication, because the operation of the nails is possible through another manner as well.

[The opponent asks: "How can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the statement 'they bind the animal to the enclosing-stick' (*paridhi*), given that [the animal] is placed in the mortar to be pounded with the nails? [The answer is:

Because it is directly enjoined as performing the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). [The Siddhāntin replies: Here too, he considers that there is no scriptural statement to the effect that "that which is the binding to the sacrificial post must be performed upon the enclosing-stick."

The meaning is: why should this not be merely another application (*niyojana*)? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since there is no scriptural statement (*śruti*) such as "having made it *aira*, one should sing," which would imply the function of the word *girā* by way of its task, the connection with the singing (*udgāna*) is possible even through the substitution of other syllables; therefore, even by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it cannot be understood that the substitution must occur specifically in the place of the word *girā*.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the term *naivāraścaruḥ* (the *naivāra* rice-porridge) is justified as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) when there is a connection with *naivāra* [rice], provided there is no relationship of original material and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*).
The meaning of this is as follows: this is an injunction for a modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta-upadeśa*), and it is fixed in place of the *caru*; it is already established—

The function is the substratum [of the injunction]. Since the function pertaining to *vrīhi* rice has already been established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this is not a separate, additional function; therefore, this injunction of *nīvāra* millet applies to that very same function. Thus, the relationship between the *nīvāra* millet and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—characterized as a modification of the archetype—is expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). Consequently, the *nīvāra* millet undergoes the function of the *vrīhi* rice, and upon that assumption of its function, the properties of that [rice] are obtained. Likewise...

1. [p. 274] With regard to the requirement of a specific purpose (*kāryāpekṣa*), the consumption of honey and ghee is not [performed] as a contingent rite (*naimittika*), because the possibility of its application exists elsewhere through the connection with the ritual structure (*saṃsthāna*). As far as—

As long as the connection with the *dadhikāra* (the curd-offering) is possible for the completion of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍahasamsthāna*), there can be no justification for it being a *nimitta* (condition), because only that which qualifies the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) can function as a *nimitta*. Here, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to the performer of the sacrificial session (*satrin*) who has completed the six-day rite, even when another task initiated by that rite is underway. In the case of a different application (*viniyogāntara*), the assumption of the function of the six-day rite—which is distinguished by its difference in objective—occurs precisely within the scope of the injunction defining the entitlement (*adhikāraniyoga*).

There is the transfer of the function (kāryāpatti). Consequently, there is the application of those factors (dharmas) that are devoid of their own specific purpose but are prompted by the supreme apūrva. In this way, is there also a transfer of the function in the case of the "shaving of the nails" (nakhāvapūta)? Why? He says: "And the state of being shaved (avapūtatā) is logically connected with the fruit [of the sacrifice], provided it is other than the performance of the action."

Therefore, here too, because the modified (vaikṛta) instructions depend upon an established effect, even for the nails, the cause of their connection is precisely the removal of husks and chaff; thus, there is a transfer of function (kāryāpatti). Since it is not prescribed that "one should bind the animal to the enclosing-stick" (*paridhi*), what else could be understood from this other than the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? If the binding were itself being prescribed, [then the *paridhi* would indeed take on that function].

In that case, there would not even be a transfer of function (*kāryāpatti*). Furthermore, no injunction to employ [the word] is prescribed here, because it is already obtained through the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, since there is a transfer of the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is an acquisition of its properties.
Likewise, because of the syntactic unity with the phrase "not with *girā*," and because swallowing (*giraṇa*) is impossible, [it is not so].
The attainment of the function [of one word by another] (*kāryāpatti*) means that two things are established even in the absence of the function of the word *girā*.
Its meaning is as follows:

no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is perceived between the word *girā* and the phrase "having substituted *aira*. And this [unity] is established only if the word *aira* indeed takes on the function of the word *girā*.
For in that case, because its purpose has already been accomplished, the cessation of the *girā* word is established; being thus already obtained, it is merely restated (*anūdyate*).

Otherwise, that [cessation] too would have to be enjoined, which would result in the fallacy of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, by the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the phrase "one should not say *girā-girā*" is stated for the very purpose of ensuring that the *irā* word is understood as taking over the function of the *girā* word. Nor is it possible for itself—

The objection that there is a fault characterized by "swallowing" (giraṇa) is stated because [that swallowing] is impossible. Whether the word "self" (ātman) refers to the body itself through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) due to its connection with the self, or whether it refers to the self itself according to the direct scriptural statement (śruti)—in either case, swallowing is impossible. Therefore, when the word *irā* is prescribed as the substitute for the word *girā*, both of these [requirements] are consistent within a single sentence: "Not with *girā*, do not say *gireti*."
One should say: "Having made it *aira*, [one performs] the *udgītha*"; because of the occurrence of the function, there is the acquisition of its properties.
But because of its origin, there would be cessation, since it is produced by that.

Furthermore, there is an objection regarding the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*): the fact that something which serves one purpose is employed for another task is not a reason for its acquisition of [auxiliary] properties (*dharma*).

Even though the enclosing-stick is prescribed for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), nevertheless, because of the contradiction inherent in employing what has already been employed elsewhere, the enclosing-stick lacks the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) with respect to the tying (*niyojana*), nor does it possess such status toward the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the animal sacrifice by way of that tying.
1. R omits *na*. [p.

275] Now, why, according to the logic of the sacrificial cake’s potsherds (*puroḍāśakapālanyāya*), is there an application through the indication of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānalakṣaṇā*) in the state [of the object]?

The designation [of the *kapāla*] as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) by way of exclusion is not accepted. Now, if it were prescribed merely as a causal factor (*kāraka*) in order to favor the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), why would this not also apply to the *puroḍāśa-kapāla*? On this point, the eminent Prābhākaras respond: "In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is the injunction: 'They bind the animal to the *paridhi*.'"

The injunction is not disregarded. Now, when the function has been established for the sake of favoring the Vedic text (*śruti*), the modified injunction (*vaikṛta-vidhi*) applies; since the function of binding is already established as belonging to the previous [substance], the injunction of the *paridhi* is justified even merely as a means (*sādhanatva*) in that very context where such a function exists. For in that case, the status of the *paridhi* as a means is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is a scriptural statement (*vacana*) regarding it.

This constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, there is the impulsion toward what is unprecedented (*apūrva*). Therefore, by the mere fact of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), the injunction regarding the binding is established as being connected to the *apūrva*; and since the binding itself is to be understood through the sentence as qualified by the specific means (*sādhana*), the unity of the sentence is established by relying on the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). [The substrate...]

The injunction as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not accepted on account of the defect of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, since the injunction regarding the *kapāla* for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this designation does not rely upon a fixed function; rather, it depends upon the nature of the constituent elements (*padārtha*). In that context, if the *kapāla* for the sacrificial cake were not to enter into a relationship with the transcendental result (*apūrva*) from the very beginning as being for its sake (*aidamarthyena*), then it would merely be connected to the essential form of the constituent element itself. And thus—

There would be a lack of authority for the sentence and an absence of its application. Furthermore, its purpose cannot be ascertained without the purpose belonging to that [underlying substrate]. Nor is it possible to establish an application toward another meaning through the sense of being for that purpose without resorting to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, by force of circumstances, a secondary indication based on the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to. In that case, there is an injunction merely as a means of accomplishment already established, and consequently, there is a lack of status as a subordinate element (*anaṅgatva*).

Regarding the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*): since that which is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) cannot possess the status of being an instrument for an effect, its [status as such] does not serve as a reason for the application of the ritual property (*dharma*); thus, there is a renewed objection concerning the enclosing-stick.
Why?

The answer is as follows: For the collection of ritual elements (dharma) observed in the archetype (prakṛti) is based on their subservience to a specific purpose; indeed, it is observed in the archetype that only those things which have attained subservience toward the injunction (niyoga) possess a connection with the ritual elements, and this remains so in the ectype (vikṛti) as well.

It must be exactly so. Therefore, even though the *aṅga* (subsidiary part) has assumed the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is no impossibility of its connection with the ritual properties (*dharma*).

With the shadow of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he raises an objection: "But surely, here the 'being-for-that-purpose' (*aidamarthya*) is for the sake of the function, not for the sake of the 'being-for-that-purpose' [itself]."

The meaning of this is as follows: since in the case of the *prakṛti* (archetype), the capacity to produce an effect (*kāryakāritā*) cannot be understood without its being for that purpose (*aidamarthya*), "being for that purpose" is relied upon in relation to the connection with the ritual duty (*dharma*). However, "being for that purpose" itself is not the cause of the connection with the ritual duty. And here [in the *vikṛti*, the ectype], "being for that purpose" is understood even without the capacity to produce an effect; so what is the use of "being for that purpose"? He replies: "True, it is so; nevertheless, 'being for that purpose' is not absent—"
It is not the case that, by virtue of the injunction’s division, those factors which come into contact with the purpose must necessarily be subordinate to it—just as in the case of the rule:
"He scatters the husks with the cake-potsherd. [R omits *na*] (p.

If the ritual acts (*dharma*) were [independent], then that which lacks *naidamarthya* (purposefulness toward that specific act) would not be a ritual act, because it would have a different purpose for its application; for without the *naidamarthya* of application, those acts would not touch upon the objective characterized by the binding of the animal, since they are bound by the unity of the *niyoga* (the primary injunction).
"And there is the restriction of the properties (*dharmaniyama*); this is established.

Its meaning is as follows: if there were only a single injunction (*niyoga*) to be accomplished for both the properties (*dharmas*) and the primary elements (*pradhānas*), then there would be a restriction of the properties. Otherwise, if they were not for the sake of an injunction, [there would be no such restriction] regarding the properties.

There must be a restriction (*niyama*). For *niyoga* (the injunction) impels those duties (*dharma*) which have the injunction as their purpose. And if the duties were not in contact with the injunction, then, since they would not have the injunction as their purpose, the consequence would follow that there is no impulsion toward them. Precisely because there is a restriction regarding the impulsion of those duties that are in contact with the injunction, and because there is no impulsion for those that do not have the injunction as their purpose, for this very reason [the rule applies] to the duties of the *paridhi*...

There would be no occasion for the contradictory sacrificial duties of the post, such as carving and so forth; otherwise, why would those contradictory sacrificial duties not be applied to the animal sacrifice? Since there is no distinction [between them] if they were applied, with this intention he says: "Otherwise, what indeed is this so-called 'contradiction' that serves as the reason for the non-performance of the sacrificial duties of the post? Or how [could there be a contradiction] regarding the *paridhi*?"
The greater strength of the *paridhi* (enclosing-stick) is such that it sublates the properties of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by means of its own properties.
The properties of the *paridhi* are for the sake of the *paridhi*;

however, although the properties of the *yūpa* are performed upon the *paridhi*, they do not result in the *paridhi* serving the purpose of the *yūpa*. Therefore, the properties of the *paridhi* are stronger.

This [substitution] is not tenable for either of the two, given that both are impelled by their own specific injunctions. And this being the case, the restatement of the Bhāṣya—that there is no modification (*ūha*) in the formula "to the sacrificial post being anointed" (*yūpāyājyamānāya*)—is intended to refute [the opponent's position].
Now, one might object: "But this is improper."
He asks, "How so? and says: "The *ūha* (adaptation) is established by the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), and its absence constitutes the reasoning of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*).
He provides the resolution: "The *ūha* is not improper."
The rebuttal: How is it unjust?

The answer: For it has been established that the mantras function as means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Since the quality of being a means for binding does not exist in the *paridhi* (enclosing-stick), [the objection] is refuted.
The statement that "the designation is logical" is incorrect.

Its meaning is as follows: by the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), who maintains the principle of modification (*ūha*), it must be asserted that there is modification of the mantra just as there is modification of the ritual property (*dharma*). In that regard, when the mantra "for the sacrificial post being anointed" (*yūpāyājyamānāya*) is applied to the enclosing stick (*paridhi*), [the modification is required].

In the absence of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the word *yūpa* certainly cannot be employed. Even if one were to use the word *paridhi*, that too would be inappropriate, because the word *paridhi* does not denote the object that serves as the means for the tying (*niyojana*). Furthermore, it is the object functioning as the means that is denoted by the mantra. Thus, this objection is resolved when there is no modification (*anūha*) of the characteristics of the sacrificial post applied to the *paridhi*.

This being the case, it is replied: here too there must be modification (*ūha*), because of the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*); for the unity of the injunction is indeed the cause of the relationship [between the mantra and the ritual act]. However, by means of direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the difference between injunctions precludes the application [of the mantra] as prompted by the specific action.

The meaning of this is as follows: for through instruction, there is indeed a unity of injunction regarding the dharmas; this is the intended sense [p. 277] once the subordination of the primary object (śeṣin) to the purpose of the injunction has been established.
This is the reason: for when dharmas are connected with something that does not have that [niyoga] as its purpose, they do not attain the status of being for the sake of the niyoga;

however, when connected with things that have attained the status of being for the sake of the niyoga, they do attain it. Since the attainment of the dharmas occurs through the task (kārya), the status of being for the sake of the niyoga is first established. Once that is established, there is merely a requirement for a substratum (āśraya) for the performance; and the substratum of the dharmas is the objective (sādhya).

The application to the function cannot be prevented; furthermore, the fact that the *paridhi* serves that function has been established. Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) cannot be prevented on the grounds that they must be performed.
Moreover, this section was deliberated upon under the premise that the properties of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are applied to its function and are not for the sake of the post’s production.

As for the claim that "the mantra is not intended to be recited," it is replied as follows: Since the mantra is employed for a specific purpose and another means of accomplishment is not intended, its recitation occurs exactly in that manner; thus, there is no contradiction with the *ūha* (modification). Because the recitation is established in that very way—since the means of binding (*paridhāna*) is not intended while the means of tying (*niyojana*) is intended—the *yūpa* word is capable of denoting that [means], and therefore there is no *ūha*.

It must be performed. If the application of the animal sacrifice entails the properties of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), how then is there the favoring of [properties] such as being smeared with ghee (*satvak*)?
The answer is: for that which is of such a nature...

Since it is taught that the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belongs to that which has become the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), it is logical that when its own form is obstructed, it is incapable of performing that function; therefore, it must be infused with qualities that do not conflict with it.
But because it is for the sake of another, the impression (saṃskāra) shares the same purpose [as that other], since its object is that [other]. || 44 ||

Furthermore, here there is not even an injunction for a specific purpose; thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering the enclosing-stick (paridhi) to be something else, states that the ritual properties (dharmas) do not apply.
He explains this very point: "For in that case, they tether the animal to the enclosing-stick."

In that case, the function of the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) was enjoined; here, however, neither curd nor the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is enjoined, but rather both curd and rice-grains for the giver. Therefore, there is a disparity from the case of the enclosing-stick: not only is there no such *tadarthya* (purposefulness), but no function is enjoined either. To this it is replied: the function is indeed the motivator of ritual duties (*dharma*), not the injunction itself. That very [function]...

For indeed, application [of a means] occurs sometimes through a direct injunction (*codanā*), as in "one should bind the animal to the *paridhi*"; sometimes through its purposefulness (*aidamarthya*), as in the case of mantras recited within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) which are to be applied by their indicative power (*liṅga*), where their purposefulness consists in being subordinate to those things that require them; and sometimes through the sense of the matter itself (*artha*), as in this very instance. Thus, there is no difference whatsoever regarding the performance of the task. Furthermore, it has been stated here that the attainment [of the application] occurs through the task itself, and not through verbal designation (*abhidhāna*) or application (*viniyoga*).

Since the connection with the properties (*dharma*) of the consecrated water (*praṇītā*) is not based on its name or its specific application to the ritual act, but rather arises merely through its association with that act, it cannot be said here that the acquisition of the properties of the consecrated water is non-Vedic. Therefore, the properties of the consecrated water must be performed for both the curd and the milk.
1. It is not applicable;
2. it is not of the nature of a surrounding rim; 3. nor does it exist.
[278] || 15 || There would be no distinction because they have the same meaning. || 46 ||

[The question is: "Are the properties (dharmas) applied according to the specific function? Regarding the statements, "There is the *bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha*" and "There is the *rathantara* *pṛṣṭha*," it is deliberated whether there is a difference in function or not. In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), considering that both things denoted by the word *pṛṣṭha* have a single function, maintains that the properties prescribed for both should enter into both, just as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*). Just as [there is a single function] for rice and barley—
Because ritual elements (dharmas) are defined by their function and are prompted by that function, the dharmas heard in connection with one instance apply to both;

likewise, here too, since the two— the Bṛhat and the Rathantara— are identical in what is denoted by the word "pṛṣṭha," they must be accompanied by the dharmas prompted by that term, even when those dharmas are heard in connection with only one of them.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: first, in the case of the instruction, there exists a difference of words, namely "Bṛhat" and "Rathantara.

Since the words "Bṛhat" and "Rathantara" are employed in the instruction of the ritual duty (*dharma*), there is indeed a difference of words. And from this difference of words, a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) is determined.
[If it is argued that] there is a single effect for the dharmas, [the author] refutes this: "And a difference in effects is observed;
otherwise, praise is understood differently in the case of the *kavati* verses than in the case of the *bṛhatī* verses."

Praise, characterized by the declaration of qualities, occurs in one manner in the *kavatī* verses and in another manner in the *bṛhat* verses; thus, a difference in function is indeed understood. If it is argued that the designation "pṛṣṭha" is the same in both cases:
He refutes this: it has been stated that the acquisition of properties does not occur through denotation.
Therefore, even when there is identity of denotation, there is no confusion of properties. What then? The acquisition of properties occurs solely through function, and through function both—

It has been stated that a distinction is perceived between the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans], just as there is a distinction between plowing and cutting, both of which result in the separation of joints. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated in the case of *nīvāra* rice and other substitutes that ritual duties do not exist merely by virtue of their results, but rather by virtue of their function (*kārya*). Therefore, since a difference in function is possible for all [the rites], it is improper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. Consequently, the ritual duties must be performed according to their specific fixed application (*vyavasthayā*).
If it is argued that no difference in function is possible between rice and barley in the production of a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), because both serve as the material cause for the cake—

otherwise, one would have to say that a barley-made cake is of one nature and a rice-made cake is of another, implying a difference in their functions even in that case— then [the following must be considered].
The answer is: it has been stated that dharmas are not prompted by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather by function (*kārya*).

Furthermore, in this context, the intrinsic nature is differentiated; there is no operation (*vyāpāra*) at the time of production. Dharmas are prompted by operation, and the distinction from the operation of denotation (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*) is [explained] in the *Bṛhatī*.
It has been demonstrated in the case of the *rathantara* and *bṛhat* [sāmans] that the praise is performed in one way for the *kavatī* verses and in another way for the *bṛhat* verses;
therefore, there is a dissimilarity between the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* and the case of rice and barley.
|| 16 || In the case of what is not archetypal (*aprākṛta*), they would remain fixed due to the contradiction with that [archetype]. || 48 ||

In the establishment of other *sāmans* within the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*), there is a deliberation regarding the *pṛṣṭha* [laud]: should the properties of one [sāman] be performed for the sake of the ritual function, or those of both? And should the properties be performed optionally (*vikalpena*) or collectively (*samuccayena*)?

There is doubt. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that there is no difference in the attainment [of the result] because the difference in the task exists in the archetype (prakṛti) and thus it is the same here as well, desires [the result] by means of the task.

The meaning of this is as follows: The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), considering that in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) there is an acquisition [of subsidiaries] through distinct functions due to the difference in their effects, maintains here too that the acquisition occurs through the function in that which possesses the archetype; otherwise, the very state of being "possessing the archetype" would not exist.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the function is acquired in that which possesses the archetype, but not the means (*upāya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: a modification (*vikṛti*), like the archetype (*prakṛti*), possesses auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*), but it does not possess constituent elements (*padārtha*). For this "being like that" (*tadvat*) refers to similarity in terms of auxiliary benefit, not similarity in terms of constituent elements. This has been demonstrated in the first section of the tenth book (*daśamādya*). Let it be so; nevertheless, how can there be a co-inherence (*samāveśa*) of properties?
To this he says: "And from the difference in means, a difference in the function within the archetype is understood.

From the difference in the *ṛc* verses, a difference in the function characterized by the act of praise is understood in the archetype. But here there is no difference in means, because another means is prescribed.

In the case of the *stuti*, because the original *ṛc* verses are set aside by the injunction of other *sāman*s, there is a requirement for other *ṛc*s; and since that [requirement] is singular, one cannot perceive any difference in the function (*kārya*). And when there is no difference in the function, who can prevent those properties (*dharma*) that are prompted by the function—just as the properties of the mortar and pestle are not prevented from applying elsewhere, except where there is a contradiction? If, at most, it is precisely due to contradiction that the properties are not performed.
Therefore, it is established that there is a coexistence of those [qualities] which are not contradictory.
And likewise in the case of a hymn containing both [sets of qualities], because of the implication of a single referent. 49.
Regarding this as well, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that both [elements] are to be applied in both places, just as in the case of the Kaṇvarathantara;
what is meant is this: that which was understood as a twofold means in the archetype (prakṛti), its function—
Here, two methods are prescribed.

He explains this very point: in the case of the *bṛhat* function, both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* [are used]; likewise, in the case of the *rathantara* function, both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* [are used]. Therefore, there is a co-inclusion (*samāveśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*).
The established conclusion, however, is that there is an entry into the means [of liberation] through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Its meaning is as follows: those two operations...

Regarding the praise, the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] as understood in that context are recognized here as being combined; therefore, it is the two means (the sāmans) that are combined, not the two effects. Furthermore, it has been stated that the properties are not occasioned by the combination itself, but rather by the effect.
Consequently, due to the difference in the effects, the properties must remain established according to their respective [original] applications. This is what was said.
In the Bhāṣya it is said: "By means of the Sāman, either a visible or an invisible result is produced. The completion of the purpose of the means is the visible effect;
praise, characterized as a specific function, is the completion of the purpose of the means, which is the visible effect. Through their coexistence, some invisible effect [is also produced].
Furthermore, when the connection of the properties with one specific action is understood, it is not possible for those same properties to be connected with another action;
therefore, a fixed restriction (vyavasthā) alone is logical.
Regarding the two *pārvaṇa* offerings, however, there is no application [of the properties], because they are connected to the purpose of the collective whole.
For that [deity] is indeed the object of worship.

[280] Here, hearing the word "functioning" (*pravṛtti*) in this sūtra, one who is mistaken raises an objection: "But surely this is a consideration regarding extended application (*atideśa*). What relevance does it have here?"

"What is the use of this fruitless discussion? Thinking that this is a sublation (bādha) and not an extension (atideśa), he says: 'There is a relevant point here, because the question of whether there is an extension or no extension depends primarily on the ritual action. He explains this very point:"

For if the two oblations were intended for the deities of the archetype (*prakṛti*), then they would not apply to the *saurya* and other such sacrifices; however, if they provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakārakatva*), then they do apply.
The meaning of this is as follows: those actions of the archetype, such as the *āgneya* and others, which constitute the deities—

If the two *pārvaṇa-homas* were intended for the sake of those [parvans] denoted by the word "parvan," that is, for the purpose of commemorating them, then they would not apply to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*). However, if they serve as indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), then they do apply, just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Thus, since their application or non-application depends upon the specific function, the mediating function of the two *homas* is now considered: is it the consecration of the deities?

Is it the effect itself, or rather the assistance rendered to the instrument, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings? In this chapter, an investigation into the effect as the means (*dvārakārya*) is indeed undertaken, since modification (*ūha*) is dependent upon that; thus, there is a logical connection (*prasaṅga*). Someone learned in the tradition raises an objection:

—But if this is the case, does it not follow that this is merely a consideration of sublation (*bādha*), since cessation occurs due to the absence of an effect? Why, then, do you, as the respondent, state that there is no extension [of the rule]? He replies: True, this is so; nevertheless, regarding the effect—

The proponent of the solution shows that this inquiry falls within the scope of the *ūha* (logical extension) because its object is the determination of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, and by implication, the sublation (*bādha*). He states: "I have not persisted [in this objection] out of mere obstinacy, but rather because [the inquiry] consists entirely of the consideration of the effect."
As for the connection: whether there be sublation by the sense of the matter or non-extension [of the rule], we have no concern with that.
In this regard, certain Mīmāṃsakas, desiring independence within the system and failing to consider the simplicity of their own intellects, [assert as follows].
They brought about its sublation. Now, even if the two *homās* are merely preparatory (*saṃskāraka*) rites for the action, why should there be a sublation?
For, even when there is a different deity, the two *Pārvaṇa-homās* should indeed be performed by means of modification (*ūha*), just as in the case of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
On this point, those whose entire dullness has been dispelled by service at the feet of the venerable Prabhākara [state as follows]:

They state the justification as follows: it has been said that ritual properties (*dharma*) are employed for the sake of a specific effect (*kārya*). Now, the intermediate effect of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices with respect to the production of the supreme *apūrva* is not the same as that of the *Saurya* and other sacrifices.
For this very reason, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no mutual confusion of the properties of the *Āgneya* and the others.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that even though the word *parvan* denotes time, its usage with respect to the ritual action is justified because of the connection with that time; thus, he considers it to be a term for time.

However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that since the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) cannot be established [if it were a term for time], it is more logical that it denotes the aggregate (*samudāya*) itself.

For if the word *parvan* denotes the ritual action (*karman*), then because the two oblations (*homa*) are the means of its consecration, the unity of their injunction (*niyogaikya*) is established; otherwise, it would not be established. And the unity of the injunction is understood because of the context (*prakṛtatva*). Moreover, even if it has the sense of a collective whole (*samudāya*), the action—

Even though it denotes speech (*vacana*), its usage at a particular time is due to its connection with an action. Alternatively, this word *parvan* is etymological (*yaugika*); since the root *pṛṇāti* has the sense of "giving," when it functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), it denotes the object (*karman*); when it functions as a locative noun (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), it denotes time (*kāla*). In that regard:

Since actions are the subject under discussion here, it is determined that the word *parvan* is employed specifically with reference to actions. Thus it is said: "The word *parvan* applies to both [actions and joints] by virtue of etymological connection (*yoga*); however, its entry into the ritual injunction (*vidhi*) is the specific reason [for its primary application here]."

Now, one might ask: even if it is a word denoting an action (*karman*), why does it not function as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*)? To this he says: "And because they are the subject under discussion, there is a rejection of being a remote auxiliary.
Since the actions under discussion are fit to be objects of refinement (*saṃskāra*), there is a rejection of their being remote auxiliaries.
This is the work. The rest has been stated.
|| 19 || Because there is no distinction between the two. || 57 ||
This discussion has arisen as a secondary consequence following the consideration of the primary matter.

In the preceding section, it was established that the two *homa* offerings serve the purpose of the ritual action; as a further consequence of that, it was raised whether these two *pārvaṇa-homas* should be performed separately.

What, then, is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*)? The answer is: he considers that because they share a single application (*ekaniyogaka*) while having the same subject matter (*prakṛtārthatva*), both [rites] apply in both places.

Since the application of the governing injunction (*adhikāraniyoga*) is one and the same in both cases, and since both [the *arthavāda* and the injunction] have that as their purpose, both must exist in both places. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that even when there is a restriction (*vyavasthā*), because it does not contradict the single governing injunction, there is no need for a [separate] ritual action (*kārya*) devoid of [independent] purpose.
This position is logical.

For that which has the deity of the new moon as its object serves to consecrate the new moon, while that which has the deity of the full moon as its object serves to consecrate the full moon. Wherever there is that which is to be consecrated, there too must be the act of consecration.

Not otherwise. Therefore, a fixed distinction alone is logical. Furthermore, when a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to assume an invisible one; thus, there is no contradiction with another effect. For it is not proper that for the very same act there should be a visible purpose in one case and an invisible purpose in another, such that the performance of the *homa*—which has a visible purpose on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)—would have an invisible purpose on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). The same applies to the other [act].
"Regarding 'therein' (taratra):
[Objection] 'If it is argued that [the rule] applies even to the *prayāja* [sacrifices]...'"
This is merely a mention of the name by way of the present context.

Its meaning is as follows: just as in the case of the two *pārvaṇa* oblations, there is no application in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) because they are intended for the deities of the archetype (*prakṛta*), so too here, even though [the rite] is intended for the archetype, there is no such [restriction], since the performance of the action is possible in the modified sacrifice as well.

Therefore, by way of incidental discussion, only the mere name is introduced here because it is relevant to the subject at hand. Just as in the case of the two *pārvaṇa* oblations, they serve the purpose of the ritual action and the deity, so too here, the *samit* and the other items serve the purpose of the deity and are objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*).
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that such an assumption is not appropriate here, because there is no evidence for the *samid* and other [offerings] being intended for a deity;
furthermore, even if they were words denoting an action, the use of the accusative case would still be justifiable, as there is no evidence that the wording of the mantra is non-factual.

Therefore, it is proven that the deity indicated by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇikī devatā*) is indeed to be accepted here, and thus [the offering] functions as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
Thus ends the second quarter of the ninth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) composed by the venerable Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra.
In the *Ṛjuvimalā*,
the third section of the ninth chapter.
Just as there is a statement regarding the origin of things in the primary creation (*prakṛti*), so it is in the subsequent evolution (*tati*),
because that is its source and because the object itself is not something produced.

But is it not the case that in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, it was demonstrated that the word-meaning is the form (*ākṛti*)? This is indeed the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), and this very point is its purpose.
The purpose is so that the designation "saṃskāra" may apply to that which is qualified by that genus;
and [thus] the saṃskāra is the designation.
It must be such that it denotes the genus (*jāti*) alone. For, under the view that words denote individuals (*vyakti*), there would be a mere statement of the means (*sādhana*);

since there is no distinction in the status of being a means between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), there would be no modification (*anūha*). Therefore, this is precisely the purpose of [the word] denoting the genus: what further advantage is produced here by the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since the word *vrīhi* lacks the capacity to denote *nīvāra* grains, that word—
It must be applied in this very way.
But if that is so, and if the word *vrīhi* does not denote that which belongs to a class other than *vrīhi*,
then the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the case of the phrase "for their sake" (*teṣām arthena*) would also be untenable.

If the word *vrīhi* were to denote both the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the cooked milk offering (*sānnāyya*), then the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) might be raised that the properties of the grain-offering (*auṣadha-dharma*) must also apply to the clarified butter and the cooked milk offering.
However, this is not possible if the word denotes only the genus of rice (*vrīhi-jāti*). He refutes [this objection] as follows: "For it is indeed something else..."
In that regard, the previous position has been refuted.

To the question "What was refuted?", he says: having raised the objection that if the action of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is intended as the object, it would not attain the status of being a constituent part of the ritual application (*prayogāṅgatā*), that [objection] was refuted therein.

If the object of the verbal root itself— such as rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth— were accepted as the purpose (*prayojana*) in the intended sense, then acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) would not serve the purpose of the injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).

Therefore, raising the objection that the object of the verbal root is not intended to be significant, but rather that [threshing] serves only as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), [the author] addresses this point:
This has been refuted. Here, however, we do not perceive any other function for the mantra than its original function in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

For in the archetype, the function of the mantra is to denote the primary substance of the oblation (*havis*); here too, it is that very same function, and since that is impossible without modification (*ūha*), it must be accomplished by modification. Nor is there a lack of connection to the relevant matter (*asamavetārthatva*), such that even if the meaning of the mantra were intended to be expressed, it would nonetheless be disconnected from the relevant matter—as is the case with the word "Agni."
It might be understood from the two words *vrīhi* and [the others]; yet even that is not the case. For it is already established that the words *agni* and *vrīhi* possess a combined meaning.
Therefore, that which is to be refuted here must be stated;
this is what is now being declared: it is true that the denotation of words as referring to the generic form (*ākṛti*) is established, and likewise—

Furthermore, since it is designated here as being in the state of a means (*sādhanabhāva*), and because there is no distinction between the original form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) regarding that state— namely, the state of being a means— it must be expressed by the *ūha* (modification). Even if it were the meaning of the word, the generic form (*ākṛti*) remains exactly as it was.
Because it indicates the nature of being a means (*sādhanatva*).
The meaning of this is as follows: even in the primary ritual (*prakṛti*), the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) does not denote its own essential form (*svarūpa*);
rather, it denotes a specific means (*sādhanaviśeṣa*), and that [means] is no different in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*). Otherwise, even modification (*ūha*) would not occur.

It might be so; and consequently, even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the generic form (*ākṛti*) would not be what is expressed, because it serves merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the defining characteristic of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Likewise, in the ectype (*vikṛti*), the species of *nīvāra* rice would not be expressed; thus, the modification (*ūha*) [of the word "rice" to "nīvāra"] would not be logical. Now, one might argue: "Even if it were an indicator, since the generic form of rice is absent in the ectype, its status as an indicator is untenable; therefore, to bring to mind the species of *nīvāra* and other grains that serve as indicators, there must indeed be the mention of a different species."

It should be said that this is logical: for when a certain genus is enjoined, only a member of that same genus is capable of being indicated; since the genus *vrīhi* (rice) is not capable of indicating the individual *nīvāra* (wild rice), another [genus] must be employed. It is not the case that the word denoting the *vrīhi* genus must be employed.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies: "In this regard it is said: this would indeed be so, if there were no intention to express what is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*)."
It might be argued that the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is to be indicated by its own genus (*svajāti*). In the present case, this [genus] is inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*);
for since that genus is enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is a proximate indicator, and thus there is a state of inseparability. However, if—

There would be an injunction of a different genus, and in that case, it could not serve as an indicative mark even by way of necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*). For in the primary injunction (*prakṛti*), rice of that specific genus is enjoined, as in "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*). In the mantra as well, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) is employed as denoting that very genus;
thus, the proximate genus serves as the indicative mark. If, however, in that case too, something of another genus were enjoined, or [if] in the mantra...

A word denoting a different genus would then not serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that which is proximate. Thus, it is established that [the word] serves as an indicator of the proximate; and it is not logical to intend that [different genus]. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the status of being an indicator of the proximate, the employment of a word denoting a different genus is not appropriate.
How, then, is it that the word *vrīhi* denotes something belonging to the species of *nīvāra*? The answer is:
in some way or another (*kathaṃcit*).
