The designation [of the mantra] is to be understood as in the case of the *aindrī* [mantra]. Therefore, the designation is an inseparable concomitant and is not intended to be expressed [as a primary meaning].

Consequently, since the two original words are seen to be employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), their designation must also be assumed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), because they are obtained there through their function (*kārya*). A different word, however, is neither obtained through its function nor through usage.

Thus, he considers [the mantra] to be without modification (*anūha*). Furthermore, the fact that its meaning is inherent (*samavetārthatva*) serves as a supporting argument for this position, because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is inherent in the ritual action, and since the individual instance (*vyakti*) possesses the status of being a direct means of accomplishment, the genus (*jāti*) exists merely for the purpose of defining it;
therefore, because the genus is necessarily concomitant [with the individual] and is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatva*), the word *nīvāra* should not be employed.
And he demonstrates another argument regarding the absence of modification (*anūha*): "Furthermore, even in the case of application (*viniyoga*), there is instruction of the words themselves.
The meaning of this is: the application of a mantra terminates in the phonemes (*varṇa*), because there exists nothing over and above those phonemes; just as it is...

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that even though the mantra serves a functional purpose in the archetype (prakṛti), it is not subject to modification; likewise, in the ectype (vikṛti) as well, it should certainly not be modified.
Even in the archetype, the mantra is employed solely for the sake of its function. In that regard, just as that very same word is employed [in the archetype], so too [should it be in the ectype].

Even in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), that very same [mantra] should be employed, because it is a constituent part (*aṅga*). To this it is replied: there must be modification (*ūha*). Why? Because when a different function is required, there is no rule—such as that which applies to the *aindrī* mantra—regarding the assumption of a different capacity for Agni and the other deities.

When postulating a different capacity for a word in relation to a different function or a different denotation— such as in the case of words like "Agni" (fire)— the same principle does not apply as it does in the case of the word "Indra. Why is the principle not applicable?
The answer is as follows: Just as in the case of the original [text], it follows that here too, the manifestation of the means (*sādhana*) must be performed by means of this mantra.
Now, it must be considered whether this is achieved through the postulation of another denotation (*abhidhāna*) or through the postulation of another power (*śakti*). In that regard:
It is not logical to postulate another power for a word whose power has already been established; for when there is a further application, one would have to postulate yet another power.
For instance, the word "Agni" and others have their powers already established, yet when that same word is used again in a different mantra application, [one would have to postulate a new power].

The postulation of a separate power is not tenable. Why? Because there is no application of that much alone. If there were no application of that much alone, then one would be forced to postulate another power. However, there is no application of that much alone; rather, it is the application of the mantra.
Nevertheless, he asks "What [is the consequence]? and says: even when there is the insertion of another expression for the mantra, nothing imagined occurs that is superior to what is perceived.
It is not an expression—
For when there is an insertion of another word, nothing is imagined [as a new entity]. However, in the view that imagines a distinct power (*śakti*), that same fault remains.

Therefore, rather than avoiding the imagination of a distinct power due to its complexity (*gaurava*), it is more logical to simply insert another word. But [it may be argued]: "In that case, the status of being a *mantra* would be lost, since it has been stated that *ūha*, *pravara*, and names are not *mantras*."

He refutes this: its status as a mantra is not lost. For that non-mantra-status was intended with reference to the *nimitta* (the causal basis), not with reference to the designation (*abhidhāna*), because [in the latter case] there is a word to be inserted.

It was stated that such [a word] lacks the status of a mantra; however, it was not stated therein that a sentence which is expressive lacks expressiveness. Since its function is already established, it is logical that the mantra possesses meaning through its efficacy, because that which constitutes a collective whole is recognized as such. And for this very reason, when only the occasion (*nimitta*) is destroyed, there is no destruction of the mantra.
For this very reason, there is no substitute [for the mantra].

For a substitute gains its existence only when the entire mantra is lost, not when merely the occasion (*nimitta*) for its use is destroyed; because when the entire mantra is forgotten, it is impossible to recognize something similar to it. However, when only the occasion is destroyed...
The reality of the mantra is precisely that; therefore, it is logical to introduce another designation rather than postulating a different power.
Why? Because it depends upon repetition.

The postulation of another power depends upon repetition. For if there were no repetition of the word "Agni" and so forth, it would have to be employed as it occurs within the mantra, and thus only in that specific form. Consequently, when it is employed in its isolated form, one must necessarily postulate another power; otherwise, it would lack the capacity for denotation. And that which is not enjoined...

"It is possible to cause repetition where there is an instruction of a word. True; however, it has been stated that such [instruction] is for the sake of a grammatical operation (*kārya*). And here, the application occurs through the operation, not through the instruction. Therefore, the denotation is according to the operation;
the denotation does not deviate from the operation.

It must be resorted to. Furthermore, attainment here occurs through its function (*kāryataḥ*), and the function here is the manifestation of wild rice (*nīvāra*). It is not logical to postulate another capacity for that [word], since that [function] is established even otherwise; therefore, modification (*ūha*) alone is the correct principle.

Furthermore, regarding this explanation of the "pregnant woman within" (*antarāgarbhiṇī*), which was first presented and then subsequently challenged and explained otherwise: why was this matter introduced as something that ought to be challenged?
Why?

The commentary on the sūtra has been composed with that as its primary focus. The answer is: it has indeed been introduced precisely because it ought to be introduced and because it is logically appropriate. If...
[Objection: "In that case, why is there an objection? [Response: It is for the sake of avoiding the lack of connection with the subsequent sūtra.
The objection is raised merely because the subsequent sūtra would otherwise be disconnected, not because it is improper. If, under this interpretation..."

"There would be no connection with the subsequent sūtras; therefore, the previous explanation is unsystematized (asūtrita). He refutes this: "And it is not unsystematized, because a sūtra indicates multiple meanings. Therefore, this is a demonstration of skill by way of an objection."
The author of the Sūtras provides [this] here.

Since the author of the Sūtras has also formulated another topic (*adhikaraṇa*) right here, he demonstrates great skill on the part of the Sūtrakāra by indicating multiple meanings with a single sūtra. The remainder has been stated along with its defining marks (*liṅga*).
For it is enjoined [as a duty] because worldly things are indeed separated from [the ultimate goal] due to their association with defects. || 9 ||
This section is incidental.

Previously, it was stated that the statement beginning with "if there is one sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is for the purpose of establishing a rule. Now, this section has arisen by way of a relevant digression. In that regard, because there is no distinction...

If one should touch a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because the scriptural statement is made without qualification, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it to serve both purposes— that is,
to serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*).

And he considers [the act] to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). However, there is this distinction: in the case of the worldly [act], one must assume a separate qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, another position is that it should be exclusively Vedic.
He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "In this case, the qualification is already established, because of the hearing of [scriptural] defects."

Even a defect mentioned as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) is more directly applicable when [the act] has the person as its purpose. He states another argument: "And because of the connection with the word 'desired' (iṣṭa), the expiation is considered to have as its object the touching that occurs after the desired [act] has been completed."
Furthermore, the acts of raising [the sacrificial post] and so forth do not occur at a later time;
he states another argument as well: "And because the raising and so forth are unavoidable, it cannot be conceived that [the sacrifice] could take place even without them."
The meaning of this is as follows: therefore, the prohibition "the sacrificial post (yūpa) is not to be touched" is logically established as pertaining solely to the human agent (puruṣārtha).
1. Otherwise, there would be no connection with the subsequent sūtra; 2. [It applies] to that which is non-worldly and Vedic.

If it were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), there would be the consequence of an option (*vikalpa*); yet an option is not tenable because acts such as raising [the ladle] are unavoidable.

If, however, the prohibition is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), then the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its transgression must also be for the sake of the person alone. Therefore, it pertains solely to the worldly (*laukika*).
This is the mantra for touching. As for what was said—that the word "punarganya" (or "punardaṇḍa") is to be connected with "praharānena"—how is that so?
The answer is: it is exactly as it is heard; such is the intended meaning.
The questioner explains: "But surely, in the case of 'syonaṃ te' as well, the avoidance of syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) would result. He replies:
"It indeed occurs when the meaning of the sentence is being understood."

Because at the time of the comprehension of the meaning, it depends upon that; however, in the case of the ritual application (*prayoga*), at the stage of the application, it is the end of the mantra.
But [this is] illogical, because in the absence of modification, there is no observed obstruction.
And from the remainder; therefore, this [is so]. || 10 ||

Considering the similarity between the second and third positions, he says the following to demonstrate the distinction: "Four positions have been presented here. But this first position is that [the word] should proceed without modification in the plural number alone."

The first [form], ending in the plural, indeed ceases; however, the second, ending in the plural, ceases while that ending in the singular comes into operation, and it must be supplied (*ūhya*). As for the third, there is the application of both: the plural-ending form remains unchanged (*avikāra*), while the singular-ending form is modified (*vikṛta*). Regarding the fourth, there is the application of both as well as modification. What is the reasoning for these four cases?
The reply: First, this is the reasoning for the initial position: if, when there is an expectancy for an expression in the modified rite, even that which is unmodified [is expressed]...
When one is unable to express [the meaning], then the application of the governing rule (*adhikāra-niyoga*) enjoins it. However, expression by means of the unmodified plural form is possible;

for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the plural form was employed with the intention of referring to the noose (*pāśa*) in general. Thus, there is the view that this is grammatically correct (*sādhudṛṣṭi*).
And as in the archetype, even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) where there are two nooses, expression by that very same unmodified form is possible. [The singular form...]

However, since the term *ekapāśā* denotes the number one, it follows that it must be modified even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) in order to denote that number. But that is not correct, because the denotation is accomplished by the unmodified form itself; therefore, it does not require modification.
This is the reasoning for the second [view]; he states it as follows—the proponent of *ūha* (modification) says:

For one who maintains that there is no modification (*anūha*), it cannot be said that the singular ending is not applicable; for you yourself have stated that only the rope (*pāśa*) is intended to be expressed. Consequently, since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is possible, the mantra must take a singular ending. And its [the singular ending’s]—

The application of what has been established is possible, because it possesses its own inherent meaning; since it refers to a meaning inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), if that [word] ending in the singular number is modified in the ectype (*vikṛti*), then the expression of the connected meaning is accomplished. He explains this very point: "Because it reveals what is inherent [in the rite], what is the use of expressing something unconnected?"
The phrase "with that which ends in the plural" continues to apply.
As for the third [case], this is the reasoning; he states it: "This is the intention. It was stated by you yourself..."

Since the mantra cannot be set aside merely because of its association with the noose, the mantra must indeed exist in that form ending in the plural number. But was it not argued that there is no need for it, because it would express something incoherent?
He refutes [this objection]: "The application of the principle of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related) does not occur in the form 'this [word] denotes a meaning already related [to others]."
It is attainment (*prāpti*) by means of which there would be non-attainment (*aprāpti*) due to its absence.
How, then, is it so? It is stated that [the word] "prāptika" is used in the sense of denoting that which is inherent (*samaveta*).
This application of meaning is the same;

for the mantra is understood to have both a singular ending and a plural ending. Its occurrence cannot be prevented. Even though it is not syntactically connected [to the specific context], it will remain grammatically correct here just as it was in the original context. Furthermore, regarding that which has a singular ending:
Just as in that case, here too it is because [the word] denotes the bond (pāśa) which is inherent and conjoined with oneness through its own meaning, and because it conveys that [oneness].

There is no fault on the grounds that the term "correctness" (sādhutva) refers to grammatical correctness in denotation; rather, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the two mantras should be employed in their modified form. But [it may be objected] that they denote things not inherent [to the ritual].

It has been stated that the mantra ends in the plural number; the sense is: "How will its grammatical correctness (sādhutā) be established? He provides the answer: "True, it is not stated here regarding the ritual action involving two nooses (dvipāśaka); however, one should act according to the model (prakṛti)."

In this case as well, the same consequence follows. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), that which is intended must be something whose meaning is inherent; however, this is not intended there. Why? He says: "True, it could have been stated here [in the archetype] regarding the ritual involving two nooses (*dvipāśaka*); but it was not. Now, [one might ask]: "Is it not [the case that it was not stated]?"
And since it is said that "one should perform [the rite] as in the archetype," here too the same rule would apply.
In the archetype, the mantra would have a meaning intended to be connected with the ritual act;
however, this is not intended there. Why? He says: because in that case, [the mantra's application] follows solely from its connection with the fetter (pāśa).

The meaning intended here is "noose" (*pāśa*); however, the connection with the verbal suffix (*vacana*) is for the sake of ensuring the grammatical correctness of the usage. It is not a case of denotation (*abhidhāna*). And if this usage is indeed correct, then, given its correctness, who would prevent its use even in this context?
He refutes [this objection]: "In this case, correctness cannot be asserted.
Why? He says: For correctness arises either from usage or, even in the absence of usage, from a grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa)."

In that regard, first of all, there is no application [of the rule] for the dual form *pāśayoḥ* ending in the plural number. Even though the characteristic of a plural suffix is found in Vedic usage according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*, it has been stated that there is no *ūha* (modification) in Vedic. Therefore, the plural ending here is merely a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*).

Therefore, for the sake of correctness, the dual-ending form must be supplied. Here, considering that a different grammatical rule has been stated because of its prior application, he objects: "How can there be a rule for that which is not employed?
The intention is: "for that whose usage is not directly perceived."

The meaning is that even for that [word] whose usage in the *prakṛti* (archetype) is not seen through direct perception, its correctness (*sādhutva*) is understood from the observation of its grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, when only two loops (*pāśa*) are intended to be expressed as the meaning of the mantra used in the *prakṛti*, why should regard be paid to the purpose of the plural number?
The answer: We say it is for the sake of correctness (*sādhutva*). Without a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the word alone is not [correct].
[This establishes] correctness (*sādhutva*). Nevertheless, [the author] asks "Why? and replies: "Because of the prohibition of what is incorrect (*asādhu*).

Likewise, even regarding words whose meaning is already understood, people are seen to respect the use of common speech for the sake of correctness, as in: "This task is to be done by Devadatta and Yajñadatta."
In cases such as "it has been done" (*kṛtam*), therefore it is well said that there is the employment of even the two modified mantras.

When there is a conflict of opinion, there should be an option (*vikalpa*), because of their equality; for in the case of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), it is improper to assume something else, since it occupies only a single part [of the whole].
The two *pāśa*-mantras are cited as examples.
By this, he states the designation of the *pāśa*-mantras, which is useful for the purpose of excellence (*utkarṣa*).
Now, an objection: the discussion was conducted by relying on the *pāśa*-mantra ending in the plural number, which is obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*). Is it not so?
How can there be an application by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) for that which has not entered into the *prakṛti* (the archetype)?
Therefore, as to how the doubt regarding "transference" (*utkarṣa*) arises again, he says: "And this section [is established] on account of the sense."

The preceding [section] should be consulted first. The intention is that this reflection was undertaken by taking up the "inclusion" (*anupraveśa*) already established in that prior topic (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, because it was not directly relevant, this reflection was not performed earlier; now, however, there is a connection through the context of the previous topic. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [argues] that because there is no syntactic connection with the entire sentence...
He maintains that there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the mantra associated with the plural number.

The meaning of this is as follows: this mantra is to be applied by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*); therefore, it should be used precisely where the untying of bonds (*pāśonmocana*) is manifested in connection with a plurality of bonds, and not merely because of the designation "bond-mantra" (*pāśamantra*).

That which has already established its general connection is applied [to its specific context]; thus, there is an *utkarṣa* (transference) of the plural-ended [mantra]. But surely, since the two mantras serve the purpose of releasing the noose (*pāśa*), even if they are applied with a plural ending, their transference is not logical as long as that purpose remains possible.
This release of the noose is to be manifested by the two mantras; it can indeed be accomplished even by a mantra ending in the plural.

"How can there be excellence in this, since it is merely for the purpose of making [the meaning] manifest? He replies: "True, it serves the purpose of releasing from bonds, but by abandoning the plural number..."

It [the plural number] is inherent in the nature [of the word]. Furthermore, there is no authority for abandoning the plural number when its meaning is already connected [to the ritual act]. Therefore, wherever there is a connection with the action as a collective whole (*sahānvaya*), this mantra—whose meaning is inherently integrated (*samavetārtha*)—must be employed. Even if one were to resort to subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*), that [subordinate sentence] does not exist within the principal sentence (*mahāvākya*).

Since there is a basis [for the plural], it is logical that the excellence [of the number] alone is appropriate. This being the position reached, it is replied: for here plurality is understood as dependent upon the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because it is cognized through the case-ending (*vibhakti*), and not independently, as is the case with words expressing number and the like.

Just as in cases such as "he offers four handfuls," where number is enjoined independently of its connection with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is not so perceived through the case-ending (*vibhakti*). The meanings expressed by the case-endings depend exclusively upon the nominal stem, as they are denoted by direct statement (*śruti*).

They say it is for its own sake. What follows from that? The answer is: consequently, there occurs the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) of plurality with that which is based on the meaning of the *pāśa* (the fetter).
It is understood. Nevertheless, he asks "why? and says: "And the meaning of 'bond' (pāśa) is understood as being connected with liberation.
It cannot be said that pride (*māna*) is not denoted by this mantra; if it is indeed denoted,
then since that is its meaning, the meaning of the mantra consists in its being expressive of that [pride],
provided that the meaning of the mantra is dependent upon its ritual application (*viniyoga*).

If the meaning of the mantra were independent of its application (*viniyoga*), then— since the gender (*liṅga*) residing in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs first and is primary, and because the gender indicated by the case-ending is stronger with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem— the plural number would be intended as the fruit of the mantra even when there is only a single rope, since the mantra would thus be applied [to that single object].

Thus it is determined. Furthermore, it has been stated that the meaning of a mantra is understood through its application (*viniyoga*). Otherwise, the mantra would have only a functional purpose (*kāryārthatā*), and in that case, it would follow that any [portion] whatsoever could be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, because of the resulting contingency of dependency, there would be a loss of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). However, when the meaning of the mantra is dependent upon its application, only as much as is required for the application must be manifested.

Since the mention of another meaning is, by the maxim "the consumption of poison is necessarily concomitant [with death]," simply unintended, there is no lack of authority. Therefore, the determination of the mantra's meaning is restricted solely by its application (*viniyoga*). Precisely because there is no displacement (*anutkarṣa*) according to the principle of the nominal stem and gender, the Commentator has introduced the context (*prakaraṇa*) as functioning as a supplementary factor (*abhyuccaya*).

If there were no other fundamental reasoning (*mūlayukti*), then the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself would constitute that fundamental reasoning; however, it is not possible for it to be a fundamental reasoning, because it is weaker than *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*. Therefore, displacement (*utkarṣa*) on the strength of *vākya* is the logical conclusion.

For this reason, he asks: "How, moreover, can there be a logical connection of reinforcement for the context? He replies: "For when a connection with a statement of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is perceptible, and a connection with an injunction of entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*) is possible, it cannot be [connected] with an imperceptible injunction of entitlement."
The intention is that the connection is logical.
He concludes: "Therefore, by virtue of the substratum, the meaning of the concordant case-ending is to be understood."

The meaning of the case-ending should be understood as being concordant with the single rope that serves as the substratum for the number; and that [meaning] is directed solely toward the accomplishment of the ritual action.

Because the singularity [of number] is not intended to be expressed, the mantra is directed toward the perception of the action alone. Or, if the number is intended to be expressed, then the meaning of the mantra is together with that very singularity.
But surely, in the case of "together" (*saha*), there will also be the assumption of a different meaning for the plural [suffix], because of the word *saha* itself.
Even the state of being a plurality [is thus established]. It is postulated that there is no referent for the plural number;

consequently, the contingency of expressing a single object arises even in the case of the plural. And thus, even when one has the freedom of usage, the contingency of using the plural for a single entity follows. [End of] the section.
It removes [the objection]: there is no contingency regarding usage that is not under one's own control, because it is understood from common worldly practice that there is no fixed rule;

for it is understood from the restriction of singularity and so forth that the singular number and so on apply. Therefore, in this case, the very correctness of usage constitutes the correctness of non-denotation. How so?
To this, he replies: "Because it denotes action alone, unity is established.
Since only the action is understood, unity is apprehended independently; for numbers such as duality and the like are based upon a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Since—

The plural number in reference to a single entity is non-expressive; for this very reason, even the authors of grammatical treatises undertake a special effort with the rule "the plural in reference to one" (*ekasmin bahuvacanam*). Otherwise, because it would be established by its own nature, it would be inexpressible. [This refers to] that which is established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*).
Therefore, there is no lack of expressibility. How then is the traditional rule (smaraṇa)—"the plural number [is used] for one when the plural is not otherwise obtained"—to be understood?

It is precisely for the purpose of obtaining [the usage]. Consequently, it is merely the grammatical correctness of the employment, as there is no semantic connection [of the plural sense] with the object.
|| 6 || But in the case of the apūrva, there would be no modification, because it is not indicated [by the archetype]. || 20 ||

Furthermore, in this case of a ritual application involving a single wife, since a connection with one's own purpose is possible, it cannot be said that there is correctness (*sādhutā*) for two or many wives. For in the case of the *pāśa* (the singular form of the word "noose"), such a resort [to the singular] is adopted because there is no other way; but here, since another way exists, there is no resort to the correctness of the ritual application.
"Surely, even here it will serve for the grammatical correctness of the formulation. He refutes this: "No, because its own meaning is impossible in a single [instance]."

The grammatical correctness of the application is not possible in its own sense; therefore, for the sake of correctness alone, the modification (ūha) must be made for both [cases] and for the plural. Now, why does its application not occur only in the case of one wife?

Just as in the case of the *vrīhi* [grain] option, the mantra "syonaṃ te" [is used]; therefore, the stated substitution (*ūha*) is not appropriate. He refutes this: it is not so established, because since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is possible everywhere, there is application (*viniyoga*) in every instance, just like the case of the *pāśa* [mantra].

For in that case [the example of *yava*], there is no inherent connection (*samaveta-arthatā*) at all. Here, however, since the nominal stem *patnī* has an inherent connection both in the dual and in the plural, it is not possible to assert a restrictive rule based on conformity with another scriptural statement. Furthermore, when an inherently connected meaning is possible, the grammatical correctness of the usage [is established].

Regarding the word "vacanasya" (of the singular number), it must be modified by means of *ūha*. To this, it is replied: first of all, neither duality nor plurality is heard in the place of the singular number, as is the case with *nīvāra* grains.
Just as *nīvāra* grains are prescribed in the place of *vrīhi* rice, so too...
In the case of a single effect, duality or plurality is not heard [in the scripture]. What follows from that? The answer is: this results from it;
namely, it cannot be said that the meaning is inherently inherent (samaveta) in that way.

Just as the word *vrīhi* has a meaning inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too can it not be said that the singular number [is inherently present], because all three— singularity, duality, and plurality— are equally inherent. But surely,
even the grammatical correctness of the usage cannot be maintained?
He refutes this: it is simply not possible to say so,

because the mere meaning of the nominal stem is connected with the act of donning [armor], and because when there are two or many [persons], the combined meaning is not understood [from that stem alone].
The meaning of this is as follows: because the mantra is connected with the act of girding the waist, which requires a specific number associated with the nominal stem *patnī* itself;

since there is no singularity when there are two wives or many, the singular number cannot be understood as referring to the actual object present (*samavetārtha*). Therefore, it can be said that the word is applicable even to a single wife without distinction.

This singular number is not used for the purpose of expressing oneness, because that would be absent in the case of two or many; rather, it is for the sake of establishing the connection with the status of being an object (*karman*) through the fact that everything possesses activity. Therefore, in this case as well, it is simply a matter of grammatical correctness in usage. Thus, it is not [the case that the singular is used to denote unity].

[Objection: There is a contradiction with usage (*prayoga-virodha*). [Question: But surely, consistency (*samanvaya*) cannot be maintained in a single instance? [Response: He refutes this: It is indeed not impossible, because through specific usage there is consistency of meaning for both [singular and plural] and for many; thus, it is correct in usage (*prayoga-sādhu*).
"Therefore, there is no fault.
|| 7 || "And also in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because of that statement. || 21 ||

In this context, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) belongs to one who considers the performance to be under his own control. Just as, thinking that in an action under one's own control the performance is likewise under one's own control, one modifies [the mantra] into the dual number, so too here in the modified ritual (vikṛti), even when there are two wives—
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that in the case of the word, the modification of the dual number alone is appropriate, because the application [of words] is under one's own control.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that since grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is possible according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no authority for an application that is not under such control.
If the purpose cannot be accomplished through Vedic usage, then an application under one's own control is resorted to. [In the case of the word] *patnī*—

Furthermore, since the word *śabda* is established in usage with a singular ending even when there is duality or plurality, there is no opportunity for its application [as plural] to depend on one's own will (*svāyatta*).

In the case of *pāśa*, however, because no usage is observed with a plural ending in the sense of duality, there is an opportunity for its application to depend on one's own will. As for what was stated in the *Bhāṣya*—namely, "and likewise, by that statement, there is no non-intentionality"—that is incorrect, because it contradicts the *Pāśādhikaraṇa*.

Even when the meaning of the case-ending is not intended to be expressed, the case-ending must still be employed according to its proper function; therefore, he offers a rebuttal by stating "or rather" (*athavā*), because it is precisely for this reason that the use of the dual and plural numbers would otherwise follow here as well.
An alternative position was stated because of dissatisfaction with the previous one; he explains that: "Because correctness (*sādhutva*) is possible in exactly that same way.
Just as in the case of the *prakṛti*, since there is usage even for the dual and plural numbers, the singular number is correct [in the case of the word] *patnī*.
Likewise, there is no modification even when there is a corruption in the word.
|| 8 || In the case of the *adhrigu* formula at the *savanīya* offerings, it is the same if they are governed by the same injunction. || 22 ||
This reflection is made on the basis that there is an identical injunction (*samānavidhāna*). By means of this distinction, he says this:
this is a general extension (*atideśa*), and no further specific detail need be stated;
the purpose of this is that it constitutes an identical injunction.
|| 9 || And because there is no modification in the case of a substitute. || 23 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that there should be modification (*ūha*) because the function of rice is transferred to the substitute, and because the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) applies directly to its primary meaning in the case of the original substance.
This would be so if both the substitute and the rice were taught as independent [options].

In that case, the mantra would certainly not apply. However, since the substitute has taken on the function of the rice (*vrīhi*), and the word "rice" denotes a meaning that is inherently present [in the substitute], modification (*ūha*) is indeed appropriate.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that *nīvāra* grains are not prescribed for the function of *vrīhi* rice;

rather, *nīvāra* grains are taken up so as to accomplish a slightly deficient objective of *vrīhi* in order to justify the prescription of *vrīhi*. And when the justification of the prescription is achieved...

Since the function [of the original] falls upon that very [substitute], it ought to be designated by that very name. Therefore, even in the case of a substitute, since they are indeed *vrīhi* grains, it is proper to designate them here by the word *vrīhi* itself. Having mentally reflected upon the correct meaning, this very point has arisen: if that which is to be conveyed has not been conveyed...

And this has been refuted: that the secondary meaning (*gauṇārtha*) consists in either the identification with that state (*adhyāsitatadbhāva*) or the superimposition of that state (*adhyāropitatadbhāva*).

Here, "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) is the non-apprehension of difference, while "superimposition" (*adhyāropa*) is erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*). Both of these are untenable when there is a clear distinction [between the primary and secondary meanings].
It has been stated that this is because of the understanding of *nīvāra* grains.

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) clarifies his own intention: "This is not a fault; for it is possible, by virtue of the greater similarity of parts, to prepare *vrīhi* rice itself [as a substitute] according to one's capacity."

The very designation [of that substance] is performed by the word *vrīhi*; thus, there is no transformation into a different word (*śabdāntarāpatti*). This is because the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) belongs to the generic form (*ākṛti*) as far as its constituent parts extend. Even in the absence of *vrīhi* grains—where there is an absence of the collection of all constituent parts—the adoption of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is for the sake of accepting some constituent parts of *vrīhi*; such is the nature of *vrīhi*.

It is appropriate that *pāṭala* flowers are designated by the very word *vrīhi*. Nor are there superimposition (*adhyāropa*) or false attribution (*adhyāsa*), because from that cognition [of "rice"], other constituent parts are understood. If the constituent parts [of rice] are thus taken up, why is the *nīvāra* grain taken up instead? To this he says:
"The taking up here is of something distinct from that," meaning distinct from the constituent parts of rice.

It is not invariably concomitant; for there is no fault, as without them one is simply unable to take up the rice-grains themselves. Therefore, this is not the domain of modification (*ūha*), because there is no assumption of its place (*tatsthānāpatti*).

On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) says: "In the event of the loss of the rice-grains, since the performance of the primary ritual must necessarily involve the employment of another substance, there is a restrictive rule that one should desire to employ a substance similar to the original. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*), however, maintains that a similar substance is employed solely for the purpose of fulfilling the requirements of the scriptural injunction itself.
And because, in the case of things that come into contact, the dimension of the object is not fixed. || 27 ||

Regarding this, the Commentator has stated as follows: "But even in the archetype (prakṛti), this is indeed an improper recitation (anyāyanigada), since there are two eyes yet a singular number is used; therefore, modification (ūha) is not appropriate. He raises an objection to that: "This objection concerning the meaning being inherent (samavetārtha) is not at all sufficient to preclude modification. How so?"

—The answer is: A singular form is observed for two [objects] in rituals involving pairs of animals; however, when there is a plurality of substrata, grammatical incorrectness (asādhutva) would result, just as in the case of the word *pāśān*.

The claim that the plural form is incorrect when applied to two nooses because it is seen used for one is likewise [invalid], since here the singular number is seen used for two; therefore, this objection is entirely purposeless. He provides the resolution—the intended meaning is as follows:
294] Regarding the challenger: if [the deity] were already inherent [in the mantra], how could there be a modification (ūha)?
The meaning of this is as follows: the intention of the objector (*codaka*) is this:

"I have raised the objection that there is a lack of inherent connection (*asamavetārthatva*) due to the difference in substrates; however, in order to establish the state of having an inherent connection (*samavetārthasiddhi*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) will offer the rebuttal that light is a single entity and thus not lacking inherent connection. Nevertheless, even in the case of two animals, [the light remains] a single...

"Because of their oneness, even though the referent is inherent [in multiple substrates], there would be no modification (anūha). Having thus supported the injunction, he explains the *bhāṣya*’s refutation:

"This is improper. As for what you have urged—that this is an illogical recitation—[we reply that] because fire is a composite entity, even though there is a difference in its substrates, one considers it to have a referent inherent in those [substrates]."

Having thus refuted [the objection], the proponent (codaka) states his own intention: "The intention is this— that even if the mantra were formed as *eṣām* or *anayoḥ*, it cannot be said to be ungrammatical (*asādhutā*), just as in the case of *pāśān*."
This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṛṣṭānta*).

Just as there is non-eternality and lack of correctness in both [cases], so too here, because of the incorrectness, there is no [application] even for a mantra ending in the singular number; such is the objection.

Here, the proponent (*pūrvavādī*), considering that there is a difference in the fire due to the difference in the animals connected to it—that is, due to the difference in the objects—advocates for modification (*ūha*).

Since the singular form is ungrammatical when there are two fires or a plurality of fires, modification (*ūha*) is appropriate; and the distinction between the fires follows from the distinction between the sacrificial animals.

When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been thus established, the author challenges it by means of the shadow of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Or why, on account of the substratum, is the distinction not intended to be expressed?"
If difference [of the sacrifice] were due to the difference of the related entities (*sambandhin*), then there would also be difference due to the difference of the substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Consequently, how could the singular number be used even in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*)? [Objection: Even when one thing is different, another may not be different;

thus, the difference of the substrata is not intended to be expressed. [Response: In that case, the difference resulting from the plurality of animals (*paśu*) should likewise not be intended to be expressed. This is the resolution.

He explains the commentary: "The [objection] regarding the absence of material cause (*upādāna*) and locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) has been refuted. The phrase "of this" (*asya*) refers again to the animal (*paśu*), implying that for it there is indeed a material cause.
The meaning of this is as follows: the distinction based on the locus is not being relied upon, because of the delimitation by that [material cause].

Because "brilliance" (*tejas*) is not explicitly denoted [by the word *caksus*], and because the animal is introduced by another word—namely, *asya* ("of this")—and because brilliance is denoted only through its delimitation by the animal, it is indeed appropriate to intend a distinction based on that. Therefore, there should be modification (*ūha*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that modification is not appropriate due to the non-difference of the word; for the meaning of the word *caksus* is that which is characterized as brilliance.

Because it is non-different and unitary, modification (*ūha*) is not tenable. Even if there were a difference in the animal which is the relatum, nevertheless, a difference in the sense organs such as the eye—the referents of other words—is not tenable. If there is no difference in the light [which is the essence] despite a difference in the animal which is the referent of another word, how could the eye [be distinct] in that case?
[Application of the term] The answer is: by means of the very definition, despite the difference in substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Intending precisely this "substratum-ness" (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) even when it is distinct, people in the world employ the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) in this manner.

In that case, because the primary intent is the substratum (the eye-organ), one understands there a desire to denote that very substratum. Here, however, in the phrase "May the sun lead his eye," no desire to denote the substratum is understood; for, since [the eye] returns to its source, that statement refers precisely to the substratum. It is not the substratum that has the sun as its source, but rather the light-element (*tejas*); therefore, the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) refers to that [light], and thus there is no modification (*anūha*). The indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated.
11. "Ekadha" (in one way) would be a designation based on repetition due to a single conjunction. 29.

[Page 295] Now this is considered: Is the meaning of the mantra in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) to be described exactly as it was explained in the model ritual (*prakṛti*), or is it to be described in another manner, since the connection with the relevant meaning is possible? In that regard, if it were exactly so in the modified ritual as well—

In that case, because the original ritual (*prakṛti*) prescribes "he should strip off his skin once" (*ekadhā*), the same act must be performed in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) as well; thus there would be repetition, expressed as "once, once. Alternatively, if the description of the mantra's meaning were otherwise, then, since it serves the purpose of providing assistance, there would be no modification (*anūha*). In that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [holds that] even in another application, just as in another assignment (*viniyoga*), the mantra has a different meaning.

Thinking that there would be no fault [in this], he stated the non-modification (*anūha*) by means of another method as well. Now, there is no evidence for postulating a different meaning for the rule "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), since it is already established through its own inherent capacity (*śakti*). However, in the case of another instruction, because the previous one becomes untenable, there must be a description of a different meaning; thus, even elsewhere, non-modification (*anūha*) will occur in that same manner.
He addresses the objection: "What is this so-called *anūha*, which is the cause for describing a different meaning?
The answer is: "It is the favor of the Ṛṣis."
He asks again: "What is that which is called *ārṣa*? The answer: "It is that which is the essential nature [of the mantra] at the time of private recitation (*svādhyāya*).
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—

He says: "The essential nature (svarūpa) as it is favored [in its primary sense] does not exist secondarily in either the original form (prakṛti) or the modification (vikṛti); rather, since its attainment is understood through its function (kārya), a description precisely according to that function is logical.
And the established [nature] is its oneness..."

Since the modification (*ūha*) is to be performed upon the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is precisely that modification which is appropriate for the sake of accomplishing the same purpose in the ectype (*vikṛti*). If, however, the application occurs through direct instruction (*upadeśa*), then the performance must conform to that very form as it is obtained. Even granting that the application occurs by way of functional requirement (*kāryataḥ*), he asks: "Why so? and replies: "There is no authority for assuming a different meaning in the function, because it is already established by the very arrangement of the archetype."
Therefore, those learned in logic maintain that modification (*ūha*) alone is appropriate here, and not the inclusion of a different meaning;
for the status of being the "lord of the sacrifice" (*medhapati*) belongs to both the owner and the deity due to their co-occurrence everywhere.
Because it has been employed [as a reason]. || 32 ||

In this case, since it is logical for both the owner (*svāmin*) and the deity (*devatā*) to serve as the cause (*nimitta*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering both the owner and the deity to be the meaning of the mantra when they constitute the ritual act (*padārtha*), maintains that there is no modification (*anūha*). This is because, having observed the dual and singular endings in various instances within the archetype (*prakṛti*), he believes that their application is possible in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well. Now, [one might object]: "But how can the word *medhapati* [be applied] by means of a single ritual act?"
Since the purpose of the indicative mark (*nimitta*) has been fulfilled, how can there be a twofold meaning for the mantra?

For it is logical that the meaning of the mantra is only that single object which the term *medhapati* brings to mind; how then can a twofold meaning be attributed to the mantra when [the object] is being apprehended?

Because of its specific nature. The intention is that both [deities] are presented by the term *medhapati*, for sentences can have two referents. However, another view is that while it is true that both are mentioned, if no distinction is perceived there, then [the application] belongs to both.

The state of being a sign (*nimittatva*) would belong to you [the opponent]. However, a distinction is perceived: when the reference is to the owners (*svāmin*), the meanings of the dual and singular numbers are justified; for the singular number is appropriate for a single owner, while the dual number is appropriate for a husband and wife. This is not the case when the reference is to the deity (*devatā*), because the deity is singular. Therefore, this mantra refers to the owners, and it should be modified (*ūhitavya*) accordingly. As for the deity—

The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, maintains that "otherness" (*paratva*) is intended; thus, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not explained by way of its having occurred in the past.
For it is understood that what is to be given belongs to the owner, and a relationship based on what has previously occurred is not appropriate, nor does it apply to the sense of "becoming."

It is logical to rely on a past precedent. As for this description of the singular number as having the sense of a group (*gaṇa*), and the reminder that the group itself possesses deity-status in order to prevent the elevation of the word ending in the singular—this [justification] is possible through the logic of the "plural of the noose" (*pāśabahuvacana-nyāya*). When a reason for non-elevation is available, why would one resort to a single reason? Regarding the correctness of the expression, it is simply the correctness of the usage.

"It is not proper to rely [on that]"—for in the case of the *pāśa* mantra, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) of the plural number is possible because of the correctness of the expression (*abhidhāna-sādhutva*). This is a recourse when there is no other way (*agatikā gatiḥ*). Therefore, by demonstrating the correctness of the expression, the singular number is explained as having the group (*gaṇa*) in mind. He asks: "What is the purpose? and replies: "And in the modification (*ūha*), there arises a specific [form], which is the correctness of the usage."
If it were intended to indicate the suffix *tva*, it would apply to external deities;
if it were intended to signify a group (*gaṇa*), then, provided the expression is grammatically correct, that [suffix] does not apply.

[Objection: But surely, even if the deity who is the substratum of the two [mantras] is one, the statement [of duality] remains untenable. [Reply: It is not untenable, because the meaning is unified by a single cause.
But how could there be such an object?
To this he says: because even that which resides in two places is logically established as having unity in its substratum.

Now, one might object: "Even if the duality residing in the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is inherent (*samaveta*), nevertheless, it does not reside in the causal factors (*kāraka*); therefore, the mantra would be purposeless in revealing that [duality]. To this, he says: "And it has been stated that a mantra is purposeful when it denotes an inherent meaning; the substratum, too," [is such].

The meaning is that a factor (kāraka) which has been made known causes [the mantra] to be remembered. Therefore, modification (ūha) occurs by virtue of the deity: when there is a plurality of substrates for a word ending in the dual, or when there is singularity, modification occurs according to the singular or plural number; thus it is established. || 13 || Or rather, there is a restriction; in the case of multiple deities, there would be a modification. || 41 ||

In this context, one considers that the mantra ending in the singular number is set aside; it does not proceed at all by means of modification (*ūha*) due to its singular ending. How is this considered?
The answer is: for when there is duality, this [mantra] ending in the singular—

Regarding the term "application" (*prayoga*): for one who is confused by many corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), it is correct that there is only one correct singular form; therefore, since there is no correctness among the many [corrupt forms], conjecture (*ūha*) is appropriate.

But has it not been stated that "deity" refers to a group of associated deities? Therefore, even here, the use of the singular number to denote them is indeed appropriate. He offers a rebuttal: [the opponent] thinks that this [singular form] would be applicable only in the case of duality.
The meaning of this is as follows:

it has been stated that the usage [of the singular] is established in the case of duality because it expresses a connection (*saṃsarga*). Therefore, here too—whether in the case of duality or in the case of a connection—it is considered that the singular is used there, and not the plural. Consequently, in the case of many [objects], it is merely a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*). "Cessation" (*nivṛtti*) means delusion (*bhrama*), as for example:
Regarding the two [verses beginning with] "pāśān," he states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): or rather, it should proceed [with the word] ending in the singular number.
Why is this? He says: for here, conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is intended [as the meaning], and that [conjunction] occurs between two or among many;
for here, mere conjunction is what remains undifferentiated. Indeed, everyone...

The connection is indeed one and the same; therefore, the singular number is appropriate there. For a restriction regarding usage occurs only when there is a disagreement over the designation (*abhidhāna*), but not even when there is agreement, merely because of non-perception. Wherever there is the capacity to designate, there alone is the usage; in that case, it is of that very same kind elsewhere as well.
The restriction [of grammatical correctness] is based merely on the observation of usage. Why? He says: because it would follow that the word *go* would be incorrect when applied to a cow born today.
Since there is no such incorrectness, here too—as in the case of the base form—the singular number is correct.
|| 14 || There would be a modification in the case of a different purpose, because of the distinctness of the deity; it would be so because of the co-inherence in one [substance]. || 43 ||

In this matter, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the singular form to be correct on the grounds that there is no distinction in the mere fact of association. Whether it be an association with a substratum or an association with a deity, in any case, because the association is one, the singular number is correct. However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the meaning of the mantra is the association with the deity, not mere association.

Because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the meaning of a mantra consists in its connection with the deity, not mere connection; for the latter is not a subordinate element. To the objection that it is proper to express even that which is not a subordinate element because it is inherent (*samaveta*) [in the ritual], he says: "For it has been stated that mantras express meanings that are inherent in a subordinate element."
Not by mere possibility. In the phrase "aṅge hi," the locative case is used according to the rule *nimittāt karmayoge*. Therefore, the meaning is: for the sake of the subsidiary (*aṅga*).

The recitation of mantras with their constituent meanings is performed in order to indicate the subsidiary element (*aṅga*); it is not, however, the mere conjunction of those that are possible. Because of the difference in sacrifices, the conjunction of the deities belonging to various distinct sacrifices is nowhere a subsidiary element. Furthermore, the mantra ending in the singular number is intended to reveal the form of the deity as a subsidiary element. Therefore, due to the plurality of deities, the singular number is incorrect; hence, there must be modification (*ūha*).
Thus it is established.

But if this were the case, would it not follow that there is a contradiction with the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on generic form)? Since specific actions are observed to be denoted [by mantras], the status of the mantra as having that [generic form] as its meaning is not thereby established.

The meaning of this is as follows: thus, it has been shown that the expression functions solely as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). And by demonstrating this, the objection regarding the section on *ākṛti* (the universal form) is raised; for since a universal form cannot function as an adverbial modifier, it would follow that it could not be denoted. He provides the resolution: "It exists here."

The distinction regarding the nominal stem’s status as a designation of a deity is already established; furthermore, one need not resort to the notion of a "deity" as a basis for the relationship merely for the sake of logical consistency.
Therefore, it is not the case that there is a combination of the deities belonging to those distinct sacrifices.
The term "deity" (*devatā*) is not the denotatum of the mantra, because if it were, it would follow that the mantra lacks logical connection (*anvaya*). In this regard,

it has been explained at length elsewhere that the cognition of the form (*ākṛti*) alone is the cause of the connection, since the connection is understood through its universal aspect (*sāmānyarūpa*).

Therefore, whether by the principle that "one does not grasp that which lacks a qualifier" or for this other reason, since the action is connected only with those things that are identical in form (*ākṛti*), there is no [actual] conjunction (*saṃsarga*).
Thus, the designation of the deity is established as the designation of non-conjunction. Consequently, there is no sublation of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
Thus ends [the section] in the work composed by the Great Teacher Śālikanātha Miśra.
The third quarter of the ninth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā* Pañjikā.
In the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the fourth quarter of the ninth chapter:
"Twenty-six [offerings] by repetition in the case of a group of animals, because it is a subordinate element derived from that archetype."

For if there were no modification [of the suffix], their connection would not be complete; because of the modification, there would be no compound, and because of the lack of conjunction with all [the words].

In this regard, five positions are presented, based on the fivefold manifestation of the meaning of the mantra. Among them, the first position is that the meaning of the mantra has the animal (*paśu*) as its primary referent. The second is that it has the number (*saṅkhyā*) as its primary referent. The third is that it has the ribs (*vaṅkrī*) as its primary referent.
Another [position] holds that it is not intended to be expressed at all. The fifth is that its connection is with the number twenty-six. And regarding this fifth position:

This being the case, a relationship between the two is expressed; for when the word "twenty-six" is repeated in the phrase "twenty-six, twenty-six—these are their ribs," it is demonstrated that each of the two animals is related [to the ribs], or rather, by the animals [collectively]. Repetition (*vīpsā*), however, is the desire to pervade; thus, because the doubling of the word is observed, it is intended to demonstrate that the number twenty-six itself is related to the animals.

It is understood that [the word] is sweet. For example, in the passage "A person reaches the Puruṣa as the Nidhana," since the singular number remains fixed for "person" (puruṣa), this is a restatement of the preceding portion.

Because the nature of the number is understood through the act of counting by means of the expression "twenty-six," and because the mantra is not employed as a means for producing a cognition when the number is primary, it follows that the meaning of the mantra is indeed not intended to be expressed; thus, its use occurs without modification.

For a mantra is a "performative mantra" (*karaṇamantra*) when that which is remembered by it is performed, and since the recitation of the *adhrigu* formula occurs at the time of leading [the victim], [it is not modified].

Therefore, because it is not an instrument of action and because it is not enjoined for the purpose of recollecting the meaning, the utterance—having its meaning unintended—is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, there is no modification (*anūha*). When the ribs (*vaṅkrī*) are primary, they are mentioned in a compound. For when there is mention in a compound, the counting of the ribs is understood; by that, their primacy is apprehended.
But how, once the meaning of the mantra has been accepted on the basis of its application (*viniyoga*), can it appear in five ways?

To whatever extent there is an application (*viniyoga*) in a particular context, that alone is the appropriate meaning of the mantra. In response: for one who considers the application to be based on the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone, the meaning of the mantra appears in five ways.
The application of the mantra occurs through context alone;
it is not by means of direct statement (*śruti*), nor by syntactical connection (*vākya*), nor by name (*samākhyā*), nor by position (*sthāna*).
But is this not improper? For if it were to be applied by context, there would be a fivefold manifestation of its utterance—

Since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) is established by the mere [mention of] the mother, it is more logical that [the number] is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*). Where would alternative interpretations of the meaning be of use? He answers:
1. *nya-mā*.

[Page 300] — You have spoken the truth; you are indeed possessed of a teacher! Even though there is application by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), nevertheless, it is entirely appropriate to consider the purpose (*artha*).

When the meaning of a mantra is being examined, if it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) regarding some specific matter, then the indicative power (*liṅga*) is not contradicted by the context (*prakaraṇa*). This is because context establishes a general connection, whereas indicative power establishes a specific connection. Furthermore, when a visible purpose is possible through indicative power, one does not assume an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

It is appropriate for the opponent to argue that, by examining the meaning of the mantra words, the application of a mantra is sometimes obtained from its indicative power (*liṅga*) and not from a direct injunction (*viniyoga*); thus, there are many ways of examining the meaning of a mantra. In that regard, if the animal (*paśu*) is the primary element, or if primacy belongs to the number associated with it, then when another [element] is performed, some benefit is rendered through the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Whether the animals are the primary elements or whether the number is.

Since it is useless for the primary purpose to manifest [the animal] either in its own form or as qualified by the animal, the meaning of the mantra does not provide an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, it is only the predominance of the ribs (*vaṅkrī*) that is beneficial. [Thus one says: "Drive them out along the ribs."
Thus, because the extraction of the whole [animal] is understood from this, it is said: "O slaughterers, carefully detach the ribs along the spine.
By this, the extraction of all the ribs is established;
[the phrase] "along the spine" refers to the backbone.

The effort regarding the third [verse] of the opponent is its state; therefore, it is indeed logical that the statement be made in a compound form. This is intended to demonstrate that "so many curved pieces have been extracted. Now, even here, because simultaneous extraction is impossible, the compound statement is certainly not prepared in various ways.

For if they were extracted together simultaneously, then the statement regarding their combination would be appropriate; thus it is well said that the combined statement itself should be performed. [Sūtra 2] The horse has thirty-four [syllables]; because of that specific mention, it is distinct. [Sūtra 17]

Here, the objection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises by the force of the negation of the word "only" (*kevala*): "He should not say 'thirty-four,'" thus only the word "thirty-four" is prohibited. It does not mean that his statement must be made exclusively as a specific alternative (*vaiśeṣika*).
But how, on this view, is there no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)? Because of the prohibition of the word "thirty-four," [the number] twenty-six—

Furthermore, because of the prescription of a specific word (*pada*), a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result. However, if it is a prohibition of the *ṛc* verse, then this is merely a restatement of the mantra obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), namely: "one should say 'twenty-six'. Therefore, there is no split in the sentence. The answer is: [it is] the word *irā*.
The intention is that this will be so.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) when the *irāpada* is enjoined, so too here, when the *ṣaḍviṃśatipada* is enjoined, the absence of the *catustriṃśatpada*, which was already established, is merely restated (*anūdyate*).
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that this is not a prohibition of the word alone. Why? Because of the hearing of the word "he should speak" (*brūyāt*).
The meaning of this is as follows: a prohibition occurs only of that which is applicable, and the recitation of the *ṛc* is what is applicable here.
But this does not apply to a mere word, because it lacks the capacity to convey meaning. Thus he says: "It is not only when words are spoken that they are engaged in conveying meaning."
For it has been stated that a sentence (*vākya*) is the cause of speech (*vacas*); therefore, it is the [sentence] that is prohibited when applicable, and not merely a word (*pada*).
But surely, as in the case of the word *irā*, there will be a prohibition of the word as well?
He refutes this: "Such a possibility does not exist here.
He asks, "Why? and says: "When it is stated that 'one should understand it as twenty-six,' the term 'thirty-four' [does not follow]."
We accept this as a prohibition. Its meaning is as follows: "One should not say 'gira-gire'"—this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

And a restatement, when describing what is already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does not entail any fault. Therefore, it is appropriate that there is a restatement of the mere utterance of the word in that context.

In this case, even though twenty-six words are prescribed, the exclusion of thirty-four words does not follow, because there is no identity of function; for even there, due to the co-occurrence with the word *udgāna* (chanting), [the phrase] "having made it *aira*,
one should chant" [indicates] that [the *aira*] enters into the function of the *udgāna*.

In the former case, there is a connection with the word *irā* through its constituent part [of the *girā*]; therefore, the *girā* word, which is the instrument for the *udgāna*, is set aside. Here, however, there is a difference because a single purpose cannot be understood except through a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Consequently, a prohibition is appropriate, not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Thus, it is not understood as a prohibition of the word itself.

He states further arguments: "And a split in the sentence is improper," as stated in the subsequent [verse]; and because of the contradiction in the [interpretation of] the *vaṅkri*, there would follow the consequence that it has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

Since the word "twenty-six" cannot denote as many ribs as there actually are, it follows that the prohibition applies specifically to the *ṛc* verses; this is established. [Sūtra 22: Because of its proximity to the *vaniṣṭhu*, the term "urūka" refers to the omentum (*vapā*).

In this case as well, since there is no specific application [of the mantra], the fault lies in the meaning of the mantra itself; therefore, its meaning is deliberated. That very [meaning] is the cause for resorting to a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), thinking: "The omentum is a vulture, the rectum..."

If it were said that [the mantra] is "possessed by Māra," the mantra would have an invisible purpose (*adṟṣṭārthatā*). For in the case of the owl's speech, there is indeed an invisible purpose. Furthermore, at the time of extracting the omentum (*vaniṣṭhu*), there would be a contradiction, because [the mantra] would be equivalent to mere scribbling. If one were to meditate on an owl and then cut the omentum...

In that case, there would be the fault of having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). Alternatively, if it were said that "the *vaniṣṭhu* should not be cut like an owl," then because it would have a contradictory meaning—since the *vaniṣṭhu* must indeed be cut—the principle applies only to the mere distinction between the words. The word *uru* signifies "extensive," while the word *ka* signifies "distinction" through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of denoting a whole, thereby establishing the word *kaśa* as a means of expressing distinction, just as in the case of the three feet.

[The term] *lakṣaṇā* [is used]. Whether there be a compound (*samāsa*) when there is a division of words or not, there is no difference in purpose; thus, because there is no cause for a definitive conclusion, there is no resolution. However, if some specific meaning is conveyed by accents (*svara*) and so forth without contradiction, that must certainly be adopted. In the absence of such [indications], however, there is no pointlessness whatsoever; the restriction is according to one's wish. Thus, both cases have been demonstrated.
By the author of the Bhāṣya:
[Sūtra 4] "The naming of it is for the sake of praise. (23)
In this case as well, that very same point is determined by an examination of the mantra;
it is the same point as in the previous case.

Let that very [act] be what determines the application here as well; however, it is rejected because it has already arisen from a previous [context], for fear of postulating a new application. For if it did not denote the axe, one would have to postulate the application of raising the arms with an axe, since otherwise the manifestation of a relevant meaning would not be possible. Nor can another application be postulated, because the application having the axe as its instrument is already established.
But surely, when praise is expressed regarding the arms by means of the sentence, those two would attain the status of deities by virtue of being the recipients of the hymn (*sūkta*).

To this he replies: praise does not, however, establish the deityhood of the arms. This is because it is also logically consistent [to take the arms] as being "entirely extracted" (*kṛtsnoddharaṇatayā*);
that is, the entire [Soma] is extracted, and not the mantra which is for its own extraction. Its state is "thatness" (*tattā*). Even though the meaning of the mantra is thus established...

And because it is possible for [the word] to designate the deities, this very principle applies by implication to the excellence of both arms. But how is it that the author of the Bhāṣya speaks of *ūha* (modification) in the case of this [word] being a name? It is said: it follows from the nature of the mantra-text (*māntravarṇika*). The sword is established by the mantra-text. Therefore, when it is praised in the singular, the form ending in the singular is used; when there are two or many, the dual or plural forms are used respectively.
And [the rule] ends with the word "vacana" (statement).

|| 5 || In the cases of the hawk, the pin, the tortoise, the *kavaṣa*, the *sreka*, and the single leaf, the statement refers to the generic form (*ākṛti*), because of the proximity of what is well-known. || 25 ||
In this case as well, since a visible purpose is possible, it is not reasonable to assume an invisible purpose that would contradict it; therefore, it is logical that the extraction should be total.
The meaning of the mantra would be: "Make his chest such that it has the form of a hawk.
By having the purpose of total extraction, it becomes a visible purpose; for when there is total extraction, the chest indeed takes on that particular form. But [is this not so]?

To the question, "How is there a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) in the complete extraction [of the portion]? he says: "Because otherwise, a deficient cutting-off (*nyūnāvadāna*) would result. For when the extraction for the sake of the oblation (*homārtha*) is performed as a complete extraction, it results in [portions] that are not deficient. [Objection: But let there be no requirement for a non-deficient cutting-off...

To this he replies: Because of the explicit mention here and because of the scriptural reference to the "cutting out" (avadāna), it is not possible for words such as *śyena* to be used in both senses [simultaneously].
For in the other view, there would be a mere indication of the shape (*ākāra*). As it is said: "The position stated..."
"The purpose" has been stated in the Bhāṣya; and that purpose is mentioned in the context of the slaughter, not in the context of the Uha.

And it is appropriate to state [the reason] as "ūhe," otherwise there would be an inconsistency with the definition (*lakṣaṇāsaṅgati*); such is the objection (*paricodanā*). The resolution (*parihāra*), however, is this intention: that in such a sense, the expression is justified; thus, those [objections] have been raised.

The *adhrigu* formula does not become defective by being recited with a modified form; rather, there is no deficiency in the entire *adhrigu* mantra because its purpose is the complete extraction [of the victim].
1. May it protect us according to the ritual application.
2. "By way of logic" [p. 303]:
In a case that is incidental, there is no expiation because it is for the sake of another.
For it is prescribed for that purpose. || 28 ||
But surely this is an inquiry into qualification (*adhikāra*). What is its relevance here in the context of the definition of *ūha*? He answers:
"However, the determination of qualification is based on the purpose (*kārya*), not on the explicit instruction (*upadeśa*); therefore, it is considered right here."

When the fire itself is the purpose of the *jyotiṣmatī* [offering], then the qualification belongs only to one who has formally carried out the fire for the sake of the *agnihotra*. However, when this performance of the rite is occasional (*naimittika*), then the qualification extends even to one whose fire has been carried away incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*). Therefore, by virtue of the purpose...

Thus, since the determination of the application (adhikāra) does not arise from the direct instruction (upadeśa), there is an inquiry into modification (ūha) during the consideration of the ritual action (kārya). The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī),
considering the principle of the section on distress (ārty-adhikaraṇa), argued in the prima facie position that the intended purpose is expressed through the act of extracting [the mantra].

Just as in the *Ārtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on distress) the dual number was not intended to be significant, so too here, the fact that the pouring out (*udvāna*) is for the sake of this [specific purpose] is not intended to be significant. Therefore, it was argued in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that even when the pouring out occurs incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*), it remains merely occasional (*naimittika*). However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that if the connection with the function were otherwise, it would not exist in the Agnihotra; thus, the fact that it is for the sake of this [purpose] is indeed intended.
It is not respected.

The meaning of this is as follows: the cause for the fire’s going out (*udvāna*) is not merely the act of going out itself; rather, for the person whose fire has gone out, the only thing to be done is the re-establishment of the fire (*agnisamādhāna*). In that case, if there were to be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) even when the fire goes out incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*), then for that [person]... the fire—

Because of the connection with the *hotṛ* priest, there would be no connection with the *agnihotra* for the *jyotiṣmatī* brick; therefore, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) applies only when the fire has been drawn out for the purpose of the *agnihotra*.
Now, it was stated in the section concerning the sick man (*ārta-adhikaraṇa*) that the qualification of the eligible performer is not intended to be significant; to this, he says:
Furthermore, it was stated that the non-intentionality of the qualification applies to the *upadeśa* (the original injunction), not to the *kārya* (the subsequent application).
Therefore, there is a disparity with the *Ārta-adhikaraṇa*.
