In that case, the non-intentionality was asserted due to syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); here, however, the entry [of the qualification] occurs through the function (*kāryataḥ*). Consequently, there is no syntactical split. Therefore—

There is no expiation for a different purpose. Now, regarding the objection that the rising of the fire (*udvāna*) is the occasion (*nimitta*), not the one who causes it to rise (*udvānavān*), he replies:

Just as the status of the rising of the fire qualified by the fire itself was refuted, so too has it been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya; for from the scriptural statement, "He whose fire rises," it follows that the fire itself [is the occasion].
Regarding the term "sign" (*nimitta*): since it is established that fire enveloped by smoke is the sign, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is thus justified; this remains settled.
|| 7 || And in the case of maintaining [the fire], because it is for the sake of another. || 29 ||
Everything previously stated is established as being taught by way of a causal sign (*nimitta*). Such [a sign] does not exist. Why? He says:
"For here, that which has accomplished its purpose is maintained, while that which has not accomplished its purpose is said to be the causal sign."

A resolution is required for that which has not yet achieved its purpose; this [text] is for the sake of resolving that required purpose. Furthermore, the fire here has already accomplished its purpose—that for which it was drawn forth and maintained has indeed been performed.
Therefore, let it be as in the case of another's purpose. As for the avoidance of the ritual sweeping, it has already been stated in the *Prayoga*.
[The action is] by way of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: because the sweeping and other such acts are auxiliaries.
304] || 8 || But it is not so when [the sacrifice] has already arisen, because the injunction does not apply at that time. || 31 ||
Time is an auxiliary (aṅga); and in the absence of an auxiliary, there is no alteration of the primary meaning of the scriptural injunction. Therefore, there is no exclusion of other auxiliaries.
The meaning of this is as follows: although when the fire is drawn out for the sake of the Darśa sacrifice, the time for drawing it out for the sake of the Agnihotra is not obtained—
Nevertheless, it is indeed proper to employ the mantra; for we observe the performance of the principal act even in the absence of its subsidiary parts, as in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice.

Just as the purpose of the scriptural injunction for the Āgneya is not lost (or omitted) even when rice (*vrīhi*) is absent, and thus its performance takes place, so too is it appropriate here. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is this: while it is true that there is a deficiency of a subsidiary part, nevertheless, it is equivalent to [the case of] a specific occasioning condition (*nimitta*).
Why is this so? He says: For it is when time exists that action is impelled, but it is not the case that time exists because of action;
[this is] because of the dependence on material causes (*upādāna*).
Because of the capacity [of the substance]. Therefore, in its absence, since there is no entitlement [to perform the rite], this [offering] is not for the sake of the *agnihotra* alone.

|| 9 || The observation of the offering (*pradāna*) occurs during the cooking (*śrapaṇa*), because it is for the purpose of consuming that which possesses those properties, and because of the mixing, as in the case of honey and water. || 32 ||
"Payas (milk) is not for the purpose of cooking.

Here, moreover, since we take the Veda as our authority regarding distinctions, we understand from the words themselves that the status of being the sentence-meaning belongs to the milk (*payas*), and not to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). [In the case of the statement] "The *caru* is for Āditya," the connection with Āditya belongs to the *caru*.

It is not understood [to apply] to milk, and for that [milk], being for the purpose of cooking is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, it cannot be said that what is cooked is raw, whereby the word would be contradicted; for even in the world, we observe that what is intended for eating serves as a means for cooking.
Moreover, even if there were no cooking as an inseparable concomitant, the "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) does not apply in the case of the Veda. Thus, in that regard—
Regarding this, it has been stated: "But the purpose of the injunction is non-different [from the original].
|| 10 || "In the case of prosperity, the removal of milking would follow its own rule, because it has already commenced. || 41 ||
Or rather, it is a removal (apanaya) because it is prescribed for another purpose, as in the case of the caru and the payas. || 46 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that, because of hearing the word *śṛta* ("boiled"), there is a lack of similarity with the *prāyaṇīya* [offering], despite the commonality of the scriptural term (*śruti-sāmānyatva*).

For it is established from observation that "cooking" (*śrapaṇa*) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); thus, considering milk to be the oblation, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that there is a difference between this and the milk used for the *prāyaṇīya*. Furthermore, this is because the sentences are similar to those of the *abhyudayeṣṭi*.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: since the status of being an offering substance (*pradeya*) is not absent, it is impossible to deny the meaning of the locative case; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is exactly as it is heard.

In the *Abhyudayeṣṭi* sacrifice, because the status of being an offering substance was previously understood, there was a denial of the locative meaning. But here, since that is not the case, such a denial is not appropriate. Furthermore, the word *śṛta* (cooked), even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), is indeed connected with the locative meaning, referring simply to the milk.
By definition, that [term] refers to the sound, for it does not occur in milk because of the mention of "pouring" (*śravaṇa*); the meaning is that it has ceased.
305] || 12 || But because the pourings (*śrayaṇa*) are unprecedented (*apūrva*), there must be an injunction for the purpose of offering (*pradāna*). || 45 ||

Regarding the statement, "He mixes the [oblation] for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the word "milk" (payas) to refer to the substance to be offered, since no visible purpose [for mixing] is obtained. Even though it ends in the instrumental case, it is connected to the deity,
just as the word "milk" ending in the locative case is connected to the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice.
We do not say, however, that because the status of being a deity is already occupied by the third [instrumental case], it cannot be connected as the object to be given (*deyatva*).

Rather, because of the scriptural hearing of a connection with *soma*, which is inherently connected to what is always to be given, it is determined that [the offering] is for its sake alone. According to the injunction "He takes the *maitrāvaruṇa* [cup]," the connection with the deity is understood to belong to the *soma* alone. That [connection] is thus understood...
The *soma* connected with the deity is restated here for the purpose of mixing (*śrayaṇa*); therefore, the milk is for the sake of the *soma*, not for the purpose of being an offering. Why?

Because in another scriptural passage (*śruti*), the mention of the deity would be prescribed solely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the substance to be offered. For that which is given is [only] for the sake of connecting it with another thing to be enjoined; and since it must necessarily be indicated when that other thing is being enjoined, in a dual case, it serves to present the principal object (*śeṣin*).
This is the position of Maitrāvaruṇa. Therefore, because of its connection with Soma as a secondary element, it is logical that the milk serves the purpose of Soma alone.
The remainder has been explained.
|| 13 || When there is the disposal of those items around which fire has been carried, they serve that same purpose, just like the placing of the bricks. || 51 ||

But how, in this case, can a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the mention of a deity be stated? Since in the injunction "One should sacrifice a parasvat to Īśāna," the sacrifice is understood through the very mention of the deity, how can there be a doubt concerning the prima facie position?

And regarding the hearing of the deities, what fragment of meditative concentration (*samādhileśa*) does he consider [to be the result]? The answer is: nothing other than renunciation (*tyāga*) can be established. This was stated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) in the midst of establishing the final conclusion (*rāddhāntasthāpana*).
Conceptual doubt should be examined.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the statement "he releases them after having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa*," the act of release itself, qualified by the *paryagnikaraṇa*, is what is to be enjoined, because no other thing to be enjoined is possible. For if [it were intended] for Īśāna...

By the statement "he seizes [the animal] for himself," the sacrifice is enjoined; however, in the subsequent statement "he releases them after they have been encircled by fire," nothing remains to be enjoined, because the encircling by fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is already established by the general rule (*codaka*). Thus it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. Therefore, what is enjoined is that the seizing must be performed while uttering the word "for Īśāna. Regarding this, he says: "The mention of the deity, moreover, [serves] the nature..."

The intention is that it will be connected [with the result] as if it were a mantra. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: this is indeed an injunction of sacrifice. Why? Because when a connection with the meaning is possible, it cannot be asserted that there is a connection with the word-form itself.

But surely, since an operation is impossible with respect to the word itself, it is logical that the comprehension occurs with respect to the meaning; for in that case, the operation is understood to pertain to the meaning. However, here, since the word exists, it is logical that the operation should apply to the word alone.
The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*) says: Who has stated that it is improper where there is comprehension of a word?
Rather, in this case, there is no comprehension of the word at all; for indeed, when there is no intention to express a meaning, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be apprehended.

Where a procedure is not possible without a formal renunciation (utsarga), the possibility of its occurrence has been demonstrated there by means of the prescribed ritual for the subsidiary parts ending with that [renunciation]. The remainder has been explained along with illustrative examples.
There may be a substitute for the clarified butter (ājya) when it consists of the offering of a substance. || 56 ||

Even though this is clear, a delusion arises from the word *śeṣasaṃsthāpana* (re-establishment of the remainder) in this general rule (*utsarga-vidhāna*), namely that the ritual action does not extend to the end [of the sacrifice]. Consequently, because two alternative views are possible, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced in order to remove that delusion.
Nor is doubt alone appropriate even in this case; as to how the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is determined, he says—the prima facie view is indeed...
Since the remaining ritual forms are mentioned,
one must conclude that by the force of this very fact, it is impossible for there to be an injunction for the performance of those final subsidiary rites.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, states that this [work] must indeed be brought to completion; yet, having said this, it is contradictory to then state a remainder (*śeṣa*) for it.

Therefore, in the statement of a remainder, there is a figurative application (*gauṇasamanvaya*). Nor can "completion" be asserted when there is no completion, because the meaning expressed by the word remains uncontradicted even under an alternative view. The proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "It is proper that it be concluded..."
Regarding the position that it is a different ritual act (*karmāntara*): [The opponent asks] "But how can there be the word 'remainder' (*śeṣa*)?

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) replies: "Indeed, it has been stated in the Bhāṣya that it is precisely because of similarity; the meaning is that it is called a 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) in the sense of being like a remainder."

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "It is true that what was stated in the *Bhāṣya* has been said; however, it is incorrect, because the word 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is heard [in the text].
He states this in a single passage: 'Or, if it is a general rule (*utsarga*), what partiality [could there be]? "

The sense is: "Why has that very same thing been described otherwise? The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) gives the answer: "This is a partiality; the word 'remainder' (śeṣa) is different from what was previously stated."

Furthermore, the remainder does not depend on what was previously stated; for a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) depends on the whole (*avayavin*) that precedes it, but the previously stated [whole] does not depend on the subsequent remainder. Therefore, because it is independent, the general rule (*utsarga*) is based on direct scriptural authority (*śrauta*). It is logical, however, that the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to that [general rule]. Thus, the remainder has been explained with an illustration.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the ninth chapter in the *Pañcikā* composed by the great preceptor Śālikanātha Miśra.
The first quarter of the tenth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
|| 1 || Since there is an extension (*atideśa*) from the original injunction (*vidhi*) to another context (*prakaraṇāntara*), the entire ritual procedure (*sarvakarma*) should apply. || 1 ||
"But surely, when there is sublation (bādha), there must be modification (ūha).

By this, he challenges the relationship of cause and effect between the definitions of modification and sublation stated in the Bhāṣya. For if sublation were to occur only when there is modification, then [modification] would stand in relation to sublation...
The status of being a cause would be reversed; however, when there is sublation, there must be an inferential modification (*ūha*).
He asks: "Who says this? The reply: "For it is perceived thus: when the word 'fire' has ceased [to apply]..."
The substitution of the word *sūrya*. That substitution of the word *sūrya* in the place of the word *agni* is not possible as long as the word *agni* has not been set aside.
Therefore, it is understood that modification (*ūha*) occurs when the word *agni* is sublated. The respondent says: "If it is indeed perceived [that the word *agni* must be set aside]..."
In the case of the *sāman* or its refinement (*saṃskāra*), what is perceived? Upon the cessation of what is there the addition of what?
Neither in the *sāman* nor in its refinement is any sublation (*bādha*) observed of anything; therefore, the application of the *sāman* and its refinement is not caused by sublation.

It follows that modification (*ūha*) preceded by sublation is merely a source of intimidation. Anticipating the objector’s question—"How so with respect to the mantra?"—he provides the answer: "In that case as well..."
Because of the principle that "one should perform the recitation according to the original form," the insertion of the word *sūrya* does not require the removal of the word *agni*.
Why? He says: for the insertion of the word *sūrya* is intended for the purpose of fulfilling the recitation.
It is not caused by the absence of the word "fire.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as the designation was performed with a mantra in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too must it be performed in the modification (*vikṛti*); for this purpose, the word "Sūrya" is substituted. For indeed, without the word "Sūrya," the designation could not be carried out as it was in the archetype.

It is accomplished as follows: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the naming of the principal deity is performed by means of a mantra. In the ectype (*vikṛti*), the Sun (*sūrya*) is the principal deity; since he cannot be made known without the word "Sun," the word "Sun" is inserted into the mantra. However, this insertion is not caused by the absence of the word "Agni. For if it were caused by the absence of the word "Agni," then there would be a sublation (*bādha*).

The modification (*ūha*) would have [the original] as its cause, but this is not the case; therefore, the relationship between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) is not inverted. If that were so, then sublation (*bādha*) would likewise not be caused by modification; rather, it is an insertion intended for the purpose of accomplishing the designation [of a deity]. Thus, in the *saurya* ritual, because Agni is not to be designated, the word "Agni" is excluded; sublation, however, is not caused by modification.
2. Following the objection: "Let there be no sublation preceded by a formal modification (ūha); what harm is there to us? [p. 308]
The intention is that nothing of ours is contradicted. The objector asks: "In that case, what is the relationship of the definition (lakṣaṇasambandha) if there is no relation of cause and effect?"
The respondent says: "An inference is obtained through its effect; what is the connection [to be understood] regarding whether a statement devoid of an effect should be put into practice or not?"

The meaning of this is as follows: since the function of the ritual items in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is the same in the ectype (*vikṛti*), by virtue of that function—the oblation (*havis*) which is to be refined by the material substance serving as its source—it follows that the purpose for inferring the threshing (*avaghāta*) applies precisely to the *kṛṣṇala* grains, which serve as the source-substance for the oblation. Now, once it is determined that the performance of the threshing is intended as a refinement of the *kṛṣṇala* grains, the threshing must be performed.

It becomes devoid of the sacrificial oblation (*havir*), because the purpose of removing the husks is absent; hence the doubt arises: "Should the performance of threshing—which is now devoid of its purpose—be carried out or not? In that case, because the means (*dvāra*) is absent, there is non-performance of the threshing, which constitutes a sublation (*bādha*).
This is the relationship between the definition of *ūha* (modification) and the definition of *bādha* (sublation). What is meant is this: [sublation] is based on the omission of the means.

Therefore, sublation (*bādha*) does not directly constitute the cause of modification (*ūha*); rather, once it is determined through modification that the threshing must be performed because of its connection with the *kṛṣṇala* grains, there arises the certainty of the loss of the means (*dvāralopa*) for threshing, since the purpose of removing husks and chaff is absent in the case of the *kṛṣṇala*. Consequently, sublation occurs; thus, modification stands in a causal relationship toward sublation by virtue of being the cause for the certainty regarding the loss of the means.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being a cause": likewise, the author of the Sūtras himself, having demonstrated that in the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice the cloth and the calf—which take the place of the ordinary *anvāhārya* rice—possess the characteristics of the *anvāhārya*, will show that the cooking is set aside due to the absence of the [necessary] means.
And there are verses on this point:
When the status of the modified sacrifice as something new for its own sake is established within the boundary of being a subsidiary to the primary rite,
it remains defined by the extended application (atideśa) of the constituent elements of the archetypal sacrifice.
When the performance is known, the omission of a subsidiary act is easily determined by the desire to perform another substance that has fallen into the place of the original one.
Furthermore, since there is sublation caused by the omission of a door, there is a dependence on modification (ūha) for the sake of establishing the reason;
thus, the connection between modification and sublation is indeed evident.

Having paraphrased the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage, "What is called sublation (*bādha*)...", he raises an objection: having stated that "sublation" is the falsity of a certain cognition of an effect produced by another cause, [he asks] what the nature of sublation is...
This has been described. However, those who know the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consider this to be contradictory. For a cognition that is certain cannot be false.

Furthermore, the falsity of a cognition consists in its being devoid of an object; yet a cognition that is certain cannot be devoid of an object, because a cognition presents its object by its own inherent power (*svamahiman*). This is especially so for the Mīmāṃsakas.

In our view, consciousness is not false, for those [who hold this view] maintain that falsity consists solely in the non-apprehension [of difference]. The Mīmāṃsakas indeed assert the falsity of cognition by way of its being a non-apprehension of difference, not by way of its being a form of knowledge. [Regarding] the distinction—

For when a cognition of memory arises from non-apprehension, it causes a person to fall into error regarding practical activity by functioning as a semblance of perception; thus, such a cognition is called "false. Therefore, falsity is based solely upon non-apprehension.

Even for those partial followers of the Mīmāṃsā school who maintain that there is indeed a "manifestation" (khyāti) which is erroneous—that is, that the cognition itself is not in accordance with reality—they too do not [accept anything other than non-apprehension].

They claim that certainty is the cause of error; for them as well, the ascertainment of the true nature of the mother-of-pearl is not the cause for the apprehension of silver, but rather the very lack of ascertainment of the mother-of-pearl's true nature. This is what he says: "For them too, the latent impression of ignorance is the cause of error."

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) and latent impression (*vāsanā*) constitute the "impression of ignorance" (*ajñāna-vāsanā*). For one who is conditioned by the ignorance regarding the true nature of mother-of-pearl, the cognition of silver arises.
It is indeed logical that ignorance alone is false, because it is precisely that which is sublated when it is removed by knowledge (*jñāna*). Knowledge...
But it cannot be removed by knowledge; therefore, since there is no sublater [of it], it is logical that knowledge is not false. Thus he says:
"And ignorance is dispelled by knowledge"; thus, it is only for ignorance that falsity is appropriate.
Therefore, the claim that certain knowledge is false is a contradiction.

Furthermore, in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), you yourself have stated that the very state of being well-ascertained is the cause of its validity: "How could the cognition of one who is awake, which is well-ascertained, be subject to subversion?"

Thus, if it is asserted that whatever cognition is ascertained by that [means] is false, there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). Therefore, how can this commentary—which speaks of a sublation (*bādha*) of such a nature—be inferred? This concludes the summary.
The respondent says: To this it is replied—how do those who know the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consider this?
[They hold that] "it is certain" and "it is false" are contradictory; the point is that this is not a contradiction. Why?

Thus he says: "We have stated that even verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us. Nevertheless, what follows from this? He says: "Those Mīmāṃsakas who understand the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that verbal testimony do not speak otherwise [than the truth]."
Since this falsity belongs only to that which is ascertained by means of verbal testimony, it is logical that what is so ascertained is indeed false. How is it ascertained by verbal testimony?

The answer is as follows: For when there arises the expectancy regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*)—namely, "How is it to be performed?"—the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is supplied by the instruction, "It is to be performed in this way. It is postulated that "it is thus" insofar as it comes to be through this [procedure].

The meaning of this is as follows: when the injunction (*niyoga*)—which is the object to be accomplished—is understood within the context of the primary ritual procedure (*prakṛti*), there arises an expectancy regarding the means of assistance (*karaṇopakāra*) as to how it is to be performed. In response to this, the performance-requirement (*itikartavyatā*) is provided by the instructional texts (*upadeśa*) as a collection of constituent elements (*padārtha*). And thus, that very [collection]...
2. Having set aside the notion of a "self," the benefit is conceived in this way: namely, in whatever manner a benefit arises through this collection of entities.

In that way, it is conceived as "by means of this door" and "in this manner. Once the "being-in-this-manner" (*itthambhāva*)—that is, the assistance rendered by the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*)—has been established, there is an extension (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) based on the principle that "the modification should be performed like the archetype" (*prakṛtivadvikṛtiḥ kartavyā*). Thus, there is an extension of both the assistance rendered by the instrument and the collection of constituent elements (*padārthasaṃhati*). Nevertheless, he asks: why is this so? He replies: "And when [the archetype] has not been attained, it cannot be said 'in that same way' (*tadvat*)."

If there were no attainment of the assistance and the collection of constituent elements (padārtha-saṃhati) for the sake of the modified sacrifice (vikṛti-apūrva), then it would be impossible to state that "the modification is to be performed as in the archetype" (prakṛtivat). Therefore, there is indeed an attainment of the collection of constituent elements, together with its assistance, for the sake of the modified sacrifice.

Therefore, the meaning is that the collection of natural (prākṛta) constituent elements, having been obtained in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), is connected as a subordinate factor (aṅga). And that which is obtained is determined; thus, its state of being determined is well-established. Having established the lack of determination [in other cases], he now states their falsity:

"But for that which [is not so]—in whatever manner, by means of a specific door of the natural [elements], there is such a state of being (itthaṃbhāva), namely, the assistance to the performance (karaṇopakāra)."

It is understood to be false because it is not to be performed due to the absence of its means (*dvāra*). To the question, "How can there be an impossibility of assisting the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the absence of a means? he says: "Even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this 'manner of being' (*itthambhāva*) is based solely upon the means."
"Because it is for that purpose.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of "because. Because even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the assistance rendered by the instrument is based solely on the means (*dvāra*), and not based merely on its being for that purpose; and because the assistance in the ectype (*vikṛti*) is likewise [based on the means], therefore, when the means is obstructed...

There is an impossibility of assisting the instrument (*karaṇa*). And when there is an impossibility of assisting the instrument, because it would be ineffective, there is no performance [of the action].

If it does not produce assistance to the instrument by way of obstructing the door (*dvāra*), how then can there be a determination of its [application] in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)? To this he says: "And this determination is based on its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*)."
It has been stated that the authority of a word extends only as far as it is uttered.

The meaning of this is: although [the auxiliary] does not produce an assistance to the instrument by subverting the door [of application], nevertheless, it [assists] the *apūrva* of the modification (*vikṛti*).

The fact that this [subsidiary act] serves that [primary purpose]—its status as a *śeṣa* (auxiliary)—is thus determined. Therefore, there is a verbal certainty, because the word possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding the mere fact of serving that purpose. However, the means (*dvāra*), such as the removal of husks and chaff through threshing and so forth, is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). And this determination was stated while accepting verbal authority; for since the means is to be known through other means of knowledge, [the word does not directly denote it].

It has been stated that this is conceived as false due to another cause (*kāraṇāntara*). He explains the term "another cause" as meaning "by the force of another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaravaśena*).
This is the underlying intention: that the fact of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is determined by verbal testimony, which is itself another means of valid cognition.

Because there is no other means [of cognition] and no door [to it], and because it produces an assistance for the instrument, it is conceptually constructed as false. It is established that what is determined to be false is so conceptualized because it does not assist [the instrument], since it lacks that purpose (*tādarthya*). But how can the falsity of the verbal [cognition's] having that purpose be established by the force of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that the fact of having that purpose is grasped by the verbal cognition itself as being true?
It is indeed real; its falsity cannot be asserted. Even though at that time there is no benefit due to the absence of a means, [it remains real].
1. R *kalpite* 2. A *dvārābhāvena*

An entity does not produce [the benefit], yet because the benefit is inherent (*prākṛta*), it is indeed produced by that [entity], since it is being produced by it within its own nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, there is a connection between the *apūrva* of the modification (*vikṛti*) and the benefit not produced by that [original]. Consequently, [this applies] to the inherent [benefit].

Even for an object whose means [of proof] have been lost, its status as being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) remains entirely unimpeded. But how can the falsity of a verbal [cognition] be established by the force of another means of knowledge?
The answer is: precisely because there is no falsity, for that very reason—
It has been stated that falsity does not arise intrinsically, but through another cause, because there is no certainty regarding the door [of the means].

In the absence of that [certainty], even if there is a purposefulness toward that [object], since it does not produce an auxiliary benefit for the instrument at that time, it possesses a commonality with that which lacks such purposefulness regarding the instrument.

When one perceives that something is the cause of an action, a recollection arises—based on what has been seen elsewhere—that it serves that purpose; thus, one considers it to have its "door" (the means) lost and not to serve that purpose. Since the door is apprehended by that other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), in its absence there arises a cognition as if it were not for that purpose; however, the lack of being for that purpose is not understood through verbal cognition alone. He clarifies this very point: "It is contingent upon another condition (*paropādhika*)."
Who can prevent the self-evident certainty of falsity, just as one cannot deny the seeing-nature of the Self?
He explains the illustration:
"It is not that because it does not see when [the mirror] is without an adjunct that its nature as a seer is lost."

Merely because one does not perceive an object during states such as deep sleep—due to the absence of the operation of the sense organs and other factors resulting from the lack of adjuncts (*upadhāna*)—the Self’s nature as a seer, its possession of the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*), is not lost. That power of vision remains innate even for one who is not currently seeing. Likewise, it assists in the effect [of perception].

Even in that state, the capacity to produce an effect certainly exists, as is seen in the case of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) even when its gateway is closed; for the self perceives objects just as it does in the waking state. Therefore, the sublation consists merely of that much.
If this is so, then one should simply say that sublation occurs due to the absence of a gateway; thus he says: "Now, why has it not been stated in this very way?"
"The absence of a door constitutes a sublation (bādha).

The reply is: "It is not so; what is meant is that there is a sublation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). But has it not been stated that there can be no sublation of a means of valid cognition in itself?

Therefore, since there is no sublation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not even appropriate to speak of "sublation by a means of valid cognition. Thus, the meaning is that its non-mention is not a fault. He refutes [the objection]:
"Even a sublation based on a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is indeed a sublation, just as [the scent] of women is 'fragrant' [only figuratively]."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the absence of a door (to the object) is understood, even though there is a state of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), if there is a recollection of its not being for that purpose (*atādarthya-smaraṇa*) acting as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), then the sublation (*bādha*) resulting from that is indeed a case of sublation.
For example, when the fragrance inherent in the bodies of women who are adorned with fragrant unguents is not perceived, it is [only] recollected [as having been present].

Just as when one perceives the fragrance residing in body-unguents, one becomes as if fragrant oneself; if it is argued that the perception of women as fragrant would thus invalidate the [logical] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then [we reply]: this is merely a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Since a metaphorical designation is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*), there is no sublation of the ultimate reality by such cognition. This is remembered as the lack of purpose in the doctrines of others, just like the fragrance residing in body-unguents.
It is experienced; however, that very [object] appears as if in women of desire due to its inherence in what is conjoined [with the sense organ]. 1. R.
said;
2. A. regarding the knowledge of reality.
He refutes this: "One cannot speak of assistance regarding the effect;
there is only a metaphorical application regarding the effect that sublates."

It does not exist. The effect of sublation (*bādhakārya*) consists in non-performance (*ananuṣṭhāna*) at the ultimate level; that indeed exists ultimately, because in the absence of a means, there is no performance of that which provides no assistance. Therefore, even if the sublation is not ultimate, the effect is indeed ultimate. Just as, for example, although the fragrance [of a woman] may not be ultimate for women who are lustful, the effect of that fragrance—consisting of the lover’s pleasure—is indeed ultimate.

In order to establish that the sublated effect is not to be performed, it was shown that the sublated effect of the means of knowledge occurs when its falsity is demonstrated; for that purpose, even a conditional sublation (*aupādhika-bādha*) of the means of knowledge was mentioned. Therefore, it is rightly said that [the cognition] is definitely false, because no distinction is observed in the resulting action.
When there is no performance of the subverting action,
no distinction or difference is observed between ultimate sublation and sublation based on adventitious conditions; therefore, it is well said that [the object] is certainly false.

Now, one might ask: why does a deficiency not arise when an auxiliary (aṅga) is not performed? [The answer is: because even the effect of an obstruction is scriptural. For by the very scripture that teaches "that which is beneficial must be performed," it is simultaneously taught that "that which is not beneficial must not be performed."

This has been stated from the perspective of the purpose (*kārya*). Therefore, the summary of the meaning here is as follows: even though it is determined that even ordinary objects serve the purpose of the *apūrva* of the modification (*vikṛti*), the cognition that arises—which is conditional and not ultimately real—that they do not serve that purpose, functions as a sublater by its result; whereas the cognition that they do serve that purpose is the sublated by its result, because there is an absence of performance [of the latter].
He restates the commentary: “In the same way, there is an addition, namely that when there is the cognition ‘this exists here,’ there is also another cognition, ‘that exists.
He raises an objection: “Because [it is said] ‘when there is the cognition “this exists here”’.”

Why? The answer is as follows: first, the connection with the assistance (upakāra) belongs only to the archetypal (prākṛta) elements by way of extension (atideśa); furthermore, it belongs to the modified (vaikṛta) elements by way of direct instruction (upadeśa). And this [distinction] applies to the modifications (vikṛtis). In the archetype (prakṛti), however, such a division is not possible, because the connection established by direct instruction lacks any distinguishing feature. For all the auxiliary elements (aṅgas) established by direct instruction...
Because the relationship of assistance [between the primary and its auxiliaries] occurs simultaneously.

Now, if the [auxiliary] is first derived by extension (*atideśika*), then once the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) has its requirements satisfied by that extended [auxiliary], how can there subsequently be a connection with the directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) auxiliaries?

The meaning is that since the requirement of the modified *apūrva* for constituent elements (*padārtha*) that produce assistance is already fulfilled by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) auxiliaries obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), there being no further requirement, there would be no connection with the directly enjoined auxiliaries in respect to the assistance produced.
1. R But even so, 2. R it is well said:
3. A another limb.
He refutes this: "Or how could there be a connection with the prescribed subsidiaries (*aupadeśika-aṅga*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*)?
He says this in a single passage:
A connection with the injunction alone cannot be asserted simply because of that desire; why is this so? He says:
for in that case, the unity of the injunction is the cause of the connection with the subsidiaries.

The fact of being embraced by the application of the principal rite (*pradhāna-niyoga*) is the cause for the connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). For if the connection were based on mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), then since that expectancy would be satisfied even by a few [subsidiaries], there would be no connection with all of them. And in this case of the modified rite (*vikṛti*), the unity of that application is undifferentiated; therefore—
Therefore,
since a single application is observed in the case of the effect— that is, in the state of the effect— both the primordial (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta) are non-contradictory.
And we shall explain this in the section on "additional elements" (*abhyuccayādhikaraṇa*) under the rule *etacca vikṛtau*. Thus it is said: "there is also another [element]."

Now, the purpose of the definition regarding sublation (*bādha*) is considered: whether the archetypal element, even if its function is lost, must be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), or whether it is excluded. But has this not already been established by one who explains *ūha* (modification), on the grounds that ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by their functions?
How can the necessity of performing it be suspected in its absence? The answer is: it is true that dharmas are prompted by the task (kārya);
however, for one who considers there to be a difference in the meaning of the extended application (atideśa) statement, doubt arises.
This is the underlying intention.

There is doubt precisely regarding the existence of the effect (*kārya*). If the door is indeed the original one (*prākṛta*), then there is a sublation of the effect; if, however, it is another door, then there is the existence of the effect as well as doubt regarding the door, due to the difference in the meaning of the extended application statement (*atideśavākya*). To the question, "What then is that extended application statement, and what is its difference in meaning? he says: "In the same way" (*tadvat*). What [are the] subsidiaries (*aṅga*)—?
Is similarity dependent on the [auxiliary] factors (*aṅga*), or is it dependent on the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*)?

"The modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is to be performed like the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*)"—this is the statement of extension (*atideśavākya*) according to the grammarians. By that, the similarity of the modifications to the archetype is stated. Is that similarity dependent on the factors, or...
"Dependent upon the assistance of the instruments.

This is what is meant: is the similarity based on the possession of constituent elements (*padārtha*), or is it based on the possession of the assistance of the instruments? In that regard, if the similarity were based on the possession of constituent elements, then the archetypal elements themselves, independent of the purpose (*kārya*), would [be transferred] to the ectype (*vikṛti*).

If they are [indeed] indicated, then another assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*) must be postulated for them; and for the sake of producing that [assistance], a medium (*dvāra*) must be resorted to by the constituent elements (*padārtha*). In that case, for that which has no perceptible medium possible, an imperceptible one is postulated. Consequently, it cannot be said that there is an absence of the effect (*kāryābhāva*). However, if instead the assistance to the instrument itself is first extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*), and subsequently its production—

When, in the event of a desire for something else, the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are extended by analogy (*atideśa*), then by whichever means they were connected to the primary purpose in the archetype (*prakṛti*), by that very same means they are connected in the ectype (*vikṛti*). Due to the absence of that [means], there is an absence of the effect; and from that follows sublation (*bādha*). In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers similarity to depend upon the auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).
What is the intention?

And this is the underlying thought of one who asks about the intention: for that which is new—the modified (vaikṛta) sacrifice—first requires assistance from the constituent elements (karaṇa), not merely the individual items (padārtha). Therefore, it [requires] the assistance itself by way of being possessed of those [elements].
It is logical that one grasps [the subsidiaries]. The reply is: "For without the apprehension of the subsidiaries, the apprehension of their performance is not possible";
thus, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by the maxim that "one does not grasp a qualified object without first grasping its qualifier."
The meaning of this is as follows: It is true that first there is an expectation of benefit (*upakāra*);

however, since even in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the benefit is something to be inferred, the benefit that arises through the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is what constitutes "benefit" here. Thus, the consideration of benefit is preceded by the constituent elements (*padārtha*). Likewise, when there is an expectation of benefit in the ectype (*vikṛti*), it is preceded by the constituent elements.
It resides within the very cognition of that [object]. In that regard, the injunction grasps only those objects that first present themselves.

For example, according to the view that the denotation of a word is based on an object qualified by its form (*ākṛti*), the word denotes the form itself as it first presents itself. This is because, as the principle "there is no cognition of a qualified object without its qualifier" dictates, the form is understood first.

If, in this way, the injunction were to grasp only the constituent elements (padārtha), then, according to the principle stated previously, the performance of even a non-original (aprākṛta) action would have to be assumed—just as the act of cooking is assumed in the case of the kṛṣṇala berries.

This being the prima facie view, it is replied: this extended application (atideśa) to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) by virtue of "being like that" (tadvadbhāva) does not depend upon the constituent elements.

The auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are not extended by analogy; rather, it is the benefit (*upakāra*) alone that is extended. Subsequently, however, when there arises a requirement for the means of producing that benefit, the extension of the auxiliary elements occurs.

To the question, "Why is there no extension of the auxiliary elements by way of the 'being like that' (*tadvadbhāva*) [of the archetype]? he says: "Because even in the archetype, [the auxiliary elements are established] through performance..."
The connection with the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) depends precisely upon [the requirement of] that [primary act]; otherwise, there would be no connection at all.
The meaning of this is as follows:

first, there arises only the requirement for the performance of the injunctional object (*vidhyartha*), which constitutes the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*); it is not the case, however, that there is a requirement for the auxiliaries independently of that [requirement for the primary].

Consequently, although the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are touched upon first, they are nevertheless disregarded at that time because they are not required then. Even though they present themselves later, it is the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) itself that must be accepted. Once that is accepted, and when there subsequently arises a requirement for its producer, those whose relationship was established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as being the producers of the performance—and who are brought to mind by that very performance—are [to be applied].

The acceptance of ritual items (padārtha) is not restricted to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti); even in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti), their connection with the subsidiaries (aṅga) depends precisely upon performance.

Although the ritual items are initially unrequited for performance and are connected to the mandate (niyoga) merely by way of being subservient to it (aidamarthya), nevertheless, even that established connection would not be tenable without a requirement for assistance (upakārākāṅkṣā).

It is postulated that the cognition of the relationship occurs precisely through the cognition [of the injunction]; or, because of the understanding of the unity of the mandate (*niyoga*), everything possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
If a relationship were postulated based on the unity of the mandate alone, without a requirement for the assistance of the instrument, it would necessarily be by way of being an instrument.

However, since the meaning of the injunction depends upon the effect characterized as the assistance of the instrument, the relationship exists precisely as its producer; thus, this is not a lack of relationship.

This is the fault [of the opponent's position]. If even in the *prakṛti* (archetype) the connection with the subsidiaries occurs solely through the requirement for assistance (*upakārākāṅkṣā*), then what is the distinction between the *prakṛti* and the *vikṛti* (ectype)? To this he says: "But this much is the distinction. Because the denotation of the related [subsidiaries] occurs merely by virtue of being for the sake of that [the primary], once the connection with the word-meanings has first taken place in the *prakṛti*, there subsequently follows the comprehension of the specific effect characterized as the assistance of the performance (*karaṇopakāra*).

The connection of the subsidiaries [with the sacrifice] arises from the understanding of that specific assistance in the modified form (*vikṛti*). He concludes: therefore, when that [assistance] is understood to exist, even the previously understood collection of subsidiaries, in its connection with the *apūrva*, serves as its own cause—the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*).
1. Since non-existence does not depend on anything else, this matter must be understood as depending solely on its own cause; that which is the assistance of the instrument—

The characteristic [of being "like that"] is the cause for the connection with the constituent parts; it is precisely with reference to this that the meaning "the modification (vikṛti) is to be performed like the archetype (prakṛti)" is to be understood.

The sense is that it is the similarity of assistance (*upakāra*) alone that is expressed by the state of being "like that" (*tadvadbhāva*). However, when there is a dependence on the constituent elements (*padārtha*), then...
There would likewise be an infinite regress regarding the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) even in the case of other constituent elements (*padārtha*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if it were the case that only the constituent elements themselves were required, then there would be no distinction between what is an action (*kārya*) and what is not an action (*akārya*).

There is no requirement [for an expectation] because, if all things were to require other things, there would be an infinite regress regarding the expectation for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). However, when the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expected, then it is logical that the expectation belongs only to the effect (*kārya*) and not to anything else.
Thus he says: "Without the assistance of the instrument, which is the effect, no systematic determination is possible."
The meaning is that when that [general rule] is taken into account, the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) becomes possible.

Furthermore, because there is no direct scriptural injunction (*codanā*) regarding the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), their connection [to the archetypal procedure] would not be understood; however, if [the connection is established] through the assistance of the instrument (*karaṇa-upakāra*)—

There is no doubt as to how there can be a connection of archetypal (prākṛta) items with the modified rites (vikṛti). For even in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it is precisely when there is a requirement for the assistance of the instrument that the items exist as qualifiers of that instrumental assistance. In the absence of that [assistance], however, there would be no presentation of those items at all; so how could there be a connection? Therefore, there is a connection of archetypal items with the modified rites.

To the objection that this would not be the case, he says: since it was established in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādye*) that the instruction of ritual elements (*padārtha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is based on the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*), a connection [of those elements] with the modifications (*vikṛti*) is difficult to obtain due to the difference in their respective entitlements (*adhikāra*). Therefore, for the new transcendental results (*apūrva*) of the modifications...
The desire for assistance (*upakārākāṅkṣā*) is that which must be resorted to; and when that [desire] is present, it is assistance itself that is connected first.

Therefore, in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the connection of ritual elements follows precisely the effect characterized as assistance. Consequently, it is established that even the state of being "like that" (*tadvadbhāva*) depends upon performance. In all cases, the fact of being for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*) is based solely on the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*).

To demonstrate this, he says: Even in cases where direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) exist as the causes for the mutual relation of word-meanings, the relationship there too is based solely on the effect (*kārya*), since the word is independent; how much more so, then, for context (*prakaraṇa*) and the rest, whose very existence is contingent upon that effect?

The meaning of this is as follows: even in cases where there are *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*— which serve as the causes and means of communication for a relationship consisting of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of word-meanings— even there, the relationship of the word-meanings is characterized solely by "assistance" (*upakāra*), insofar as they possess the capacity to serve that specific purpose (*aidamarthya*).

But how is it that another relation, characterized as an effect (*kārya*), distinct from the meanings of the words themselves, is accepted? To this it is replied: although the word is independent [of other means of knowledge] in the sense that its meaning is not established through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, it is indeed understood through the word itself. For those [factors] such as context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*), their very existence is dependent solely upon the effect.

1. Since it is not understood [in that way], their connection is all the more based solely on the effect (*kārya*). Even the syntactic relation (*padārthānvaya*) of word-meanings is based solely on the assistance rendered by the instruments (*karaṇopakāra*).

It has been demonstrated in the third [book] that in the *Prakaraṇa* and other [sections], the application of the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof occurs solely through the syntactic connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*).

Therefore, since one who knows the sublation (*bādha*) holds that "that which is devoid of a purpose (*kārya*) should not be employed," there is a cessation of its performance. However, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* [beans], there is a difference due to the specific injunction (*upadeśa*). By the force of the injunction, even though it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the cooking is performed in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*.
And here is the summary of the meaning: expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) are the causes for the expression of what is connected (*anvitābhidhāna*).

Among these, first, there is the injunction’s expectancy for the assistance of the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the form of "how? (*katham*). And that archetypal assistance is brought into proximity by direct statement, by name, or by the indicative mark of a scriptural injunction (*codanāliṅga*). Since it is also semantically competent, the meaning of the injunction is connected with that [assistance].

It is denoted by its own specific term. Furthermore, this "attainment of assistance" (*upakāraprāpti*) is an extension (*atideśa*), because it involves the connection of something belonging to one thing with another. It is also "instructive" (*aupadeśikī*), because it is to be known through direct instruction (*upadeśa*). Whatever is directly taken up by the word for the sake of the injunction’s purpose, or whatever is [taken up] by the injunction’s purpose as cognized through the sentence—that is all indeed instructive. And the assistance is to be presented by the injunction’s purpose.

It is exactly like the archetype (*prakṛti*). In the archetype, the purpose of the injunction brings about the assistance by postulating it; however, in the ectype (*vikṛti*), the purpose of the injunction merely brings into proximity the very assistance already postulated for the archetype as being connected with the purpose of the injunction. The operation of the indicative marks of the injunction (*codanā-liṅga*) and so forth consists in the restriction of this specific [application].

Furthermore, that which is brought forward by a direct statement (*pratyakṣavacanopaneyo*) and that which is brought forward by name (*nāmnopaneyaśca*) are even more clearly *aupadeśika* (based on explicit instruction), because they are presented through the syllables being recited. That which is brought forward by the indicative mark of an injunction (*codanāliṅgopaneyaḥ*) becomes present in the mind only when there is an expectancy for a rule (*vidheḥ*), and not otherwise;

thus, it too is brought forward by the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyarthopaneyaḥ*). In this way, the state of being explicitly taught (*upadiṣṭatvam*) and the state of being extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭatvam*) are contradictory, because they consist in being objects of knowledge through explicit instruction (*upadeśaprameyatayā*).

*Atideśatva* (the state of being extended) consists in the extension (*atideśa*) of that which belongs to one thing to another due to its connection with it. Furthermore, when the assistance (*upakāra*) of the form of the injunction has been obtained, there arises an expectancy for its producer; at that point, just as in the *prakṛti* (archetype), the constituent elements (*padārtha*) enter into syntactic relation (*anvaya*), being presented by that very assistance produced by them, because the causes of syntactic relation—expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*)—are present. And the syntactic relation is...

Since it is not possible [for the meaning of an injunction] to exist without a relationship of primary and subordinate status, the meaning of the injunction is understood as being primary and the ritual elements (*padārtha*) as being subordinate. Therefore, the meaning of the injunction, conjoined with the subordinate archetypal ritual elements, is denoted by its own word. This being the case, the extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual elements themselves is also established.

For if even the constituent elements (*padārtha*) were not connected to the *apūrva* of the modification (*vikṛti*), then, because they would have no connection elsewhere than with the archetype (*prakṛti*), there could be no extended application (*atideśa*). It has already been shown that these elements also possess a connection toward the *apūrva* of the modification, characterized by their subservience to it (*aidamarthyam*). However, for one who does not accept that these [elements] constitute subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) in the modification—in the case of the *satras* which adopt the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*)— [The text continues: ...in the case of the *satras* which adopt the ritual procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice, [the following would apply]. There would be no attainment of the Jyotiṣṭoma subsidiaries, because they are not subsidiaries in the Dvādaśāha sacrifice, and there is no recognition of the sublation of what is not a subsidiary. Furthermore, for that which is not a subsidiary—just like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the *pavamāneṣṭi* offerings, or the *godohana* vessel—there is no attainment [of the archetype]. Nor is there attainment of the archetypal elements through the injunction of the primary rite; rather, there is merely the communication of their performance. And that applies without distinction to those [elements] taught in the specific instruction.

And [this applies] to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements as well. Consequently, the performance of the modified (*vaikṛta*) elements would not occur subsequent to the archetypal ones. If the archetypal elements were recited within the injunction of the primary rite (*pradhānacodanā*), then their performance would logically follow immediately after the primary rite due to that textual sequence. Likewise, by accepting a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), that which is enjoined in the modification (*vikṛti*) along with the archetypal element—[that would not occur].

It might be so. For if the constituent part (*aṅga*) were a primary ritual element (*prākṛta-padārtha*), then there would be an option (*vikalpa*) due to their equal strength. However, if it is not a constituent part, then—as in the case of the prohibition against speaking untruth—there must be an absolute prohibition, because the prohibition functions as a constituent part and is therefore applied more rapidly. For application is rapid in the case of a constituent part; but in the case of what is not a constituent part, it is delayed by way of the application of a constituent part. And the text [states]:...
For one who does not accept the extension of word-meanings everywhere, this [position] is contradicted; so, enough of this excessive digression.

Nor should it be argued: "How can word-meanings belonging to one thing be connected elsewhere, given the contradiction between what has been employed and what is being employed? For the contradiction of cognition occurs only in the case of employing what has already been employed, provided that [the meanings] were equal [in status].

If a relationship were admitted even in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), then there would be a contradiction with experience, as in the case where that which belongs to Devadatta is said to belong to Yajñadatta. However, when the connection of assistance is established through the state of "possessing that" (*tadvadbhāva*), and subsequently the objects are connected because they produce that [assistance], then there is no fault whatsoever. For example, having been connected to the assistance by way of the state of "possessing that"—
There is no contradiction with experience regarding the *māna* (the means of knowledge), for otherwise, how could even a benefit (*upakāra*) belonging to one thing be connected to another?

Nor should it be argued that the benefit does not constitute a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the primary rite (*prakṛti*), because that would lead to the consequence of there being no connection at all; for otherwise, its connection with the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual potency) would not be possible. And if there were no such connection, the very principle that "that which belongs to one thing is connected to another" would be undermined.

It would not be so. Furthermore, this extension (*atideśa*) of word-meanings is based on the authority of the *kārya* (the ritual function), not on the authority of direct instruction (*upadeśa*). This is because [the extended meaning] is neither established by the recitation (*pāṭha*) nor by the injunctive sense (*vidhyartha*). For word-meanings are not established by the injunctive sense; rather, they are established by the *kārya* known as "assistance" (*upakāra*), which is itself established by the six chapters (*adhyāya-ṣaṭka*) that constitute the authority for the injunctions. As it has been said: "[The application] is based on direct instruction... (*aupadeśikī*).

Cognition has been examined; now, comprehension through the effect (*kārya*) is being considered. And by "effect," what is intended is the instrument, the assistance, and so forth, not *niyoga*. For if *niyoga* were taken as the effect, then the deliberations of the fourth chapter would have to occur within the second section (*ṣaṭka*).
Now, since the benefit (*upakāra*) is directly taught (*aupadeśika*), why are the constituent elements (*padārtha*) that are conveyed by it not also considered directly taught?

It is said in reply: An "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is indeed a textual composition that conveys the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*); it does not depend upon the meaning of an injunction [for its own validity]. It is said: An instruction is indeed a textual composition that conveys the meaning of an injunction; it is not dependent upon the meaning of an injunction.

There is an instruction (upadeśa). Therefore, whatever is understood from a word that depends upon the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely what is "taught" (*aupadeśika*). And both that which is understood through the effect (*kārya*) and that which is understood through the instruction are indeed verbal (*śābda*). Regarding their status as verbal, this is the distinction: some are taught, while others are understood through the effect. Enough with excessive elaboration.

What is the purpose [of this], or what is the intention behind asking how a modification (*vaikṛta*) is illustrated? He states it in a single passage: "The purpose is stated as 'that which has its function sublated is set aside'; by that, the purpose is first established. And in all modifications, there is cessation because of the absence of [original] function."

The example, moreover, is not clear. Therefore, with what intention is the question regarding the purpose and the example? The answer: this is the intention—that where there is an independent injunction of something else for the sake of a particular effect, from that very [injunction] follows its exclusion [from other applications].
"What is the scope of the general rule?

This is its meaning: where there is no positive injunction, such as "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin*," or where there is an injunction of something else for the sake of a specific ritual purpose, such as "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds"—in those cases, it follows from that very [general rule].

[The cessation] is not [due to the absence of its effect]. As for this cessation by way of the general absence of its effect, what is its object? Because he did not know the object, and thus—failing to regard even the cessation already stated as a purpose due to his ignorance of the object—he asked about those two. When he had asked thus, [the author] demonstrated that "this is the object," and the object—
There are two purposes. Or rather, by what specific distinction is this section commenced?
The reply: Thus far the aphorism concerning the general subject has been explained; now, however, it is explained in detail regarding the particular and the general.
The intention is that there is no tautology because they function as distinct objects of cognition. He raises an objection: "But has this not already been considered in general?
Therefore, all intended particulars serve as examples; what is the use of a specific consideration? He provides the answer:
There is a distinction in this matter. What, then, is it?—even acts such as threshing, though they are non-natural (apākṛta) effects, certainly do occur; what is the intended meaning?
The reply: Because of hearing the word *caru*, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that cooking itself is what is obtained here as well.
The meaning of this is: this use of the word *caru* occurs even where there is no *caru*.

How could the properties of *caru* be independent of their purpose? For the purpose of the *āgneya* [offering] has already been established; it is for that purpose that the word *caru* exists. However, even if independent of its purpose, the word *caru* serves to extend (*atideśa*) the properties of *caru* to what is not *caru*. Consequently, cooking (*pāka*) also follows from the very hearing of the word *caru*. And just as there is cooking, so too must there be threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts. It is with this intention that [the author speaks of] the *apūrva*.
1. Having asked, "Does the *barhis* become [the vessel]? [p. 319], the proponent now states that intention: "But surely, it follows from the very statement, 'He cooks in ghee'..."

[The opponent asserts] that it is for the sake of cooking. [The author] refutes this: the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the clarified butter is for the purpose of the substance itself, and not for the purpose of the injunction regarding cooking.

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that here too, the application [of the ritual details] is based solely on the word *caru*. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*) asks: "Does the word *caru* preclude the fact that the ritual details (*dharma*) are prompted by the purpose to be accomplished (*kāryaprayuktatā*), or are they prompted by the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇopakāraprayuktatā*)?"
The sense is that, as long as the fact of being prompted by an effect is not obstructed, the effect itself is the motivator.
The proponent of the prima facie view says: "In this example, it obstructs the state of being prompted by an effect. How does it obstruct it?

The reply is as follows: This word *caru* is conventionally established as being used for well-cooked rice; however, in the case of these *kṛṣṇala* grains, there is no cooking—the meaning of the root *pac*—which results in softening (*viklitti*). Therefore, this sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consists of food that is already well-cooked and ready to be eaten.

Therefore, this word *caru* [used] with respect to what is not a *caru* should be understood as figurative (*gauṇa*), namely as "like a *caru*" (*caruvat*). Consequently, by means of the word *caru*, this is what is stated: "The properties (*dharma*) of a *caru* are to be performed even for that which is not a *caru*. Similarity is the basis for the properties. But why is it figurative? To this he says: "Because the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is not direct (*anāñjasa*)."

Therefore, since there is no clear proof [of its primary sense], the word "other" (*para*) when applied to something else is used figuratively (*gauṇa*). To the question, "Why does it not simply follow the literal meaning (*vācanika*)? he says: "It has been shown in various places that even by a hundred verbal injunctions, one cannot postulate a different capacity for a word."

Therefore, it is not primary in that context because it does not produce a specific modification in the performance; rather, this word *caru* is devoted to the ritual application due to its similarity in nature to the *dharma*, just like the term *agnihotra*.

The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, maintains that because the word *caru* is applicable even on the basis of similarity to the sacrificial oblation (*havissāmānya*), or due to its connection with the act of cooking (*śravaṇa-yoga*), whatever is stated in the scriptural injunction is authoritative exactly as expressed.
The meaning of this is as follows: the word *caru* applies even by virtue of similarity to what has already been established.

[The objection regarding] the application [of the procedure] is resolved. Furthermore, similarity is established by way of being an oblation (*havis*) and by way of being cooked; and the purpose is merely to produce a specific activity. In the case of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, however, when there is an expectation of assistance, one resorts to similarity of function (*kārya-sādṛśya*) because they provide what is required. Here, on the contrary, the expectation for assistance is already fulfilled; rather, it concerns the performance of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth, which were not previously required.
Thus, it is independent of any injunction. Therefore, only that which is directly enjoined by the scriptural statement—namely, cooking—is to be performed, not threshing and the like.
But surely this scriptural statement is not appropriate for enjoining cooking, because there is no softening [of the grain].
The objection that "this is because it has the sense of the root *pac* (to cook)" is merely a challenge. The reply is: we shall explain later how the statement is logically consistent.
1. She was indeed swift.
Or rather: what is the distinction here?
The answer is: when [the object] is not yet ascertained, there is no possibility of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: for sublation (*bādha*) is supported by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when the absence of the effect is certain; however, where the absence of the effect is doubtful, the sublation lacks a basis in valid cognition. [The author] raises an objection: "Or [is it] the performance [of the rite]?"

How so? Just as sublation is not possible because of the lack of certainty regarding the non-existence of the effect, so too is performance [of the rite] impossible because of the lack of certainty regarding the existence of the effect. How so?
The reply is: "An extended application (atideśa) does not depend upon certainty regarding the performance.

The meaning of this is as follows: although the performance is not certain because the sacrifice to the Wide-striding One (urukrama-ijyā) is a mere act of dedication (pratipatti); for an act of dedication does not employ a substance [as a primary means], but rather—

It is employed with a substance alone—that substance which is occasionally present, namely that which is touched by the wooden sword (*sphya*) or trampled upon. Therefore, this restorative rite (*pratipatti*) is one whose application is not certain. Nevertheless, the extension (*atideśa*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries to it is indeed certain.
In that regard, if the invocation of Viṣṇu is performed, then if the sacrifice to Urukrama should happen to occur, it becomes endowed with its constituent qualities (*saguṇa*).

For otherwise, if it were to occur [only] by chance, it would be defective; and if it were not to occur at all, then there would be no harm even if the invocation (*āvāhana*) had been performed—this is the meaning. Even when there is doubt, the invocation must be performed; for doubt regarding the purpose (*ārtha-saṃdeha*) is also a factor that prompts action. If there is an extended application (*atideśa*), there is certainty regarding the performance.
He does not depend on anything else; rather, what does he depend upon? To this he says: "For he follows the determination of the scripture.
And the scripture has determined that "that which would be crushed below. Therefore, in accordance with the scripture, this one action is first determined.

In this case, the extended application (*atideśa*) is also certain. Therefore, the uncertainty regarding the performance (*prayoga*) is not capable of subverting the extended application; and since the limb has been extended, the invocation (*āvāhana*) must indeed be performed. Furthermore, as in the case of addressing a king or his minister, nothing visible here is contradicted; thus, this extended application remains unopposed.

This being the case, it is replied: You have spoken the truth, provided that the scope of the scriptural meaning (*śāstrārtha-adhikāra*) were also certain in this instance. According to the scripture, the nature of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is determined; the scope regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) is based on the substance to be disposed of as the occasioning factor. However, this substance which serves as the occasioning factor is not certain.
And the scripture following that [is] likewise.

Although the scripture is certain in its own nature, it is nevertheless said to be uncertain insofar as it establishes the qualification for the ritual (*kratvadhikāra*). Therefore, extension (*atideśa*) is not [applicable], just like sublation (*bādha*).
It is impossible to speak without certainty;

just as it is impossible to speak of sublation (bādha) without the certainty that the effect is not lost, so too an extension (atideśa) cannot be spoken of without the certainty of the qualification (adhikāra). Therefore, in this case, there is simply non-performance.
This has been stated more fully: "And when the ritual application (*prayoga*) has not commenced, a performed subsidiary (*aṅga*) does not become beneficial.

[Page 321] By the non-commencement of the preliminary application (*prayoga*), he demonstrates the lack of qualification; and in the absence of qualification, there is no extension (*anatideśa*); consequently, that which is not an auxiliary member (*anaṅga*) is non-beneficial.

[Objection: But surely there is no sublation (*bādha*) here of that which is certain; for you have stated that this scripture is indeed uncertain. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is a sublation here characterized by the certainty of falsity (*mithyātva*), as was proposed. [Reply: It is said: No.

When a scripture is ascertained, if it is not ascertained due to another cause, its falsity is indeed established. Even if this scripture is ascertained by its own nature, it remains unascertained due to the lack of ascertainment regarding its cause, by virtue of another factor. This is because the cause is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like a door. Just as a door is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge and its absence constitutes falsity, so too is the case with the cause.

If that [object] is cognizable by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then in the absence of certainty regarding it, the scripture itself lacks the status of being a cause for qualification (*adhikāra*). Now, it was stated that sublation (*bādha*) consists in falsity, not in uncertainty;
therefore, there would be a contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñā*).

The sense is that there is no connection here because [the object] is external to its own nature (*svarūpa*). The answer is: even non-determination (*aniścaya*) is indeed a state of falsity (*mithyābhāva*). Why? And since non-apprehension (*anadhyavasāna*) is equal in both cases—both in the case of absence and in the case of the non-determination of the effect—there is indeed sublation (*bādha*), as there is no difference in their being false. Not so.
"And performance is not possible when [the object] is uncertain.

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever is certain yet not performed results in a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), because the state of being deficient depends upon the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And when something uncertain is not performed...

Since there is no deficiency [in the ritual], it is appropriate here that there be simply no performance of the invocation (*āvāhana*). Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is indeed certain in its essential nature.
