Even here, the state of falsity is based solely on limiting conditions (*upādhi*); thus, because the cause does not arise, there is no undertaking of the sacrifice to Viṣṇu (*urukramejyā*), and this is not due to uncertainty regarding the meaning of the scripture. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "that which is connected to the undertaking..."
[This refers to] the performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

Therefore, it is certain that the performance of the auxiliaries occurs through the commencement of the primary act (*pradhāna*). Yet, because there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) [to the result], the primary act has not been commenced. Consequently, there is no one who would be motivated (*prayojaka*) to perform the auxiliaries.

For this reason— that there is simply no performance of the invocation— it is well said: “And when the ritual application has not been commenced, that which is performed as an auxiliary does not become a benefactor.”
The *iṣṭi* sacrifice should cease [at the first attempt], because it is connected with the commencement and is a subordinate element; for the commencement is connected with the primary rite.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites possess the status of being subsidiary members (*aṅga*) precisely because the undertaking (*ārambha*) has not been abandoned.
Even though the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others are subsidiary members of the Jyotiṣṭoma, nevertheless their undertaking certainly exists; thus, by virtue of that undertaking—

The Ārambhaṇīyā [rite] should be performed for the sake of removing defects. However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that this is indeed an injunction for a distinct performance; namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."
That injunction is an injunction for another performance, namely the Soma sacrifice of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). And it has been stated that the commencement depends upon the performance.

Whether that ritual act (*padārtha*) is the very first one, or whether there is a falling away due to negligence—in either case, it does not depend on the performance of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering]. To the question, "How is it that they have no performance?", he says: This is an injunction for the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma, not for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*.

Since [the cause] has ceased, therefore the *ārambhaṇīyā* and other rites, whose occasion has been lost, should not be performed for the sake of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rituals. Furthermore, the phrase "api ca" (moreover) is merely an additional argument, as this section is devoted to establishing the underlying logic (*nyāya*). From this point onward, the occasion being established—

When there is a sublation (*bādha*) regarding the door, one should observe that it is merely an examination of its state. It has been stated that sublation occurs by way of the cause (*nimitta*), because it is dependent upon the absence of the cause.
|| 3 || Furthermore, from the primary [cause] when conjoined with another, all undertakings cease.
Because they are its limbs. || 5 ||

In this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that there is an injunction for the performance common to both the subsidiaries and the principal, maintains that the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [is required].
For in the previous case, it was held that there is performance of the principal alone, not of the subsidiaries; therefore, [the opponent argues] regarding the commencement of the subsidiaries—

Because [the sacrifice] exists [as a distinct entity], the *ārambhaṇīyā* should not be performed as its motive; however, in this case, since even the *iṣṭi*-offerings are primary, the *ārambhaṇīyā* must be performed. Furthermore, it is not only the performance-injunction (*prayogacodanā*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma. He explains this very point: "This is not the performance of the *iṣṭis* alone, nor is it the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma alone; rather, it is a common performance."

Therefore, the commencement (*ārambha*) is also common [to all sacrifices]. Since it is the commencement that must be performed, it is called the *Ārambhaṇīyā* [offering]. And this does not bring about a contradiction with the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, according to the maxim: "Like one who eats from a brass vessel, [the rule applies] even when [the primary object] is not present."

For there is no contradiction whatsoever in performing the *ārambhaṇīyā* for the *saumika*, *dārśa*, and *hautraka* rites; whereas if it were not performed, there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the *aiṣṭika* rites, just as a disciple who eats from a bronze vessel suffers if he does not take up a bronze vessel [for his teacher].
A proponent of a partial conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) challenges the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Does this person not see the scriptural statement regarding the *agniṣṭoma*?"
"Because it brings [the fire] for the first time.

By this statement, he indeed thinks that since the Agniṣṭoma is prescribed for the purpose of the Anvārambhaṇīyā, the Anvārambhaṇīyā is excluded—just as the Barhis is excluded by the prescription of Śara grass. He provides the resolution: "Certainly, he sees [this]."
However, this statement refers specifically to the first performance of the Agniṣṭoma for the sake of its fruit;
one perceives that it is not an injunction for the sake of the Ārambhaṇīyā,
but rather that this statement is intended solely to prescribe the sequence, not the Ārambhaṇīyā itself.
This is for the purpose of substitution.
This being the position reached, it is stated in reply: the Ārambhaṇīyā rite need not be performed, because this is the commencement of the Agniṣṭoma.
The preliminary application has been stated. Without having understood the meaning of this text, [some claim] that this is intended as a rule for the performance of the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite.
Having considered this, the opponent objects: "It is true that it was stated that the injunction for the Agniṣṭoma is not for the purpose of the Anvārambhaṇīyā.
The proponent (the Siddhāntin) replies: "By whom was it said that the injunction for the Agniṣṭoma is for the purpose of the Anvārambhaṇīyā?"

Even so, not understanding this intention, he raises an objection: "If the performance [of the *ārambhaṇīyā*] is not possible for the sake of the commencement, why then is the *ārambhaṇīyā*, whose purpose is not lost, not performed?"
He refutes this: because there is no loss of commencement for the *iṣṭis* due to the commencement of the *agniṣṭoma*.
The meaning of this is as follows: since the *agniṣṭoma* is being performed for the first time, it possesses a specific character that is being grasped; therefore, its—

[This is] the commencement. Since the performance of the *iṣṭi*-related rites occurs precisely through that commencement, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should not be performed because their commencement has already taken place. Furthermore, the commencement of the *agniṣṭoma* does not necessitate the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, nor does it occur for one who has already performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*;
this has been stated on the grounds that other causes are not the motivators (*aprayojaka*) with respect to the *ārambhaṇīyā*. Therefore—
Thus it is established that here too the performance is indeed without the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering.
But in that [sacrifice], there may be [the offering] as in the case of the Prayājas. || 4 || 6 ||

Here, he raises an objection to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But surely, in the scripture concerning the *ārambhaṇīyā*, the injunction 'as in the archetype' (*prakṛtivat*) is not capable of enjoining the function of the *anvārambhaṇīyā*. Why? Because we understand the function from this very scriptural injunction that prescribes the function of the *ārambhaṇīyā*, and it is precisely here that we perform the extension (*atideśa*)."
This is merely the play of a child, because it entails the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, we do not see anything here that truly requires refutation.

A partial respondent (*ekadeśin*) offers this resolution: "To this it is said: [the injunction] 'one should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices' refers to those [sacrifices] whose properties (*dharma*) are not yet fully completed."
How can it be extended [by analogy] to be like that?

The meaning of this is: the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is conceived together with the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] itself. Therefore, having set aside the *ārambhaṇīyā*, [the procedure] of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—

The modeler (rūpakāra) cannot be extended [to the new sacrifice]. Therefore, the sense is that if one accepts the extension of the *prayāja* and other elements, then the *ārambhaṇīyā* must also be extended.
The objector asks: "Or how does the *anvārambhaṇīyā* depend on the assistance (*upakāra*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa? [This refers to its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.]

The effect requires the assistance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, because otherwise the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) would follow. This is simply a logical principle and not some defect; as he himself says: "Or what is the loss of direct perception of the self?"
Although it was stated that [the *nārambhaṇīyā*] is not for the purpose of the commencement (1.
R), [it is] for the sake of the primary [rite] (2. A).
3. It is conceptualized.
4. From this, [it] proceeds.
The performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), being incomplete in its constituent elements, is not extended [by analogy]; nevertheless, nothing is lost for us.
An opponent who holds a partial view says: "If the *ārambhaṇīyā* [introductory rite] is not extended, then the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would likewise not be extended."

Because it is impossible to extend an injunction when the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is incomplete; yet you yourselves accept the extension (*atideśa*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Therefore, that very [extension] is lost. He states this in a single passage: "Therefore, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* must also be performed.
If the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are extended, but the *ārambhaṇīyā* is not extended, then conversely, there would be no extension of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth."
The objector says: It is better that there be no extension (atideśa) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth when it is logically established,
rather than an extension of an unestablished benefit (*upakāra*).

But when the function of the *ārambhaṇīyā* is being extended [to another rite], it follows that an as-yet-unestablished benefit is what is being extended—just as this statement [suggests]; and that is improper. The supreme resolver says:
"This is like asking about mangoes and answering with *kovidāra* trees."
Thus it follows:
for example, someone who is counting in the dark, being asked "What are these mangoes?", not understanding the meaning of those words, says: "These..."
"Regarding the term 'kovidāras,' it is just as you have been urged by failing to understand this entire statement of ours.
The respondent reveals his own intention: "For it is one who has already performed the *ārambhaṇīyā* that is enjoined to perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
it is not, however, an injunction [for the *ārambhaṇīyā*] as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*."

The meaning of this is as follows: the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] is not enjoined as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Why? Because it is only for a person who has already performed the Ārambhaṇīyā that the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are enjoined. Therefore, the Ārambhaṇīyā does not have the status of being a subsidiary part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa modifications (*avikāra*). What follows from this?

This follows from that: it is not possible to preclude the extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) regarding the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering]. Why? Because the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is already fully understood as providing its assistance even without the *ārambhaṇīyā*.

The meaning of this is as follows: the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) is postulated by taking the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) themselves [as its basis], because it is those very subsidiaries that produce it. By virtue of their being for the sake of the apprehender (*grāhakaidamarthya*), even an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) quality is postulated as the assistance to the instrument. And that [status of being] "for the sake of the apprehender" belongs to the subsidiaries alone; therefore, apart from the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice, which is not a subsidiary [of the main sacrifice], there is no [need for it] since the assistance is already known [from other sources].

In the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is no contradiction in the extension (*atideśa*) of the *prayāja* offerings and other elements to the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite. Now, one might object that the *ārambhaṇīyā* itself ought to be treated in the same way. The meaning of this is as follows: just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), once the commencement has been performed—

The sense is that since the *ārambhaṇīyā* is an undertaking (*ārambha*) performed by one who has already been assisted [by it], the *ārambhaṇīyā* would follow [ad infinitum]; thus, even in the case of the *ārambhaṇīyā*, another *ārambhaṇīyā* would be required. Therefore, because of the fault of infinite regress (*avyavasthā*), it is more appropriate to abandon the extended application (*atideśa*) in order to establish a fixed rule.
He refutes this: "This is true; for this very reason, he raises the doubt regarding a lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*)."
The proponent of the prima facie view [says]:
Since the commencement performed by a person consecrated by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is beneficial,
therefore [one may act] with a distracted mind.

[Page 325] Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) suspects that there is no entitlement to perform a second *ārambhaṇīyā* when the first *ārambhaṇīyā* has already been performed;
he demonstrates this under the guise of a conclusion by stating: "Therefore, by implication, the more excellent arrangement..."
It is considered that in all circumstances, power alone is the regulator; therefore, there is an extension of [the ritual] as far as the power extends.
However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: regarding the Ārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi], for one who is "commencing" the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices...
He is the one authorized.

The meaning of this is as follows: since the one who has begun the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) is already authorized for the Ārambhaṇīyā, there is no separate commencement of the Ārambhaṇīyā. Thus it is said: "Therefore, one should perform the Ārambhaṇīyā without a further commencement."

It is fit [to be performed]. Therefore, the meaning is that because it does not depend upon qualification (*adhikāra*), it does not depend upon having already commenced the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice. Thus, although this commencement of the *ārambhaṇīyā* has been established, its falsity—being based on the causal condition (*nimitta*) of qualification—is set aside.

The meaning is that there is falsity (mithyābhāva) precisely because of the absence of the cause consisting in the form of an undertaking (*ārambha*). As for this second resolution—that the same scripture is not capable of conveying two meanings, namely, to make known the performance of the *ārambhaṇīyā* and to extend it (*atideṣṭum*) to that [other sacrifice]—that is not the case if its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is admitted; for if it were an auxiliary, the *ārambhaṇīyā*—

The scripture (*śāstra*) also functions toward the conceptualization of subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*). Now, one might object: this acceptance of subsidiary status would also preclude the extension (*atideśa*) of the *prayāja* and other such elements, because that which assists while possessing incomplete properties is not subject to extension. [The author] refutes this:
No, because its purpose is merely to demonstrate non-existence.
This statement—"In the Ārambhaṇīyā [rite], there is no Ārambhaṇīyā"—is intended solely as such. Nor does the acceptance of this position entail any further fault. Therefore, it is well said.

And the ritual action would cease because its purpose is the conjunction with the substance; since that purpose no longer exists, it ceases, for its subservience to that purpose is established by direct scriptural statement. || 9 ||
The opponent’s position— that this oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) does not have the purpose of producing the post—

is the intention of one who asserts that the oblation for the post must be performed even in the case of the *khalevālī* (the wooden hitching-post used instead of a post). What is the reasoning behind its not having the purpose of producing the post?

The answer is: Just as in the case of [the preparation of] the sacrificial post (yūpa), no specific function is perceived in its production; therefore, because it serves an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti) must be performed even for the threshing-floor post (khalevālī), just as in the case of the encircling (parivyāṇa) and other rites. [Regarding] the Khadira—

For indeed, various substances become sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). In that context, it is logical that whatever ritual action is performed upon *khadira* wood and other such materials has the purpose of producing a sacrificial post through the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that very material. Furthermore, no functional role for the *yūpāhuti* (post-offering) is observed in relation to the *khadira* wood and so forth.

Therefore, since its purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the *yūpāhuti* must be performed even for the *khalevālī* (threshing-floor post), just as in the case of the *parivyāṇa* (encircling) and other rites.
The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is as follows: it is true that no visible benefit is perceived at the time of production;

nevertheless, by means of the word *takṣaṇa* (hewing) and others, we understand that the purpose is production, as in the statement: "One who is about to carry the sacrificial post (yūpa) must offer an oblation."
How so? For the learned teach that the word *accha* is well-established in the sense of "to reach" (*āptum*). Let it be that its meaning is "reaching";
nevertheless, how can it mean "origination"? He says: "And the origination of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is its reaching."

Since one obtains the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) only by producing it and not by any other means, and since its purpose is for the production of the post, it need not be made in the form of a threshing-floor pillar (*khalevālī*). For it is established that the animal is tied to what is not a sacrificial post; therefore, there is no purpose for [the *khalevālī*] as a post. Thus, being intended for the sake of the post—
It is not performed.
|| 6 || But in the case of a sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*), because it is merely a location, its non-cessation would be understood. || 10 ||
Now, it has been stated that because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is something to be produced, its connection with all [the rites] is for the purpose of its production.

It was stated that when the connection with the post is understood from the phrase "for whom one will cut the post," that [connection] is for the purpose of producing that specific post, because the post is something to be produced. Therefore...

The *sthāṇvāhuti* (offering to the sacrificial post stump) is for the purpose of producing the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). He provides the resolution: "True, what you have said is true; however, that very point is now being challenged. How is it challenged? Because the *sthāṇvāhuti* is connected merely with a stump in general, its connection specifically with the stump of the sacrificial post is not understood."

What then? There is merely a connection with the post (sthāṇu); consequently, no connection with the sacrificial stake (yūpa) is understood. Since it is not connected by context (prakaraṇa), it is grasped as an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakāraka). This is the underlying intention here: by means of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), the khadira wood and others become the sacrificial stake. And this purificatory rite is a worldly matter, or rather, it is performed upon that which is connected to the purificatory rite.

It is produced by an action. And since the *sthāṇv-āhuti* (the oblation for the sacrificial post stump) is not performed upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) itself, nor upon that which is connected to the post, it is non-sanctificatory (*asaṃskārikā*).
Furthermore, the word *accha* must be explained in some way or another. Thus, the *yūpāhuti* (the oblation for the sacrificial post) is also a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārikā*).
For even that is not connected to the sacrificial post; rather, being performed in the vicinity of the post, it is for the sake of the post. To this, he says: "Moreover..."

This must necessarily be accepted: that the *yūpāhuti* (post-offering), because it is performed in the vicinity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), does not belong to the post itself. Otherwise, there would be no principle of commonality (*tantratā*) for the *yūpāhuti* in the case of the set of eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*).

If the oblation related to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) were performed in the vicinity of the post, then, due to the difference in location, there would be no *tantratā* (commonality of performance) for the *yūpāhuti*.
Now, it was indeed stated that the *yūpāhuti* is for the sake of the post; that is true as far as it goes, yet that very point is considered untenable.
The intention is that either the status of being a subsidiary (*tantratā*) must be abandoned, or the purpose of producing the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) must be accepted.

However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: because of the statement "he shall offer," it is understood that the *sthāṇvāhuti* (the oblation to the stump) is indeed for the sake of the sacrificial post.
And the word *riti* is understood as referring precisely to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) itself;

for there is no authority for abandoning a qualification that pertains to the subject under discussion. This word *sthāṇu* is etymological (*yaugika*) and denotes an individual; and words denoting individuals refer to the individual present [in context].

"They do not overstep" means that the stump is indeed related to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Now, one might object: even if this [stump] is not related to the sacrificial post, how can there be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the post by means of its connection to that [stump]? To this he replies: "Even when the consecration is disconnected from the tree...
Ordinary people maintain that purification pertains to the person possessing the object;

for example, when a garland is removed from Devadatta’s head and purified by being placed in a clean location, it is considered that Devadatta himself has been purified. And this is the worldly meaning of the term "purification."

It is accepted as being like [the acts of] threshing and so forth. From the word, however, there is merely a restriction. Therefore, because of its connection with the post (yūpa) through its connection with the stump (sthāṇu), the offering at the stump (sthāṇvāhuti) serves the purpose of the production of the post. As for the offering at the post (yūpāhuti), the proximity of the location is not intended to be significant; this is because proximity is relative, as it has been stated. Thus, the offering at the post performed in one place is considered as having been performed in the vicinity of the fresh post.

Because the proximate portion is relative, there is no fault in its being a *tantra* (a common performance). The meaning is that since the *yūpāhuti* (sacrificial offering at the stake) performed even near the stakes is logically established as a *tantra*, the fact of its being a *tantra* does not invalidate its purpose for the stakes.
Thus, the scriptural observation has been explained.
And [the rule applies] to the *prayāja* offerings as well, because that name is applied there. 14.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the mention of *svāhākāra* to be a designation of a deity because of its being indicated by the accusative case in the injunction "one sacrifices to *svāhākāra*" (*svāhākāraṃ yajati*).

Just as Viṣṇu is the deity because of the accusative indication in "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajati*), so too is *svāhākāra* [the deity]. Furthermore, he states another argument: even on the view that it is a designation of an action, it would still be merely an auxiliary that assists from afar (*ārādupakāraka*).
Because of the primacy of the ritual action (*karman*).

Although the word *svāhākāra* is the name of a ritual action, nevertheless, because it is indicated in the accusative case, it is understood as a primary action; therefore, its purpose is the recollection of that deity. Consequently, it is better that it has a distinct meaning. For if...

If the action were to function as a direct auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka*), then, out of that desire [for such a status], one would accept that the word *svāhākāra* has a non-distinct meaning from the word *yajati*. However, when it functions as an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) even while being the name of the ritual action, why is its distinct meaning not accepted? It would be better for it to have a distinct meaning; for if that were the case—
What is the merit [of this position]? He says: "In this view, a distinction of words (*padabheda*) is logical because of a distinction in meaning.

Otherwise, one would have to admit a distinction of words even when there is no distinction in meaning; and this is not appropriate. Furthermore, it is illogical for multiple words [to denote the same thing]."
Regarding the word "you" (*tvam*):
[the opponent asks] "But in this case, how can there be a denotation by words such as 'Agni' occurring within the mantra of the mere sound *svāhākāra*?
To this he says: "And for words such as 'Agni,' the establishment of denotation is possible even through a secondary quality (*guṇa*); thus it is consistent."
If [the term] does not have its primary application through the connection with qualities, then there will be either a secondary (gauṇī) application or the postulation of another power (śakti),
as in the case of words such as "light" (jyotis). Just as words like "light" apply to ritual actions, so too do words like "Agni" [apply to ritual actions].

This is likewise shown in the Bhāṣya regarding the utterance of *svāhā*: the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) denotes not only one's mother, but also the "mother" of grains and other things. Furthermore, if Agni and the others are deities, then [the term applies] because of the conceptualization of Agni and the other deities as well.
There would be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the mantra, and there would be a division of the mantra. By imagining parts that reveal each respective deity, he says this:
otherwise, indeed, there would be a conceptual construction of the deities and a division of the mantra.

Therefore, this [mantra] is also a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), just like the other *prayāja* offerings; thus, even the argument based on association has been presented. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he now raises an objection: "But surely, when a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) is possible, it is not logical to postulate a separate primary power (*śakti*). For where..."

The apprehension of another meaning is established according to the power already inherent [in the word]; therefore, it is not logical to postulate a further power there, since the effect can be accounted for otherwise. He replies: "True, this would be the case where the constituent meaning is present through syntactic connection (*anvaya*), or where there is an injunction elsewhere regarding a connection with another meaning. But here, thinking that neither of these two exists, it was said thus."

For secondary (gauṇa) [terms] are of two kinds: those that function through connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*), such as the word "Indra" when applied to the *gārhapatya* fire due to its specific application; and that [secondary term] occurs where the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) remains applicable. Likewise, there is the secondary [term] functioning by virtue of similarity (*sādṛśya*), such as [the term] "Agnihotra."

The word [“mother”] occurs in the context of the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice during the oblation. And that [usage] arises because the ritual details (*vidhyanta*) connected to the regular (*naiyamika*) *agnihotra*—which is a distinct entity—are prescribed elsewhere for the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana* oblation. However, in this case, since neither of those two conditions exists, metaphorical usage (*gauṇatva*) is impossible; therefore, one must assume a different primary power (*śakti*). Thus, what was stated in the Bhāṣya—that “even a mother [is called ‘mother’]”—is justified.
That alone is correct.

This being the case, it should be stated: this is an injunction for the mere act, namely, "one should sacrifice with the *svāhākāra*," and not an injunction for an act qualified by a deity, because of parsimony (*lāghava*). But is this not an injunction for a deity?
It has been stated that "one performs the sacrifice with the utterance of *svāhā*.

[The author] refutes this: for there is no authority here for making known a deity who is not already known. Nor is the accusative case prescribed in the grammatical tradition (*smṛti*) to denote the status of a deity.

But surely, the fact that the two words have distinct referents is itself the proof for their being the deity; to this he replies: "For the status of being a deity [is established] when there is a distinction, and the distinction [is established] when there is the status of being a deity."

There would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). However, there is no such defect because the deity is understood through another injunction (*codanā*), namely, "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu. Therefore, it is proper that this [term] denotes the action (*karman*), on account of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But was it not already stated that even when the action is enjoined, the primacy of the action itself is understood?
He refutes this: Or rather, by whom is predominance not accepted for the injunction—that is, in the state of being an injunction? For the sacrifice, being intransitive, is itself the primary element.
Thus, at the stage of its arising, when there is a purpose— that is,

when one postulates a purpose— it possesses the status of a subordinate factor; it does not possess the status of a subordinate factor inherently by itself, as is the case with [the threshing] and so forth.

Furthermore, the predominance established by an injunction does not preclude a subordinate status known through another means of knowledge. Therefore, it is logical that in this case the sacrifice has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the deity.
1. [Regarding] the option of mantras (R); 3. because of the connection with the parts (R).
2. It is appropriate to say "O Mother. A 4. For the sake of the deity.
R [p.
329] But has it not been objected that this results in a conceptualization of the deity and a division of the mantra?
The answer: It does not [permanently] fail to perceive, because of a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
He explains this very point: "For it is not [the case that it] is not perceived..."

There is a distinction regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*): [the question arises] whether the consecration belongs to this deity or not. Therefore, since the ritual procedure requires the consecration of all deities, it is logical that the status of being a deity (*devatābhāva*) is likewise established in that very same way.

The meaning of this is as follows: since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of all deities is required, the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) postulates both the refinement of all deities and their status as deities (*devatātva*). It is not the case that the status of deity is postulated for the combined [deities] in the *svāhākāra* merely in accordance with all the refinements. Thus, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated.
If it be argued that the Ājyabhāga fire is likewise [to be taken up]. || 16 ||

Having raised the objection that, as in the previous case, it is logical that the *ājyabhāga* (clarified butter portion) serves a visible purpose here as well by way of being a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the deity, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) was established: there is no visible purpose because the deity is not recognized [as being the same]. For if there were a recognition that the deity Agni who is in the *āgneya* sacrifice is the very same one in the *ājyabhāga*, then it would indeed be a consecration; but that is not the case.

And there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna) here. Furthermore, non-recognition has been demonstrated in the invocation formula (āvāhana-nigada), where it is recited: "Bring Agni," "Bring Soma," "Bring Agni.
In that context, if [the word] "Agni" belongs to the [deity] Āgneya, even in the case of the butter-portion (ājyabhāga)—

If it were [the case that] "devatā" [is the term], then by the first word "agni," the deity of the principal *āgneya* offering would be manifested; by "soma-agnim," the deities Agni and Soma of the *upāṃśuyāja* would be manifested, and there would be a reversal of order. However, in the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings belonging to other deities, Agni and Soma are the deities of the two *ājyabhāgas* to be manifested, and immediately thereafter—

And it is logical that Agni is the principal deity. How, then, is there a subordinate status for the deity? The answer is: because the deity is an accomplished entity (*bhūta*) and the ritual action is something yet to be accomplished (*bhavya*), the propriety of its subordinate status has been stated.
The meaning is that subordination is logical, not merely based on scriptural statement.
|| 9 || If it is argued that this applies even to the animal sacrifice, || 19 ||

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering the term "fire" to refer to the fire being carried for the sake of the *latā-soma*, maintains that there is no recognition [of the same entity] based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). From the explanatory passage, "They carry it toward the *soma*," [he concludes that the fire being carried is for the sake of the *latā-soma*.]

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that the designation [of the animal] applies to the words "Agni" and "Soma," and maintaining that there is an absence of recognition because the two terms do not necessarily denote the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as well, asserts that the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) is a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka). In this context, regarding the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, there is a concern for displacement (utkarṣa) under the view that it is a purificatory rite (saṃskārakarma), because the deities are different from those [of the model sacrifice].

Regarding the animal sacrifices and the *puroḍāśa* offerings: where the deity is the same, there should be a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *puroḍāśas*. However, if they function as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), there is no displacement; furthermore, the subordination to the primary act (*guṇābhidhāna*) is equal in both cases, just as it is in the case of the animal sacrifice. [p.

"Likewise, [the rule applies] to the *dhānā* and the *puroḍāśa* as well. How is it that its predominance (*prādhānya*) and the primary application of ritual properties (*mukhyā dharmaprāptiḥ*) must be stated otherwise? For if Agni and Soma were subordinate (*guṇabhāva*), the primary application of ritual properties would [belong to them]; indeed, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the ritual property was taught for Agni and Soma precisely when they were subordinate, and that becomes primary when they are in a state of subordination. But if predominance were the case, [the properties would apply] by virtue of performing the function of a subordinate element.

The attainment of dharma must be explained; that [attainment], which is accomplished through ritual affliction (*kleśa*), is thereby set aside by accepting the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the deity even in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake. This very point has been stated in the Bhāṣya: “Even when defeated, a reason is sustained by some particular qualification.”
Thus it is said.
This is the distinction.
But the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: there is no cause for non-recognition here, as there was in the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. There is recognition.
If it is argued that this is not so because the abandonment of the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) is impossible, it has already been stated [in response].

As for the specific reason that sustains the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the refutation has been stated by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Now, if it is objected that an explanatory passage was stated as the reason for the difference in expression, and that [objection] was refuted by another explanatory passage—
"By this [statement], 'the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has the same deity as the animal (paśu),' [it is established].
But surely, in the absence of the context (prakaraṇa), its status as a preparatory rite (saṃskārakarma) is not possible.
This is the meaning:"

If there is contact through the application of the context (*prakaraṇa*), then it is a sanctificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*); otherwise, why would it not be an independent primary act (*svatantrakarma*)? If there is contact with the context, then its helpfulness is direct; therefore, its helpfulness is remote—this is the hidden intention.
He refutes this: "Who has said that it is possible?

We too say that, apart from an investigation of the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no status as a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarmatā*). Again, he objects: "In that case, by virtue of the context, it must be merely an indirectly contributory act (*ārādupakāraka*)."
Let it be so.
He avoids [this objection] by asking: "Is it not the case regarding a perceptible object? It is an assistance to the context.
He states this in a single passage: "Regarding the perceptible—"

And since there is no difference in the connection with the context when no visible purpose is seen, it was stated in the case of the *svāhākāra* that a visible purpose cannot be set aside; therefore, one must resort to the view that it assists the context through a traditional sequence in accordance with its visible purpose. The rest has been explained.
The *caru* should be a modification of the *havis*, because of its connection with the sacrifice. || 34 ||

Considering the pot (*sthālī*) to be the primary meaning [of the term *caru*], and because a sacrifice cannot be performed with a substance unfit for consumption, he maintains that the *caru* is a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*). The meaning of this is: since the pot is already established [as a vessel], it is indeed denoted by that very word.
1. In the case of partial negation (aṃśe nirākaraṇe), there would be the status of a subordinate element (guṇabhāva).
2. "R" [indicates] the reason for its being a statement of commendatory meaning (arthavādābhidhānatve hetu).
3. By means of the context (prakaraṇena).

The word *caru* refers to boiled rice (*odana*) because of its connection with that [cooking]. Even in that case, the cooking pot (*sthālī*) cannot be enjoined as the sacrificial offering (*havis*), because it is not edible.
Furthermore, if a sacrifice were performed with something inedible, it would contradict the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). [Therefore, the pot is mentioned] as the substratum for the cooking.
In place of the skull-cup (kapāla), a cooking pot (sthālī) should be employed; this view has already been demonstrated. He states another subsequent position:
"Because the meaning of the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is untenable, it is established that [the term] refers to a modification of the oblation (havirvikāra).
This is indicated by the secondary derivative suffix in the word *saurya*.

The deity is connected with the oblation (*havis*), not with the vessel that serves as the locus for cooking; therefore, the injunction regarding the pot (*sthālī*) is based solely on its status as an oblation. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): since the primary meaning is possible even in the case of cooked rice (*odana*), and because the application to the pot is justified through its connection with that [rice], and because there would be a contradiction with the scriptural mention of "that which is to be eaten" (*adanīya*); furthermore, because in some instances the word "he cooks" (*śrapayati*) is heard in reference to the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
It is established that the oblation (*havis*) is exchanged for cooked rice (*odana*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the word *caru* were to denote the cooking vessel (*sthālī*), then its status as an oblation would have to be predicated of that vessel; consequently, the sacrifice would be performed with something unfit for consumption—this is the view of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

The term *caru* must denote the cooked rice; for if it were to denote the vessel, there would be no contradiction with established usage (*śiṣṭācāra*). Thus, it is determined that the word *caru* denotes the rice itself. Its denotation of the rice is possible, and through its connection with that [rice], its application to the pot is also justified. The denotation of the vessel is abandoned because it contradicts established usage. In some instances, the cooking of the *caru* is prescribed.
Thus, it is established that the oblation is indeed the boiled rice (*odana*). The remainder has been explained.
|| 11 || That [oblation] should be on the potsherds by its original nature, because there is no scriptural injunction for anything else. || 45 ||

In this case, whatever is contradicted is set aside; however, there is no contradiction regarding the *kapāla* (potsherd) itself, but rather with respect to the number. Therefore, having abandoned the number eight, the *caru* should be cooked in the *kapāla* itself—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The potsherd is not able to assist as the primal material does; for that [potsherd] is the cause of baking, whereas the primal material assists by serving as the substratum for the baking.

Furthermore, since the rice (*odana*) is cooked by the heat residing in the water, the [application of the term] is not established due to the loss of its primary meaning, just as in the case of the number [of the potsherds]. Now, when the restriction of the vessel has been reached, [it is concluded that] "the *carus* are those vessels in which the Soma-juices were kept," because of the observation of this indicative mark (*liṅga*); and because the cooking denoted by the word *caru* is accomplished only in a vessel (*sthālī*).

It is established that it should be cooked in a pot itself for the sake of convenience; and this is merely stated as a friendly suggestion, not intended to mean that the pot has been specifically assigned for that purpose. The rest has been explained.

What is the purpose? [It is to determine] whether the *caru* is a modification of the potsherd, or whether the oblation (*havis*) is modified by the boiled rice (*odana*). In this regard, the specific distinction regarding the vessel (*sthālī*) in the modification of the oblation has not been considered, because the sublation of threshing and other such rites is easily understood.
Or rather, it is as follows: [p. 332] || Thus.

In this section, however, having explained the omission of grinding and other such acts on the grounds of [their] being for a specific purpose, the intention is that because another section is subsequently commenced, there must be something to be removed in certain cases.
Now, one might object: "But a weak doubt is not to be removed," to which he replies: "Even by a weak poison... as has been shown.

Just as one who has been bitten by a scorpion with mild venom does not die and thus is not to be treated, so too is a disciple agitated by a slight suspicion; this is shown in the Bhāṣya. In that regard, [the Bhāṣya] shows that when many [factors] are possible, there is no loss of purpose in the performance [of the rite].

The opponent has argued as follows: in some cases there is no cessation [of the original form] due to lack of contradiction, while in other cases he considers that the very purpose of the injunction is the meaning itself.

He maintains the conviction that for acts such as *saṃvapana* (pouring together) and so forth, there is auxiliary benefit merely through the possibility of performance because they are capable of being performed; and since here too there is the "non-loss of purpose" (*anarthalopa*) characterized by the possibility of performance, there is no contradiction for visible purposes such as grinding (*peṣaṇa*), and thus [the cake] consists of flour.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position was argued on the grounds that, because both the cooked rice-oblation (*caru*) and the act of extraction (*vyuddharaṇa*) are seen [in the text], they must be understood as objects of injunction.
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is not a matter of performance based on feasibility, nor is it due to lack of contradiction;
nor is it a matter of the object itself.

What, then, is being indicated? It is the performance of duties (*dharma*) by way of their purposeful effect (*kārya*), and their cessation due to the absence of that effect. Furthermore, the postulation of an effect arises from scriptural statement (*vacana*). Therefore, it is well said that there is no extension (*atideśa*) because the object does not enter into the assistance toward the performance of the effect.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Ṛjuvimalā* composed by the venerable Śālikamiśra.
The first quarter of the tenth [chapter] in the Pañcikā.
The second quarter of the tenth chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā*.
|| 1 || In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds, there would be non-cooking because the purpose [of cooking] is absent. || 11 ||
But how, then, is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) here? For even in the prima facie position, there certainly exists a scriptural statement.
He provides the resolution: not even by a hundred statements can an impossible matter be established as a mandate.

To the question "How is it impossible?", he replies: For in the case of cooking, softening is the primary meaning; and since that does not exist in the *kṛṣṇala* grains, what will the scriptural injunction accomplish here?

The meaning of this is as follows: The author of the Mahābhāṣya has stated, "For the primary meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is softening (*viklitti*). "Primary" means principal. And it is observed even in common worldly usage that *pac* denotes softening, as in the expression "the rice grains are being cooked" (*pacyante taṇḍulāḥ*). Even in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), [the result] is likewise connected with the rice.

Devadatta is the agent only with respect to the softening (*viklitti*) occurring within the wind; for that [softening] is dependent upon him. And this softening consists of specific qualities such as odor, color, touch, and taste. By this, the cooking of the *puroḍāśa* cakes and other such items is established. However, since there is no change in color and other qualities in the case of golden *kṛṣṇala* seeds and the like—which are composed of fire—cooking is impossible, and thus it cannot be effected even by a hundred scriptural injunctions.

The injunction is thus established. He says in a single passage: "But even if cooking (*pāka*) consists merely in the production of heat, since it would be obtained by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) itself, what is the purpose of the explicit statement? [It serves] if that which has softening as its result is indeed the very operation [intended]."

The meaning of *pac* is [cooking]; therefore, that very same [meaning] is prescribed even in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, since it would apply to the *kṛṣṇala* grains by the rule of extension (*codaka*) alone, the explicit prescription [in the ectype] would be purposeless. Furthermore, he states another defect: "In that case, acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) would be difficult to avoid."

When verbal roots denote an activity (*vyāpāra*), then even in the case of the root *han* (to strike), since its meaning consists merely of the acts of raising and lowering [the weapon], only the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is understood. Now, it might be argued that because the fruit consisting of the separation of husks and chaff is absent, the non-performance [of the action] is equal in the case of cooking (*pāka*).
Even when cooking has been taught, there is non-performance due to the equal absence of a result;
therefore, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) belongs to one who considers it simply not to be performed. Now, for what purpose is this statement, if cooking is indeed not to be performed?
The answer is:
it is also purposeless.
For a statement is meaningful only by virtue of its meaning being understood; it is not the case that there must be a statement simply because there is a meaning.

There is a means of valid cognition [for this]. However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is as you have truly stated: because there is an absence of a result, there is no attainment through action.
Furthermore, a scriptural statement cannot be set aside; therefore, there will be cooking as prescribed by the text.
334] But was it not already stated that an objective which cannot be accomplished even by a hundred statements cannot be enjoined?
He refutes this: "This too is true; an impossible matter cannot be enjoined.
Furthermore...
The proponent asks: "How then can there be the necessity of performing cooking, given that it is impossible to enjoin it because it cannot be accomplished?
The respondent says: "Because the meaning of the word is possible."

That very operation which results in softening (viklitti) is what is expressed by the root *pac* (*pacati*), because it occurs first. Through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on being its effect, the root *pac* is used in the sense of softening, as in "the rice grains are being cooked" (*pacyante taṇḍulāḥ*). And thus, in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), [the action] resides in Devadatta himself.

Devadatta’s agency resides in his activity (*vyāpāra*). Now, if that very activity—which is the cause of the transformation of the odor and other qualities and results in conjunction with the particles of fire—is the meaning of the word [“cooking”], then it is possible even in the case of *kṛṣṇala* berries, since a conjunction of their own parts is indeed perceived there. For the movement of the particles of fire within them is inferred from their hot touch; therefore, the meaning of the word...

Because it is possible, the cooking can be enjoined there. [Objection: Even if it is enjoined, it might not be performed because there is no fruit, since ritual duties (dharmas) are prompted by their effects. To this, he says:
When a verbal meaning is enjoined, there must be a purpose, whether visible or invisible. That which has a visible purpose...
Its purpose is indeed visible,

as in the case of cooking in the archetype or of threshing and so forth. However, for that which has no visible purpose, an invisible (adṛṣṭa) result is postulated to effect the fulfillment of the relationship with the enjoining cognition, since that [relationship] would otherwise be untenable without such a means.

Just as in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed upon the raw materials themselves; for there too, because the accusative case is heard, it is inferred that the action pertains to that substance.

Therefore, here also in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains, it is determined that some kind of refinement produced by cooking (*pākaja-saṃskāra*) serves as the purpose. It is not, however, a negation of the injunction on the grounds that no visible purpose exists; rather, the literal meaning of the word is indeed possible.

Now, one might object: "An injunction is seen to have a purpose; yet an injunction itself is not possible prior to the comprehension of that purpose, since a person's application (niyoga) occurs only when the operation culminates in a purpose. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the scope of an injunction is indeed only as far as the activity of the person extends, and does not include the actual attainment of the fruit."
For a person is indeed enjoined to his own specific activity;

therefore, when only that much has been prescribed, the postulation of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphala*) is entirely appropriate. Furthermore, it was stated previously that the result of the root *pac* (to cook) is the state of being softened (*viklitti*), which is the meaning of the act of cooking, and not that [softening] itself is the meaning of the root *pac*. How then is the statement of the author of the Mahābhāṣya to be understood? To this, he says:

Furthermore, it is observed in the *dhātupāṭha* that even a verbal root is stated by means of its result, as in "gaḍi [means] a part of the face. For a root indeed denotes action; thus, *gaḍi* also denotes action alone—namely, the action characterized by the initiation of a part of the face.

He says: by that result, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is stated; the sense is that *gaḍi* refers to an activity whose partial result is speaking. Likewise, as for the question "What is the primary meaning of *pac*?", the explanation must be given precisely in terms of its result: the meaning is that the primary meaning of *pac* is simply an activity whose result is softening (*viklitti*).
1. By this, that which someone has said in the *Dhātvarthapāṭha* is refuted: namely, that [the two roots] depend solely on a specific conceptualization of mere softening (*viklitti*).

Because they are understood to have that [specific] purpose, the two [terms *prokṣaṇī* and *avahanti*] do not denote anything else in the case of the *iṣṭi*. Therefore, it is well said that "cooking is performed for the *kṛṣṇala* grains on account of the scriptural injunction.

As for the objection that if the meaning of a verbal root were merely the general activity (*vyāpāramātra*), then even acts such as threshing would be unavoidable [as the root meaning], it is replied as follows:
The cessation of threshing and other such acts follows from the absence of their original purpose.

The meaning of this is as follows: even when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists merely of an activity, its visible means (*dvāra*)—such as the removal of husks and chaff—is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, that very same purpose is obtained in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well.

Due to the absence of the original purpose, there is a cessation of the threshing and other such acts. Likewise, because of the absence of the transformation of the smell and other qualities of the *puroḍāśa* cake—which constitutes the original purpose—there is also a cessation of the cooking. However, a subsequent, scripturally enjoined cooking is prescribed; for that, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated as the means. As it has been said, "We shall explain later how this is logically established," so this has now been stated.
2. [Sūtra 2] 3. [Sūtra 3]: Because the purposes of the spreading and the pouring over are already established by other means, these two acts should not be performed.

But is it not the case that the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is already evident? For what purpose, then, is this section (*adhikaraṇa*)? To this he replies: "In this [section], the causes for cessation are examined. Is the reason for the cessation [of the rites] in the case of *kṛṣṇala* grains—that the spreading of the base (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) have the purpose of making [the oblation] immortal (*amṛta*) due to the impossibility of sweetness (*svādima*)—or rather, is it because of the attainment of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*)? This is the statement regarding the attainment of the fourfold portion.
The meaning is that this section is intended to refute a fallacious conclusion, namely, that the cause of cessation is either [mere] absence or that the absence of contact is the cause of cessation.

For some indeed hold that, in the archetype sacrifice, the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) have the purpose of providing flavor (*svādima*); therefore, since flavor is absent in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains, these two acts are excluded.
Others, however, hold that the under-spreading and the sprinkling have the purpose of effecting the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), and that this fourfold portion [is what matters].

The requirement [for spreading and pouring] ceases because it has been fulfilled by the mere offering of four *kṛṣṇala* grains, as there is no further purpose for it. Likewise, another opinion holds that the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) are intended to prevent the sacrificial food (*havis*) from adhering to the ladle (*sruc*). Since there is no adhesion of the *kṛṣṇala* grains to the ladle, the spreading and pouring should not be performed for the sake of preventing such adhesion.

In that regard, one reason for desisting—namely, the preparation of an oblation of nectar (*amṛta*)—has been refuted by treating it as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). For sweetness cannot be the ultimate purpose [of the rite], because it is useless; moreover, the sacrifice is accomplished even with what is not sweet.
Thus, the second reason for desisting has also been refuted.
The connection: To the question "By what reason? he says—1.
Not by way of an undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti).
Because the number four pertains to the primary substance to be offered;

as in the statement "he cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* seeds," this number four refers to that which is the primary sacrificial oblation (*havis*) to be offered, not to the act of cutting itself. Therefore, the attainment of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) occurs through a single [act].
There is no [such thing as] a single *avadāna*.

One might object: "Even if there is only one *avadāna*, nevertheless, the attainment of four portions (*catur-āvatta*) by means of that [single portion] is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*. To this, he says: [this is not so], because of the explanatory passage regarding the attainment [of the four portions], namely: "He cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* grains; that is one *avadāna*."
The connection is with the term "refutation" (*nirākaraṇam*). Likewise, because they are understood to have different objects, there is a refutation of the number [of portions].

The number four is understood to have a different object; it pertains to the *kṛṣṇala* seeds, not to the portions (*avadāna*) [of the sacrificial cake]. Therefore, this is merely for the sake of praise (*stuti-mātram*). Furthermore, there is a refutation due to the contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the repeated offering of four *kṛṣṇalas*. [The text says: "four..."

"One cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* [weights of gold]. Since there is another act of cutting off (*avadāna*), repetition is appropriate. If the fulfillment of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) were achieved by the cutting off of the four *kṛṣṇalas* alone, then there would be no intermediate occasion for the rule at all, and thus the scriptural injunction regarding repetition would be contradicted.

Now, as for the objection that the scriptural injunction of repetition may be justified in view of the *sviṣṭakṛt* portioning, it is said in response: "The repetition belongs to the principal [act], because of the context. Thus, this refutation shows that this repetition concerns only the portioning of the principal [oblation], and not [the subsidiary].

The *bhāṣya* demonstrates that the context of the offering depends upon the portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* deity; for this reason, it is rejected because [the context] has the purpose of attainment (*āpti*). Therefore, the very fact that the *kṛṣṇala* seeds do not come into contact with the ladle (*sruc*) is the cause for the sublation (or rather, the absence) of the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), since those two have the cessation of contact as their purpose. Why is that the specific purpose?

To this he replies: "And since the purpose of negating the connection is already seen to be possible, it is not tenable to claim that even in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), another effect must be postulated;
therefore, it is rightly stated that non-connection alone is the cause of sublation."

Now, one might object: "If there is no under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*), then how will the requirement of four portions (*caturavattatva*) be fulfilled when only two cuttings (*dvayavadāna*) are made from the principal oblations? To this he replies: "As for the injunction that 'one offers what consists of four portions,' that is accomplished through [the inclusion of] those [other elements]; thus, there is no fault."
"He cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* seeds for the sake of obtaining the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*).
Since this very statement regarding attainment expresses the favoring of the fourfold portion, [the rule] stands.
|| 3 || But as for the portions to be consumed, because they serve the purpose of satisfaction, there would be no ritual action [required]. || 13 ||

[Objection: But in the archetype (prakṛti), eating is for the purpose of the disposal of the substance; why is this notion that it is for the sake of pleasure raised as a ground for sublation? [The author] replies: It is true that eating is for the purpose of the disposal of the substance, but while it is indeed so— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
1. There is no occasion for praise at all. 2. For the sake of the attainment of the sacrificial oblation (havis).

The meaning is that [the term "eating"] is intended for the sake of comprehension without abandoning its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, eating is invariably concomitant with pleasure (*prīti*), for it is observed in the world to have as its object things fit for consumption. In the world, what is called "eating" has as its object only those substances that are earthy and flavorful; and that is invariably concomitant with pleasure in the form of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Therefore, because of the absence of that pleasure—
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is logical that the consumption [of the remnants] ceases precisely because of the absence of the essential nature of the sacrificial items (padārtha).
However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that consumption occurs by virtue of the scriptural injunction.
He raises an objection to this: "But if this were so..."
The statement would also become meaningless because it would enjoin an impossible thing. The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) refutes this:
"It is not meaningless, because the mere substance is possible."

Even when eating is for the sake of pleasure, that activity is indeed expressed by the verb *bhakṣayati*; therefore, its injunction will be established by that verbal expression, since it is possible even in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains. But is it not observed in common usage that eating has edible food as its object, and that [eating] is invariably concomitant with pleasure?

And it has been stated that there is no pleasure in the *kṛṣṇala* grains. True, [pleasure] is observed, but it does not become the object of the injunction; rather, it is merely an activity (*vyāpāra*), and that exists even in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*. Thus he says: "And eating, which is the object of the injunction, is found even in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*."

It is correct to state that the word *viṣaya* refers to the act of eating, and thus the neuter designation *viṣayam* is appropriate. Furthermore, this applies specifically to the *kṛṣṇala* [gold berry] and not to the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), because the clarified butter is subordinate while the *kṛṣṇalas* are the primary element; so it has been stated in the Bhāṣya.

But is it not reasonable that this injunction for consumption is like that of ghee mixed with poison? For in the case of that [ghee] being consumed, the mention (*anuvāda*) of *cucchūṣā* and so forth is possible;

however, since *cucchūṣā* and the rest would not otherwise be established when gold is being consumed, they too must be enjoined, which results in the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhigaurava*). To this, he replies: because the mention (*anuvāda*) of *cucchūṣā* and so forth is impossible [in the case of gold].

When the gold, which serves as the vessel for cooking and is mixed with clarified butter, is being consumed, the act of making a sucking sound is already established; thus, there is no incurrence of the fault of over-complication in the specific injunction.
4. In the case of a single offering, there is joint participation because the consumption of the *brahma-bhakṣa* portions is prescribed for all in the archetype sacrifice. 17.

In this regard, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), fearing that if the position of "simultaneity" (*sakṛttva*) were adopted, it would entail the sublation of other [prescribed] portions (*bhakṣa*) obtained through the *codaka* rule, has therefore relied upon the position of "togetherness" (*sahatva*) and stated: "But surely, this portion is based solely on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), not obtained through the *codaka*.
In that context:

Having further stated this—namely, that because it serves the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*), this consumption (*bhakṣa*) is already obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), and that the scriptural statement is for the purpose of enjoining *cucchūṣā* and so forth—he objects to that: "In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), having declared the consumption to be based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), how can it now be said to be obtained again as being for the purpose of disposal? Or how [could there be] a restatement (*anuvāda*) of *cucchūṣā* and the others?"
1. A. Having first stated the general rule regarding eating at once, a further restriction is now set forth.

He provides the resolution: this contradiction is not possible, because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), one observes that the effect of the worldly consumption—which consists of edible food—is the form of pleasure; since that [pleasure] is absent in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), there is no attainment of the prescribed [result], as was stated previously. And the scriptural statement is [intended for] the prescribed—

It is established as an object [of the injunction], like the act of cooking. Here, however, it is said: if in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) this very mere activity (*vyāpāra-mātra*) is what is to be enjoined, then the effect of the injunction (*kārya-kalpanā*) pertains to the injunction itself, not to the word-meaning (*padārtha*). And this is possible here as well; for even in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the effect of that injunction is a counterpart to the substance. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is a sublation (*bādha*). Consequently, the eating (*bhakṣa*) occurs by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).

It is not established that [the rule] applies to piercing (*vedha*) and so forth; rather, only *cucchuṣā* and the like are the objects of the statement. Since *cucchuṣā* and the like are non-eternal (*anitya*), it is well said that their status as objects of the statement can be asserted for the sake of what is eternal (*nitya*). This is what is meant:

just as there is an injunction of the mere performance (*vyāpāra*) in a modification (*vikṛti*), let it be the same in the archetype (*prakṛti*); and its purpose is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the substance.

Since the primary result is [the sacrifice] and the pleasure of the person is incidental, the consumption [of the soma] is indeed established by the general injunction (*codaka*). However, the specific statement is for the purpose of restricting the particular manner, that is, for the purpose of restricting the specific verbal expression. How then was it stated previously that the attainment [of consumption] is based on the text?
To this he says: "For what purpose is the preceding section now [repeated]?"

The answer is: for the sake of establishing this reasoning. The meaning is that it is for the purpose of proving this very reasoning. Merely the activity itself is the object of the injunction (*vidhi*).

The intent here lies in establishing this [point], and not in the literal injunction regarding eating; therefore, there is no fault. To the question, "For what purpose is the establishment by reasoning? he says: For reasoning that has not been established is not truly reasoning, because it fails to accomplish its purpose.
And their universality would follow from their [respective] entitlements. || 18 ||
The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is possible to provide a method for avoiding something that is otherwise unavoidable.

Even if the formulation of the statement is such that "whatever one offers to Brahman, all that [is the sacrificial fee]," nevertheless, regarding that which constitutes a portion of the Brahman's share...

It follows that [the portion] must be avoided; therefore, the rule "everything" is prescribed for the purpose of avoiding it. Even as for the portion belonging to Brahmā, it is not the case that the whole of it must necessarily be given to Brahmā, because its status as being for his sake is established even through a single part.
Likewise, even if the verbal construction were "whatever belongs to Brahmā, all of that he avoids," nevertheless, regarding what is not to be avoided—

The meaning is that "he wears [it] solely for the sake of a necklace" is what is to be enjoined. To the question, "If there is only one single meaning even in these two modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*), why then were both stated?", he says: "The demonstration of the modes of expression is merely a statement of possibility."

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that since the use of the word "all" (*sarva*) would otherwise be untenable, an injunction for what has not been previously obtained is impossible; thus, there must be a partial exclusion (*bhāgāpanaya*).
The meaning of this is as follows: in the syntactical formulation of the statement, "Whatever he offers to Brahman, all that [is for the gods]," the referent of the word "all" is—
1. It is not to be enjoined. 2. It is to be enjoined.

It is not something to be enjoined, because it is already established; for indeed, whatever is intended for the purpose of disposal (*parihāra*) regarding the *brahman* is already established as being for the purpose of disposal, since disposal is for the sake of the disposal of the substance (*dravya*). Disposal is appropriate only so long as the substance exists. For if the substance were subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), then the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled even when the operation is performed upon only a portion of it. But since the substance is primary (*pradhānya*), [the whole must be disposed of].
The exclusion is logically applicable only to the substance itself; otherwise, by means of this consecration (*saṃskāra*), there would be an abandonment of that [substance].

Likewise, even in the formulation of the statement, "He excludes everything for the Brahman," the term "everything" remains untenable because the qualified object is not fully understood. Therefore, [the correct interpretation is]: "He excludes the entire *caru* for the Brahman. If it were the case that "whatever is everything... [the following would apply].
By resorting to one of the two possible modes of expression—namely, that "he avoids that which is non-Vedic" (tad-abrāhmaṇam)—this removal of the portions belonging to other persons is enjoined;
and it has been shown that the meaning of the word "all" (sarva) is impossible in all modes of expression.
|| 6 || Because of the removal of the persons, [the rite] belongs to its own time. || 20 ||
It is considered how much is sublated by this.

In that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering everything to be uncontradicted as far as it is heard in scripture, has argued the prima facie position: that "he gives everything to Brahman," according to the Śruti, at one and the same time.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that since avoidance (*pariharaṇa*) is understood, time (*kāla*) is also sublated. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the injunction (*niyoga*) has a single purpose, no other purpose is possible; therefore, it culminates in mere removal (*apanaya*). Whatever else [is involved] must be performed, as it is not sublated.
The meaning of this is as follows:

although simultaneous performance is heard [in the scripture], nevertheless, because it is impossible for a single injunction (*niyoga*) to enjoin multiple matters, only the removal of a portion is enjoined;
the time is not enjoined either. Therefore, since no other time is prescribed, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the time as it has already been established.
Therefore, the avoidance [of the conflict] must be performed at its own proper time.

Why, then, is simultaneous occurrence—notwithstanding that it is heard in the text—not enjoined? To this he says: it has been established that an injunction does not extend as far as the verbal expression nor as far as the application.
Because the mandate (niyoga) is primary, the description of those two [the word and its application] is not according to their denotation or application, but rather solely according to the mandate.
|| 7 || There would be no distinction because they have a single purpose. || 21 ||

Since only the removal [of the original substance] is enjoined, the thought that "whatever else [is used] is not sublated" might arise even with respect to the *vyādeśa* (the assignment of the name) according to the logic of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*). To address this potential misconception, the following statement of reasoning is provided. Of what nature is it?
1. He says that this has been demonstrated regarding individuals:
"In this case, even though there is this statement of exclusion, for whom it follows by implication... [p. 340]

If the purpose disappears, that [act] also should not be performed. For non-performance results from the disappearance of the purpose; therefore, it is logical that there should be a sublation even of that [act] for which the purpose does not disappear when it is directly enjoined, and of that for which it is obtained through implication, since the disappearance of the purpose is equal in both cases. Therefore, there is no [sublation] of the *vyādeśa*.

The purpose [of the instruction] would be that, once the person has been removed, that which is to be given to those [others] should be assigned to them. However, since there is no giving to anyone other than Brahman, there is no purpose for the assignment.
|| 8 || The gift to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) would be merely a matter of religious duty (dharma), because of the force of the verb "to give" (dadāti). || 22 ||
Here, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the number] is not fixed because of the lack of restriction on means and because of the scriptural statement.

The meaning of this is as follows: since there is no restriction on the means for men, the prescription of a fixed measure is not logical; however, it is logical if it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

Likewise, regarding a gift for the purpose of bringing [the recipient] under one's influence (*ānatyartha*), what is the use of a verbal statement? Even without a statement, the gift is already accomplished.

Nor is the statement intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), because such a restriction is impossible; for it is precisely because men are not subject to [such] constraints that they are unpredictable. Thus he says: "He considers that there is no purpose whatsoever in a statement made for the purpose of bringing [someone] under one's influence."
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that as long as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is possible, one cannot claim it has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*),
just like a religious vow (*vrata*). If the visible benefit for the person— the very purpose of giving— were not present, then this scriptural statement would be rendered meaningless.

Since the statement has the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—to the effect that "this must necessarily be performed"—it is not devoid of meaning; for a statement indeed serves as a restrictive rule, such as: "The milk-vow belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. The example given by the mere mention of a restrictive rule illustrates this: the restriction of a vow (*vrata-niyama*) is for the purpose of excluding other [foods], whereas this [present case] is for the purpose of excluding non-connection (*ayoga*). Furthermore, it was stated in the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that even through a restrictive rule, the injunctions possess purposefulness.

Therefore, it is established that the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the purpose of purchase; the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated. But what is the relevance of this section to the definition of sublation (*bādha*)?
The answer is:
the objection (*prasaṅga*) is that, since persons are not to be purchased, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is sublated in the *sattra* sacrifice.
And likewise, those who eat the remnants [of the sacrifice]. || 29 ||

But how can one consider the substance intended for another purpose to be for the sake of purchase? [The author] says in response to the objection that this would involve a contradiction between what has been assigned and what is being assigned: "In this case as well, thinking that the two portions are to be brought together and that in the *soma* sacrifice they are for the purpose of the offering until the oblation is completed, he considers it to be for the sake of purchase."
