The purposefulness toward the sacrifice pertains not merely to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), but rather to the double-portion (*dvayavadāna*) alone. 1. When [the cause] is absent, the motive arises. 2. Indeterminate. A.

[Page 341] (Thus it has been concluded: However, in the case of *soma*, since only as much as is offered remains for the purpose of what is left over, there is no contradiction between what has already been employed and what is subsequently employed; therefore, the purchase (*parikraya*) is appropriate—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

But how can there be an exchange with such a very small amount of substance? To this he says: "And whatever measure of pleasure arises from substances being consumed for the sake of pleasure, [that much is obtained]; therefore—"
"Foodstuffs are for the purpose of satiation.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "For a substance would necessarily be taken up for the purpose of satiation."

If the *bhakṣas* (consumptions) are for the purpose of consumption, it follows that the substance to be consumed should be taken for the purpose of consumption. Consequently, why are the *bhakṣas* heard of as having the taken-up substance as their object? And that taking-up [of the substance] is for the sake of the sacrifice, because the whole [substance] is intended for the sacrifice;

however, the operation [of consumption] takes place by means of a single part. Furthermore, it is not possible for something intended for one purpose to serve another purpose. Therefore, this [consumption] belongs to that which is intended for the sacrifice itself.

It is established that *saṃskāra* (consecration) consists of performance and is not for the purpose of [obtaining] something else. The remaining [categories], including those with visibility (*sanidarśana*), have been explained.
[Objection: Since the *varaṇa* (choosing) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is for the purpose of honoring them, it should not exist in a *sattra* sacrifice.
Because it is its own action. || 24 ||

Now, one might ask: since choosing (*varaṇa*) consists of a request for the purpose of hiring (*ānati*), how can there be a suspicion that it serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)? To this, they reply: since hiring is already accomplished through payment (*parikraya*), the Śruti considers the act of choosing to be for an unseen purpose.

This being the case, it is replied: indeed, when something already possesses a purpose, a subsequent request for it cannot be assumed to have a visible purpose. Furthermore, because the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) occurs at a later time, the act [of choosing] does not achieve its purpose through it; for if the choosing (*varaṇa*) occurred earlier, then the purpose would have been fulfilled by that very act.
He refutes [the objection]: "The state of being bowed (*ānatyarthatā*) does not destroy the act of giving.
Why? He says: for it is precisely that [state of being bowed] which is favored by it."
It becomes successful—that is, purposeful—and not merely in vain.
Why is this? To this he says: for in the world, the giving of the virtuous is observed to be preceded by respect, and thus results in the accomplishment of its purpose.

For in this world, it is observed that the giving by virtuous people for the sake of accomplishing a purpose is preceded by respect; therefore, since lack of respect serves as an auxiliary factor by functioning as a modification of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the gift, it cannot negate the gift itself. As for the selection of a ritual season (*ṛtuvaraṇa*), however, it has already been refuted on the grounds that, because its purpose has already been achieved, it serves only an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
Since the acts of choosing and supporting have already been performed, no further choice serves a visible purpose; therefore,
what remains above is merely the nature of a formal petition.
3. The interval between the *varaṇa* (choosing) is for an unseen purpose.
|| 11 || And the hiring (*parikraya*) is also for that same purpose. || 35 ||

But has it not been stated that it is "purchase" (*parikraya*)? Since "purchase" is derived etymologically as "that by which one is purchased," and since that is not possible in the case of the Self, how can there be a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)? [The answer is: It is because of the observation of prohibitions, according to the maxim of the "poisonous snake" (*mandaviṣanyāya*).
Seeing that "no cow is sacrificed here," a weak doubt arises; by means of that [doubt], the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established,
on the grounds that there can be no prohibition in the absence of a prior application (*prāpti*).
The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, has been stated: this is not a prohibition; rather, it is a perpetual restatement (nityānuvāda).
The Udavasānīya sacrifice should possess the characteristics of a Sattra because it is a constituent part of it; therefore, in that case, there should be only the duty of giving.

It is not logical to assume a separate qualification (adhikāra) based on the mention [of the sacrifice] in proximity to the *satra*, because it is established by the principle that "that which is fruitless in the vicinity of something fruitful is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it.
Having emerged from the *satra*, [one performs] the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* Jyotiṣṭoma.

In the sentence "They should sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee," the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* rite is mentioned within the same syntactical unit as the *sattra*. Therefore, its mention in the proximity of the *sattra* is like that of something fruitless in the proximity of something fruitful; thus, it shares the same qualification (*ekādhikāra*) with the *sattra*. And when there is a shared qualification, that which lacks a fruit becomes a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of that which possesses the fruit. Since the *sattra* possesses a fruit, whereas the *udavasānīya* is fruitless, [the latter is subordinate]. Therefore...

It is a constituent part of the *satra*. And since it is a constituent part of the *satra*, the injunction regarding the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) serves solely for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because one is oneself the performer [of the sacrifice].
This is like the statement "a mare and a woman who has borne a child, both milch-cows" in the *kāmeṣṭi* which is a constituent part of the *sārasvatasattra*. Furthermore:

If there were a separate injunction [for a distinct ritual] at the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, then the expression "having emerged from the *satra*" (*satrād udavasāya*) would have to be understood as indicating time;
and that is improper. Therefore, since it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *satra*, the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* is simply the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*).

This being the position reached, it is replied: this is not correct, that the statement regarding the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Because the *udavasānīya* is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *satra*; for here there is no co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the *satra*, but rather this is a co-utterance with the abandonment of the *satra*.
Indeed, the suffix *-kta* is not heard as belonging to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); what then? It belongs to the root *ava-so* (to conclude).

Regarding the term *udavasāya*: it does not denote a sacrifice, as in the case of [the expression] "having sacrificed with the Vājapeya. For if this were an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *satra*, then there would be no abandonment of the *satra* at all; consequently, the scriptural mention of "abandonment" (*tyāga*) would be contradicted. Therefore, [this is] not a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*).
2. Because it is produced by its own agent;
3. This is the southern course.

Because of the mention of "renunciation" (*tyāga*), it is understood that this rite is not to be entered into as a *sattra* sacrifice. Therefore, it is established that for those who have relinquished the *sattra*, this constitutes a different qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) serves a visible purpose;
thus, the word "fee" does not [apply here].

It is contradicted. Under the view that the action is independent (*svatantra-karma*), since the agency of another performer obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) is not sublated, the giving of a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is solely for the purpose of hiring (*ānati*).
This being the case, he asks: Is the state of having abandoned the *sattra* the occasion (*nimitta*), such that there is an entitlement based on that occasion?
Is this [the case], or rather is there the assumption of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*) as in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice?

If there were an assumption of a separate qualification, then it would be considered a definition of time. He states the answer: "This is not what is being deliberated here; first of all, its status as a non-constituent part (*anaṅgatva*) is established."

In this regard, if the application of the original context (*adhikāra*) is logical, then let that very one be adopted. If, however, it is illogical, then another context should be postulated. Furthermore, there is no fault of indicating time (*kāla-lakṣaṇā*), because the *udavasānīya* sacrifice lacks the status of an auxiliary (*anaṅgatva*) due to its being mentioned in conjunction with the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
But according to their statement, there should be a simultaneous performance, like that of two sacrifices.
Now, one might ask: how can it be suspected here that there are multiple performers, given that this is merely another qualification for those who have already commenced a *sattra* sacrifice?
Since they are necessarily many, their plurality is simply being restated; it is not that there is a qualification for a rite performed by multiple agents.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this case, because of the use of the plural form in the word *yajeran*, and because [the action] is connected with another constituent element (*padārtha*)."

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that, just as there is an understanding [of plurality] through connection, so too there is an application (anvaya) of plurality even with respect to the action (kārya).

The meaning of this is as follows: by the use of the plural number in the word "yajeran" (they should sacrifice), the entitlement (adhikāra) is understood to apply to a subject involving multiple performers.

Nor can it be conceived that this plurality [of performers] is a mere restatement (anuvāda) with reference to the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, because the meaning of the injunction—which pertains to a complete ritual act consisting of a sacrifice performed by many agents—is already understood; for [the injunction] is connected with another ritual element, namely the *udavasāna*. If the injunction, without regard for plurality, were to concern the sacrifice alone, [it would be connected with the *udavasāna*].

In that case, one might say that plurality is being restated (*anūdyate*). However, when there is a connection with another [element] of a word-meaning that is already complete, even then—since the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) has been understood as referring to a sacrifice performed by many agents—the plurality is not something to be restated.
Therefore, just as the connection of plurality occurs in the cognition, so too does it occur in the ritual action (*kārya*); thus, the agency in the *udavasānīya* rite belongs to many alone.

Thus, since it is established that there are many performers [of the ritual], one can consider the possibility of self-performance (*svayaṃkartṛkatā*). Otherwise, if there were only a single performer, the performance by oneself would not even be conceivable because of the impossibility of such capacity; thus, the mention of the pregnant woman is inserted as an intermediate example.
This is for the sake of a perceptible purpose, just as in the case of understanding a relationship.

344]: Having stated that what was established there remains unfinished, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was advanced that the application (*prayoga*) has the self as its agent.

That appears to be incorrect. For if there were an injunction for the sacrificers themselves to perform the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*), then it would be appropriate to raise this as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, the priestly function of the sacrificers is not heard [in the scripture]. If, indeed, the sacrificers who have performed the *udavasa* (departure) were heard [in the text] as being employed by other persons, then their mention would apply to the priestly function. But it is not so.

To this he says: for at the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, those performers are not perceived as being prompted by another, that is, as being prompted by a different person, because they are themselves subject to the prompting of others.

By which [reason] they ought to be such [performers] in the sacrifice. To the objection that by the word "they should sacrifice" (*yajeyuḥ*), agency is expressed even in the office of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he says:
"For they do not sacrifice. What then? They cause [others] to sacrifice (*yājayanti*).

[They] go [to the sacrifice]. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) do not perform the sacrifice themselves; rather, they cause others to sacrifice. Furthermore, in the verbal form *yajeyuḥ* ("they should sacrifice"), agency is understood with respect to the act of sacrificing (*yajana*), not with respect to the act of causing to sacrifice (*yājana*). If the officiating priests have no agency in the act of sacrificing, how then is it that [the text] says "they sacrifice"?
"Yājakāḥ" (sacrificers) is a counter-example. The answer is: that is to be seen when there is actual usage; when it is being employed—

It is understood that the term *yajati* (sacrifices) is applied by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the activity of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), which is prompted by the activity of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This is the counter-example. In this regard, the word *yājaka* itself is the authority; for the word *yājaka* denotes the officiating priests, as it is derived from the root *yaj* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the agentive suffix *ṇvul*.

Furthermore, this application—"they should sacrifice"—is established as being independent only when the agent is [the sacrificers themselves], because of the hearing of the *ātmanepada* ending; thus, there is no understanding of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) [as the agents]. Therefore, how can there be a doubt regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) being performed by the sacrificers? He provides the answer: "True, as you have said. However, in this case, since the plural number is mentioned in connection with the *satra* at the time of the *udavasāna*, it is thus—"
The objection that "a suspicion regarding the actual state of things arises" was raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to refute that [view].

Its meaning is as follows: just as the performers are of such a nature in the *sattra* sacrifice, they are perceived to be of that same nature even at the time of the *udavasāna* (concluding rite). Those very ones who are the performers at the *udavasāna* are the same ones who perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*.

Even those who perform the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*) themselves at a sacrificial session (*sattra*) are considered the performers (*kartṛ*); thus, it was raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that here too they should be considered performers in that same way.
However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) has already been stated by means of the very objection (*paricodanā*) previously made. This is the objection that was formulated earlier.

For it has been stated in that very [work] as the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) that there is no injunction for the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) to perform the office of the officiating priests (*ārtvijya*). Therefore, the statement "the *udavasānīya* sacrifice must be performed just like the archetype (*prakṛti*)" does not sublate the fact of its being performed by another; rather, it [establishes] the state of being performed by another.
It must be understood that [the injunction] is indeed uncontradicted in its capacity to bring about [the result].
For if it were based on the *sattra* sacrifice as its archetype (*prakṛti*), then there might also be self-performance;
however, the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* does not have the *sattra* as its archetype. Therefore, it is established that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be chosen.
But how is it understood that the state of being such [as the archetype] itself precludes performing the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) oneself?
The answer is: it has been stated, "like the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*).

It has been stated that the very fact which is understood from the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) — namely, that just as there is agency by another in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too it exists in the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice — is precisely the reason for negating its being of such a nature. Therefore, that which—
It is the mere abandonment of the sacrificial session (*satra*) that is to be respected as heard in scripture, and not the performance of the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) oneself;
this is the reply to the established position (*sthitāt*).
A complete word requires another word; however, in this case, the application is based on what was previously understood.
This refers to many [words] that are mutually independent.
The meaning of this is: because of the hearing of the suffix *ktvā* in the term *udavasāya*.
First, the procedure for the concluding rite (*udavasāna*) must be understood; for the suffix *-ktvā* is employed when a preceding action is to be understood.
And that [procedure] involves many agents who are mutually independent. [The opponent] objects: "If they are many and mutually independent, as you say, then on what basis does their plurality rest?"
For plurality is based on mutual dependence;

otherwise, the establishment of plurality would not be possible, since it is dependent upon enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). The respondent says: "We say that its basis is the substrate (*sattā*)."

In a sacrificial session (*sattra*), plurality is appropriate because of mutual dependence; however, at the conclusion (*udavasāna*), there is independence, since each person performs it individually. Even if this be so, what follows?—namely, that such [individual] performances were understood previously.
It is understood in the same way even later on.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the performance of the *udavasāna* (concluding rite), many independent agents are first understood; and the state of having a common agent would not be possible without a second performance.

Furthermore, as for that second performance (*prayoga*), since it has the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) as the first performance, it is understood as having many agents who are mutually independent. Therefore, the *udavasānīya* sacrifice must have a single agent.
[Objection: But since the word "they should sacrifice" (*yajeran*) is heard, the second performance is enjoined as having many agents; to this he replies:
However, since only the act of sacrificing (*yajimātra*) remains uncomprehended, the injunction of its meaning remains; thus, the conclusion rests precisely there.
The meaning of this is as follows: because of the comprehension of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*), there arises a performance by an agent distinct from the previous performance.
The injunction is not for the purpose of dedication (*samarpaṇa*), but rather for the purpose of establishing the mere nature of a second performance that was previously unknown;

thus, its finality lies precisely there. Even when there is a plurality of agents, the operation of the injunction does not extend [to them]. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why would it not be exactly the same in the case of the *rājapurohita* and other such [compounds]? To this he says: "But in the case of the *rājapurohita* and so forth..."

Because no other application is understood and because no distinction is perceived, the meaning of the word (*vacana*) must also be enjoined, just like the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); thus there is a disparity. Just as the meaning of *yaj* is enjoined there because it was not previously understood, so too is the meaning of *vacana*. However, in this case, the meaning of *vacana* is not to be enjoined, because its prior application—
Precisely because there is a single agent, the number of that agent is understood; therefore, only the sacrifice itself is to be enjoined.
Consequently, as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), a single agency must be intended for the *udavasānīya* rite. Thus, it is well said that the performance is to be carried out by each individual.
And in the Kāmeṣṭi sacrifice, [the result follows] from the connection with the gift. || 44 ||
In this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering it a specific thing to be given, maintains that the agency of another applies to the auxiliary rites (aṅga).

The meaning of this is: even though the Kāmeṣṭi is an auxiliary part of the Satra, the agency of another is established by the rule of extension (codaka); therefore, in the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—
This is the prescription of specific offerings obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). Nor does the statement "those who are the sacrificers" preclude the agency of others;

rather, the statement "those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)" applies to the primary act. Since the injunction for self-agency applies even to the primary act alone, the use of the plural number is entirely appropriate; thus, it does not preclude the agency of others obtained through the *codaka* with respect to the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*). Therefore...
"This [purchase] is indeed a barter, as in the case of 'a mare and a man-woman'.
To this it is replied: for the bending down is an auxiliary to the performance.

This act of giving is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the preparatory rite (*prayoga*). Furthermore, this sacrificial session (*satra*) constitutes a single preparatory performance; moreover, the rule regarding the auxiliaries pertains only to the constituent elements (*padārtha*), not to the performance as a whole. And it has been stated that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is not an auxiliary of the constituent element. Therefore, the statement is for the purpose of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and not for the purpose of prescribing a specific object to be given. This is the point here.

The true meaning is as follows: this rule regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) indicates only the existence of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), not their performance (*prayoga*). Only the rule concerning the primary act (*pradhāna-vidhi*) is the indicator of performance; and that [primary rule], being without distinction, indicates a single performance for both the subsidiaries and the primary act together. Since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is an integral part of the performance, if this fee were to belong [to each subsidiary] individually, then it would have to be given with every separate performance.

Nor can it be a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*), because the primary act is declared to have the sacrificer himself as its agent. Therefore, this [gift] is not a *dakṣiṇā* (priestly fee).

It is logical that it is merely a subordinate element of the ritual action (*padārtha*), and not a constituent of the performance itself. Consequently, it is determined that the giving is for the sake of an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
And in the case of one who is hateful, there should be a removal of the *dakṣiṇā*, because there is no injunction [to give to him]. (Sūtra 4.3.46)
Now, one might ask: "Since the *anvāhārya* has been prescribed as a purpose, why is there a suspicion of another sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)? To this he says:

"Because it is occasional (*naimittika*), a modification of the sacrificial fee is logical"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). [The opponent argues: "One should set aside the regular *anvāhārya* fee for the sake of the occasional ones..."
The rule regarding the *kahāyanī* cow sets aside [the general rule], and the term "dakṣiṇā" (sacrificial fee) is thereby justified. For a dakṣiṇā is that which makes one capable (*dakṣakārī*).

If even a hated person were to become a priest (*ṛtvij*), then the gift given to him would indeed make him capable; however, in the case of one who is not a priest, the status of being a dakṣiṇā is not possible. Nor is there any need to postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), for [this status] is established when a hated person is accepted as a priest.
In the case of giving, there is no assumption of an unseen force (adṛṣṭa); this is a mandatory injunction (vidhi). 1. R [p.

To this it is replied: This gift is not for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), because it contradicts the *smṛti*. For if the officiating priest were someone detestable, then this would be a gift to the officiating priest;
however, the officiating priest is not detestable, nor is he one to be hated.

This is the meaning: according to the Smṛti statement, "The officiating priest (ṛtvij) and the teacher (ācārya) are not to be transgressed against. Therefore, because there is no such thing as a "hated" officiating priest, this gift is not for an officiating priest.
[Objection: But surely, even an officiating priest can sometimes become hateful to one who has violated the meaning of the scriptures?

Precisely because there is the possibility of aversion, there exists the scripture of prohibition; otherwise, if such aversion were not possible, the statement of prohibition would not apply. He refutes this [objection]: "And from scripture, the destruction of that aversion toward its object is obtained through effort."
The meaning of this is as follows:

the operation of the scripture (*śāstra*) proceeds by taking those who abide by the scripture as its basis. Furthermore, one who abides by the scripture is not to be reviled by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). On the other hand, for one who does not respect the scripture, there is no qualification even for being chosen [as a priest], because of his unrestrained nature. This very point he states:
If he does not follow the scriptural injunction or choose [the priest], why [is there a fine]?

If it is because of the scripture, then since his decision has been made, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) cannot be an object of hatred. Therefore, because a hated officiating priest is impossible, this gift for a contingent occasion (*naimittika*) is not for the purpose of expiation.
It is established that [this is] because another scripture has not been seen.
|| 17 || The bone-sacrifice (asthiyajña) should belong to others because there is no prohibition; it belongs to the bones because there is a prohibition [against others]. || 47 ||

But how can there be a suspicion of sacrifice regarding bones, given their insentience? For that which is insentient cannot perform a sacrifice, nor would the qualification (*adhikāra*) for ritual action be possible for insentient things; for it is the conscious agent who is qualified. Nor are those [bones] themselves enjoined.

Precisely for this reason, it is said that animals lack qualification; to this, he replies: "In this case, by the force of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), [there is] the application of the designation."

And since an injunction depends upon feasibility, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts that the meaning of the injunction must be carried out in such a way that it is possible without abandoning what is explicitly stated in the scripture.

The meaning of this is as follows: no qualification for the bones can be established, because the Bone-Sacrifice (*asthiyajña*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*). The suspicion that the bones possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) in the sacrifice arises from the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding both the designation and the application. First, the designation "one should cause the bones to sacrifice" (*asthīni yājayet*) is directly heard (*śrauta*) with respect to the bones; likewise, the connection of the bones with the act of sacrificing is also directly scriptural. Therefore, [the sacrifice]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument presented in the Sanskrit passage.*

The agency of the bones is indeed established by Vedic scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, as for this meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) that the sacrifice having the bones as its agent must be performed in such a way as is possible through what is not [yet] present—
because in a *sattra* sacrifice the injunction depends upon capacity— and because it has been demonstrated that there is a relinquishment according to one's capacity.

2. Because it transgresses the scriptures, when people perform a sacrifice after taking the substance of a corpse while other men are performing the sacrifice, the bones become the performers of the sacrifice; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

The proponent’s pride is [unfounded], and the indicative mark has been shown. The presence of the bones at the end of the hymns for those who have become the sacrificers shows that the bones are the sacrificers.
This being the position reached, it is replied: True, the injunction conforms to capacity; however—
The literal meaning of both the designation and the application is not possible, because it is impossible for bones to function as the agent in a sacrifice.
Nor can agency be established through the mediation of hiring, because there is no hiring. For if they were to cause [others] to perform the sacrifice...

One might purchase men [as priests], and thus that purchase might indeed take place; however, this is not the case. For the bones have no property by which a purchase could be made, nor is there any capacity directed toward them. Indeed, the meaning of the scripture cannot be something for which one lacks the capacity.
How, then, is it that one acts according to one's capacity when there is a substitute?

The answer is: that [capacity] is described as belonging to the *niyoga* (the injunction) itself. One performs the purpose of the *niyoga* exactly as it can be accomplished; however, the taking of a similar [substitute] is...
For the sake of the perfection of the expression, that is, for the sake of the perfection of the meaning as it has been expressed,
and not for the sake of the perfection of expressing some other meaning;
therefore, the consistency of the causal basis according to the literal hearing is not possible for the expression and its application alone.

Just as in the expression "the Ganges is polluted," a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be resorted to; by the word "bone" (*asthi*), those possessing bones—the living performers of the sacrifice (*sattrin*)—are to be indicated. Therefore, there is consistency in the fact that the agency belongs to those possessing those bones who performed the sacrifice together with the *sattrins*, as they possess the constituent parts of that [act]. Consequently, it is logical that the sacrifice belongs only to those who are alive. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is as follows:
The Bhāṣya states that this [mantra] is of the same form as the sacrificer's vessel (yājamānakumbha), or rather, it is expressly enjoined by the scriptural text (vācanika).
If, however, on account of the scriptural injunction, their muttering (japa) and consecration (saṃskāra)— which would otherwise be purposeless— are to be performed along with the sacrifice (seṣṭi)...
Because it is for that purpose. || 49 ||

This presentation of the *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical argument) is for the purpose of stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and its practical application (*prayojana*) regarding the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, when stating the application, no further purpose needs to be mentioned, because it is itself of the nature of a purpose. And therein [is found] the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of recitation (*japa*).

There is a sublation of the [rules] for the merchants according to their respective order. Because of the absence of hair on the head and beard, and because of the absence of speech and mind, there is cessation [of certain rites].
|| 19 || But that which is for the sake of the sacrifice should be performed, because it is subordinate [to the sacrifice]. || 50 ||

In this case as well, because there is an absence of autonomy, agency is not possible even for bones in acts such as the measuring of the *audumbarī* post; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
For bones, being insentient, cannot themselves be agents anywhere.
The intended meaning is that they are actively engaged.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that independence is logically tenable because the object to be expressed is possible.
The meaning of this is as follows:

independence (*svātantrya*) consists in being connected with the operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not, on the other hand, in acting by oneself. To explain this very point, he asks: "Is independence merely the accomplishment of an action?"
The answer is: it is said that "om" [is the response]; the pervasion of the operation delimited by the verbal root (dhātu) is the cause of agency.
That which is delimited by the verbal root—

The operation has been established; its possession [of that operation] is independence (*svātantrya*), and this alone is the cause of agency. Thus, with reference to their own operation—namely, the burning and so forth which constitute the operation of the fuel and other materials—the sentence "the fuel and others cook" is employed.
Therefore, since the agency of bones is possible, there is no contradiction regarding the acts of honoring and assisting.
But rites performed for specific desires do not exist [in that way], because they are not recited for one who lacks desire and knowledge, just as they are not for the other. || 51 ||
In this regard, what is the intention behind the statement that rain occurs for the sacrificer even in the absence of desire?
For as long as the sacrificer’s desire exists, there ought to be the fruit corresponding to that which is desired.

The answer is as follows: this is the intended meaning— namely, that in the case of desire (*kāmanā*), the sacrificer is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) nor is the fruit (*phala*), because both are primary (*prādhānya*) due to being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*).

The meaning of this is as follows: where there is desire (*kāmanā*), a person possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*); in that case, the qualification does not constitute a subsidiary factor (*aṅga*) because the qualified person is the primary element. Furthermore, since desire is a qualification of the qualified person, it too is not a subsidiary factor. He asks, "What follows from this? and replies: "Due to the absence of a subsidiary factor, the fruit is not produced."

But this is not the case even when a non-essential element is being adopted. Therefore, the result must come about even without a desire for it. Consequently, it is logical that from the measuring of the *sadas* accompanied by qualities such as being low, there must arise results such as rain, even in the absence of a desire for those results.
How, then, is the *ātmanepada* [justified] in this view?

Its meaning is as follows: the *ātmanepada* indeed brings about the fact that the fruit accrues to the agent (*kartṛgāmitā*). But if the fruit occurs even when the agent has no desire for it, then [the rule does not apply].
The fruit goes to the agent. For the connection of the fruit is through its being experienced, and not otherwise. The reply is:
this principle has already been stated. And when that principle is established, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) itself expresses that the fruit goes to the agent, according to the circumstances.

However, it indicates that which is obtained through entitlement (*adhikāra*). In that regard, where there is an acquisition by virtue of entitlement, there exists the indication of the fruit of the action as residing in the agent; where this is not possible, let it not be so. And because this [action] has already commenced during the state of being alive, it is established that Pāṇini’s [definition] expresses that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
The meaning of this is as follows:
that fruit of the measurement of the sacrificial hall (*sada*), such as rain and so forth, which exists here in the *asthi-yajña* (bone-sacrifice), is not directly stated [in the scripture].
Rather, [it is obtained] because it has been previously established.

[Page 350] It proceeds from the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the existence of its substratum. And in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the middle voice (ātmanepada) is employed to indicate that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent during his living state; and since that is possible, the designation is correct.
[The objection of] Pāṇini [is as follows].

This being the case, it is replied: It is true that the sacrificer is not a constituent part [of the sacrifice]; nevertheless, he remains qualified [to perform it] even in the absence of a specific desire.

And it is only when there is eligibility (*adhikāra*) that the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is understood for the ritual action; for one who is eligible can produce the fruit, whereas one who is not eligible cannot. How is there a lack of eligibility? The answer is:
the absence of desire (*kāmitā*).
The cause [for eligibility] lies in this very qualification; in its absence, there is no eligibility. And that being absent, the ritual action is not a means of accomplishment.
Due to the absence of the means, there is an absence of the fruit—so what is the use of considering whether something is a subsidiary (aṅga) or not?
This is what is meant: even if [the qualification]...

Even though the subsidiary (*aṅga*) does not [directly] produce the fruit, nevertheless, because it serves as a means (*sādhana*) for the production of the fruit of the primary (*pradhāna*), the absence of that [subsidiary] results in the absence of the fruit.
Therefore, due to the absence of the fruit, there is a cessation of the optional rites (*kāmya*) and others, such as the *Sado-māna* and so forth.

Furthermore, the mention of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the Bhāṣya is intended to indicate the qualification (*adhikāra*). It is precisely by virtue of the qualification that the fruit [is attained].

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. But as for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), it is precisely that which causes [the action] to be experienced by oneself; thus there is the mention of the middle voice. || 21 || And because of the absence of the sense of effort (*īhā*), it is like the *sūktavāka*. || 52 ||
What, then, is the suspicion regarding this distinction?

Its meaning is as follows: just as there is a cessation of optional rites (*kāmya*) due to the absence of a result, so too it would be proper that there be a cessation of the *sūktavāka* due to the absence of a result. He provides the resolution: "But surely, [there is] the purpose..."
It has been stated that this is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), for this result—longevity and so forth—is not [the actual fruit]; rather, this is an *arthavāda*.
He raises an objection again:
its status as an *arthavāda* is improper because it is not supplementary to the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*).
For an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is a supplement to an injunction (*vidhi*).

Since that [injunction] is absent here, this is not an explanatory passage. He replies again: it has been stated regarding the verse "Four are the horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*) that encouragement toward performance is purposeful.

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *arthavāda* may serve as a commendatory statement during the stage of performance. However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is this: such [an interpretation] applies when the purpose is not directly inherent, as in the case of "four horns. But here, since the purpose exists as a result, its inherent connection is indeed possible. And thus, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated that the sacrificial animal is of the bovine species and that the deity is derived from the words of the mantra.

It has been shown that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) has longevity and so forth as its fruits. Therefore, since there is no fruit despite the presence of a fruit [in general], there is a sublation (*bādha*) here as well—just as in the previous case—of the *sūktavāka* mantra which indicates the fruit, because of the absence of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
1. Because of the absence of the means.
2. The state of being a fruit [p. 351].
|| 12 || Or rather, there may be the desires of the Hotṛ priests. || 55 ||

An eligibility for this cannot be asserted here, because desires such as [long] life and so forth already exist; for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) indeed desire the *arka* sacrifice. Therefore, there must be desires on the part of the *hotṛ* priest, just as [in the case of the others].

In the case of [desires] such as long life and so forth, the sacrificer alone is the qualified person for the optional rite; it is not so with the desires of the Hotṛ priests, because the officiating priests also possess qualification. Therefore, there must indeed be those who possess desire regarding the desires of the Hotṛ priests.
This being the position reached, it is here stated in reply:

It is true that there is no lack of entitlement; however, cessation [of the ritual] occurs due to the absence of an object. For the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the object of the fruit to be desired, and the desire for that fruit as its object is the cause of the officiating priests' (*hotṛ*) entitlement.
But it is not possible for bones to be the object of a fruit, because they are insentient. Therefore, for those whose desire lacks an object...

Those desiring the office of the Hotṛ priest undertake the state of being the cause for that qualification. Therefore, since the qualification is absent here as well, there is also the cessation of those desiring the office of the Hotṛ.

Here, an objection is raised: what is the relationship between the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the qualification (*adhikāra*), such that by the absence of the subject matter [the qualification ceases]? By which...

[Objection: There is an absence of qualification (*kārābhāva*). [Response: Certainly, there is a connection. A desire that lacks an object does not attain the status of being a cause for qualification (*adhikāranimittabhāva*). Therefore, in this case as well, there is indeed no qualification. For what purpose, then, [is it mentioned]?
It was stated previously that this is true: there is no lack of entitlement, but rather cessation due to the absence of an object, for the sacrificer is indeed the object. The reply is:
this was stated with reference to those who are entitled.

For it was stated that there is no lack of qualification with the intention of implying the existence of appointed officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who possess consciousness and are capable of desire; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*),
even though there are those who desire, because of the absence of objects (*viṣaya*), there is no desire, and due to the absence of desire, there is no qualification.
23. There is no completion of the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice upon the death of the patron, because the ritual action is connected with the living person. 57.

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya reflects as follows: "Should that karma be abandoned once the final destination has been reached, or must it be completed? Regarding this, he states the cause for doubt: "Now, this is doubted: does the qualification [to perform rites] last only so long as one has not reached the destined destination? Or, once that destination is reached, is there a relinquishing of karma due to the absence of qualification?"
Or rather, there is the continuation of qualification even for one who has died; that is, there is qualification for the fruits [of action] even beyond death.

In this regard, the connection is that the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) has argued as follows. To the question "By what reasoning? he says: "No one indeed... [proceeds in such a manner].
From the scripture, one understands one's qualification [to perform the rite], thinking, "I have the qualification for this even though I am dead.
Therefore, as long as [the qualification exists]—1. R [this applies] even in the subsequent cases.
It is understood from the scripture that one does not proceed to a state of rebirth as long as there remains the thought, "This must be done by me. Beyond this point,
action ceases due to the absence of qualification, just as it does for optional rites (*kāmya*).

Just as a desired fruit does not come to fruition due to the absence of qualification (*adhikāra*), so too there can be no action subsequent to death; for agency in an action is possible only while one is alive, and qualification extends up to that very agency. Thus, regarding actions subsequent to death—
There is no lack of qualification.
However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that since qualification is understood to persist until the completion [of the rite], the cessation of qualification is not determined.

The entitlement (*adhikāra*) is understood to pertain to the primary rite together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*). Now, it was argued that while it is understood that "it must be performed by one who is dead," the agency (*kartṛtva*) of a dead person is untenable.
He refutes this, asking: "By whom was it said that [this] is understood?"

How, then, is it said that [the rite] must be performed? The answer is: that duty of performance belongs only to one who is living; only while living does one have authority over those matters that follow after death. And it must be performed by one who is living in that manner.

Just as the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of one who has entered [the path] as prescribed ceases with respect to ownership, how does it cease? It ceases because of the injunction regarding the equipment (*sambhāra-vidhi*).
For the scripture teaches that one must complete the collection of requisites while still living.

It is understood as follows: furthermore, that which is impossible constitutes a sublation of the *yajamāna*-rite precisely because of its impossibility, just as in the case of other impossible elements even while the sacrificer is alive—for example, the purchase (*parikraya*) and so forth in *satra* sacrifices. And by the gathering of the ritual materials (*sambhāra-sambharaṇa*), [the role] of the owners...

The status of being an agent does not cease; thus it has been said: "Without doubt, there is no difference whatsoever between one who is living and one who is dead," because both possess agency by way of the equipment [of the ritual].
Furthermore, as for what was asked—how can there be agency for that which does not exist—it is said in reply:
there is no non-existence, because the self is eternal and it possesses agency. Furthermore, when [the body] has died...
The objection regarding the impossibility of the means has been answered by the means of providing the materials.

Furthermore, the purpose of the injunction "O Brahmins, complete my sacrifice" is established as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) only if the sacrifice is to be completed; otherwise, it would have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
It should be concluded with the word "syāt" (may it be), for it is established that [the sacrifice] must be completed;
when [the patron] has passed away, [the ritual continues] like a bone-sacrifice (asthiyajña). || 24 || || 59 ||

Since the purpose of a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical inquiry) is that it is useful for practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*), the extended application (*atideśa*) is intended to demonstrate the possibility of its subject matter.
This is done in order to show the fruit of the principle established through *kṛtvācintā* when it is put into practice.
This has been stated:
1. This is the well-known subject matter.
|| 25 || The word "lives" (*jīvati*) is not [a mere] statement; it is a benediction (*āśis*), because its purpose is that [benediction]. || 60 ||
Now, it is considered whether or not there is an obligation regarding injunctions that oppose death until one goes to the destined state.
By this, the doubt concerning the cause [of the soul's departure] arises from the doubt concerning the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*).
It has been established.
In that regard, since the qualification [for the rite] is caused by death, the opposing qualification ceases; such is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).

The final conclusion, however, is that because the desire for death is restricted to a specific time, no contradiction regarding eligibility is perceived in those [acts] occurring prior to it; thus, there is an absence of sublation (*bādhā*).

There is no contradiction in the fact that one should first pray for longevity specifically for the purpose of dying at a fixed time; therefore, there is no cessation of the prayer for longevity. (26) Ritual action should consist of those things which are merely dharma. (62)

To introduce the doubt, he restates the matter: it is heard in scripture, "Those desiring prosperity should undergo [the initiation] for twelve days. Regarding that, a doubt arises as to whether there is the choosing of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests and the giving of gold to the descendant of Atri, or not.
Akṣiti—But surely this doubt itself is improper due to the absence of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
For it cannot be asserted that there is a loss of purpose for that which has an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Its meaning is as follows: the selection of the *ṛtuyājyā* [priests] is for the sake of an unseen result.

Furthermore, since it cannot be said that there is an omission of the door [of the ritual] even in their *sattra* sacrifice because an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) is possible there as well, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable;

thus, the doubt is not appropriate. He resolves this: "True, it is so; nevertheless, according to worldly logic, even when something is given to another or a *sāman* is employed, the servants [of the giver] also receive a share."

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that there is an elision [of the meaning], thinking: "Thinking 'this person is a good and noble speaker,' they will exert themselves even more in his service.
The meaning of this is: according to worldly logic, the proponent of the prima facie view considers that there is an elision of the intended meaning.

The proponent says: For in the world, even when a gift or the employment of conciliation is given to another, there certainly arises a return toward the giver on the part of the servants. To illustrate:

servants, perceiving that "this man is virtuous, pleasant-spoken, generous, and charitable," are seen to exert themselves all the more in the service of that donor, the patron. And thus, even in the case of those who reside with another person...

The purpose of conciliation (*sāman*) and bribery (*dāna*) is solely the hiring of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); since this does not exist in a *sattra* sacrifice, these two are excluded due to the disappearance of their purpose.
However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that a secondary purpose cannot constitute the primary purpose of the scriptural injunction.
The meaning of this is as follows:
since the incidental honor of the officiating priests cannot constitute the purpose of the scripture, there is no need for conciliation or bribery.

It must be that which serves as the motive; however, the motive is indeed the unseen (adṛṣṭa) result. As it has been stated: "And the primary purpose of the scripture is for the sake of the unseen alone"—this was established in the context of the archetype (prakṛti). Therefore, there is no cessation of these two, conciliation (sāma) and bribery (dāna).
And when the primary [meaning] is impossible due to the loss of its qualities. || 63 ||
The injunction regarding the pouring out [of the oblation] (nirvāpa-śāstra) is completed together with the Agnihotra-ladle.

Its meaning is this: the injunction for pouring out the sacrificial offerings, namely "he pours out the oblations with the Agnihotra-ladle," is concluded along with the Agnihotra-ladle. Nevertheless...
He asks: why is this so? [The answer is: "And there is no division of the meaning of the scripture.
Since the scripture is one, its meaning is also one.
For it is the individual categories (*padārtha*) that are divided, but not the meaning of the scripture. Without the *agnihotra* ladle, the very meaning of the scripture does not exist.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that in the Pavamāneṣṭis, the act of pouring out the oblation (nirvāpa) is not to be performed; even if the pouring were performed, it would be as if unperformed, because it would not serve the purpose of the scriptural injunction. The final conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is that while this would indeed be the case if the performance were based on direct instruction (upadeśa), here the performance is rather based on the requirements of the ritual context (kārya).
Furthermore, when a portion of the task is possible, its abandonment is without any basis for proof.
Even in the absence of the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the performance of the rite can still be accomplished; and there is no justification for abandoning a portion of the task that is indeed possible.

There is authoritative evidence for this. And upon its abandonment, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) must also necessarily be performed, because the performance of a ritual action is prompted by the task to be accomplished.

If the performance were merely for the sake of fulfilling an injunction, then non-performance might be possible; however, in this case, the performance is solely for the sake of accomplishing the task, and thus the pouring out must be performed. Furthermore, if it were the case that only the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle is consecrated by the pouring out, [then the same would apply].

In that case, in the absence of one to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), the pouring of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) would not take place; yet such an absence does not occur. Thus he says: "But surely the *agnihotra-havaṇī* [ladle] is not what is to be consecrated, such that in its absence the performance of the rite would be omitted."
In the case of the offering (*nirvāpa*), however,

the substance being offered is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*); and since that purpose is not sublated, it cannot be said that there is any contradiction, and thus the act of offering remains established.
But because of the loss of the handful, there should be a repetition of the entire formula, since that [repetition] is a subordinate quality of it. 64.
But surely, it is heard in the scripture that "one pours out four handfuls," whereby both the number four and the handfuls are prescribed in relation to the pouring out (*nirvāpa*);
whereas the number seventeen and the material of the earthen bowl (*śarāva*) pertain to the measure of the cooked rice (*odana*).
Therefore, how can there be a difference in their respective objects?

Anticipating the objection that, due to the absence of contradiction, both might sublate each other, he says here: although the scripture has different subject matters, he described the omission of both by considering them to have a single subject matter in terms of their function; for otherwise, [there would be] the enjoyment of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
The intention is: by what cause is there the elision of even one of the two?
The meaning of this is: although, in the case of the *nirvāpa*— [The remainder of the sentence is not provided in the source text.]

From the scriptural injunction, "He pours out four handfuls from the vessel," the teaching regarding the seventeen *śarāva* measures of rice is a statement concerning a different subject matter; nevertheless, through an examination of the purpose (*kārya*), they indeed come to have a single subject matter, because such a quantity of rice is impossible to obtain without pouring out that much [grain]. Thus, having attained identity of purpose by implication, it is like [the use of] the *godohana* vessel and so forth.

It is logical that the number seventeen of the *camasa* vessel—which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—is set aside by the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), and that the substance of the four *śarāva* measures and the substance of the handfuls are likewise set aside. However, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that if a commonality of objective domain (*samānaviṣayatā*) based on function is not accepted, then the sublation (*bādha*) of either one, which is the intended conclusion (*rāddhānta*), would not be established. Thus is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: first, the scriptural texts refer to distinct objects; for one text prescribes a *caru* oblation measured by seventeen *śarāva* vessels, while another prescribes an offering (*nirvāpa*) measured by four handfuls. In this regard, there is no evidence for their having a single purpose.

The meaning of this is as follows: if there were an injunction of modified number and substance in place of the functions of the original number and substance, then indeed there would be a sublation of the two by the two; and such sublation must occur when there is identity of scope. However, there is no identity of scope here, because the original number and substance have the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) as their scope, whereas the modified ones have the cooked rice offering (*caru*) as their scope.
Because it is heard [in scripture].
But was it not stated that, if the offering were of such a limited quantity, the seventeen-śarāva measure of the sacrificial pap (caru) would not be established?

He refutes this: "In that case, then, the sublation is objective (ārtha), not because it has fulfilled its purpose. Nevertheless, what follows from this? To this he says: "If this sublation is objective, then..."

It ought to be as much as is necessary for the purpose. Only that much should be set aside by way of sublation (bādha) as is required so that the measure of the *caru* is established without sublation. Since the purpose is accomplished even by the sublation of either the number or the substance, it is not possible for both to be sublated. This section [of the treatise] concludes with just this much.
It is concluded. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is a sublation of both; the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that there is a sublation of one or the other.
Furthermore, this is another principle (*nyāya*) presented here: of those two, is it the substance of the handful (*muṣṭidravya*) or the number that is sublated?
In that regard as well, it has been stated that the primary element is indeed the act of taking up (*grahaṇa*). Just as there is the taking up of the first and the last.

In this case as well, there is a renunciation (tyāga): namely, the adoption of the primary number which exists previously, and the omission of the subordinate substance; for both the number and the substance serve as qualifiers for the act of pouring out (nirvāpa). If the number were subordinate to the substance, then the substance alone would be followed and the number would be omitted. However, in this instance, the number is denoted by a distinct nominal stem.
They are subordinate solely with respect to the act of extinguishing, just as the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is subordinate with respect to the purchase.
1. Regarding the scope of measurement; 2. Because its [the measurement's] establishment would not otherwise be possible.
But in the case of that which is innate, there would be a modification in substance, because it is not something produced.

Considering the *codaka* (the general rule) to be equivalent to a *upapada* (a secondary word), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) does not consider there to be a sublation (*bādha*) of the goat-substance (*ajadravya*).
The meaning of this is as follows: just as in the case of "a goat-bull" (*aja ṛṣabha*), upon hearing the word "goat" (*aja*) functioning as a *upapada*, [the term "bull"]...

In this way, the bull (*ṛṣabha*) is included; likewise here as well, when there is a scriptural injunction (*codaka*) that prescribes a goat, only a bull that is a goat is to be taken, and thus the substance of the goat is not excluded. Now, one might argue: "Since a cow is understood merely by hearing words such as 'bull,' it is more logical that the goat, which was obtained through the scriptural injunction, should be set aside. To this, he says: "If, at the very moment of the utterance of the word..."

If one thinks that the substance "cow" is perceived only after an interval [from the word], then even the usage "goat-ox" (*aja-ṛṣabha*) would not occur, because there would be no mutual connection between the two, just as in the case of "goat-cow" (*aja-gauḥ*).

Now, [an opponent might argue that] because it is not applicable in its primary sense, this word "bull" (*ṛṣabha*) is used figuratively; thus, the usage "the goat itself is the bull" is indeed possible. To this, he replies: "And it cannot be said that this is figurative, because it does not abandon its own primary meaning."

For that which functions elsewhere by abandoning its own primary meaning is secondary (*gauṇa*), as in the case of "the boy is fire. However, words such as *ṛṣabha* do not abandon their own primary meaning even when applied to a goat; for by the very same property—such as age—which constitutes the denoted object (*abhidheya*) through which words like *ṛṣabha* apply to a cow, they likewise apply to a goat here. Thus, [the word] *ṛṣabha*, etc.,...

There is no contradiction with the direct scriptural statement (*śabdaśruti*) regarding the goat (*aja*), since the injunction by extension (*codaka*) is supported even when applied to a non-goat substance; thus, there is no sublation of the goat.

However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the injunction by extension operates only when the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) has been fully completed; for [the extension] occurs only once the [direct rule] has been understood.

Since the meaning of a word is established by direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), the extended application (*codaka*) occurs only subsequently; therefore, the meaning of the word cannot be altered in accordance with that subsequent extended application. Words such as *dhenu* (milch cow), however, denote qualities residing in a cow, and not merely the quality itself.

[They are] expressive words. Furthermore, at the time of the instruction [of the ritual], there exists no substance such as a goat (*ajā*) that could serve as an opposing substrate for the cow-form and so forth of the "cow" (*dhenu*) and other terms;

by means of which one might postulate a figurative denotation of qualities residing in another substrate, even though those qualities are not themselves directly denoted. Moreover, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) occurs subsequently and is not capable of altering the meaning of the word as it existed at the initial stage. If [it were] a cow—
If words such as *dhenu* (cow) and others denote qualities based on superimposition (*adhiṣṭhāna*), how then is the usage *aja* (goat) and *ṛṣabha* (bull) employed? The answer is:
because the primary instruction is not yet complete, this usage will be figurative (*gauṇa*).
Since both words are heard [in the text],

the instruction cannot be completed without a syntactical connection (*anvaya*). And since a syntactical connection is not possible without a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*), one must determine that a figurative sense is intended.
But how can there be figurative usage when that [primary] meaning is possible? The answer is: because no such direct denotation is observed.
If the denotation of a mere quality were observed in common usage, then there would be the status of expressing a mere quality; however, that is not the case.
Therefore, a mere quality is not the meaning of that word. But how is it that no such denotation is observed? Upon hearing the word in isolation...

Because that [quality] is not perceived in the mere [denoted object], whereas the quality residing in the cow is perceived; therefore, by the force of the sentence, one must somehow explain the cognition of the quality residing in the goat through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). But here, since there is nothing standing as an opponent to the cognition of the quality residing in the cow, the directly expressed meaning (*śrauto'rthaḥ*) cannot be abandoned. Furthermore, these words such as *dhenu* [and so on] [signify] that quality residing in the cow.
They say that even "cowness" (gotva) is not denoted.
[Objection: If these words do not denote cowness, then how can they be terms expressing specific qualities?
It is replied: For there are certain things that are distinct by their very nature; when such a thing is differentiated by the difference of its substrata, it remains distinct by its own nature.

It does not depend on the denotation of a qualifier. Furthermore, things such as "grains" (*dhāna*) differ according to their respective substrata (*āśraya*). In that regard, those grains and so forth which reside in a cow are denoted by words such as *dhenu* (cow); thus, they do not require the denotation of a substratum for the sake of being qualifiers.
There is some object that is not qualified in itself, but attains qualification solely through the power of a qualifier; that [object], being qualified—

When something is being denoted, it cannot be so denoted without the denotation of its qualifiers, as is the case with "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like. In this context, words such as *dhenu* (milch cow) do not denote cowness as qualified by the act of milking and so forth; for without the denotation of the qualifiers—such as milking—it is impossible to denote the qualified cowness, since cowness itself is inherently undifferentiated. [This applies] when both the qualifier and the qualified are being denoted.

Because of the conceptual burden (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating a [separate] potency (*śakti*), whereas if words such as *dhānā* were to denote [the act of] threshing in dependence upon a cow, they would inherently express that meaning and thus have no need for a further expression of a qualifier; therefore, by virtue of this parsimony (*lāghava*), words like *dhānā* denote the act of threshing itself. In that case, although these are adjectives (*guṇavacana*), they are employed in other scriptural contexts to refer to substances possessing those qualities when the substance "cow" is not being directly taken up.
Therefore, because another substance is prescribed, the goat-substance is set aside.
But in the case of an occasional rite, because it is something to be performed, there would be the application of the archetype due to its occurrence.

But here, if a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), being heard in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), attains the status of a causal indicator (*nimitta*) only as far as its own substrate (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) according to the previous principle, then this word *śveta* (white) also conveys its own meaning as extending only to whatever substrate it possesses, without requiring a specific class (*jāti*). Thus, the substance that is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*)—

That is indeed a sublation. For since the general term has the substance in its entirety as its referent for the purpose of instruction, the specific detail obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is sublated.
To this it is replied: You yourself have stated that the word "white" conveys its own meaning by having the mere substance as its substratum.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: In that case, it does not convey a specific distinction, nor is there an apprehension of the qualities of the substrate.
It makes known the specific distinction.
As long as the specific distinction is not understood, it is difficult to state the exclusion of other distinctions, because there is no contradiction.

If the word *śveta* were to convey a distinct substrate different [from the original], then there would be a contradiction with that which is obtained through the *codaka* (the transfer rule). But this is not the case; therefore, it is logical that there is no sublation of the *codaka*. In the event of a conflict, there should be an omission of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) quality because of that specific statement, and by that...
Because of the connection with karma. || 70 ||
In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya considers only the sublation and non-sublation of the *khadira* wood and others.
Therein,

lest someone who grasps only what is explicitly stated should have the notion that it applies to those alone, [the author]— on the basis of equal reasoning— [establishes that] for all sacrificial posts (*yūpa*)...

He provides examples of substances and ritual preparations intended for the production [of something else]. Regarding the statement, "The threshing-pole becomes the sacrificial post" (*khalevālī yūpo bhavati*), there is a doubt: should the properties (dharmas) intended for the production of the sacrificial post be performed in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, or not? How should they be performed? How...
Or rather, they should not be performed.
The answer is: if their purpose is lost, then they should not be performed; but if their purpose is not lost, they should be performed.

If the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is sublated here, then [the rites] should not be performed, because they exist for the purpose of producing the sacrificial post. If, however, it is not sublated, then they should be performed.
But how can there be the omission or non-omission of the purpose?
Question: Because of doubt regarding the sublation or non-sublation of the sacrificial post (yūpa).
Question: How can the sublation or non-sublation of the sacrificial post itself be doubted?
Answer: The doubt arises from the difference in the grammatical interpretation (vacanavyakti) of the statements.

When the syntactical formulation is "that which is a threshing-floor post (khalevālī) becomes a sacrificial post (yūpa)," then there is a loss of purpose [for other materials]. In that case, the threshing-floor post is prescribed for the function of the sacrificial post; and consequently, since the function of the sacrificial post is accomplished by that very post, [other requirements are dispensed with].

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would be omitted. Now, if it is stated that "the threshing-fence (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post," then, because its purpose is not lost, the ritual properties (*dharma*) apply; for in that case, the state of being a threshing-fence is enjoined for an existing sacrificial post. What, then, is the correct position here? He adopts the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
the meaning of the sentence is correctly understood as "the threshing-fence is to be made into a sacrificial post."

What, then, is the reasoning here? The Vedic term *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is upheld, and the general rule (*codaka*) is not violated. But [it may be objected]: in this view, the term *khalevālī* (threshing-floor fence) is made to abandon its Vedic meaning.
He asks "Why? and replies: for the word *khalevālī* denotes a wooden post;
it is etymological (*yaugika*) by virtue of the derivation "that which keeps [grain] out of the threshing floor" (*khala-vārayati*). Thus, *khalevālī*—
The word denotes a sacrificial post made of *medhī* wood, and not merely the act of making a threshing-post. Nevertheless, he asks "why?
and says: "And it is not possible to enjoin another piece of wood for a sacrificial post whose wood is already determined.
The meaning of this is: [the wood] is already determined...
1. R Therefore, also because of non-affliction;
2. A Of those whose purpose is the production of what has not previously existed.
One for whom the wood—such as *khadira* and so forth—is already determined is a "person of known wood"; in that case, it is impossible to enjoin another kind of wood.

It is impossible to enjoin that the *khadira* or other wood becomes something else. Therefore, the act of making a threshing-floor fence (*khalevāraṇa*) must be performed upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) which consists of wood. The sacrificial post is to be made into a threshing-floor fence; that is, the act of making a threshing-floor fence is to be performed upon the sacrificial post.

"The ritual preparations (saṃskāras) must be performed for its sake. Consequently, there would be the abandonment of the substance prescribed by the Vedic text and the injunction of a different action through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), as in the case of the word "cook" (*pācaka*), which refers merely to the act of cooking.
Now, if this is the intention: if the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) can exist in its own form even as a threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), then—
Thus, the scriptural injunction is indeed appropriate for a non-literal sense.

The meaning of this is as follows: if the injunction were stated with reference to a threshing-post made of some other kind of wood, then it would be an injunction of something possible to perform; however, if [it refers to] a threshing-post made of *khadira* wood—

The intention of the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) is that if the injunction regarding the *khalevālī* (threshing-floor post) is based upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then there is no contradiction, and thus it is simply the injunction of the Vedic meaning. The objector refutes this: "In that case, the injunction is even more untenable;
for the *svādira* wood is already established [by another rule]."

The quality of being made of *khadira* wood is already established and need not be enjoined. With a single sentence, the proponent himself raises this doubt: "Now, if it is argued that what is enjoined is that [wood] which has been consecrated as a threshing-floor post (*khalevāra*), then even though it need not be enjoined because it is already obtained through the *khadira* requirement, it is nevertheless enjoined by virtue of its being consecrated as a threshing-floor post."
He refutes this:
"In that case, it is simply figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for the word *khalevālī*, which denotes a wooden post, because its referent is a post prepared at the threshing floor."
When the prima facie argument has been thus raised, the proponent of that view says: "In that case, one should not level a criticism against a fault that is common to both sides.
For instance, even if the formulation of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) were reversed, the word 'sacrificial post' (*yūpa*),"
It is to be described by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Again, the objector says: "In that case, what is your specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) as the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*)?
The proponent replies: "This is the specific reason: when it is stated, 'The threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),'..."

The word *yūpa* indicates properties (*dharma*), not the function (*kārya*); for if the function were indicated, the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) would be the thing enjoined. And if that were enjoined, there would be a mediated connection, namely: "the threshing-floor post becomes the function of the sacrificial post" (*yūpakārye khalevālī bhavati*). [This is] from the word *yūpa*.

The word *iti*, being separated [from the preceding], should be connected with the word *khalevālī*. Even if there is a figurative indication (*dharmalakṣaṇā*) [of the sacrificial post by the threshing-floor post], he asks "What then? and replies: those ritual properties (*dharma*), when enjoined in relation to the *khalevālī*, result only in its consecration (*saṃskāra*).

The meaning is that they are for the purpose of consecrating the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*). Consequently, since a threshing-floor post is impossible within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the sublation of the context, the assumption of a separate governing topic (*adhikāra*), and the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would otherwise follow; therefore, this very position—that "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) becomes the threshing-floor post"—is the most logical one.

This being the case, it is replied: the meaning of the sentence is that "the threshing-floor post (khalevālī) becomes the sacrificial post (yūpa)" because there is no intervention; it is not, however, that "the sacrificial post becomes the threshing-floor post."
[Page 360] But if this is so, it has been stated that the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*). He replies: This has already been answered.
The objection was raised by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) himself when he stated that "the fault applies to both";
for even in the prima facie view, the word *khalevālī* was explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

"But surely there are defects such as the assumption of a different scope [of application]? He replies: "Indeed, these defects apply when [the word] has the nature of denoting a property (dharma); but here, the word 'sacrificial post' (yūpa) denotes an action (kārya)."
To the question, "Why does it not characterize the *dharma*s themselves?

he replies: "The definition by way of function (*kāryalakṣaṇā*)—and not a definition by way of the *dharma*s—is for the very purpose of avoiding faults; that is, for the sake of avoiding faults such as those pertaining to a different scope (*adhikārāntara*) and so forth."

But if this were the case, the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) would not be connected with the verb "becomes" (*bhavati*), because it is the object of an injunction (*vidheya*). For it is the threshing-floor post that is to be enjoined as the thing to be produced, not the production in the threshing-floor post. Thus he says: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not to be enjoined in the threshing-floor post, because it serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, because it is the subject of reference (*uddeśya*)."
And therefore, that very [relationship] is one involving mediation. How is it said to be "without mediation"?
