It is replied: Or how [could it be so] in the case of "the sacrificial post (yūpa) comes into being," since when an effect is indicated, [it cannot be expressed] by way of the nominative case?

The connection is established. For it is not the case that "the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," but rather that "the threshing-floor post serves the function of the sacrificial post.
To this, it is replied: [it is] qualified by the threshing-floor post...
The sacrificial post (yūpa) is enjoined for a purpose. What does it mean to say that this threshing-fence (khalevālī) is enjoined as a specific sacrificial post?
The answer is: this [is what it means].

Just as in the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there is an injunction for an oblation qualified by curd, so too here there is an injunction for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) qualified by the threshing-floor fence (*khalevālī*). Since an injunction has as its object an action (*bhāvārtha*), it is the very function of the sacrificial post—characterized by being an action—that is enjoined as qualified by the threshing-floor fence; thus, there is no syntactic connection across a gap (*vyavahitānvaya*). [The term *khalevālī* refers to a wooden beam used as a boundary marker on a threshing floor.]

The meaning of this sentence is that "it becomes a sacrificial post" (yūpa). To the question, "From what source does this meaning of it derive? he says: "Because of its connection with the verb *bhavati* (to become) [with the word] *yūpa*.
To the question, "How is the word *yūpati* [formed]? he says: "According to some, [it is formed] from all nominal stems (*prātipadika*), as in the cases of *śvatigardabhati*."

Thus, by the rule *kvip* for the sense of "conducting oneself" (*ācāra*), the word ending in the nominative case is also justified. This word *yūpa* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) to refer to something resembling a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Therefore, the meaning is this: "the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes like a sacrificial post. And this similarity is said to be based on function (*kāryanibandhana*). Consequently, if the function of the sacrificial post as qualified by the threshing-floor post is enjoined, then how is this...?

"It is stated that the *khalevālī* (the threshing-fence post) is prescribed to take the place of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). To this, he replies: since that which was not previously established is what is being prescribed, and by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, the prescription of the *khalevālī* is stated; thus, there are no defects such as the sublation of the context (*prakaraṇa-bādha*)."

Nor is there any intervention. Therefore, there is no application of *khadira* wood and the like—which would otherwise serve as the means for producing a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—when [the door] has been omitted.

Now, why is it that the threshing-floor beam (*khalevālī*) itself is not employed as the sacrificial post? For in that way, the purpose of the sacrificial post would not be frustrated, and the function of the post would be accomplished by the threshing-floor beam. To the question, "Why is there no application of the sacrificial post? he says:
[361] ...Because it expresses a specific quality that has been implied, just like the word *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post) is like a *dhenu* (milch cow).
The meaning of this is as follows: just as...

The word *dhenu* (cow) culminates in a substance and does not terminate in the quality alone; likewise, the word *khalevālī* also denotes a specific substance implied [by the context] and does not denote the mere act of threshing on a floor. In that case, if the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) itself were employed for the purpose of being made into a threshing-floor-post (*khalevālī*), then it would follow that there is merely an injunction for the act of threshing on a floor as a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the post; and in that situation, there would be the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, by the very sublation of the sacrificial post (yūpa), there is the favoring of the Vedic meaning.
|| 31 || There would be a prohibition of the opposing views. || 71 ||

It has already been stated that materials such as *khadira* wood are excluded because they denote specific [materials] that have been superseded, since the prescription of one substance entails the exclusion of another substance. Now, the question is considered regarding whether acts such as planing (*takṣaṇa*) and so forth should be performed on the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post).
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that they should be performed, because there is no contradiction with the direct injunction (*upadeśa*).

The meaning of the injunction that "the function of the sacrificial post (yūpa) must be performed upon the threshing-floor" is not contradicted even when [operations] such as carving are being carried out; therefore, the carving and other such acts must be performed. For there is no contradiction with this injunction here, as there was in the case of the *khadira* wood and others.

But surely there is no purpose for the carving and so forth; what contradiction will there be here? As for the selection and the cutting, once the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) has been selected and cut, its purpose is lost; the carving as well [is for that same post].

"Due to opposition to the hair (vālī), what non-existent effect could non-opposition produce here? The answer is: the intention is that one cannot say that very same effect has ceased simply because there is no opposition. This is the intended meaning:
[The text continues: "This is the intention—"

In its own nature, there is no contradiction; therefore, since there is no contradiction, one must postulate a purpose for these [acts] which appear as things to be performed. Thus, even for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the smoothing and cutting would not be performed again, nor would the planing be for an unseen purpose. To this it is replied: because that [purpose] has a visible effect, and because it is impossible in the case of a threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*).
"Expectation of another function.

The meaning of this is as follows: since those [functions] whose functions are already established are obtained through the original archetype (*prakṛti*), that very same function appears; thus, there is no expectation of another function by which another function might be postulated without contradiction. Therefore, it is not [the case].

The existence of an effect can be asserted merely on the basis of its non-contradiction with the effect [of the archetype]. However, that which is the natural (prākṛta) effect of these [substitutes] has been lost. And when their effect is indeed the natural one, then—since [in the archetype] it serves the purpose of producing the sacrificial post (yūpa)—here too they must serve solely for the production of the sacrificial post. Furthermore, there is no need for a sacrificial post here, because the function of the post is prescribed for something other than a post, namely, for the threshing-floor post (khalevālī).

And because [the post] is different [from the sacrificial post], consequently, due to the absence of the effect (kārya), the acts of hewing and so forth do not apply. Thus it is said: "Furthermore, it was stated in the archetype (prakṛti) that hewing and so forth are for the purpose of producing the sacrificial post (yūpa). But since this [wood] is prescribed for the binding (niyojana) as a non-post (ayūpa), hewing and so forth cannot take place; and since [the selection] and so forth have already been performed, they need not be done again."
This has been demonstrated.
In the absence of an object, there would be the status of a mental impression (saṃskāra).
The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that because the purpose has been accomplished, there is no further requirement for another purpose;
since that purpose has been fulfilled by means such as sprinkling with water, it does not require any other purpose, and therefore these [rites] cease.

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): It would be true [that the rite is not performed] if the visible effect itself were not present. But when the visible effect is indeed present—as in the case of a threshing-floor post (khalevāra) that has been loosened—the sense that "it has already been done" does not apply.

And since there is the task of producing firmness, there is no state of having already accomplished what was to be done, because even that which has been done does not persist [without further effort]. Therefore, those [scriptures] whose purpose is not lost are uncontradicted.
And even if there is a reversal [of cognition] due to the object, it would still be reality itself because it has that as its purpose.
Here, the proponent (pūrvavādī) considers that even the sequence of ritual elements (kramapadārtha) is sublated.
The meaning of this is as follows:
in the archetype (prakṛti), threshing (avaghāta) occurs prior to cooking; here, however, threshing would occur after cooking, which constitutes a sublation of the sequence. Therefore...
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that when the sequence is sublated, the *avaghāta* (threshing) is also sublated.

But is it not already established that in the case of "one offers with the Agnihotra-ladle," the primary act is not sublated for the sake of a subordinate detail (*guṇa*)? Furthermore, sequence is a subordinate detail, while the constituent acts (*padārtha*) are the primary elements. Therefore, even if the subordinate detail [sequence] is sublated...
It has been stated that the primary act must indeed be performed, and its application here is established by the very nature of the task;

furthermore, since the visible result of that task—characterized by the removal of husks and chaff—is observed, it is entirely appropriate to carry out the threshing, as there is no loss of purpose. Therefore:
This appears to have its meaning already established, since the reasoning has been stated.
To this it is replied: it was said that sequence is merely the expansion of injunctions (*vidhi*). There is no such thing as "sequence" apart from the fire-altar (*agni*) and so forth.
Just as in the case of the *hotṛhavaṇī* ladle, we describe a separate sublation for something distinct;
therefore,
the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when there is a difference from the sacrificial canopy (*vitāna*), there is indeed a sublation of the ritual act (*padārtha*).

For if the sequence of ritual items were independent, then even in the absence of that sequence, the performance would indeed be carried out, since the essential nature of the items themselves would remain unchanged. However, the sequence is inherent to the very nature of the item; it is the items themselves that are perceived as being "extended" [in sequence]. Therefore, in the absence of that sequence, the essential nature of the item itself would also be absent. Thus, when the sequence is sublated, the item is likewise—
Being urged, he is oppressed.
1. R. It indeed exists;
2. R. even in the absence of qualities.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: when an effect is observed, that which has been applied cannot be sublated.
As for the husks and grains—
Since the purpose of liberation is possible, the act of threshing cannot be sublated. If the threshing, being prompted by that purpose, is not sublated, then what is it that is sublated?
The answer is: the repeated performance [of the ritual].
We reply:

Since the rule for thrice-shelling is prescribed for the subject matter at hand, the threshing is to be repeated. In this case, if that repetition were performed upon the roasted grains (*dhānā*), they would become flour-meal (*saktu*); therefore, because it contradicts their essential nature, the repetition of the threshing is precluded.
The threshing is performed only once; indeed, only that much is done as is required for the removal of the husks and chaff.

Furthermore, this repetition can be said to be a "subsidiary" (guṇa) because it is prompted by the purpose [of removing the husks]. Since the proper production of rice grains is impossible without the repetition of threshing, the repetition of threshing is implied by the purpose itself; thus, being a subsidiary, it is subject to sublation.
But what is this "transgression" (vyatikrama) that the author of the Bhāṣya speaks of?

If it is a transgression, then by the previously stated principle, even the threshing (avadhāta) would result in being sublated. The answer is: with reference to the substance [of the mantra] as it is heard in the scripture.
This is explained as follows:
this statement is made with reference to the substance of grain that has been prescribed in the scripture. In the archetype (prakṛti), threshing is performed prior to cooking;
here, however, it is performed after cooking, and thus a transgression is said to occur.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, there is no transgression at all; for the threshing occurs immediately after the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of that very substance which was prescribed. And here, the prior state of the grains (*dhānā*) is not what is prescribed, but rather their state as *dhānā* itself. Thus it is said: "But the prior state of the principal substances is not prescribed. Therefore, it is well stated that the threshing applies to the *dhānā*.
"It should be performed.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*.
The second quarter of the tenth [chapter].
In the *Ṛjuvimalā*:
The third quarter of the tenth chapter.
In the case of a modification, because it possesses the same word as the original, there is the addition of the qualities of the primary substance due to their proximity.

In this context, the author of the Commentary has cited those modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) in which there are injunctions regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*) with respect to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries. Fearing that someone who grasps only what is explicitly stated might take up only that much, he says: "All modified examples are indeed joined with the injunctions of direct instruction (*upadeśavidhāna*)."

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the author of the Bhāṣya has adopted this specific example for the purpose of providing a supplementary argument, namely that even a single name might be assumed to have multiple meanings.
But what, then, is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) here?
The answer is as follows—the intention is this:
the extension [of a rule] occurs by virtue of the purpose (*kārya*).
Nevertheless, he asks "why? and replies: "If it is by virtue of the purpose, then it is precisely through that attainment."

The principal [element] is free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*). For the attainment that results from the effect—characterized by the assistance rendered by the instrument—is solely due to its being the producer of that assistance. Consequently, the principal element is free from expectancy precisely through the attainment of the entity that produces the assistance; and when it is free from expectancy...
In that case, even though a quality (guṇa) has been prescribed, there would be the consequence of its non-performance because it lacks connection with the primary injunction;

furthermore, in the absence of an injunction for the quality, the sentence would be purposeless. Nor is it possible to postulate a separate qualification (adhikāra) regarding the quality, since the unity of the qualification under discussion is understood. Therefore, since an injunction for a quality is impossible, it is logical that these are indeed distinct ritual acts (karmāntara).
Here he raises an objection: "Or, if another action is postulated, how can there be a cessation of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer)?

And if there is no cessation, its purposefulness is indeed difficult to maintain. Therefore, even by one who maintains that it is a different action, a solution must be stated regarding its connection with the primary rite."

It is said: this samādhi exists. For the primary [means] depends upon the means of practice. As long as one considers the ordinary means that have ceased following the rules of instruction, so long does instruction exist here just as it does in the case of *prakṛti*; thus, it does not depend upon a means bound by the instruction of another.

The meaning of this is as follows: In the view that there is an injunction for a separate action (*karmāntara*), since the elements already accepted as part of the task through the unity of the mandate (*niyogaikya*) would otherwise be independent by virtue of adopting the archetypal procedure (*prākṛta-itikartavyatā*), the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) ensures that there is no sublation of the inclusion of those elements directly taught in the original injunction.

It is not accepted [as a primary injunction]; rather, assistance is inferred according to the principle of the *darvihoma* based on whatever is explicitly heard in the text. However, in the case of a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), this resolution is not possible because the purpose is the accomplishment of a specific ritual action.

1. Regarding the word *rāyatteḥ* [p. 365], its meaning is as follows: under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is the inclusion of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) constituent elements by virtue of being their own substratum and by virtue of being the constituent elements under discussion (*prakṛtapadārtha*).

It must be considered as follows: since the requirement for further information is satisfied by the very set of constituent elements (*padārtha*) belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is impossible for them to enter again into the subordinate group (*gaṇa*);

this is the stated distinction. Furthermore, words such as *prayāja* and so forth—which clearly denote distinct actions—should, just as in the archetype, be understood here too as denoting many [actions], because we accept that a single word may have multiple meanings. Just as, for example, a single...

The word *prayāja* denotes many [subsidiary acts] such as the *samid* and others in the archetype (*prakṛti*); likewise, it denotes these other acts as they arise, because by virtue of usage it possesses multiple meanings.
This being the prima facie position, it is replied: True; [the archetypal acts are included] on the basis of their function, characterized by the assistance rendered to the cause.

The extension (*atideśa*) of ritual elements consists in their connection with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) for the sake of its *apūrva*. And it is true that there is no further expectancy because the means have been fully determined. Furthermore, the unity of the injunction (*niyogaikya*) cannot be denied due to proximity (*sannidhāna*), just as in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Just as in the archetype, by mere proximity alone, there is a single injunction for both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*).

Just as the goal (*sādhya*) is accepted [in the archetype], so too it is perceived in the modification (*vikṛti*) in that very same way; and because of their identity, the inclusion of additional auxiliary elements (*adhikāṅga*) is not without authority. Once the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) is understood, the capacity to produce the archetypal benefit (*prākṛtopakāra*) is attributed only to those auxiliaries exactly as they are taught. For in the absence of such a teaching, the accomplishment of that benefit here would have to be through the very same set of constituent elements as in the archetype.

The modified injunction (*vaikṛta-vidhi*) accepts only that means of assistance which has been established by the original archetype (*prakṛti*). When additional auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are taught, their entry into the production of that assistance is postulated for the sake of achieving their integration [into the ritual]. Nor should it be suspected that the injunctive force (*codaka*) itself will not operate, because the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would otherwise fail to be obtained. And there are verses on this point: [The verses follow.]

It is established that an injunction, being initially devoid of the attainment of a restriction and supported by the force of the indicative mark (liṅga), first accepts the assistance provided by another [element]. || 1 ||
The group of entities that constitute the source of assistance is intended in the archetype;
by virtue of being for that purpose alone, it comes into proximity in the ectype through its mode of operation.

Certain dharmas that are heard as falling under the category of instruction (upadeśa) attain the status of being for that purpose (tādarthya) therein by virtue of their necessary connection with it. || 3 ||
Then, from the mass of primordial objects, the modified portion is presented;
the Creator, for the sake of producing benefit, ordains it as an auxiliary factor.
1. As in the case of the *prakṛti*, it is indeed singular; 2. A. they too are enjoined.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the prescription is by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), whereas in the case of an injunction regarding an action (*karmavidhi*), it is by means of direct statement (*śruti*); to this he replies: "There is no difference whatsoever in the application (*viniyoga*) whether it concerns a quality or an action. For it has been stated that even in an injunction regarding a quality, the injunction has as its object only the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*). Therefore, in sentences that have the form of an injunction regarding a quality, where the constituent word-meanings are possible, there is no injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).

It acquires for itself the status of being a source of ritual gravity (*vidhigaurava*). Furthermore, its possibility has been stated on account of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). Therefore, it is logical that these are indeed injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*). The remainder has been explained with illustrative examples.
[The meditation on] the Golden Embryo [is prescribed] for the former [mantra], because of the indicative mark of the mantra. || 13 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that, on account of the *liṅga*— that is, the capacity for manifestation— the injunction regarding the mantra applies specifically to the previously mentioned base (*ādhāra*). Otherwise, the mantra would serve a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as it would lack the capacity to manifest Indra.
If its application were accepted in the second substrate, the mantra would have a visible purpose;
furthermore, the sublation of another mantra— namely, "ūrdhvo adhvaraḥ"— which is obtained through the *codaka* rule, would not be assumed.
If it were accepted that [the mantra] performs that effect despite not being capable of performing it, then by accepting the performance of that effect by one mantra,
there would be a sublation of one mantra by another mantra.
This being the case, it is replied: the assumption of a different function is not possible, because the instruction is exhausted by merely enjoining another means.
The meaning of this is: the function of the mantra pertains to the second fire-altar (*ādhāra*).

Since a function for another mantra has already been established in the preceding substrate, no further assumption (kalpanā) should be made; for there is no means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for such an assumption, as the instruction is justified by the mere injunction of another mantra, and because this applies equally even when the mantra designates Indra.
And the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated this equality. Therefore, the injunction of another mantra applies only to the subsequent one.
This is well said.
But in the case of consecration (*saṃskāra*), there is a separate ritual action, because it serves as its injunction. || 18 ||

But is it not already established by the statement, "He performs eleven *prayāja*s"? For when a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is possible, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) is not possible.
The meaning of this is as follows: [it refers to] the very two original acts of placing and offering...

Since the two sentences are rendered consistent through the prescription of qualities characterized by the *utkara* and *paridhi*, it is not appropriate to resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). He provides the resolution: "This is true; however, because it is impossible, it is suspected again as follows: [as understood].

Since the ordinary methods of placing (*āsādana*) and tying (*niyojana*) are impossible for the two *svaru* and *paridhi* sticks—which are high, sharp-pointed, and slender—because they serve no visible purpose, there arises a further doubt that these must be injunctions for other distinct acts serving an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). To this, he says: "Not [the ordinary] placing..."
1. In the case of the application of the original forms,
when the purpose is visible, there is the displacement of the *utkara* and the *paridhi*.

The intention is that [the two qualities] can occur in things that are both high and sharp-pointed and thin. Furthermore, this was previously refuted only by accepting that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even when prescribing a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) must be performed to the full extent of what is possible.

The meaning of this is as follows: let the injunction of qualities apply to the two [sacrifices] that are already archetypal (*prakṛta*). Among those, whatever is possible will be performed; however, since "having a high tip" and "thinness" are impossible in that context, they are not required, and "having a broad tip" and "thickness" will be adopted according to what is feasible.
Regarding this, he says: "And that [injunction] will be carried out for the purpose of the application of the *utkara* by means of its broad tip and of the *paridhi* by means of its thickness;
therefore, it is not proper to assume an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*), because the understanding of the injunction is grounded in what is to be done (*kartavyatā*)."

For an injunction (*niyoga*) culminates in the duty to act (*kartavyatā*), not in the purpose (*prayojana*). Therefore, there is no need to postulate a further purpose, since the performance of the rite is established even by resorting to the already determined effect. Consequently, in this case as well, it is logical that it is merely an injunction regarding a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, having concluded the topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*), he introduces a hypothetical argument (*kṛtvācintā*): "And here, [there would be] the fault of restating a qualified [entity], etc."
This need not be doubted. Since such an instruction has for its object a matter whose purpose is already well-known, there is no fault even if it constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Although, due to the hearing of multiple qualities, this is not an injunction for a separate act of placing or tying, nevertheless, with respect to the original function (*prākṛtakārya*)...
There is no fault regarding the result because it is equal;

for whatever kind of result exists in the case of an injunction of a subordinate element (guṇavidhi), exactly the same kind exists in the case of an injunction of a qualified entity (viśiṣṭavidhi). And this has been stated everywhere.
"He initiates with six" refers to a modification of those [mantras],
because of their connection with the Vedic revelation.

On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the modified (*vaikṛta*) mantras are indeed employed for the very same function as the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ones, just as *śara* grass is used for the function of *barhis* grass. Therefore, because their function has been subsumed, there is the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of the archetypal mantras.
Now, one might object that because of the repetition of the oblations, both the original (prakṛta) and modified (vaikṛta) mantras are combined; to this he says:
"And no other function for the mantras is possible in the case of repetition, even though there is a repetition of the oblations.
Regarding the mantras:

There is no other purpose [for the second mantra], for if the purpose were different, repetition would be impossible; repetition is defined as the performance again of exactly that which has already been performed. If there were a difference in the purpose of the mantra, it would not be "exactly that same thing"; and if the purpose is one and the same, then the injunction of another mantra would apply to that very same purpose.
Therefore, sublation (bādha) is the logical conclusion.

The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is as follows: it is true that there is an injunction regarding the primary action because that action has already been performed; nevertheless, we do not consider the repetition of the mantra to be logical.
Since the purpose of the action has been accomplished by means of what was taught once, the instructional authority of that mantra is fulfilled.
The practice of mantras is not appropriate even when there is the practice of ritual action. But surely, when that very ritual action exists, practice is justified?
It does not apply to other matters.
He refutes this: "This too is true—that there is no practice [of recitation] when there is another matter. Why, then, is there no practice of the mantras?
The sense is that even the practice of mantras by one who has business [to attend to] is proper.
The reply is: we say that it is accomplished by that instruction.
The meaning of this is: by the instruction in the mantra.

The performance of the mantra has been accomplished; and there is no authority for the non-performance of that mantra-repetition. For here, the connection with the ritual action of the modified rites is for the sake of the perfection of the instruction, not a connection with the action arising from the action itself.
Action—

The mere fact that [the mantra] exists does not mean the task has been accomplished; rather, it is for the sake of the completion of the instruction (*upadeśa*). Therefore, since the instruction is fulfilled by performing it even once, it ought to be capable of setting aside [the requirement for] further repetition. If, however, the task were to be performed solely because of its necessity, then, since the task would already exist, there would be only the setting aside of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) [mantra] upon the attainment of this specific mantra. It is not so.
To this he says: "But from the perspective of the effect, there is indeed sublation. And it has been stated that this [sublation] does not occur from the perspective of the effect.
Therefore, there is a combination [of both]. The remainder has already been explained.

The recollection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Thus, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇādāna*), which has cooked food as its means (*annasādhana*), will not be impaired.

Now, it is heard in scripture that "the calf is the sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā); how then can its flesh be the fee? This being the case, it is stated in reply: "The calf is the sacrificial fee" (vatsaḥ dakṣiṇā); thus, the status of the calf as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇātva*) is heard in the scripture.
As for that which...

In the case of rice grains (*brīhīṇām*), this is understood. and because cooking is performed by means of food. || 37 ||

In the *Manvāhārya* (the monthly ancestral rite), it is well known that [cooking] does not take place on the garment because of the omission of the door; thus, even for the garment, cooking must be set aside.

Furthermore, ritual elements (*padārtha*) are not performed for the sake of fulfilling the literal meaning of the words; rather, it has been stated that they are performed for the sake of the purpose (*kārya*). The proponent [states]: the meaning of this is as follows—the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the effect of cooking to be merely a transformation of the substance to be cooked.
And since a transformation resulting from cooking is possible even for clothing, there is no omission of the means (dvara); such is the prima facie view.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that in common usage, "cooking" (*pāka*) is well-known as having the sense of a specific transformation (*viśiṣṭa-vikāra*). What is this specific transformation? We say it is the cause for being designated by the word "food" (*anna*).
That is to say, when this [transformation] exists, there is the state of being denotable by the word "food."

That modification is accepted as something to be performed in the *anvāhārya* [offering]. Furthermore, just as in the case of the calf, there is a cessation of the cooking process in the sense that "the garment being cooked does not attain the state of food";
so too is it with the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*). || 38 ||
[Page 371] Now the pouring over (*abhidhāraṇa*) is considered: should it be performed on the calf and the garment, or not?
Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering the invisible refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) of the *anvāhārya* to result from the pouring over—
[The opponent] considers that pouring [the clarified butter] over [the sacrificial food] must be performed.

However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: since it is not logical to postulate an unseen result when a visible one is possible, the purpose of the pouring is indeed for the sake of making [the food] savory, as it serves to satisfy the officiating priests.

For it is well known in the world that one is satisfied by delicious food, and not so by other [kinds of food]. Furthermore, there is no need for that deliciousness in the calf or in the garment, because those two are inedible. Indeed, deliciousness residing in edible substances leads to the satisfaction of persons.
It is employed [for that purpose], and not even when it consists of inedible substances; thus, due to the absence of a purpose, the pouring over (abhidhāraṇa) is set aside.

What, then, is the relevance of this section to the definition of sublation (*bādha*)? The answer is: this section is incidental (*aupoddhātika*), intended for the purpose of establishing the sublation of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

For the sublation of those things associated with number will indeed be described both partially and in its entirety. If there is a connection of cows with a number, then when another number is heard in the modified rites (*vikṛti*), there is a sublation of those very [cows]; in that case, when another number is heard regarding the portion belonging to the priests (*ṛtvij*), there is a sublation only of the portion belonging to the cows.

Upon hearing of another number, there is a sublation of all the cows without exception. Not only is this particular section (adhikaraṇa) for this purpose, but the distribution and the giving are also considered for this very purpose;
the section concerning the assembly (pariṣad-adhikaraṇa) likewise serves as an introductory supplement (upoddhāta).

This is the meaning. Therefore, this section (adhikaraṇa) is applicable to the definition of sublation (bādha). For it is not the case that by the word "of that" (tasya) in the phrase "twelve hundred for that," the sacrifice itself is denoted because of its being the subject under discussion, rather than the cow and so forth.
How then can there be an investigation by taking up that word as referring to cows and so forth? To this he says: "Having set aside the word from the sacrifice, this is the inquiry.
This inquiry concerns whether the reference by that word applies only to substances. Even granting [the opponent's position]...
This deliberation is undertaken in order to state that, among the substances included within the scope of that word, the connection with number belongs to the cows alone.
In this regard, either no distinction being perceived, the cause for the connection with number applies to all of them;
or, because the purpose is fulfilled by a single one, the connection with number pertains to each individually, and it is precisely this [latter] view—that it is by any single one—that holds.
This is the specific reason (*viśe�ṣahetu*).

Its meaning is as follows: the number and the cows and so forth are connected with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that case, according to the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*), the connection of the number must be experienced by depending upon a substance; therefore, [it refers to] some substance whatsoever—
It is not the case that all [factors] are relied upon; rather, due to the connection with the word "ca" (and), there arises the intuition that the collective aggregate is related to the number.
1. R. Prākṛta [p. 372].
Although number requires only a substratum, nevertheless, upon hearing the word "ca" (and), a conjunction of substances is understood;
that [conjunction] alone will be what is connected with the number—this is a mere appearance.
Or rather, the verbal suffixes (*bhāṣā*) are the relata because of their immediate proximity, since the number is heard immediately after them.

Because they function merely as numbers, living beings are connected with number. Living beings are capable of being used in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by means of number alone; they do not, like speech and so forth, depend on delimitations such as *kuḍava* measures. Therefore, because they are dependent [on other factors], rice and the like have no connection with number; rather, it belongs only to living beings. Or, it is due to their greater utility.

There is an application [of the term] to cows and horses, for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform a great service; and it is the practice of the virtuous that one must repay the service of those who have assisted. Therefore, cows or horses, which provide great assistance, are connected with the number. And in this view, the horse is excluded by the prohibition, for the use of animals with teeth in both jaws is indeed forbidden. Thus, it is not [the case that the horse is included].

Horses are of great utility; therefore, they too are not connected with the number. Rather, it is the cows alone that are so connected because of their great utility, for they are indeed highly blessed.
In this context, the possibility of each [cow] being connected with the number was suspected on the basis of the primacy of the substance. In that regard:
He states the objection: "But surely the presentation of the view that substance (*dravya*) is primary has been refuted more than once in the ninth [book]. Why, then, is it presented again?
For it was stated that [the injunction] would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) if it were connected with the mere substance. He states the reply:
The proponent of the primacy of substance (dravyaprādhānyavādin) intends that the pointlessness [of number] due to its being a subordinate element (upādāna) is avoided.

Just as for animals and the like, qualities such as oneness (ekatva) and so forth—which relate solely to the substance—become purposeless when the substance is taken as the primary factor because they are subordinate to that taking (upādāna), so too is this number. How, then, is this position refuted? It must be refuted...
And this is so because the principle of *aruṇā* (the red cow) does not apply when [the number] is not set aside;

and as long as that principle has not descended, there would be no connection of the number with the mere cow. To this, he says: "Because it is included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is not [separately] taken up..."
The refutation [of the opponent's view] is that being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is possible only through the act of giving (*dāna*).

For the number denoted by the nominal stem is connected with the action alone by virtue of the word; thus, according to the principle of the *aruṇā* (the red cow), it would indeed be a subordinate element in terms of its application (*viniyoga*).

There is no status of being a remainder of the *upādāna* (the thing taken up). However, that which is expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and is related solely to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is denoted by the case-ending itself through direct audition (*śruti*); thus, it becomes a remainder of the *upādāna*. Granted that the principle of the "red [cow]" (*aruṇānyāya*) applies, one might still ask: why does the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) not become connected with the number? To this he says: "Furthermore, the meaning of the word 'and' is not at all [directly] connected; for it denotes a meaning already [otherwise] connected."
For these [particles] are possessors [of meaning].

The meaning of this is as follows: the meaning of the word *ca* does not participate in the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the word-meanings, just like the word "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), because the isolated meaning is not denoted by the word *ca*. Indeed, one does not say, "The *ca* is beautiful."
However, particles (nipātas) denote their own meaning as accompanied by or conjoined with another;
[in this context], substance (dravya) is primarily suspected [to be the referent].

Now, if there is no connection with number for those [elements] when they are combined here, then how is their combination indicated by the word *ca*? To this he says: "The word *ca* has its purpose fulfilled through its connection with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it will be stated that the status of being a sacrificial fee belongs to those things combined."

Thus, the meaning of the word "ca" (and) has been refuted. Because there is no worldly transaction based on a connection with number, [entities] that are not living beings have been refuted; for in the world, there is no transaction involving rice seeds and the like that are merely delimited by number alone, independent of measures such as a *kuḍava*. Therefore, because they do not conform to worldly transaction, [they are not the self].
This refers to their connection with number.
Now, one might ask: "Why are all living beings not connected with number when they are gathered together? To this he says:
"Number is applicable even by means of a single living being," which serves to exclude the category of living beings in general. And the word *mātra* here [indicates]...
This refers to the sense of totality (*sākalya*). When all living beings have been excluded and the connection with a single living being remains,

it is determined that cows alone are the entities connected with the number, because they are primary, because they are the first to present themselves, because they are of great utility, and because they are not prohibited.
